story:
Connor had built the lemonade stand out of two sawhorses and a door someone had left by the curb, and by eleven in the morning he had sold four cups at a dollar each, which meant that at this rate he would afford the used moped by sometime around his fortieth birthday. He was still doing the arithmetic on the back of a napkin when Priya biked up the street with her backpack flapping open.

"Your econ notebook is in here," she said, holding it out like evidence at a trial. "You left it in chem. Also, Mr. Okafor moved the quiz to tomorrow, and I don't understand a single word of chapter twelve, and your handwriting looks like a spider fell in the ink."

"That's the good spider. She works cheap." He poured her a cup without being asked, because that was the kind of hospitality his grandmother had tried to inculcate in him since he was small, mostly through threats involving no dessert. Priya sat on the curb and flipped the notebook open across her knees.

"So the graph," she said. "Inflation over time. There's this mountain in 1980 and then it just falls off a cliff and I don't know why I should care."

Connor leaned over her shoulder. He had spent last night on that exact page, squinting at the line that shot up and then dove down like a seagull changing its mind. "Okay, so, read the peak."

"Fourteen point eight percent, March 1980."

"And then find where it lands."

Priya traced the line downhill with one finger. "Below three percent by 1983. That's a huge drop. Did everyone just stop buying stuff?"

"I looked it up. It happened after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates, sharp increases, that's all the book says." He tapped the page. "The quiz just wants us to read the graph, not perform surgery on it."

"That's a relief, because I was about to say something dumb about presidents."

Down the block, a smaller stand had appeared on the Delgados' lawn, where eight-year-old Miguel was selling iced tea out of a wagon, badly, at fifty cents, mostly to his own sister. Connor watched him spill a pitcher into the grass and felt an inchoate sense of opportunity, the feeling of a plan arriving before its details did.

"Priya. Say you can make lemonade better than Miguel. Obviously. He's watering his down and calling it 'tea style.'"

"Tea style," she repeated, delighted.

"And say you could also make cookies better than he could. You're better at both things. So Miguel should just give up, right?"

"He's eight, he should give up at everything except being eight."

"That's what I thought too. But that's absolute advantage, and it's not the point." Connor grabbed the napkin with his arithmetic and started writing columns. "What matters is what you give up. If I spend an hour juicing lemons, I'm not doing something else. Same for him. The question isn't who's best. It's who loses the least by doing which thing."

Priya frowned at the napkin. "So even if I'm better at both, there's some split where we're both better off trading than each doing both?"

"Comparative advantage," Connor said, and then heard himself and grinned. "I've been saying it in the shower all morning, don't tell anyone."

"It's called that? Okay. Fine. Say it to Miguel."

So he did. He walked over, negotiated with the gravity of a trade delegation, and came back with an arrangement: Miguel would supply iced tea at cost, Connor would sell it at his stand alongside the lemonade, and they would split the take. Priya claimed the title of witness and demanded a commission in cookies. By two o'clock they had sold out of both drinks, and Miguel had made more money than any Saturday of his life, which he celebrated by doing a cartwheel into the lawn sprinkler.

"Okay, but explain to me again how we both gain when he's worse at everything," Priya said, counting the coins into stacks.

"Because my hour is worth more squeezing lemons than pouring tea, and his hour is worth more pouring tea than whatever else an eight-year-old does. The trade lets us both be the least-wrong version of ourselves."

"That's the most romantic thing I've ever heard about economics." She handed him the notebook, now marked up in green pen. "I still don't get why the Fed raising rates makes inflation fall off a cliff. The graph shows it happens, fine, but not how."

Connor turned the napkin over, wrote "why?" in the corner, and sat with it. "I don't know yet either. Maybe that's the next chapter."

"Or maybe it's one of those things you just trust the graph about and move on."

"Or maybe," Connor said, and pocketed the napkin with the question still on it, because the moped fund now stood at forty-one dollars and Miguel's mother was already asking whether they'd want to do Sundays too.

The deadline was Friday at five, and it was already Tuesday, so Elliot sat at the small upright piano in Ms. Reyes's studio with his manuscript paper in front of him and exactly four bars written down. They were, he thought, the four best bars anyone had ever written, which was possibly the problem, because he was afraid to ruin them with the other twelve.

"Play it again," said Ms. Reyes, who was famous for being taciturn and for drinking tea that smelled like a forest fire. She said everything once and never twice. "Now backwards. Now somewhere in the middle. Tell me what you find."

What he found was that his four bars had a chord change in them that he liked, G to E minor, but that when he tried to extend the melody it kept circling back like a dog chasing its own tail. He had read enough about composition to know that a sixteen-bar melody wanted a shape, an arc, a place to go and a way home. He had also read enough to know that reading was not the same as being able to do it, which was a distinction he found personally insulting.

"It needs a second idea," he said. "But when I put one in, it sounds like a different song crashed into mine."

"Good," said Ms. Reyes. "Two ideas crashing is called music. One idea alone is called a ringtone." She set a deadline with the serenity of someone who had watched a hundred students panic before: the county young composers showcase wanted a notated score by Friday, sixteen bars minimum, chord symbols included, and she had already told them he was entering. "Bring me something honest tomorrow," she said, "even if it's ugly."

That night he lay on his bed with headphones on, listening to a Mozart piano sonata for no reason except that Ms. Reyes had once said, "If you're stuck, eavesdrop on the masters," and he wanted to feel like he was working. His phone buzzed. A text from Dana, who played trumpet and had never voluntarily listened to piano music in her life.

"ok I'm doing the listening assignment," she wrote, "and either the pianist on this recording had a stroke or the file is broken, because he plays like 2 minutes and then STARTS OVER from the exact same place. I've checked twice. It's the same notes. Is this a joke."

Elliot sat up. He pulled up the same recording and counted along. She was right: the pianist played a stretch of music and then began again from the identical spot. He was about to text back "broken file" when he remembered the score reprint Ms. Reyes kept on her shelf, the sonata he'd flipped through once while waiting for his lesson. He found a PDF online and followed it measure by measure. There, at the end of the first section, were two dots stacked vertically like a colon, and back at the beginning, another pair. Repeat signs. In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition was often marked that way, so the performer played it twice before the development began. The pianist hadn't made a mistake. The piece itself asked for the rewind.

"it's not a mistake," he texted. "the exposition is marked with repeat signs, so he plays it twice on purpose." Then, because Dana would not let this go without a fight, he added, "You get to hear the beginning twice and act betrayed both times." Her reply was a single trumpet emoji followed by "i want my 90 seconds back." Somehow this exchange assuaged some anxiety he hadn't known he was carrying: even the masters, apparently, built repetition into their structures on purpose, said "here it is again" and trusted the listener to want it.

He sat back down at the keyboard, but differently now. He had been treating his two ideas as rivals, A material and B material, and trying to pick a winner. What if he let the first idea play, then let the second one crash in, then played the first idea again, changed? It wouldn't be a retreat; it would be a return. He notated eight bars, then borrowed the opening phrase for bars thirteen through sixteen with the chord underneath shifted from G to C, so the same melody landed in a new place, like a familiar street seen from a bus going the other direction. At one in the morning he wrote "DONE (ish)" on the manuscript and fell asleep with his cheek on the piano bench, which his neck would punish him for in the morning.

On Thursday he played all sixteen bars for Ms. Reyes, who listened with her eyes shut in a way that could mean rapture or a nap. When he finished she was quiet for a long moment, long enough for him to consider faking a phone call and fleeing the county.

"The return at bar thirteen," she said finally. "Where the melody comes back over a different chord. What made you think of that?"

"A guy on a recording started over," Elliot said, "and my friend thought he'd had a medical event. So I looked at the score." He told her about the repeat signs, the exposition played twice before the development, and Dana demanding a refund of her time.

Ms. Reyes almost smiled, which on her face was the equivalent of a standing ovation. She wrote one word at the top of his score in red pencil, and he leaned in to read it, and it said: "Again." Then she turned back to the first page and said, "From the top."

The room smelled of the radiator and someone's microwaved noodles, and Oliver had claimed the corner terminal because its monitor didn't flicker. He was on his third attempt at the Player class, the one Ms. Reyes wanted stored properly, and this time he had gotten the fields private on the first try.

"No, look," said Dev, leaning over from the next chair. "You wrote the getter wrong."

"I wrote it fine."

"You named it getScore but you're returning name. It compiles. It'll even run. That's the worst part."

Oliver looked at the line. His getter handed back the wrong field, polite and quiet about it, and the compiler had said nothing because both were Strings and both existed. He fixed it, wrote a test in the main method, created a Player, set the score, printed it, and watched the correct number appear. Something loosened in his chest. Encapsulation, Dev called it, keeping the fields locked behind the methods like water behind stone, and Oliver thought of the aquifer under his grandfather's town, the one that had fed every well for a century until the summer the levels dropped and nobody could agree who had drained it. Hidden things stayed healthy until suddenly they didn't.

The competition dataset arrived at four o'clock, a file called round3_large.txt, forty megabytes. Their club had entered the regional algorithm contest mostly as an excuse to order pizza, but they had actually made the final round, and now the search routine had to find player records in the giant sorted array. Oliver had written the binary search himself two weeks ago, and it had passed every test since.

He ran it. The terminal printed one found record, then a second, then a stack of red text he had never seen before.

"That's an overflow," Dev said, pulling his chair over.

"It can't be. The array's not even full."

"Line forty-one." Dev tapped the screen. "You're doing low plus high, then dividing by two. On this thing, low plus high runs right past what an int can hold."

Oliver stared at the line. mid = (low + high) / 2. He remembered the night he wrote it, a Sunday, rain against his window, his mother watching something downstairs with the volume too low to hear. He had been so pleased with himself that evening, the search cutting the array in half and in half again, elegant as folding paper, and he had tested it on the club's sample file of two hundred records and it had worked perfectly. He remembered thinking, briefly, that he was getting good at this. Now forty megabytes of competition data sat in memory and his beautiful line was producing a negative number somewhere deep in the loop where nothing checked for it.

"So it works on the small file because low plus high never gets big enough," Oliver said slowly. "And on this one it does."

"Yes. Write low plus, open paren, high minus low, close paren, divide by two." Dev was already reaching for the keyboard, and Oliver put his hand flat over the trackpad.

"Let me."

He changed the line himself. mid = low + (high - high) / 2, no, he'd mistyped, delete, again. mid = low + (high - low) / 2. Same middle, Dev said, without the overflow. Oliver read it twice. It looked worse than his version, uglier, a workaround dressed as arithmetic, and some small stubborn part of him wanted to argue that his original was cleaner, that the ugliness should count against it. But the red stack trace was still on the screen, impervious to his opinions, and he could not impugn the dataset or the judge or the clock. The code was his. He had written low plus high.

He ran it again. The terminal filled with found records, hundreds of them, then thousands, scrolling faster than he could read, and when it stopped the last line said 2,047,993 matches, 0 errors. Dev exhaled. Priya, who had been watching from the whiteboard with a slice of pizza held like a wand, said, "So we can still submit?"

"We can still submit," Oliver said.

He copied the fixed file onto the flash drive for the upload, and Priya pointed out that they had eleven minutes left, and Dev said the deadline was in eleven minutes or they were dead, it was one of those. At the terminal, Oliver opened his Player class one more time before sending it, hovering over the wrong-getter fix, checking it was really there. He had tested a class today and it had caught his lie. He had tested an algorithm and it had caught his pride.

"Send it," Dev said.

Oliver pressed upload, and the progress bar crawled and crawled across the screen.

The living room smelled like the lasagna his mother had left warming, and Marcus pushed the coffee table against the wall for the third night in a row. He had promised the drama club he would direct Priya's play for the spring one-act festival, and tonight the two of them were going to rehearse for the first time, except that Priya arrived with her script under her arm and a face that said she already knew something was wrong.

"Read the stage directions on page four," she said, dropping onto the couch. Marcus read them. The play was called June Through August, and in ten minutes of stage time it wanted a backyard, a bus station, a lake, a diner, a hospital waiting room, and Priya's own grandmother's kitchen. Six places, and seven characters besides, two of whom appeared for a single exchange.

"We can't do this," Marcus said. He said it carefully, because Priya had written the whole thing over winter break and had read it aloud to him twice over the phone, her voice going soft at the parts she liked best. "The festival gives us ten minutes. Ten. A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." He had read that in the directing guide the club advisor had lent him, alone, at midnight, and it had landed on him like arithmetic.

"So cut it," Priya said, but her jaw was set in a pugnacious way that meant don't cut it. "It's a whole summer. That's the point. Everything that matters happened across the whole summer."

Marcus sat down on the arm of the couch. He thought of the lake scene, the one where the little sister finally says what she saw, and the bus station scene where their mother leaves, and he understood suddenly that the summer itself was not the subject. The subject was one afternoon wearing the costume of three months. "What if we don't show the summer," he said. "What if we show the moment the summer ended? The backyard, the last night, before the sister goes inside. Everything else can live inside what they say to each other."

Priya didn't answer. She took the script back and flipped through it, and Marcus watched her fingers stop at the hospital scene, the diner, the kitchen, and he could see her weighing each one and setting it down. "The grandmother could be on the phone," she said at last, slowly, like she was testing a plank across a gap. "We never see her. She's just a voice off, and it's the last call before the sister flies out." Two characters, one backyard, one phone. Marcus wrote it on the back of his hand.

They rehearsed it that way for two hours, using the couch as the porch step and the lamp as the porch light. Marcus blocked the actors in his notebook, since the actors themselves wouldn't come until Thursday, drawing small arrows and Xs, deciding that the sister should start upstage and drift downstage as she confessed, so that the distance between them closed while the truth came out. When Priya read the sister's lines, doing all the parts at once, her voice cracked on "you weren't even there," and Marcus made her do it again, and again, until the crack was something she could place deliberately instead of something that happened to her.

By ten o'clock the living room had achieved a kind of homeostasis, the two of them passing the script back and forth, revising a line, testing a pause, neither one fighting anymore. Priya cut the bus station herself. She cut the diner without being asked. But she refused to give up the lake, and Marcus refused to stage it, so they compromised on something uncertain: the sister would describe the lake, in the dark, in the last minute of the play, and Marcus did not know yet whether that would play as revelation or as a writer holding on too hard. He marked it in his notebook with a question mark, and Priya saw him do it and didn't object.

His mother came home at eleven and found them still on the floor with pages spread out around them, and she said, "Are either of you eating that lasagna," and Priya said, "In a minute," and reached for a pencil.

Marcus looked at the single drawn room on his page, the two Xs, the arrows converging, and thought of all the summer that wasn't there anymore, and then underlined the question mark once, hard.

"Do it again from the top," he said. "Just the backyard. I want to hear it whole."

The pamphlet in Grace's hands had a cartoon condom on the front, winking, which she thought did not portend anything good for her credibility at Friday's assembly. She was sitting in an exam room at the Riverbend clinic, waiting for Marisol, the health educator who had agreed to cram six weeks of peer-educator training into one afternoon, because Grace had volunteered for the presentation before fully understanding what she had volunteered for.

"Read the chart while we wait," Marisol had said, ducking out to fetch a demo kit. So Grace read the chart. It was a blood pressure table mounted at eye level, the kind she'd seen a hundred times and never once looked at, and it said that under the 2017 guideline from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association, normal adult blood pressure was below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. Below both numbers, not just one. She stood and pressed her finger to the column, following it down, because that seemed like the kind of thing a person should know how to do before standing in front of two hundred classmates talking about health.

On the counter lay the file from the previous patient, left open, which felt like a thing she shouldn't look at and also a thing she couldn't not look at. The last reading said 118 over 76. She did the comparison slowly, systolic against systolic, diastolic against diastolic, and found that both numbers sat underneath the thresholds. She caught herself smiling at the paper as if it belonged to someone she knew.

"That's not yours to smile at," Marisol said from the doorway, carrying a plastic tub of pelvic models and flip charts. But she said it lightly, setting the tub down. "Well? Is it normal?"

"Under 120 and under 80," Grace said. "So yes."

"Both numbers. People forget the second one." Marisol pulled a folding chair over and sat, close enough that their knees almost touched, which Grace noticed and then deliberately did not move away from. "Okay. You're seventeen. By Friday you're supposed to explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested here, to a gymnasium of people who think they already know all of it. So start. I'm a sophomore who doesn't want to be here."

Grace began with consent, because Marisol had told her to always begin there, and she got through the part about it being freely given and ongoing, and then Marisol crossed her arms and said, "But I already said yes at the start. Doesn't that count?"

"It counts until it doesn't," Grace said. "You can take it back. Any time." She heard her own voice go flat, reciting, and stopped. She tried again, slower. "If you said yes Tuesday, and Thursday you're not feeling it, Thursday is what matters. Tuesday can't speak for you."

Marisol's arms uncrossed a little. "Better. Now the harder thing. Somebody's going to say, well, if you didn't want it, why did you go to his room. What do you say?"

Grace had prepared an answer, a good one, about how going somewhere isn't a contract, but when she opened her mouth the prepared part felt extrinsic to her, like a borrowed coat. What came out instead was, "I'd say I've done that. Gone somewhere not knowing what I wanted yet. And it still counted as no, because I said no, and because I got to decide after I knew what I wanted." The room went quiet. The ceiling fan ticked.

"You don't have to tell them that part," Marisol said.

"I know. But if I don't, they'll hear a rule. Rules sound like sophistry when they come from someone standing safely behind a podium. If I tell them the truth, they might actually check in with somebody. Someday. When it matters." Grace turned the winking pamphlet face down on her lap. "That's the part I can't test in advance, though. I don't know if honesty persuades or if it just makes Friday longer."

Marisol didn't answer right away, which Grace was learning was her way of agreeing to take a question seriously. Instead she lifted a diaphragm out of the tub, then a packet of pills, then a row of condoms, and lined them along the counter like evidence. "Contraception," she said. "Go."

Grace went. She fumbled the diaphragm, mixed up the sponge and the ring, got the condom onto the demo model on the second try with the room's one unbroken condom, and explained the clinic's walk-in testing hours almost correctly. Almost. Marisol corrected the day, Thursday not Tuesday, and Grace wrote it on her wrist in pen, where it would smudge by Friday, where she would have to look at it while talking, where her sleeve would slide down over it at exactly the wrong moment, and she decided she would let it.

At the end Marisol stood, and Grace stood too, and they faced each other in the small room with the chart on the wall and the evidence on the counter. "You'll be fine," Marisol said, "or you won't, and you'll do it again next year better." She held out the tub for Grace to carry, which Grace understood was not about the tub. Grace took the heavy end, and the models shifted, and they walked out through the waiting room together, past the blood pressure machine, past a boy about her age filling out a form with his hood up, his pen pausing over the line for a phone number he maybe didn't want them to have.

"Hey," Grace said to his back, quietly, not stopping. "The machine's free. It tells you both numbers."

Cole sat on an overturned milk crate in his uncle's garage, a sandwich in one hand and a photocopy of his first apartment lease in the other, because his uncle Ray had promised that parking lessons would only begin after Cole read every page he'd been ignoring. The lease was for a studio near campus, eight hundred dollars a month, which had seemed possible until Cole hit the paragraph about insurance. It required the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covered the tenant's own belongings rather than the building, and it added a monthly premium. He read it twice, then a third time, mouthing the words like they'd been transcribed from a language he only half remembered.

"I'm broke," he announced. "The lease makes me buy insurance. It's not even for the building, it's for my stuff, and it costs extra every month."

Ray looked up from checking the tire pressure on his ancient Corolla. "So your stuff isn't worth insuring?"

"My stuff is two duvens of clothes and a lamp."

"Duvens," Ray repeated, delighted. "That's not a word. Say duvens again."

"It's a unit of measurement I invented. One duven is what fits in one duffel bag." Cole waved the lease at him. "The point is I budgeted eight hundred a month and now it's eight hundred plus a premium and I don't have a plus."

"That's a real problem," Ray admitted, screwing the cap back on the tire valve. "Also your mother says you told her you'd read the whole lease already."

Cole examined the sandwich with great concentration. "I read the parts about the deposit."

"So the veracity of your earlier claims is, what, partial?"

"Situationally accurate." His uncle snorted, and Cole allowed himself a grin. "Fine. I should have read it. That's why I'm in a garage learning to park instead of moving in."

"It's why you're in a garage learning to park on a Saturday," Ray said, jingling the keys. "The parking was always happening. Come on. Cones."

They had set up six traffic cones behind the garage in a mockery of a curb, and Cole had spent an hour wedging the Corolla between them, easing backward, turning the wheel, killing the engine twice, and once mounting the neighbor's grass at an angle Ray described as "bellicose." Cole preferred the word "assertive." The car, he argued, was simply making its position known.

"You're overcorrecting," Ray said from the hood of the car, where he sat eating the second half of the sandwich like a judge at a livestock fair. "You see the back cone, you panic, you crank the wheel. Small adjustments. Adjust, look, adjust again."

"That's easy for you to say from the hood."

"I'm saying it from thirty years of not hitting things."

Cole tried again, slower. He reversed until the rear tire neared the first cone, turned the wheel one rotation, drifted back, straightened, and slid into the gap with maybe a foot to spare on each side. Nobody spoke for a second. Then Ray said, "Do it again but worse, so I know it wasn't luck."

It was luck. The second attempt ended with a cone under the rear tire, crunching like an empty soda can. Cole rested his forehead on the steering wheel.

"Here's my theory," he said. "You commit to one strategy, full lock, and you either fit or you don't. Binary. Or you do the small adjustments thing, which gives you more chances to fix it but also more chances to panic mid-fix."

"Those are your two theories of parking."

"They're my two theories of everything. The lease, for instance. I could have read it in one sitting like a commitment machine, or I could have gone page by page and adjusted. Instead I did neither, which turns out to be its own strategy, and not a good one."

Ray slid off the hood and came around to the window. "And the insurance? You still short every month?"

"Twelve dollars short. Maybe fifteen, I haven't done the exact math because I'm afraid of the answer."

"Monday, call the company and ask what the premium actually is for your situation. Don't guess at numbers. Then call me and tell me, and I'll tell you whether to panic." Ray leaned in through the window. "Now pull out and merge onto the pretend highway."

"The pretend highway is a gravel road behind a funeral home."

"Traffic's lighter there." Ray walked back to the cones and righted the fallen one, setting it precisely in its scuffed circle in the dirt. He stood with his hands on his hips, waiting.

Cole started the engine, checked his mirrors with exaggerated ceremony, and pulled out onto the gravel road, which stretched empty in both directions under a wide gray sky, no oncoming cars, no ramp, nothing to merge with but possibility.

The folded notice sat under the cashbox all morning: debate camp tuition due by five o'clock, and Clara forty dollars short. She had until the afternoon heat died to sell enough lemonade, and between customers she rehearsed the thing that had sunk her interview last week, the question she would get again when she called the camp director at five. How does a central bank raising interest rates slow inflation? She knew the words. She could recite them like a poem and, like a poem, they dissolved the moment anyone looked at her expectantly.

"You're mumbling again," her grandmother said from the porch, shelling peas into a blue bowl. "Your elocution was better when you were eight and charging a quarter."

Clara reset the pitcher, sliced another lemon. "When rates go up, borrowing costs more, so people buy less, so prices stop climbing." She said it to the street, to the mailbox, to a boy on a skateboard who rolled past without stopping. "That's the whole sentence. Why can't I make it land?"

"Because you don't believe it yet," her grandmother said, which Clara thought was unfair, because she did believe it, the way she believed that ionize meant to strip electrons off an atom, a fact she could hold without being able to feel.

At noon Mr. Aldous came down the sidewalk, the retired economics professor from two doors over, impecunious in his frayed canvas shoes but never too poor for a cold drink on a hot day. He counted out coins and then lingered, because he always lingered. Clara braced for a lecture. Instead he pointed at her hand-lettered sign, which read COLD, and asked why she sold only lemonade and not iced tea as well.

"Too much work."

"Suppose it weren't. Suppose you could make both better than the kid on Maple Street makes either one."

"Then I'd outsell him at everything."

"Would you?" Mr. Aldous settled onto the curb. "When you spend your afternoon making tea, what do you give up?"

Clara started to say nothing, then stopped. Lemons. Lemons and time and the customers who wanted lemonade, who were most of them. If she made tea, she gave up a lot of lemonade. If the kid on Maple Street made tea, he gave up very little, because nobody on his street bought lemonade from him anyway. "He loses less by making tea than I do," she said slowly.

Mr. Aldous smiled at the curb.

"So even if I'm better at both, I can't have the advantage in both," Clara said. "It's called comparative advantage, isn't it. A lower cost for one thing means a higher cost for the other, so it evens out." She stood very still, holding the pitcher, and something shifted, not in the facts but underneath them. Being better at everything wasn't the same as being better off doing everything. Everyone was giving something up, always, and the price of what you chose was the thing you didn't.

"Grandma," she called to the porch. "When the central bank raises interest rates, what does borrowing give up?"

Her grandmother looked up from the peas. "It gives up being cheap."

"No, I mean the borrower. What does a person give up when they take a loan now instead of waiting?" The answer assembled itself as she spoke it. The money they would have saved. The cheaper price later, the interest not paid, the other uses of their cash. Borrowing had an opportunity cost too, and the central bank, whatever else it was doing, was turning that dial. Raising rates made the thing people gave up bigger, so more of them waited, and she could see it now as a street of small decisions rather than a sentence to memorize.

"Rate," Mr. Aldous said, raising his paper cup. "One more, and put nothing in the tip jar but your own conviction."

She poured it, and poured three more in the next hour as the heat peaked, and at four forty she counted the cashbox with her grandmother's cool hand steadying her elbow. Forty-six dollars and change. She had enough, barely, if the camp would take cash dropped at the office before five. She also had a question she couldn't answer: whether cooling prices was worth the neighbors who wouldn't borrow this year, and she decided she would say that on the phone, out loud, as part of her answer rather than as a weakness in it.

She carried the cashbox up the porch steps and reached for the phone.

"Dial," her grandmother said.

Victor's mother left on Sunday night for a week of night shifts at the hospital, and on the kitchen table she had set down a bank card, a pad of yellow paper, and a sentence she clearly considered sufficient instruction: "Feed yourself." He was sixteen, and until that moment his contribution to the household's food had been locating things in the refrigerator that other people had cooked. The pad of paper looked back at him with the blank patience of an exam he hadn't studied for.

He stood at the counter and tried to introspect, which was a word his English teacher used and which Victor privately suspected meant "staring at a wall with your eyes open." It didn't work on meals. What worked was a list, and what made the list survivable was a plan his mother had once mentioned in passing: cook in batches, eat the same thing twice, buy everything at once so you weren't in the store every day losing money to impulse. He wrote Monday through Sunday down the side of the paper, then, because seven distinct dinners felt like seven separate defeats, wrote "chili" beside two days and "pasta bake" beside two more.

The grocery store on Tuesday afternoon was a landscape he had never properly visited. He had been in it a hundred times, but always downstream of the decisions, grabbing bread his mother had phoned ahead about. Now he stood where the decisions were made. He bought dried beans because they were cheaper than canned, a fact he discovered by standing in the aisle doing arithmetic on his phone, and cumin because the recipe said so, and an onion, and a block of dark chocolate because the same shelf held it and because Saturday was Delia's birthday and he had, three weeks earlier and in a moment he preferred not to examine, volunteered to make her chocolates.

The chili took four hours, mostly because of the beans. He had not known that dried beans needed soaking, and the bag had told him this only after he had already begun. He soaked them overnight, cooked them Wednesday, and ate chili Wednesday and Thursday, and by Thursday he had formed a considered position: batch cooking was less like cooking than like logistics, and logistics rewarded the person who thought ahead and punished the person who merely responded. His mother texted a photo of hospital vending machine noodles at 3 a.m. and the words "you're eating better than me," which he chose to take as a compliment.

The chocolate was the part he had not planned honestly. He had imagined himself Saturday morning pouring neat squares into the silicone mould he'd ordered online, and the mould arriving in a padded envelope with a small insert that said, in four languages, nothing useful. He broke the chocolate into a bowl over simmering water, melted it all the way, stirred in cream because a video had said ganache, and spooned it into the little heart-shaped cavities with the focus of someone defusing something. Then he put the tray in the fridge and went to read about pasta bake.

Two hours later he turned the mould over and tapped it, and nothing happened. He tapped harder. One heart broke at its waist and stayed in the mould, half in, half out, like something alluvial deposited there over geological time. He dug at another with a spoon and it came out smeared, dull, and wrong, its surface bloomed with pale streaks. He stood at the counter holding a ruined heart and felt the specific embarrassment of a person who has claimed a skill in public that he does not hold in private.

He did not call anyone. He looked it up himself, and the looking up was a small humiliation of its own, because the answer was everywhere, and the fact that he hadn't known it made him feel like the last person to arrive at a meeting everyone else had left hours ago. Somewhere in the forums, in a thread from 2017, someone with the username cocoa_mum had written the whole thing in one line: properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould. Victor read it twice. His batch had been melted and poured and never tempered at all, whatever that consisted of, and it had sat in the mould like a tenant who refused to acknowledge the lease had ended.

Finding out what it consisted of took most of Friday evening. He learned to melt most of the chocolate, then take it off the heat and stir in the reserved unmelted chunk until that melted too, and to test a smear on his lower lip, which was cool enough to tell him something, though he wasn't entirely sure what. He worked the bowl with a spatula longer than seemed reasonable. At some point his friend Marcus texted asking if he was coming out, and Victor answered "making chocolate," and Marcus replied with three crying-laughing faces, and Victor put the phone face down without holding a plebiscite on whether it was funny. It was, a little. That wasn't the point.

Saturday morning he filled the mould a second time, set it in the cool of the garage because the kitchen was warm, and waited with the particular discipline of a boy who had already lost once. When he turned the mould over and flexed it, the hearts dropped out one after another onto the plate, glossy and exact, each with a soft click against the ceramic. They had shrunk, just slightly, just enough. He picked one up and turned it in the light. He still couldn't have said why the method worked, only that it had, twice in a row now, the second heart-shaped batch and the fact of it, and that somewhere between the ruined first tray and this plate the difference had been patience he hadn't known he could operate.

Delia arrived at four. He gave her the box, and she opened it, and she said, "You made these?" and Victor, who had prepared several modest and self-deprecating answers, heard himself say, "They're in temper."

"What?"

"The chocolate," he said, and turned the plate toward her. "Listen." He tipped it, and they clicked again against the rim.

Sara spread the towel flat on the sand and weighed its corners with a cooler, a sneaker, and a paperback copy of the oceanography text she was supposed to have finished by now. The morning was already warm, the kind of warm that made the parking lot shimmer, and she had until four o'clock to learn how to explain, out loud, to an actual audience, how greenhouse gases trapped heat and how to read a century of carbon dioxide measurements off a single line. On Monday she had to stand in front of her seminar and teach it for eight minutes. Teaching it was the assignment. Faking her way through it was not allowed.

Marcus arrived with his board under his arm and a folded map in his teeth, which was typical, since he had one want all summer and it was the water. He dropped the board, spat the map into his hand, and knelt beside her.

"Read this to me," he said. "Quiz is Tuesday. If I fail again I have to retake the unit, and my dad said he's not paying for summer school twice, that the first time was supposed to indemnify him against me being lazy. His word."

"You can't be insured against yourself," Sara said, and he laughed, though neither of them was entirely sure it was a joke.

He smoothed the map across the towel. It showed the Atlantic with arrows threading across it, some red, some blue, a few fat and short, some long and skinny. Marcus tapped a long red arrow off the eastern coast.

"So this one's fast," he said. "Red's fast, blue's slow. That's why they're colored like that, right? Like a speedometer."

Sara looked at it. She had been staring at graphs all week, a rising line of carbon dioxide climbing and sawtooth-ing across a hundred years, and she had learned the hard way not to assume what a picture was telling her. Her eyes moved over the arrows. There was a red one crawling down the western side of Africa, slow and wide. There was a blue one running fast up the eastern coast of North America, narrow as a pencil stroke. If red meant fast, the map contradicted itself.

"Wait," she said. She held her finger over the red arrow near Africa. "This one's huge and it's going south. If it were speed, it'd be flying. But it's labeled with temperatures, look, at the edge. Degrees."

Marcus squinted. "So what's the color for?"

"I think it's temperature. On current maps, red arrows are warm currents and blue arrows are cold ones." She said it slowly, testing it against the shapes on the page, and the whole map reorganized itself in her mind like a sentence she'd been misreading. "The colors aren't speed at all. They're warm and cold."

He sat back on his heels. "So I've been studying it wrong for two weeks."

"You've been studying it wrong for two weeks."

"That's why I failed the practice questions." He dragged his hand through his hair, leaving it salty and crooked. "I kept answering how fast the water moved. Okay. Okay, warm red, cold blue. Say it again so I get it stuck."

She said it again, and he repeated it back, and then he made her quiz him, pointing at arrows while a gull screamed over the dunes and the tide chewed steadily at the slope below them. He was quick when he wasn't wrong, which Sara thought was the most frustrating kind of smart.

"Okay, your turn," he said finally. "Teach me the greenhouse thing. I'll be your practice dummy. But make it good, I want to actually get it, not just nod."

Sara took out her printed graph, the long sawtoothed climb, and flattened it on the towel beside the current map so the wind couldn't take it. She began where the book began, that sunlight came through the atmosphere and warmed the ground, and that the ground gave heat back as a different kind of light, and that certain gases let the sunlight in but were much less willing to let the heat out, so the heat lingered. She used the word physiology once, by accident, saying the planet's physiology was the way heat moved through its skin, and then stopped, because it wasn't quite right, and she was honest about that out loud. "Scratch that. It's more like a blanket than a body. I have to pick one and stick with it Monday."

"With the graph," Marcus said, leaning over the printout. "Why does it sawtooth like that, up and down every year, but always climbing?"

"I don't fully know yet," Sara said. "There's a yearly cycle, the teacher said so, something about seasons and plants, but I couldn't explain the mechanism if someone paid me. I'm going to say that part carefully." She traced the long rise with her finger, the line going up and up across the decades. "The main thing is the trend. Whatever the wiggles are doing, the whole thing climbs. It's not flat, and it's not coming down."

Marcus looked at the graph for a while, then out at the water, which was blue and glittering and, she now understood, crossed by currents whose colors on paper had nothing to do with their speed. He stood, picked up his board, and waded in, and Sara stayed on the towel with the two maps side by side, the rising line and the red and blue arrows, rehearsing under her breath. When he caught his first wave and stood up on it, she held the graph above her head so he could see the line climbing even from the water.

The laminated menu at Marisol's had a coffee ring on it shaped, Rebecca decided, like Portugal, and she kept rotating it while she read the article for the fourth time. The article was Spanish, from a paper in Seville, about a city council debating whether to grant amnesty to shopkeepers who had occupied an abandoned market building for six years. Her college required a language placement test in August. Her debate coach had told her, more or less, that reading aloud was the only way to make a language live in your mouth instead of your head, so here she was, at the corner table by the window, muttering at a newspaper.

"¿Más café?" The waitress, Doris, was maybe twenty-five and had already corrected Rebecca's pronunciation twice, once with great gentleness and once laughing so hard she had to hold the coffee pot with both hands.

"Sí, por favor. And also." Rebecca turned the paper around. "I have to summarize this. Out loud. In Spanish, then in English, without looking. For my placement prep."

"Then you will need more than coffee," Doris said, and poured.

The trouble was that Rebecca could summarize in English forever. She had spent four years on the debate team building arguments like walls, brick on brick, and she knew exactly how a wall went up. She could still hear her coach at the state semifinal last spring, leaning over the flow pad: "You've got the logic, Reyes, but you're arguing at a jury made of computers." In the flashback she'd rolled her eyes at him. Now, seven weeks from a campus where nobody knew her, the memory sat differently, the way a song you skipped in June becomes, by August, the only one you can hear.

She tried the summary anyway, staring at the sugar dispenser as though it might prompt her. "El consejo, uh, debate. The council debates amnesty for the shopkeepers, porque the building, la edificio, is..." She lost the thread, found it, lost it again. "They are not destitute, exactly, but the article says some are. The reporter says the city should not, no debe, historicize the occupation, should not treat it like a piece of the past in a museum, because people still work there."

Doris set down the pot and folded her arms, which was either judgment or interest. "That part was good. The last part."

"The grammar or the idea?"

"The idea. The grammar was a crime scene."

Rebecca laughed despite herself, and something about the laugh loosened the knot she'd been carrying since she'd opened the paper. Because she realized, mid-chuckle, what had been bothering her about the summary. She had explained what the article said the way she always explained things: reasons, evidence, a clean line from claim to conclusion. If the shopkeepers had stood up at that council meeting and argued the way Rebecca summarized, listing clauses like ingredients, nobody would have moved. But the article quoted one shopkeeper, a woman named Pilar, who had only said that her daughter had learned to walk between the stalls. That was the sentence the reporter had chosen to end on. Not the zoning law. Not the six years.

"Okay," Rebecca said slowly, "this is going to sound like a class I'm not taking yet. Aristotle. Three means of persuasion." Doris raised an eyebrow and said nothing, which Rebecca took as permission. "Ethos, that's the speaker's credibility. Pathos, the audience's emotions. Logos, the logic of the argument." She tapped the newspaper with each word like she was dealing cards. "My whole summary was logos. Just logos. Pilar's one line was pathos, and it probably did more than the council's whole file of documents."

"And ethos?" Doris said. "You said three."

"I don't know. Hers, maybe. Six years in the building. You can't fake six years."

Doris considered this while wiping a table that was already clean. "So for your test, you will say the facts, but also you will say the woman's daughter learned to walk there."

"Maybe." Rebecca turned her cup in its saucer. She wasn't sure, honestly, whether a placement test wanted Pilar or wanted clauses, whether a summary was supposed to have a heartbeat or just a skeleton. Maybe both. Maybe the summary in Spanish would be clumsy no matter what she did, her accent a crime scene for another month, and the best she could hope for was that the ideas arrived dented but recognizable. What she did know, with a certainty that surprised her, was that the next time she built an argument, she would count the walls and find only one, and she would look for the other two on purpose, even if she couldn't always tell where logic ended and feeling began.

She spread the paper flat, took a breath that fogged the window for a second, and started over, slower this time, saying the woman's sentence first: "Su hija aprendió a caminar entre los puestos."

"There," Doris said. "Now more coffee."

The debate tournament shared its building with the theater program, which was how Andrew ended up holding a script in the black box room while sixty debaters argued about jurisprudence two hallways away. He had come to compete, but his partner had the flu, and Ms. Okafor from drama had cornered him near the sign-in table: their student director for the one-act was suspended, the performance was in two weeks, and Andrew, who had done lights for the fall play, was apparently the only person in the building who knew where the board was. He said yes before he had decided to.

The cast was three people: Priya, who talked fast when she was nervous; Marcus, who was calm the way a lake is calm before something drops into it; and a sophomore named Dani who had never performed anywhere. They stood in a loose clump on the stage, scripts rolled in their fists, waiting for him to know what to do. He did not know what to do. He had watched directors work for years and had absorbed nothing except that they said things like "hold that beat" and drank a lot of coffee.

"Okay," he said. "Scene one. Priya, you enter from, uh, the left, and Marcus, you're at the table." Priya walked toward the table from stage right, crossing the whole playing area to get there, and stood behind Marcus's chair looking faintly betrayed. Andrew blinked. He had said left. She had gone right. "No, your left," he started, and then stopped, because she had gone to her own left and that was somehow the wrong direction anyway, and he could feel Marcus watching him work this out in real time.

Marcus set his script down. "Stage left," he said. "That's what it's called." He pointed across the stage. "Stage left and stage right, they're from the actor's point of view, facing the audience. So they're the reverse of what the audience sees." He said it without any edge, the way you'd tell someone which door stuck. Priya crossed to the other side, and this time her entrance worked, and Andrew wrote SL in the margin of his script with a hand that was not quite steady.

He found Ms. Okafor at lunch and told her, half apology and half accusation, that nobody had explained any of it. "Nobody explained debate theory to you either," she said. "You read it, you lost rounds, you figured it out." That was true. His first year he had run a case about obsolete constitutional doctrine, some argument about obsolescent clauses that a senior had handed him, and he had defended it without understanding a word of it until he lost to a girl who simply asked him what the standard was. Losing had taught him more than winning ever did. He went back to the theater with a legal pad and began, for the first time in his life, to write down what he did not know.

The rehearsal that afternoon went badly and then went well. He blocked the whole first scene, drawing boxes on the pad, and when Dani froze in her monologue he almost fed her the line, and then didn't. Instead he called a break, sat on the edge of the stage beside her, and asked what the character wanted. "To be heard," Dani said, so quietly he almost missed it. "Then walk toward him while you say it," Andrew said. "Stage right, two steps." She looked at him to check, and he nodded, and she crossed and delivered the line to Marcus's face, and it was the first true moment of the day. Something in Andrew's chest went hot and clean, the way it did after a round he knew he had won on the merits, though this was better, because it wasn't his.

By evening he had found the two ways of thinking and could not get them apart. Debate had trained him to hold positions he did not hold, to argue a side to its limit and then drop it the second the bell rang. Directing wanted the opposite: a conviction about the scene that he had to keep pressing toward, take after take, without a bell to release him. Yet the arguing had a use here too. When Priya wanted her character to lie and Marcus wanted her to tell the truth, Andrew made them swap sides and defend each other's choice, and out of that argument came a third thing, a compromise that was better than either and that he could not have planned. He still did not know whether he was a person who could commit to one truth long enough to build anything on it. He knew he had blocked eleven pages and the entrance directions were all correct.

At eight o'clock Ms. Okafor looked in from the hallway. "You're missing your own round," she said. Andrew checked the time, and he did feel it, a pull toward the pairing sheets and the fluorescent rooms where he was good at things. But Dani was running her monologue again, unprompted, and Priya had moved a chair without being told.

"I'll take the loss," he said, and turned back to the stage. "From the top. Priya, enter stage left."

Elizabeth had forty minutes before her mother's headlights swept the parking lot, and the exam was at eight the next morning. She sat on the coping at the top of the quarter pipe with her review book open on her knees, working the same problem for the third time: two charged plates, a point between them, compute the field strength. The numbers kept sliding away from her, the way the park slid into shadow once the sun dropped behind the equipment shed.

Marcus wanted to film something before the light died entirely. He had a channel, ninety-three subscribers, and a plan involving his little brother's skateboard and a bucket of water he'd carried from the bathroom in a jaundiced old mop pail. "Five minutes," he said, holding up his phone sideways. "I need the drop test."

"Drop test," she repeated, not looking up.

He produced two hacky sacks from his hoodie pocket. "Dev says if you throw one out sideways and just let go of the other one, the thrown one takes longer to land. Dev owes me a dollar if he's wrong."

"They hit at the same time," Elizabeth said, and then heard herself say it, and frowned at the sentence as though someone else had left it on her page. She knew it the way she knew her own locker combination, without being able to say when she'd learned it.

"Prove it." Dev had come up the ramp without his board, chewing a straw, and there was the dollar, held out flat between two fingers like a card trick. Marcus set his phone on the ledge, propped against a skate left on its side, and started recording.

They used the top of the concrete picnic table, which put the drop at roughly waist height. Marcus held one hacky sack at the table's edge and Dev crouched with his arm extended, the second sack in his hand, ready to fling it horizontally the instant Marcus let his fall. Elizabeth stood back by the fun box with her book still open, half of her attention on the variable E and half on the two boys arranging themselves in the fading light.

"Listen for the sounds," Dev said. "Both hits. One-two and you win, one and then a gap and I win."

They ran it three times. The first was botched, Dev threw early; the second was clean, two taps so close together they overlapped into a single knock against the concrete; the third, Marcus insisted on doing himself, holding both sacks, dropping one straight down while flicking the other sideways over the table's edge, and again the taps landed together, a doubled click like a single syllable. Dev paid the dollar without ceremony, folding it into Marcus's palm and immediately demanding a rematch, best of five, different table.

Elizabeth looked down at her problem and felt the two halves of her evening titrate into each other, the memorized fact and the empty grid on her page, until the concentration of one in the other changed the whole thing. Between the plates, the field was what it was at the point; it did not care how the charge had gotten there, only where it was, and her mistake had been carrying a distance from the wrong side of the diagram. She erased two lines and rewrote them, and the answer arrived with the flat certainty of those two overlapping taps.

She checked her phone. Twelve minutes before her mother. Marcus was still filming, Dev was out another dollar, and the light had gone copper along the coping. She closed the book without checking the answer again, because she was done being jaundiced about it, done treating her own work like it came from antiquity, some dead relic she was obliged to memorize rather than something she had watched happen on a picnic table.

"Hey," Marcus called, phone still sideways. "That thing you said. Same time, no matter what. Put it in the video?"

She zipped her bag. "If you split the dollar."

"Two-fifty each," Dev said, already counting.

Behind them, the sprinklers hissed on across the soccer field, and her mother's headlights turned in at the gate.

Victor spread the two books across his grandfather's card table, one propped against the other like feuding relatives at a holiday dinner. Outside, the sprinkler ticked across the brown lawn of the retirement community, and the smell of his grandfather's coffee, half cocoa, half regret, drifted from the kitchen. The assignment was due in September, his first week at college: compare two historians' explanations of the Cold War and decide which the evidence actually supported. He had picked Gaddis and a revisionist named Kolko because they seemed to disagree about everything, and now, four days before deadline, he realized he could not even say what counted as evidence.

"Grandpa, who started the Cold War?" he called.

His grandfather shuffled in with two cups and set one down near Victor's elbow, on a coaster, always on a coaster. "The Soviets," he said. "Obviously. They wanted to subjugate Eastern Europe, and they did."

"That's what Gaddis says. Kind of. But Kolko says the United States wanted markets and used the atomic bomb as blackmail." Victor tapped the page where Kolko had called American policy economic expansion dressed up as defense. "So which is it?"

His grandfather lowered himself into the chair across the table. "I lived through part of it. Does that count as evidence?"

Victor considered this seriously, pencil hovering. "It counts as something. Kolko would call it a confounder. You were raised on one story, so your memory is shaped by the story." He regretted it immediately; it sounded like he was calling his grandfather brainwashed. But his grandfather only laughed, a dry creak like the screen door.

"Read me the part you're stuck on."

Victor read aloud, the bit where Gaddis argued that Stalin's ideology made confrontation unavoidable, and then the Kolko passage arguing that American leaders inflated the Soviet threat to justify their own ambitions. Both cited the same events. The Yalta conference, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin blockade. Same facts, opposite arrows.

"That's the thing about historians," his grandfather said. He turned his cup slowly on its coaster. "You know who Thiers was? Adolphe Thiers. There's a statue of him in Paris, or there was. I saw it on leave, back in the fifties." He squinted at the ceiling. "He ran France later. But before that, he wrote the History of the French Revolution. Published from 1823 to 1827, three volumes, while the memory was still warm. And in it he praised the moderates, men like Mirabeau and Lafayette, and condemned the radicals, especially Robespierre."

"So?"

"So he wasn't lying. He wasn't stupid. He was a moderate himself, writing about a revolution where moderates got eaten. His position was inside the book." His grandfather leaned forward, forearms on the table. "You're trying to find the historian with no position. There isn't one. The question is whether the position bends the evidence or the evidence bends the position."

Victor wrote that down, then crossed out "position bends evidence" because it sounded cleverer than he understood it to be. He pulled the books back and tried the thing he had been avoiding: testing each claim against something outside both books. The telegram from Moscow that Stalin sent about Berlin, which Kolko quoted partially and Gaddis quoted at greater length, and which, when Victor found the full text online in the room where his grandfather's dial-up wheezed like an asthmatic dog, said something neither historian had said it said. Not the opposite. Something murkier. Stalin had been conciliatory and threatening in the same paragraph, which refused to support either clean story.

He worked until the sprinkler stopped and the lawn went quiet. His grandfather watched the evening news with the sound low, glancing over now and then. Victor filled eleven pages of a legal pad, crossed out eight of them, and discovered that Gaddis held up better on Soviet actions in Eastern Europe and worse on American motives, which Gaddis treated as innocent where the record showed them mixed. Neither explanation proved tenable on its own. The honest paper, he realized, would say that.

At ten his grandfather brought in a plate of sandwiches and found Victor staring at the pad.

"Well?" his grandfather asked. "Who started it?"

"I don't know yet. Both of them, probably, in different ways, and I can't make the proportions exact." Victor rubbed his eyes. "Is that an acceptable answer for a college paper?"

His grandfather set down the plate and picked up the pad, reading Victor's scrawled margin note, the one that said: Thiers problem. Check who benefits from the telling.

"You know," his grandfather said, "that's the first honest thing anyone in this family has written about history." He put the pad down and tapped the sandwich plate. "Eat. You can't weigh the world on an empty stomach."

Victor took a sandwich and pulled the pad back toward him, writing at the top of a fresh page: unfinished.

The black box theatre smelled of dust and old paint, and Alexandra had claimed it for every free period of the past week. Her one-act, which she had also written, was scheduled for the spring showcase, and between now and then she had two actors, a bench, and the growing suspicion that she did not know what she was doing. She had watched Mr. Delgado direct the fall musical from the back of the house, taking notes on how he moved bodies through space, and she had assumed the knowledge would transfer. It did not. On Tuesday she had told Marcus to cross downstage left and he had walked into a chair.

The problem, she decided by Thursday, was that she was moving her actors the way she moved words on a page, one at a time, wherever they seemed to fit. At lunch she spread her script across a cafeteria table, and Priya from her drama class sat down across from her with a napkin and a pen. Priya had gone to drama camp the summer before and talked about it the way other people talked about foreign countries.

"You're trying to block without knowing where your climax is," Priya said. She drew a triangle on the napkin, then bisected it with a rising and falling line. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid, exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution. In his book on drama technique. Eighteen sixty-three."

"That old?" Alexandra said.

"Older than the building." Priya tapped a point near the top of the triangle. "Your climax lives here. Find it first, then block toward it."

Alexandra studied the napkin. Her play was about two sisters who meet at a riverbank to divide their dead mother's belongings, and she had written eleven pages of quiet conversation because quiet was what she trusted. She found the moment where the older sister reveals she had already sold the mother's house weeks before, and marked it. Then she drew her own pyramid in the margin of the script, a small neat slope, and set the reveal at the peak. Underneath she wrote: everything before must rise toward this. It was a mechanical thing to do to something she had made out of feeling, and she did it anyway.

That afternoon she ran the scene like an experiment. She placed the bench upstage right, near the painted backdrop of the riparian shoreline she'd begged the art class to make, reeds and a strip of water. The sisters began far apart, one at each edge of the playing space, and Alexandra blocked them moving inward along the rising action, a step closer each time a secret surfaced, so that by the time the house was sold they were nearly touching. Then, in the falling action, she sent them apart again, not to where they had started but to a middle distance, close enough to speak, too far to touch. It worked. She could feel it working, the geometry doing something the words alone had not.

Except that Marcus, who played the younger sister's silent boyfriend for all of six lines, kept watching from the doorway, and on Friday he finally said what his face had been saying for two days. "They're moving like chess pieces. It's clean. It's dead."

She wanted to defend the pyramid. She wanted to say that structure was not the enemy of feeling, that a river needs banks or it's just a flood. But she had also seen it herself, the moment in Wednesday's run when Nadia, playing the older sister, abandoned her mark to pick up a scarf that had slipped from the props box, and the small unscripted gesture had been the most alive second of the entire rehearsal. Alexandra had said nothing about it at the time. She had underlined the mark in her script instead.

She spent the weekend trying to metabolize the contradiction. On Saturday she walked the actual creek path behind her house, the one the play's riverbank was borrowed from, and found she could not hold both ideas in her head at once. Freytag's pyramid was true; the sisters' slow approach and withdrawal was the best thing she had made. Marcus was also true; the approach was legible as approach, it looked planned, and looking planned was a kind of lie. Two true things, refusing to fit.

On Monday she ran the scene a third way, which was not a compromise so much as a surrender she had thought her way into. She kept the pyramid as the floor plan, the deep map, the rise and the peak and the fall, and she told her actors what it was. "The shape's mine," she said. "The steps are yours. Break the marks whenever the moment asks you to. I'll fix the lights around whatever you do." Nadia grinned. Marcus stopped leaning in the doorway.

The run that followed was rougher and better. Nadia picked up the scarf again, this time on purpose, and carried it to the top of the rising action instead of her assigned mark, and Alexandra watched the reveal land in a place she had never planned, three feet from where the pyramid said it should be, and it was still, unmistakably, the climax. The shape held. The actors were not inside the shape; they were leaning against it, pushing at it, and the pushing was what made it visible.

Afterward Priya came to watch the last ten minutes and sat with the napkin pyramid folded in her pocket. "So which one won?" she asked in the aisle, meaning structure or freedom, and Alexandra found she could not say, could only say that she had stopped needing them to fight. There was no rapprochement exactly, no tidy treaty; there was a truce she re-negotiated at every rehearsal, and some nights the actors would keep every mark and the scene would be cold, and some nights they would wander and she would lose the ending in the reeds, and both failures taught her something she could not yet name.

She turned back to the stage, where Nadia was still holding the scarf, standing in her wrong place, exactly right.

"From the top," Alexandra said. "And this time, Nadia, take your time coming in."

Annabelle had five days to learn to argue about carbon taxes for five minutes in French, and her grandmother's kitchen table had become the debate hall. The table was maple, older than her mother, and it smelled faintly of the clove cigarettes her grandfather had given up a decade before he died. Her grandmother set down two cups of tisane and slid into the chair opposite her, palms flat on the wood like a judge about to call a session to order.

"Encore," her grandmother said. "Dès le début."

Annabelle began, and fell apart almost immediately. The word for tax escaped her the way a cat slips under a fence, present one moment and gone the next. She stopped. In the silence she could hear the refrigerator ticking, and behind it the small humiliation of a girl who had won her school's English debate finals in the spring and now could not produce a single noun.

Her grandmother did not correct her. She folded her hands and waited, which was somehow worse.

"I don't have it," Annabelle said in English. "The word. La, the thing the government makes people pay, for carbon." She gestured, drawing a rectangle in the air, then pointing at the window toward the invisible government.

"Ah." Her grandmother tapped her own temple once. "C'est de la circonlocution. When you cannot find a word, you describe it instead of stopping. It keeps you talking. A speaker who talks around a missing word, we say she uses circumlocution. It is a real strategy, not cheating."

"It sounds like drowning politely."

"It sounds like a debater," her grandmother said. "The judges cannot mark you down for a word they never noticed was missing."

So Annabelle tried again. She acclimated to the rhythm of it slowly, the way she had once acclimated to the cold water of the lake at her aunt's cabin, by degrees and without dignity. When "pollution" vanished, she said "the smoke that cities breathe." When "economy" deserted her, she said "the money that moves between everyone" and kept going, and her grandmother lifted one eyebrow a millimeter, which in her language was applause.

The problem was not only vocabulary. The problem was that Annabelle did not actually know what she believed about a carbon tax. Her debate coach had assigned her the opposing side, the bellicose one, the side that attacks, and she was good at attacking. But her grandmother, she had learned over the summer, had worked thirty years as a hospital administrator and thought about policy the way a gardener thinks about weather, with patience and resentment in equal measure. Over dinner on the second night her grandmother had said, in English, "The tax works only if poor families get the rebate back. Otherwise it is just a fine for being born without money." Annabelle had argued back, coach-style, listing the studies, and her grandmother had waved her off and gone to wash the lettuce.

On the fourth day, Annabelle stood at the sink drying dishes while her grandmother washed them, and tried out a position in French, haltingly, talking around every third word. She said that the tax could be a good tool and also a cruel one, that it depended on the rebate, that she would defend the policy only with that condition attached. The water ran. Her grandmother handed her a wet plate and did not say anything for a long time.

"That is not what your coach asked you to argue," she said finally.

"I know. I'm supposed to destroy the tax, not fix it."

"Then you must decide whether you are a person who argues what she is told, or a person who argues what she has decided." Her grandmother rinsed a fork and set it in the rack with great care, as if setting down the question itself. "Both are honest. Only one is yours."

Annabelle did not sleep well that night. She lay in the guest room under a quilt pieced from her grandfather's old shirts and rehearsed both speeches against the ceiling. The attack speech was easier and stronger; it had statistics in it like flares, and it would win. The other speech had a hole in the middle where her certainty should have been. She could admit, in it, that she did not know whether the rebate would actually reach the families who needed it, that this was the part the studies disagreed about, that she was arguing for a version of the tax that might not exist yet. That was either honesty or weakness, and lying awake she could not tell which, and by morning she still could not.

The day of the trial run, her grandmother cleared the table, set the kitchen timer to five minutes, and stood at the end of the room with her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. Annabelle took a breath and began in French, slow and then steadier, the attack rising in her throat and the other argument rising underneath it. Halfway through, the word for "rebate" abandoned her completely, and she did not stop. "The money," she said, in French, "that the government gives back, to the families, the poor ones, so the tax does not fall only on them," and her grandmother's mouth curved, and the timer ticked on.

"Time," her grandmother said, when it rang. She took off her glasses, looked at her granddaughter across the maple table, and asked, "Which speech was that?"

Annabelle was still catching her breath. "Both," she said. "I don't know yet if that's allowed."

Her grandmother turned the timer over in her hands, considering it, then wound it again and set it back to five. "Then tell me the parts you are still unsure of," she said. "Start now."

The kitchen table had been cleared of everything except the launcher, a meter stick, a roll of masking tape, and a bag of marbles that Vanessa's little brother kept trying to steal. The regional engineering fair was in forty hours, and the fair's judges awarded points for hitting a target eleven meters away with a projectile fired at a set angle. Every other team would bring a launcher. Only the teams that could explain their own numbers would advance.

Vanessa had spent the evening doing what her textbook demanded: dichotomize the motion, treat the horizontal and vertical components as separate problems linked only by time. The marble left the barrel at eight meters per second, tilted at forty degrees, so the horizontal piece was a steady 6.13 meters per second and the vertical piece started at 5.14, rose, decelerated, fell. She worked the vertical equation for the time of flight, carried that time across to the horizontal equation, and got a range of just over five meters on paper. Then she set the launcher on the kitchen tile, aligned it with the tape line she had stuck to the floor, and fired.

The marble hit the floor at four and a half meters. She measured it twice. She fired again, and again, and marked each landing spot with a small pencil tick on a strip of painter's tape, because her mother had already objected to pencil marks on the tile. Four ticks clustered tightly, all short of the calculation, all short by roughly the same margin. She checked her arithmetic, found nothing, and checked it again with her calculator upside down for no reason she could defend.

Her brother Marcus came in for a snack at nine and stood over the tape marks with a plastic cup of apple juice. "You missed."

"I didn't miss. There's no target yet. It landed short of where the math says it should land."

"Then the math is wrong."

"The math is not wrong." She said it with more force than she felt, and he shrugged and went to the living room, where her mother was watching something with the volume low. Vanessa sat back down. The launcher was a project she had inherited in a sense: her physics teacher had announced the fair three weeks ago, and her lab partner, Priya, had done the building while Vanessa had done the deriving. Priya was asleep by now, or studying for the calc exam they both had on Monday, and Vanessa had agreed to handle the trajectory model. The agreement had seemed fair at the time. Now the model and the machine were telling different stories, and she had until Saturday morning to reconcile them.

She tried a different angle, thirty-five degrees, recalculated, refired. Short again, by a comparable fraction. She tried the marble her father had brought home from a trade show, slightly lighter than the others, and it landed shorter still. At ten thirty she drew the parabola from her equations on graph paper, then plotted her four tick marks below the point where the parabola met the floor, and stared at the gap between the curve and the dots. In class, the problems always ended with the marble landing exactly on the parabola, because the problems were about the parabola. The textbook had a footnote she half remembered, something she had skipped because footnotes were a disincentive to finishing problem sets on time. She got the book from her backpack and found it, small type at the bottom of the page: the calculations ignored air resistance, and real projectiles did not.

She read the sentence three times. The problems in the book assumed the marble flew through nothing, through a vacuum, and her kitchen was full of air. The gap on her graph was not an error in her algebra. It was the difference between the clean world of the equations and the tiled, air-filled world where the marbles actually flew. A thrown or launched ball would land shorter than the calculation predicted, because the calculation had never promised anything about air.

Her mother appeared in the doorway in her robe, dour about the hour but holding a mug of tea, which she set down beside the graph paper without comment. Vanessa explained anyway, fast, pointing at the parabola and then at the tick marks. "The math assumes no air. The air is real. So it lands short, every time, by about this much."

"So add the this much."

"It's not a constant this much. It changes with the speed and the angle and probably the marble." Vanessa looked at the ticks again. "I can't derive that. Nobody in our class can derive that. There's a whole drag equation and it's not in our book."

"Then what will you tell the judges?"

Vanessa turned to a fresh page. She could not make the model match the machine exactly, but she could make the model honest. She would present the clean calculation, then present her measured landings, then state the difference plainly: air resistance slows real projectiles, so a real ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts. She would show the graph with the parabola and the ticks and let the judges see the gap. If they asked why the gap had the size it had, she would say she didn't know yet, and that this was the next problem. Some teams would hide the discrepancy or fudge the launch angle to compensate. She wrote a note to adjust the launcher's angle by trial until the marble covered eleven meters, then wrote a second note beside it: do not pretend the adjustment is part of the theory.

She texted Priya a photo of the graph, the parabola and the four ticks, with the message: we land short of the math, it's the air, I'll explain on the bus. Priya's reply came as a single question mark, then, a minute later: ok good, I knew the launcher wasn't crooked.

Vanessa fired the last marble of the night at forty degrees and watched it thump down short of the tick cluster, half a tile's width short of the rest, and she picked it up and turned it under the kitchen light looking for the reason. She set it aside in its own spot on the counter, labeled with a torn piece of tape, and turned off the light over the table.

"How late are you planning to do this?" her mother asked from the hallway.

"Until Saturday," Vanessa said, and clicked the launcher empty to check the spring.

I am not a competitive person, which is why I let Dara talk me into the race in the first place.
