That's what I told myself on the walk to the coding club, the January dark pressing against the classroom windows when I got there, and it was almost true. Really I wanted to lose. Losing to Dara in front of people would prove something I needed proven: that I was here to learn, not to win, and a person like that could afford to lose.

Mr. Okafor's room still had the antiquated desktops along the back wall, the ones nobody used since the laptops cart arrived, but the club met here anyway because it was the only room with the good whiteboards. I claimed a seat near the middle and opened my laptop on a half-finished file called WordList.java. Dara dropped into the chair beside me and spun a marker like a baton.

"New project," she said. "Dictionary lookup. Whoever finds a target word in the club's word list faster wins. I'll go front to back. You do your weird halving thing."

"It's not weird. It's called binary search." That was the whole of my authority on the subject, a name and a rumor.

"Fine," she said. "I'll do it the normal way."

Theo, who kept the club's data files on a drive shaped like a rubber duck, announced that the list had a million entries, sorted, and he proposed to commandeer the projector so everyone could watch our screens magnified and merciless. A million sounded infinite to me. I imagined the evening ending with Dara somewhere in the C's and me apologizing.

But first, homework review. Mr. Okafor had asked us to build a Java class with private fields and getter methods, and to test it, and I had done this at my kitchen table with a confusion I hadn't admitted to anyone. The confusion was this: why hide the data? If the whole point of a WordEntry class was to hand out its word and its definition, why wrap them in private and make callers go through getWord() like a customs gate? It seemed ceremonial. It seemed like something invented to give tests something to check.

My test file was a small embarrassment. I had written one test that constructed an entry and one that didn't. "That's not testing," Theo said, leaning over, "that's attendance." So I wrote a real one: build an entry, call getWord(), assert it equaled what I'd put in, try to change the field directly and watch the compiler refuse. The refusal was the interesting part. I had expected to resent it and instead felt something closer to relief, the way you feel when a railing turns out to be solid. Dara, whose own class had public fields everywhere, watched my error message scroll up and frowned at it like it had insulted her family.

"Private just means you have to knock," I said, and immediately worried it sounded smug.

"It means extra typing," Dara said, but she opened her file and started changing her fields to private anyway, jaw set, typing getters with the aggression of someone losing an argument she'd started.

Then the race. Theo loaded the million-entry list into both our programs and picked the target: "perspicacity." He wrote it on the whiteboard in his terrible handwriting so we wouldn't claim spelling errors later. Dara started at index zero, her counter ticking on the big screen, one, two, three, a march into a desert. I halved. Take the middle of the list, compare, throw away half the world, take the middle of what's left. The screen made it look casual, my index leaping like a skipped stone, and my counter climbed in a way I didn't believe: single digits, then twelve, then it stopped.

Seventeen.

Dara was at forty thousand and somewhere deep in the B's. She kept going for a while out of dignity, then closed the lid of her laptop, which on the projector looked like a curtain falling.

"Twenty," Theo said, reading off something on his own screen. "Halving a million twenty times leaves a single item. So a search like yours never needs more than twenty comparisons." He said it flatly, the way he said everything, and I sat with the number. At most twenty, out of a million. Dara would have needed, in the worst case, the whole million, or half of it on average, I didn't know which and it didn't matter against twenty.

Here is what I told Dara on the bus afterward, and I want to be honest that I made it sound more finished than it was. I said the class exercise and the race were the same lesson: you accept a constraint, the private field or the sorted list, and the constraint pays you back, order at the door, speed at the counter. I said the railing and the railing's solidity were one thing. Dara listened with her forehead against the window and said, "So hide the data and halve the world. Great slogan. Doesn't tell me what to do when the list isn't sorted."

I opened my mouth and found nothing in it. Because that was the part I hadn't worked out, and the part I'd skipped in my kitchen-table sulk, and the part my neat speech on the bus had papered over. The getters guard the door only if everyone agrees to use the door. Binary search buys its twenty comparisons only if the million entries are already in order, and sorting a million of anything is its own expensive question, one nobody had asked me and I hadn't asked myself. I had been congratulating myself on not being competitive, and then on losing gracefully, and now on winning gracefully, and somewhere in that chain I had stopped checking what I actually knew.

"Theo," I said, texting him from the bus, "how long does it take to sort the list before we can search it?"

Three dots appeared, stopped, appeared again. Dara watched me watch the screen.

"Ask him if the sort's worth it for one search," she said, "or only if you're searching all night."

The dots kept pulsing, and I typed, deleted, typed again, while outside the window the streetlights came on one at a time, in order, all the way down the hill.

The assignment was due at eleven fifty-nine, and Sienna had until then to submit a Book class with private fields, getter methods, and a test file proving it all worked. She'd brought her laptop to Grandma Ruth's house because her own internet was down and Mom had said a change of scenery would do her good. Now she sat at the kitchen table between a bowl of walnuts and a jigsaw puzzle missing its edge pieces, watching forty red compiler errors crawl up her screen like ants finding spilled sugar.

"Still fighting with it?" Grandma asked, setting down two mugs of tea. She had her diurnal rituals so firmly fixed that Sienna could have set a clock by them: tea at four, crossword at four-thirty, the porch from five until the light failed. Today the schedule made a kind of cage around the deadline, and Sienna found it oddly steadying, the way the world kept its ordinary shape while her code refused to.

"Forty errors," Sienna said. "All the same error, which is somehow worse."

She scrolled to the first one. Her test file had a line that said assertEquals("Beloved", b.title) and the compiler complained it couldn't see title, that the field was private. She'd written private String title in her Book class herself, the way the assignment sheet told her to, without really pausing over what the word committed her to. Apparently it committed her to a lot. She tried a different line, tried to set b.title directly, and got the same complaint. She looked at the two files side by side, the test and the class, and began to understand what she'd built: a field marked private could be read or changed only by code inside the same class. Her test file was a different class. It lived outside the wall, knocking.

"So the wall is real," she said aloud.

"Wall?" Grandma settled into the chair across from her with the crossword and a pencil she refused to sharpen.

"Nothing. Talking to my program." But she kept turning it over, because she'd started the afternoon with two ideas that now refused to sit together. One was that private was a hassle, a rule from the assignment sheet designed to trip people up. The other, older one, came from Grandpa's old shed talk about how a well-made thing keeps its insides where you can't reach them, how you don't poke the wiring in a radio, you turn the knob. She'd half-listened back then. Now she introspected, as her English teacher would say, on which idea was actually hers, and found the second one had more weight. If anyone could scribble on the fields from anywhere, the class couldn't promise anything about its own contents. The wall wasn't a hassle. It was the promise.

The trouble was practical: her test still couldn't read anything. She stared at the assignment sheet again and found the phrase she'd skimmed past, getter methods, and then a line near the bottom: "your test should call public methods only." She'd been so sure the test was the important file that she'd treated the class like paperwork. She typed public String getTitle() into Book, returned the field, and changed her test line to assertEquals("Beloved", b.getTitle()). The red error there vanished. She added getters for author and pages, fixed each test line, and watched the errors fall from forty to eleven to three to none.

Grandpa came in from the porch at some point and read over her shoulder, which he did without apology. "Forty mistakes this morning," he said. "How many now?"

"Zero. It runs." She hit the test button and the little green bar filled, and she felt a ridiculous pride in it, a bar the width of her thumb.

"Runs correctly?"

"Runs and passes." She hesitated, because honesty seemed owed to the green bar. "Mostly I'm trusting it. I tested three things. There are probably ways it breaks that I haven't thought of, and I won't know which until they happen." It was a travesty to call a program finished just because a deadline said so, but it was also eleven fifteen, and she submitted anyway, watched the confirmation page load, and closed the laptop on a screen still showing the green.

Grandpa put a walnut half on the table in front of her like a medal. "So what did you build, exactly?"

"A class that keeps its own secrets," she said, "and decides what to tell."

Grandma looked up from the crossword. "I'd like to meet her."

Connor had two hours before the pharmacy closed and one night before he had to stand in front of a sophomore health class and explain things he was not entirely sure he understood himself. The peer education program had assigned him the unit on consent, contraception and testing, and Mr. Reyes had said, "You'll do fine, you just have to know it cold," which was exactly the problem. He did not know it cold. He knew it the way he knew the bus schedule, well enough to ride it, not well enough to drive.

He stood in aisle four with his phone out, comparing the shelf against his notes. Condoms were locked behind plastic, which meant he had to press a button and wait for someone to come unlock the case, and while he waited he practiced his first line under his breath. Consent is a yes you can give freely, and can take back. The words felt like someone else's coat. He had learned them in a training where the facilitator had tried to inculcate the idea through roleplay, and the roleplay had been awkward in a way that made the idea feel smaller than it was.

"You're the peer ed kid," said a voice behind him. Maya from his civics class was standing there in her work polo, name tag crooked, holding a clipboard. "Reyes sent me an email. You're presenting fourth period tomorrow, and I'm supposed to be your backup if you freeze."

"I'm not going to freeze."

"Okay." She did not look convinced. She glanced at the locked case, then at his notes. "Since you're here, can I ask you something? Off the record. Not as your backup."

A pharmacist came and unlocked the case without a word, and Connor bought a box he did not need, just so he would have something in his hands. In the parking lot Maya sat on the curb and told him, in a flat hurried voice, that she had an appointment at the clinic across town at eight tomorrow morning, before school, and that she had been reading about options all week and the reading only confused her more. "I have to decide there," she said. "They said decide at the appointment or wait a month for the next opening. And my mom works at the school, so waiting means her finding out before I do it."

"What are the options?"

"Pill, shot, implant, IUD thing. The nurse on the phone said something I wrote down." She pulled out her phone and showed him a photo of her own scribbled notes. Under implant and hormonal IUD she had written less than 1 in 100 a year, and next to the pill a number that was much worse, and then a question mark.

Connor looked at the question mark for a long moment. The training binder had a chart, he remembered, and he had skimmed it, but the numbers had slid past him because they were all just numbers. Now, sitting on a curb with someone who had to choose in sixteen hours, he saw what the chart had actually been saying. "Okay," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "The pill fails more not because it's weaker, but because it's a pill. You have to remember it every single day, and people are people. The implant and the hormonal IUD fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use. They just work, sitting there. It's not about the hormone being stronger. It's about not trusting memory."

Maya was writing this down. "So the smart choice is the one I don't have to think about."

"That's not a rule I can give you," Connor said. "That's the thing I keep running into with this whole presentation. I can tell you the numbers, and the numbers are real, I'm not doubting them. But which one is right for you depends on stuff I can't know. Needles. Your period. Whatever else." He rubbed the box of condoms with his thumb. "That's the part that made the training feel dishonest. They wanted me to hand out certainty."

"You could say that part," Maya said. "To the sophomores. The part where you don't know."

The light over the pharmacy door flickered on, that early melancholic blue of autumn evenings, and Maya stood and brushed off her jeans. She said she would text him after the appointment if he wanted to know how it went, and he said he did want that, genuinely, and then asked if she would still be his backup at fourth period. She said yes, but that if he froze she was going to do more than stand there, she was going to talk, and he told her that was the deal anyway.

That night he rewrote his outline on the back of a receipt. Under consent he wrote: it's about volition, a yes that is actually chosen, and you have to say what that means out loud even though it's uncomfortable. Under contraception he drew a crude copy of Maya's question mark. Under testing he wrote the clinic's address and the walk-in hours, because the nurse had given those to Maya too, and Maya had read them aloud to him like they were directions to somewhere ordinary. He practiced the whole thing once in his kitchen, to the refrigerator, and got through it without stopping.

At 7:52 the next morning his phone buzzed. It was a photo of a clinic waiting room, beige chairs and a fish tank, and beneath it Maya had typed: going in, tell the sophomores the truth. Connor put the phone in his pocket, picked up the box of condoms and the receipt and the marker he'd borrowed from his mother's drawer, and walked toward the school with the sun still low behind him and the outline already softening where his thumb had smudged the ink.

Sophie had claimed the corner table by the periodicals on Tuesday because it was farthest from the children's room, and by Thursday she had spread across it entirely: the case packet from Mr. Ruiz's constitutional law elective, two highlighters gone pale, and a legal pad ruled into two columns labeled FOR and AGAINST like she expected the arguments to fight each other without her.

"You're going to have to argue the school's side," Nadia said, dropping her backpack on the FOR column. "That's the whole assignment. Both sides. Mr. Ruiz wants you to lose to yourself on purpose."

"I know that. That's the problem." Sophie tapped the packet. Tinker v. Des Moines was settled, obviously, but the packet went further: a hypothetical extension where a student group had hung a banner reading CONDEMN THE COMPACT from a rail along the riverwalk, city-owned riparian land adjacent to school property, and the city had cut it down in the night. The mock court would hear arguments on whether the banner was school speech, public speech, or something in between, and Sophie had been assigned to argue both positions in sequence, an arrangement Mr. Ruiz called a dialectic, as though the two of her were supposed to arrive at a synthesis by Thursday.

Nadia, meanwhile, had a petition of her own, which was that Sophie write it. She had been trying to file a formal complaint against the vending machine in the student lounge for two weeks, on the grounds that it took her dollar and gave nothing back, and she believed Sophie's new legal powers could be turned to this purpose.

"You can't sue a vending machine," Sophie said.

"Students sue schools. Schools own vending machines. Interpolate."

"That's not what interpolate means. You can't interpolate a lawsuit."

"You're the lawyer." Nadia pulled the packet toward her and frowned at the fact sheet. "Okay, so. Your government. The president. If your congress decides they hate him, what happens?"

"Nothing, basically. He stays."

"For how long?"

"His term. The whole fixed term. He's elected separately from the legislature, so they can't get rid of him just for disagreeing with them." Sophie said it the way she'd say the date, and then heard herself saying it, because Nadia was already shaking her head.

"Where I'm from, prime minister, parliament, one election. They vote no confidence on a Tuesday, he's packing by Friday. Your president could be fighting with everyone and still sit there for years."

"Years," Sophie agreed, and something about the shape of that, a leader insulated from disagreement by design, made her look back at her two columns. The FOR column said the banner stayed because unpopular speech was the point of the First Amendment, the school's authority stopped where the riverbank began, and riparian land was public forum land by tradition. The AGAINST column said the school had sponsored the riverwalk cleanup, so the banner was school speech wearing a borrowed coat, and schools could discipline that. The columns were equally good. She had assumed that meant she hadn't worked hard enough.

A toddler escaped the children's room trailing a puppet fish, and the librarian, a large man named Gerald whom Sophie had watched shush a table of law students into submission, intercepted the boy with the gravity of a bailiff. The boy pointed the fish at Sophie's case packet and said, "Guilty," and was carried off.

"See, even the fish has a ruling," Nadia said.

Sophie laughed, then stopped laughing. Because the fish was right, in a way: somebody had to rule, and the ruling wouldn't come from the arguments agreeing with each other. In Nadia's system, the disagreement itself was the mechanism; losing confidence meant losing power. In Sophie's, the disagreement was weather. The president stood out in it. And maybe, she thought, that was actually the strongest version of the AGAINST column, not that the students deserved punishment but that the school, like a president, had to be able to hold an unpopular position for a fixed term without the argument of the moment dissolving it. She wrote that down, then wrote under it: but students are not presidents, and underlined it twice, and did not have an answer.

She worked until the lights dimmed for closing, then past it, interpolating Nadia's question into her closing statement for both sides, so that each argument ended by conceding what the other one proved. It felt less like winning and more like standing in the middle of a river with the water going both ways.

Friday, the mock court convened in the library's meeting room, because the classroom was being waxed. Gerald had been drafted as a justice and wore his shushing finger like a gavel. Sophie stood, arranged her notes, and began, "May it please the court," and got four sentences into the school's side, the side she had privately come to distrust, delivering it with a conviction that surprised her, before Mr. Ruiz leaned over to Gerald and whispered something. Gerald rapped the table.

"Ms. Okafor. The assignment sheet says you're arguing for the students first. You've prepared the rebuttal as the opener." A pause. "Which is against you, apparently. You argued it very well."

From the second row, Nadia raised her hand and said, "Your Honor, I'd like the record to show I predicted this."

The community theatre smelled of dust and burned coffee, and the stage was smaller than Aaron's bedroom, which he kept forgetting when he drew his blocking diagrams on graph paper. He had been given the one-act because nobody else wanted it, a forty-minute play about two brothers arguing over a dead father's watch, and he had spent two weeks drawing arrows that meant nothing once actual humans stood where the arrows pointed.

The trouble was Marcus. Marcus played the older brother with a kind of pugnacious energy that Aaron had first mistaken for talent and now recognized as a habit of charging across the stage whenever he forgot his lines, as if movement could stand in for memory. Every time Marcus crossed, Priya, who played the younger brother's wife and had the only quiet scene in the play, ended up with her back half-turned or her body swallowed behind Marcus's shoulder, invisible from the folding chairs that passed for an audience.

"You're blocking me out again," Priya said on the fourth night, not unkindly, which somehow made it worse.

"I'm acting," said Marcus.

"You're a wall," said Priya. "You're a wall that walks."

Aaron sat in the third row with his graph paper and tried to see the stage the way an audience would, as a flat picture rather than a room. He had read somewhere that theatre was a two-dimensional art pretending to be three-dimensional, and he hadn't understood it until now, watching Marcus erase Priya every time he moved. He rubbed out an arrow and drew another, and then, sitting very still, he drew a second, smaller arrow next to Priya's mark, a small adjustment rather than a new position. When Marcus crossed left, Priya needed to shift right, just slightly, to keep both of them in the picture.

"Okay," he said, standing. "Marcus, do your cross again. Priya, when he moves, you move too. Just a half step, opposite direction."

They ran it. Marcus swept left with the dead father's watch in his fist; Priya drifted right, unhurried, and the stage, which had been collapsing all week into a single stubborn column of one actor, opened into two visible people. From the folding chairs it looked almost intentional.

"There's a word for that," said Dolores, the volunteer stage manager, who was seventy and had been threading her way to the coffee pot. She paused by the fourth row. "Countering."

"Countering," Aaron repeated, and wrote it down.

Dolores went on to the coffee pot, and that was all she said about it, which Aaron appreciated more than he could have said. He worked the principle through the rest of the scene himself, calling out adjustments, wrong twice before he was right: once he moved Priya so far she faced the wall, once he moved her into the doorframe. By nine o'clock the cross and the counter ran clean, and Priya, who had privately seemed ready to quit on Tuesday, was smiling at Marcus as though he were a scene partner instead of an obstacle.

That night Aaron lay on his bed and composed a message to his older sister, Maya, who was doing her second year at a conservatory and would, he knew, mock him for the graph paper if he didn't get ahead of the mockery. "I used to think directing meant telling people where to stand," he typed, "like furniture arrangement. Tonight I learned it's more like that thing where you watch a flock of birds on a nature documentary and every bird is adjusting to every other bird, except the birds have lines and one of them keeps forgetting his. Also the word 'countering' is now the most important word in my life. A seventy-year-old woman told it to me and then walked away, which I think is how wisdom is supposed to arrive. I still don't know if I'm directing this play or just preventing disasters in sequence. Possibly those are the same job. Don't answer that." He sent it before he could edit it into something cooler, and Maya replied only with a bird emoji and the sentence "The disasters ARE the job," which he read three times and decided not to interpret.

Opening night was a Friday, and the audience was thirty-one people, four of whom were there for the free coffee. Aaron stood in the wings with his graph paper rolled in his fist like a bad idea he couldn't put down, because the play was no longer on the paper; it was out there, happening. Marcus did his big cross in the second scene, the one with the watch, and Priya countered him, a half step right, smooth as a bird adjusting on a wire, and from the wings Aaron could see both of their faces at once, lit and turned to the house. Something in him that had been clenched for two weeks let go.

Afterward, in the lobby with its folding tables and its plate of abandoned cookies, Marcus found him. Marcus, who had never once apologized for anything, who had once argued for fifteen minutes that a missed entrance was the lighting designer's fault, stood holding a paper cup and looking at his shoes.

"I watched the video Dolores took," Marcus said. "Of Tuesday's run. I couldn't see Priya at all and it was my fault. Every time." He looked up. "How do I fix it, the crossing thing? Do I cross less? Do I cross on her lines instead of mine?"

Aaron opened his mouth to answer and found he didn't have one yet. Cross less and the scene went flat; cross more and it was a chessboard with pieces nobody could see. There was some balance in there he hadn't found, and he suspected he wouldn't find it tonight, or maybe before the run ended, which was in six performances.

"Run it with me tomorrow," Aaron said. "You cross, I'll counter, and we'll see what it looks like from the house."

Marcus nodded, drained his coffee, and glanced at the cookie plate.

"Take the oat ones," Aaron said.

The kitchen table had been Samantha's since eight that morning, and by noon it was a landscape of highlighters, torn notebook pages, and her mother's anatomy textbook, borrowed without asking. Her placement exam was in two days. If she scored well, she'd skip the intro biology lecture and go straight into the second-semester course, which mattered only because it would free a slot for the poetry seminar she actually wanted. So she sat there, rehearsing the central dogma out loud, because the test had an oral component and she could not yet say the words in order without stumbling.

"DNA gets copied into RNA," she said to the room. "Transcription. Then the RNA gets read three letters at a time, and each three letters makes one amino acid, and the amino acids chain up into a protein. Translation."

"Who are you talking to?" Her brother Danny stood in the doorway with a peanut butter sandwich, thirteen and incorrigibly curious about anything that looked like suffering.

"Myself. Go away."

"You sound lugubrious," he said, which was their father's word, deployed whenever one of them moped. "Like a funeral for a science."

"It's not a funeral." But she was saying it wrong somehow, and she knew it. She could recite the steps and still not hold them together, the way you could know every word of a poem in a language you didn't speak. She flapped a hand at the chair opposite her. "Sit. Be an audience."

He sat, chewing, and she started over. "Okay. In the nucleus, an enzyme unzips the DNA, and it builds a messenger RNA strand off one template. That's transcription. The mRNA travels out to a ribosome, and transfer RNAs bring amino acids that match the codons, three bases at a time. The ribosome stitches them together." She paused. "That's it. That's translation."

"Okay," Danny said, in a tone that adjudicated nothing. "So why is it called the Krebs cycle?"

She blinked. "What?"

"Mom's book. That page you keep flipping past. It says Krebs cycle. Why does it have a guy's name on it if it's just, like, how cells work?"

Samantha turned the book toward herself. There it was, a wheel of reactions, citrate at the top, and she had been skipping it because the exam outline said it was covered in the second-semester course, the one she was trying to test into. She read the caption twice. "It says Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937," she said slowly. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it." She looked up. "Sixteen years later. He figured it out and then waited sixteen years."

"So why only Krebs? What about Johnson?"

The caption didn't say. Danny leaned over the book, leaving a smudge of peanut butter near the margin, and Samantha felt something shift, small and unwelcome. She had been treating the whole subject as a machine that had always existed, facts the way water exists, and now the machine had builders in it, and the builders had been people who got prizes or didn't, and one of them had apparently vanished from the name.

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe he died. Maybe he did less of it. Maybe it's unfair."

"You always say life's not fair like that's an answer."

"That's not an answer, it's a weather report." She pulled the book back and stared at the wheel again, and the question she'd been circling all morning came back with a different weight. She had wanted to memorize the mechanism. Now she wanted to tell it, actually tell it, the way you'd tell how something was found. "Okay. New version. Listen and tell me if you follow."

Danny nodded, sandwich suspended.

"Everything in you is built from instructions, and the instructions stay locked in the nucleus, like an original document you don't want smudged. So the cell copies the part it needs. Transcription makes the copy, and the copy is messenger RNA, and it goes out through a pore to a ribosome, which is basically a factory sitting in the cytoplasm. The ribosome reads the copy in threes. Translation. Each three-letter word calls for one amino acid, and the amino acids get linked in that order, and the order makes the protein, and the protein is hemoglobin or an enzyme or keratin, whatever the cell ordered." She stopped. "And the enzymes that do all of it, including the ones in that cycle on the page, they're proteins that were made the same way, by other instructions. It's all built out of itself."

Danny frowned. "So who built the first one?"

"I don't know that either." She heard her own surprise at how little it bothered her. For two days she had wanted certainty, clean steps, a mechanism she could recite like a train schedule. Now the honest version had a seam running through it, names and dates and gaps, and it felt truer in her mouth than the recitation had. She would learn the rest of the gaps in the second semester. That was, she realized, the whole reason to take it.

"So did I pass?" Danny asked. "As an audience?"

"You were terrible. You ate through the second half."

He grinned and closed the book on her finger, gently, and slid the whole thing toward his side of the table.

Isaac had taped the diagram to the refrigerator door so he would see it every time he went for water, which was often, because the kitchen was the only room in the house with decent light since his father had started sleeping through the afternoons. The diagram showed a long, wavering strand labeled mRNA and a lumpy shape sitting on it like a bead on a wire. He'd redrawn it twice. Both times the lumpy shape came out looking like a potato, and both times his sister Dara had laughed at it.

"You're going to fail," she said now, from the table, where she was ostensibly doing her own homework but mostly watching him.

"I'm not going to fail." He uncapped a marker and held it over the paper without writing anything. The placement exam was in nine days, the one that would let him skip the intro biology lecture his schedule couldn't hold, and the packet the college had mailed described transcription and translation in a prose so dense it read like a legal contract. He'd underlined a sentence about RNA polymerase and then un-underlined it, because underlining had started to feel like a ritual rather than understanding.

"Explain it to me, then," Dara said. She was fourteen and relentless. "You always say if you can explain something you actually know it."

He could feel the moment stretch. Their father's furlough had entered its eleventh week, and the house had gone quiet in a way that made any conversation sound louder than it was, so that even Dara's challenge seemed to hang in the air. He sat down across from her and pulled the diagram between them.

"Okay. First part, transcription. The cell copies a gene. DNA stays in the nucleus like a reference copy at a library, the kind you can't check out. The copy that travels is mRNA, messenger RNA." He tapped the wavering strand. "It carries the instructions out to where the protein gets built."

"That part I get. It's the second part that's garbage." She rotated the diagram toward herself, squinting at the potato. "What is this thing?"

He had written "ribosome" beneath it in small letters, and he looked at those letters and realized that although he had copied them faithfully, he had never once managed to say out loud what the ribosome did. In the packet it was a sentence he'd read maybe thirty times: something about movement, something about joining. He knew it moved along the mRNA, and he knew the words amino acid and peptide bond were in there somewhere, but when he tried to assemble them they scattered like beads dropped on a floor.

"Give me a second."

"Nine seconds," Dara said, and started counting.

He looked past her at the window, where their mother's wind chimes moved without sound. In his mind he tried to picture the potato, the strand, the small units waiting. His grandmother used to restring her broken necklaces at this table, and he could still see her hands, a saucer of loose amber beads beside her, her thumb pressing each one down onto the thread in order. She had a pattern laid out on a paper towel, little pencil marks, and she never looked up, just moved along the marks and pressed bead after bead onto the string until the necklace was whole.

"Stop counting." He took the marker and, on the back of the diagram, drew a thread with pencil marks on it and a thumb above the first mark. "It's like this. Somebody restringing a necklace. The paper towel with the pencil marks is the mRNA, the pattern. The beads are amino acids, the building blocks. The person threading, the thing doing the work, that's the ribosome, the potato." He drew a bead going onto the thread, then another. "It moves along the pattern, and as it goes, it joins the amino acids together with peptide bonds, one after another, building the whole protein chain." He looked up. "That's translation. That's the whole thing."

Dara studied the drawing, her mouth slightly open, and he understood that he had just performed the exact test he'd set himself, because she had known nothing an hour ago and now she was nodding.

"Wait," she said slowly. "So the protein is the necklace."

"The protein is the necklace."

She picked up the marker and added a clasp to the end of his thread. "Grandma would like that you used her beads."

He almost laughed, and then didn't, because the reason he needed to skip the intro lecture, the reason the schedule mattered at all, was the scholarship condition he hadn't told either of them about yet, the one requiring him to hold a campus job from the first week. He put the cap back on the marker.

"Nine days," Dara said.

"Nine days." He taped the necklace drawing to the refrigerator beside the potato, over the note from the plant about his father's insurance paperwork, and went to fill his glass again.

On Monday Mr. Okafor announced that the ten-minute plays would be staged Friday night in the black box theater, which gave Amelia four days to finish a draft, hear it read, and revise it. The assignment required a moment from her own life, and she had chosen the night last spring when her father sat in the parked car outside the driver's license office and told her he was moving to Phoenix in June. She had written seven pages over the weekend, working at the kitchen table until one in the morning, and she believed the script was finished.

Tuesday, Mr. Okafor collected the pages and assigned casts. A junior named Dante got the part of the father, and a quiet girl from her economics class, Priya, got the part of Amelia-as-character, called simply Girl. When Amelia asked what happened next, Dante said, "Table read tomorrow, right? Where we all sit and read the script out loud so we can hear how the dialogue sounds before we do any staging." Mr. Okafor nodded and said to bring pencils. Amelia said she didn't need to change anything, and Dante looked at her the way people look at a homeowner describing a house they have only seen from the street.

The table read was Wednesday, fourth period, in the drama room with its racks of costumes and its smell of dust and hairspray. Eleven students sat around a rectangle of folding tables pushed together. Amelia took the seat nearest the window so she could watch the parking lot instead of the readers. Priya's voice was smaller than she expected, and the first two pages went fine. Then Dante read the line Amelia had been proudest of, the one where the father says, "I have impugned my own integrity by staying silent this long," and the room went still in the wrong way. Nobody laughed. It was worse than laughing. A boy named Marcus looked down at his copy of the parking map he was supposed to hold as a prop and turned the page too early, twice.

Amelia kept her eyes on a gray sedan outside until Dante reached the end of the scene. Her father had never talked like that. Her father had said, "I should have told you before I signed the lease," and then he had apologized for the lease, not for himself, and she had understood in that moment that his apology was ductile, something she could bend into whatever shape she needed for the next three years if she wanted to. She had written the stiff sentence because the truth sounded too small, like a city ordinance posted on a chain-link fence, technically correct and unread.

"Can we stop," she said. Mr. Okafor lifted his hand and the readers stopped. "Page four," Amelia said. "Cross out the line about integrity. He just says he should have told her before he signed the lease." Dante asked whether that wasn't blaming the lease instead of himself, and Amelia said that was the point, that was exactly what he had done, and Dante wrote it in the margin. Priya asked whether the Girl character would let that pass, and Amelia said she had, out loud, she had said "okay" and turned up the radio, and the radio had been playing a song she still could not hear in grocery stores.

They read the last three pages. The smaller lines held better than the polished ones. When Priya said "okay" and Marcus, unprompted, made a small turning motion with his hand as if adjusting a volume knob, Amelia wrote volume knob in the margin and underlined it. Mr. Okafor said they had twenty minutes left and told each writer to take notes on what their ears had caught. Amelia wrote until her hand cramped. Some of the script was true and some of it was a better-shaped version of true, and she could not always tell from the page which was which. At the table she could hear the difference, though she could not have said what the difference was made of.

Thursday night she retyped the play in her room, cutting four lines and adding two. She left the ending where the Girl says "okay" and the lights go down on the radio playing. She did not add a scene where the Girl forgives him or a scene where she doesn't, because she had not decided, three years later, on Friday mornings when his number came up on her phone, whether the deciding was finished.

Friday at six, the black box theater filled with forty folding chairs. Priya sat on a wooden bench that was supposed to be the front seat of a car, and Marcus stood behind a music stand holding a boom box that was not plugged in. Dante sat in a chair beside the bench with his copy of the script on his knees. Amelia stood at the light board in the back. The house went dark and she pushed the slider up halfway, the way she had practiced, and Priya said the first line.

Thomas had until eight o'clock, which was when his mother would drive Marisol home and when, by unspoken agreement, the physics quiz would stop being something he could still prepare for. It was Tuesday evening in the backyard, the grass still giving off the smell of the rain that had come through at four, and the only light came from the kitchen window and a citronella candle his father insisted worked. Thomas had the textbook open on the dry part of the picnic table, a bag of tennis balls at his feet, and the strong suspicion that projectile motion was about to ruin his grade.

He was trying to expiate a semester of doing just enough, the homework copied half-understood, the labs passed off as group work. His father had used the word once, lightly, about his own year off after high school, and Thomas had looked it up and found it heavier than his father had made it sound, all that guilt worked off through effort. Anyway, tonight he was throwing tennis balls at the fence and writing down where they landed.

The rule he kept circling was that the horizontal and vertical motions didn't interfere. The ball went sideways at a constant rate, the way a puck on ice would, while at the same time it fell the way anything falls, faster and faster, and you solved them separately and only married the two answers at the end through time. It felt like a lie until he tested it. He tossed one ball gently and one hard, marked the landing spots with his heel in the soft ground by the fence, and found that both hit within a hand's width of the same moment, thud, thud, almost together. The hard-thrown one had simply gone farther before the ground caught it. He wrote it down, the pencil wet where the grass had brushed it.

Marisol arrived at six-thirty, cutting through the gate with her phone in her hand and a plastic binder under her arm. She also had a history outline due tomorrow, a five-paragraph thing on Iran as a theocracy, which she claimed she could write in her head while walking, and she said this in the slightly disaffected voice she had been using all spring, the one that said school was a performance she was tired of giving. But she sat down at the picnic table anyway, which Thomas took as the real signal. She was worried about the quiz too, though she'd never have said so plainly.

"Look at this," she said, tilting the phone at him. It was a photo she'd taken of her older brother's diagram from when he took the class, two parallel plates, one marked positive and one marked negative, with arrows drawn between them pointing from the negative plate toward the positive one. Her brother had gotten an A, she said, so the diagram had to be right. "I've been staring at it for an hour and I can't make it match the textbook."

Thomas squinted at it in the candlelight, then carried it closer to the kitchen window so he could see. He was supposed to know this; the quiz covered it after the projectile problems. He thought about the tennis balls, about how you had to ask what a thing would actually do rather than what a tidy picture suggested. There was a way to check the diagram that didn't depend on trusting anybody's arrows.

"Which way would a proton go?" he asked her. "If you dropped one in there."

Marisol looked at the plates. "Toward the negative plate. Protons are positive, and it's like the negatives are pulling it." She said it with confidence, then heard herself and frowned. "Wait. Is that right?"

Thomas found the passage in the textbook, but before he read it aloud he worked it through the way he'd learned to that evening, splitting the question the way he'd split the motion of the ball. "The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate," he said slowly, reading and checking it against the picture in his head, "and that's the direction a positive charge would be pushed." He looked up. "So the field is the direction a positive charge would be pushed. Your brother drew his arrows backwards."

Marisol took the phone back, looked at the diagram for a long moment, and then, instead of arguing, laughed one short syllable and tipped her head back at the sky. "He got an A," she said. "He got an A and his arrows are backwards."

"Maybe the teacher never checked the arrows," Thomas said. "Or maybe he copied it wrong."

She was already fixing it, redrawing the arrows on the screen with her finger, from the positive plate across to the negative one, and saying the fact back to herself under her breath, positive to negative, the way a proton gets pushed, so that it would be there in the morning. Thomas watched her and realized he had done the same thing with the tennis balls, said the rule aloud until it stopped being words and became something he could see in the air, an arc with two invisible stories running along it at once, one steady and one gathering speed.

They worked until his mother called that it was almost eight. Marisol gathered her binder, and at the gate she stopped, one hand on the latch. She said she'd write the theocracy paragraph in study hall, and then she looked back at the yard, at the heel marks Thomas had left near the fence, and said, "Throw one more. I want to see if they land together again."

Thomas picked up two tennis balls, weighed them, and threw the first one easy and the second one hard, both of them crossing the candlelight and dropping somewhere into the dark by the fence.

The museum's French Revolution wing smelled like dust and radiator heat, and Jordan had been standing in front of a diorama of the storming of the Bastille for ten minutes without writing anything. His essay was due Monday. Not a report on the Revolution, his teacher had said, but a historiographical essay: an essay about the historians, about how views of 1789 had shifted since 1800, and why. He had three pages of quotations from Carlyle and Aulard and Simon Schama, and no idea what any of it added up to.

He moved to a glass case holding a small printing press, the label explaining that pamphlets had spread revolutionary ideas faster than the authorities could suppress them. That was the kind of detail his paper was full of, and the kind his teacher kept crossing out. This is about events, not historians, she had written in the margin of his draft, in green ink. He needed perspectives, arguments, revisions. He needed, apparently, to care about who had told the story and what they wanted.

His grandfather had offered to pick him up at four, which gave Jordan two hours. He sat on a bench beneath a portrait of some deputy in a grandiose collar and opened his notebook. The early writers after 1800 had mostly mourned or celebrated, depending on which side their families had been on. Later, Marxists read the Revolution as a bourgeois seizure of power. Later still, revisionists questioned whether anything so tidy had happened at all. He wrote the sentences and they felt like inventory, a warehouse of opinions with no one inside them.

At four his grandfather was early, waiting in the lobby with his coat still buttoned. On the drive home he asked what Jordan had found, and Jordan admitted the problem: every historian seemed certain, and they all disagreed. His grandfather laughed and said that was the point, that he'd written a paper like that himself once, in 1960, his second year of college.

"You wrote about historians?" Jordan asked.

"About the Cold War. There was a book the year before, 1959, William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. Started the whole revisionist school." His grandfather changed lanes, unhurried. "Williams argued that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War."

Jordan stared at him. "An American blamed the United States?"

"That's what the book said."

"Was he right?"

His grandfather didn't answer for a long moment. "People argued about it for twenty years. Some of them still do."

When they got to the house, Jordan followed him inside, essay forgotten. The book itself was gone, sold in a move decades ago, but his grandfather remembered the fight it started in his seminar, how half the room thought Williams had committed treason against history and the other half thought he'd finally told the truth. Jordan sat at the kitchen table taking notes on a napkin. What struck him was not who was right. It was that Williams had looked at the same documents everyone else had, the same speeches and cables, and seen something different, and that the difference had lasted, had forced every historian after him to say where they stood.

That night he spread his sources across his desk. The Marxists had a framework, the revisionists had a corrective, the early memoirists had their wounds. He began a new draft arguing that each generation's account of the Revolution told him as much about the generation as about the Revolution, and that the honest move was not to pick a winner but to say plainly what each view revealed and concealed. He could see, dimly, where this left him: with an essay that ended in uncertainty. His teacher might call that a failure to conclude. He kept typing anyway.

At one in the morning his cursor sat blinking after the last sentence, which was about how the historiography had no ending, only revisions. He read it twice. Then he opened his phone and texted his grandfather: was there ever a book that settled it? He waited, watching the screen. The reply came as a photo, the napkin from the kitchen table, on which his grandfather had written a single word, underlined twice. Jordan leaned closer to make it out.

Liam had cleared the coffee table of his mother's catalogs and set out six folding chairs like a tiny theater, which meant the living room now smelled of popcorn because Dex had brought a bag and refused to eat it anywhere but the "audience." The assignment was a ten-minute play about a moment from their own lives, due Friday, and Liam had chosen the night his father missed his regional swim final because of a work call. He had written three drafts, and each one had a letter in the first scene, a letter his father left on the kitchen counter saying he'd be home late, a real letter, laminated in Liam's memory.

"Okay," he said, standing on the hearth like it was a stage. "Read-through. Priya, you're Dad. Dex, you're the letter."

"I'm a prop," Dex said, delighted. "I've always wanted to be a prop."

Priya held the pages at arm's length the way she held everything, as though the world were slightly suspicious of her. She read the first scene with surprising tenderness, and Dex performed the letter by waving it over his head, and by scene three the swim final had happened and the father had apologized and the lights, per Liam's stage directions, went "dim, like a pool at night."

Then Priya lowered her script. "The letter."

"What about the letter?"

"It shows up in scene one, big dramatic close-up, Dad practically setting it on fire with his eyes, and then it never comes back. Why is it there?"

Liam opened his mouth and closed it. He picked up Dex's popcorn and ate some, thinking. "It's realistic. Dads leave letters."

"It's a play," Priya said. "Nothing on a stage is just realistic. A table read isn't life, it's life with the boring parts cut out." She flipped back a page. "There's a principle for this, I think. Chekhov's gun. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play."

"Chekhov had guns," Dex said, waving the letter again. "You have stationery. That's the parochial version."

"That's not what parochial means," Priya said.

"It could mean small-town stationery."

"It couldn't."

Liam sat down on the hearth, letting the argument wash over him like lane water. The letter was real; that was the problem. His father really had left it, and in real life it really had mattered to nobody but him, a rectangle of paper that meant a broken promise to exactly one sixteen-year-old. In a play, though, Priya was right, it sat on the stage glowing like a flare, promising the audience a payoff that never arrived. Real life could afford unexploded bombs. Ten-minute plays could not. He held both ideas at once, the true thing and the useful thing, and they did not fit together neatly, and he suspected they weren't supposed to.

"So I cut it," he said slowly, "or I pay it off."

"Or," said Priya, "your character keeps it. Carries it into the final scene. Doesn't say anything about it. The audience does the math."

Dex pointed at her with the letter. "That's ominous. I love it."

From the kitchen doorway, unnoticed until now, Liam's father stood with his coat still on, keys in hand, home early for once. He had heard the last few minutes, apparently, because his face had that careful blankness he wore at school concerts. He watched Priya, standing there with her script, feeling the room's awkwardness arrive like weather.

"You gave me a letter?" he said to Liam. Not angry. Almost curious, the way a debilitated swim coach had once asked Liam why he'd flipped on the turn.

"It's a play, Dad. You're a character. He's not exactly you."

"I'm the guy who misses the meet."

"He's the guy who misses the meet," Liam said. "You're the guy who came home early on a Tuesday to watch a table read in his own living room. There's a difference, and I'm still figuring out how much of one."

His father took a folding chair, sixth row of a one-row house. "Then I'm audience. Do I have to eat the popcorn?"

"It's mandatory," Dex said, passing the bag.

Liam stood back on the hearth, script in hand, and looked at his father, at Priya with the answer already circling her like a shark, at the letter Dex was now folding into a paper airplane. Cut it, pay it off, or let it sit in his character's pocket through the final scene, weightless and enormous at once. He honestly did not know which was truer, and the not knowing felt less like failure than like the first honest line he'd written all week.

"From the top," he said. "Priya, you're Dad. Dex, you're the letter. Try to be a serious letter this time."

Dex sailed the paper airplane across the living room, and it landed, perfectly, in his father's lap.

The argument had been going since Tuesday, and Connor was losing it in his notebook. His aunt's dining room table was buried in photocopies of the Haggadah, a folded calendar from the synagogue, and two slices of pizza going cold, because his cousin Noa insisted that ancient rules earned their authority by surviving, and Connor, who had agreed to debate her at the youth program on Friday, insisted nothing survived on survival alone. The topic was whether the commandments about festival observance still bound people who lived by train schedules and term papers, and the rules of the debate required them to argue from the text itself, no modern commentary allowed, which meant Connor had spent three evenings reading Exodus like a lawyer reading a contract.

The complication arrived when he finally called the synagogue office to confirm the social hall for Friday night. "You booked it for the twenty-third," the secretary said, "but the Seder is the night of the twenty-second." Connor stared at his own handwriting on the reservation form, where he had circled the twenty-third because the calendar on his phone called the twenty-third the first day of the holiday. He thanked her, hung up, and sat very still while the pizza congealed.

"It's my fault," he said to Noa. "I read the date off the phone. It said the holiday starts on the twenty-third, so I booked that evening."

Noa tilted her head at him the way she did when she thought he was being slow on purpose. "The day begins at sundown," she said, and went back to her photocopies. Connor sat there doing the arithmetic in reverse. If a day began at sundown, then the evening that started the festival was the one before the day the phone named, and every plan he had made was off by a night. He thought about apologizing to the secretary, about the folding chairs, about how a person could be careful and still be wrong by exactly the length of one dusk.

He spent the afternoon on the phone. The hall was free on the correct evening, the folding chairs could be moved, the custodian would stay late if Connor brought him coffee, and the rabbi, who had signed off on the debate, said only, "I'm glad you called before printing the flyers," which was somehow worse than a lecture. When Connor finally sat down at the table again, Noa pushed a passage across to him without comment. It was the verse about the festival being kept on a specific evening, and beside it she had written, in her terrible handwriting, one question: starts or ends?

He understood what she was doing. If the text itself anchored the festival to an evening, then the calendar question was not a bureaucratic accident but the very hinge of their debate. A rule that could organize time this way, that could take a day apart and reassemble it starting from darkness, was either a fossil or evidence that the text thought about time more carefully than his phone did. He had planned to argue that such rules were beautiful and finished, museum pieces; now he found himself annotating his own notes with questions he could not answer. He worked until Aunt Ruth turned on the porch light for no reason he could determine, since it was barely five and the sky was the color of weak tea.

Ruth stood in the doorway drying her hands and watched the two of them bent over the table, her nephew's earlobe red the way it got when he was thinking hard, her daughter's pen moving in circles while she read. She had watched Connor all week treat the Haggadah like a chess problem, all cerebral, no skin in it, and she had wondered whether to say something. She had decided not to. Whatever the boy was looking for, being handed it would spoil it. But now he had moved the folding-chair order and the Exodus commentary into one pile, as though they belonged together, and he was muttering about whether the custodian took his coffee with sugar.

"Uncle Marco takes it with sugar," she said. "The custodian plays chess with him. Bring two cups."

"Two cups," Connor repeated, writing it down.

Noa looked up. "You're going to argue my side now, aren't you. I can see it on you."

"I'm going to argue that the text knows what it's doing with time," Connor said, "and that I still don't know if that obligates anybody. Both of those can be true. That's allowed."

"It's sloppy."

"It's honest. There's a difference, and it's not small." He said it with more force than he intended, and Noa, who won most arguments by waiting, actually set her pen down.

Ruth went back to the kitchen and took the brisket out to thaw, because whichever evening it was, they would need it, and she had lived long enough to prognosticate about appetites rather than arguments. Her own view of the old rules had shifted twice in her life, once toward them and once at an angle, and she had stopped believing that probity required picking a side permanently. Through the doorway she heard Noa say, "Fine. New topic for Friday. We debate whether a rule has to bind you to mean anything," and Connor say, "Deal, but I book the hall this time," and the scratch of two pens starting over.

Kaitlyn had been student-directing the one-act for eleven days, and the sofa had been in a different place for all of them. On Monday it sat stage left of the window frame. By Wednesday it had migrated four feet toward center, dragged there by Marcus during his big monologue, presumably because moving furniture felt like acting. She had said "hold your position" so many times the phrase had desensitized everyone, including her; it entered the room and dissolved, like a note played too often.

The play was hers in name only so far. Mrs. Okonkwo had signed the form, taken the club's disbursement paperwork to the main office, and otherwise stayed in the back row of the auditorium with her coffee, watching. "It's your room," she'd said on the first day, which Kaitlyn had initially heard as generosity and was beginning to hear as a verdict pending.

Her instinct was to leave the blocking loose. Her drama teacher last year, Mr. Farelli, had talked about letting actors discover movement from the inside out, and Kaitlyn had believed him, mostly. But Priya had a different education: two summers of community theater, where the director taped the floor and heaven help you if you wandered. "Some people need a map," Priya said now, stretching on the sofa in question. "Some people need a fence." Kaitlyn suspected the truth was less symmetrical than that, but she didn't say so, because Priya was also the one playing the sister who sat on the sofa for eleven of the play's fourteen minutes.

"Places," Kaitlyn called. "Top of scene two. Marcus, this time stay where I put you."

Marcus did not stay where she put him. He crossed to the sofa on his entrance, which was correct, but by the end of his monologue the sofa had traveled again, and Priya, who had been sitting on it, was suddenly four feet upstage of where her scene partner needed her to be. Devon, playing the brother, gamely pivoted to compensate, and the whole blocking collapsed like something tangential had been substituted for the actual scene. Kaitlyn stopped them. She stopped them again. The third time she didn't call anything at all; she just sat in the third row with her binder and listened to the pause where a line should have been.

From the stage, Devon could see her better than she thought. He watched her chew the end of her pen, cross something out, uncross it. She was eighteen days from festival and she looked like a person doing arithmetic with too few numbers. He had been in three shows at this school and directed by four kinds of director, and his private theory was that the good ones knew one big thing and the great ones knew two things that disagreed. He wasn't sure yet which kind was in the third row. Marcus, beside him, whispered, "She's going to make us run it again." Devon whispered back, "She's building up to something," and, unusually, he hoped he was right.

At the next rehearsal Kaitlyn came in with a roll of colored tape she had bought with her own money from the hardware store after the theater supply site wanted two weeks for shipping. She knelt on the stage during warmups and put a short strip where the sofa's front legs belonged, another at stage left where Priya entered, a third at Marcus's mark. Priya recognized it immediately and crouched beside her, delighted. "Spike tape," Priya said, running her thumb along the fluorescent orange. "It marks where furniture and actors go. Real directors use it for everything." Kaitlyn said, "Then we're real now," and Priya laughed in a way that suggested she had changed her mind about something and was not going to announce what.

But Kaitlyn did not tape everything. She left Marcus's cross open, one strip at the start and nothing after; and when he asked, she told him the sofa had a home now, and he could find his own way to it. She was not fully sure this hybrid worked. The fence people got fences and the map people got a map with blank sections, and there was a possibility she was just splitting the difference rather than choosing. She noted it in her binder under a question mark, next to a note that read "Marcus: does he want direction or permission," which she suspected was the same question about herself.

The run that Friday held together. The sofa stayed spiked; Priya hit her mark in the dark without looking; Marcus made his cross slowly, differently each time, and Devon stopped bracing for furniture and started listening. Mrs. Okonkwo, in the back row, said nothing at all, which Kaitlyn decided to take as the office stamp on the disbursement of her opinion. After notes, Priya gathered her bag and paused at the edge of the stage, looking down at the small orange geometry of the last three weeks.

"Leave the tape down over the weekend?" Priya asked. "In case the janitor doesn't get it."

Kaitlyn looked at the marks, at the one blank corridor where Marcus walked, and said, "No. Pull it up. We'll spike it fresh on Monday."

The sign outside city hall read Youth Assembly on Local and National Government, and beneath it, in smaller letters, Bring Your Position Papers. Nathan's position paper was two paragraphs long, which was one paragraph longer than his actual position. He had written it at eleven the night before, arguing that a president fixed for four years gave a country stability, a claim he had lifted from a columnist whose reasoning he could no longer remember. He followed the crowd of teenagers through the brass doors and up the marble stairs, where a woman with a clipboard handed him a lanyard and a room number and, unprompted, a granola bar, because she had noticed him checking his pockets for the breakfast he'd forgotten.

The room had been a council chamber once and still held its curved wooden desks, though the microphones at each seat were dead, vestigial, wired to nothing. Nathan found his assigned table near the window. Across from him sat a girl he recognized from the regional debate, Priya, who was already arranging her notes with the calm of someone who had finished early. Beside her, a younger boy in a school blazer was reading his own paper with visible dread. Priya slid her spare highlighter across the table to him without a word, and he took it like a rescue line.

The morning session was a structured debate on a motion Nathan had helped draft three weeks earlier: that a parliamentary system serves voters better than a presidential one. He had proposed it on a whim, assuming it would be easy to argue either side, and had spent the weeks since discovering that he believed both sides on alternating days. The moderator, a councilwoman with a hoarse voice and a thermos of tea she kept asking people to pass back and forth, gave them twenty minutes to prepare opening statements.

Priya went first for their side, parliamentary. She started with something Nathan hadn't heard before. "My aunt lives in Manchester," she said, leaning into the dead microphone out of habit, then abandoning it. "In 2022 the UK had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, and there was no general election the whole time, because the governing party changed its leader. My aunt texted me a photo of her calendar with all three names crossed off." She let that sit for a second. "So my question for the other side is what you do with that."

Nathan had been half listening while scanning his paper, and the sentence stopped him. Three prime ministers. He turned to the kid in the blazer, whose name tag said Theo, and asked whether that was right, whether a country could really swap leaders twice in a year without anyone voting. Theo nodded. "That's why I picked the presidential side," he said. "You at least know who you're getting until the term ends."

During the break, Nathan stood by the window with the granola bar and looked down at the plaza, where a crew was setting up folding chairs for some ceremony. He had spent three weeks treating the question like a scoreboard, one system winning and one losing, and the scoreboard approach had quietly atrophied his ability to notice what was actually being traded. Priya's aunt had watched three faces cycle past without casting a ballot. But Theo, who had looked genuinely frightened behind his highlighter, had a point too: a fixed term meant that when you lost, you at least knew exactly how long you'd lost for. Two different fears, and each system was a way of managing one of them.

When they reconvened, the moderator asked Nathan for the rebuttal. He pushed his prepared opening aside, which made a small tearing sound because the pages were still stapled, and spoke from the window-view version instead. "The other side will tell you that in a parliamentary system the party can ditch a leader you never got to vote on, and they're right, that happened, three times in one year in the UK with no election," he said. "But a presidential system has its own version of being stuck. You can't remove a president for being bad at the job, only for committing crimes, so a bad four years runs all four years. I don't think either side gets to claim voters are always in control. I think the real difference is whether you'd rather be able to fire the leader quickly and unpredictably, or rarely and predictably."

He paused, and to his surprise the room was quiet rather than bored. "I'll be honest," he said. "I don't know which of those I'd choose, and I've been switching all morning. But I know they're the actual choice, and every platitude about stability or democracy I was going to open with doesn't touch it."

The debate ran another hour. Theo, who turned out to speak better than he read, gave a closing for the presidential side that borrowed Nathan's framing and argued predictability mattered more when you were eighteen and trying to plan anything at all, and Nathan found himself nodding along to the case against his own side. When the assembly voted, the motion passed by four votes, thin enough that nobody treated it as settled. Priya gathered her notes and looked over at him.

"So which system do you actually want, after all that?" she asked.

"Ask me next week," Nathan said, and began pulling the staple out of his dead pages.

The sign taped to the double doors read MODEL GOVERNMENT DAY, ROOM 2B, and beneath it, in smaller letters, DELEGATES MUST PICK A SYSTEM BY 4:00. Victor read it twice, then pushed through into the echo of a municipal chamber that smelled of floor wax and old paper. Rows of folding chairs faced a dais where the mayor usually sat, though today the dais belonged to a graduate student with a clipboard and a megaphone she did not appear to need. Victor had signed up because his civics teacher had promised it would look good on applications, and because his father, who had grown up in a country where the parliament fell every eleven months, had said only, "Learn both, then tell me which one lets you sleep."

They drew assignments from a coffee tin. Victor pulled the card that said PRESIDENTIAL SYSTEM, DEFENSE, and a girl named Priya, from the junior college across town, pulled the card that said PARLIAMENTARY SYSTEM, DEFENSE. The graduate student explained the exercise in a voice that carried to the fire exits. Each side would design a country, write the rules for choosing and removing a head of government, and by four o'clock the whole room would vote on which constitution to adopt. Victor sat down at the long table with his team, four strangers shuffling index cards, and realized he had no argument beyond a vague loyalty to the system he had grown up under.

The parliamentary table worked fast. Priya stood, laid out their design in five minutes, and sat down. The parliament would elect the prime minister, she said, and the same parliament could withdraw its confidence and remove him, usually within days, without any trial, without any court. "The majority that makes him can unmake him," she said. "That is the whole idea." Around Victor's table someone muttered that it sounded like the prime minister worked on a leash, and someone else said the leash was the point, and Victor wrote both sentences down without deciding between them.

His own side argued for an hour about the removal rule. One boy, Khalil, wanted impeachment to require a simple majority of the legislature, so that a rogue president could be fired as easily as any other official. An older delegate, a gap-year student with a trenchant manner of speaking that flattened disagreement rather than inviting it, insisted that anything so easy would turn removal into a routine weapon and every president into a tenant. Victor, trying to referee, pulled out his phone and searched for the only removal case he half remembered from class, the one from 1868. He read the result, then read it again, and stood up without quite deciding to.

"In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote," Victor said. "Thirty-five senators voted to convict. That was one short of the two-thirds they needed." He let the room absorb it. "So the bar they set was high enough that a president everybody in that chamber apparently wanted gone survived anyway." Priya turned in her chair, and Khalil said what Victor had been thinking, which was that one vote deciding the fate of a president seemed like a terrible way to run a country. The gap-year student said it was the opposite, that a bar a single vote cannot clear was the only thing standing between them and a government that changes heads every season.

The graduate student called a recess, and Priya crossed the room to Victor's table. She did not gloat, which he had expected. Instead she asked him what he thought a president and a prime minister were actually for, and he found he could not answer quickly. They walked out into the corridor by the water fountain and argued in low voices, half as rivals and half as two people trying to get something right. She argued that her system emancipated the legislature from a leader it no longer trusted, that confidence was a living thing, withdrawn the moment it died. Victor argued back that a fixed term gave a leader room to act against the mood of the moment, that some decisions needed a horizon longer than the average quarrel. He heard himself defending a system he had never before bothered to defend, and he heard her conceding, quietly, that her prime ministers rarely had time to be anything but careful.

When the vote came at four, Victor did something neither table had proposed. He stood at the dais and offered a hybrid: a parliament elected by their new country, a prime minister who served at its confidence, and a directly chosen president with a fixed term who could be removed only by the two-thirds rule, the one that had saved Johnson and would probably save most presidents who deserved it too. "I am not sure the bar is at the right height," he said. "I only know that in 1868 it was one vote tall, and I would rather argue about that number every generation than pretend either system solves it." A delegate called out that he was an egoist, inventing a whole new constitution just to avoid losing, and Victor said maybe, but an egoist with two systems in his pocket was still better than a partisan with one.

The room voted. The hybrid lost, nineteen to fourteen, to Priya's clean parliamentary design, and she shook his hand with both of hers and told him the margin was smaller than she had predicted. Outside on the city hall steps, Victor called his father and gave the honest summary, that the parliamentary side had won, that he still could not say his side was wrong, and that the one thing he now knew for certain was a single Senate vote from a century and a half ago. His father listened all the way through, which he rarely did, and then said only, "So which one lets you sleep?" Victor looked back at the lit windows of Room 2B, where delegates were still stacking chairs, and said, "Ask me again after I've seen both break."

Grandpa's driveway sloped toward the lake road at an angle that made Dylan nervous every time he backed out, and today the cones were waiting for him. Five of them, salvaged from a road crew two summers ago, spaced to the length of Grandpa's Buick plus what Dylan had read was a car and a half. He had set them out himself at seven in the morning, before the heat, and now he stood at the curb while Grandpa lowered himself into the passenger seat with the slow ceremony of a man boarding a ship.

"You're going to memorize this driveway instead of learning to park," Grandpa said, adjusting the mirror he never adjusted while driving. "New lot today. By the post office."

Dylan drove them there with his hands at ten and two, and on the way he passed the orange signs for the bridge construction, the right lane closing in a mile. A line of cars had already gathered in the left lane, nose to tail, while the right lane sat open and empty. He signaled early and slid in behind a pickup, feeling righteous about it, and Grandpa said nothing at all, which was worse than being corrected.

At the post office lot he parallel parked eleven times. Twice he clipped a cone with his rear tire, once he ended two feet from the curb, and by the ninth attempt he had begun to feel the maneuver as something he could parametrize, distances and angles feeding into one another, wheel speed tied to the cone vanishing from the side mirror. It stopped being a sequence of memorized steps and became a single motion. He did not celebrate the good ones. He had learned, from seasons of cross country, that celebrating in practice was a form of attrition, each small satisfaction wearing down the edge he needed for the race itself.

On the drive back they hit the construction again, and this time the left-lane backup was longer, and the open right lane taunted him. His test was in nine days. He wanted, suddenly and badly, to understand what the examiner would think of a boy who sailed down the empty lane while everyone else waited in line like good citizens. It felt like cheating. It also felt like the only sane thing to do.

"Go," Grandpa said, before Dylan could ask.

So he went. He drove the full length of the empty lane, past the patient faces of drivers he could not look at, and at the cone where the lane died, a woman in a hatchback let him in with a small wave, and he took his turn, and the cars behind hers did the same, one and then another, teeth of a zipper. At the narrow bridge Grandpa turned the radio up for half a minute and then off again.

That night, in the guest room with its smell of cedar and old newspapers, Dylan looked it up on his phone with the window cracked to the lake air. Minnesota's Department of Transportation said the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, could cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. He read it twice. The state was telling him the thing that felt like cheating was the thing that worked, and he sat with the discomfort of that, because his mother had raised him on early merging as a species of courtesy, and he did not think she was wrong, exactly. Both lanes full to the end, everyone taking turns. Or everyone queueing early out of politeness, and the line stretching back past the county road. He could hold both ideas at once, but he could not make them agree, and he suspected the examiner might hold either one, depending on the examiner.

In the morning Grandpa was at the kitchen table with coffee and the crossword, and Dylan asked him which he had done yesterday, the polite thing or the right thing, and Grandpa filled in a word before answering.

"I merged late in 1988 and a man in a Grain Belt truck called me a name I won't repeat in this house." He turned the paper sideways, studying it. "He wasn't pithy about it, either. Took him a while."

"So which is it?"

"Ask the examiner," Grandpa said. "Or don't ask, and drive."
