On the ninth day, in St. Cloud, the examiner climbed in smelling of pencil shavings and hand sanitizer, and three blocks from the DMV they came upon a lane closure Dylan had not known about. He held the empty lane to the merge point, took his turn at the cones when a box truck let him in, and watched the examiner make a small mark on the clipboard without expression. Dylan kept his eyes forward, ten and two, waiting to find out which kind of man was sitting beside him.

"Turn left at the light," the examiner said. "Then we'll do your parking."

Sarah spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted the corners with her father's least favorite bricks, the crumbly ones he kept meaning to throw out. The map had come rolled in a cardboard tube from her cousin Theo, who was doing a semester at sea and had sent it with a note that read, in his terrible handwriting, "You like weather. This is weather's big sister." She didn't like weather, particularly. She liked knowing why things happened, which was different, and which nobody in her family seemed to understand.

Her little brother Wren wandered out with a popsicle and planted himself on the far bench, dripping orange onto the grass. "What's that," he said, in the tone of someone prepared to be unimpressed.

"Ocean currents," Sarah said. "There's a river of warm water that goes up the Atlantic, and it's the reason England isn't frozen like Canada, even though they're at the same latitude. Look, the lines with the arrows."

Wren leaned over the map, popsicle hovering dangerously. "That's it? It's just a map."

"It's not just a map," Sarah said. "It's an argument."

She had actually said that before she was sure it was true. Her geography teacher, Ms. Okoye, had assigned them each a question to answer for the class, and Sarah's was this: explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. It sounded easy until Sarah tried it, at which point she discovered she had two maps that appeared to disagree. The laminated one from school showed the Gulf Stream ending somewhere west of Britain, while Theo's map showed warm water continuing northeast in a branch labeled North Atlantic Current, curling up toward Norway and beyond. One of them, she had concluded grimly, was a liar.

Wren tapped a spot far in the north, past Norway, where the coast made a hook. "Why is this city in a circle? Did you draw that?"

"I didn't draw anything." Sarah leaned in. The city was Murmansk. Beside it, Theo had penciled something, and she had to tilt her head against the sun to read it. WARM ALL YEAR, ICE-FREE PORT, his note said, and then, less helpfully, GOOGLE IT, I'M OUT OF MINUTES.

"That can't be right," Sarah said. "It's above the Arctic Circle. Ports up there freeze in winter. Every port freezes up there."

"Maybe the map's wrong," Wren said, cheerful. "Maybe your cousin's a dissident. Like he disagrees with the map on principle."

"That's not what dissident means. A dissident is somebody who speaks out against a government, not somebody who's rude about arrows." She got her phone out and typed, shielding the screen from the glare. The first three results were about submarine bases, which she skipped, and the fourth said it plainly: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current. She read it twice, then a third time, mostly to enjoy the sensation of being wrong in an interesting way.

"It's real," she announced. "The ships can get there in January because the warm water keeps going. The school map just stops drawing it too early, like the ocean got bored."

"The ocean can't get bored," Wren said. "It's water."

"Water is extremely boring," Sarah agreed. "That's the whole problem with it."

They sat with that for a minute. Wren worked on his popsicle stick, and Sarah traced the warm line with her finger, from the Gulf of Mexico up past the Carolinas, across the Atlantic, northeast past Britain, up along Norway, all the way to that circled city in the dark latitudes where the sun barely bothered showing up in winter. It mesmerized her, the way a small warm thing could travel so far and still have something left to give. Though she was honest enough with herself to admit she wasn't sure she could say why the water stayed warm that long, and the websites she'd found used words like thermohaline circulation, which she refused to say out loud in case she got it wrong.

That evening she wrote to Theo, because he owed her a reply anyway and because Wren had suggested, with his dour eleven-year-old solemnity, that if she was going to lecture the class she should have her sources in order. Dear Theo, she wrote. Your map won the fight with my school map. Tell your professor the Murmansk fact did all the work. Also Wren thinks you're a dissident now, which you should consider a promotion. Then, because it was Theo, she added: I still don't get why the water doesn't cool off on the way. Nobody explains that part. If the ocean tells you, write back.

She read the letter over, decided it was fine, and left the map on the picnic table overnight, weighted down with the bricks, so the dew would soften the paper into the shape of the table. In the morning Wren came out first and drew a tiny ship with a flag near Murmansk, sailing through water that, on the map, was warm.

The physics hall on the second floor smelled like hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Addison had been standing at the capacitor exhibit for eleven minutes. Two brass plates faced each other across a gap the width of her palm, and a laminated card invited visitors to compute the electric field strength at the midpoint between them. Divide the voltage by the separation, the card said, in a tone that reminded her of a substitute teacher pretending the material was fun. What the card did not say was why anyone should care, and Addison had come to the museum that afternoon specifically to decide whether she cared.

She was here because of her brother's tutor, a man named Dr. Pemberton who charged forty dollars an hour and had told her parents that Addison "lacked the temperament for quantitative work." Her mother had repeated the phrase at dinner without irony, as though temperament were a thing you could be diagnosed with, like a peanut allergy. Addison had wanted, with a fierceness that slightly embarrassed her, to walk into her first physics exam in September and desiccate that sentence. Not refute it. Drain it of moisture entirely, so it crumbled.

"Excuse me," said a voice beside her. A boy about her age, lanyard from some robotics camp, was holding a clipboard and squinting at the brass plates. "Are you doing the midpoint problem? Because I got forty, and the card says check your answer against the dial, and the dial says forty, but I don't know if the dial is a measurement or if it's just, like, displaying what you're supposed to get."

Addison looked at the dial. The needle sat at a lazy forty. "If it were a real measurement," she said, "it would jitter. Needles always jitter. That thing hasn't moved since we started talking." She felt a small, unexpected satisfaction in saying it. Maybe the museum was full of charlatan dials, needles pretending to sense the world.

"I'm Marcus," the boy said. "My sister dragged me here and then abandoned me for the butterfly room."

"Addison." She copied her own work onto the corner of his clipboard, since she'd left her notebook in the locker. Half the voltage, divided by half the distance, which came out to the same forty as the full quotient, a coincidence she found elegant until she realized it couldn't possibly be a coincidence. She wrote a question mark next to it and moved on.

Two exhibits down, a demonstrator in a blue polo was resetting a machine that launched a steel marble horizontally off the edge of a table into a sandbox. A strip of tape on the floor marked the table's edge, and a prize basket sat beside a bucket sunk into the sand. "Predict the landing spot," the demonstrator announced, in the cadence of a person who had said it four hundred times. "Closest prediction wins a holographic pencil. Launch speed is on the sign. Time in the air, I'll tell you, because the light gates measure it: half a second."

Marcus went straight for the bucket, pacing out distances by eye, but Addison stood at the table's edge with her hands in her pockets. The marble left the launcher moving sideways, nothing pushed it sideways after that, nothing slowed it down, so the horizontal speed it started with was the horizontal speed it kept, all the way to the sand. The sign said six meters per second. If it traveled sideways at six for the entire time it was airborne, then the horizontal distance was simply that constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air. Six and a half of a half. Three meters. "Get your tape measure out of my bucket," she said, and Marcus stepped back.

She measured three meters from the tape line on the floor, at a right angle to the table's edge, and dropped the museum's wooden marker into the sand. The demonstrator raised an eyebrow at her, either at the marker or at the fact that she had measured from the edge line rather than the launcher, which sat two centimeters back. She moved the marker two centimeters. It seemed judicious.

The demonstrator loaded the marble, counted down with theatrical patience, and released. The marble left the rail, dropped in its smooth sideways-falling curve, and hit the sand with a sound like a small coin, four finger-widths from her marker. "Holographic pencil," the demonstrator said, and dropped it in her palm.

Marcus leaned over the sand, frowning at the marble's crater. "Half a second," he said. "That's all we needed after the time. One multiplication and you had the whole spot." He sounded slightly betrayed, as if the machine owed more difficulty than it had delivered.

"It needed the velocity too," Addison said. "And a right angle." But she was only half attending. She was looking back down the hall toward the brass plates, where a field of forty-something per something existed invisibly between two metal sheets, uniform and patient, and where a question mark sat beside her arithmetic on a borrowed clipboard. The voltage divided by distance gave the same answer as half over half; she didn't yet know whether that meant something or nothing. She turned the pencil over in her fingers and said, "Come on. We're going back to the plates, and this time I want to know why the dial doesn't jitter."

Elizabeth sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with a practice dummy between her knees and a condom in one hand, timing herself. The training manual for peer health educators said you had to be able to explain contraception in under three minutes without blushing, and so far her best was four minutes twelve seconds, a record that included one full sentence about dolphin biology she still could not account for.

"Is that a plastic pelvis?" her father asked from the doorway, holding the mail.

"It's a demonstration model, Dad. Don't be dour about it." She snapped the condom onto a wooden dowel with what she hoped was clinical authority. "Consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic. Those are my three topics. The whole ninth grade health fair is my three topics."

Her father set a pharmacy printout on the counter and did not leave, which was how she knew something was wrong. She stood, still holding the dowel, and looked at the paper. His blood pressure reading from the machine by the pharmacy counter, a number he read aloud twice, as if saying it again might make it smaller.

"I thought those machines were a scam," she said.

"So did I." He tapped the number. "Nurse at the counter said it was high."

What Elizabeth remembered, suddenly and vividly, was being eleven and trailing after her father at a county fair while he historicized every ride, explaining that the Gravitron had terrified children since 1983, that cotton candy predated the lightbulb, that the Ferris wheel was an engineering rebuttal to the Eiffel Tower. He had an aphorism for every occasion, most of them borrowed from her grandfather, all of them useless when the occasion was a number on a receipt. For once he had nothing to say, and neither, for a moment, did she.

Then she remembered the binder. She had read all four hundred pages of the training binder, mostly to avoid her chemistry homework, and somewhere past the diagrams there had been a page about blood pressure. She retrieved it from her backpack, flipped past a section she had annotated with the note "DO NOT MENTION DOLPHINS," and found it: a chapter on lifestyle basics for peer educators, because students asked about parents, not just about themselves.

"Okay," she said. "Listen. It says here regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people. Including people who already have hypertension." She looked up. "That's you. The already part."

"That's a grim way to put it."

"That's a medically accurate way to put it." She was already getting a notebook. "You walk to the pharmacy every day anyway. That's not brisk. You stop to talk to Mrs. Okafor about her cat for twenty minutes."

"The cat has opinions," her father said. "She expresses them."

"Then we go at night. After dinner. Both of us, brisk, most days. Which days?"

He had changed his mind about something, she could see it happening, some private verdict about the plastic pelvis and the dowel and his daughter's chosen vocation rearranging itself behind his face. "Monday through Friday," he said. "Saturday is for the cat."

"Deal." She wrote it down, and beneath the schedule, in her real handwriting, she added the three topics again. "But you have to be my practice audience. Consent, contraception, testing. Three minutes. I need to get it under three minutes."

Her father sat down at the table, folded his hands like a man braced for jury duty, and said, "Start with the testing. I want to know if you'll blush."

Elizabeth set the timer, took a breath, and began.

The air cannon at the science museum fired every ninety seconds, and Hayden had timed his whole afternoon around it. A yellow ball left the barrel at a speed the plaque promised was constant, and visitors dialed the launch angle themselves, then watched the ball clear a wall of plastic pegs or fail against it. He had failed six times in a row, which was the thing itself, because he was supposed to be good at this. In the physics notebook on his lap, angle after angle, his predictions were all wrong the same way.

"You're up," said Priya, leaning on the railing with her chin in her hand. She had come only because he'd promised her the planetarium after, and she was making her boredom as visible as weather. "What's the big deal? Point it and shoot."

"It's math," Hayden said. "That's the big deal." He showed her his page, where he had written the launch velocity split into pieces. He'd decided that the horizontal part was v sin θ and the vertical part was v cos θ, and he'd been building his predictions from there all afternoon. He dialed the angle down to almost flat, ten degrees, barely a slant off the ground. His notebook said the vertical component would be enormous, nearly the full speed, and so he told her, "Watch. Almost flat launch, and the ball's going to shoot almost straight up."

The cannon thumped. The ball skimmed out low and true, a hard little line, and dropped into the net long before it reached the peg wall. It had not gone up at all. Priya laughed, not unkindly, but the laugh was visceral to him anyway, a thing felt in the stomach rather than heard. He stared at the arc hanging in his memory and then at his own handwriting.

"Say that again," he said. "What I just said. Almost flat goes almost straight up." He said it aloud himself and heard how absurd it sounded against the actual flight of the ball. He flipped back a page. Earlier he had tried a steep angle, seventy degrees, and predicted the ball would race forward barely off the ground, when in fact it had gone high and come down nearly on top of the launcher. Both predictions were wrong in mirror image. The components had to be the other way around. He crossed out his equations and wrote them fresh: the horizontal component was v cos θ, the vertical v sin θ. Almost flat meant a tiny angle, and sine of a tiny angle was a tiny number, so the vertical push was small and the ball flew out level. Sine and cosine, each in its right place.

"Congratulations," Priya said. "You've discovered that things fall down."

But he wasn't done, because the wrong version had its own logic, a kind of bogus logos, and he wanted to understand how he'd believed it for three hours. He had wanted the components to be interchangeable, one clean rule instead of two, and wanting it had been enough. That was the uncomfortable part. He looked down the exhibit hall at the water table, the pendulum, the tesla coil behind its cage, and thought about how many of his certainties might be that kind of thing, tidy and reversed. He couldn't know. He noted it in the margin anyway, a small question mark he would carry into the school year.

He tried to interpolate between his two best data points, ten degrees and seventy, and picked forty as his guess for clearing the peg wall, whose height he had already paced off in sneaker lengths. He dialed forty, wrote the number down like a bet, and gripped the railing. Priya pulled her phone out to film it, which meant she had, without saying so, decided it was worth watching.

The cannon fired. The ball climbed, hung for a blink, and cleared the pegs by what looked like a hand's width, clipping the top row so they scattered like dropped coins before it rolled off the far side. Hayden checked his numbers against where it had landed, and they were close but not close enough, off by some length he couldn't name yet. Air, probably, or the sneaker-length wall, or something he didn't have a word for at all.

"Planetarium," Priya said, tucking her phone away. "You owe me stars."

"In a minute." He copied the new equations into the inside cover of the notebook where he couldn't lose them, then flipped the dial back to ten degrees and fed the machine another ball.

The chocolate came in slabs, and Audrey had promised truffles for Priya's going-away dinner by seven o'clock, which gave her four hours and a kitchen that still smelled of the morning's burnt toast. She set the double boiler over low heat and chopped the bar into pieces the size of buttons, because the video had said small pieces melt evenly, and because she wanted, for once, to follow a recipe exactly instead of improvising the way she did with everything else. Her mother's handwritten notes on tempering were pinned to the fridge: seed with unmelted chocolate, work between 88 and 90 degrees, test on marble. The notes were less a recipe than a set of instructions someone had tried to codify after years of doing it by feel, and Audrey suspected her mother had left out the part that mattered.

She had a second problem. The dinner required her grandmother's mole sauce, which her mother had frozen in a brick-shaped container a month ago, and the plan had been to move it from the freezer to the refrigerator this morning so it would thaw slowly overnight. Audrey had remembered at two in the afternoon, when the brick was still hard as a paving stone. She stood holding it now, cold biting through her fingers, and considered her options the way she considered most things, by talking to her brother, who was at the table doing nothing in particular.

"I forgot to move this into the fridge," she said. "Is it ruined?"

Dario looked up. "You can't just leave it on the counter to thaw. That's the one thing you can't do." He shrugged. "Fridge, cold water, microwave. Those are the safe ways. Cold water's fastest if you keep the water cold."

"You know this how?"

"Food safety unit, sophomore year. It was riveting." He went back to his phone, but he had said it plainly enough that she believed him. She filled the biggest bowl with cold water, plunged the sealed container in, and set it near the sink, deciding she would change the water when it lost its chill. It felt like a small competence, knowing that, and she filed it away next to the tempering notes as one more piece of kitchen law she had acquired secondhand.

The chocolate, meanwhile, was melting, and she watched it with the attention she usually saved for exams. It occurred to her that chocolate was almost suspiciously particular, that a food could have a personality, and she smiled at herself for half-suspecting it of something like sentience, of deciding whether to cooperate. The melted chocolate reached 115 degrees on the candy thermometer, and she pulled it off the heat and began dropping in the reserved seeds, the unmelted buttons, stirring until each one dissolved. The temperature fell. At 90 she smeared a streak on the back of a spoon and waited five seconds, and it set with a faint satin sheen, and she felt something in her chest loosen.

Then Dario opened the microwave to heat his coffee, and the fan roared, and the vibration traveled through the counter and into her bowl, and a bead of water slid down the side of the double boiler and landed in the chocolate. She saw it happen in slow motion, a single drop, and the mixture seized almost instantly into a stiff, grainy paste, like wet sand deciding to become concrete. She stood over it with her spatula useless in her hand.

"No," she said. "No, no."

"What?" Dario came over, still holding his coffee.

"One drop of water. It's ruined." She poked at the paste. "Forty minutes to melt, and it took one drop."

"You could start over. You have time?" He checked the clock, and she checked it too, and neither of them liked the answer. Sixty-two minutes until Priya arrived.

She could have cried, and instead she found herself thinking about the mole, sitting in its bowl of cold water, minding its own business, thawing safely while everything else went wrong. Two ways of thinking were tugging at her, and she let them argue while she scraped the seized chocolate back into the pan. One voice said follow the rules exactly, the temperature, the seed, the marble test, her mother's codified certainty. The other said her mother had never owned a candy thermometer and had tempered chocolate for thirty years with her fingertip and a marble slab, and that the rules were a map drawn after the territory. Neither voice was wrong. The problem was that a single drop of water could defeat both of them, and no recipe had warned her about the microwave fan.

She started over with the last bar in the house, and this time she moved the bowl to the far end of the counter, laid a towel under it, and told Dario he could heat his coffee on the stove like a person from an earlier century. While the chocolate melted she ran cold water into the mole's bowl, feeling the old water go tepid against her wrist, and the small ritual of it steadied her. She checked the thermometer less often this round and the streak test more, and when the streak set glossy in four seconds she did not quite trust it, so she did it again.

The doorbell rang at seven while she was still rolling the first truffles, her palms dusted with cocoa, and Priya came into the kitchen saying she could smell chocolate from the street. The mole, warmed through and glossy, sat in its pot on the stove, and the truffles on their tray caught the overhead light in a way that made them look almost lit from within. Audrey broke the test streak off the spoon and it snapped, cleanly, like a knuckle cracking.

"Snap," she said, and held out the piece.

The graph was printed on the last page of the folder Marcus's professor-to-be had mailed out, a jagged line climbing like a staircase from left to right, and Marcus had brought it to the lake because he didn't know where else to put it. He spread it flat on the picnic table and weighted the corners with two coolers and a tin mug. His cousin Dana sat across from him peeling an orange, unbothered, while their fathers took the canoe down to the water and argued, pleasantly, about who would steer.

"You're doing homework at a campsite," Dana said.

"Orientation packet. They want us to be able to explain it before we get there. To anyone. Like a test you give yourself." He turned the page toward her. "Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, every year since about 1958. See how it wiggles?"

"It wiggles and goes up."

"The wiggles are the seasons. Plants breathe it in during the northern summer, so it dips, then climbs again in winter. But every year the top of the wiggle is higher than the last one. That's the part that matters." He traced the line with his finger and stopped where it steepened, the last decades rising faster than the first, and he understood suddenly that the graph wasn't a picture of air, it was a picture of accumulation, of everything poured out and not yet taken back.

Dana pulled a segment of orange loose and pointed it at the page. "So explain the trapping part. My dad says the ocean handles it. He says the Gulf Stream moves more water than every river on earth put together."

Marcus had read that claim two nights ago in a library book with real gravitas, a thick oceanography text, and he had liked the number so much he'd copied it into the margin of his folder. "That part's true," he said. "About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream." He tried to picture it while he said it, 30 million of the milk crates stacked behind the school cafeteria, every second, through one strait, and failed, the way you fail to picture a billion of anything.

"So Dad's right."

"Not about what follows." He had gotten this wrong earlier in the week, in an email to a girl from his biology class, and she had sent back a correction so polite it stung. He'd spent an hour with the book after that. "Oceanographers have a unit for it. That flow is called 30 sverdrups," he said, and Dana repeated the word under her breath like a password. "It's named after some oceanographer guy. But the water moving doesn't mean the heat disappears. Greenhouse gases trap heat near the surface because of how their molecules absorb the radiation the earth sends back out. Shortwave light comes in fine. Infrared going out gets caught, partly, on the way through. The ocean can shuffle heat around, and does, enormous amounts of it, but shuffling isn't the same as getting rid of it."

Dana chewed on that along with her orange. Down at the shore their fathers had settled the steering question and were paddling out, the canoe sliding through the reeds where a heron stood with its neck folded, patient as punctuation.

"Then why do people say the ocean handles it?" Dana asked.

"Because it's easier to believe something big than something invisible." Marcus looked at the graph again, at the little sawtooth rising and rising, and thought about his uncle's certainty out there on the water, the way a man could love a lake his whole life and still trust that bigness meant forgiveness. He didn't think his explanation would change the man's mind, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't entirely understand why. He understood the mechanism. He could say it in plain sentences now, could draw the arrows, incoming and outgoing, in the dirt with a stick. What stayed uncertain was everything around the arrows, what people did with a fact once they had it.

The evening came on slowly. Their mothers called that dinner was close and the smoke from the fire drifted sideways, low and warm across the table, and Marcus noticed, in the way you notice things when a lesson has invigorated you, that the smoke hung beneath the canopy of branches instead of rising straight through, pooled and drifting, held a little by the leaves and the still air, and he almost said so and didn't, because it wasn't the same thing at all and he refused a bad comparison even when it was flattering to his side.

At the fire his uncle tore a foil packet open and steam rose and vanished. "Marcus," his uncle said, "Dana says you're going to be a scientist. Tell me the ocean's not going to rise up over Tampa."

"The ocean moves 30 sverdrups through the Florida Straits," Marcus said. "30 million cubic metres a second. I can't tell you what it's going to do."

His uncle laughed, surprised, and handed him a fork. "First honest answer I've gotten all year."

Dana caught Marcus's eye across the flames and raised her orange segment like a toast. The heron lifted off the reeds in the last light, unhurried, its great wings taking the whole slow air beneath them.

The chocolate had to reach exactly the right temperature, and Violet had already ruined it twice. She stood at the back of Marta's stall at the Saturday farmers' market, where the awning threw a stripe of shade across the folding table, and stirred the bowl of melted dark chocolate with a metal spatula. Marta had agreed to teach her because Violet had shown up four weekends in a row, buying a single bar each time and asking one careful question, until the questions became too specific to answer from the customer side of the table.

"Slower," Marta said. "You're beating air into it. Air is not your friend today." Violet slowed her wrist. The chocolate had come off the heat glossy and loose, and now, as it cooled in the bowl set over a pan of cool water, it thickened against the spatula with a resistance she could feel in her forearm. The trick, Marta kept saying, was temperature and patience: warm it, cool it, warm it again just slightly, so the cocoa butter set in the form that made chocolate shiny and hard, the form that snapped when you broke it instead of bending like an eraser. Tempering, it was called. Violet liked the word. It sounded like something you did to a horse or a sword, and only later did she learn you did it to chocolate.

The problem was that Violet had promised tempered chocolate to her roommate Devi by Sunday night. Devi's birthday. Violet had announced it two weeks ago with the confidence of someone who had watched three videos, and now the videos seemed like a fraud, because nothing in them mentioned how fast chocolate seized if you let even a drop of water into the bowl, or how the whole batch went dull and streaked if you missed the window by a degree. The first failure sat in a plastic container at home, a gray-bloomed slab that bent like a shoe sole. She had put it in the freezer, thinking cold would fix it, and had texted Devi a photo with the caption "saved it."

When Devi arrived at the market that afternoon, lugging a canvas bag of peaches, she picked up Violet's phone and looked at the photo again. "You know that didn't clean it," she said. "Freezing at minus eighteen Celsius stops bacteria from growing, but it doesn't kill most of them. So when it thaws, it can spoil again." Violet frowned at her. "It's chocolate. It's not leftovers." "You said you were going to eat the failures. You've been eating the failures." Devi set the phone down on the table, screen dark, and Violet realized she had been treating the freezer like a reset button, a way to pause her mistakes instead of dealing with them. It was the same instinct she'd had all summer, honestly: she had deferred her college deposit twice, told everyone she was just deciding carefully, and let the deadline drift toward her like weather.

"It's not pedantry," Devi said, reading her face. "You'd have eaten a thawed brick of old chocolate on Monday and blamed the temper." "The temper is already to blame," Violet said, and Marta laughed from the front of the stall where she was weighing out apricots for a woman in a sun hat.

Violet went back to the bowl. She had been thinking of tempering as a rule to memorize, the way her father had tried to inculcate rules in her all through high school, curfews and formulas and the correct order for writing thank-you notes, as if a person could be proofed against error in advance. But Marta taught differently. She pressed a dab of chocolate onto her own lip to test the warmth, and when Violet asked how she knew, Marta said, "I don't know. I feel it. Nine years of failing." The two ways of thinking sat side by side in Violet's head: the rule that said 31.5 degrees, and the feeling that said this, now, almost. Neither was enough alone. She thought of her deposit, still unsigned, and of Devi's incisive little lecture about the freezer, which had stung precisely because it was right: freezing a mistake didn't kill it. You had to take it back out and work it warm again.

"Test it," Marta said. Violet dipped the tip of a knife and touched a smear of chocolate to a piece of parchment, then waited, counting under her breath while customers moved along the row, buying tomatoes, arguing over eggs. Thirty seconds. A minute. The smear set. She pressed her thumbnail to the edge and it came away clean, no smudge, and when she tilted the parchment in the light the small patch of chocolate shone like a lacquered button.

"That's it," Marta said. "That's tempered. Now you pour."

Violet poured the chocolate into the bar molds Marta kept in a crate under the table, tapping each one flat against the table's edge so the bubbles rose and popped. Devi leaned on the stall's post, eating a peach, juice running down her wrist. "For the record," Devi said, "I'm still eating whatever you give me, spoiled or not." "It won't be spoiled," Violet said. "Nothing's been frozen. Nothing's going to be frozen." Her voice was more certain than she felt; she had one afternoon, one batch, no guarantee the next bar would set the same way, and the college deposit was still sitting unsigned in her email, which was its own kind of unfrozen problem. But the chocolate in the molds was cooling evenly, losing its wet look gradually, the way Marta said it should.

When the bars came out, an hour later, Violet held one up to the sun coming in low between the stalls. She snapped it in half and it broke with a clean, high click, like a knuckle, and the broken faces were smooth and dark.

"Hear that?" Marta said.

Violet broke the second half again, just to hear it once more.

The article was about a city council proposal to raise the minimum wage, and Hailey had agreed, in a fit of confidence two weeks ago, to argue the opposing side entirely in Spanish for five minutes. Five minutes. In English she could talk for five minutes about almost anything, but Spanish arrived in her mouth in pieces, like furniture that had to be assembled each time before use. She spread the article across the library table and began circling words she could use: aumentar, empleo, salario. Then she hit the sentence "Según el sindicato, el aumento creará doscientos nuevos puestos" and stopped.

Según. She had skipped over that word a dozen times, reading it as filler, the way she skimmed past "like" in casual English. But something about it snagged her now. The sentence said the increase would create two hundred new jobs, and she wanted that claim, badly, because it supported her side. Only the sentence did not quite say it would happen. It said "según el sindicato", which was not quite the same thing at all.

She texted Marisol, whose mother was from Quito and who took the class mostly for an easy A. Hailey typed: does segun just mean "according to"? like according to who?

Marisol's reply came back fast: "yes! según = according to. spanish news writers use it all the time to show a claim comes from a source, not from the reporter. it's like a little flag on the sentence." Hailey read the message twice. A little flag. So the reporter was not promising two hundred jobs; the union was promising them, and the reporter was only holding the claim up, at arm's length, for everyone to see. She wondered how many times she had imputed certainty to articles that were being careful, how many facts she had absorbed that were really just someone's statement, faithfully carried.

The wondering changed her argument. She had planned to say the raise would cost jobs, a clean counterclaim, but now she saw that she could not stand behind a clean counterclaim either. Her other source, an editorial, was itself full of hedges: according to economists, according to a study, according to the chamber of commerce. Everyone was quoting everyone. She drafted a debate position on a napkin, abandoned it, and drafted again: the evidence was contested, the unions said one thing, the economists another, and maybe, she wrote in Spanish, teniendo dudas es razonable. Having doubts is reasonable. Her teacher would probably find that noncommittal, and part of Hailey worried she was right. A debate was supposed to be a fight. Standing in the middle saying "the sources disagree" felt like showing up to a duel and complimenting both pistols.

On Thursday the classroom smelled like the whiteboard marker Mr. Okafor refused to replace. He called her name third. She stood, and the opening she had rehearsed dissolved, and what came out instead was clumsy but hers: "Mi posición es complicada, pero voy a intentar explicarla." The class laughed a little, not unkindly. She laid out the proposal. She quoted the union's claim, and then she said, carefully, "pero la periodista escribe 'según el sindicato'. No es un hecho. Es una declaración." A boy near the window, Danny, who usually slept through these debates, looked up at that. When her five minutes ran out and Mr. Okafor invited a rebuttal, Danny raised his hand and argued, in serviceable Spanish, that doubting everything was its own kind of dodge, that someone had to decide. It was aimed at her and it was a fair hit.

She got the rebuttal slot and stood again, palms damp. She could feel the pull toward pretending certainty, toward grabbing the union's two hundred jobs or the economists' losses and wielding whichever one won the room. Instead she said, "Danny tiene razón que debemos decidir. Pero quiero decidir con los ojos abiertos." We must decide, yes, but with open eyes. The claim was the union's, the losses were the economists', the reporter's job was carrying both, and hers, she said, was choosing among them anyway, knowing they were claims. She finished eleven seconds early and stood there in the silence, unsure whether she had argued or merely described.

Afterward Marisol caught her at the door. "You argued doubts and still took a side. That's harder than either thing alone."

"I don't know if I won," Hailey said.

Mr. Okafor was writing something at his desk, and when he looked up, his pen still hovering over the grade book, he said, "Come look at this rubric line. I'm not sure what to give you for 'position.'"

The practical exam was Thursday, and Sophie had until five o'clock, or until Mr. Bell decided his saturnine patience had run out, to prove she understood the whole sequence. He had written one question on the board in his cramped hand: How does a gene become a protein? She was supposed to demonstrate with the plastic base pairs and the laminated diagrams, talking the whole time, as if to a student who knew nothing.

Her cousin Daisy sat on the far stool with her boots swinging. Daisy was nine, up from the farm for the week because her mother was at a conference, and she had followed Sophie to school the way she followed the border collie, out of habit and lack of alternatives. Sophie's aunt had said, "She'll be quiet, she's good at quiet," which was true, and also beside the point, because Daisy was not quiet when something interested her.

Sophie began as she had practiced: the gene, the copy, the protein. Mr. Bell had given them a heuristic in September, a recipe to follow, and she had followed it straight into a fifty-eight on the practice test. The score was still folded in her pocket. She had not shown it to anyone, not even Marcus, who had offered her his notes with a generosity that felt, in Mr. Bell's fluorescent room, slightly like a performance. Marcus wanted the single seat on the regional team, and he had been telling anyone who would listen that he'd already booked the hotel.

"So the DNA goes out to the factory part," Sophie said, moving the blue plastic strand across the table, "and the factory reads it and builds the protein."

Daisy frowned. "Out of the middle part?"

"The nucleus. Yes."

"Isn't that the important part? The only one?" Daisy had spent the summer watching her father refuse to take the good tractor onto the wet field, taking the old one instead, and she had a farm girl's suspicion about risking the thing you could not replace. "If the book's the only copy, you don't take the book to the barn. You take a picture of the page."

The lab went quiet except for the tick of the cooling oven. Sophie looked at the blue strand in her hand, halfway across the table, in transit, exposed. On the practice test there had been a question she could not answer, question eleven, and she had assumed it was about the protein part, the factory, the part with all the vocabulary. She unfolded the score sheet now and looked at eleven again. It was not about the factory.

She pulled Mr. Bell's textbook toward her, the heavy one on the back shelf, and turned pages with her thumb. RNA polymerase, the passage said, and she read it twice, then set the book down between their stools. In transcription, the enzyme read one strand of the DNA and built a matching strand of messenger RNA, and the messenger RNA carried the gene's instructions out of the nucleus.

"RNA polymerase," Sophie said aloud, mostly to fix it. "It reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. That's the copy. That's what goes out."

"So you were wrong," Daisy said.

"I was wrong." Sophie laughed, one short breath. She put the blue strand back inside the ring she had drawn on the butcher paper for the nucleus, and cut a strip of yellow paper with the scissors from the drawer. She wrote the matching letters on it, A where the DNA said T, and walked it across the table herself, holding it up like a note passed in class. "The DNA stays in. The messenger goes to the factory." She said it again to Daisy, slower, then once more fast, then asked Daisy to say it back, and Daisy did, with the vowels flattened by her farm cadence, and it held.

Mr. Bell looked up from his crossword. Marcus had come in twenty minutes ago and was at the other bench with his own models, and Sophie realized she had not once heard him talking through the sequence out loud, only moving pieces with his head down. He could not hear her now, or he was pretending not to. She thought about the missing page in his notes, page forty, which she had assumed he'd lent her without, and about how convenient it would be to blame him for question eleven, and how page forty was probably in his binder the whole time, and how the missing page did not exonerate her anyway, because she had never gone looking for it until a nine-year-old asked about a tractor.

Thursday she would stand at this table and talk for five minutes. She still did not know about the factory part, the ribosome, the folding, the parts where the real question lived. She slid the yellow strip back toward the nucleus to run it again.

Daisy said, "From the top," and pointed at the blue strand with her chin.

The swings at Miller Park had been Laura's thinking spot since sixth grade, and tonight she had brought the whole problem with her: Priya, a copy of Priya's practice interview on her phone, and forty-eight hours before they had to give each other feedback in front of the rest of the robotics team. The competition's scholarship interviews were on Saturday. Priya's hands were fine, her answers were fine, and she had looked, for the entire twenty minutes, at a point somewhere above the camera lens.

Laura sat on a swing, not swinging, and watched the video again. Priya's grandmother had coached her first, in the living room, with tea. Look down when the interviewer speaks, she had said, glancing away herself to demonstrate; steady staring at an elder is disrespectful, it makes a conversation into an interrogation. Two days later Priya's Aunt Meena, who did hiring at a logistics firm, had said nearly the opposite: hold eye contact, look interested, look confident, because in a North American interview the candidate who keeps looking away reads as nervous or, worse, as having something to hide. Priya had tried to satisfy both and satisfied neither, and now the video existed.

Laura's own problem was narrower and somehow harder. Last year, when Marcus had crashed the robot into the field wall in the final round, she had said only, it's fine, don't worry about it, and Marcus had gone on believing his turning code was fine, and it was not. She had learned that kindness without truth was just delay. But she had also watched their old captain deliver brutal, precise critiques that ionized the team, splitting everyone into factions over whether he was right, a sectarian little war about feedback style that had ended with two people quitting. She did not want to be either person. She wanted to be the third thing, and she did not yet know what it looked like.

Priya arrived at seven, sandals slapping, and dropped onto the swing beside her. "Tell me the truth," she said. "Everyone keeps saying I seemed shy. I'm not shy."

"I know." Laura turned the phone toward her. "Watch this part. When he asks about your design decisions. Your answer's good and then you look at the ceiling."

"That's my grandmother in my head," Priya said. "She drilled it into me. You don't stare at a senior person in our family, not for long. It's rude, like challenging them."

"And your aunt said the opposite?"

"My aunt said, look the interviewer dead in the eye the whole time, that's what confidence looks like here. She interviews people for a living. So which one of them is wrong?"

Laura pushed off the swing slightly, let the chains take her weight. "Neither," she said slowly, working it out as she said it. "They're describing two different places. Your grandmother's rule fits how she grew up; your aunt's rule fits a North American interview room. The problem isn't that one of them lied to you. It's that you tried to obey both at once, and your eyes ended up in the middle of nowhere."

Priya was quiet for a moment. A jogger passed behind them; somewhere near the slide a toddler was being persuaded, at length, that it was time for bed. "So Saturday I do it my aunt's way."

"That's the part I can't decide for you," Laura said. "Because there's more than one interview in your life coming, and more than one kind of room. Maybe the honest answer is: you learn to read the room, and you get to choose." She stopped, aware of how glib it sounded, like a peroration she hadn't earned. "What I can tell you for Saturday specifically is this. Look at the interviewer when you answer. Not a stare-down, not the ceiling. Just, when you finish a sentence, let your eyes land on theirs and stay there a second. Try it on me now."

Priya turned on the swing, chains twisting. "Hi, I'm Priya Nair, and the lifting mechanism was my subsystem." Her gaze held Laura's, wobbled once, and held again.

"Right there," Laura said. "That wobble. That's the whole note. Everything else in your interview is already good, I mean it, your answer about the torque tradeoff was better than anything I could do. The one thing to change is the eyes, and now you know exactly what to change." She heard how specific it was, how it named the thing instead of the person, and felt something settle that she couldn't have articulated: this was the third thing, or near it, and it had only taken saying it out loud to find out.

"On Monday," Priya said, "when we do Marcus's code review, you're talking first."

"Deal," said Laura, and jumped off the swing while it was still moving, just to feel the ground take her.

The clinic smelled like the inside of a binder, all paper and antiseptic, and Victor sat on the crinkling exam table with his sleeve rolled up, trying to look like someone who belonged in a body that was being inspected. He was here for his college physical, but also, according to the packet in his backpack, for something else: in September he would start training as a peer health educator, and before the first session he was supposed to be able to explain consent, contraception, and where a person could get tested for infections. His own doctor, Dr. Okafor, had agreed to let him practice on her, which was either a kindness or a trap.

The blood pressure cuff tightened around his arm like it had opinions. Dr. Okafor watched the numbers and frowned, just slightly, the way you frown at a typo in someone else's essay.

"That's high," she said. "Were you nervous coming in?"

"A little," Victor admitted. "Also my mom has hypertension. Congenital stuff runs in my family, or maybe it doesn't, I don't actually know what counts as inherited and what's just... habits."

She wrote something down. "Do you know what your pressure reads at home?"

"We don't have a cuff."

Dr. Okafor nodded and unwound the cuff from his arm. "There's a thing called white coat hypertension," she said. "Pressure reads high here in the clinic, often from nervousness, but it's normal at home. So before I conclude anything, I'd want to check it with home readings, or a monitor you wear all day. One number, one time, in one room, doesn't tell the story."

Victor looked at his own arm, at the pink crease the cuff had left. He had walked in here certain that one reading would instantiate his fate, that the machine would look into him and hand him his heredity like a sealed envelope. The idea that the building itself could be a variable, that the same body could say different things in different rooms, was strange and a little relieving. "So how would I get the monitor?" he asked, and she wrote him a referral and told him the pharmacy kept loaners, and he folded the paper into his packet, where it sat on top of the health educator checklist.

"That's what you wanted to practice?" she said, tapping the packet. "Go ahead. Pretend I'm seventeen and clueless."

He stumbled at first. Consent, he said, was about permission that could be taken back, that had to be clear and ongoing, not assumed from silence or from what happened yesterday. He made her repeat it back to him, which felt absurd with a woman who had checked his tonsils since he was four, but she played along, and the repetition was the point: he was supposed to make the other person say it, not just nod. With contraception he did better, laying out the options like islands in an archipelago, condoms and pills and IUDs, each with its own failure rates and its own logic, no single one the whole answer. She asked questions a real seventeen-year-old might ask, whether two methods were better than one, whether you could feel an IUD, and he answered, and where he didn't know he said so.

The testing part was where his voice thinned. He explained that the campus clinic did it, that it was often free or cheap, that results were confidential even from parents, that you could ask for a full panel and not just what they offered by default. He heard himself say the words and realized he had never said any of them out loud before, only read them in the training modules at midnight with his door shut, and that some part of him had planned to keep that silence going even while standing in front of a classroom teaching other people to break it.

"Better," Dr. Okafor said. "You'll get smoother. You should also know you're going to get it wrong sometimes, say something clumsy, have a kid laugh at you. That's the job."

"Great," Victor said. "The job sounds terrible."

"The job is the reason a kid who's too embarrassed to ask me might ask you." She looked at the referral slip, then at his arm again, and said that in the meantime he should take his own pressure at the drugstore machine, twice, on days he felt calm, and bring her the numbers. Not to decide anything yet. Just to see what his body said when nobody in a white coat was in the room.

In the parking lot he called his mom to say the physical was fine, mostly, probably, pending. He sat on the curb afterward with the packet open on his knees, the referral slip beside the checklist, and texted the friend who had dared him to apply for the training in the first place: guess I have to practice on you next. He pressed send before he could reread it, and watched the three dots appear.

Aaron had signed up for the playwrighting elective because it met during the last period on Fridays, which meant he could leave through the gym doors and avoid the parking lot entirely. This plan lasted exactly one week, until Ms. Rojas announced that the final project was a ten-minute play drawn from the writer's own life, and that each playwright would have to stage it with volunteer actors from the class. Aaron's life, as he understood it, contained no ten-minute moments. It contained, mostly, waiting rooms.

He wrote about the afternoon his father taught him to drive in the empty lot behind the landfill, which was the flattest place in town and smelled like an epicurean experiment gone wrong. In the draft, the father said things like "you're overthinking the wheel" and the son said nothing, and somehow that silence took up four pages. Priya read it over his shoulder during lunch and said it was good, which from Priya meant it was good, and then she volunteered to act in it, and dragged along Marcus, who had failed driver's ed twice and considered this thematically appropriate.

The first rehearsal happened in the choir room on Tuesday, because the drama teacher had the auditorium until four. Marcus played the father with his backpack still on, holding an imaginary steering wheel at chest height like a man praying to a very small god. Priya played Aaron, which Aaron had not expected to find unsettling and did. They read the landfill scene, and then they read it again, and by the third time they were standing in the same square meter of choir room, bumping elbows, both reaching for the same invisible door handle.

"You're on top of each other," Aaron said.

"That's the playwright's fault," Marcus said. "You gave us nowhere to go."

Priya, who had done a summer at the community theatre, looked up from the script. "In scene two of my one-act there last year, we kept colliding, and the director fixed it in one night. She drew the stage on the whiteboard and moved little magnets around, like war planning. It's called blocking. It's the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals."

"I'm the director," Aaron said, slowly, as if discovering a tumor.

"You are," said Priya. "Congratulations."

So on Wednesday he came in with the whiteboard markers he had stolen from the math wing and drew the landfill lot, more or less to scale, and put an X for the car and a circle for the passenger side and small arrows like migrating birds. He moved Priya's circle three feet stage left when she stood up to argue a point about momentum, and he discovered that if the father crossed behind the car while the son stayed put, the scene had a shape, a tension, two people orbiting a machine neither of them fully trusted. He had written the scene about driving. Staging it, he found he had written it about distance. He wasn't sure which one was truer, and he decided, for the moment, not to decide, just to draw the arrows.

Ms. Rojas circulated on Thursday, notebook against her chest like a shield, and watched two minutes of the run-through. "Who's blocking this?" she asked.

"I am," said Aaron.

"Hm," said Ms. Rovas, and wrote something, and left. Marcus insisted this was either a compliment or a death sentence, no third option.

The problem was the ending. In real life, the landfill afternoon had ended with his father getting out of the car, walking to the fence, and saying nothing for a while, and Aaron had never known what that silence meant, whether it was disappointment or pride or just a man who liked looking at garbage. In the play, he needed Priya to do something with her body that carried all of that, and every time he tried to place her, it felt like a lie, like he was deciding what his father had felt and pinning it to another person's shoulders. He tried her walking away. He tried her staying still. He tried, briefly, having her get back in the car and mime adjusting the mirror, which made Marcus laugh so hard he knocked over a music stand.

Friday came, and the class performed in the Little Theatre, ten minutes each, alphabetically, which put Aaron second to last. The drive scene worked. The garbage smell did not, but Priya's stillness did; the audience, thirty bored teenagers, went quiet in the way that meant something, and Aaron watched from the light booth, transfixed by his own life being held by other people. Priya stepped out of the car at the end, walked to the taped-off edge of the stage that stood for the fence, and stood there, and did not explain herself, and the lights came down on her back.

Afterward his father was in the lobby, holding the program folded into a small square, which he did when he was thinking.

"Who was the kid playing you?" his father asked.

"Priya."

"She walked away at the end." His father turned the square over once. "I remember I was going to say something, that day. Can't remember what now."

"You could tell me," Aaron said.

His father pocketed the program. "Write it into the next draft," he said. "You're the director, aren't you?"

Alexander's grandfather had led the Passover seder for forty-one years, and this year, three weeks before the holiday, he handed Alexander a worn Haggadah and said, "Your turn. All of it, from the candles to the last cup."

The kitchen where they stood smelled of his grandmother's simmering brisket, a smell that had presaged every family gathering Alexander could remember. He took the book. The spine gave way at the page with the Ten Plagues, where forty years of thumbs had pressed grape juice stains into the paper. "All of it," he said, not quite a question.

"You'll be at college next year," his grandfather said. "Somebody has to know how." He said it lightly, but Alexander understood it as a kind of countdown, a deadline with a date on it, and after that date nobody in that dormitory would need him to know anything.

The family WhatsApp group, meanwhile, had erupted into war over the seder's timing. His cousin Maya wanted it moved an hour earlier so she could take photos before sunset, and her brother Daniel, home from his first year at yeshiva, had posted a long message about how the seder couldn't begin after dark anyway, which was wrong, Alexander was fairly sure, and which Daniel defended with a confidence that made Alexander want to prove him careless rather than correct. Alexander scrolled and scrolled, and then, past midnight, he stopped scrolling and started searching instead.

He found it in a fragment of Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2. The Mishnah listed thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle. Thirty-nine. He read the list twice: sowing, ploughing, kindling, extinguishing, striking a hammer for a final blow. Somewhere online Daniel was arguing that posting a photo to the group counted, and Alexander typed out the Mishnah's line and pasted it into the chat, then deleted it, then typed something shorter: "Look up the list, then tell me which category a phone falls under." He put the phone face-down on his desk and did not entirely sleep.

At the family gathering that weekend, a pre-Passover dinner his aunt hosted so that everyone could argue in person instead of by text, Alexander was put at the head of the table to practice. His grandfather sat at his right, silent in a way that felt like an audience rather than a rest. Daniel sat across from him, arms folded, still holding his phone.

"So," Alexander said, lifting the cup of juice they were using as a stand-in, "we start with Kiddush." He got through it, voice steadier than he expected. When he reached the part where his grandfather always paused to ask the youngest child a question, he paused too, and his eight-year-old niece beat him to it: "Why is this night different?" She grinned, missing a tooth.

"Because we're practicing," Alexander said, and a ripple of laughter went down the table, which he decided to take as warmth rather than mockery. But when he reached the second cup, Daniel cleared his throat and said, "You skipped the paragraph about the sages in Bnei Brak."

"It's a rehearsal, Daniel."

"A rehearsal that leaves things out presages a performance that leaves things out." Daniel said it smugly, an epicure of other people's errors, tasting each one. Alexander's ears went hot. He almost said that at least the rabbis in Bnei Brak hadn't had a WhatsApp group, and then a better thought arrived, unbidden, and he let it stand.

"Maybe I skipped it because we're not at the seder yet," he said. "Or maybe I skipped it because I don't know everything yet. I looked up the thirty-nine categories last night, the ones the rabbis linked to the work of building the Tabernacle, because I wanted to know whether turning on my phone for the Haggadah app would be a problem." He turned to his grandfather. "Would it?"

His grandfather rubbed his jaw. "On the seder nights, which are festival nights, not the Sabbath itself, the rabbis had opinions." He smiled, withholding the opinions the way he had always withheld answers, handing over questions instead.

"Fine," Alexander said, "then before the seder I'll print everything I need, and I'll tell Maya when sunset is, and she can take her photos then. And I won't skip the sages in Bnei Brak, because you're right that skipping things becomes a habit." He said it without heat, and Daniel, who had visibly prepared a rebuttal to heat, uncrossed his arms.

They finished the rehearsal with the youngest child asking the Four Questions off-key and everyone singing anyway. Afterward, in the hallway, his grandfather pressed the Haggadah into his hands for good. "Three weeks," the old man said. "You'll want to know what you don't know by then."

Alexander carried the book out to the car under his arm, and in the driveway he stopped under the streetlight and, judicious about nothing at all, opened it to the page with the wine stains and began, quietly, to read aloud.

Mr. Okafor put the problem on the board before the bell finished ringing: two countries, two goods, one question. "Explain why both of them gain from trading," he said, "even if one country is better at making both. Presentations Friday. No reading off slides."

William copied the numbers into his notebook. Alpha could make twelve shirts or six computers in a day; Beta could make four shirts or four computers. He understood the arithmetic by Tuesday, could compute the opportunity costs, could see that Beta gave up less to make a computer and should therefore specialize in computers. But when his lab partner Dana asked him at lunch why anyone would trade when Alpha was simply better at everything, he opened his mouth and nothing came out. He had the rule without the reason, which felt like owning a key to a house he'd never seen.

"You're doing the face," Dana said, spearing a fry. "The face you do before you decide something's stupid."

"It's not stupid. I just can't say it in a sentence."

"Then say it in two."

He couldn't. That was the problem, and it had a deadline.

Thursday night his mother dropped him at his grandfather's apartment so she could take the car to her shift, and William spread his notes on the kitchen table while his grandfather made tea. He'd hoped for quiet. What he got was the news playing low, and his grandfather standing at the counter saying, "They finally did it, huh. Raised the rates. About time somebody took inflation seriously." He said it the way he said most things, flat, final, a verdict already rendered.

"Is that good?" William asked, mostly to be talking.

"Good? Inflation's a thief. You save thirty years and it melts your savings. They jacked the rates up like this once before, early eighties, and it broke inflation's back. Best thing that ever happened to the dollar."

William nodded and looked back at his numbers. Then his grandfather sat down across from him, slower than he used to, and turned his mug a quarter turn without drinking.

"I was on second shift at the plant then," he said. "They let go of sixty of us in one afternoon. Unemployment went over ten percent that year. Ten percent. Whole parking lot empty by Friday."

William put his pencil down. His grandfather was not a man who told stories for effect; he told them the way a carpenter sets a nail, once, squarely. The tea steamed between them. On the news, a man in a suit was still praising the rate hikes, and William heard both voices at once, the man on the television and the man at the table, and could not make them into one true thing.

"So it worked," William said carefully, "and it also cost jobs."

"It worked," his grandfather said. "And it cost jobs. Both of those are true, and don't let anybody tell you different."

William drove the idea home in the passenger seat, his mother's headlights carving the dark. He had been trying to parametrize the whole problem as one line, one equation where you solved for the answer. But the numbers on his page were like his grandfather's decade: Alpha gains, Beta gains, and inside each country somebody's parking lot goes empty. The shirts-and-computers version let you total the gains honestly, because the gains were real, both countries could end up with more of both goods than before. What the totals hid was distribution, and hiding it was not the same as lying about it, but it wasn't nothing, either.

Friday he stood up with one index card, on which he'd written nothing. He walked the class through Alpha and Beta, let Dana object that Alpha was better at everything, and then said, "Right, that's the whole point. Better at everything isn't the question. The question is better at what compared to what else you could be doing. Beta's worse at both, but it's less worse at computers. So Beta makes computers, Alpha makes shirts, they trade, and both end up ahead." He saw it land, a small rippling of heads, and felt a flash of exhilaration he tried not to show. Then, before sitting down, he added the part he'd decided he couldn't leave out. "Ahead in total. My grandfather lost his job in the early eighties when they raised rates to kill inflation, and unemployment went above ten percent, and the inflation died anyway. Both happened. I don't know how you weigh that. I'm not sure anybody does."

Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. "That's not on the test," he said. "But it's germane."

"Is it right, though?" Dana asked as they packed up.

William zipped his bag. "It's honest."

The gym smelled of floor wax and vinegar, which meant somebody two tables over had brought a baking soda volcano, the same one that had won the year Brayden was a freshman. He set his beakers in a row and checked the balance for the third time. Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole; he had written it on his palm in ballpoint before he found the index card, and now both records disagreed with each other by a decimal place, and the bag of salt on the scale was telling him nothing either way.

"You're the equilibrium kid," said Priya Raman, who had the next table and a poster about moss that looked like it had been designed by a connoisseur of Swiss typography. Her want was obvious and she didn't bother hiding it: the regional slot went to one project, and the judge with the lanyard had already paused at her moss for four full minutes.

"I'm the salt kid," Brayden said. "Equilibrium is just what the salt does." He had dissolved sodium chloride in hot water, cooled it, watched crystals come out, then warmed it again and watched them go back in. Le Chatelier's principle, temperature shifts, a reaction running one way and then the other like a tide that couldn't make up its mind. He had twelve trials, a graph, and one number he could not make lie down.

The problem was the number. His bag held 500 grams of table salt, and table salt, sodium chloride, had a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole. He had done the division on the bus: 8.55 moles, give or take, 8.5556 if you didn't round like a coward. But his first trial note said he'd weighed out one mole as 5.844 grams, a factor of ten off, and every concentration on his graph was built on that. The crystals hadn't cared; the salt dissolved the same whether he called it a mole or a tenth of one. Chemistry, it turned out, did not grade your arithmetic.

He was turning the index card over, as if the back might remonstrate with him, when the judge arrived. She was young, maybe a grad student, and she picked up his beaker of saturated solution and held it to the fluorescents like a gemologist, which he chose not to point out was exactly what he had done an hour ago in the bathroom mirror.

"So when you cool this," she said, "what happens?"

"Crystals precipitate. Heat it back up, they dissolve again. The equilibrium shifts with the temperature." He moved the beaker over the hot plate, and the little igneous-looking cubes at the bottom, sharp as basalt chips, began to lose their edges, one by one, the way the gym lost students as the afternoon announcements started. She watched the last crystal go under.

"And how much salt is in there, in moles?" she asked.

Here it was. He could show her the graph, which was beautiful, all smooth curves and confident error bars, and let the mole question slide past on a generality. Or he could tell her that a kid who had built twelve trials on a decimal error had gone back that morning, weighed exactly 58.44 grams, seen with his own hands how much a single mole was, and redone the concentrations in pencil on the train, arriving forty minutes before the doors opened with his tie still in his pocket.

"I got it wrong the first time," he said. "I used 5.844 grams for a mole. It's 58.44. Sodium chloride, whole bag's 500 grams, so about eight and a half moles. The trends are the same either way, the shifts are the same, but the concentrations were off by ten. I fixed them this morning. The pencil parts are the fixed parts."

Priya, pretending to adjust her moss, had gone very still. The judge turned the graph sideways, then right side up, and tapped the penciled column.

"Which is the more honest version," she said, "the one that was wrong confidently or the one that's right in pencil?"

Brayden looked at the beaker, where the warm solution sat clear again, holding all that salt invisibly, ready to give it back the moment things cooled. "The pencil one," he said. "Ink dries before you find out what you don't know."

She wrote something on her clipboard, and Priya drifted over with her moss poster held like a shield, and the hot plate ticked as it cooled.

The vial in Violet's hand was the color of a bruise, and when Mr. Okafor set it in the ice bath, it went the pink of bubblegum, which felt like an insult to something serious. The whole class was bent over the same demonstration, hot water on one side of the lab bench, ice on the other, and everyone was supposed to write down what the color change meant about heat being a product or a reactant. Violet wrote nothing. She was watching the thermometer instead, the way the line of alcohol crept down as though retreating from something.

"Your prediction," said Priya beside her, tapping Violet's blank worksheet. "Which way does it shift?"

"I don't know yet. That's the point of a prediction, isn't it? You're supposed to stake something."

Priya rolled her eyes, but Priya had already filled in her answer with the confidence of someone who had never once been wrong in a way that cost her. Violet had. Last spring she had told her father she would not move with the family to Phoenix in June, that she would stay with her aunt and finish senior year here, and he had said fine, and the fineness of it had sat in the house ever since like furniture nobody moved. She had predicted that the household would shift, absorb it, find a new arrangement. It had mostly just gotten colder in one room.

At the front of the room there was a laminated poster about the principle itself, and she had read it the first week without interest. Today she read it again. The principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. She said the name out loud, quietly, and Priya said, "Le Chatelier. He's the equilibrium guy," without looking up from her vial, and Violet thought that being remembered for one sentence spoken a hundred and forty years ago was either a triumph or a kind of erasure, depending on what else the man had wanted.

The demonstration was the concrete thing. Heat the solution and it went blue; chill it and it went pink; and the class was meant to conclude that the equilibrium shifted to oppose the change, pushing back toward the temperature you had taken away. Mr. Okafor wandered the rows asking questions without giving answers, which was his way of refusing to disenfranchise them of the discovery, though mostly it produced an ennui of blank stares. When he reached Violet's bench, she slid the vial back into the hot water and watched the purple climb through the pink like weather reversing.

"So," he said.

"So if you add heat, it consumes heat. If you take heat away, it makes heat. It leans against whatever you do to it."

"That's the principle."

"It's a bit smug," Violet said. "The system never actually wins. It just softens the loss."

He laughed, one syllable, and moved on, and Priya whispered that Violet thought everything was a metaphor for her home life, which wasn't fair because it was only sometimes true.

After school she took the long way past the science museum, because the new chemistry exhibit had a wall of panels and she had a free hour and no desire to go home to her aunt's subterranean apartment, its windows at sidewalk level showing nothing but shoes. On the historical wall, between Lavoisier and Curie, was the name again, and beneath it the sentence she already knew: the principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. A kid at the panel, maybe ten, was reading it aloud to his mother, stumbling on the surname, and Violet almost corrected his pronunciation and then didn't. He would say it his own way and it would still be the same sentence.

What she kept circling, standing there, was the disagreement between the two versions of the idea she had collected. Mr. Okafor's version was hopeful: systems resist, they compensate, they find their way partway back. Her version, the one she had tested against her father's spare bedroom and the phone calls that had gone from weekly to whenever, was harder: the system only ever absorbs a portion of the blow, and everyone calls that balance. Both were true of the same sentence. She could not make them agree, and she noticed she didn't especially want to, because the wanting was the interesting part.

She took out her phone and texted her father a photograph of the panel, the name and the date and nothing else. Then she stood at the window with her hands in her pockets, watching the shoes go by, pink and blue and brown in the late light, until the phone buzzed against her hip.

Brayden had promised his host brother, Tomás, that he would read the news article aloud twice, but by the second pass he was already speeding up, flattening the Spanish into a rhythm he could control. The kitchen in Tomás's apartment in Salamanca smelled of coffee and scorched milk, and the table between them held the newspaper, folded to a page about water restrictions. In three days Brayden had to stand in front of his summer language class and debate the issue for five minutes, entirely in Spanish, and so far he had managed forty seconds.

"Slower," Tomás said, sliding his own cup across the table so Brayden could finish the milk he had been ignoring. "You are running from the verbs."

"I'm not running. I'm pacing myself."

"You are sprinting toward the end so no one notices the middle." Tomás tapped the article. "Also, you said the restrictions are in Spain."

"They are in Spain. It's a Spanish newspaper."

Tomás leaned over and put his finger on the line above the first sentence, where three words sat alone before the text began: SANTIAGO, CHILE. "This," he said. "The dateline. Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence." He said it lightly, as if pointing out a step Brayden had tripped on, not a lecture. "So this was reported in Chile. About Chile."

Brayden read the line again, feeling the small collapse of a summary he had built his whole argument on. He had spent two evenings assembling notes about Spanish farmers and Spanish reservoirs, and now half of his evidence belonged to a country he had never given a thought to. He wanted to defend himself, to say the dateline was easy to miss, small print pretending to be nothing, but that excuse sounded like exactly the kind of thing his father would say at home when he drove past an exit he didn't want to take. Instead he pulled a clean page toward him and started over, writing the word Chile at the top.

He worked through the afternoon while Tomás studied for a chemistry exam, and when Tomás's grandmother came in from the market, Brayden stood up to take the heaviest bag from her arms before she asked. She thanked him in a rapid, affectionate Spanish he caught only pieces of, and she left him the apricots she had bought too many of, which he took as a sign that his accent had not yet offended anyone past forgiveness.

By evening he had a draft, and the draft had a problem he could not sprint past. The Chilean article argued that water should be priced higher so households would waste less, and it quoted a man in the desert north who already paid more than he could afford. At home in Ohio, Brayden's uncle farmed on wells that ran low every August, and his uncle's answer to everything was the free market, which Brayden had spent years rolling his eyes at. But the Chilean argument was not stupid. Higher prices did make people careful. And the man in the article was real, standing in his yard with a dry tap. Brayden wrote one paragraph for pricing and one against, and then sat looking at them, because the assignment required a position, not a display of indecision.

He read both paragraphs to Tomás after dinner, on the narrow balcony where the putative breeze was actually just warm air shifting, and Tomás listened with his eyes closed, which Brayden had learned meant concentration, not sleep. "Which one do you believe?" Tomás asked.

"I believe pricing works and it's unfair at the same time. I think I want to say the price should rise, but the money should go back to the poorest households so the burden lands somewhere else. Someone smarter than me probably has a reason that fails."

"That's fine," Tomás said. "Say that it might fail. Five minutes is not so long. You can be honest in five minutes."

The morning of the debate, Brayden's teacher, Señora Iriarte, called him third, and he walked to the front with his notes folded in his pocket, a paper he mostly did not intend to open.
