"I've been staring at it for ten minutes. Starting is generous." She had bracketed the first theme in pencil and then rubbed it out twice. The opening eight bars kept pulling at her. They ended, and yet they didn't; the sound arrived somewhere and stood there, leaning.

Theo dropped his bag and played the opening, and at the eighth bar he lifted his hands deliberately, so the sound stopped exactly there. The room held the absence of the next phrase like a held breath. "There," he said. "That's a half cadence. The phrase ends on the V chord, so it sounds unfinished. Your ear expects another phrase to follow." He said it as if reporting the weather, and Naomi wrote V in the margin, and then, underneath, unfinished.

"Play it again," she said, "but keep going into bar nine." He did, and the second phrase arrived like an answer that had been waiting to be asked. She felt something settle that she could not yet name, which annoyed her, because she preferred to name things before she trusted them. Her chemistry teacher liked to say you couldn't manage what you couldn't operationalize, and Naomi had carried the phrase around until it felt like a tool she could apply anywhere: break the thing into marks you could actually make. Pencil marks. Roman numerals. Brackets. If she could mark the form, she would own it.

But the marking fought her. The exposition was supposed to end at the repeat sign, and it did, only the second theme had already started dissolving into things that belonged, she thought, to the development, wobbles and dark turnings that arrived before their appointed hour. She drew the bracket, then extended it, then rubbed the extension out. "It's not clean," she said. "Mr. Okoye said it wouldn't be."

"So mark where you think it starts and argue from there." Theo was playing the passage again, quietly, his foot off the pedal so the notes came out dry. He ended at the eighth bar again, on purpose this time, and looked at her, and she understood he was showing her something a second time not to teach it but because he liked the waiting it made. Maybe that was the whole reason people loved this music, she thought, and maybe that was also why her mother had left the packing until the last week: some part of a person prefers the unresolved chord, the phrase that demands its answer, to the answer itself.

She wrote a small question mark next to the development, then softened it to a wavering line. Her position, if she had to give one, was that the form was real and the edges were real and the edges were also where the music lived, and she could hold the first half of that and only gesture at the second. Mr. Okoye came back at last, hair damp from the front-desk argument, and asked what they had found. Naomi turned the score toward him. "Exposition, development, recapitulation," she said, and put her pencil on the eighth bar, where the half cadence waited for whatever came next. "Start here."

Mya's one-act had a narrator problem, and she had known it since Tuesday. The black box theater smelled like dust and radiator paint, and her three actors sat on stacking chairs in the crepuscular light that leaked through the half-shuttered doors, waiting for her to tell them where to stand.

"Same question as before," Marcus said. He played her brother, sort of. "When I'm talking to the audience, where is everybody else? Frozen? Gone? What?"

"Let me try something," Mya said, though she did not have the something yet. She moved Priya, who played her mother, downstage left, and Marcus up to the lip of the stage, and she said, "Stay there, don't move," and then she just looked at it. The frozen tableau behind the speaking actor looked bad, like a wax museum. She scratched it in her notebook and told them to take five.

She had written the one-act about the year her father left, and she had defended it fiercely at auditions when Deshawn asked whether it was too close, whether she could be trusted to direct her own past. "I'm not on trial," she'd told him. "Nobody has to exculpate me." But privately she suspected he was right about one thing: the script kept trying to prove that everyone had behaved badly except her. That was not directing. That was lawyering.

In the library at lunch she found Deshawn at a table with a battered anthology open to The Glass Menagerie. "Is that for Okafor's class?" she asked, sitting down without waiting for an answer.

"Memorizing Tom's opening speech." He tapped the page. "You should read the intro. Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie a memory play. It was first staged in Chicago in 1944, and it's narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family." He said it lightly, the way he recited facts he liked, and went back to his lines.

Mya read the speech over his shoulder. Tom telling the audience the play is memory, that it is sentimental, not realistic, that in memory things don't move the way they should. She read it twice, and something in her chest went quiet, like a room when the refrigerator shuts off. She had been staging her past as if it were a news report, blocking every entrance and exit to match what actually happened, and it kept refusing to work because the actual events were not the point. The point was that she was the one remembering them, and memory is soft, guilty, and unfair, and you have to admit that out loud or the whole thing curdles into self-defense.

After school she taped a new mark on the floor, a chalk-white X far stage right. "Marcus, this is your island," she said. "When you step on it, the past goes dim. The lights on everyone else drop to half. You're the only one who's real, because you're the one telling it."

"So I'm Tom," Marcus said.

"You're me," Mya said, and Priya laughed before she could stop herself. "No, it's not a joke. I'm not acting in it, so I'm borrowing his body. When I step out, the memory is allowed to be wrong. You can look at your mother and love her and blame her in the same breath, and the audience doesn't get to decide which one wins." She ran the dinner scene that way, Marcus stepping off his island into the half-light, correcting his own memory mid-sentence, saying, "That's not how she said it. She said it quieter," and saying it again quieter, and Priya answering as if she hadn't heard him, locked inside the remembered moment. It was the first thing in three rehearsals that had made the hair on Mya's arms stand up.

There was still the ending, which she had not solved. Deshawn found her after rehearsal stacking chairs and asked how the memory thing was going, whether it had fixed everything. "It fixed the middle," she said. "The ending is still a hostage situation. I want my mother to be forgiven, and the scene wants her to be forgiven, but I don't know yet if those are the same thing, and I won't know until I stage it wrong at least twice." He asked what she'd do if it stayed wrong, and she said she'd stage the not-knowing, because that was also true, and he said that sounded like a dodge, and she said maybe, and wrote it in her notebook anyway.

On Friday the lights were better than the words. Priya stood in the half-dark holding an invisible dish, and Marcus stepped onto his island and told the empty seats, "I left too. Nobody talks about that part," and the shuttered doors leaked their last stripe of daylight across his shoes. Mya, sitting in the back row with her notebook open on her knees, underlined the line twice, then crossed out the ending she'd planned and left the space blank for Monday.

The screen door banged behind Chase before he remembered to close it softly, and his grandmother looked up from her crossword without complaint, as she always did. He set his laptop on the kitchen table beside the bowl of tomatoes she was sorting, one hand still warm from the walk from the bus stop, and opened the document he had been fighting all week. The assignment was due in nine days, for the freshman seminar he would not even start until September, a placement essay the college had mailed with unsettling confidence: apply a critical lens to a passage from a classic novel. He had chosen Jane Eyre, the chapter where Rochester's wedding is interrupted and Bertha Mason is dragged into the light, mostly because it was the one classic he had actually finished.

The trouble was that he had two lenses and only one essay. His annotated copy of the novel was bristling with pink tabs for the feminist reading, blue for the Marxist one, and the margins had become a small civil war. The pink notes said that Bertha existed only as a plot device, a woman whose entire ontology was reduced to a growl in an attic so that Jane could have a conscience and a plot. The blue notes said the whole marriage was an economy, that Rochester wanted to expropriate Jane's youth and legitimacy the way his family had expropriated Bertha's fortune thirty years before, and that the novel never once blushed at this.

"What's the face for?" his grandmother asked. She had a pencil behind her ear and another in her hand, and the morning light came through the lace curtain in a fine grid across the table.

"I wrote this sentence," Chase said. He turned the laptop toward her. "Rochester is an unreliable narrator, and the novel asks us to notice it."

She read it, tapping the pencil once against her teeth. "Where did you get that phrase, unreliable narrator?"

"Everyone says it. It's all over the internet. It's basically the first thing anyone learns about the book."

"Mm," she said, and slid the laptop back, and returned to seven across, which was some word for a kind of pigeon. Chase sat with the small cold feeling of having been found out without knowing for what. Her "mm" was not disapproval; it was the sound she made when something needed looking up.

He went looking himself. He typed the phrase into the library database with the tomatoes smelling sharp and green from the bowl, and the result surprised him: the term had not drifted down from ancient Greece or been coined by some Victorian man with side-whiskers. It was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth, in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction. Sixty-some years old, younger than his grandmother. He said it out loud before he could stop himself. "It's from 1961. Wayne C. Booth. The Rhetoric of Fiction."

"Wayne C. Booth coined it," his grandmother said, filling in her square. "The Rhetoric of Fiction, 1961." She said it the way she recited phone numbers, a fact held flat in the hand, and then she was quiet again, which was her way of letting him keep it.

The fact sat strangely with him. The phrase felt like a law of nature, and it was younger than the Formica table. It made him wonder what else in his pink-and-blue margins was younger than it pretended to be, and that thought folded itself into the larger problem, which was that he had been treating his two lenses as rivals when they might be witnesses to the same scene. If Jane told the story, and Jane was shaped by money she did not acknowledge and by a marriage market she thought she had transcended, then the unreliability was not a trick Rochester played. It was the water Jane swam in. The feminist reading asked who got to be a person in the story; the Marxist reading asked who got paid. Both of them, he saw now, were asking about the same wedding morning, from opposite ends of the same attic stairs.

He typed a new sentence, deleted it, typed it again. Rochester does not only conceal Bertha; the novel expropriates her, taking her fortune in its backstory and her humanity in its plot, so that Jane's moral victory can be purchased at a price Jane never counts. He read it over and hated and liked it at once, which he suspected was the correct condition for a first draft. What stayed uncertain was the part he could not wedge into either lens: whether Jane, a fiction shaped by a woman writing for money under a male pen name, was unreliable in the way Booth meant or in some other way the term did not yet cover. He left a note in the margin to think about it in September, when there would presumably be a seminar table and other people's faces to watch while he tried out the sentence aloud.

His grandmother rose to put water on for tea, and outside a mourning dove started up its low questioning note from the fence, and Chase closed the laptop on the pink and blue tabs both. "Nine across," she said. "Six letters, 'untrustworthy.'"

"Try unreliable," he said.

Isabelle had told herself, on the bus downtown, that she did not care whether Ms. Okafor liked her theme. This was not quite true, but she kept it in place the way you keep a bookmark in a page you mean to return to. She carried her ten sketchbooks stacked against her chest, and the gallery door was heavier than she expected, so that she entered the Saturday critique group slightly out of breath and slightly late.

The group met in the back room of the Meridian, where the walls held a touring print collection and the floor held eight folding chairs. Ms. Okafor, who ran the teen portfolio program, had one rule: bring a theme, not a pile. "A portfolio of ten pieces around one idea," she said each week, as if repeating it might make it true for all of them. Isabelle's idea was wounds. She had nine pieces about wounds and one about her grandmother's hands, and she had written an artist's statement claiming the hands were also a wound, which she privately suspected was a lie.

A boy named Theo, who was applying to the same schools, went first. He had brought a print of Kahlo's The Broken Column because he wanted to argue with it. "In it, nails pierce her face and body while tears run down her cheeks," he said, "yet she looks straight at the viewer. Every time I meet her eyes I want to apologize and look away." He turned to the room. "That's a flaw. The tears do the feeling for you, and then the stare dares you to react, and I don't like being dared."

Isabelle, who had spent three weeks staring at a reproduction of that painting, said nothing at first. She did not want to preempt him with her own reading, or perhaps she did, and the wanting was the problem. She smoothed the edge of her top sketchbook instead.

When her turn came, she laid out the nine wound pieces in a grid on the floor: the stitched apple, the cracked blue bowl, the self-portrait with the bandaged forearm that she'd told everyone was about her cousin, though it was about her. Ms. Okafor walked the grid slowly, hands behind her back, and Isabelle noticed that she walked around it twice, and that the second circuit was slower.

"In every piece," Ms. Okafor said, "the damage faces outward. You've made the viewer the one who flinches. But there's no stratum underneath, nothing that shows me what the wounding sits on top of. It's surface all the way down." She stopped at the tenth piece, the grandmother's hands, folded in lamplight. "And this one is the only honest thing here, which is probably why it doesn't fit."

Isabelle heard that as a compliment at first, the way you hear rain as restful until you remember the window is open. She looked at the hands again. Her grandmother had been obdurate about the move to the care home, refusing for months, gripping the doorframe of the house on Delancey while her son explained and explained. The drawing showed the hands folded, at peace, and Isabelle had drawn them that way because it was easier than drawing the doorframe.

She took the statement out of her bag and unfolded it. Ten pieces about wounds, it said, exploring how damage is carried. Theo leaned over from his chair. "But the hands aren't wounded," he said. "They're just old." He said it without malice, which was somehow worse, because it left her nothing to argue against.

"That's the problem," Isabelle said. She heard her own voice go flat. "The Kahlo you showed us. She's pierced and crying and she still looks straight out. I keep doing the opposite. I look at the wound and refuse to look at whoever's looking at me." She picked up the grandmother drawing and held it, then set it down again, in the center of the grid, where it broke the pattern entirely. "I think my theme isn't wounds. I don't know what it is yet. Maybe it's who's allowed to watch."

Ms. Okafor said nothing for a moment, which Isabelle chose to read as permission. She took out a pen, turned the statement over to its blank side, and at the top wrote the word watching. Underneath it she wrote a question she could not yet answer, and then, because the group was waiting and the afternoon light had moved across the prints on the wall, she began to read the nine pieces again, one by one, starting with the apple.

The kitchen thermometer, the cheap dial kind that had lived beside the stove since before Edouard could remember, read thirty-four degrees Celsius, and the chocolate refused to cooperate. He had the notebook open on the counter, the one with TEMPERING written on the first page in his own careful hand, and above that word a grid of temperatures he had copied from a video: melt to forty-five, cool to twenty-seven, bring back up to thirty-one and a half, hold, hold, hold. The problem was that his kitchen was already hotter than the chocolate was supposed to get at the end. He stirred the bowl over a pan of warm water and watched the surface sheen go dull at the edges, which the video had said meant the crystals were forming wrong, forming fat and soft instead of tight and glossy.

His brother Marcel was home from his first year of university, and Marcel's contribution to the afternoon was a paper bag of leftover noodles from lunch, sitting on the counter in the sun since noon. It was nearly two o'clock. Marcel lay on the floor of the living room with his phone above his face, fanning himself with a pizza flyer.

"Put those in the fridge," Edouard said.

"They're fine. Cold noodles are disgusting anyway, I'll microwave them at dinner."

"That's not how it works." Edouard wiped his hands on the towel and picked up his own phone, because he was the kind of person who checked. The page he found said that the USDA advised refrigerating cooked food within two hours. He read further, because two hours had almost passed and something in him wanted the noodles to be guilty. There was more: within one hour if the air temperature was above thirty-two degrees Celsius, ninety degrees Fahrenheit. He looked at the dial thermometer again. Thirty-four.

"It's over thirty-two in here," he said. "So it's not two hours for your noodles. It's one. And that hour's gone."

Marcel sat up. "You're telling me the heat makes the food go bad faster, so the deadline is shorter, and since it's already past the short deadline, my dinner is dead."

"That's what it says."

"This heat wave has desensitized me to everything," Marcel said, "including food safety and joy." But he got up, took the bag to the fridge, and stood in the open door for a while, letting the cold air wash over him, and Edouard didn't say anything about the electricity because he was doing the same thing with the bowl of chocolate, holding it near the fridge's breath.

The chocolate was for their mother. It was her birthday on Saturday, and she was supposed to arrive Friday night from Lyon, where she had been since spring, teaching a term of seminars that had somehow become two terms and then a summer contract. Edouard had decided in June that he would make her a box of tempered squares, dark with candied orange, milk with hazelnut, each one snapping clean like a promise about order. He had failed four times already. The first batch bloomed white and streaky. The second never set at all and had to be scraped off the parchment like mud. The third he had refrigerated in desperation, and the video's comment section, full of sycophants praising the chef's every syllable, had still been unanimous about that: fridge chocolate sweats, dulls, softens. Cold sets the outside before the inside and ruins the snap. Tempering had to happen at room temperature, in a room cooler than this one.

He went back to the bowl and began the work of the final stage, warming it in short passes over the water, stirring, testing a smear on his inner wrist the way the video showed, watching for the smear to set dull and dry within a minute instead of staying wet and dark. Marcel had drifted back in and was leaning against the fridge, watching him.

"You know you've been talking to yourself," Marcel said. "Like a whole narration. Now we stir. Now we check."

"It helps me keep the steps straight. The guy in the video does it."

"The guy in the video is performing for an algorithm. You're performing for chocolate."

"It's not a performance, it's precision. If the cocoa butter forms the right crystals, the chocolate sets shiny and it snaps when you break it. If it forms the wrong ones, it bends. It's just chemistry." He caught himself starting down a long explanation of crystal forms and stopped, because Marcel's eyes had already gone vague. "Sorry. That was tangential."

"I understood one word in three, but I liked hearing it," Marcel said. "You sound like her when she talks about her seminars. The same voice."

Edouard stirred and did not answer. The smear on his wrist set, dull and dry, faster than it ever had before, and something in his chest went light and careful at the same time. He poured the chocolate into the molds, tapping each one against the counter to release the air bubbles, and set them on the cool tile of the kitchen floor, away from the window, away from the fridge's warm exhaust at the back. He put the fan on them. Then his phone buzzed on the counter.

It was his mother. He read the message twice. Her Friday flight had been cancelled by the airline, the earliest rebooking was Monday, she was sorry, she was so sorry, could they celebrate on Monday instead, she would make it up to them. She had put a heart. Marcel read it over his shoulder and exhaled through his teeth.

The molds were setting anyway, because chocolate does not wait for airlines. In twenty minutes the first one had gone matte and firm at the edges, and Edouard turned it out onto the board, and the squares came loose whole, glossy as lacquer. He took one and snapped it in half, and the sound was exactly the sound from the video, a clean high crack, and the broken face was smooth and dark with no bloom at all. Five batches, and on the day it finally worked, it was three days early.

Marcel ate the other half of the square without asking, standing there with the cracked piece held between two fingers. "So they keep till Monday?" he said. "In this heat?"

Edouard looked at the board of shining squares, and at the dial thermometer, which still read thirty-four, and at the fridge where the noodles now sat, rescued by the one-hour rule, taking up the shelf. He got out the parchment and began wrapping the squares one by one.

"Help me," he said. "We'll put them on the bottom shelf, behind the yogurt, and we'll bring them back to room temperature slowly, before she sees them."

Parker had spent forty minutes on the last paragraph, because the last paragraph was where the hard words thinned out. The article was in Spanish, from a paper in Valdivia, and it concerned a flood, a river, a regional official, and something the dictionary kept translating as "turbid," which made no sense applied to water until he looked it up a second time and found it meant muddy, clouded, stirred full of sediment. The final paragraph was about a farmer who had lost forty sheep. It was the easiest part to read and he had started there, and when Sra. Ibarra called on him he had forty sheep and no idea what the article was actually about.

Their regular teacher was away on sabbatical that term, and Sra. Ibarra, who had come from the university to replace him, did not believe in translation exercises. "You summarize aloud," she said on the first day. "One minute. In Spanish. From memory." Parker had assumed this would be like the vocabulary quizzes he could pass by cramming on the bus. It was not. In the third week he still had not made it through a full article, and the oral summaries counted for most of his grade, and his mother had already paid the deposit for the spring exchange trip that the district's language grant underwrote, the trip everyone said would change how he thought about everything.

He went second that day, after Marisol Vega, who spoke Spanish at home and summarized the article as though reading it from the air. Parker stood, held his printout, and said that a farmer in the south of Chile had lost forty sheep in a flood. He said the river was turbid. He said the farmer's name might be don Pedro, or the name might have meant something else entirely.

Sra. Ibarra folded her hands. "And what happened in the article?"

He looked at the last paragraph, the sheep, the mud. "The flood," he said.

"Where did you start reading?"

"The end. The end was easier."

She nodded once, which was neither approval nor its opposite, and moved on to Deshawn, and Parker sat down with his ears burning and the article still mostly a locked room in front of him.

Marisol watched him from two seats over. She had noticed him at the start of the term, the way he attacked the page from the bottom like a climber who thought the summit was the easy part, and it had puzzled her, because in her house the newspaper came every morning and her father read the first paragraph of everything, sometimes only the first paragraph, and considered himself informed. She had assumed everyone knew this. But watching Parker, she understood that he did not, and that nobody was going to tell him, because Sra. Ibarra believed in finding things out and because the class was arranged in a quiet competition that made admitting confusion expensive. After the bell she caught him at the door, the printout still in his hand.

"You read it backwards," she said.

"I read the easy part first."

"News is written front-loaded," Marisol said. "It's called the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the less important details follow after, so the opening paragraph carries the core story." She tapped the top of his page. "You did the sheep first. The sheep are the least important thing in there. That's why they're at the end."

Parker looked at the first paragraph, which he had avoided for three weeks because it was dense with official titles and numbers and verbs in tenses he had not yet been taught. He sat down at the nearest desk, and Marisol, instead of leaving for lunch, sat across from him, and for twenty minutes they worked through it with her refusing to translate and him refusing to give up. The first paragraph, it turned out, was the whole story: a regional official had announced that the river's flood defenses had failed, that three towns were being evacuated, and that the blame lay with the previous administration's budget. The sheep were a closing detail, a human face stapled to the end.

The following week he summarized an article about a bus strike in Lima in fifty-three seconds, starting from the top, hitting the core of it in the first sentence, and Sra. Ibarra said "mejor," which from her was a standing ovation. Walking out, Parker found the English teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, in the hallway, who had been laid off by the same budget fights the article described and rehired only after the teachers' union threatened to strike in sympathy. Parker told him about the inverted pyramid, feeling like someone passing on a family secret. Mr. Okonkwo smiled and said that was exactly how he taught it in journalism, back when the school still had a newspaper, and then he paused. "Of course, my students always buried the news in their own articles anyway. Last line, every time. They figured the ending was where the important stuff went." He nodded toward the main office, where the principal's weekly bulletin had just been posted, its announcement of next year's program cuts printed in small type at the very bottom. "Apparently the administration figured the same."

The garage smelled of oil and cut grass, and the Toyota's hood was still warm from the afternoon. Sienna folded herself into the driver's seat, adjusted the mirror the way she'd practiced, and looked at her mother, who sat in the passenger side holding the clipboard from the driving school like a warrant.

"Cones again," her mother said. "The test is Saturday morning, so tonight we do the cones."

They had set up the two orange cones eleven feet apart behind the car, an approximation of the space between parked vehicles that Sienna had measured twice with a tape measure because she distrusted her own eyes. She backed up, turned the wheel, straightened, and clipped the second cone with a soft plastic knock.

"That's a fail," her mother said, not unkindly.

Sienna got out and reset the cone. Her mother had volunteered for this after the driving school charged eighty dollars an hour, a number that had ended the lessons after two sessions, and there was something strange about the arrangement, because her mother had not been on a highway in fifteen years. Sienna had begun to notice it the way you notice a door that is never opened: every route her mother drove looped around the interstate like water around a stone. When Sienna asked once, her mother said she preferred the scenery, and changed the subject to Sienna's grandmother's car, which needed selling.

The third attempt was clean. The car slid into the space with room on both sides, and Sienna sat with her hands on the wheel, breathing.

"There," her mother said. "Now the other thing."

"The merge."

"The merge."

They drove out past the hardware store to the on-ramp at Route 9, the one Sienna dreaded most, the one she'd failed at during her lesson because she had slowed down instead of speeding up. The ramp curved right and then straightened into a long added lane beside the traffic, and as they came around the curve Sienna's foot drifted toward the brake.

"Why are you slowing?" her mother asked.

"Because it's safer. Because everything out there is going so fast."

Her mother was quiet for a moment. "It's called the acceleration lane. That's what it's for."

Sienna looked down the lane, then at the headlights coming up behind them in the through lanes. She pressed the gas. The engine climbed, the speedometer needle swung up, and suddenly the cars in the right lane were not monsters overtaking her; they were moving alongside her, at nearly her own speed, and one of them changed lanes to the middle with a lazy flash of its signal, leaving her a gap the size of a room. She eased into it. Nobody braked. The highway carried them both.

"See," her mother said, and her voice was not quite steady.

They merged twice more before dark, and on the drive home Sienna began assembling the pieces, the way she did with anything cerebral, turning the problem until its faces lined up. Hesitation had felt like caution, the responsible choice, the thing her driving instructor had called defensive driving, but the on-ramp had taught her the opposite: caution could be the danger. Slowing down on the ramp had forced other people to make sudden decisions. Speed, used correctly, was a form of consideration. She wasn't sure the two ideas could be made into one rule. Maybe they stayed in tension, and you had to judge which one the moment wanted. She liked that it didn't resolve neatly. Most of what she'd been taught in school had resolved neatly, erudition handed over in tidy conclusions, and she was beginning to suspect the world outside the classroom did not traffic in tidy conclusions.

In the garage, under the single buzzing bulb, her mother sat on an overturned bucket and told her the twist of the evening, or maybe of the whole fifteen years: she had failed her own highway test at nineteen. Merged too slowly, caused the examiner to grab the wheel, and never gone back. "Your grandmother never knew. She thinks I've been driving Route 9 my whole life." She turned the clipboard over in her hands. "Tonight I watched you do the thing I couldn't, and I thought, if an eighteen-year-old can learn it in three tries, maybe the fear isn't a fact about the world. Maybe it's just a habit I never expiated for."

"You want to try it," Sienna said. "The merge."

"After your test. If you pass Saturday, you drive us to your grandmother's to sell her car, and on the way back, you sit in the passenger seat."

Sienna laughed and picked up the cones, stacking them by the lawnmower. "Deal. But you have to use the acceleration lane."

Her mother stood, took the keys, and jingled them once in her palm.

The assignment was due at eight the next morning, and Jaxon had written nothing but his name. On the kitchen table his laptop glowed with a passage from Great Expectations, the scene where Pip comes into his expectations and begins to be ashamed of Joe. Apply one critical lens of your choice, the prompt said, as if choosing were the easy part. His mother had gone to bed an hour ago, leaving him a plate of sliced pear covered in foil, and the house had gone quiet in the way that made every unread page louder.

He got up and went to the whiteboard he kept in the garage, the one he'd claimed for chemistry formulas last year and never cleaned. The marker was half dead; he pressed until the squeak turned into a line. At the top he wrote BOURGEOISIE and under it PROLETARIAT, then sat on an overturned milk crate and stared at the words, because he wasn't sure yet who went where.

Miss Havisham went at the top. She owned a brewery and a whole decaying estate, land and business both, and Pip's benefactor, whoever that turned out to be, sat beside her in his head. Then the trouble started. Joe was a blacksmith, but he owned his forge, or did the forge belong to someone else and Joe only worked it? Jaxon drew a question mark that looked like a hook. Estella he left hovering between columns, because she owned nothing at all and was herself, he thought, something owned.

A floorboard creaked behind him and his sister appeared in the doorway in her dressing gown, hair tied up, holding two mugs of tea. Naomi was home from her first term at college and had spent the evening Skyping someone in Lisbon, which had made her seem suddenly cosmopolitan, a person with an address book that crossed water. She handed him a mug without being asked, which he accepted without saying thank you properly, only tilting his head, and she seemed to understand that as thanks.

"You're still on that," she said. "It's midnight."

"It's due at eight. I'm sorting the characters." He pointed at the board. "Owners on the left, workers on the right. But Joe's in the middle."

Naomi came closer, steam rising off her mug. "What's your rule? What makes somebody an owner?"

"That's the part I keep losing," Jaxon admitted. He'd read the definition an hour ago and it had slid off him like water off the pear plate. He looked at the board instead, at Miss Havisham's name sitting alone up top, and tried it aloud. "The bourgeoisie owns the means of production, the factories and the land. The proletariat owns only its labour, and has to sell it for wages."

"Okay," Naomi said slowly, waiting, the way she did when she wanted him to go on rather than rescuing him, which he both appreciated and resented.

"So Joe," Jaxon said, and the crate creaked under him as he leaned forward. "If the forge is his, he's a small owner. But Orlick, who works for him, sells his labour for wages, so Orlick's the one on the right. And Magwitch in Australia, he ends up owning land and cattle, so he moves columns. He can buy Pip." He drew an arrow with his thumb smudging the ink. "That's why Pip's shame is stupid. Joe at the forge, the man Pip maligns in his own head, is closer to Magwitch's money than Pip will ever be by standing around in a borrowed suit."

Naomi laughed once, quietly, mindful of their mother sleeping down the hall. "And the feminist part?"

"That's what I was going to do first. Estella. She's raised to be given away, her whole self is somebody else's project. But when I look at her through this column thing, she's got no labour and no property either, she's not even allowed the worker's one thing. She's just, transferred." He put the marker down. "I think the two lenses overlap. I think that's my thesis. Or part of it."

"That's more than most of my seminar manages," Naomi said, and touched his shoulder once, briefly, before heading back inside. "Drink the tea before it goes cold."

Jaxon stayed on the crate. The thesis was half a thesis, honestly, and he could feel where it went soft, the places a teacher might press. He didn't know yet what to say about Pip himself, who seemed to want to be owned by the left column and never quite managed it. But he had the board, the names, the arrow. He took a photo of it on his phone, drank the tea in two long swallows, and carried the plate of pear slices back to the kitchen table, where he opened a blank document and typed the first line: Miss Havisham owns the brewery; Estella owns nothing, not even her own choices.

Justine had come to her grandmother's house to escape the group chat, which was not really an escape, since the phone sat on the kitchen table buzzing like a wasp under a glass. Priya had missed practice twice that week and their quartet had eleven days until the regional competition, and everyone expected Justine, as first violin, to say something. She had typed and deleted four drafts. The last one had begun, "You always do this," which was exactly the sentence her mother used on her father, and Justine knew how that conversation went, because she had listened to it through her bedroom wall for three years.

"Do you want tea or do you want to sulk," her grandmother said. She was at the sink re-proofing an old canvas jacket, working the wax in with a rag, and she had already lost the argument about whether Justine should help.

"Both," Justine said. "It's called multitasking."

"Then you'll be mediocre at both, like everyone who multitasks." Her grandmother held the jacket up to the window. "This used to be impermeable. Now the rain gets through anywhere I've forgotten to touch. One untreated spot and the whole thing soaks." She went back to the cloth, working in small circles, and Justine, against her will, thought about Priya, and about how one missed rehearsal seemed to leak into everything else.

They played Scrabble while the kettle heated, because her grandmother believed in Scrabble the way some people believed in voting. On her second turn the old woman laid down IONIZE across a triple word square and looked insufferable.

"That's not a real word," Justine said.

"It is a real word. To ionize is to give an atom a charge, positive or negative. Your grandfather taught me that, and he was a chemist, and I have never once needed it, which is how you know it stuck." She counted her points out loud, twice, savoring them.

Later, while her grandmother took her arthritis pills and her constitutional nap, Justine wandered to the sunroom shelf, which was mostly Reader's Digest Condensed Books and one shelf of her grandfather's things nobody had moved since the funeral. She pulled down a paperback with a cracked spine, some popular psychology thing about marriage, and read it standing up out of boredom more than anything. She was halfway through a chapter about couples arguing when she stopped, then read the page again.

The book said the psychologist John Gottman distinguished a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character. You missed practice twice, the book implied, versus you always mess up. Justine sat down on the arm of the wicker chair. She thought about her four deleted drafts, every one of which had been about who Priya was rather than what Priya had done. She thought about her mother saying always. She could admit, in the quiet of a sunroom with a dead man's book on her lap, that she had no idea whether the distinction would fix anything. It might just be a nicer way to hand someone the same weight.

Her grandmother appeared in the doorway in her reading glasses, hair flattened on one side. "You found his book."

"There's a part about complaints," Justine said. "Versus criticism."

Her grandmother considered this, or seemed to; it was possible she was only considering the kettle. "Your grandfather criticized me once about how I loaded the dishwasher. For eleven years." She straightened a curtain that did not need straightening. "It was never about the dishwasher, and it was never a complaint."

Justine texted Priya: can I call. The reply came back fast, which meant Priya was awake and afraid, and Justine dialed before she could draft anything worse.

"Hi," Priya said. Then, "I know."

"I'm not calling to break up with the quartet," Justine said, and Priya laughed, a small cracked sound, which helped. "Okay. I practiced this on my grandmother's Scrabble board, so bear with me." She took a breath. "You missed practice twice this week. Tuesday and Thursday. And at regionals we're one desk of four, and when we're a desk of three, Marco rushes and I can't hear Renee's cello under him. That's it. That's the whole complaint." She heard the word leave her mouth and understood she had chosen it on purpose, had aimed at the behavior and not the girl.

There was a silence long enough that Justine counted the ticks of the sunroom clock. "My mom's schedule changed at work," Priya finally said. "I've been watching my brother. I didn't want to say that because it sounds like an excuse."

"It sounds like a Tuesday and a Thursday," Justine said. "Can Renee's mom drive him those nights? I'll text her, she loves being asked, she'd drive him to the moon."

"Okay," Priya said. "Okay." Her voice did something unsteady, and Justine let it, did not rush to paper over it. "You're weirdly good at this all of a sudden."

"I read a book by a dead chemist's wife's dead husband," Justine said. "I'll explain later. Tuesday, six o'clock. Bring the Shostakovich."

When she hung up, her grandmother was in the doorway again, holding two teacups, having clearly heard everything and pretending she had not. "You're an aesthete about your music," she said, handing one over, "but apparently you can be practical about people. I find that suspicious."

"It's just a complaint," Justine said. "It's a technical term."

Her grandmother sniffed and settled into the wicker chair, and outside the first rain began against the sunroom glass, running off the canvas jacket where the wax had taken, and Justine drank her tea.

The festival had taken over the whole park by the time Henry found the language tent, its canvas sides pinned open so the noise of the drummers came and went like weather. His mother had signed him up for the newspaper workshop weeks ago, when his college acceptance still felt hypothetical, and he had agreed mostly to stop her asking. Now he stood at the back holding a photocopied article, its headline reading MAYOR DENIES BRIBES IN PORT DEAL, and waited for the session to start.

The instructor, a graduate student named Samira with a lanyard and a whistle on a string, paired them off and gave the task: read the short article, then summarise it aloud to your partner without looking at the page. Henry's partner was a girl his age named Priya, who had a laminated badge that said she was a volunteer and clearly wished she were somewhere else.

"Summarise in English," Samira said, "but you have to read it in the new language first. Out loud. That's the hard part."

Henry looked down at his article. It was in a language he had never studied, printed in a script he could mostly sound out thanks to a semester of Spanish and one regrettable month of Duolingo. He could pronounce it, haltingly, like a child walking on ice. But when he reached the English gloss at the bottom, a single translated sentence, the headline above it stopped him. DENIES. Just that. No he, no had. As if the mayor were being erased from his own denial.

"Wait," he said to Priya. "Why does it say DENIES? He denied it. Last month. It says so in the first line."

Priya glanced over. "That's just how headlines are."

"How they are how?" He read it again, quieter. "MAYOR DENIES. There's no is, no has, no anything. It's like someone took a sentence and pulled out all the small bones."

She laughed despite herself. "Small bones. Okay." Then, because she was a volunteer and felt obliged, she added, "I think it's called headlinese. My cousin does layout at a paper and complains about it constantly."

Henry turned the word over. Headlinese, as though newspapers had their own dialect, a compressed country he had been walking through for years without a passport. He thought of all the times he'd skimmed past headlines and absorbed them without parsing them, the way you hear a language you don't speak and understand nothing but the feeling. This one had seemed to have no grammar at all until he looked closer and saw that the grammar was there, just smuggled out.

"I'm going to try it," he said.

He read aloud. His tongue stumbled on the long words and he had to go back twice, and a family with a stroller paused at the tent flap to watch, and Priya waited with her arms folded but her foot had stopped tapping. When he finished, the two-minute sand timer Samira had flipped was long empty.

"So," he said, closing his eyes because the rule was no peeking. "The mayor denied taking money. From the port deal." He opened one eye. "Denied, past. Even though the headline says DENIES."

"Because?" Priya said, testing him, or maybe testing herself.

"Because headlines drop the small words. And they use the present tense for things that already happened." He said it slowly, watching her face to see whether it landed, and it did, a small nod, the nod of someone confirming a thing they half knew.

Outside the tent, a man at the cultural advocacy booth was telling anyone who would listen that the local paper had run a story to denigrate the festival committee, and he was waving a photocopied headline of his own like a subpoena. Henry heard the words through the canvas: biased, slander, who asked them. He thought about how easily a headline could be read wrong, or read as wrong when it was only compressed, and how quickly people decided they were being attacked. He wondered whether the man had misread it or whether the paper had meant exactly what he thought. He couldn't tell from here. That unsettled him more than the foreign article had.

Samira drifted over during the break and looked at his worksheet. "Nice work. Most people just paraphrase. You noticed the structure."

"It felt cerebral at first," Henry admitted, "like a puzzle with missing pieces. Then it felt like the pieces weren't missing, they were just... implied."

Later, walking out past the drummers with the photocopy folded in his back pocket, he passed the advocacy booth again. The man had pinned his headline to the corkboard. Henry stopped, read it once, and caught himself doing automatically what he had learned an hour ago: supplying the dropped words, translating the present into the past, deciding what had actually happened versus what had merely been said.

"You agree with me, right?" the man asked, seeing him linger. "This paper is against us."

Henry looked at the pinned headline, then at the man's expectant face.

"I'd have to read the whole article," he said, and kept walking toward the food stalls, where the line for dumplings had finally shortened.

Ethan had promised his grandfather a summary, in Hungarian, of a real news article, read aloud by Sunday dinner, and it was Saturday morning.

The kitchen of the old house smelled of paprika and dish soap, and his grandfather sat at the table with the folded newspaper between them like a referee. Ethan had chosen the front page himself, a piece about flood defenses along the Danube, because it seemed important, and importance had felt like the point. Now, four paragraphs in, every sentence arrived like a lock with too many tumblers. He knew víz meant water. He knew a city or two. Everything else was guesswork stacked on guesswork, and when he tried to say a sentence back in his own words, the sentence fell apart before it reached his mouth.

"Again," his grandfather said, and poured more tea.

They went paragraph by paragraph. His grandfather would not translate, only tap the paper and wait, patient in a way that made Ethan feel the patience more than his own failure. Twice Ethan tried to impute meaning to a word from its neighbors, inventing a definition that sounded plausible and turned out wrong, and his grandfather laughed, not unkindly, and shook his head. By lunch Ethan had understood perhaps two of the twelve paragraphs, and he had summarized neither aloud. He shut the notebook and sat with his hands flat on the oilcloth.

In the afternoon, while his grandfather napped in the chair by the window, Ethan went looking for the dictionary and found instead a shelf of his grandfather's old teaching books, spines cracked, margins dense with tiny annotations. One, a battered applied linguistics text, fell open to a page he had marked years ago with a tram ticket. In the margin, in his grandfather's handwriting, was a single underlined line: readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. Below it, his grandfather had penciled, in English, "So choose the text, don't let it choose you."

Ethan sat on the hallway floor with the book open on his knees and thought about the arithmetic of it. If he had to know ninety-eight words out of every hundred, then the flood article, where he perhaps knew sixty, was never going to be readable, no matter how long he stared. It had not been a failure of effort or of intelligence. It had been a failure of selection. He had assumed reading a language meant grinding through whatever hard thing appeared first, and the grinding itself was the virtue. His grandfather's stoicism about it, the endless tapping and waiting, had let him believe that the suffering was the lesson.

He went back to the kitchen and counted. He took the easiest article he could find in the paper, a short piece about a village baking festival, and made two columns in his notebook, one for words he knew and one for words he didn't. The numbers came out to something like one unknown in sixty. He circled it. Then he worked the article until the unknown words gave in, or nearly did, and found that when he understood nearly all of it, the few strangers stopped mattering; the sentence carried them. The Danube article had felt like a puzzle because it was one, at his level, all the way down.

At dinner he summarized the festival piece aloud. It was clumsy. He put the tenses in the wrong places and his grandfather corrected him only twice, which Ethan had learned to read as a kind of applause. When he finished, he said, in English, "I picked the wrong article first. I thought it was cheating to pick an easy one."

"Easy is not cheating," his grandfather said. "Hard is not a virtue." Then he stood to refill the water jug, and Ethan noticed, not for the first time that week and not for the first time that month, how slowly his grandfather crossed the kitchen now, one hand trailing along the counter, as if the room had grown slightly unsteady beneath him. Something subterranean was happening in the old man, some fault Ethan could sense but not name, and the language they were trading back and forth was beginning to feel like a rope thrown across it.

On Sunday, before the relatives called, his grandfather slid the newspaper across the table, folded to a different page. "This one," he said. It was a short notice, half a column, about a women's choir in a town Ethan had never heard of, and beneath the printed name of the town his grandfather had written a name Ethan knew: his grandmother's name, before she married. She had sung in that choir, sixty years ago, and the notice recorded that the choir had disbanded this spring after its last concert.

Ethan read it through once silently, counting without meaning to, and found he knew nearly all of it. He read it aloud, and then he summarized it aloud, in Hungarian, slowly, and his grandfather listened with his eyes closed, his thumb moving along the edge of the table, and when Ethan finished, the old man kept his eyes closed for a while.

"Again," his grandfather said. "The last part. Slower."

Madison's mother had a rule about the Saturday shop: whoever rode along got to carry the baskets, and whoever was learning to drive got the car afterward. So Madison stacked tins of beans into the trolley with the grim efficiency of someone earning wages, and her mother hummed along to the radio playing above the dairy aisle, and the whole time Madison was thinking about the letter from the test centre. Her practical driving test was on Thursday, and in the margin of the confirmation email, in her instructor's neat handwriting, was a note that had been bothering her for a week: "We've done bay parking. We should talk about the others."

"There's more than one?" Madison had asked, and Priya had said, brightly, too brightly, "We'll cover it Tuesday," which was the day before the test, which was like being told about a pop quiz the night before it happened.

At the checkout her mother fumbled for her card and Madison loaded the bags, and the boy at the till, maybe nineteen, wearing a lanyard that said TRAINEE MANAGER, asked if she'd found everything all right. She said yes. Then, because the queue behind them was long and nobody was talking, she said, "Do you drive?"

"Passed last year," he said, scanning a bag of spinach with a beep that sounded almost sarcastic. "Failed once first. Parallel parking. I'd only practised in car parks, so when he asked me to do it at the side of the road, I just sort of... stopped."

"At the side of the road?"

"That's where they get you. Bay parking's the safe one, in the car park. Out on the road it's one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner can ask for. Mine picked parallel. My mate got the bay. It's luck of the draw."

Madison stood very still with a bag of potatoes in her hands. Her mother said, "Madison, love," and nudged her forward, but Madison was doing arithmetic. Tuesday. One session. One manoeuvre she had never once attempted, out of a hat she could not see into, on a road where the examiner might simply point at a parked car and say there, please.

In the car park she took the driver's seat while her mother fussed with the receipt. Between the trolley bays, an old Vauxhall sat at the kerb, and Madison studied it the way she imagined an examiner might. Two car lengths of empty road behind it. A delivery van ahead. She put her seatbelt on.

"What are you doing?" her mother asked.

"Practising."

"On what?"

"On that." She nodded at the Vauxhall. "Parallel parking. At the side of the road." She reversed out of their space, looped the car park twice, and drew up alongside the Vauxhall, close enough that her mother made a small sound, not quite a word. Madison checked her mirrors, which she did now the way other people checked their phones, constantly and without thinking. Then she began the reverse, turning the wheel full lock, watching the nearside wing mirror like it owed her money.

She ended up eighteen inches from the kerb and a foot from the Vauxhall, angled slightly. Not perfect. But a car, in a space, at the side of a road.

"Is that it?" her mother asked. "Are we done? Can we go home?"

"One more." She pulled forward and did it again, worse, then a third time, better, and a fourth, when a woman with a trolley stopped to watch with the frank interest of someone at a zoo. Madison wound down the window. "Sorry. Test on Thursday."

"Bay or road?" the woman asked.

"Road, if I'm unlucky."

"Both," the woman said. "Practise both, then luck's got nothing to do with it." She pushed her trolley on toward the Vauxhall, which, Madison now noticed, had a man asleep in the driver's seat, undisturbed by any of it.

Driving home, Madison felt something settle, not into certainty exactly, but into something adjacent to it. Priya's cheerful vagueness had impugned nothing and promised nothing; the trainee manager's confession had given the thing its true shape: not a hidden trap but a known list, one item short in her case. She could not make Thursday's examiner choose the bay. She could only remove the difference between the choices, and she had until Tuesday, and Priya, she suspected, had known she'd figure that out, had counted on a kind of complicity between them, the unspoken agreement that a panicked pupil is worse than an informed one.

The motorway ramp came up on her left, and she signalled early, matched her speed to the flow, and merged into the gap behind a lorry whose driver flashed his lights at her, which she had learned meant well done, come on. Her mother gripped the door handle less than she used to.

"They might not even ask for it," her mother said, as their junction approached. "The parking. You might get the easy one."

"Or I'll reverse around a corner," Madison said. "That's a manoeuvre too, apparently. The internet is a pugnacious place at two in the morning."

At the roundabout she slowed, looked right, and waited. Behind the grocery bags in the boot, something shifted and rolled, one of the tins, probably, finding its level.

"Left at the next one," her mother said. "Then you can practise the hill start on our road, and after that, honestly, you're on your own, because I've done my part and my part was tins."

Madison indicated left.

The writing club met on Tuesdays in the library's back room, where a poster about plagiarism had been curling off the wall since roughly the beginning of time. Mia arrived early, set her laptop on the long table, and opened the document titled, with great optimism, "Paper Draft 1 FINAL final." Mr. Okafor had told them at the last meeting that their next project would be a real research paper, with an argument, footnotes, and a bibliography in Chicago style, a phrase that had made her think of jazz until she saw the handbook.

"Chicago style," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from her. "Do we have to write it in a windstorm? Is that the citation?"

"You joke," said Deshawn, "but I spent forty minutes last night trying to footnote a website. Forty minutes. I could have learned to juggle."

Mia turned her laptop so they could see. Her topic was vaccines and public trust, mostly because her aunt had sent the family group chat an article about autism that Mia had found unsettling and vague. She had gathered two sources. The first was the article her aunt sent, which said that a study had shown a connection between the MMR vaccine and autism. The second was a much longer review article that had looked at hundreds of thousands of children across several countries and found no connection at all. She had assumed the disagreement was like a debate, two sides with roughly equal evidence, and her job was to pick one.

She read the first article again, hunting for the footnote that would lead her to the study. When she found it and pulled up the original, she sat back. "Wait," she said.

"What," said Priya, who was coloring a lugubrious skull in the margin of her outline for an essay on Hamlet, evidently planning to argue that the play was a comedy.

"Look at this." Mia scrolled. "The study my aunt's article is based on, Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet, the one claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, was based on only twelve children."

Deshawn leaned over. "Twelve."

"Twelve children. And the other paper is like half a million." She said it twice in her head, as if the number might grow. It did not. The two articles had been presented to her, side by side in the group chat and in her own imagination, as rivals of equal weight, two gladiators. Now it looked more like a rowboat parked next to a container ship.

Priya set down her pen. "So when my uncle says 'studies show,' I should ask how many kids were in the study?"

"That's the thing," Mia said slowly. "I almost didn't look. The headline sounded so certain." She had been ready to write a paper that impugned the study's honesty, its funders, its authors' motives, all the dramatic accusations, and she suspected that would have felt satisfying and proved nothing. What the numbers proved was smaller and stranger: a claim could travel around the world on twelve children, and it could sound identical, in a headline, to a claim built on a mountain of evidence. She started a new document and typed a footnote, then deleted it, then typed it again, getting the punctuation exactly wrong in three fresh ways.

"Yours looks right," Deshawn said, peering over. "Mine looks like the footnote got into a fight with a semicolon and lost."

"There's a whole page on commas in the handbook," Mia said. "Just about commas. Page forty-one."

Priya groaned with feeling. "The etiology of my headache is page forty-one."

They worked for a while in the good quiet of the back room, the radiator ticking, someone shelving carts somewhere behind the biography section. Mia discovered that Chicago style wanted her to decide, up front, what she actually argued, and she kept circling it. She didn't want to say the small study was a lie, because that wasn't what she'd found. She didn't want to say the big study settled everything either, because she'd read enough of the review to see its edges, the places where the authors themselves admitted uncertainty. What she had was a difference in scale, twelve against hundreds of thousands, and a question she liked better than either article's headline: why do we weigh them the same?

She wrote that question at the top of a fresh page. Then she wrote the first footnote, correctly, on the second try, and felt an unreasonable pride, as though she had landed a small plane.

Mr. Okafor came around the table on his way out and paused at her screen. "Interesting," he said, and moved on, which was somehow the highest compliment available.

At ten to six they packed up. Priya photographed her skull for reasons she declined to explain. Deshawn handed Mia his flash drive. "My bibliography's on there," he said. "Tell me if it's in Chicago style or just sad."

Mia took the flash drive and looked at the clock. Her aunt's article was still open in a tab at home, waiting, along with a group chat she had not answered in four days.

"I'll tell you tomorrow," she said, and zipped her bag.

Joshua stood in Priya's kitchen on Sunday afternoon with a legal pad, a pen, and the growing suspicion that he had never really looked at food before. Next fall he would be in a dorm with a shared kitchenette, and Priya had offered to teach him what his mother called, with a dismissive flick of her wrist, "that batch cooking thing." He had defended it, a little too loudly, at dinner. Now he had to prove he could actually do it.

"Start with the week," Priya said, sliding a cutting board across the counter. "Seven dinners. You pick, I'll cook alongside you, and we make them all today so you just reheat."

He wrote Monday through Sunday in a column, then stared at the blank space beside each day. At home, meals had simply appeared. In the dining hall, they would appear again, at a price he had now calculated twice. The gap between those two systems, between his mother's kitchen and the swipe of a card, was exactly the size of the legal pad in front of him, and he found he didn't know how to fill it.

"What do you actually eat?" Priya asked.

"I don't know. Food happens to me."

She laughed, not unkindly, and pulled open a drawer of recipes her sister had left behind. They settled on a rotation: chicken and rice on two nights, lentil soup stretched across three, pasta with frozen vegetables for the rest. Then she sent him to the grocery store two blocks away with a list and forty dollars of his own money, and he walked the aisles holding his phone like an instrument he was learning to read, comparing prices per ounce, putting back the pre-cut onions when he saw what they cost. He noticed, with a curiosity that surprised him, that the store had a logic to it, that cheap and expensive versions of the same thing sat side by side, and that the difference was mostly labor he could supply himself.

Back in Priya's kitchen, the real work began. He browned chicken thighs in a skillet that spat at him, burned his thumb through a folded dish towel, and learned to sharpen the knife her sister had left disgracefully dull. "How do you live with this?" he asked, running the blade against the steel the way a video had shown him, listening for the change in the sound.

"You excoriate the previous tenant, apparently," Priya said, watching him with her arms crossed. "Which is what my sister did to me when she found out I'd been using it like that."

By late afternoon the counter held five labeled containers and the kitchen smelled like onions and thyme, and Joshua felt a competence in his shoulders he hadn't expected. That was when he decided to add the chocolate. His youngest sister's birthday was Wednesday, she was staying home while he left in three weeks, and he wanted to bring her something when he visited Tuesday night. Simple bark, the recipe said. Melt chocolate, pour it on a tray, sprinkle pretzels on top, chill.

He set a pot of water simmering and balanced a metal bowl over it, breaking dark chocolate into pieces the way the photograph showed. He was stirring, watching the shards soften and slide into something glossy, when he leaned to grab the pretzels and his elbow nudged the bowl. A bead of condensation slid down the outside of the bowl and dropped in. Then another, from the steam, before he understood what was happening.

The chocolate changed in seconds. It went from liquid to stiff, from glossy to dull, thickening around his spoon until he was dragging a grainy paste in slow, resistant circles.

"Did I burn it?"

Priya leaned over the bowl and sniffed. "It doesn't smell burned." She touched the edge of the paste with a fingertip and rubbed her fingers together. "It's grainy. That's seized."

"Seized?"

"That's what my sister called it when it happened to her. A few drops of water in melted chocolate and it seizes up into this thick, grainy paste. Something about the sugar and cocoa particles clumping together." She said it the way she repeated anything her sister told her, half quotation, half fact.

Joshua stared into the bowl. He hadn't put water in. He hadn't done anything but breathe over it, and reach for pretzels, and let the steam do what steam does. "So the water can't touch it at all? Even from the pot underneath?"

"Even a little, apparently."

He turned the burner off and lifted the bowl free, setting it on the counter. The paste held the impression of his spoon. He poked it, and it held the impression of his finger too, like clay. He was quiet for a moment, working through it. At home he would have thrown it out and asked his mother what went wrong, and she would have said chocolate is temperamental, and that would have been the end of it. But he had just spent an afternoon learning that chicken thighs were cheaper on the bone, that dull knives were dangerous knives, that a week of food could be planned on a single sheet of paper. It seemed wrong to let this be the one thing that stayed mysterious.

"Can it be fixed?" he asked.

Priya found her sister's number in her phone and read from a text. "If it happens, you can stir in a spoon of cream or butter, it loosens it, but then it's not for dipping anymore."

"So it's ruined for the thing I wanted, and saved for something else." He got the heavy cream from the fridge, measured a tablespoon, and stirred it in with more patience than he'd shown anything all day. Slowly the paste loosened, went smooth again, darker and softer than before. Not what the recipe had intended. Something that would still taste like chocolate with pretzels pressed into it.

He poured it onto the tray anyway, uneven at the edges, and scattered the pretzel pieces across the top.

"It's not going to look like the photo," Priya said.

"I know." He carried the tray to the fridge and cleared a shelf between the lentil containers, sliding it in level. Then he stood there a second longer, looking at the week of food he'd made, and the crooked tray at the top of it, and wondered what his sister would say when she saw it, and whether it would matter that the chocolate had seized, and whether his mother would be able to tell from the taste. "Do you think anyone can tell it went wrong?"

Priya was already wiping down the counter. "Only if you tell them."

Daniel pushed his rice to the edge of the plate and said, "I have to tell Marcus something tomorrow and I don't know how to say it."

His father didn't look up from the chicken. "Then don't say it."

"He's my co-captain. He missed the deadline for the robotics roster, and now Priya can't compete because her paperwork went in late." Daniel's voice came out flatter than he intended. "If I say nothing, she thinks I don't care. If I say something, he'll quit. He's threatened to before."

His mother set down her fork. "What were you planning to say?"

"That's the problem. I keep drafting it in my head and every version sounds like 'you're lazy.' Which isn't even true. He stayed until eleven last Tuesday." Daniel caught himself introspecting instead of eating and picked the fork back up. His little sister, Amara, was watching him with the particular attention she saved for his problems, which she treated as theater.

"You could text it," she offered.

"He'd screenshot it."

Their father laughed once through his nose. "So don't text it."

"Helpful."

After dinner, Daniel's mother found him at the kitchen table with his laptop open to a half-written message he'd already deleted twice. She put a folded napkin beside him and sat down across from where he wasn't looking. "Your coach mentioned something once, when you were having trouble with the scrimmage feedback. Some model the Center for Creative Leadership uses. She said it changed how the whole team talked to each other."

"She told you this?"

"She told all the parents, hoping we'd use it at home. Your father lasted a week." His mother smiled at the laptop screen rather than at him. "It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model."

"That sounds like something a consultant made up on a golf course."

"It probably is. But she said you frame the feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. When, what, effect. That's the whole thing."

Daniel turned this over while pretending to read his own dead draft. In his head he had been building a case against Marcus's character, brick by brick, every missed practice and slow reply stacked into a wall with LAZY chiseled on it. The model wanted him to tear the wall down and hold up one brick instead. Friday, the roster deadline, Priya benched. One brick, held out flat in his palm.

"That's it?" he said. "No part where I say what I think it means about him?"

"Why would there be?"

"Because otherwise it sounds like a weather report. 'On Friday, the deadline passed, and Priya was affected.'" But even as he mocked it, he could feel where his old drafts had gone wrong. He'd been leading with conclusions, and a conclusion gave Marcus nothing to do except defend himself or leave. A disincentive, his economics teacher would have called it. Every word of judgment was a reason not to listen to the next word.

In the morning he found Marcus in the shop room before first period, soldering iron in hand, safety glasses pushed up into his hair. Marcus saw him and set the iron down slowly, the way people do when they expect bad news and want their hands free for it.

"Friday was the roster deadline," Daniel said. His mouth was dry. "You told me you'd submit it that night, and it didn't go in until Sunday. Priya's form bounced, so she can't compete at regionals." He stopped. The three sentences sat in the air between them, small and unadorned, and Marcus stared at him like he was waiting for the second half, the part where Daniel told him what kind of person he was.

"That's it?" Marcus said finally.

"That's what happened. I don't know what was going on for you, and I'm not going to guess. But I need to know what to tell Priya, and I need to know if you can handle the roster for state, or if I should take it."

Marcus pulled the safety glasses down off his hair and looked at the bench for a long moment. "I was at my mom's appointment on Friday. I forgot." He turned the soldering iron over in its stand. "I should have told you."

"Maybe. I'd have covered it."

"Take the roster for state," Marcus said. "I'll do the travel forms instead. And I'll talk to Priya myself."

Daniel nodded and didn't push further, though he was aware he was choosing not to, that judicious silence was its own decision and not necessarily the right one. Whether the model had actually fixed anything, or whether Marcus just hadn't wanted to fight in the shop room, Daniel couldn't know from here. Priya would still miss regionals either way.

He was almost to the door when Marcus called after him.

"Hey. That was better than the last time you yelled at me."

Daniel raised a hand without turning around and walked out past the trophy case, tapping the glass once with his knuckle as he passed.

The newspaper had come from Lisbon three days late, wrapped in brown paper that smelled faintly of the sea, and Mathis's grandfather set it on the kitchen table beside the honey pot with the ceremony of a man laying out cards. "Página sete," he said. "You will read it aloud, and then you will tell me what it says." Mathis had agreed to this in June, when failing to place into the advanced Portuguese class had seemed like a small thing, a scheduling annoyance. It was August now. Placement retesting was in eleven days, and his grandfather's kitchen in the hills above the town had become his last chance.

He began badly. The first paragraph concerned a municipal debate over the old tram line, and every second word snagged him. His grandfather sat across the table with his saturnine face giving nothing away, drinking coffee, correcting nothing until Mathis had finished a whole sentence, and then correcting everything at once. "Acento on the second syllable, not the first. Again." Mathis said the sentence again. The old man listened, nodded once, and turned the page slightly toward his grandson, as if handing over something heavy.

The article itself was stranger than the tram line. Two candidates had shared a stage in a small town near Coimbra, and one of them, instead of answering the other's argument about water rates, had spent three minutes imitating his accent. He did a version of the northern vowels, rolled them around for the audience, got his laugh. The writer seemed to disapprove, but the disapproval was buried in long clauses, and Mathis wasn't sure he was reading it right.

"Slower," his grandfather said. "You are guessing. Guessing has no verisimilitude. Read it as though you mean it."

Mathis read the passage again, and this time the rhythm carried him. Something clicked open in the middle of a sentence about how the audience had laughed and the moderator had not intervened, and he heard the sentence the way he would have heard it in English, which was: this isn't right. He looked up. "The other one had made a point about the water rates. A real point. And this guy answered by doing his voice."

His grandfather put down his cup. "And?"

"And so nobody ever dealt with the water rates." Mathis heard the shape of what he'd just said and sat with it for a moment. He had spent the whole summer convinced his problem was vocabulary, that if he could just hold enough words in his head the newspaper would open like a door. But he had understood nearly every word of this article and still almost missed the thing that mattered, because the thing that mattered was a gap, a place where an argument should have been and wasn't. "He tried to vilify him," Mathis said, testing the word in Portuguese first and then in English. "The whole three minutes. Making him sound like a fool so nobody would listen to the numbers."

His grandfather's face did something unusual, a loosening around the mouth. "In a formal debate," he said, "they call that ad hominem. It is a fallacy." He said it the way he said the names of chess openings, briefly, and then reached for the coffee pot as though the subject were closed. But it wasn't closed for Mathis. Fallacy was a word he half knew from an English class unit he'd slept through, and now it had a body, a face, an accent being mocked on a stage in Coimbra. A person's voice was not their claim. You could destroy the person and leave the claim standing there untouched, waiting to be answered, and nobody in that hall had answered it.

"Now," his grandfather said. "The summary. Aloud, in Portuguese, in your own words. Not the writer's words, yours."

Mathis pushed back from the table and stood, because somehow it came easier standing. He started with the tram line context, fumbled, restarted, and found a cleaner path: two candidates, one argument about water rates, one answer that was not an answer, one audience that laughed, one moderator who let it stand. His Portuguese creaked in places and his grandfather's eyebrows marked every creak, but he got to the end of it, and the end of it was the sentence he most wanted to say: "Ninguém respondeu ao argumento." Nobody answered the argument. He wasn't sure his grammar had survived, and he wasn't sure he'd summarized the writer fairly, because the writer, now that Mathis thought about it, had spent more words on the accent imitation than on the water rates too. Maybe that was the same trick in a smaller size. He said so, in clumsy Portuguese, and watched his grandfather consider it.

"Eleven days," his grandfather said, gathering the newspaper and folding it back into its creases. "Tomorrow you will read the editorial page, and you will tell me where the writer is fair and where he is not." He carried the paper to the sideboard, and paused with his hand on it. "Tonight, the accent. Practice the accent in the shower, where no one can hear you."

"Everyone can hear me in this house," Mathis said.

"Exactly," said his grandfather, and turned out the kitchen light.

The garden center smelled of wet peat and cut pine, and by the second Saturday in October Evan had learned to tell, by the weight of a bag in his hands, whether it held seed mix or potting soil. He had taken the job for the money, plainly enough, and for the fact that his grandfather had worked a similar yard on the other side of the city thirty years ago and still brought it up at Sunday dinners as if it were a family inheritance. What Evan had not expected was Priya.

Priya ran the register and was in her second year of economics at the university, and she had a habit of turning the slow afternoon hours into an informal seminar. That day a customer had come in wanting only New Zealand-grown plants, only local, nothing shipped across oceans, and after he left with his native grasses and his certainties, Priya asked Evan whether the man had been right to insist. Evan said it seemed obvious that buying local kept the money here. Priya smiled in a way that suggested the smile itself was a kind of argument.

"Say you're good at two things," she said, stacking clay pots. "And someone else is worse at both. Why would you trade with them?" Evan said you wouldn't, or you'd cheat them. She shook her head and set down a pot from New Zealand and a pot from down the road.
