She walked him through it for the better part of an hour, between customers, interrupting herself to ring up bulbs and bags of gravel: the idea that what mattered was not who was best at what, but who gave up less of one thing to make another. Evan kept resisting, then stopped resisting, then said slowly, "So both of them end up with more, even though one of them is better at everything," and Priya said, "Now you're dangerous."

Driving to his grandfather's house that evening, he turned it over the way you turn a stone in your pocket. It bothered him a little, honestly, that something so tidy could also feel like a trick, like a proof that left the world outside the proof unaccounted for. His grandfather, who had grown reticent since the funeral in the spring and answered most questions with weather, was watching a news program about interest rates when Evan came in. An announcer said something about the inflation target, and Evan, half to fill the silence, asked whether central banks had always aimed at a set number like that. He expected no answer. He was already sorry he'd asked.

His grandfather reached for the tablet Evan's mother had set up for him, and for a while the two of them searched together, Evan typing, his grandfather dictating corrections in a tone that had not been used in the house for months. They found it: New Zealand had been the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent. His grandfather repeated the numbers back as if confirming a fishing weight. "Nineteen ninety," he said. "I was loading trucks then. Thought about money every day and never once wondered who decided what it should do." He looked at the screen a long moment. "0 to 2 percent. Tight."

Evan asked him whether he thought that was the right way to run a country's money, and his grandfather said he supposed the Kiwis had done fine, and then, after a pause, that he had once quit a job over two dollars a week and still could not decide, all these years later, whether it had been principle or pride. It was the most he had said at one time since April. Evan recognized the shape of it, the arithmetic that never quite closes, the choice you keep auditing. He did not try to assuage him. He only said he'd quit over less, probably, and his grandfather laughed, a short dry sound like a branch giving way.

The following Saturday the local-only customer came back. Evan carried his grasses to the counter and found himself wanting to say something about trade and comparative advantage, about New Zealand and what its central bank had done first, and he understood that saying it would be showing off a lesson he had owned for six days. He also understood, standing there with the pot in his hands, that he was not sure the customer was wrong, that "both countries gain" was a statement about totals and the man's objection seemed to be about something totals might not see. Both things could be true at once, or close to once, and Evan could not yet say how close.

He rang up the plants without a lecture. Priya watched him from the register with one eyebrow up, and when the customer had gone she asked, "You didn't tell him he was wrong."

"Still deciding if he is," Evan said, and went back for the next bag, weighing it in his hands before he read the label.

The compiler message appeared for the fourth time in a row, red and indifferent: cannot access private field. Peyton sat in the back row of the lab, third period, the radiator ticking under the window, and stared at the line where she had tried to write student.name directly instead of calling getName(). Somewhere in the room Marcus was explaining, loudly, that his code was perfect and the machine was wrong. Peyton knew better than that now, mostly.

She had started the unit thinking privacy was a formality, a hoop Mr. Reyes made them jump through so the rubric would have enough boxes. Last week they had been arguing about it at the robotics table, of all places, waiting for a judge to come score their robot. Dev had been scrolling through the team's code on his phone when he said, "Wait, this language is older than we are. Java came out in 1995." Someone asked who made it back then, and Dev had shrugged until his brother, home from college, texted him the answer: it was Sun Microsystems, and the lead designer was a guy named James Gosling. Peyton had written the names in the margin of her notebook because they seemed like facts a person ought to keep. She hadn't expected them to matter.

They mattered now, in a small way, because the whole idea of private fields had come from somewhere. Somebody, in 1995 or before, had decided that a program was less fragile when its data was locked away and you had to knock politely, through getter methods, to get at it. Peyton could see the shape of the argument. She could also see Dev's argument, made over the robot's scattered screws, that locks just slowed you down when you knew exactly what you wanted.

The flashback came unbidden: she was eleven, sharing a room with her sister, keeping a diary with a combination lock her sister had cracked in a week. When Peyton found out, she hadn't cried. She had started writing in a code of her own invention, substitution, tedious to encode and decode, and her sister had lost interest long before Peyton did. The diary had become useless as a diary. She had protected it into a rock. That was the tangential thought, anyway, one she kept pulling herself back from, because the lab was not about sisters.

Or maybe it was, a little. She deleted the direct access, wrote String n = student.getName();, and the red message vanished. The test turned green in the runner, one small square of confirmation that something she had built held together under inspection. She sat with the satisfaction of it for a moment before testing the edges, the way Mr. Reyes kept telling them to. What happened if getName() returned the actual reference to a mutable object? What happened if the class trusted whoever knocked?

At the next table, Dev was declaring that getters were for cowards, that he was an iconoclast, though he mispronounced it and then looked it up on his phone with theatrical disappointment. "Fine," he said, "it means what I thought." He came over anyway, chin on his fist, and watched her test fail on purpose, a null she had planted in a field the getter was supposed to guard against. "You broke your own thing," he said. "Why would you do that."

"Because the grade isn't for the class," Peyton said. "It's for the test." Which was true, and also not the whole reason, and she found she couldn't say the whole reason out loud without sounding like a poster in Mr. Reyes's room. She believed in the locks, mostly, and she believed Dev was right that locks could calcify into rocks, and she had not yet worked out where the line fell between them. She suspected the line moved depending on who was trying to get in. That was as far as she had gotten, and she let it stay there, unresolved, the way the green square in the runner stayed green without telling her whether it portended anything about the program's future or only its present.

Mr. Reyes circulated, looked at her screen, and moved on without comment, which from him was praise. Peyton added one more test, then saved her work to the shared drive, checked the filename twice, and closed the laptop feeling something adjacent to competence.

At lunch, Dev found her in the courtyard with his phone out. "Gosling," he said. "You know he has a tattoo of the Java logo on his ankle?" Peyton said she didn't see how that was relevant, and Dev said it wasn't, it was better than relevant. Then he turned the phone around to show her the diagram of Gosling standing in front of a Sun Microsystems banner, and she leaned in to look. "So the guy who invented privacy for your data," Dev said, "put his own name where everybody can see it."

Jade had told her mother she had everything under control, and by the second Saturday of driving school she had almost convinced herself. She sat in the back row of the classroom above the strip mall pharmacy, two folders open on the desk while the instructor droned about shoulder checks. The folders held her future: one lease for a basement apartment near campus, all-inclusive, eight hundred a month with utilities bundled in; the other, a bright sixth-floor studio with a balcony, six-fifty plus hydro and water, which meant reading meters, estimating kilowatt hours, adding columns. She was good at columns. She had a calculator app and a pen with four colours, and she had told her mother she would decide by Monday, calmly, the way an adult decides.

The basement lease was typed on plain paper, headed with the landlord's name and a logo that looked designed on a home computer. The studio lease was dense and grey, every page stamped with a small Ontario government emblem, standard form, standard form. She had assumed the plain one was simply more personal. Her instructor, Mr. Okafor, paused the video on a diagram of a four-way stop and caught her circling numbers. "Apartment math," she said, holding it up. "Rent plus utilities, total monthly cost." He nodded and moved on, but at the break he leaned against the radiator beside her desk, coat still on, and asked which one was cheaper once she added it all up.

"The basement," she said. "Eight hundred flat. The studio comes to about seven-eighty, but it's close, and the view is better."

"Which one is on the government's standard lease form?"

"The studio. Why?"

He shrugged, the shrug of a man who had been a landlord once and a tenant twice. "In Ontario, most private residential landlords have to use that standard form for new leases. And if a tenant doesn't get one, she can ask for it in writing." He straightened his coat. "Make of that what you like." Then he was back at the projector, and Jade sat with her pen stopped mid-circle, the four colours suddenly useless. The plain lease, the friendly lease, was the one that wasn't standard. The landlord could be made to fix that, if she asked, in writing. It was not a flaw exactly. It was a fact with a door in it.

She spent the last hour of class half-listening to merging procedures and half drafting a letter in her head. She had told her mother she would decide by Monday, but that had been before the folders stopped being arithmetic and started being judgment: total cost on one axis, something harder to total on the other. During the in-car session afterward, on the quiet streets behind the plaza, she signaled early and braked late, thinking about meters, about a request in writing, about whether asking for the standard form would sour the basement landlord before she even moved in. She told herself she was calm. Her hands on the wheel said otherwise.

From the passenger seat, Mr. Okafor watched her take the corner by the school too widely, correct, correct again. He had seen this before, students whose bodies were in the car and whose minds were somewhere else entirely, negotiating with futures they hadn't signed yet. She was a careful driver fundamentally, he decided, just not presently. "Full stop at the sign," he said, and she stopped fully, hands at ten and two, eyes flicking to the mirror, to the road, to nothing, to the glovebox where her phone held photos of both apartments.

When she parked, she took out the phone before unbuckling. "Mr. Okafor. If I ask for the standard form and the landlord says no, then what?"

"Then you know something too," he said. He didn't elaborate, and she found she preferred that.

She sat in the school parking lot after he went inside, engine off, folders on the passenger seat where he had been. The basement was cheaper in a way that might not stay cheap; the studio cost more on paper and was exactly what it claimed to be on every page. Her mother would say take the cheaper one. Her mother had also never read either lease. Jade wrote at the top of a blank page, "Request standard lease form in writing," and underlined it, and then, after a moment, wrote "total monthly cost, studio: $780, all in" beneath, the two lines sitting side by side, neither one crossing the other out. It occurred to her that she had been insouciant about the whole thing for weeks, mistaking confidence for knowledge, and that the feeling of the mistake was not shame exactly, but something quieter, like discovering a room in a house she thought she knew.

She texted her mother: not decided yet, both are real options, will call you tonight. Then she folded the letter draft into the studio folder, the basement folder, both, her thumb leaving a crease down the middle. Somewhere behind the pharmacy a car door slammed. She started the engine, checked the mirror, and pulled out onto the road, the two folders riding beside her like passengers who had not yet agreed on a destination.

Eve found the two articles at the library's third-floor printer, which had jammed on the first one and then, in a fit of mercy or contrition, produced the second. Both were about the same question, whether a poet's letters should count as evidence when reading her poems. One article said the letters exhumed the poet's real intentions. The other said the letters were performances too, costumes the poet wore for posterity. Eve needed to compare them in a critical review for Ms. Okafor's class, and she had no idea how to begin.

"You just have to pick a side," said Dani, sliding her tray next to Eve's at lunch. "Say one of them is right."

"But I don't think either of them is completely right," Eve said. "The first one treats the letters like they're more honest than the poems, which is a weird assumption. And the second one is so suspicious of everything that it can't explain why the letters are moving at all."

"So you'll write that they're both wrong. Very brave. Everyone loves a sixteen-year-old with an opinion about scholarly methodology."

The problem was not only having a position. It was the format. Ms. Okafor had spent one breathless Thursday on citation, and Eve had been at the orthodontist. Her friend Priya, who had transferred from English into Mr. Lancet's history class that semester, had her own troubles, which she described in the hallway before sixth period.

"He keeps circling my heading in red," Priya said, holding up a paper. At the bottom of the page, in Eve's view, was the phrase Works Cited, circled twice, with a note in the margin. "Every single paper."

"That's the heading," Eve said. "That's what we use."

"Not in history. He wants a bibliography. And we don't put the name and page number in parentheses in the text either. I keep doing it anyway. Muscle memory."

"But in English we do put the name and the page number in parentheses," Eve said slowly, working it out, "and then the full sources go at the end, under that heading."

"Congratulations," said Priya. "You've now learned what I learned in September, at the cost of three red circles."

That night Eve sat at the kitchen counter with both articles fanned out and a legal pad that had belonged to her father, back when he still claimed he would write a novel. She made two columns. On the left she wrote what each article claimed. On the right she wrote what each article assumed but never said. The first assumed sincerity was possible. The second assumed it wasn't. The poet herself remained mercurial, resisting both columns, quoting her own letters in her poems and then denying she'd written the letters, which Eve found genuinely funny and wrote in the margin as "a flex, honestly."

By ten o'clock she had a draft that said, roughly, that the two articles were not opposites but neighbors who refused to speak, and that a reader could stand in the doorway between them. She liked the sentence. She suspected Ms. Okafor would find it too cute. She kept it anyway.

She also had citations to do. She remembered Priya in the hallway, and she put the author's name and the page number in parentheses at each quotation, which felt strange at first, like signing every word she borrowed, and then useful, like leaving breadcrumbs back to the source. At the end, on a fresh page, she typed Works Cited and listed both articles in full. It looked official. It looked like something a person had produced who knew what she was doing.

In class on Monday, Ms. Okafor read the reviews while they worked silently on a grammar sheet about commas, which Eve found rich, given the parentheses. When Ms. Okafor reached Eve's paper she stopped, read a page, and read it again.

"The doorway," she said, not looking up. "That's yours?"

Eve nodded, then realized the teacher wasn't watching and said yes.

"Your uncertainty paragraph is the strongest part. Most students hide the part where they don't know. You put it in the middle and built around it." She set the paper down. "The second article's author is coming to give a lecture in April. You could ask her about your objection to page twelve."

"I don't have an objection to page twelve."

"You will by April," said Ms. Okafor, and moved on to the next paper, pen already circling.

Wyatt had come to his grandfather's house for the weekend with two jobs: help clean out the study, and avoid sharing anything else he was ashamed of. The second job was newer. On Thursday he had forwarded a video to forty people in his class chat, a clip of a flood swallowing a parking lot, captioned as happening two towns over, and by Friday afternoon a girl named Priya had replied with a single link showing the same footage, watermarked and dated, from three years ago and four hundred miles away. Nobody mocked him outright, which felt worse. The silence just sat there, noxious, like milk gone off in a fridge nobody would claim.

Grandpa's study smelled of pencil shavings and the particular dust of paper that has outlived its usefulness. "You check the source before you pass it on," Grandpa said, not looking up from a drawer he was emptying. "Your grandmother has been saying that since the party line." He meant it as a joke, but Wyatt heard it as a sentence handed down, and he didn't want it. He wanted to figure the thing out himself, on his own screen, in his own way.

While Grandpa sorted, Wyatt sat at the old desktop computer and practiced what Priya's link had taught him. He took a still frame from another viral video, one of a shark swimming down a highway, and ran a reverse image search. The results came back like a family tree of lies: the earliest dated entry was from a storm years ago, and every newer copy had simply shed its date the way a rumor sheds its source. He took a screenshot to send to Priya, then didn't send it. He wasn't sure yet whether he was apologizing or showing off, and until he knew, the screenshot stayed in his camera roll.

"Found my disks," Grandpa announced, holding up a stack of labeled CDs like a man presenting treasure. Grandpa's want was simple and long-standing: before he gave the computer away, he wanted to print one last report, a list of every customer his old shop equipment business had ever served. "Fifty years of accounts," he said. "I'm not leaving them on a hard drive to rot." He had been a bookkeeper who taught himself databases in his sixties, and he still spoke of SQL the way some men spoke of fly-fishing, with affection and grievance in equal measure.

Wyatt, the designated neophyte, was put in front of the keyboard while Grandpa hovered. They built the query together, joining the customers table to the orders table, and when the results appeared, Wyatt scrolled and frowned. Some customers appeared with no orders at all, the order columns just blank, the word NULL printed where a date should have been. "It skipped people," Wyatt said. "That's wrong, isn't it? I expected every customer in the list."

"That's the LEFT JOIN doing its job," Grandpa said. "Every row from the left table comes through. Where there's no match on the right, it fills in NULL." He tapped the screen beneath one of the blanks, a customer named R. Okafor who had apparently ordered nothing ever, and Wyatt understood that the empty cells weren't errors. They were information. The list was complete precisely because it showed what was missing.

Wyatt sat with that for a moment, and it connected itself to his morning without his permission. The reverse image search had done the same thing, in its way: it kept every copy of the shark video in the results and marked where the truth was missing, the date stripped out, the origin NULL. Two practices he had thought were unrelated, his grandfather's half-forgotten databases and his own bruised afternoon, turned out to underwrite the same idea, that a complete picture includes its own gaps. Whether that was wisdom or just a coincidence he could parrot, he honestly didn't know. He was sixteen, and he had been confidently wrong once this week already.

"You're smiling at a customer list," Grandpa said. "Concerning."

"I forwarded a fake video to my whole class," Wyatt said. "Flood footage. Turned out it was old and from somewhere else."

Grandpa lowered himself into the desk chair across from him. "In my day a rumor took a week to circle the church picnic. You lot can do it before lunch." He was quiet a second, then added, "There was a man in 1988 who told everyone at the hardware store that I'd gone bankrupt. I knew inside a day who'd started it, because I asked, and asked, and checked. Nobody taught me that either. You just decide you're tired of being a relay station." He shrugged, as if to say he might be remembering his own embarrassment more fondly than it deserved.

They printed the report, all eleven pages, R. Okafor and his blank line included, and Grandpa folded it into a folder with the care of a man filing a deed. Wyatt pulled out his phone, opened the class chat, and typed a message he deleted twice before settling on the third version: the shark video was fake, the flood one was too, here was how he'd checked, sorry for the flood of floods. Priya replied within a minute with a thumbs up and the words "finally," which could have meant anything.

"Supper's at six," Grandma called from the kitchen, where she had been listening to the whole thing, they both knew, without appearing to. Wyatt hit send.

Denny had swum the same two thousand yards every morning since June, and by August he had stopped getting faster, which he announced at the community pool on Tuesday while holding a kickboard over his head like a shield against the inevitable. "Same time as June," he said. "Two weeks ago I was eight seconds faster. Now I'm back."

Michael, seventeen and certifying for the junior lifeguard program in October, had his own problem, which was that he needed to swim five hundred meters in under nine minutes and currently managed it in ten forty. He also had a phone full of conflicting advice. His club coach back home believed in volume above all things: if you were tired, you hadn't done enough yet. His sister Priya, who was two years into a physiotherapy degree and insufferable about it, believed in rest the way some people believed in weather, as a force you did not argue with. He had been trying to follow both at once, swimming hard every day and then lying very still on his bed in the evenings, ache pooling in his shoulders, feeling that he was honoring neither philosophy especially well.

The pool at six a.m. was a concrete rectangle with a friable edge near the deep end, where the years and the chlorine had softened the lip so that grit came away under your fingers if you rested your hand there. Michael rested his hand there now, sitting with his legs in the water, watching Denny churn through another identical two thousand.

That night Priya sent him a message, which he read while eating cereal over the sink because the table was covered in his mother's tax papers. "You asked about plateaus," she wrote. "Look up progressive overload. Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt. The key words are gradually and reason. If nothing changes, nothing changes. Also, warm up before, and take at least one full rest day a week. Two is not cowardice." He read it three times. There was something in the pragmatics of the last line, the way she'd said "not cowardice" instead of "is fine," that told him she was answering a question he hadn't typed out loud, the one about the mornings he'd gone to the pool anyway with his arms feeling like wet rope.

He thought about Denny. Two thousand yards every day since June, identical, and a body that had adapted to exactly that and then closed the file. Michael had been doing a version of the same thing, swimming his ten-forty five hundred every morning and treating each repetition as if effort alone were the whole mechanism. Priya's message and the coach's sermon on volume were not, he realized, actually opposites. Both were underpinned by the same idea: the workout had to ask something of the body that the body couldn't already do. The coach just never said what happened when the asking stopped changing.

On Wednesday he sat at the friable end of the pool with a pencil and the back of a registration flyer and drew a grid, seven boxes. Monday, hard intervals, five hundreds at a pace just past comfortable. Wednesday, distance, but longer than last week by a little. Friday, hard again. Saturday, easy, drills, warm-up laps taken seriously instead of skipped, which he'd been doing, sprinting cold off the blocks like an idiot. Sunday, nothing. He wrote "nothing" in the box and then, hearing Priya's voice in his head, underlined it. Thursday he left blank and stared at it for a while, because rest days were the part he didn't fully trust. One or two? He wrote "one, maybe two" and left it at that.

Denny floated over during the warm-up Michael was now actually doing, slow laps, arms loosening, and asked what he was reading off the flyer. "Progressive overload," Michael said. "It means gradually increasing training demands, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt." Denny looked at him with the expression of a man being told his house had been on fire for years. "I've been doing the same workout since June," Denny said. "Exactly the same." "I know," Michael said, and pushed off the wall into his first slow lap, letting the water take the plan out of his hands.

The next morning his arms still ached from Monday, a good ache, and he swam the five hundred in ten thirty-one without having tried to, and stood in the shallow end breathing, looking at the pencil-marked flyer folded into a Ziploc bag on the bench, Thursday's box still empty, the question still open. "Bring the flyer," Denny called from the far lane. "I'm copying it."

Arianna taped the tenth blank sheet to her bedroom wall and stood back. The application wanted a portfolio of ten artworks organized around one theme, plus an artist's statement, and so far she had nine paintings of doors: a screen door in a storm, a hospital door propped open with a chair, the cabinet under her grandmother's sink. The tenth refused to arrive. Three nights ago she had painted a door with no wall around it, just hanging in gray, and it looked like a poster for a motel.

Her brother Marco knocked with his elbow because his hands were full of his telescope parts. "Can I borrow your desk lamp? Mine died and the astronomy club meeting is Thursday. I need to collimate the mirror before then." He wanted the club's single travel slot for the spring trip to the dark-sky site in the mountains, and he had been talking about nothing else for two weeks.

"You can have it if you sit still for twenty minutes," she said. "I need someone to look at something."

He set the mirror down on her dresser, careful as a sleeping cat. She opened the library book to the page she had flagged and turned it toward him. "Tell me what you see."

"A woman lying on a bed kind of, or standing, with a cracked Greek column where her middle should be. Why is there a column inside a person?" He leaned closer. "It's broken down the middle. Like something cracked it from inside her."

"That's what I couldn't stop thinking about." She had found the painting on Tuesday, looking for references for the statement she hadn't written: The Broken Column, 1944, by Kahlo. Her spine painted as a cracked Ionic column, visible through an opening in her body, the flesh pulled aside like a curtain. Arianna had sat with it for an hour before she understood what bothered her, which was that it worked both ways at once. The column was architecture, something built, ordered, old, and it was also bone, private, hers. The painting took two completely different vocabularies and made them hold still together in one figure.

"I don't get art," Marco said. "But the nails are visceral. I actually flinched."

"I need to paint something like that. Not like it, but like it." She pulled the ninth painting off the wall, the door in the storm, and set it face down on the bed. "I've been painting doors from the outside. What if the tenth is from the inside?"

"A door from the inside is just a wall."

"Unless the door is open." She was talking faster now. "All my other doors are closed, or about to close, or broken. Everyone reads closed doors as the end of something. But the whole portfolio is actually about my grandmother's house getting sold, and the last time I was in it I stood in the kitchen doorway, from the inside, looking out at the moving boxes. That's the tenth painting. The door from inside, the room already empty."

Marco looked at the taped-up blank sheet, then at her. "That's the theme? Grandmother's house?"

"Leaving. Doors as the exact moment of leaving." She sat down at her desk and pulled the statement draft toward her, the one with three crossed-out opening lines. It had said something about journeys, which was a lie. She wrote: "These paintings are about the last year of my grandmother's house, and about what a door does that a window doesn't." She stopped. "I don't know how to end it. Every ending I write sounds like a greeting card."

"Say what you actually think. You think the painting with the column is the best thing ever, say that."

"I can't put Kahlo in my statement, that's not how statements work." But she wrote on the back of an envelope, where she kept things she wasn't sure about yet: an Ionic column holds up a building and a spine holds up a body, and a door holds up the difference between inside and outside. She didn't know if she believed the third part. She might believe it by Friday.

"You owe me a lamp," Marco said, gathering his mirror.

"Take the good bulb, the daylight one." She gave it to him and he left with the telescope parts balanced against his chest, and she heard him on the stairs explaining something about mirrors to their mother, who was asking whether the dark-sky trip would presage an actual career or just a very expensive hobby, a word choice that made Marco groan audibly through the floor.

Arianna turned the envelope over. Her grandmother had called the house the family patrimony, once, at Thanksgiving, and everyone had laughed because it was a small house with a damp basement, and the word seemed too grand for it. But the word had stuck, and now the house was sold, and the word was all that was left of it. She wrote that down too, then crossed out the sentence and wrote it again shorter.

Before starting the tenth painting she taped a fresh sheet where the blank one had been, mixed a gray for the empty kitchen, and sketched the doorframe first, from the inside, the light coming in from beyond it. Then she painted the open door.

Justin had been first into the gym every morning that August, sneakers squeaking on the empty court an hour before anyone else arrived, and by the last week of the month he was getting slower. His vertical, which he measured nightly with chalk on the backboard, had dropped an inch and a half. He told himself it was the heat, or the old ball, or the scale in the locker room lying about the four pounds he'd apparently lost, but on Tuesday he missed a layup in pickup that he would have dunked in June, and Marcus, who was taciturn about everything except basketball, actually laughed out loud.

"You're running yourself into the ground," Marcus said afterward, sitting on the bleachers retying his shoes. "My cousin did that before his senior season. Trained twice a day, every day, got worse all fall."

"That doesn't even make sense," Justin said. "You work more, you get better. That's the whole deal."

Marcus shrugged, which was most of his vocabulary, and pointed at the bleacher beside him until Justin sat. He pulled out his phone and showed Justin a screenshot from some training forum, a graph with a dip and then a rise above where the line had started. "Read the caption."

The caption said the gains happened after the stress, not during it. Justin read it three times and felt something rearrange behind his eyes, the same feeling he got when a math proof suddenly closed. "So the workout doesn't make you better."

"It makes you worse, temporarily. Then you recover, and you rebuild past where you were." Marcus tapped the peak of the curve. "It's called supercompensation."

Justin looked at the graph for a long moment. "But you have to rest for that part."

"Got it in one."

The problem, Justin decided on the walk home, was that rest felt like nothing, and he had been raised, quietly and thoroughly, to believe that nothing was a sin. His father ran a landscaping business and was out the door at five-thirty; his mother graded papers at the kitchen table past midnight. Nobody had ever said idle hands to him outright, but the ethic was there anyway, tacit and load-bearing, and every morning he had gone to the gym to instantiate it. He bounced the ball against the garage door and thought: what if the nothing was the work?

That night he did something he'd never done, which was to plan the coming week on paper instead of just intending it in his head. Monday, court work and lifts. Tuesday, nothing. Wednesday, court work, lighter. Thursday, nothing, or maybe just shooting, easy stuff. Friday, the hardest session, after two partial recoveries. Saturday, game. Sunday, nothing again. He wrote warm-ups at the top of every active day, ten minutes of skips and lunges he'd always skipped himself, pun he now caught, because his left ankle had a history of rolling when he went cold. The schedule looked sparse and almost embarrassing. It looked like the opposite of effort. He pinned it above his desk anyway.

The hard part wasn't the plan, it was Tuesday. He woke at six out of habit, lay in bed with his heart already in gym-day rhythm, and had to consciously talk himself down, a small civil war inside his own consciousness between the boy who wanted the chalk mark on the backboard and the boy who had read the graph. He went downstairs and made eggs and watched his father's truck pull away, and the morning felt like a held breath. Wednesday he went back and his legs were light in a way that scared him, like borrowed money.

By Friday the plan was working; he could feel it in the spring of his first step, and on Saturday he jumped higher than he had all summer. But the cost had its own shape. The other guys had started a noon run on Tuesdays and Thursdays, full court, the loud funny kind of basketball, and he had missed both. Marcus had gone without him and posted a video of a buzzer beater that Justin would have been there for, in the old life. Sunday he sat at the kitchen table staring at his own schedule, wanting to cross out one of the rest days, and his mother looked up from her grading and said, "You've been different lately. Quieter."

"I'm resting," he said. "On purpose. It's a thing I'm trying."

She considered this the way she considered a student's excuse, then went back to her red pen. Justin picked up his phone and opened the thread with the Tuesday crew, typed a question about next week, deleted it, typed it again. Outside, the light was going amber over the driveway, and he could hear somebody's ball going up and down the street.

He typed, "Tuesday I have to sit out. Wednesday though. Who's in?"

Violet had sequestered herself in the garage with a bag of corn chips, a voltmeter borrowed from her uncle's toolbox without permission, and two aluminum baking sheets she intended to charge and hang facing each other like the plates in her physics textbook. The textbook was propped open on a sawhorse, its diagram showing two parallel lines bristling with little plus signs and minus signs, and beside it a formula for the electric field between them. Her physics exam was in nine days, and the field between two charged plates was the one topic that still sat in her mind as an inchoate mess of symbols she could not yet picture.

The problem was that she could not see an electric field, and she distrusted anything she could not see. So she had decided to build one. She clipped a wire from each sheet to opposite terminals of a battery she had pulled from her mother's dead cordless drill, and then she stood between the two sheets on an upturned milk crate and held up a ping pong ball wrapped in foil, dangling it from a thread of fishing line, wondering if it would swing. It did not swing. It hung there with the serene indifference of an object that had no idea what a physics exam was.

Her younger brother Marcus opened the garage door halfway, saw her on the crate between two baking sheets, and said, "Is this a seance."

"It's a parallel plate apparatus," Violet said. "Go away."

"You don't have an apparatus. You have bakeware." He came in anyway, because he was fourteen and had nowhere else to be, and picked up the textbook. He read aloud with mock oratory, one hand raised like a man addressing a parliament: "The electric field between two charged plates may be taken as uniform, and its strength equals the potential difference divided by the separation." He looked at her. "What does any of that mean."

"It means," Violet said, climbing down, "that if I know the voltage across the plates and how far apart they are, I can divide one by the other and get the field strength, in volts per metre. And then if I put a charge in that field, I can find the force on it." She said it flatly, and then heard herself, and frowned, because saying it flatly was not the same as believing it. "In theory."

Marcus had found the tennis ball she kept in the garage for no reason she could name, and he was bouncing it against the concrete while she rechecked her battery connection. "I got a question," he said. "When I throw this up, it slows down on the way up, right? And then it speeds up coming down. Is that the same amount? Like the same rate?"

"That's gravity, not electricity," Violet said, but the question snagged on something. She took the tennis ball from him. "Timer on your phone. I'll throw it, you call out the seconds at the top." She tossed the ball straight up, harder than she meant to, and it cracked against the ceiling and came down fast. Marcus laughed so hard he forgot to time anything.

They tried again, softer. Marcus called "now" at the top, and she wrote the numbers on the back of a paint can label with a carpenter's pencil, threw it again, threw it a third time. The ball rose and fell in almost the same span each side of the peak. "It's the same," she said slowly. "Near Earth's surface, the vertical velocity changes by about nine point eight metres per second every second. Whether it's rising or falling. Exactly the same rate both ways." Marcus said, "So it loses nine point eight going up and gains nine point eight coming down," and she nodded, and then stood very still.

She was thinking of her foil ping pong ball. Gravity pulled every ball the same way, steadily, whether the thing was climbing or dropping, and the field between two charged plates was supposed to act on a charge the same way: uniform, constant, the same everywhere between the plates. That was what the word in the diagram had meant all along. She did not need to see the field. She needed to trust the symmetry. She grabbed the pencil and, on the paint can label, wrote out her plate separation, twenty centimetres, and the battery voltage, and divided, and got a number of volts per metre, and then a small number of newtons for a charge the size of the one in her homework problem, and the arithmetic came out clean.

"It's working," she said. "The field. I can compute it. I don't have to see it, I just have to do what the numbers do."

"You still have bakeware," Marcus said. He had eaten most of the corn chips. He held up the empty bag as evidence.

Violet sat down on the milk crate and copied the paint can numbers into her notebook, and then, because she was honest with herself even when it was inconvenient, she added a note: that her garage battery was dying, that the foil ball had not swung, that she had not actually measured a field tonight, only computed one on faith. Some uncertainty would stay. But the division was right, the symmetry was right, and tomorrow she would bring the voltmeter back before her uncle missed it.

She stood, picked up the tennis ball, and tossed it straight up toward the ceiling, watching it slow, stop, and fall, the same nine point eight all the way.

Levi had the museum's third-floor gallery almost to himself on the Tuesday before school started, which was the point of coming. His backpack held two books on the French Revolution, a photocopied packet of excerpts, and a half-empty notebook with the words "HOW VIEWS CHANGED SINCE 1800" underlined twice at the top of a blank page. He stood in front of a case holding a cockade, its ribbon faded to the color of rust, and tried to imagine Burke looking at one of these and feeling the world come apart.

The assignment terrified him in a way he had not admitted to anyone. His older sister, Devi, had told him that a historiographical essay was not about what happened but about how historians had argued, and the distinction, which had sounded simple in her kitchen, kept dissolving when he tried to write. He had Burke's reaction, Carlyle's drama, the Marxist reading, the revisionists of the 1980s who said class had been the wrong lens all along. He had the facts. What he lacked was a way to hold them together without flattening them into a timeline with a moral at the end.

He moved along the cases slowly, because the gallery guard, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor whose badge he had read on previous visits, had once told him that slow looking was the whole trick of museums, and he had decided to believe her. "You're back," she said, coming over to straighten a label someone had knocked crooked. "Same bag, same frown."

"College essay," Levi said. "Sort of. It's about how people have seen the French Revolution differently since 1800, and I can't figure out if the historians are arguing about the Revolution or about themselves."

Mrs. Okafor considered the cockade case as if it might answer. "Maybe they're arguing about the present, using the past as the room to do it in." She pointed down the corridor. "There's a display on how museums change their own exhibits. Same idea, smaller scale. And the library room is open if you need to sit."

The library room, it turned out, was less a library than a reading alcove with a shelf of exhibition catalogs and a few donated books of history. Levi sat down anyway, mostly to have somewhere to put his despair, and texted Devi: "I have nine historians and no argument. Every time I line them up they cancel each other out."

Her reply came while he was still staring at a catalog called Revising the Revolution. "Stop trying to make them agree. Pick two who genuinely clash and build the essay on the seam between them. Also: look up what historians do in other fields when the big interpretation breaks. That's your model. It doesn't have to be France."

He almost put the phone down. Then he thought about what she had said, the seam rather than the summary, and began pulling catalogs off the shelf. The Cold War was not his subject, but a fat blue book had a prize sticker on its spine, and he opened it because the sticker said Bancroft, which Devi had once mentioned the way other people mentioned the Pulitzer. The book was Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, and its argument, compressed into the introduction, stopped him cold. Leffler had won the 1993 Bancroft Prize for maintaining that American leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. Where other historians Levi had heard of, especially someone named Gaddis, saw defense and containment, Leffler saw the pursuit of preponderance itself, security achieved by standing above everyone else.

He read the introduction twice. What gripped him was not the Cold War at all but the shape of the disagreement: two historians, the same archive, opposite readings, and the argument was really about what the country was for. That was his seam. If historians of the Revolution had split the same way, then his essay was not a timeline but a set of running questions: who feared the crowd, who trusted it, and what present danger each historian was answering when he looked back at 1789.

He worked for two hours, filling pages, and at some point Mrs. Okafor brought him a cup of water without being asked, setting it on the far side of the table away from his notebook. "You looked like a man in the desert," she said. He thanked her and noticed that the afternoon light had shifted through the tall windows, and that the museum's diurnal rhythm was closing around him, guards rotating, voices thinning, the front desk cashing out.

By closing time he had a plan and a problem. The plan: pair the Marxist historians with the revisionists and show that the disagreement was about the present, not the past, using the Leffler model as his structuring idea without pretending the Cold War explained France. The problem: he did not actually know whether the Marxist reading was really dead after 1989 or whether the revisionists had overcorrected, and every time he tried to resolve it he circumscribed his own argument until it said nothing. He wrote in the margin of his notebook, "I don't know who is right. I know what each side was afraid of. Is that enough?" and, after a minute, added, "Maybe that's the essay."

He packed slowly. At the door Mrs. Okafor was logging the last visitors out, and she nodded at his bag. "Did you find your seam?"

"Maybe," Levi said. "I found a book about the Cold War instead of the French Revolution, and it told me how to write about the French Revolution. But half my historians still won't line up."

"Good," she said, and held the door for an elderly couple shuffling toward the exit. "The ones who line up too neatly are usually hiding something."

Arianna had forty-one dollars, a market full of October, and a theory that if she planned the whole week's meals in advance she would stop buying the seven-dollar cheese croissant every time her roommate Dana said the word "brunch." The theory was untested. So was she. In three weeks she would be at college with a shared kitchen and a meal plan that covered dinner only, which meant five breakfasts and five lunches a week depended on whatever she could learn now, standing between a pumpkin stall and a man selling honey with his dog's face on the label.

She had made a list, which was a kind of victory. Onions, carrots, a sack of potatoes, dried lentils from the grain vendor who called everyone "friend" in a way that made her trust him less. At the tomato stand she hesitated over a bruised half-basket marked down to two dollars, and the vendor, a woman with soil in her knuckle creases, said, "Those are for sauce or soup. Can't eat them raw." Arianna took them. It felt like being let in on something, though she wasn't sure what.

The problem revealed itself slowly, the way a stain does. She had never cooked a meal before, exactly. Her mother made dinner the way other people took showers, privately and without commentary, and Arianna had absorbed nothing except that garlic went in everything and complaining did not. What she wanted, she realized on the bus home with potatoes rolling under the seat, was not one good dinner. It was a system. Something she could do on Sunday and then live off all week, the way Dana lived off one pedicure for a month. Dana had systems. Arianna had cheese croissants.

The community kitchen on Fuller Street ran a Sunday session where anyone could cook, and the woman at the desk said the lentil soup they were making that day was "the same idea you're describing, honey, we make forty servings and freeze them." Arianna had come intending only to watch, but watching lasted four minutes before a man named Renato handed her a wooden spoon and said, "Stir from the bottom, they settle," and after that she was staff.

The kitchen had a huge pot, wide as a truck tire, and Renato ladled the finished soup into containers while narrating his life to anyone within earshot. When Arianna asked whether she could just put a pot like that straight into the fridge, full, he looked at her with something between pity and delight. "You could," he said. "It'd sit warm in the middle for hours. That's why we split it into these shallow ones, it cools fast." He stacked the flat containers like bricks. Arianna wrote it on her list under "onions": shallow containers, not the deep pot. It was the first piece of information all day that felt like a tool rather than a fact.

Her own soup happened the following Sunday, in her mother's kitchen, while her mother was at work and her brother Theo narrated from a stool. Theo was fourteen and blase about nearly everything except the instant noodles he ate like a sycophant praising a king, groaning "so good" at the package before the water even boiled. When Arianna's soup was done, a genuine double batch with the bruised tomatoes cooked down into it, Theo watched her divide it into six flat containers, two inches deep each, and slide them onto the fridge shelf.

"Why not just put the pot in?" he said. "Like Mom does."

"Mom puts it on the counter with a dish towel over it, Theo. It sits there steaming all night." She had looked this up, or rather she had remembered Renato, which felt more reliable than looking things up. A deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours; she'd filed that away the way other people filed phone numbers. Theo shrugged and went back to his noodles, exculpated of all culinary responsibility by his age, or at least using it that way.

The week that followed was not a triumph so much as a series of small, survivable events. Monday's soup needed salt. Tuesday she burned the flatbread while reheating it and ate it anyway, charcoal edges and all, standing at the counter because dishes were already a negotiation she was losing. Wednesday Dana tried the soup, said "this is actually good" in the tone of someone announcing a lab result that had surprised her, and asked for the recipe, which Arianna recited from memory and realized, mid-recitation, she was making half of it up. She hadn't written anything down. She'd been so pleased with the list, the containers, the system, that she'd forgotten the part where the system needed to be repeatable.

Thursday she sat in the empty kitchen with her notebook and tried to reconstruct what she'd actually done, which was also, she supposed, the moment she combined her mother's wordless competence with Renato's loud, narrated method and got something third, something hers: plan the list, buy the marked-down tomatoes, cook double, split it shallow and fast, write it down. What stayed uncertain was everything else, whether Sunday cooking would survive homework and homesickness, whether Dana would keep eating it, whether five dollars of lentils could really carry a week. Friday she found Theo at the stove with one of her containers, and he said, without turning around, "There's one left after this, so."

The garage smelled of motor oil and cold metal, and Mia had spread her chemistry homework across her grandfather's workbench, weighting the pages with a wrench and a jar of screws. She had come to his house for the weekend to recuperate from a week of exams, or that was what she'd told her mother, though mostly she wanted the quiet. The quiet was not cooperating. On the page in front of her, an equilibrium problem sat like a locked door: a reaction at equilibrium, the temperature raised, and the question of which way the system would shift.

She understood shifting fine when the changes were concentrations. Add product, the reaction ate some of it back; remove reactant, the reaction made more. That part felt like a seesaw, like common sense. But temperature was different. Temperature wasn't a substance. It wasn't on either side of the arrow, and her teacher's phrase "the system opposes the change" kept sliding off her mind without catching on anything.

Her grandfather was at the far end of the garage, stripping a bicycle wheel with a rag, and he had said almost nothing since she sat down, which was one of the reasons she liked working here. He let problems stay problems. At home her father would have leaned over her shoulder within two minutes and started guessing, and guessing out loud was worse than silence.

She copied the equation onto a scrap of sandpaper, the only paper left in her bag. Nitrogen and hydrogen on the left, ammonia on the right, the double arrows of equilibrium drawn between them. Below it she'd written, in her own handwriting, "exothermic," because the textbook had said so, and then a question mark so fierce she'd torn the paper slightly with the pen. The forward reaction released heat. So where did the heat go? It came out of the reaction, so it came out the right side, like the ammonia. Like a product.

She sat with that for a moment, then wrote the word heat on the right side of the equation, after the ammonia, in lowercase, almost apologetically. Nitrogen plus hydrogen gives ammonia plus heat. It looked wrong, like graffiti on a textbook, but it also looked like something. She raised the temperature. If heat was on the right, then raising the temperature was like adding product, and the system would oppose her by shifting left, consuming nitrogen and hydrogen, undoing ammonia. She checked the answer in the back of the book and the letters came up correct. She pressed the pen down so hard the sandpaper dented.

"Did you figure it out?" her grandfather asked, not turning around.

"I think so. I wrote heat into the equation, like it's a product. Then everything got easy." She held up the scrap. "If it were endothermic instead, heat would go on the other side. As a reactant. You'd treat it like something the reaction takes in and uses up."

He set down the rag and came over, adjusting his glasses to look at the sandpaper. He had never taken chemistry, she was fairly sure, but he studied her handwriting the way he studied a bicycle chain, patiently, without pretending to expertise he didn't have. "So hot weather would be like adding fuel," he said slowly. "For that kind."

"Sort of backwards from that, actually, but yes, it changes the direction." She heard the hedge in her own voice and decided to keep it there rather than smooth it over. There was still a question she couldn't answer, and she didn't want to hide it under confidence she hadn't earned. She didn't know why temperature behaved like a substance when it wasn't one. The trick worked; she had watched it work; and she could feel the outline of something underneath that she hadn't reached. Maybe the why came next year, in college, or maybe it came from no one, the way most understanding seemed to arrive at her, sideways and unannounced.

"It's like apportionment," her grandfather said, tapping the double arrows. "You move something in, and the balance moves somewhere else to pay for it." He meant it loosely, she thought, the way he used words he'd collected from decades of invoices and hardware catalogs, but the looseness helped. The system had a budget. Everything you added had to be paid for somewhere.

She copied the sandpaper version into her notebook, heat and all, and wrote a small margin note to herself: true, even if I can't say why yet. Outside, the afternoon had started turning that melancholic gray that came before October rain, and the light through the garage door's small window had gone the color of pencil lead. She gathered the screws back into their jar and put the wrench where it belonged, not because he'd asked but because the bench felt like a place that deserved order.

On Monday there would be a quiz, and she would probably get the exothermic ones right, and possibly the endothermic ones too, and possibly she would encounter some third kind that undid her. That was fine, or fine enough. She had one working tool and one open question, and for now, at seventeen, that seemed like an honest apportionment of what a person could know. She folded the scrap of sandpaper and put it in the pocket of her jacket.

"Supper at six," her grandfather said, picking up the wheel again. "Bring your notebook. I want to see those arrows."

Jordan had told his mother the assignment was basically finished, which was true in the sense that a house is basically finished when the frame is up. He'd brought the folder to his grandmother's house for the long weekend because she had a real desk and because nobody at school would be around to ask him how it was going. The assignment asked for a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and he had chosen two papers about whether remote learning narrowed or widened achievement gaps. He had read both twice. He had opinions. What he did not have was any idea how to make the opinions sit next to each other on the page without one of them winning by default.

His grandmother set a mug of coffee beside the folder and said she was going to the garden and that he should not let the desk go to waste. He arranged the two articles side by side. The first, by a researcher named Achebe, argued that gaps widened, and it underpinned the claim with test scores from three districts. The second, by a Dr. Lindqvist, argued the data were too noisy to say anything yet, and Jordan had privately decided Lindqvist was just being a coward about it. Privately, and somewhat unfairly, because Lindqvist's tone was mild where Achebe's was acerbic, and Jordan had confused mildness with weakness before.

He wrote for an hour and a half. It went badly. Every paragraph he produced was a summary with a verdict stapled to the end, like Achebe says this, and he's right, and then Lindqvist says this, and he's wrong. He could feel the essay becoming a courtroom where he was judge, prosecutor and stenographer, and the verdict never changed no matter what the witnesses said, which suggested the courtroom was decorative. He deleted two pages. Then he ate a peach on the porch and told himself he was thinking, which was half true.

His grandmother came back with tomatoes and asked, not looking at him, whether the work was going well. "It's fine," he said. "It's basically done." She said that was good and put the tomatoes in the bowl with the peaches, and something about the way she did it, the older fruit to the top where he'd see it, made him feel caught, though she hadn't said anything catching. He went back to the desk and opened the folder again.

This time he tried the opposite of what he'd been doing. Instead of deciding who was right, he wrote down what each article assumed before it argued anything. Achebe assumed the test scores measured the thing that mattered. Lindqvist assumed that without knowing who had actually logged on during remote instruction, the scores could be measuring attendance rather than learning. Jordan sat back. The two men weren't disagreeing about the answer. They were disagreeing about what the question was even made of. He wrote a sentence that began "Where Achebe treats the scores as evidence, Lindqvist treats them as an artifact," and it was the first sentence all day he actually liked.

He kept going until dark, and somewhere in the rush he assembled his list of sources, which he typed up in the order he'd used them: Achebe first, then a school district report, then Lindqvist, then a statistics textbook. He sent the draft to Priya, who was in the writing club with him and who had agreed weeks ago to trade reviews over the weekend. Then he went down to the kitchen and told his grandmother, with more honesty than he'd managed at noon, that it had been going badly and now it was going better. She said the peaches were the ripe ones.

Priya called at nine. "Your argument part is good," she said, which he made her repeat. "Like actually good. But your sources list is wrong." He said it couldn't be wrong, it was just a list. She said she'd made the same mistake last year and lost points for it. "In Chicago, MLA, and APA, entries in the final list of sources are alphabetical by the author's surname," she said. "Not in the order you cited them." He looked at his page. Achebe, then the district report, then Lindqvist, then the textbook, exactly the order of use, exactly wrong. He told her the system was arbitrary and she said maybe, but it was the arbitrary system everyone used, and then she asked whether he really thought Lindqvist's position was weaker or just less fun to read.

That question sat in him while he reordered the list, Achebe first anyway by luck of the alphabet, then the district report under D, then Lindqvist, then the textbook under T. It occurred to him that alphabetical order didn't care who was right either. It didn't care about the order of ideas, or the order of anything. It was a convention, a flat surface the actual thinking had to sit on, and nobody confused the surface with the thinking. He wondered whether his earlier draft had made that exact confusion, treating the sequence in which he'd encountered the articles as if it were the structure of his judgment.

He wrote one more paragraph that night, at the desk with the lamp on and the window open to the sound of the garden. He put both positions together and then was honest about the seam: he wrote that his own reading leaned toward Lindqvist's caution, but that he could not rule out that this was because Achebe's tone had irritated him, and that the evidence Achebe presented was real evidence even if it was thinner than Achebe believed. He read the paragraph over twice. It did not conclude. It ended with a question he didn't answer, and for the first time all weekend that felt like strength rather than failure.

In the morning his grandmother asked if he'd finished, and he said mostly, and she raised an eyebrow at the difference between that and basically done. He laughed. He told her the list of sources at the end had to be alphabetical, and she said she didn't know that, and he said neither had he until yesterday. She poured him more coffee and said his grandfather had once written a whole thesis with the footnotes on cards spread across the kitchen floor, and that some things you learn late and some things you learn just in time.

He packed the folder, and Priya texted a picture of her own reordered list with the caption check yours twice, and he texted back a photo of his, Achebe, district, Lindqvist, textbook, all in a row. "Read it one more time on the train," she wrote. He said he would. He slid the articles into the folder with the final list on top.

Sofia had volunteered to run the peer health table at the pharmacy on Saturday mornings because the alternative was a second shift shelving shampoo, and the pharmacist, Mrs. Okafor, had said the table counted as community service, which Sofia needed for her scholarship application. The table itself was a folding card table between the cough drops and the photo counter, and her job was to hand out flyers about the teen clinic two bus stops away and answer questions, even though she had only been trained once, in a conference room with bad coffee, by a nurse who talked fast.

The training was supposed to have a second session, on consent and contraception and testing, but it had been cancelled twice, and Mrs. Okafor had told her, do your best, you're not diagnosing anything, you're pointing at a door. That had felt like enough until a girl from her chemistry class, Dana, appeared in front of the table at nine-forty with her hands in her hoodie pocket, looking at the vitamins behind Sofia's head.

"I need to ask something but you can't tell anyone," Dana said.

Sofia came around the table, which was a gesture she had learned from the nurse, get on the same side of the thing, though she was aware of how it might look, two girls whispering between the antacids. Dana's question came out in pieces. She had been with a boy from the archipelago of magnet schools across the county, someone Sofia vaguely knew, someone with a reputation she did not fully trust, and the condom had broken, and now she wanted to get tested but her mother read the mail, and her mother read the insurance statements, and her mother would need to sign.

"Does she, though," Sofia said, and realized as she said it that she did not know.

The fact surfaced slowly, from a folded pamphlet in the box under the table, the one with the small print she had skipped during the single training. All 50 states and Washington, DC, let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections themselves, without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age. Sofia read it twice with the pamphlet tilted away from the photo counter, where a man was waiting for his blood pressure pills. She told Dana the shape of it, that no form was coming home, no signature required, that she could walk into the clinic Monday. Dana asked what the minimum age was in their state, and Sofia had to say she didn't know that part, and that the clinic would. Dana nodded, wrote the address on her wrist in pen, and bought a pack of hair ties so it would look like she had a reason to have been at the pharmacy, which Sofia thought was a strange and careful kind of planning.

It was the consent part Sofia had not prepared for, and it kept coming up. A boy from the middle school stopped by to take a flyer because his friends dared him to, and Sofia found herself saying, it means yes, and it means you can change a yes, and it has to be a yes you actually said, not one somebody decided for you. She was transliterating, really, taking what the nurse had said in her fast conference-room voice and putting it letter by letter into ordinary words, and she could feel the places where the translation was thin. A girl asked whether the pill made you gain weight and Sofia said some kinds can, and you can switch kinds, and the clinic helps you do that, and she heard herself sounding almost like a person who knew things, which was itself a kind of warning she decided to notice rather than ignore.

By eleven she had explained condoms to two boys who were too embarrassed to hold still, walked one woman toward the emergency contraception shelf with the flatness Mrs. Okafor had modeled for her, and given out the clinic's number nine times. When Mrs. Okafor passed with a cart of deodorant, she paused and said, "You're better at this than the last one," and Sofia said "than the last what," and Mrs. Okafor said "than the last volunteer, obviously," and rolled the cart on.

At noon Dana came back. She was holding a receipt and a pharmacy bag with a toothbrush in it, and she said her cousin had driven her to the clinic on a Saturday hunch, and they had been open, and the intake nurse had not asked for a single parental thing. "I signed my own name on my own line," Dana said, as though the line itself were the discovery. Then she leaned in and said, "I told them you sent me, and they asked if you'd want to train the next peer group. They said you already know the law." Sofia looked at the pamphlet still in her hand, at the paragraph she had read to one person, once. "Tell them I know one paragraph," she said.

Dana zipped her hoodie and walked out past the photo counter, and Mrs. Okafor set a second folding table against the wall beside the first one.

The cones in the driving school lot were orange and scuffed, and Kate had backed between them eleven times before Mr. Reyes said anything at all. He sat in the passenger seat with his clipboard against his knee, the window cracked to let the August heat escape in slow degrees. On the twelfth attempt she came in too wide, corrected too late, and ended with her rear tire resting against the curb like an apology.

"You're looking at the cones," he said. "Look where you want the car to be."

She tried again. The car slid in on a smooth arc, and when she straightened the wheel and looked up, the cone behind her was close enough to touch through the rear window, and the one ahead had a hand's width of clearance. Mr. Reyes made a small mark on his clipboard that could have meant anything.

Kate had a reason for being here that went beyond the ordinary one. Her mother was moving at the end of the month to an apartment across the river, closer to the hospital where she'd taken the night shifts, and Kate would be staying in the old house with her father on the weeks he wasn't traveling. The two addresses were forty minutes apart by two buses and one transfer, and the transfer never came on time. A license would emancipate her from the bus schedule entirely, from waiting under a shelter with a broken panel, from arriving places already tired. She had explained none of this to Mr. Reyes. He knew only what the clipboard said.

Between parking runs, while another student took the car, Kate sat on the metal bench at the edge of the lot with her math homework on her knees. The chapter was on induction, and the book kept using a word she'd had to look up twice: lemma, a smaller result you proved first, on your way to the thing you actually wanted. She liked that there was a word for it. Almost everything in her life at the moment felt like a lemma, a preliminary step whose only meaning was that it came before something else.

That afternoon her mother had texted her a phone number and a question about the new apartment. Her mother was at work and couldn't call the landlord, so it had fallen to Kate, who was sitting in the driving school office with the landline and a scrap of paper. When the landlord picked up, he was eating something, and he set it down.

"I can do the rent," Kate said, "but I'm trying to figure out the electric bill. Do you know what the last tenant used?"

"Six hundred kilowatt-hours a month, give or take," he said. "That's a pretty normal month there. Electricity gets billed by the kilowatt-hour, so you can work it out yourself if you know the rate."

"What's the rate?"

"Fifteen cents a kilowatt-hour, out there."

Kate wrote the numbers down. On the paper, under the scrap of the lemma she'd copied out at the bench, she multiplied six hundred by fifteen and got ninety dollars, and then, remembering something the landlord had muttered about service fees, she asked whether anything else got added on.

"There's fixed monthly charges from the utility, whatever those are," he said. "The ninety is just the usage part. Before those."

She thanked him and hung up. Ninety dollars, plus whatever the fixed charges turned out to be, on top of rent, out of a night-shift paycheck. She sat with that number for a moment. It was not catastrophic, and it was not nothing, and she could not decide which it was more of, because the fixed charges were still unknown and she had learned this year not to round unknowns in either direction.

Back in the car, it was highway merging, which Mr. Reyes said was where students failed who had passed everything else. The on-ramp rose and curved, and the traffic in the right lane came on at highway speed, and Kate's hands were damp on the wheel. She signaled, checked the mirror, checked it again, and then made the error Mr. Reyes had warned her about on paper and never yet in person: she slowed instead of speeding up, hunting for a gap so perfect that it would never arrive. A truck bore down, flashing its lights, and she had to ride the shoulder for a hundred yards before an opening came.

"Braking on a ramp," Mr. Reyes said calmly, as they came back around for another try. "It's a pernicious habit. It feels careful, and it's the most dangerous thing you can do up there."

"But what if there's no gap?"

"There's always a gap if you're going the speed of the traffic. You're asking the highway to accommodate you. Don't. Arrive at the speed it's already going, and the gap makes itself."

She thought about that on the second run. It ran against something in her, the same something that had made her creep between the cones with inches to spare, the belief that safety came from minimizing your presence, from taking up exactly the room you were given and no more. But the merge required the opposite: to meet the traffic at its own speed, to claim a space. Somewhere in the two ideas there was a middle she couldn't yet name, a way of being careful that didn't mean shrinking.

The second merge was not perfect. She came on a little fast, corrected, and slid into the lane a half-length behind a blue hatchback whose driver never even looked at her, which was somehow the point. On the way back down the off-ramp, Mr. Reyes made another mark on the clipboard, the same mark as before, she thought, though she couldn't be sure.

"One more week of this," he said, "then we book the test."

That evening she texted her mother the number, ninety dollars a month for the electricity usage before the fixed charges, six hundred kilowatt-hours at fifteen cents, and asked if that changed anything. The reply took an hour to come. While she waited, she carried her math book to the kitchen table and worked through the lemma again, proving the small thing first, the preliminary thing, the thing you needed before you could need the rest. Her mother's answer arrived at last, and it was only three words long, and Kate read it twice before she set the phone face-down beside the book and picked up her pencil. "It'll work."

The museum was nearly empty on weekday afternoons, which was exactly why Felix came. He had a physics placement exam on Monday that would decide whether he started college in the introductory section or one level up, and his bedroom had stopped being a place where thinking happened. Here, at the ballistics exhibit, a small brass cannon fired a ball across a dark chamber once every eight seconds, and a strobe light froze it into a string of pearl-bright positions against a gridded wall. Felix had his notebook open on the railing, and he was losing to the problem.

He kept trying to compute the whole arc at once, one velocity, one angle, everything tangled together, and the numbers collapsed every time. On the fourth shot he stopped writing and simply watched the strobe. The horizontal spacing between the pearls was even. Every single image, the same distance across. The vertical spacing, though, widened going down, ball images spreading apart like a dropped handful of coins. He wrote that in the margin, then drew two small axes, and something loosened. Nothing pulls the ball sideways, he thought, so across it just keeps whatever it started with. Up and down is where the gravity gets to act, alone, on its own clean problem. The motion wasn't one thing. It was two, stacked.

A boy of maybe ten arrived at the railing with a half-eaten pretzel and an expression that augured poorly for Felix's concentration. The boy's name, announced unprompted, was Deshawn, and he wanted to know why the ball went farther when the cannon tilted up but not when it tilted up too far.

"Forty-five degrees," Felix said, and then, because that would mean nothing, "watch the even spacing. When you tilt it, you trade across for up. Too steep and you have tons of up, which gravity just eats, and barely any across." He angled his notebook so Deshawn could see the two axes. "You have to split it. That's the trick. That's the whole trick."

"Split every throw?" Deshawn said. "Like my dad throws footballs?"

"Every one," Felix said. "Rockets, spitballs, everything."

Deshawn nodded with the gravity of someone being inducted into a secret, then wandered off toward the electricity hall, and Felix, surprisingly, missed him. He worked the problem again with the split, and the pearls lined up with his arithmetic almost exactly. The gap he couldn't close was small, and he suspected his strobe timing, not his physics, which was a feeling so unfamiliar it took him a moment to recognize it as confidence.

He found Deshawn ten minutes later at the Van de Graaff exhibit, where a docent named Renata was demonstrating field effects, and Deshawn was looking worried that the machine's crackle would hurt him. Renata noticed too. She crouched to his height and said the dome was loud the way thunder is loud, and that she would hold his hand the whole time if he wanted to touch the field meter's wand. He did want. She kept her word.

The wand read out the electric field strength at different distances from the dome, numbers on a small screen. Renata asked the small crowd to guess which nearby speck of dust, floating in the air, would feel the bigger push: the speck carrying a small charge or the speck carrying twice that charge, both sitting in the same field. Someone said it made no difference. Deshawn, with total intransigence, said the small one, because it was lighter.

"Field's the same for both," Felix said slowly, working it aloud, watching the screen. "The force on a charge in a field is the charge times the field strength, F equals q E. Same field, double the charge, double the force." Renata glanced at him, checking, and he nodded to say he'd stand behind that. Deshawn squinted at the floating specks as though they had personally deceived him.

"So the dust with more charge gets pushed harder," Renata said, "just like that, straight from the field." She let Deshawn move the wand and watch the field numbers climb as he neared the dome, his fear apparently filed away under matters already handled.

Walking out past the ballistics chamber, Felix stopped at the railing one last time. The cannon fired. The strobe caught the ball mid-air, pearls strung even across, spreading down, and he copied the spacing into his notebook without doing a single calculation. Deshawn's father probably threw better footballs than Felix ever would, but that was fine. He had what he'd come for, and he wrote at the bottom of the page, underlining it twice, "split it first, always."

"Forty-five degrees," said Deshawn, appearing at his elbow with the last of the pretzel.

"Forty-five degrees," Felix agreed.

Carter had exactly one day left before his driving test, and the cones at the far end of the school parking lot were waiting for him like a verdict. His mother had left the car keys on the kitchen counter beside a note that said only "5pm," which was when she got home and when, by prior arrangement, the test would already be behind him. So the afternoon was his, and the empty lot with its faded lines was his, and the recalcitrant cone at the corner of his imaginary parking space refused, on his first three attempts, to remain upright.

"You're turning the wheel too early," said Priya from the curb, where she sat cross-legged with a chemistry textbook she was visibly not reading.
