She had agreed to come on the condition that Carter drive her to her debate tournament on Saturday, win or lose, license or no license. "You keep cutting it before your back wheel is even with the cone."

"I know what I'm doing," Carter said, which was untrue in a way they both understood. He had watched four videos that morning, each ascribing slightly different timing to the same set of motions, so that the advice had begun to cancel itself out. One instructor swore by the two o'clock method; another called that an oversimplification and recommended watching the rear tire. Carter had tried to apportion his trust between them, giving each video half his confidence, and the result was a parking job that would have flattened a mailbox.

He backed up, reset, and tried again, this time counting aloud. The car slid in close to the curb on the fourth attempt, close enough that Priya stood and walked over to eyeball it. "Maybe eighteen inches," she said. "That's passing distance." She tapped the roof twice, the way his mother did, and Carter felt something loosen in his chest. It was not joy exactly. It was more like the feeling of a proof coming out, the answer arriving after the work rather than before it.

But the parking lot was the easy part, and they both knew the test ended with a short drive, and the drive included the on ramp to Route 9. So at four o'clock, with the sun going low and orange across the windshields of the teacher lot, Carter signaled, checked his mirrors, and pulled out of the school drive toward the highway. Priya came with him because she refused to let him face the ramp alone, and also, she admitted, because her tournament was Saturday and she intended to arrive in a vehicle, not on two buses.

The ramp climbed and curved, and the merge lane shortened faster than the videos had suggested it would. Carter checked the side mirror, saw nothing, and began to drift left. Priya made a sound, a short inhale, and Carter glanced over his shoulder through the rear passenger window and there it was: a gray sedan sitting beside him, close enough that he could see the driver's mouth moving, the driver talking to someone Carter could not see. He straightened the wheel and stayed in his lane until the sedan passed and the road behind him emptied.

"Mirrors," Carter said, when they had pulled into a gas station and stopped, both of his hands still on the wheel. "Mirrors leave blind spots, right there beside the car." He turned in his seat and looked at the space where the sedan had been, then at the mirror that had shown him nothing. "I looked. I actually looked, and it wasn't there."

"That's why you turn your head," Priya said. "My dad calls it the shoulder check. He made me practice it forty times before he'd let me near his car." She checked her phone, saw three messages from her debate partner about rebuttal evidence, and typed a quick reply. "So you look twice now. Mirror, then shoulder. Both, every time."

Carter nodded slowly. The two views of driving he had been trying to reconcile all week, the videos that treated it as a system of rules and his mother's way of treating it as a matter of habit and feel, were not actually opposed. The rule was the shoulder check; the habit was doing it until it was as automatic as breathing. What he still did not know, and could not know until the examiner slid into the passenger seat tomorrow morning, was whether a half day of practice was enough to make a habit out of anything. He started the car, checked the mirror, and turned his head anyway.

"Okay," he said. "Once more around the block, then your turn to buy the gas station coffee."

"Deal," said Priya. "But if you pass tomorrow, I'm picking the music on Saturday."

The theory room above the concert hall smelled of radiator dust and old coffee, and Logan spread his staff paper across the table just as the piano downstairs began the afternoon rehearsal. He had sixteen blank bars to fill by Friday, a melody with chord changes written in standard notation, and so far he had four bars he liked and twelve he was faking.

His friend Dev slid into the chair across from him and pulled the sheet over without asking. "Bar three's good. The rest is you avoiding bar three."

"It's development," Logan said.

"It's wandering." Dev tapped the empty measures. "You've got a D minor seven going nowhere and then this G that sounds like you got bored."

That was accurate, which annoyed Logan, because he had spent two evenings on the G. He took the sheet back and played the four good bars on his phone keyboard, then the rest, and heard it the way Dev must have heard it: a sentence that started and then cleared its throat for eight bars. The rehearsal downstairs broke off mid-phrase and started again, and he listened to the pianist play the same passage twice, the second time slower, the way you'd repeat something to make sure it was true.

He tried a new approach. Instead of inventing bars five through sixteen, he wrote a return: bar one's melody, brought back over a different chord, then under the original chord, the way the rehearsal downstairs kept circling its opening theme. When he played it for Dev, Dev shrugged in a way that was equivocal, half nod and half wince, and Logan made him point to the wince. It was bar fourteen. The melody had come home, the chords had settled onto the tonic, and then there were two more bars on the page that did nothing but repeat the final chord like a guest who did not realize the party had ended.

"So end at fourteen," Dev said.

"I need sixteen. The assignment is sixteen bars." Logan stared at the last two measures. The problem was not that he lacked notes; it was that he lacked a reason for them. Everything before bar fourteen had a job. These two bars were after the job was done.

Downstairs the rehearsal reached its ending, and then, after what Logan had assumed was the ending, the piano kept going for another phrase, brief and firm, hammering the home key twice and landing hard on the tonic. Logan stopped writing. He listened to the whole thing again in his head. The melody had ended, resolved, and then this extra bit had come after and made the ending feel finished rather than merely over.

He leaned over the railing by the stairs and caught the rehearsal assistant, a conservatory student named Petra, coming up with a thermos. "That last part," he said. "After the piece ends. What is that?"

"A coda," Petra said. "Optional closing section. Comes after the recapitulation, reinforces the home key, brings the movement to an end." She stepped past him, then paused. "You can also skip it."

Back at the table, he wrote the word in pencil above his final two bars and then tried to make the bars earn it. Not a repetition of the ending, but a reinforcement: the tonic chord voiced lower, the melody's first three notes descending instead of rising, a quiet echo rather than an announcement. He played it for Dev without saying anything first. Dev listened all the way through, which he rarely did.

"That's it," Dev said. "The last two bars sound like they mean to be there."

Logan erased the pencil word and wrote it again more neatly. He was aware of a small, dishonest impulse to explain to Dev what he had done, to frame the coda as a plan he'd had from the start, and he let the impulse pass without acting on it, though he could not exactly exculpate himself either, since he had already half-opened his mouth before deciding not to. Some things you just didn't do, and that was the whole of it.

At the piano that evening, in the empty hall after the rehearsal crew had gone, he played the sixteen bars through at tempo. Bars one to four still worked. Five through thirteen still wandered a little, and he heard it plainly now, without Dev needing to say so. The return at fourteen landed. The coda landed after it. He played the whole thing a second time and then, because Petra had said it was optional, he played it once more ending at fourteen, no coda, to hear the difference.

Both endings were defensible. The one without the coda stopped like a held breath; the one with it settled like a door closing on a soft latch. He sat with his hands on the keys and could not decide which was truer, and he thought that might be the actual thing he was learning, though he would not have said it that way to anyone. He wrote "with coda" in the corner of the page, then looked at it, then left it.

He packed his sheet music, checked the practice room was empty, and let himself out through the stage door into the parking lot, still humming the last three notes.

Jeremy had signed up to be a peer health educator mostly because the training counted for service hours and because Priya Raman had signed up too, and he was not proud of the arithmetic, but there it was. On the first Tuesday of training, Ms. Okafor handed out a plastic bin of demonstration kits and told them they would learn to explain consent, contraception, and clinic testing well enough to teach it to freshmen. "You will be asked questions you cannot answer," she said. "Practice saying 'I don't know, but I know who does.'" That sentence alone felt worth the whole hour.

The second Tuesday was held in the empty seminar room with the good chairs, and a nurse from the county clinic came with a rolling suitcase that clattered like a fish cart. Her name was Dee. She spread out brochures in fans, burnishing each one flat with the heel of her hand as though the creases were personal insults. Then she had them pair off and role-play. Jeremy drew Marcus Wei, who folded his arms and announced, in the voice of a difficult freshman, "I feel fine, so why would I go get tested for anything?"

Jeremy opened his mouth and closed it. He had been about to say something about being responsible, which he understood instantly would sound like a poster. Dee drifted over, not to rescue him, just to listen with her arms crossed. "Here's the thing," Jeremy tried instead. "You could still have something." Marcus, staying in character, said feeling fine was proof enough for him. Jeremy faltered, and Dee crouched beside their chairs. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all," she said. "Testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." Then she straightened up and walked away, leaving the sentence sitting between them like a coin someone had dropped.

Marcus broke character. "Wait, seriously? None?" Jeremy shrugged, but the fact had already rearranged something in his head, the way a hallway looks different after you learn there's a room behind the wall. He thought of his cousin Daniel, who two years ago had sworn up and down that he was clean because he felt clean, the way people swear a car is fine because it starts. Daniel had ended up at a clinic anyway, in March, for reasons nobody in the family would state out loud at Thanksgiving. Jeremy had been fifteen and had not asked a single question.

The role-play went on. Priya, across the room, was handling her freshman with a kind of brisk comedy, miming a condom package instructions leaflet like a flight attendant, and Jeremy laughed despite himself. When it was his turn to play the reluctant student, he made himself truly obnoxious, drawling, "But I feel amazing," until Priya's partner, Sasha, laughed so hard she had to put her head on the table. Dee let the noise run itself out. "Good," she said. "If you can survive this room, you can survive a freshman who thinks he's immortal."

At the end, Ms. Okafor asked each of them to say one thing they would carry into the presentations. Priya said something about the clinic's walk-in hours. Marcus said, to Jeremy's surprise, "The no symptoms thing. That one's going to stick with people." Jeremy had been planning to say something more abstract, about listening before informing, which he privately suspected was an encapsulation of everything he'd absorbed in two Tuesdays, but the word felt too polished for the room, so he abandoned it at the last second and said, "Say 'I don't know, but I know who does.' It actually works." Ms. Okafor nodded like she'd already known that.

Walking out, he caught up with Marcus by the water fountain. "You argued pretty hard in there," Jeremy said. "For a fake freshman." Marcus drank for a long time. "My brother," he said finally, "spent a year feeling fine." He didn't add anything, and Jeremy didn't ask, because some things you leave where they're set down. The hallway smelled like floor wax and somebody's microwaved lunch, and outside the windows the November light had gone the color of dishwater, capricious enough that it might storm or might turn gold within the hour.

Jeremy thought about Daniel again, on the bus home, and about how he'd never once said the word clinic in that house, and about whether honesty was a duty you owed family or a presumption. He didn't land anywhere. He took out his notebook and wrote, "feeling fine is not proof," and underlined it twice, then added a question mark, because he was seventeen and had learned just enough to know that certainty was usually somebody else's confidence borrowed without permission.

The following Tuesday, Ms. Okafor scheduled the first real presentation for December, ninth graders, forty minutes, no co-teacher. She asked for a volunteer. Priya's hand went up fast as a shutter. Jeremy's went up a half second later, and he kept it there.

Lucas arrived at the community center twenty minutes early, notebook against his chest, because Ms. Ferreira had offered the only extra credit she offered all semester: attend the town hall on the county charter question and transcribe the public comments verbatim for the school paper. He found a folding chair near the back, third row, where he could see both the podium and the exit. The room smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and a fan in the corner turned its head slowly, like it was deciding whom to blame.

The meeting opened with the Pledge, then a budget item about the firehouse roof, then the charter amendment itself. When the moderator called for questions, a woman at the microphone said the whole thing felt rigged, like some foreign parliament where nobody votes for anything directly. Lucas's pencil stopped. He was supposed to be neutral, a transcription machine, but his own government class was swimming in his head, and he wanted, suddenly and badly, to be the one who answered her.

He got his chance in the lobby afterward, at a folding table where volunteers handed out voter registration forms. A girl from the college, tabling for a civic engagement club, had been explaining something to an older man in a gravel trucker cap, and Lucas drifted close enough to hear. "So they got a king over there," the man said, "and a prime minister under him? What's the king for, then, decoration?"

"Basically," the girl said. "In a lot of parliamentary systems the head of state is separate from the head of government. The monarch or the ceremonial president does the ribbon cuttings and the prime minister actually runs things." She tapped her stack of forms square. "In the United States our president is both."

Lucas had written a paper two weeks ago claiming the opposite, that a prime minister was just a president with a British accent, and Ms. Ferreira had marked it with a single question mark that he had not followed up on. The question mark had been sitting in his folder since, half shame and half splinter. Now the splinter moved. He waited until the gravel man took his form and left, then stepped up to the table.

"I got that backwards on a paper," he said. "I said the prime minister and the king were the same office in different centuries."

The girl laughed, not unkindly. "Half my intro class did too, first week."

"Is there a way to test which I actually understand," Lucas asked, "besides writing it again and hoping?" He explained about the town hall, the transcript, the woman who thought anything parliamentary was rigged. He asked whether he could quote the exchange at her table. She said that depended on its veracity, which he should check somewhere better than a folding table, and slid a thin blue textbook across it. "Chapter four. Borrow it, bring it back to the next meeting."

He sat on the curb outside with the book while the parking lot emptied, headlights sweeping the brick face of the firehouse. Chapter four laid the two systems side by side, and what struck him was not the diagram but the removal part: a parliament could withdraw its confidence and the head of government was gone, sometimes inside a week, while here a president served out the term unless the whole cumbersome machinery of impeachment turned over. One made it easy to fire the boss and hard to know who'd be next; the other made the boss nearly immovable and the succession perfectly predictable. He had always assumed predictability was the obvious good. Now he wasn't sure which he'd choose if the choice were his, and the not-sure felt less like failure than like the room had gotten bigger.

Inside, the cleanup crew was stacking chairs, and Ms. Ferreira was zipping her bag by the door. She saw the blue book on his knees. "You followed the question mark," she said.

"I got it wrong first," Lucas said. "Then a girl at the registration table, she's from the college, she set me straight, and I'm not done deciding which system I'd actually defend." He stood. "The woman who called it rigged, in there. Part of what bothered her is that in the parliamentary version you never vote for the head of government directly, and part of what bothers me about our version is the opposite. I can argue both sides now. That's new."

Ms. Ferreira looked at him for a long moment, the fan still turning its slow head behind her. "Then write that," she said, "the both-sides version, with the transcript attached," and held the door open.

Outside, the October air had gone cold and the last car's exhaust hung white under the streetlight. Lucas tucked the blue book under his arm where he wouldn't drop it, took out his phone, and typed a note to himself: return book, next meeting. Then, underneath, still standing in the emptying lot, he added a second line and read it back to himself aloud: "Ask her name."

Gavin stood in his mother's kitchen on the last Sunday of August, five days before he left for college, with a legal pad on the counter and a pen that kept dying. She had handed him the pad that morning and said if he was going to refuse the meal plan, he had to prove he could do this, and she wanted to see a full week by tonight. Not intentions. A list, a budget, a cooking plan, all before she drove him to the train station at seven.

He started the way he started most things, by writing headings and admiring them. Monday. Tuesday. Then he got stuck, because he realized he did not know how many meals a week actually contained. Twenty-one sounded hedonistic and impossible, like something from a banquet, but skipping breakfast was how he had lived for years and his mother would circle it in red if she saw it. He texted his cousin Dana, who had survived two years of apartment life on rice and stubbornness.

Her reply came as a long message he read aloud to the empty kitchen. "Batch cook on Sunday, one big pot, portion it out, and get a food thermometer, the instant-read kind. Mine saved me twice. Leftovers aren't a vibe, they're a temperature." He read the last line twice. He had been imagining leftovers as a matter of smell and confidence, the way his father reheated chili from 1998 on pure faith. Dana made it sound like math.

The deadline tightened around lunchtime when his mother came through in her coat, car keys already out. "I'm doing the shopping run at four," she said, not unkindly. "If your list is done, you come and buy it yourself. If it isn't, I'll buy what I think you need." He heard the offer inside the threat, that she would feed him either way, and it made him want the other thing more. He called Dana from the pantry while he inventoried.

"Rice, chicken thighs, two kinds of beans, onions, whatever vegetable is on sale," she recited, the sound of her own chopping undulate... he smiled and corrected himself under his breath; her voice undulated with the rhythm of the knife, rising and dipping. "Cook it all at once, portion it into containers, fridge for four days, freezer for the rest. And when you reheat, check the middle with the thermometer." He asked her what number he was looking for. "The USDA says 74 degrees Celsius," she said. "That's 165 Fahrenheit." He wrote both on his hand, because the pen had died again.

At the store he learned that planning and shopping were separate humiliations. The chicken cost more than his spreadsheet claimed it would, and the sale vegetable was cabbage, which he bought out of principle and without a single idea for it. In the checkout line an older man ahead of him muttered something about prices never coming down no matter what the news said, a word Gavin half caught, stagflation, and filed away to look up later. His mother watched him count out the total in bills and said nothing, which was its own kind of help.

The cooking itself filled the kitchen with steam and took two hours longer than the plan said. He cubed the chicken badly, wept over the onions, and discovered that cabbage, shredded and fried with the beans, was actually good, which felt like a small and private victory over the whole concept of planning. By six he had nine containers cooling in rows on the counter, and a thermometer in his pocket that he had not yet used.

He used it at ten to seven, reheating a test portion of rice and chicken in the microwave, the train now an hour away. He stuck the probe into the center of the pile and watched the number climb and stall at 61 Celsius. Under. He stirred the portion, put it back in, and tried again. 74 on the display, 165 on the small secondary line, and he stood there holding the thing like it was proof of something. He still did not know if he would actually eat this way in October, when the novelty wore off and midterms ate his Sundays, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open on the pad, in the margin, unanswered.

His mother honked from the driveway at seven. Gavin grabbed his bag, then went back for the thermometer and the container of rice and chicken still warm in his hand, and carried both out to the car. "You can test it when we stop," he said. "It hit 74 in the middle."

Blake found the box in his grandfather's study on the second morning of the visit, wedged between a set of encyclopedias nobody had opened since the nineties and a photograph of soldiers posing in front of a canvas tent. The box held his grandfather's old college papers, and on top, yellowed and soft at the corners, was an essay titled "Atomic Diplomacy and the Revisionist Case." Blake sat down on the carpet with it before he had decided to.

His grandfather found him there an hour later, holding the essay under the window light. "That was a long time ago," his grandfather said. "A professor made us argue a position we didn't hold. I got the side that lost, more or less." He set a mug of coffee on the desk, within Blake's reach but not offered, which Blake understood as an offer anyway.

The argument was this: that the atomic bombs dropped on Japan were not only about ending the war. Blake read the paragraph twice. The paper cited a historian named Gar Alperovitz, who had argued in a book called Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, that the bombs were used partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Not instead of ending the war. Partly. Blake kept coming back to that word, because his friend Dominic had shouted something like this at the war memorial on the school trip in April, and Blake had shouted back, and neither of them had known enough to know who was right.

He had said to Dominic, at the memorial, under the long wall of names, that the bombings were the last act of World War II, and Dominic had said they were the first act of the Cold War, and they had argued until the teacher moved them to opposite ends of the group. Blake had gone home angry in the specific way that meant he knew he had been arguing from nothing. He had wanted, since then, to be the kind of person who had actually read things, though the wanting had inured him mostly to scrolling summaries on his phone at midnight rather than to any real study. He recognized that now, sitting on his grandfather's carpet with the primary source of a fifty-year-old term paper.

"Did you believe it?" Blake asked. "When you wrote it."

His grandfather moved a stack of mail off the chair and sat. "Belief is a strong word for a nineteen-year-old with a due date. I believed the sources, where they were honest. I distrusted the ones that were tidy." He nodded at the pages in Blake's hands. "The trouble with that argument is it can explain too much. If you already think the diplomats were monsters, everything looks like a weapon aimed at Moscow. And if you think your country was always good, nothing does."

Blake looked at the margin notes, cramped pencil in his grandfather's younger handwriting. Next to one paragraph the note said only "check." He flipped to the bibliography, then back. The Alperovitz claim sat there with a page number, and beside it, another historian's rebuttal with its own page number, and his grandfather's "check" between them like a small flag planted in disputed ground.

That night Blake took his phone to the porch and texted Dominic instead of searching. The porch smelled of his grandfather's pipe tobacco, though nobody had smoked it in years, and the impecunious state of the house, the porch rail gone soft, the gutters pulled straight by hand each fall instead of replaced, meant the tobacco smell would probably outlast the house itself. He typed, "Ok so I found something. This guy Alperovitz argued in 1965 that the bombs were partly to intimidate the Soviets. Partly. Not instead of. I keep getting stuck on partly."

Dominic's reply came in three bubbles. The first said "so I was right." The second said "wait." The third said "partly is annoying though. If it's partly then it's both and we were both yelling about it at the memorial like idiots."

Blake thought about his grandfather saying tidy sources were the ones to distrust, and about how a person could want history to have an autocrat's clarity, one ruler deciding everything, one motive, one clean sentence you could carry to the top of a monument and shout. The truth seemed to be more like the margin note, a check in pencil beside two page numbers, an admission that you had to go read both.

"We weren't idiots," Blake typed. "We were just loud." He looked up at the yard going dark, then back down. "Want to read the book with me? I can get it from the library when I'm home Sunday. You take his side, I'll take the other one, and this time we actually finish it before we fight."

Dominic's answer was a single thumbs up, and then, a minute later: "bring the essay too. Tell your grandpa his handwriting is terrible."

Blake laughed, locked the phone, and carried his grandfather's mug inside to wash it.

The article was four paragraphs long, in Spanish, and Isabella had read the first paragraph six times before the words stopped sliding off her. She sat in the far corner of the school library where the carrels faced the window, her phone face down beside a dictionary she was trying not to open. The piece was from a Chilean paper: the port authority in Valparaíso wanted to expropriate a strip of hillside houses to widen a cargo corridor, and the city council had split over it. She had volunteered for this. Five minutes, in Spanish, in front of the whole class on Thursday, arguing one side and then summarizing the article aloud. Her teacher had said the word "B2" when she assigned it, and Isabella had nodded as if she knew what that meant.

She did not know what that meant. She copied the first sentence into her notebook, then underlined every verb she recognized. Queria. Expropiar. She looked up long enough to see Dana from her class slide into the opposite carrel, drop a binder, and start highlighting something with the concentration of a person performing concentration.

"Ask your phone," Dana said, without looking up.

"I'm not asking my phone."

"You asked your phone for the debate topic."

Isabella turned the phone over. The course outline was in her email, a PDF her teacher had sent in September, and she had never scrolled past the second page. She scrolled now. Under "Trimestre 3" it said, in English, that students at B2 level should be able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. She read it twice. It didn't say argue. It didn't say win. It said explain, and it wanted both sides, advantages and disadvantages, laid out.

"That's it?" Dana leaned across the aisle. "That's all B2 is?"

"That's what the outline says." She turned the screen so Dana could see it.

"So you don't need to beat Tomas. You just need to sound like you read the article."

Isabella pulled the screen back. She had been planning to beat Tomas. Tomas had spent a semester in Madrid and rolled his r's like a native, and she had spent a semester ordering the wrong sandwich at the deli on Fulton Street. She had planned to memorize a script so dense he couldn't get a word in.

She read the second paragraph again. The port handled more cargo than the rail line could carry; a city planner was quoted saying the throughput of the corridor had to double or the shipping companies would move to San Antonio. Throughput. Rendimiento. Even in English the word was a kind of wall. She wrote "throughput" in her notebook and drew an arrow to a house.

Because the third paragraph was the houses. Eleven of them. A woman named Rosa Herrera had lived in hers for forty years, and the compensation offer covered the market price and nothing else, and her street was the only one where the fishermen still repaired nets outside in the evenings. The reporter didn't editorialize. The reporter gave the planner his numbers and gave Rosa her sentence about nets, and then the article ended.

Isabella tried out the summary in a whisper. "El puerto quiere expropiar las casas." Her accent flattened every vowel. She tried it again, louder than she meant to, and a boy two carrels over looked up. She mouthed the rest. To widen the corridor. The throughput. The advantages. She stopped. What were the advantages? Jobs, she guessed, or the city not losing the shipping companies, and she wrote "ventajas" and then nothing under it, because the article hadn't said jobs. She had invented jobs. She crossed it out.

She sat with the crossed-out word for a while. The B2 line wanted advantages and disadvantages of various options, and the article gave her one option, widen and expropriate, and one alternative mentioned in half a sentence, let the companies leave. Rosa Herrera's nets were not an advantage or a disadvantage. Rosa Herrera's nets were a cost that didn't fit in the planner's column, and Isabella did not know whose job it was to say so. Maybe hers. Maybe that was what explaining a viewpoint meant, standing in the gap between the columns.

Dana was watching her. "You're making a face."

"I'm missing something. The article says the companies would go to San Antonio, but it doesn't say what happens to the workers here if they stay. So if I say that's a disadvantage, I'm making it up."

"So say you don't know."

"In Spanish?"

"That's the whole language. 'No se sabe.' That's three words."

Isabella laughed before she could stop it, and the librarian turned from her cart of returns. Isabella lowered her voice. "No se sabe," she said, trying it. The syllables sat more easily than the argument had.

She started over, whispering the summary from the top. The port wanted the houses. The corridor's throughput had to grow. The companies had another option, another port, another city. Rosa Herrera had forty years and a street and an offer that measured neither. "Por una parte," Isabella said, and then, more slowly, "por otra parte." On the one hand. On the other. The scales in the sentence felt honest, like the sentence knew it was leaving something out and was willing to say so. She wrote "no se sabe" at the bottom of her notes and starred it.

Thursday was two days away. Tomas would still roll his r's, and the class would still hear every flat vowel she produced, and she was not sanguine about winning. But the outline hadn't asked her to win. It had asked her to stand there with both hands open, advantages in one, disadvantages in the other, and admit which palm was empty. She read Rosa Herrera's sentence once more, closed the notebook, and slid the article between its pages, the side with the nets facing up.

Xavier arrived at the library twenty minutes before it opened, which was a kind of asceticism he practiced only during exam week, standing in the cold with his backpack straps gripped in both fists. Inside, he claimed the corner carrel by the window, the one with a wobbly leg he had learned to balance with a folded napkin, and laid out his assignment sheet: a comparison essay on how a parliamentary system chooses and removes a head of government, versus how a presidential one does it. Mr. Okafor had written a single comment in red ink at the bottom. "You have listed facts. Now take a position, and admit what you cannot settle."

The problem was that Xavier did not want to admit anything he could not settle. He liked the clean logic of the parliamentary column: the party that wins seats chooses the prime minister, and if the party withdraws confidence, the prime minister falls, sometimes within days, without any election at all. The presidential column was messier: a fixed term, a direct mandate, removal only through the cumbersome machinery of impeachment, which in his sources had rarely succeeded anywhere it had been genuinely attempted. He copied citations, underlined the word "fusion" where one textbook described the blending of executive and legislature, and felt the pleasing click of a system that seemed to hold together.

"Excuse me. Are you the guy who knows where the law books are?" A girl about his age stood at the edge of the carrel, holding a printed outline with the front page curling. Her name, from the badge on her debate binder, was Priya, and she was preparing a moot court argument against a school dress-code policy, along with two classmates who had scattered toward the computers. "We need the most famous line there is about student speech," she said. "Everyone says it exists, nobody remembers the case."

Xavier almost said he was busy. Then he found himself standing, because the assignment in front of him had begun to feel evanescent anyway, the facts thinning out the moment he tried to build a conclusion on them. He led Priya to the constitutional law shelf and they ran fingers along spines until he pulled a casebook with a battered index. She flipped pages while he read over her shoulder, and there it was, in the section on students and the First Amendment.

"Tinker v. Des Moines," Priya read aloud, slowly, getting each piece into her memory. "1969. The Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." She wrote it down twice, then a third time on her palm. Her teammate Marcus came back from the printers waving a copy and she made him recite the case name back to her, and he got the year wrong twice before he got it right. Xavier watched her insist, and something about her insistence rearranged his thinking more than the textbook had.

He returned to his carrel and looked at his two columns again. Priya's problem had a specific question, a famous line, a ruling, and she was building an argument out of them. His essay had no such spine. He had been trying to compare the systems as though one could be proved better, the way he might prove a math answer, and it occurred to him that political systems were not problems with solutions but arrangements with trade-offs. He took out a fresh sheet and began to contextualize the comparison: the parliamentary system made leaders accountable quickly but made governments unstable; the presidential system made governments stable but let an unpopular leader cling to a fixed term. Both columns were describing the same human difficulty from opposite directions.

He wrote for an hour, crossing out whole paragraphs, then a better hour in which he crossed out less. When he could not decide whether quick removal or fixed stability mattered more, he wrote that down instead of hiding it: that the answer depended on whether one feared disorder more than entrenchment, and that reasonable people in the sources disagreed. His pen slowed at that sentence, because admitting uncertainty felt like a failure, and then kept going, because it also felt, strangely, like the first honest sentence in the draft.

At the study table across the room, Priya's group had begun a practice round, Marcus standing to argue in a voice pitched too loud for the library, Priya leaning over her notes correcting him. A librarian drifted toward them with a look of mild warning, and Xavier watched Priya lower her voice without lowering her intensity, one hand flat on the page where the famous line sat.

On his way out, he stopped beside her. "Which case did you say it was?" he asked, testing her, and himself a little.

"Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969," she said. "Seven to two. Students don't shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate." She tapped the page twice and turned back to Marcus, already arguing again.

The writing club met in the spartan back room of the public library, four folding tables pushed into a square, and Ava arrived first with her laptop and two printed articles, which she laid side by side like hands of cards. The question her professor had assigned was whether a river could legally be a person, and the two articles disagreed: one argued that granting rivers legal personhood empowered indigenous communities, the other that it was symbolic gesture, a way for governments to look virtuous while changing nothing. Her review draft was due in nine days, and she had written two pages she already suspected were dead on arrival.

Ms. Ferreira, the librarian who kept the club going, had left a note in her returned draft folder, but Ava hadn't opened it yet. She'd seen the envelope at breakfast, slid it under her laptop lid, and carried it around all day like a stone in her pocket.

Priya came in shaking rain off her jacket, then Marcus, then Dee, who was writing a novel about a haunted laundromat and never read anyone else's work but came anyway for the chairs. "Read yours," Priya said, dropping into the seat across from Ava. "You look like you're guarding a body."

"It's a review of two articles. Not exactly a thriller."

"Everything's a thriller if the stakes are real." Priya tapped the printed pages. "So what's your argument?"

Ava opened her laptop and read the first line of her draft. "Both articles agree that legal personhood for rivers is a significant development in environmental law."

Marcus winced. Dee looked up from her notebook for the first time all evening.

"Wait," Priya said. "Both articles agree. So what are you arguing?"

"That it's significant."

"Ava." Priya leaned forward. "A research paper's thesis has to be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, not a fact everyone already accepts. If nobody could disagree with you, there's no paper."

Ava had heard something like this in ninth grade and filed it away as one of those teacher rules, like margins. She looked at her two pages, which summarized each article politely and then said, in her closing paragraph, that the truth probably lay somewhere in between. Somewhere in between. She felt her ears go hot.

Flashback: last spring, in chemistry, she'd written a lab report whose conclusion stated that deposition occurs when a gas turns directly into a solid, and Mr. Okafor had circled it and written, correct, but so what? She'd been insulted for a week. Now, in the library's back room, the insult rearranged itself. The fact had been true and useless, because no one alive disputed it. She had spent her draft being correct in the same way.

She pulled out the envelope, finally, and slit it open with a car key. Ms. Ferreira's handwriting was small and even. Your draft is careful and fair to both authors. But a research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts. What is this paper actually arguing? Ava read it twice, then set it face down on the table.

"That bad?" Marcus said.

"It's the same thing you just said. Almost word for word." She laughed once, without much humor in it. "So what do I actually think? That's the problem. I don't know yet."

"So find out," Dee said, not looking up. "That's what the two articles are for. Put them in a room together and watch what happens."

Ava turned the articles toward each other, physically, so the first page of one faced the first page of the other. The author who supported river personhood had spent three years collecting testimony from Māori iwi whose river, the Whanganui, had been declared a legal person in 2017. The skeptic had never been to New Zealand; he had read the legislation and found the river's new rights narrow, its guardians underfunded. One measured the law by the dignity it restored, the other by the budget line attached to it. They weren't disagreeing about rivers at all, she realized. They were disagreeing about what evidence counts.

The library's overhead lights buzzed and dimmed for a second, the way they did before closing announcements, and everyone kept talking anyway, and Ava started typing in the dark of her screen. Priya moved her chair around the table to read over her shoulder. On the page, Ava wrote: The dispute between these authors is not about whether rivers should have rights but about what a law must do before it can be called meaningful, and I will argue that the skeptic's standard, though harsher, cannot account for the testimony the first author records. Then she stopped, cursor blinking, and said out loud, "But I might be wrong. The budget thing is real. The guardians can't sue without money."

"That's fine," Priya said. "Say that too."

The closing bell chimed through the building, twice, the sound it made when the doors were about to lock. Dee closed her notebook, Marcus stacked the chairs, and Ava kept typing, both articles open under her hands, the envelope with Ms. Ferreira's note pressed flat beneath the Whanganui one like a bookmark holding her place.

The library smelled of warm dust and the glue of old bindings, and Angelina had claimed the corner table by the window before anyone else could, spreading out six books on the French Revolution like a hand of cards she did not know how to play. The essay was due in nine days. How have historians' views of the Revolution changed since 1800, the prompt asked, and she had underlined the word "historiography" three times in her notebook until the paper tore. Her first draft had come back with a single comment in Mr. Okafor's green ink: this is a chronology of opinions, not an argument. She had stared at it for a whole evening, feeling like a neophyte let into a temple where everyone else already knew the rituals.

What she had assembled so far was a parade. Early writers saw the Revolution as a catastrophe or a heroic birth of liberty; Marxists later read it as a class struggle, the bourgeoisie rising against a feudal order. Then, somewhere in the late twentieth century, the ground shifted, and Angelina could not see what had shifted it or why. She kept copying out positions the way you copy phone numbers you intend to memorize later and never do.

Her friend Priya dropped into the chair across from her with a paper cup of coffee and a rolled museum flyer. "You're still doing the Revolution thing?"

"Two thousand words on why historians can't agree," Angelina said. "So far I have four hundred on the fact that they don't."

Priya unrolled the flyer and flattened it with her cup. It advertised a traveling exhibit at the history museum downtown, prints and ephemera from revolutionary France. "We're going Saturday. Come. My mother wants company and you need to not sit here all weekend turning petulant."

"I'm not petulant."

"You hissed at the printer on Thursday."

Saturday, in the museum's cool second-floor gallery, Angelina stood in front of a broadside from 1793: a woman in a Phrygian cap planting a liberty tree while citizens in simple dress looked on, all of it drawn in confident, heavy lines. She had seen the image before, in textbooks, always reduced to the size of a postage stamp and treated as decoration. A placard beside it cited its provenance and then, at the bottom, gave a reference for further reading. Lynn Hunt, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution, 1984. She read the line twice, because the placard said something else too: that scholars since Hunt's book had come to treat such images, along with political language and public festivals, as evidence for understanding the Revolution, not merely as its illustrations.

"Look at this," she said to Priya, tapping the glass. "The picture is the evidence."

"It's a nice poster."

"No, it's a source." Angelina heard her own voice go strange and quick. "In 1984 this historian, Lynn Hunt, published a book, and it turned attention to symbols, language, festivals, this whole layer of culture, and that's the shift I couldn't find. It's not that people stopped arguing about class. It's that they started asking a different question."

Back at the library on Monday, she found the book itself in the stacks, its spine softened by decades of hands, and carried it to her corner table like something perishable. She read with a pencil, sitting forward. Hunt was not arguing that class had nothing to do with the Revolution; she was arguing that you could not understand political change without its symbols, its rhetoric, its staged festivals, that culture was not a reflection of the struggle but part of the machinery of it. Angelina copied the title page into her notebook, then sat back and looked at the window, where late light was transfiguring the parking lot into something gold and provisional.

The problem was that she liked the Marxist historians too. She had spent a week inside their argument, the long grind of economic interest and class conflict, and she could not make herself believe it had all been an illusion, a story later scholars had simply outgrown. Her instinct was to pick a winner, to write that the old view was wrong and the new view was right, the way you pick a side in an argument you overhear. But the essay prompt had not asked which historian was correct. It had asked how views changed. She wrote at the top of a fresh page: not a contest, a widening. The Marxists asked who benefited. Hunt and those who followed her asked how revolutionaries imagined the world they were trying to build, in images and speeches and civic rituals. The questions were not enemies. They were successive, and each one had remade the field because it made new kinds of documents speak.

She drafted through the afternoon, pausing to reread a paragraph in Hunt where the argument turned on a festival she had never heard of, some orchestrated public ceremony whose details Angelina could not fully reconstruct from the page. She left a bracket in her draft: check this. There were other brackets too, places where she had inferred a connection between the social historians and the cultural ones that she was not yet certain the sources supported. She did not delete them. She formatted the document, set the margins, and read the last paragraph aloud under her breath, hearing where it rang true and where it only sounded sure.

Priya appeared at the table at closing time, coat over her arm. "Done?"

"Mostly." Angelina closed the laptop and slid the worn book into her bag to return on the way out. "The part I'm sure of is what changed. The part I'm not sure of is whether I've earned everything I wrote about why."

"Is that allowed?"

"It has to be. I put it in a footnote."

At the circulation desk, the librarian stamped nothing, scanned nothing, only nodded at the returning book, and Angelina set it gently on the counter, cover up, title facing the room.

The lasagna had gone cold at Charles's end of the table because he kept forgetting to eat it. Across from him his younger sister, Priya, was describing her science fair group in escalating detail: a partner who had promised the model volcano and delivered nothing until the night before, a poster finished at two in the morning by Priya alone. "So I told her," Priya said, sawing at her garlic bread, "you ruined the whole project."

Their father looked up from his plate. Their mother said, "Priya," in the tone she reserved for minor crimes.

"She did ruin it," Priya said. "Everybody says so. Cora says so, and Cora's her best friend."

Charles said nothing, but something in his chest tightened with recognition. Three weeks ago he had stood in the hallway outside the media lab after his own presentation, and he had said almost the same words, in almost the same voice, to Dex, whose slides for their joint talk had arrived at eleven p.m. the night before, half of them out of order. He had said, "You tanked it, man," and Dex had gone very still, and then quiet, and they had not really spoken since, except in the flat shorthand of people sharing a hallway.

He had gone home that night and, unable to sleep, searched through the communications workbook their seminar teacher had assigned but never discussed, a soft-covered thing with interminable chapters on conflict and listening. In one chapter he found something that stopped him. It described "I-messages," such as "I felt stuck when the slides came in late," and said they were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming. He read the page twice, then closed the book and lay in the dark, turning the sentence over. What he had said to Dex was a you-message, though nobody called it that: you tanked it, you ruined it, you, you.

At dinner now, his mother was asking Priya whether she had talked to the teacher. "No," Priya admitted, "because then it looks like I'm the problem." Their father suggested, mildly, that the girl might have had reasons. Priya rolled her eyes so comprehensively that even Charles, seventeen minutes older and theoretically above such things, felt the pull of solidarity.

"It doesn't have to be a choice," Charles said. Both of them looked at him. He felt the familiar heat of being suddenly the entertainment. "Between saying nothing and saying she ruined it. There's a way to say what happened without the blame part. Like, instead of you ruined it, you say how it was for you. I felt stuck when the model didn't show up. Something like that."

"That sounds fake," Priya said instantly. "Like a therapy contrivance."

"It kind of is a contrivance," Charles admitted, and was surprised to find he meant it as a defense. "But it's a useful one. It's called an I-message. Some psychologist pushed it back in the sixties." He pushed a piece of lasagna around his plate. "I read about it after I said something to a guy on my project team. Something like what you said. And it went bad, and I was trying to figure out what I should have done instead."

His mother set down her fork. "You and Dex? I thought you two were fine."

"We were fine until I opened my mouth." He told it plainly: the late slides, the presentation that had lurched, the sentence he had chosen in four seconds of anger and would apparently be carrying around much longer. He did not dress it up. He noticed, as he spoke, that telling it this way, with the I of it, felt different from telling it the way he had rehearsed it in his head, where Dex was always the villain and the lateness of the slides was the whole crime.

"So did you apologize?" Priya asked, which was, from her, almost tenderness.

"I sent him a text that said, my bad about how I handled that." He winced at himself. "Which is a different contrivance. The kind that doesn't enfranchise anybody, it just closes the account." Dex had replied with a thumbs-up, which had settled exactly nothing.

Priya was quiet for a moment, tearing her bread into smaller and smaller pieces. "So if I say to Hazel, I felt panicked when the volcano wasn't there," she said slowly, "she can't really argue with that. Because it's just what happened to me." Then, suspicious again: "But it still feels like a trick. Like I'm getting her to feel bad on purpose."

"It's both, maybe," Charles said. "A trick that happens to be true." He honestly did not know. It was possible the whole method was just politeness with a manual, a way of dressing the same complaint in softer clothes; it was also possible that naming what had happened to you, instead of what was wrong with the other person, changed the thing you yourself carried afterward. He had no evidence yet. He had one failed you-message and a workbook chapter.

Their father started clearing plates. Priya pulled her phone toward her, typed something, deleted it, typed again, and held the screen out across the table for Charles to see. The message to Hazel read, I felt really stuck when the model wasn't done the night before, and I want to talk about it without us both being mad. She raised her eyebrows at him. Charles gave a small nod, the kind that tries not to seem like a verdict, and she pressed send, then put the phone face-down beside her water glass and did not look at it, though she looked at it twice before helping stack the dishes.

Later, drying the pan his mother had washed, Charles pulled out his own phone and found Dex's name. He sat with the blank message field for a while. Then he typed, I felt lost up there when the slides were out of order, and I took it out on you, and I'd like to actually talk about it. He read it four times. He could hear Priya's word, contrivance, and he could hear his own doubt, and neither of them had the last word. He pressed send, set the phone on the counter, and went back to the pan.

The biology test was on Friday, and by Wednesday Sadie still could not keep transcription and translation straight in her head. She had copied the diagrams from the textbook twice, once in blue pen and once in black, and both times the arrows had multiplied until the page looked like a turgid city map, swollen with lines that went nowhere she could follow. Mr. Okafor had told them the essay question would ask them to explain how DNA is copied and then turned into protein, and he had said it in that flat voice that meant he would not be repeating it.

The field trip to the science museum was scheduled for Thursday morning, which everyone treated as a reprieve from studying and Sadie privately treated as one more thing standing between her and Friday. She rode the bus with her flashcards face down on her knee. Across the aisle, Marcus and Priya were arguing before the bus had even stopped.

"Look," Marcus said at the big rotating model in the genetics hall, a double helix the size of a flagpole, its two strands untwisting and zipping back together in a slow mechanical loop, "when a cell copies its DNA, the old molecule opens up and two new ones get built. So the copy is all new."

"That's not how I read it," Priya said. "My notes say something about old strands. Half of it's old, I'm almost sure."

"New," Marcus said. "It's a copy. Copies are new."

Sadie stood a little way off, arms crossed, pretending to read a wall panel about ribosomes. She wanted to say something and did not trust herself to say it correctly, which was the whole problem with the test too. If she opened her mouth and got it wrong, Marcus would remember it forever.

"You're both doing that thing," said Dana, drifting over with her museum map folded into a triangle. "Where you equivocate until the other person gives up. 'Sort of new.' 'Kind of half old.' That's not an answer, that's a fog."

"I'm not equivocating," Marcus said. "I'm right."

Priya pulled out her phone and scrolled through a photo of her notebook. Sadie leaned in without deciding to. Under Priya's heading, DNA REPLICATION, there were two hand-drawn helices with the strands colored differently, and a note in the margin: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original and pairs it with one newly built strand.

"There," Priya said. "One old, one new. Both of the new molecules."

Marcus frowned at the model, which had chosen that moment to unzip itself again, its two halves wheeling apart like doors. "So when it copies, the original doesn't just stand there being a template and then leave? The original strands actually end up inside the new ones?"

"That's what my note says."

"My dad would hate this," Marcus said. "He thinks everything in biology is designed toward a purpose, like the cell knows what it's building. He's got a whole teleology thing."

"That's not it either," Dana said. "Nobody's designing it. It just keeps a strand and builds on it."

Sadie had been quiet through all of this, and the quiet had been doing something to her. She had spent the week trying to memorize the process as a list, arrows on a swollen page, and Priya's margin note had landed differently: the copy was half inheritance, half construction. The old strand stayed. It was less like photocopying and more like a sentence passed down where half the words were kept and half were new. She found she could suddenly hold transcription and translation in the same grip, because the point of keeping a strand was that the information survived the copying, and the point of copying was that the information could be read out, transcribed, and then translated into protein. The two ideas she had been holding apart were one continuous thing.

"Semiconservative," she said. Everyone looked at her. "That's what it's called. Half conserved. One strand from the original, one strand new." Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Transcription makes the message off it, and translation turns the message into protein. If the strand weren't conserved, the message wouldn't survive being read."

Marcus opened his mouth, then looked back at the model, which was zipping shut again, half its length gleaming with fresh color. "Fine," he said. "Half old. I'll say that on the test."

"Say it right," Priya said.

On the bus back, Sadie turned her flashcards over one at a time and found she knew them, not because she had drilled harder but because she had stopped treating the process as a list and started treating it as a thing that keeps hold of something while it changes. She was honest enough with herself to admit the part that still wavered: she could not yet say why the cell kept a strand, only that it did, and Mr. Okafor's essay question might ask for the why. She wrote one question in her margin for the morning.

Dana leaned over the seat. "So tomorrow, when you get the why wrong, are you going to equivocate?"

"I'm going to write what I know," Sadie said, "and star the rest."

She put the flashcards away and looked out the window at the museum shrinking behind them, its helix still turning somewhere inside, half of it old, half of it new.

Jacob stacked the last bag of dark red potatoes, each one smooth and heavy as a lump of igneous rock from the geology unit he'd half forgotten, and looked at the slip of paper in his hand. On it his orientation advisor had written two questions for the small seminar he'd been placed into at State: be ready to explain comparative advantage, and be ready to say why two countries both gain from trading. Three weeks until move-in. He had read the textbook chapter twice on his phone behind the customer service desk, and each time the words dissolved the moment he tried to hold them.

"You're muttering again," said Priya, sliding cartons of eggs onto the belt. She was a sophomore at the community college and had taken the same course, and she enjoyed reminding him of it.

"I'm rehearsing," Jacob said. "Say you're a country."

"I refuse."

"Say you make two things. Say eggs and bread. And say you're actually better than me at both."

Priya scanned a bag of lemons. "Flattering so far."

The register beeped through her answer while he worked it out under his breath. He was better than her at both, yet they still both gained if he specialized in whichever he was comparatively better at. The word wasn't "better." The word was about what you gave up, the loaf you didn't bake. Every time he approached the idea it rearranged itself, and he could feel his advisor's seminar, forty strangers around a table, waiting for him to say something coherent.

An older man came through the lane with a handbasket, banks statements folded inside a newspaper. He asked Priya whether the store had a bulletin board, because he was trying to compare two mortgage offers and kept losing track. He read a line from one sheet, then a line from the other, and shook his head. "The numbers are nothing like when we bought in 2020."

"My mom says the same thing," Jacob said, carrying the man's basket to the end of the lane. "She was at the bank Tuesday. She said the loan officer told her the Federal Reserve started raising its policy rate from near zero in March of 2022 and got it up to between 5.25 and 5.50 percent by July of 2023. She has it written on her hand."

The man frowned at his sheets. "From near nothing to that, in under a year and a half. Different world."

Priya leaned on the register. "Okay, your mom's world, the bank world, the mortgage world, whatever. Get back to your country speech."

Jacob picked up a lemon and a lime and set them side by side on the bagging counter. "Fine. Here. You're the lime country. I'm the lemon country. Say we both grow both." He turned the lemon in his fingers, the oil sharp on his thumbnail. "Say I can grow way more of both. Double the lemons, double the limes. Everyone in my country is better at everything."

"You win."

"Except." He stopped, because the shape of it had finally assembled itself, whole, for the first time. "For every lemon I grow, I could have grown four limes. That's my cost. And for every lime you grow, you only give up half a lemon. So even though I'm better at everything, I'm only really better at lemons, the way that counts. If I grow only lemons and you grow only limes and we trade, there are more of both than if we each did both. Both of us gain. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"Both gain," Priya said slowly. "Even the one that's worse at everything."

"The worse-at-everything country isn't worse at the thing it costs it least to make. That's the point. That's what the chapter kept trying to say."

The man with the mortgage papers had paused at the end of the lane, listening. "So what you're saying is everybody's got something," he said, half to himself, and rolled his newspaper tighter. He said it like a question he intended to carry out to his truck.

Jacob didn't answer right away, because the honest part was still unresolved. His chapter's last page had included critics who maligned the whole framework, who called global trade a machine for plutocracy, a system where the gains from trade pooled at the top while the egg-packing country stayed egg-packing for a generation. He believed both things somehow, that the math held and that the math left people out, and he could not yet say in one sentence where one truth ended and the other began. He would have to say something in three weeks. He could start with the lemons.

Priya picked up the lime and tossed it to him, underhand. "Okay, lemon country. Trade me."

He caught it, cold from the cooler, and held out the lemon in his other hand, and they stood there in the fluorescent hum of lane four, each of them holding the thing the other one wanted.

The launch station had a dial for speed, a dial for angle, and a row of tin buckets bolted to the floor at measured distances, and Hailey had already missed the two-hundred-centimeter bucket four times. Marcus leaned on the rail eating fries from the museum café, which they weren't supposed to have in the exhibit hall, and offered commentary she did not request.

"You're going to lambaste me for this," he said, "but you're doing the same thing every time. Same angle, more speed, like the ball's going to politely go further because you asked harder."

"That's not what I'm doing." But it was close to what she was doing. She had gotten a 61 on the projectile quiz on Friday, and Ms. Ruiz had written in red at the top, See me about components, and Hailey had decided that seeing her before Tuesday would be an admission she couldn't afford. So she was at the museum on a Saturday, standing at a machine that shot foam balls, trying to figure it out before anyone could explain it to her. She had a notebook. She had a protractor. She had the incipient headache of someone who has been squinting at the same problem for an hour.

"Try less speed," Marcus said.

"Then it won't reach."

"Reach isn't the question. Where it lands is the question." He pointed his fry at the bucket. "You keep thinking about how hard you throw. Think about how long it's in the air."

She almost threw the protractor at him, except that the sentence snagged on something. How long it's in the air. She wrote it down. Then she wrote what she'd been assuming, which was that the ball slows down as it flies, that its forward motion bleeds away the way a skateboard bleeds to a stop when you stop pushing. That was the whole reason her predictions fell short. She was aiming like the ball would get tired.

She reset the station, dialed the angle to thirty degrees, and fired. The ball rose, arced, dropped, hit the floor short of the bucket. She watched it again, and this time she watched sideways, from a crouch, tracking the ball's shadow across the tile. The shadow crossed the floor in equal spans the whole flight. She counted the tiles under its path. Four tiles out, the shadow took the same time as the first four tiles, and the last four, and all of them.

"It doesn't slow down," she said. "Horizontally. The whole way."

Marcus came off the rail. "Say that again?"

"The forward part. It's the same the whole flight." She was already writing, pencil fast. If you ignored air resistance, and in here there was basically nothing but air and foam, then nothing was pushing the ball forward and nothing was dragging it back. So the horizontal part never changed. Only the vertical part pulled at it, only that fought the launch, which meant the whole shape of the arc came from the up-and-down fight while the forward motion just carried on, indifferent, constant, all the way to the floor.

"So the distance," Marcus said, slowly, like he was handling it with gloves, "is just how fast it's going sideways times how long it's up."

"Speed times time." She looked at her quiz, folded in her back pocket, the problem she'd missed: a ball launched at twelve meters per second at forty degrees, how far does it travel. She'd need the trig to split the launch into its two parts, sideways and vertical, and she couldn't do trig at a museum railing. But the syllogism was there, simple and ugly: if the sideways part never changes, and the height determines the time, then the distance is fixed by both together, and her answer Friday had failed because she'd treated one number as if it were shrinking.

She stood, dialed the speed to the mark she'd used before, and raised the angle from thirty to forty-five. Higher launch, longer time in the air, same constant carry forward. She fired. The ball sailed over the two-hundred-centimeter bucket entirely and knocked the rim off the bucket behind it.

"Too far," Marcus said.

"Too far is information." She lowered the angle ten degrees and fired again. The ball dropped into the two-hundred bucket with a sound like a coin in a well.

Marcus raised his fries in salute. "Write that down before you forget which angle."

"I'm not forgetting." She copied the dial settings into her notebook anyway, twice, and underlined the word constant. Then she slid the quiz out of her pocket, smoothed it on the railing, and started drawing the arc over her wrong answer, splitting it with two arrows, one sideways and flat, one rising and falling, both of them hers.

"Sixty-one," Marcus read over her shoulder. "You're going to fix all of it?"

"Every problem. Right here." She tapped the page. "Hand me the protractor."

The printmaking shed at Camp Wren smelled of ink and pine sap, and Alexia had claimed the corner table by the window for eleven days straight. Her counselor, Dana, had proposed the portfolio project on the first evening: ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement to bind them. Everyone else had chosen by the second morning. Priya was doing doorways. Marcus was doing his grandmother's hands. Alexia had forty sketches and no theme, and the camp art show, where portfolio students would exhibit and sell to parents and visiting locals, was nine days away.

She had been drawing the lake. That was the trouble, she thought, smudging graphite dust off her wrist. Not the lake in general, but the same drowned log at the north shore, the one that surfaced at low water each August, silvered and split, half in and half out. She had drawn it at dawn, at noon, in rain, once by flashlight. On Sunday she'd taped the drawings in a row along the shed wall and stood back, and Dana had walked past and said only, "Huh," which Alexia could not interpret at all.

"Nobody's going to buy ten pictures of a log," Priya said on Wednesday, licking a stamp for the invitations. The shed had emptied after dinner except for the two of them and the moths orbiting the porch light. "My mom buys one thing a year. One. Who wants a set?"

"I don't know if they're a set." Alexia turned her compass case over in her hands. "They might just be ten mistakes with a common subject." The worry had begun to coagulate into something worse than worry, an actual reason to quit, and she had almost torn the drawings down that afternoon.

Then Marcus came in late, shaking rain off his jacket, carrying the art history book he kept under his bunk for the pictures. "I was looking for something for my statement," he said. "You know Monet did haystacks?" He dropped the book on the table, open to a page of pale grain stacks against winter light. "He showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month. Fifteen haystacks. Same field, basically."

Priya leaned over the book. "People bought those? On purpose?"

"Most of them. In a month." Marcus shrugged, as though he had merely reported a score.

Alexia sat very still. She was thinking less about money than about what the fact meant for her wall of drawings, the dawn one and the flashlight one, the version where her brother's canoe had blurred past the log. She had been treating the repeated subject as a weakness, an absence of imagination, when it might be the opposite, a discipline. But she also distrusted the comfort. Monet was Monet. A dead log in a Massachusetts lake was not haystacks in Giverny, and the parents at this show were not Parisian collectors. She said so, and Priya said, "Then it's a gamble either way, so pick the version you'd rather lose with."

The next morning Alexia went to the north shore at five and drew the log again, deliberately, the eleventh version, because she wanted to know whether the repetition had a genealogy, whether each drawing descended honestly from the one before, changing as the light changed, or whether she was simply copying herself. When she laid it against the earlier drawings, she saw it: the first pictures had been about the log's shape, and the later ones had quietly become about the water holding it, the way the current moved around an obstruction. The theme had been there the whole time, underneath her, patient.

Her statement took her two evenings. She wrote and cut and rewrote, and the paragraph that survived was four sentences long, about persistence and what a fixed object can teach you about everything around it. Marcus read it and said it was "almost trenchant," and she made him look up whether that was a compliment before she thanked him.

On the day of the show, the portfolios hung along the boathouse wall, and people drifted through with paper cups of lemonade. Alexia's ten drawings went up in a row, unframed, pinned with binder clips, priced at fifteen dollars each or a hundred for all ten. She stood behind the lemonade table pretending to pour, and watched a woman in a sun hat stop in front of the flashlight drawing for a long time, then move down the row slowly, hands clasped behind her back, the way you move through a gallery.

The woman found Dana and asked who the artist was. Alexia wiped her hands on her shorts and came around the table. "I'll take the whole set," the woman said. "My husband drowned in that lake when I was seventeen. I've never once seen it painted." Alexia looked at her hands, then at the wall, and understood that she had made something she could not fully account for, and that the sale and the grief were tangled together in a way she would think about for a long time. She took the drawings down one by one, careful with the pins, and rolled them together with both hands.

Hannah found the article on Tuesday, third from the top in the database, and printed it before she had finished reading it because the abstract said the finding was significant. That word had been sitting in her thesis outline for a week: Students who use school libraries score significantly higher on standardized tests. It was going to be her central claim, and here was a study that seemed to prove it, with tables, with p-values, with a bibliography she could mine for eight more sources.

Mr. Reyes had given them the format that morning: one argument, sustained; footnotes in Chicago style; a bibliography that did not pad. "A research paper is not a pile of quotations," he had said, walking between the desks. "It is you, taking a position you can defend." Hannah had written that in her notebook. She liked the sound of it, the idea of a position she could hold like ground.

The article was forty-one pages. She read it at the back table of the library during her free period, highlighter uncapped, and it was near the end, in a paragraph she almost skimmed, that she stopped. The sample was enormous, tens of thousands of students across an entire district. And the difference in scores, the actual difference, the one the significance test had been run on, was less than half a point on a two-hundred-point scale.

She read the paragraph again. Then she flipped back to the tables and read the numbers a third time, pressing the highlighter so hard against the margin that it tore the paper a little. Half a point. Her little brother's score had swung thirty points between October and March just because he had slept badly in March.

Last fall, before any of this, there had been an evening she kept returning to without wanting to. Her father had come home with a brochure from a tutoring center, florid with testimonials, a woman's face lit like a saint's, and he had set it beside her college applications at the kitchen table. Two thousand dollars, he said, and their guarantee was statistically proven. She had pushed the brochure back toward him and he had pushed it toward her again, and neither of them had said anything for the rest of dinner, and in the morning the brochure was still there, between the salt and the applications, like a border neither would cross. They had reached a truce by not mentioning it. She had not thought about the word proven since.

Now she thought about it constantly. She found Priya at the periodicals shelf and held out the article, folded open to the page. "Tell me what this says."

Priya read for a minute, chewing the end of her pen. "Significant. It says significant like five times."

"Look at the actual numbers. The difference. Half a point." Hannah tapped the table so hard the pen jumped. "How is that significant?"

"Because that's what the test says. It's a word they use." Priya shrugged. "So it's a big deal."

"It's not a big deal. It's the tiniest possible deal." Hannah lowered her voice; the librarian had looked over. "But the sample is huge. Like, whole-district huge. So the test says significant anyway. It can be significant and basically nothing at the same time."

Priya frowned at the page, then at her. "Then why do they write it that way?"

"That's what I want to know."

She spent her study hall deciding. The easy path was to use the article the way it wanted to be used, quote the abstract, and let the word significant do her arguing for her. The harder thing, the thing Mr. Reyes had half-adumbrated with his talk of defensible positions, was to build her argument on what the numbers actually said: that the libraries study showed something real about how the word significant works, and that her thesis, the way she had written it, was built on sand. She could still argue for libraries. She believed in libraries. But she would have to argue them honestly, on grounds this study did not give her.

She opened a new document and typed a footnote after the citation, Chicago style, checking the handbook twice for the punctuation. In the footnote she wrote that the study reported a significant result and that the measured difference was smaller than half a point on a two-hundred-point scale, with a sample of tens of thousands. She read it back. It was not an attack on the authors. It was just what the paper said, placed where a reader would find it.

At the kitchen table that night, her father asked how the paper was going, and she told him about the word significant, and the half a point, and he was quiet for a moment and then pulled the tutoring brochure out from under a stack of mail. "So this," he said.

"Maybe," she said. She took it from him and turned it over, the saint-lit face and the guarantee, and set it facedown beside her laptop, next to the salt.

The coding club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiators clanked and the whiteboard still held last week's ghost of a half-erased binary tree. Maika arrived early because she wanted the seat by the window, and because she had a problem she hadn't told anyone about: her Song class refused to initialize. She had a plan for the club's showcase, a small app that matched students with local volunteer shifts, and everything depended on this one class behaving itself.

Priya dropped into the chair across from her, already talking. "I redid the pitch deck. Three slides on revenue this time. Mr. Okafor says if we can't monetize it, it's just a hobby with extra steps." Priya wanted the app to win the regional showcase, wanted it badly enough that she'd started saying things like "user acquisition funnel" without irony, and Maika had learned to nod at the deck and then go back to her code.

"Look at this," Maika said, turning her laptop so Priya could see. The test was still red. She had a class called Song with private fields for title and lengthInSeconds, getter methods that compiled cleanly, a test that constructed a Song and asserted on its title. The constructor was right there, name and everything: public void Song(String title). The test failed anyway, insisting the title was null.
