Priya leaned in, chewing the end of a pen. "It compiled, though. That's the evil part. If it were broken it would yell at you."

"Java doesn't yell about things it thinks are fine." Maika highlighted the constructor and stared at it the way she stared at a page of French, waiting for a word to resolve into sense. Her mother debugged sewing machines the same way, running her thumb along a seam until the snag showed itself. Maika had always thought of that as the less useful kind of cleverness, patient and physical, nothing like the brisk logic she associated with code. She was less sure of that division now.

Across the table, Theo was showing his own project to a freshman, and Maika caught the word "sycophant" in the middle of his pitch. "The app's too nice," he was saying. "It agrees with everything you type. Like a little sycophant. I want it to argue back." He wanted his chatbot to disagree with people, which struck Maika as a strange thing to want, and also as the kind of wanting that had nothing to do with slides about revenue.

She went back to the constructor and read it aloud, quietly, one token at a time. Public. Void. Song. Then she deleted the word void and ran the test. It went green so fast she thought she'd clicked the wrong button. "It's the void," she said, louder than she meant to. "A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void. With void in front of it, it's not a constructor at all, it's just a method that happens to share a name and never gets called." Priya frowned at the screen. "So it compiled because Java thought you wanted a regular method?" "Exactly. It did what I said instead of what I meant." Maika sat with that for a second, honestly unsure whether she found it infuriating or beautiful, that the language had obeyed her so literally.

Then came the twist she hadn't planned. Priya slid her own laptop across, and there on the screen was the same shape, the same quiet betrayal: public void User(String name). "I copied your style," Priya admitted, ears going pink. "From the file you shared last week." Maika laughed before she could stop herself, and Priya laughed too, and for a moment the showcase and the revenue slides and the funnel didn't matter to either of them. Maika reached over and deleted the void, then sat back. "Your turn. Run it."

Priya hit run, and the test went green, and she said, very quietly, "Okay. Okay, we might actually have something."

The waiting room had nine chairs and Tyler had counted them twice before Dr. Okafor's office door opened and Mrs. Haddad, the health teacher, waved him and Priya inside. It was a field trip with a purpose: the clinic had agreed to let students training as peer health educators practice on real staff, explaining confidentiality, consent, contraception and testing while a nurse listened and scored them on a clipboard. Tyler had signed up because the college applications wanted evidence of leadership, which felt like a cynical reason, and because his older brother had once stood in a pharmacy aisle for twenty minutes trying to decide which condom brand would least embarrass him at the register, which felt like a real one.

Priya went first while Tyler sat in the hallway on a folding chair, running the script through his head. His problem was straightforward and stubborn: he could memorize facts, he had done it his whole academic life, but the moment someone asked a question the script didn't cover, his mind emptied itself like a sink. Mrs. Haddad had warned him. You're going to get a curveball, she'd said, and Tyler had lain awake composing answers to curveballs he invented, each one more catastrophic than the last.

Priya came out looking flushed but intact. "She asked me how the oral swab works," she said. "I described it in way too much detail. She was laughing." Then it was his turn.

The office had been rearranged for the exercise: a desk, two chairs facing each other, a nurse named Beatriz seated behind a clipboard, playing a patient. "Okay," she said. "I'm sixteen, I'm here because my mom made the appointment, and I don't want to talk to you. Go."

Tyler started with confidentiality because it was first in his notes, and it went well, explaining that the clinic wouldn't call her parents, that she controlled what happened next. He offered her the pamphlets on contraception, the one comparing methods, and when she said she'd heard the pill made you gain weight, he said the honest thing, that side effects varied person to person and a clinician could walk her through options, rather than the confident thing he didn't actually know. Beatriz made a small check mark. He mentioned the testing window, that STI testing was routine and free here, that a nurse could do it in ten minutes. Another check.

Then she uncrossed her arms and delivered the curveball. "What if I said yes to a guy already," she said. "Like, we already started. And then I want to stop. Am I allowed to change my mind, or is it too late once I've said yes?"

The sink drained. Tyler's script covered what consent was, that it had to be freely given, and he opened his mouth to recite exactly that, but the question wasn't asking for a definition, it was asking about time, about whether yes was a contract that locked shut behind you. He thought of his uncle, who called any teenager who waited a certain kind of ascetic, as though choosing not to do something was a costume you wore for show; and he thought of a kid in his grade who argued online like a professional ideologue, treating every position as either pure or traitorous, no room for the middle where actual people lived. Neither of those voices would help this girl. Both of them would turn her question into a debate, and debates had winners, and she hadn't come to lose.

"No," Tyler said, and then heard how that sounded and corrected himself. "I mean, it's not too late. Consent has to be freely given, and you can take it back at any point, even after things have started. Saying yes at the beginning doesn't mean you gave up the right to say stop." He paused, checking his own sentence against the fact sheet in his memory, and it held. "So if you change your mind, that's it. It's over. He has to stop."

Beatriz leaned back. "And if he doesn't?"

"Then it's not consent anymore," Tyler said. "It's assault." The word sat in the quiet office, heavy and correct, and he was surprised that saying it hadn't killed him. "And this clinic can connect you to people who help with that, if it ever came up. It's not something you'd have to figure out alone."

Beatriz set the clipboard down and dropped the patient voice. "That was the one most students fumble," she said. "They either hedge or they lecture. You did neither." She told him his contraception rundown had one weak spot, he should practice naming the methods out loud until they came easily, but the consent answer had been clean. Tyler nodded and wrote the weak spot on his hand with a pen, because that was a solution he understood: identify the gap, drill it until closing it was automatic.

In the hallway afterward Priya asked what the curveball had been, and Tyler told her, walking her through it, testing whether he could say it twice. She said the withdrawal thing sounded obvious, and Tyler said it wasn't, not when you were sixteen and scared you'd already forfeited something. She thought about that longer than she usually thought about anything.

On the bus back to school, Mrs. Haddad passed through the rows collecting permission slips, and when she reached Tyler she said, "Well? Survive it?"

He held up the hand with the pen ink on it. "Mostly," he said. "Ask me again after I can say diaphragm without laughing."

The painting Ms. Okafor had chosen for their first formal analysis was Frida Kahlo's The Broken Column, and Julia had been staring at it for ten minutes without writing a word. The figure stood in a desert, split down the middle like a door left ajar, an Ionic column where her spine should be, the white corset straps pressing into her skin. Nails punctured her face and torso like a map of pins. Julia's worksheet asked for three observations on colour, three on composition, three on symbolism, and every blank line looked like an accusation.

"You're supposed to start with what you see," said Priya, sliding into the next seat. "Not with what you feel about it. Ms. Okafor marked me down for that last term."

"I know that." Julia turned her pencil over. "But look at the greens. Everything is green and brown and grey, and then there's the blue of that corset, and the white of the column. It's like the landscape doesn't care about her at all."

Priya leaned in, chin on her hand. "Write that down, then. That's an observation about colour, even if it sounds like a complaint."

Julia wrote it down. The green, she noticed, was not one green. The ground was an olive murk; the sky behind the cracked earth was a flat, almost cheerful green, the green of a school hallway painted by a committee. Against it the tears on the figure's face caught the light like glass. She wrote that too, and then, in the composition column, that the body was centred and frontal, symmetrical almost, except for the fissure running down the middle, which the eye followed whether you wanted it to or not. The tears led you there. Everything led you there.

The symbolism column was where she stopped again. Ms. Okafor moved through the rows of desks, pausing at Tim's laptop, where he had pulled up a larger image. "Don't ascribe meaning to the nails yet," she said to him. "Ask first why there are so many, and why the smallest ones are in her face." She said it quietly, and Tim nodded, and Julia copied the question into her margin because it was better than any answer she had.

At lunch, Priya spread her notes across the table in the cafeteria and pushed half her sandwich toward Julia without comment, the way she did when Julia forgot to eat. "The column," Priya said. "It's a real architectural thing, right? Those are the ones on old buildings. So she's comparing her spine to architecture."

"Or to a ruin," Julia said. "Columns like that are usually broken in pictures of ruins." She had a thought she couldn't shape yet, something about the difference between a spine and a building, between something that heals and something that merely stands, and she was reaching for it when Dev dropped his tray across from them, already talking.

"I found the date," he said. "For my slide. September 17, 1925. A streetcar crashed into her bus. She was eighteen."

Julia looked up. "Eighteen?"

"Eighteen." Dev tapped his phone. "And the injuries left her in pain for the rest of her life. That's why the corset, the nails, all of it. She painted this almost twenty years later."

Julia sat very still while the cafeteria noise went on around her, the clatter of trays, someone laughing near the window. Eighteen was her age. Eighteen was a number she had been carrying around all year like a ticket, the age at which everything was supposed to begin. She had spent the morning thinking the painting was about pain in the abstract, something she could hold at the length of a worksheet, and now the woman in the desert had an age, and the age was hers.

That afternoon they reconvened in the art room for the presentations, the print pinned to the corkboard under the window. The light had shifted and the greens looked duller, and Julia found this useful. When her turn came she stood with her notes, and instead of the symbolism paragraph she had drafted she said, "I want to change my analysis."

Ms. Okafor folded her arms, which was how she listened.

"The colour makes it look like the landscape is indifferent, and I first thought that was the point, the world not caring. But she chose those greens. She built the indifference. So the painting isn't just showing pain, it's showing the effort of standing in a world that was made, deliberately, to look like it doesn't notice you." Julia paused. "The composition is frontal and centred, like a portrait, except the fissure breaks the symmetry, and the column is standing in for the spine. A column holds a building up. A spine holds a person up. But a column doesn't heal."

"That's formal analysis plus biography," said Tim from the back. "Aren't we supposed to stick to the form?"

"I don't think you can split them here," Julia said. "She painted the form out of the life. The nails are where the pain was, and the smallest ones are in her face, where pain shows. But I can't prove that from the image alone. That part stays a guess."

Ms. Okafor was quiet a moment longer than was comfortable. "Say the last part again."

"The part that stays a guess. I can defend the colour and the composition. The symbolism I can argue, but I can't be certain."

"Good," Ms. Okafor said. "Write it exactly like that."

Walking out afterward, down the corridor with its interregnum of late afternoon, the bell gone but the clubs not yet started, Julia found Priya waiting by the water fountain, holding Julia's worksheet, which she had retrieved from the front table without being asked. "You crossed out your whole symbolism section," Priya said. "Then you wrote something in the margin."

Julia took the page. In the margin, in her own handwriting, she had written: she was eighteen, and then, smaller, the same age as me, the line trailing off without a period. She looked at it for a long moment while the fountain dripped.

"Keep that part," Priya said. "Even if it isn't analysis."

Julia folded the worksheet once, carefully along the crease, and put it in the inside pocket of her bag, the one where she kept the things she did not want bent.

The camp van went into town on Thursdays, and Alexandra had volunteered to ride along so she could restock the first aid kit at the pharmacy. She wanted to be useful in a way that counted. In September she would start college with a declared interest in nursing, a declaration she had made mostly to stop her aunts from asking what she planned to do with herself, and she was beginning to suspect that wanting to be useful and being useful were not the same thing.

She was standing at the counter with gauze and antiseptic wipes when Mrs. Ferreira came in. Mrs. Ferreira was the camp cook's mother, seventy-one, visiting her daughter for a month, and she was waving a slip of paper at the pharmacist with the particular impatience of someone who has been told something once and resented it. The pharmacist was on the phone. Alexandra watched her wait, then give up and drift toward the machine near the window, the one with the cuff and the chair, the one she had seen people use without ever watching closely.

"That thing talks to you?" Mrs. Ferreira said when Alexandra drifted over too. "My daughter is busy. The nurse drove someone to the clinic. Nobody has time."

"It's quiet for a minute," Alexandra said. "Sit. I'll press the button."

Mrs. Ferreira sat and pushed her sleeve up. The cuff tightened with a sound like a slow exhale, and the numbers climbed and fell and settled. One hundred and forty-two over eighty-eight. Mrs. Ferreira looked at the screen, then at the paper in her hand, then at Alexandra, as if the arrangement were obvious.

"Which one is the bad one," she said. "The doctor wrote mine down and I lost the paper. There's a top and a bottom and I can never keep them apart."

Alexandra had a page in her notebook from the CPR certification she'd done in June, and she had copied things onto it without really inhabiting them. The top number, she remembered, was the one while the heart was beating. She turned the notebook sideways, thinking. "The top is systolic," she said. "That's the pressure when the heart beats. The bottom is diastolic, when the heart relaxes between beats. It's millimeters of mercury, that's what the little mmHg means." She pointed at the screen. "So one forty-two over eighty-eight."

"The heart beats, the heart rests," Mrs. Ferreira said. "Like everything else."

The pharmacist came off the phone and looked at the numbers with the practiced face of someone who prognosticates about twenty readings an hour and knows better than to dramatize any single one. She asked Mrs. Ferreira whether she'd had coffee that morning, whether she'd walked up the hill from the camp, whether she was upset about anything. Mrs. Ferreira admitted to two of the three and refused to specify which.

"Rest five minutes and do it again," the pharmacist said, and went back to the register, and it was suddenly Alexandra's problem again, which was what she had wanted, though not in this shape.

They sat on the bench outside with a paper bag of the orange candies Mrs. Ferreira liked. Alexandra turned her notebook right side up. She knew, in a general way, that diet and exercise were supposed to change these numbers, the way she knew that studying changed grades, a fact that had never stopped being abstract to her even when it worked. But she had spent the summer watching the campers arrive obstreperous on Monday and go home calmer on Friday, and she had watched her own resting self change shape over eight weeks of carrying canoes, and she was starting to believe the body kept a ledger whether or not you read it.

"They gave us a handout," she said. "At the CPR thing. It said the numbers go down if you walk most days and cut back on salt. Not all at once. It takes weeks."

"Weeks," Mrs. Ferreira said. "I have been eating my daughter's cooking for a month. She puts salt on the salt."

"You could ask her not to."

"You could come to dinner and ask her yourself. She listens to people with notebooks."

Inside, they did the machine again. One thirty-six over eighty-four. Mrs. Ferreira studied the screen as though comparing two photographs of the same landscape. "The top one came down," she said. "Six points from sitting on a bench. That seems dishonest."

"Maybe it's like a quiet classroom," Alexandra said. "The numbers behave differently depending on who's in the room." She heard how it sounded, the sentence reaching for something it hadn't quite landed, and she let it go. She did not actually know how much of the six points were the bench, the candy, the company, or the machine's own opinion.

At dinner that night Mrs. Ferreira introduced her to the whole mess hall as "the girl who reads hearts," which was, Alexandra thought, either a compliment or an oxymoron, since hearts mostly insisted on being felt rather than read. She sat across from the cook, who had a pot of something behind her and an expression that suggested she had been sent three people's opinions already.

"My mother says you told her the top number is the heart beating," the cook said.

"Systolic," Alexandra said. "When the heart beats. The bottom is when it relaxes between beats."

"And she says I salt the salt."

"She said it more colorfully than that."

The cook looked at her mother, who was ladling soup for a line of eleven-year-olds and doing it well, and then back at Alexandra, and something behind her face decided to concede. "Fine. Wednesday we do the low-sodium thing. You're at my table, and you're explaining it to my mother again, because she'll have forgotten by Wednesday."

"I'll bring the notebook," Alexandra said, and went to clear tray thirteen.

"Higher," said Marcus, which was exactly what Joshua needed him to say.

They were in Marcus's basement, the good kind of basement, carpeted and dim, with a desk lamp whose switch had to be jiggled. Marcus's laptop sat open between two mugs of cocoa that had gone tepid an hour ago. On the screen was a half-written function, and the half was being generous.

"Lower," Joshua said. "But that's not the point. The point is I'm still on track."

Marcus had proposed a warm-up before they attempted the homework: he would think of a whole number between 1 and 100, and Joshua would guess it, getting only higher or lower in reply. Joshua had opened with fifty. Then, after "higher," seventy-five. Then, after "lower," sixty-two. He was walking down the middle of every remaining range like a man crossing a river on the most boring stones available, and it was driving Marcus insane in a way Joshua found deeply satisfying.

"Sixty-nine," Joshua said.

"Higher."

"Eighty-one."

Marcus put his face in his hands. "Seventy-seven. It was seventy-seven. That was five guesses, which, fine, is good, I guess."

"It's better than good." Joshua spun the desk chair a quarter turn and back. "My grandfather taught me this over Thanksgiving, except he taught it by losing to it. He'd pick a number, I'd pick the middle of what was left, and he kept losing. He made me play maybe ten rounds because he was sure he'd catch me cheating. Then he said the whole thing out loud like he'd discovered fire: never more than seven guesses. One to a hundred, always the middle, seven guesses tops."

"He counted?"

"He counted. He had a little notepad. It was the most suspense my family has produced in years."

Marcus pulled the laptop toward himself and typed GUESS LIMIT: ??? into a comment, which was the closest he'd come all evening to admitting Joshua had a point. "Okay, so the homework. Sorted array, find a value, and I have to implement this and then, and this is the part I hate, explain why it beats checking every element one at a time."

"That's the linear search. The dumb way."

"It's not dumb, it's honest. It's the search equivalent of introducing yourself to every person at a party."

"To every person at a party of two million," Joshua said, because the assignment's test data was two million records, and he had looked. "By the time you'd finished, the party would be over, the building would be condemned, and your grandchildren would have taken up the task out of respect."

Marcus laughed the way he did when he was annoyed to be laughing, through his nose. He wrote a loop that walked the array from the front, index zero to the end, and it ran on a small test file fine, which was the trap. Small tests flattered the honest approach. "See, it works."

"Now run it on the big one."

They ran it on the big one, and the two of them sat watching the cursor blink for long enough that Marcus got up, went upstairs, and returned with chips. He ate some chips. The cursor continued to blink with what Joshua felt was a smugness no cursor should possess.

"Okay," Marcus said, dusting salt off his fingers. "Middle of the range. Show me."

Joshua took the keyboard and set a low index to the start, a high index to the end, and, inside a loop, picked the middle. Compare the target to the middle value: if the target was smaller, throw away the top half; if larger, throw away the bottom half; if equal, you were done. It was the party with his grandfather, translated, except that now the party was a sorted array and his grandfather's notepad was a variable.

"That's it? That's the whole thing?"

"That's the whole thing. One catch. The data has to be sorted. If it isn't, this is worse than Marcus at the party."

"Hey."

"It's a compliment. You met everyone. That's the point of you."

They ran it against the two million records and the result came back so fast that both of them leaned in, suspicious, as though the machine had skipped the work out of laziness rather than efficiency. Marcus ran it again. Then a third time, with a value he chose from the very back of the array, a corner case, the last seat in the last room, and it still returned before the cocoa ring on the desk had time to dry.

"So the explanation part." Marcus opened a new file for the write-up and cracked his knuckles, a habit he'd been threatened over. "Why does it beat the linear one. I want to say something better than 'it just does.'"

Joshua thought about his grandfather, about the notepad, about how the old man had insisted on one more round and then one more after that, as if losing seven times in a row were a statistical fluke the eighth round would correct. "Here's how I'd phrase it. The linear way asks one question at a time: is it this one? No. Is it this one? No. The other way asks questions that cut the whole remaining world in half every time. Half, then half of that. Think about the guessing game. One to a hundred, you guess the middle every time, and you never need more than seven guesses. That's not luck. That's the same thing we just implemented. Same idea, wearing a party hat."

"Binary search," Marcus said, typing the words as he said them, and the term sat there in the write-up looking official, a colloquialism promoted to a job title.

"Write it down, though. The part you're glossing."

"What part?"

"That it only works on sorted data. That's not a footnote, that's the deal." Joshua tapped the screen. "And be honest about what you don't get, because I don't fully get it either. I can tell you it works. I watched it work. But if Mrs. Okafor asks me tomorrow why the halving gives you seven and not eight or six, I'm going to say something vague and then ask if I can demonstrate with a guessing game, and she's going to say yes, because she likes it when we turn things into games, and I'll be reifying my way out of a real answer."

"Reifying."

"Making it a thing so it feels like I understand it. My dad's word. He uses it when I organize my room instead of studying."

Marcus typed for a while, the honest loop of his keystrokes filling the basement, and then he turned the screen around. He had written half a page, and at the bottom, under a heading that said WHAT I STILL DON'T FULLY GET, he had put two sentences, one of which was a question. Overconfidence was endemic to both of them, Joshua knew, but the question mark was new, and he decided to take it as a good sign.

"Read it out loud," Joshua said.

"'It beats the linear search because every comparison removes half of what remains instead of one item. Also: does the same logic apply to a range of a million, and if so, how many guesses? Investigating.'" Marcus looked up. "Can we investigate?"

Joshua pulled the laptop back toward himself and started a new file.

Cohen's grandfather kept the good dictionary on the lower shelf of the bookcase in the hall, the one with tissue paper between the color plates. Cohen sat cross-legged on the carpet with his laptop balanced on an encyclopedia, hunting for the word "quotidian," and his grandfather, who was in the armchair recuperating from a cold he refused to call a cold, watched him turn pages from the beginning.

"You're on A," his grandfather said. "Quotidian is in the back half."

"I was going to read my way there."

"Your choice." He pulled the blanket higher and closed his eyes.

Cohen flipped to the middle of the dictionary and landed on "molybdenum." Q came after M, so he split the back half and found "reproach." He split again and again, and on the fifth try there it was, between "quotable" and "quotient." He counted the pages he had actually opened: five. Reading from the front would have taken a hundred and eighty. He had a programming assignment due Sunday, a search method on a sorted array, and he had written a loop that checked every element one at a time because that was the only thing he could picture. Now he could picture something else, a fence narrowing and narrowing, and he opened the laptop right there on the carpet.

The class assignment wanted two methods, linear and binary, and a written paragraph arguing which was better on sorted data. Cohen typed the linear one in four minutes. The binary one he typed slower, drawing arrows on a napkin: low, high, middle, then throwing away half the world each time. The napkin began to smell of the orange juice he'd spilled on it at lunch. When he ran the tests, the linear method passed all eight. The binary one passed seven and failed the last, and the failure made no sense. He checked his arithmetic twice, and it was right.

The problem wasn't the search at all. He had built a small class to hold a word and its definition, and when he printed the results, the definitions came out blank. He went back to the constructor and found the line where he had written "name = name." He stared at it for a long moment, then put his cursor on the first "name" and his screen dimmed with inactivity while he thought about it. The putative assignment, the one he'd assumed was happening, was not the assignment that was happening. He tried a small change, "this.name = name," and the tests went green, all eight.

"So the keyword this," his grandfather said from the armchair. Cohen hadn't realized he was being watched. "I heard you talking to yourself."

"This means the object's own field," Cohen said. "When the parameter has the same name. That's what the book says. The constructor wasn't broken, it was just assigning the parameter to itself, over and over, politely, forever."

"Silent failure," his grandfather said. "Worst kind. In my day it was punch cards, and the machine would at least have the decency to shred one." He coughed, considered it, and went on. "What were you building?"

"A search. Two searches." Cohen carried the laptop over and sat on the edge of the ottoman. The screen still held the napkin diagram beside it, arrows narrowing like a river gorge. He typed "perspicacious" into the test field and ran the linear search first. It ground through the whole array, and the counter at the bottom of the screen said 401 comparisons. Then he ran the binary one: 9. "It only works because the data's sorted," Cohen said. "That's the trade. If the list were shuffled, I'd have to sort it first, and sorting costs more than the search saves, maybe, once. But if you search a thousand times, the sort pays for itself and everything after that is almost free. Almost. I haven't worked out when it stops being worth it."

"You don't have to know everything about it tonight."

"I know. I'm going to write that part down as a question, though. Not a conclusion." He set the laptop on the side table, next to his grandfather's teacup, and the counter still read 401 and 9, one above the other, and his grandfather reached over and tapped the screen once, on the smaller number, with one dry finger.

Olivier had three days to write an essay on how interpretations of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, and so far he had written one sentence and deleted it twice. The kitchen table had become his territory: laptop, four library books fanned open like cards, a mug of tea gone cold beside the salt. His sister Camille came through in her socks, carrying a bowl of cereal, and paused at the far end of the table.

"Is this the one that's due Friday?"

"Thursday. And I don't have an argument yet, only a pile of other people's arguments."

"Then write down that they're all wrong and you're right."

"That's not historiography, that's a tantrum."

She sat down anyway, which meant he was not going to work for the next twenty minutes, and dragged one of the books toward her. It was the Soboul, a thick paperback with a cracked spine, and she read the back cover with the skepticism she usually saved for his music. "Who's this guy?"

"Albert Soboul. A Marxist historian. He argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class."

"That's a lot of words for the rich people won."

"It's not exactly the rich people. It's," and he stopped, because he had read the chapter twice last night and was not sure he could say what it was. "It's a class, not just money. He thought 1789 was a social change underneath the political one. The politics was almost the symptom."

Camille ate her cereal and considered this. "And the museum says that too? We saw a placard about the Revolution when we went to the city, remember, it called it a bourgeois revolution."

Olivier sat very still. He remembered the placard, the little brass rail in front of it, his mother reading it aloud in her museum voice. He had walked past it without thinking. Someone had written that label, some curator with a view of history, and the view had a name and a spine and a cracked cover sitting on his own kitchen table.

"Say that again."

"Which part?"

"The placard part. Exactly."

"I don't remember exactly. It said bourgeois revolution. I remember because I thought it was weird that a museum would pick a side."

He got up and found his notes from the trip, a folded page in the pocket of the jacket by the door, and there it was in his own handwriting from six months ago: 1789, label, "a bourgeois revolution," and a question mark he had drawn next to it without knowing why. The label was not neutral. It was Soboul's position, or something like it, dressed up as plain fact and mounted under glass. He copied the line into his draft and then, after a minute, deleted it and wrote instead that the label itself was evidence, that what a museum says without argument can show which interpretation has quietly won.

Camille leaned over his shoulder. "Is that your essay now?"

"It's a paragraph. Maybe two."

"You're welcome," she said, and carried her bowl to the sink.

The rest of the day he spent on the counterattack, because there had been one. Revisionist historians in the middle of the twentieth century, English names mostly, had gone at Soboul's account with parish records and tax rolls, arguing that the lines between noble and bourgeois were blurrier than he allowed, that many bourgeois had behaved like nobles and some nobles like capitalists. Olivier read until the light through the window turned crepuscular and the tea was replaced, eventually, by dinner. His father set a plate beside the laptop and said only, "Thursday, you said," and left him to it.

What he could not do was choose. He tried drafting a conclusion in which Soboul was right, and it felt too tidy, a machine with one gear. He tried drafting one in which the revisionists were right, and that felt like dismantling the machine and calling the parts a clock. Late that night he typed a third version, the honest one: that Soboul's account explained why the Revolution kept being cited by every later movement that wanted a founding moment, and that the revisionists had shown the social engine was less clean than the story it underwrote, and that both readings could be true at different levels, the way a map of roads and a map of rainfall could both be accurate and never overlap. He did not know if that was allowed. He suspected his teacher wanted a verdict.

On Thursday morning he reread the paragraph once, at the counter, while toast browned. He thought about the placard under its glass rail, how it had told him a fact when it was really telling him an opinion that had aged into a fact, and how every book on the table was doing the same thing with more footnotes. Camille came down for breakfast, hair unbrushed, and looked at the laptop screen.

"Did you decide who won?"

"No. I decided it matters that they disagree."

"That's such a you answer." She took the last slice of toast and, chewing, pointed her crust at the screen. "Put your name on it before you forget."

Mackenzie locked the bathroom door, set her phone on the edge of the sink, and turned on the fan so her roommate would think she was showering. On the mirror, the steam was already creeping up from the pipes below, and she wrote nothing in it, though she had read somewhere that people did that, in films, to seem decisive.

"Consent is a yes you can take back," she said to the mirror. "A yes for one thing isn't a yes for everything. If someone's been drinking, or they freeze, or they go quiet, that's not a yes." She paused, rewound, started again, and this time the sentences came out level, less like a girl repeating a pamphlet and more like someone who had actually thought about it. Which she had, though not in ways she liked to exhume. There was a night in October, at Devon McCrae's party, when she had said yes to going upstairs and then not said much of anything after, and she had spent months filing that night under things that were probably fine. Probably. She was eighteen now, and the word probably was starting to feel like a debt accruing interest.

Her phone buzzed against the porcelain. A text from Priya: "You've been in there 40 min. Are you alive. Do I need to exhume you."

"Practicing my presentation," she called through the door.

"For peer health training? In the bathroom?"

"It's the only room with a lock."

Priya's voice came closer, warm through the wood. "Then practice on me. I'll be your dumb first-year."

Mackenzie flushed the toilet for cover, then opened the door a few inches. Priya sat down on the hallway floor with her back against the wall, knees up, holding a granola bar like a microphone.

"Okay," Mackenzie said. "Condoms. Every time, start to finish, and yes, for oral too. The pill, if someone's on it, the nurse is obsessed with setting a daily phone reminder, and it's not because she likes notifications. With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. Typical use means real life. Real life means you forget."

"Seven out of a hundred," Priya said. "That sounds low until it's you."

"That's what I keep thinking." Mackenzie looked at her own hands on the sink. She had missed two pills in November, one because of a stomach bug and one because she'd left her pack in a jacket at Devon's apartment, and she had told herself the stomach bug one didn't count and the jacket one was only four hours late. She had never said any of this out loud.

"Next part," Priya said. "Testing. Because that's the part nobody wants to rehearse."

"You don't need an appointment at the campus clinic. You walk in, they ask what you want tested for, and most of it is a urine sample or a blood draw. Chlamydia and gonorrhea can show up in urine. HIV and syphilis are blood. If you have no symptoms they still test you, because most infections don't announce themselves. Results in about a week, through the patient portal, and it's confidential, they won't tell your parents even though you're on their insurance, you just ask billing to keep it off the statement." She ran out of air. "Some infections, like herpes and HPV, need an exam or a swab, so you tell them everything that's happened and they figure out what to check."

Priya was quiet for a second, chewing. "You know you sound like you memorized a manual, right? Which is fine. But you also sound like a person who's about to go to that clinic."

Mackenzie turned off the fan. The silence under it was bigger than she expected. "I missed doses," she said. "Two. And the October thing, the maybe-fine thing. I keep treating that night like it's synecdoche for my whole first semester, like one bad decision stands in for everything I am now, and I know that's a category error, I literally learned that word this week, but knowing doesn't stop it."

"Then don't let it stand in for anything. Go tomorrow. I'll walk over with you and sit in the waiting room doing a crossword like a sagacious old aunt."

"You don't know what sagacious means either, do you."

"Contextually, yes. Like a wise aunt. Same thing."

Mackenzie laughed, then stopped laughing, because her eyes had gone hot without permission. She sat down on the cold tile with her back against the tub, on the same side of the door as Priya now, only the threshold between them. Tomorrow the clinic opened at nine. She had an eleven o'clock class she could miss, or arrive at late, or she could not go at all and keep carrying the word probably around like a stone in her coat pocket, and she understood that both of those futures were fully available to her, and that nobody was going to choose except her.

She picked up her phone and set an alarm for 8:15, labeled it simply with the clinic's address, and turned the screen toward Priya, who nodded once and pushed the rest of the granola bar under the door.

The paper was due at eight the next morning, and Elizabeth had spread six books across the long table by the library's west window, where the radiator ticked and the October light came in flat and gray. The assignment had seemed simple a week ago: trace how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, showing where historians disagreed and why. Now, with a candle's worth of hours left, the disagreements had multiplied faster than she could chart them, and she had two authors whose conclusions flatly contradicted each other.

The older book, checked out in a rubber-banded stack, was by a Marxist historian writing in 1983, a man who all but eulogized the Jacobins, calling Robespierre's committee a necessary defense of the republic, its violence the price of feudalism's collapse. The newer one, published in 2002, called that whole tradition an apology for terror, and it did so with a strange confidence, as if something had been settled in between, some evidence arrived that made the older view untenable. Elizabeth could not find what that something was. She flipped back and forth, two fingers keeping the pages, a pencil behind her ear going cold.

Denise arrived at seven with a cardboard cup of tea and slid into the chair across from her, unwinding a scarf that smelled of wet wool. "You look like the books are winning," she said.

"They're arguing in a language I don't speak yet." Elizabeth turned the 2002 book toward her friend and tapped a passage. "This guy keeps saying the radicals were protecting a real conspiracy, that the paranoid style wasn't paranoid. But the French conspiracy isn't documented, it's just asserted. And the 1983 guy treats every accusation of conspiracy as invented from nothing. Somebody has to be wrong and I can't tell which one, or how wrong, or wrong in what way."

Denise sipped her tea and pulled the older book closer, because she was pre-med and therefore constitutionally unable to leave an unsolved problem alone. "When did they each write? That part matters, right? You said the whole essay is about change over time."

That was when Elizabeth noticed the copyright pages. 1983. 2002. Nineteen years apart, and the second author wrote as if the first had been refuted by events, though the events he cited were not French at all. She read the footnote again, and then the page before it, and then she sat back so fast the chair legs barked against the floor. The librarian at the desk glanced over, and Elizabeth raised a hand in apology.

"It's not about the Revolution directly," she said, low, leaning across the table. "The 2002 guy is comparing. He says the old left historians trusted the Soviet project the way they trusted the Jacobins, and then he cites the Venona decrypts. Soviet intelligence messages, decrypted, that the US government released in 1995. They confirmed spy networks actually ran here, in the United States. Real agents, real networks, all along." She was talking faster than she meant to. "So the 1983 writer, the one defending the tradition, he finished his book twelve years before that came out. He couldn't have seen it. It's not that he was dishonest, it's that the ground moved under him and he never knew. He was a virtuoso of the archive and the archive itself was incomplete."

Denise frowned into her tea. "So the second guy wins?"

"I don't think that's how it works, actually." Elizabeth pulled the legal pad toward her, where her outline had stalled at the word INTRO for two days. "The Venona messages say something about Soviet spying. They don't automatically say anything about Robespierre. The 2002 guy proves one kind of paranoia was justified and then implies another kind was too, and that's a leap. But it's an interesting leap." She began writing, the pencil scratching against the radiator's ticking. "Maybe the essay isn't about who was right. Maybe it's about how each generation argues with the evidence it has, and how some evidence arrives late, and the honest ones admit the gap."

The library announced closing in fifteen minutes. Around them students were stacking books with the dull urgency of the exiled, and somewhere a cart of returns rumbled through the biography section. Elizabeth copied the two copyright pages, the footnote, the sentence she had underlined twice, her handwriting going jagged where she hurried. She had no conclusion yet, only a shape: two writers, a secret kept and then not kept, a revolution two hundred years dead still rearranging the living. Outside, the streetlights came on, and the glass of the west window held both the room and the dark, layered like rock, sedimentary over igneous.

"Same time tomorrow?" Denise asked, winding her scarf back on.

"Tomorrow it's due." Elizabeth closed the last book and held it a second longer than she needed to, thumb along the page edges. "But Wednesday I'm coming back for the one he wrote after, the 2010 one, where he answers his critics. I want to know if they changed his mind, or just his tone."

Payton taped a rectangle of masking tape to the living room floor and stood at the edge of it, holding her mother's old copy of the script like a clipboard. The rectangle was supposed to be the stage at the community theatre where her one-act would go up in three weeks, and the fireplace was supposed to be the audience, though the fireplace had so far offered no notes.

Her actors arrived at four. Dara, who played the older sister, came first, carrying a bag of clementines and a lot of opinions. Then Marcus, who was nineteen and had done two musicals at the theatre and therefore considered himself, in his own phrase, semi-professional. Last came Imani, quiet, already off book, which embarrassed the other two into running their lines in the kitchen while Payton set out chairs.

"Okay," Payton said. "Opening scene. Dara, you enter downstage left and cross to the table."

Marcus raised a hand. "Quick question, director. The stage at the theatre is flat. Why is the back of it called up? Downstage, upstage, I've said them for years and I don't know what they mean."

Payton opened her mouth and then closed it. She had used the words for a year herself, in her stagecraft notebook, in notes she'd written to herself, and she had never once asked. "Upstage means away from the audience," she said slowly, working it out as she said it, "and downstage means toward it." She frowned. "Which makes no sense on a flat floor."

"Raked stages," her mother said from the couch, not looking up from her book. Then she went back to reading, offering nothing further, which was her way of making Payton do the work.

Payton looked it up that night at the kitchen table, laptop open beside her cold tea. The old stages had been raked, sloped down toward the audience, so the back of the stage really was up and the front really was down, and the words had outlived the slant. She wrote it in her notebook and then, because something about it pleased her, drew a little slope with stick figures on it. She texted Marcus: "The floor used to tilt toward you. You've been walking downhill your whole career without knowing it." He sent back a single actor emoji bowing.

The real problem announced itself on Tuesday. Marcus kept drifting upstage during their big argument scene, near the fireplace, his back half-turned to the imaginary audience, because it was easier to play anger facing away. "You're stealing the scene," Dara said, not kindly.

"I'm playing it truthfully," Marcus said.

"You're aggrandizing it," Dara said. "There's a difference."

Payton let them argue for a minute because the argument was useful, then raised her hand the way her mother did. "Here's the thing," she said. "If you stand upstage of Dara, she has to turn her back to the audience to face you. If you stand downstage, she keeps them and you keep them. Downstage toward the audience, upstage away. The whole scene can live downstage if you let it."

"That feels exposed," Marcus said.

"It is," Payton said. "That's the disincentive. Being downstage means they can see your face." She paused. "That's also the whole point."

They ran it. Marcus stayed downstage this time, jaw tight, and when he broke and turned away, he turned as a choice, once, at the line about their father, and the turn landed. Imani, watching from the couch, said quietly, "Do that again," which was the most anyone had said all afternoon.

Thursday's rehearsal nearly fell apart. Dara had a shift, Imani had a chem test, and Marcus texted that he was "running late" with a photo of himself at a farmers market, which Payton felt was a profligate use of a Thursday. She texted back: "Market closes at seven. Curtain metaphorically rises at seven fifteen." He arrived with peaches and distributed them, and they ran the middle act with Payton reading Dara's part from the fireplace, doing a voice that made Imani laugh so hard she missed an entrance.

That night Payton sat on the floor of the taped rectangle and looked at her notebook. Half of it was the director's plan she'd imagined, blocking charts with arrows, and half was what had actually happened, which was messier and better. She had started out thinking directing meant knowing everything, and now she thought it might mean knowing the difference between the things you could know, like why upstage was called up, and the things you had to guess at in the moment, like whether an actor's bad instinct was bad or just unfinished. She still wasn't sure where that line was. She wrote a question mark in the margin and left it there.

The night before the theatre rehearsal, she found a note taped to the inside of her script, in her mother's handwriting: "Raked stage: the audience sat level, the actors walked uphill. Consider who was doing the work." Payton read it three times, then laughed, alone in the kitchen.

At the theatre on Saturday they ran the whole one-act on the real stage for the first time. Marcus hit his marks. Dara's cross worked. Imani's quiet final speech filled the back row. When they finished, the stage manager, a woman named Ruth who had watched from the house without comment, stood up and said, "Who taught you to keep them all downstage?"

Payton looked at her taped-up script, at her actors catching their breath under the lights, and said, "Nobody. We worked it out."

Ethan had stayed through lunch in the geography room because the current map refused to explain itself. Red arrows swept up the Atlantic like a warm river drawn over cold water, and beside the legend, in the neat print of the textbook, sat the question he was supposed to answer for his report: how the Gulf Stream carries heat toward northern Europe and keeps winters there milder than latitude alone would allow. He traced the arrows with two fingers, then with a pencil, then with a highlighter that bled through to the next page. Ms. Okoye had made the assignment sound simple. Explain, she had said, in your own words, why Britain is warmer than Newfoundland. His own words were the problem. He had other people's words, whole paragraphs of them, and no way to tell which ones he believed.

"You're going to get marker on your sleeve," Dana said from the doorway, holding two sandwiches. She came in without waiting for an answer and set one on the desk beside his elbow, angling it away from the map so the grease wouldn't touch the paper. Dana took oceanography the period before his, and she had already finished her report, which she mentioned the way people mention the weather, without cruelty, just as a fact in the room.

Ethan accepted the sandwich and told her the truth, which was that the Gulf Stream part made sense, the water moved, the water carried warmth, the warmth went north. What he couldn't fit together was the atmosphere. If the ocean delivered the heat, why didn't it simply leak off the top of the world and vanish into space. The report needed a mechanism, and every source he'd found online used the phrase greenhouse effect as though it were as modern as the phone in his pocket, something invented alongside satellites and anxieties he'd grown up with. He had written that in his first draft, actually, that scientists had recently discovered how the atmosphere traps heat, and Ms. Okoye had circled it in red and written a single word in the margin: check.

"Check what," Dana said, pulling a chair around backwards and sitting with her arms folded across its back. She ate the way she did everything, quickly and with full attention, watching the map while she chewed.

Eathan opened his phone and typed the phrase into the search bar, expecting a page of recent papers. Instead the first result was a scanned diagram from something called the Royal Institution, dated 1859, and below it a paragraph about a man named John Tyndall. He read it twice. In 1859, Tyndall had begun laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat. Water vapor and carbon dioxide absorbed it. Nitrogen and oxygen did not. He read the sentence aloud, slowly, and Dana stopped chewing.

"That's it," she said. "That's the whole thing. He just measured it."

"But look at when," Ethan said. He turned the phone toward her, and she leaned in, and he could smell the orange peel she kept in her lunch bag. 1859. Before electric grids, before cars, before anyone had the word for what they were doing to the sky. He had assumed the whole idea was new, something that belonged to his generation's particular dread, and here it was older than the school building they were sitting in, older than the state they lived in. It unsettled him in a way he couldn't immediately name, the way antiquity always unsettled him, the sense that the ground he stood on had been surveyed long before he arrived.

Dana reached past him and tapped the margin note on his draft, the red circle and its single word. "So fix it. It's not modern. The experiments aren't modern. He measured it with whatever they had then."

Ethan pulled his draft toward him and crossed out the sentence with the highlighter, then realized he'd highlighted his own error, which seemed like a fitting accident, and laughed, and Dana laughed, and the tension in his shoulders let go a notch. He started a new paragraph. The Gulf Stream carried the heat north, he wrote, and the atmosphere held a portion of it near the surface, which was not a modern discovery but a measured one, a laboratory finding from before anyone had reason to be afraid of it. He stopped. That last part wasn't for the report, that was for him. He kept it anyway, in the margin, in small letters, and would decide later whether it was extrinsic to the assignment or the only part that mattered.

The light through the tall windows went amber and then gray, and Ms. Okoye's classroom two doors down emptied with a clatter of chairs. Dana gathered their sandwich wrappers and, when Ethan's pencil rolled toward the edge of the desk, caught it before it fell and set it back across his notebook like a fence post. He was still writing when she stood, and she didn't say goodbye, just nudged the second sandwich, the half he hadn't touched, an inch closer to his hand. Some cold front was coming, the kind of gray afternoon that seemed to presage snow, though the map on the wall, with its patient red arrows, showed heat still moving, still traveling north across the whole drawn ocean, and Ethan followed it with his eyes all the way to the Arctic and back down again.

Paige had taped the problem to the inside of her locker door so she would see it between classes: a water balloon launcher on the roof of the gym, a height equation, and the question of the exact angle that would send the balloon the farthest distance before it burst on the parking lot. Mr. Okoye had told the physics club that whoever solved it cleanly would run the launch on Friday, in front of the whole school, and Paige wanted that launch more than she had wanted anything since she'd been cut from the cross-country team in September. The only trouble was that the height equation was a polynomial, and she had never taken a derivative in her life.

She stayed after fifth period in the math lab, a long room of chipped desks where the afternoon light came in sideways and turned the whiteboard into a glare. Devon was already there, working on the same problem, because Devon also wanted the launch. They had been friends since seventh grade and rivals since tenth, and had worked out an arrangement that was less a truce than a habit: they sat at the same table and told each other nothing.

"Do you know what a derivative is?" Paige asked him, breaking the habit within a minute.

Devon kept his eyes on his paper. "It's the slope," he said. "For each term, the exponent comes down and multiplies, and the exponent goes down by one." He slid his notebook six inches toward her, then put his hand flat over the page. "That's all you get."

She copied the rule onto a fresh sheet. Her equation had four terms, the tallest of them an x cubed, and she brought the three down the way Devon had shown her, then the two, then the one, and watched the last term become zero and vanish entirely. What remained was a new polynomial, and she understood, slowly and then all at once, that she was looking at the slope of the balloon's climb, the instant-by-instant steepness of it, and that where that slope crossed zero, the balloon would hang for a fraction of a second at the top of its arc. That was the maximum. She set the derivative equal to zero and solved, and the number she got made her sit very still, because it was the number the whole problem had been hiding.

"I got it," she said, before she could stop herself, and Devon looked up with an expression she could not read.

At home that night she found a message from her sister Ruth, who was a sophomore at a college four hours north and wrote real letters because she claimed texting made her introspect too shallowly. The envelope was thin, and inside was a single page and a photocopied exam. "I lost two marks," Ruth wrote, "and I'm not even angry anymore, but I want you to see it. I left plus C on a definite integral answer. The professor took the marks off without a word. For an indefinite integral you need the constant, because any constant works, so you write plus C to stand for all of them. But a definite integral has limits, real numbers at the top and bottom of the sign. You evaluate at the upper limit and at the lower limit, and the constant is in both answers, so when you subtract the lower one from the upper one, the constant just cancels out. It cancels! It's gone before the end, like it was never there. Two marks, Paige. I've decided to be at peace about it, mostly."

Paige read the letter twice, then sat with the exam copy in her lap, tracing the professor's red circle around her sister's stray plus C. Ruth had put the constant into both evaluations and subtracted, and it had vanished, and Paige felt the odd vertigo of watching something disappear that had seemed, a minute earlier, indispensable. She had been defensive about her own work all week, reactionary almost, snapping at Devon when he looked over her shoulder, treating every question as an ambush. Now she turned her launcher solution over and thought about what in it was load-bearing and what was decoration.

The next afternoon she went back to the math lab early, before Devon arrived, and checked her maximum against the original height equation the slow way, plugging in numbers on either side of the critical value and watching the heights rise and then fall, bracketing the peak like hands closing around a bird. Then she wrote out the whole thing clean: derivative, zero, solve, verify. At the bottom she started to add a constant, because Ruth's habit had migrated into her head, and she stopped with her pen above the paper. This wasn't an integral at all, but she wanted the habit right anyway: constants mattered when they could, and didn't when they couldn't.

When Devon came in, she did something she would have called unthinkable on Monday. She slid her paper across the table to him, all four terms, all her work, the maximum circled in blue. "Check me," she said.

He read it for a long time. His pen hovered, recalcitrant, over her factoring of the cubic, and she felt the old urge to snatch the page back and tell him to fight for the launch like everyone else. She let the urge sit there and exhaust itself. "Your algebra's right," Devon said finally. "Your maximum's right. Mine's different because I set mine up from the parking lot, not the roof."

They looked at each other across the difference, which was, she realized, the actual problem, the one neither of them had been told to solve. Mr. Okoye wanted one launcher, one angle, one clean answer, and the two of them had found two true ones.

"Half each," Paige said.

"I want the last launch," Devon said.

"Then I want the first." She held out her hand and he shook it, quick, like a deal concluded at a market stall, and outside the window the gym roof stood empty and waiting against the cold sky, its launcher still locked in the equipment closet, its angle still, for two more days, undecided.

Grayson had prepared everything, which is why his hands were shaking as he taped the sign-up sheet to the folding table outside the town hall. The sheet read, in his own handwriting, Mock Court Exhibition, Tinker v. Des Moines, Arguments by G. Fielding, and beneath that a line for audience votes. He had not expected the shaking. He told himself it was the tape, which was old and pulled at the paper.

The town hall smelled of floor wax and the coffee Mr. Dunmore had been brewing in the back since six. Mr. Dunmore ran the building, and the building ran the Tuesday meetings: zoning complaints, a proposed stop sign at Marsh and Fourth, and, tonight, a mock Supreme Court argument by a high school senior who had to argue both sides because his actual team had dissolved over spring break. Grayson had volunteered for both sides. He wanted to say he'd volunteered. He had said so, twice, to Priya, and she had looked at him the way she looked at the microwave when it claimed to be a convection oven.

Priya arrived at seven with a stack of index cards and a paperback she'd borrowed from the library, thick and soft-cornered, the kind of book that had been rebound twice. "You need a hook," she said. "For the closing. Nobody votes on doctrine, they vote on stories."

"I have doctrine," Grayson said. "I have precedent going back to Debs."

"Debs is antiquated. Nobody under sixty knows who Debs is."

The room filled the way these rooms filled: slowly, then with an audience of eleven, eight of whom had come to argue about the stop sign and stayed because there was coffee. Mr. Dunmore took the seat nearest the outlet. A woman in a Green Bay Packers hoodie sat in the back with her arms crossed, guarding, as far as Grayson could tell, a personal grievance against the concept of teenagers.

He argued the school board's side first. He explained that schools were not public squares, that the armbands had disrupted learning, that a principal had to be able to act before the hallway became a pamphlet war. He heard himself do it and it sounded, disturbingly, like something he believed. Then he turned to the other lectern, which was the same lectern moved two feet to the left, and argued that students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate, that the record showed no disruption, that calling a quiet protest a disruption was a way of denigrating the message by mislabeling the messengers.

The Packers woman raised her hand. "Which side are you actually on?"

"That's the assignment," Priya said from the side. "Both."

"So you're lying one of the times."

"No," Grayson said, and then, because he was honest or because he was eighteen and hadn't learned better, "or both times. I'm not sure yet."

Mr. Dunmore cleared his throat. In his experience, he said, most of what passed for principle was people choosing a team first and a reason second. He had seen it on the school board for nine years. He said this at length. Grayson tuned back in at the words "revisionist history," which Mr. Dunmore was applying to a colleague's memory of a budget vote, and understood that the old man was not talking about the Supreme Court at all.

During the break, Priya handed him the paperback, open to a dog-eared page. "Read the second paragraph. Out loud, later. It's your closing, whether you know it or not."

He read it now, silently. It was about a different parliament, a different country. On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election. One vote. He read it again, checking the numbers against each other, then against the margin note some previous reader had left, which said only "wow." A government, the whole apparatus of it, brought down by the distance between 311 and 310.

For the closing, he stood without the cards. He told the eleven people about the armbands, the girls, the silent protest, and then, because he couldn't find a way to say anything without saying everything, he said: "On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election." He let it sit. "When you vote tonight, you're not deciding whether I was right. I argued both sides, and I meant both, and I still don't know which one I actually believe, and I think that's the point of the whole exercise, or at least it's what I've got. You're deciding whether speech like the armbands gets protected, and your votes count the way that one vote counted. One of them, somewhere, always does."

Mr. Dunmore passed out the ballots. He counted them at the coffee table with his glasses down his nose, tonguing the numbers as he went. Six for the school board, six for the students. He counted again. Six and six.

"There's twelve of you," Grayson said. "Eleven voted."

The Packers woman hadn't taken a ballot. She stood, crossed the room, and plucked one from the stack in Mr. Dunmore's hand. She looked at Grayson for a long moment, pen already uncapped.

"Stop sign's next," Mr. Dunmore said. "After this."

Annabelle's mother had been debilitated since March, the fatigue arriving without announcement and settling in her like weather, so the cooking had drifted first to her father, who made three dishes and all of them pasta, and then, by unspoken agreement, to Annabelle. She had fifty dollars in an envelope and a Saturday morning, and she meant to leave the farmers' market with a week of actual meals, not one heroic dinner and four nights of cereal. She had written a list on the bus, and the list had a plan behind it: cook in batches on Sunday, portion everything into containers, eat like someone in charge of her own week.

The market occupied a parking lot behind the library, its stalls angled to catch whatever light November had to offer. At the entrance a man in a canvas hat sold coffee she could not afford, and past him the tables began: apples in paper bags, bread, a fish vendor whose mussels were stacked in mesh sacks and whose sign said they were harvested from the littoral beds, where the tide covered and uncovered them twice a day. Annabelle stood in front of that sign a moment, thinking that she had never considered the strip of coast that was neither fully sea nor fully land, and then moved on, because mussels were ambitious and this was a week for realism.

Realism, however, had a rival. At the dry-goods stall, where oats and flour and dried beans sat in stacked packages with printed labels, she found the five-kilogram bag of rolled oats she had imagined herself buying. She had already pictured it in the cupboard, generous and permanent, the kind of purchase a competent adult made. Beside it sat a one-kilogram bag, small and almost apologetic. She reached for the big one and only then noticed the small print on the shelf label beneath it, a second price next to the first.

The smaller bag's label read a lower cost per gram. She picked up both packages and checked again, tilting the labels toward the light, because surely the large bag, the adult bag, was supposed to win. It did not. The shelf labels gave the cost per gram for each, and by that measure the small bag was cheaper. She had been about to pay more for the pleasure of bulk.

"Unit price," said the stall's owner, a woman with flour on her forearms, taking the bags from Annabelle's hands to weigh them for her. "Cost per gram, per litre, per item. It's how you compare packages of different sizes fairly." Annabelle thanked her and set the small bag in her basket, and did not mention that she had spent four years assuming big meant cheap and had never once checked.

The correction followed her down the row of stalls like a small dog. At the oil vendor she read the label on the litre bottle and then the half-litre one, cost per litre printed on both, and discovered the same inversion. At the egg table the label priced them per item, and the carton of fifteen beat the carton of twelve by a fraction. She began to feel that everything she'd guessed about value had been guesswork, and that the market, quietly, had been offering to correct her all along if she would only read the small print.

This presented her with a problem, though, because the list in her pocket was built on a different theory of the week. She had planned seven separate dinners, seven small acts of invention, and the arithmetic of the labels told her the truth she'd been circling all morning: invention was expensive. Chicken thighs were cheaper per kilo than breasts. A single large cabbage would cost less than the three different vegetables her plan demanded. She stood between the cabbage and the carrots with her envelope in her hand and argued with herself in the patient, unhurried way her mother had taught her to argue with a knitting pattern when it went wrong.

"You could do two batches," said a voice, and she turned to find Priya from her chemistry class weighing tomatoes. "My sister calls it batch cooking. You make the same base twice and change the toppings."

"That's just doubling," Annabelle said.

"That's semantics," Priya said, and grinned, and the word loosened something in Annabelle's chest. It was, and it wasn't. If she roasted the chicken with the cabbage and the carrots and half the chickpeas on Sunday, then on Wednesday the leftovers became soup with the oats' smaller cousin, barley, and on Friday the soup became something else entirely with an egg on top, that was not doubling. That was a single investment paying out in three currencies. She took out her list and, standing at the cabbage table, drew a line through four of the seven dinners and wrote "same thing, differently" over the wreckage.

She spent forty-two dollars and left with a basket she could barely close: the small bag of oats that had beaten the large one, the litre of oil, the fifteen eggs, the chicken thighs, the cabbage, the barley, two loaves from the baker at the end of the row, who threw in a third heel piece for free. Walking to the bus stop she weighed what she still didn't know, which was whether Tuesday's version of the batch would taste like Saturday's, and whether her father would eat chickpeas two nights running without commentary, and whether the money saved would survive the week or vanish into the coffee she'd been refusing to buy. She decided she would find out in the ordinary way, one labeled container at a time.

At home she laid everything on the counter and turned the oven on, and her mother drifted in from the couch to watch from the doorway, wrapped in the grey blanket, her face suggesting appetite for the first time in weeks. Annabelle sliced the cabbage in long ribbons and salted the chicken and set the timer, and when her mother asked what it was going to be, Annabelle said, "Dinner, mostly. The same thing all week, differently."

Luca's grandmother had a sunroom with a littoral view, or close enough: a sliver of harbor between her neighbor's garage and a bank of hydrangeas, boats tilting at their moorings like punctuation marks. She had offered it for rehearsals because, as she put it, the alternative was his mother's living room, and his mother had opinions. Six of them crowded in on Saturday, scripts rolled into tubes, and Luca stood on a footstool because it was the only furniture that gave him any authority.

He was directing a one-act for the fall festival, which meant he had three weeks to learn how to tell people where to stand, when to move, and why, without becoming the kind of director everyone maligns behind the snack table. His friend Priya had written the play, a family argument about a grandmother's house being sold, and Priya sat in the corner taking notes with the serene menace of a court reporter.

"Okay," Luca said, clapping once. "Top of the scene. Dana, you're at the window. Marcus, you enter from the kitchen."

"Why the window?"

"Because it looks like you want to leave."

Dana considered this, then moved to the window. Marcus entered, delivered his first line, and stopped, because the scene as written ended there, twelve minutes later, mid-argument, lights out. Nobody moved. Priya looked up from her notes.

"So what happens?" she asked. "At the end. Do they sell it?"

"They keep arguing."

"That's not an end, that's a pause with ambitions."

They ran it twice more and the problem got worse instead of better, the way problems do when you rehearse them lovingly. The argument had a beginning, two sisters arriving with casseroles and grievances, and it had a middle, the grievances graduating into accusations about who had visited the hospital and who hadn't. Then it stopped, like a bus driver noticing the end of the route and simply turning off the engine. On the third run Luca called a break and sat on the floor with the script, and Priya came over with two glasses of lemonade and an expression she reserved for watching him think.

"I read this thing last night," he said. "For the theater elective. Aristotle, the Poetics. He says a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end."

"So?"

"So yours has two out of three. That's a solid B-minus in ancient Greece."

"Excuse me, the middle is excellent."

"The middle is excellent. The end is missing. Aristotle would say it's not whole." He said the last part carefully, testing it, the way he tested a math formula before trusting it with his homework. Priya drank her lemonade and didn't argue, which for Priya was practically a standing ovation.

"But I don't know the end," she said finally. "That's why it stops. Families like this don't resolve. They just refreeze."

Luca looked at the harbor sliver, where a small boat was coming in against the tide, making almost no progress and refusing to stop. He thought about hermeneutics, a word he'd found in the same late-night reading spiral, the idea that you understand a part by the whole and the whole by its parts, around and around. He did not say the word out loud because Dana would mock him until spring.

"Maybe the end isn't resolution," he said. "Maybe it's just the sisters choosing the same room. Dana's at the window the whole play. Marcus's character keeps leaving. What if, at the end, neither of them moves? They just stand there together for ten seconds. Lights fade on them, not on the argument."

Priya wrote for a long moment. "That's not an answer, you know."

"I know. But it's a shape of one. Aristotle didn't say it had to be happy, right? He said whole."

They ran the scene again with the new ending, and it was strange how much the middle changed once it had somewhere to arrive. Marcus stopped rushing his lines as if hoping to exit early. Dana let one accusation land without flinching, because now she had somewhere to be standing still. When the ten seconds came, the sunroom was quiet enough to hear a halyard clinking against a mast in the harbor, which Luca decided to count as a review.

Grandmother appeared with a plate of biscotti and watched the last minute from the doorway, arms folded. Afterward she said, "The one at the window. She's the one you wrote about me, isn't she."

"No comment," said Priya.

"Good girl," said Grandmother, and put the plate down in front of Dana.

Luca stayed after the others had gone, resetting the furniture by feel in the dark. Priya's script lay open on the footstool, the new stage direction in her handwriting: They stay. He read it twice, then turned off the lamp and stood a moment at the window himself, out of habit or curiosity, watching the last light fail over the water.

The packet on Maelie's bench had a red dot in the corner, which everyone in fourth period knew meant a retake, and the retake meant she had to stand at the whiteboard on Friday and explain DNA to RNA to protein without notes. Mr. Okafor had said only that. He had not said how, or for how long, or what would happen if she froze again the way she had frozen on Tuesday, standing in front of thirty people with the marker dying in her hand.

She stayed after school on Thursday because the lab was empty and the models were all hers. The plastic DNA ladder unzipped with a sound like a zipper, and she walked the free nucleotides down one strand, pairing them, whispering the letters to herself. Then she built the mRNA strand, peeled it off, and carried it to the second bench where the ribosome model sat like a hungry clam. Transfer RNA, she thought, was the delivery girl, the one who read three letters at a time and dropped off the matching amino acid. Protein came out the other end, one bead at a time.

"It's like a recipe," said Priya from the doorway, home late from track and looking for her forgotten water bottle. "DNA is the cookbook you can't take out of the kitchen. So you copy the one page you need."

"That's transcription," Maelie said. "And then translating the copy into the actual dish. Protein is the dish."

Priya hoisted herself onto the stool across the bench. "Why do you keep stopping and staring at the ceiling?"

"Because I'm trying to watch myself think. There's a word for it. Metacognition. If I can see where I lose the thread, I can fix it before Friday." She said it lightly, but her hand was tight around the marker. The truth, which she had not told anyone, was that on Tuesday she had not lost the thread at all. She had known the material. Something else had gone wrong, and she did not yet know what, and that frightened her more than ignorance would have.

Priya watched her rebuild the mRNA, unbuild it, build it again. "You do it the same way every time," she said. "Same order, same words. Is that how it happened Tuesday?"

Maelie stopped, marker in the air. That was the question she had been circling without naming it. "No," she said slowly. "Tuesday I started in the middle. Someone asked why cells bother with the RNA copy, and I jumped to answer it, and then I couldn't find my way back." She looked at the ladder model, half unzipped, and at the amino acid beads waiting in their tray. "Maybe the order is the problem. Maybe I should start from the question, not from the beginning."

Priya grinned and rolled up her sleeve, showing the pale track wristband she still wore. "Want to hear what I think about when my legs are dying at the end of a four-hundred? Because I do think about cells, and it's weird, but it helps." She hopped off the stool and mimed driving her arms, sprinting in place between the benches. "Yesterday Coach made us sprint the farm field behind the track twice. Grass, mud, everything. By the end my legs were on fire and I remembered something from bio last year. When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate. That regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis can keep going, making 2 ATP per glucose. Two. Per whole glucose.
