It's like the cell's emergency generator, this wheezing little backup that runs on fumes."

"Lactate," Maelie repeated, writing it on the corner of the whiteboard without thinking. "So that's the burn."

"That's the burn," Priya said. "Or near enough. Anyway, that's my version of watching myself think. My legs hurt, so I go looking for why, and the why turns out to be a whole invisible factory running out of air."

Maelie sat very still, looking at the word she had written. Something had just shifted in her, and she let it shift. She had been treating the DNA lesson as a sequence to be memorized front to back, the parsimonious approach, one path, no detours, nothing wasted. But Priya's sprint worked the other way. Pain first, then question, then answer. The body asked why it burned, and the answer was a molecule. Maybe that was how she should build Friday's explanation: not from the cookbook's first page but from the finished dish, from some visible thing a protein did, and then trace it backward through the copy and the code to the locked shelf it came from.

She stood and wiped the corner of the board clean, then drew a muscle cell, a sprinting figure beside it, and an arrow. "Okay," she said. "New plan. I start with your burning legs." She wrote pyruvate, then lactate, then NAD+, and after NAD+ she drew a long arrow back toward glycolysis and wrote 2 ATP per glucose in small letters. Priya leaned in and read it, nodding. Then Maelie drew the question mark that had been forming in her all afternoon: where does the protein come from that builds all this machinery in the first place? She uncapped the marker.

"Hold on," she said, and began to draw the ladder.

Natalie had the music room above the synagogue's sanctuary to herself on Thursday afternoons, because the choir didn't rehearse until six and Rabbi Wexler believed, somewhat mysteriously, that teenagers with intentions would not burn the place down. She spread her manuscript paper across the folding table beside the old upright piano, the one with the chipped C above middle C, and wrote the number four in the upper left corner. Four bars of melody. Then four more. Sixteen in all, with chord changes written underneath, due to Mr. Alvarez on Monday, and she had nothing.

The problem was not notes. She could invent notes all day, hum them in the stairwell, lose them walking home. The problem was that a melody, to count as composed rather than found, had to return somewhere. It had to end settled, and everything she wrote either wandered or circled back too neatly, like a dog on a leash she could see the whole time.

Her grandmother had left her the scores. That was the part Natalie still couldn't quite weigh: two years ago, when Grandma Ruth was dying and parceling things out with terrible efficiency, Natalie had been handed a shopping bag of sheet music and a look that she'd interpreted, at fourteen, as an obligation. She'd said thank you. She hadn't opened the bag until this week.

On top of the stack was a Mozart piano sonata, and tucked inside it an envelope with Natalie's name in her grandmother's handwriting, postmarked the week before the hospice admission. She'd read it four times since Sunday.

Dear Natalie. If you are reading this you finally went through the bag, so you got stubborn about something, which is the best I could hope for. In the slow movement of this sonata there is a melody I played at my audition in 1968 and butchered, and I got in anyway, which tells you something about what judges are actually listening for. I am not going to tell you what to do with your music. I only want to say that I stopped composing at twenty-three because I decided I was a performer and not a creator, and that decision was a door I shut myself. Maybe it was even correct. I never found out. Don't shut doors before you know what's on the other side, or shut them, but notice you're doing it. Love, Grandma.

Natalie set the letter face down and opened the score to the first movement. She played the opening theme at the keyboard, one finger at a time, then hunted for it again in the later pages. There it was, nearly the same passage, printed twice. She set her finger under the first version and leaned down to compare, and this was where it stopped being homework. The same theme, both times, but the second time the key signature had changed to match the beginning of the piece. The first time through, the melody had traveled into a different key, five sharps away, and the second time through it came home. She checked the measure numbers twice, laid a pencil across both passages like a ruler.

"You're going to scratch the page doing that," said Danny from the doorway, holding the choir's box of kazoos, which was a real object the youth group owned for reasons no one explained.

"Look," Natalie said. "This theme. Here it's in the key the piece started in, and earlier it's in the other key, the dominant. In the recapitulation, the second theme comes back in the home key instead. That's why it feels like it ends where it began." She heard her own voice say the words and they were true, she was almost sure, though the word recapitulation felt borrowed, like wearing her grandmother's coat.

Danny put down the kazoos and looked. "So it's the same tune but it lands differently."

"That's the whole thing, maybe." She played both versions back to back, and the second one settled, no argument left in it. Or that was what she thought. There was a version of herself, the one who'd quit piano at eleven because her teacher called Hanon exercises non-negotiable, that suspected any feeling of settledness was a trick, that the composer was a kind of charlatan arranging your relief for you. There was another version, the one who had cried at the funeral without knowing whether she was sad or just performing sadness for the relatives, that thought returning home was not a trick but the actual shape of loving something. She could not get those two Natalies to agree, and she was tired of pretending they did.

Mr. Alvarez had once told the class that a sixteen-bar melody circumscribes its own small world; you can do anything inside the fence, but you have to build the fence. She'd rolled her eyes at the time. Now she sat with the pencil hovering over bar five and understood the fence differently. Her grandmother had built one at twenty-three and called it a career, and maybe it had held a full life, and maybe it had just held her.

She wrote four bars that quoted the Mozart theme's rhythm, not its pitches, because that felt like conversation rather than theft. Then she modulated, moved the whole thing up, the way the exposition had, letting the melody travel somewhere it would have to answer for later. At bar twelve she brought it back down, and the return made a small seismic shift in her chest, the floor of the piece rearranging itself, and she did not trust it, and she wrote it anyway.

At six the choir tromped in, and Danny collected his kazoos, and Mrs. Ostrow asked if Natalie was staying to sing. Natalie looked at the eight bars left to fill, at the home key waiting at the end like a porch light left on, and started gathering her papers.

"Can I lock up when I'm done?" she asked. "I need twenty more minutes."

Mrs. Ostrow tossed her the key ring from across the room, and Natalie caught it against her chest, still holding the Mozart.

Ella had volunteered to be a peer health educator because the poster said six hours of training and a free lunch, and because her mother had said, in the tone she reserved for funerals, "Well, someone has to talk to girls about these things." Now she sat in the clinic's back room with a laminated folder, a plastic model of nothing she wanted to examine closely, and a workbook that smelled like the inside of a copier. The trainer, a nurse named Priya, had gone to answer the phone twice already, which left Ella alone with a page titled "Contraception at a Glance."

She read the page twice, then a third time, because the numbers refused to sit still. The box in her memory, the one her ex had held up like a trophy in tenth grade, said ninety-eight percent. The page said that with typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time. She looked at the phrase typical use the way you look at a word in a language you thought you spoke.

"That can't be right," she said when Priya came back.

"Which part?"

"Thirteen out of a hundred. The box makes it sound like basically nothing happens."

Priya shrugged, which was not the assuaging gesture Ella wanted. "The box describes perfect use. The page describes people."

Ella wrote typical use in her notebook and underlined it twice, then felt embarrassed about the underlining and crossed it out lightly, so it was still visible, which she decided was honest.

The problem, the actual problem, arrived on Thursday. Ella's first assignment was to explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections to a small group at the teen center, and Priya's rule was that every peer educator had to practice on a live audience first. The live audience, due to a scheduling collapse, was Marcus. Marcus was nineteen, worked at the tire shop, had once corrected Ella's pronunciation of "niche" at a barbecue, and carried his erudition around like a wallet he was always flashing.

"You're going to teach me about condoms," Marcus said, settling into the one good chair. "This should be incredible."

"I'm going to teach you about typical use," Ella said, "because you clearly think you know everything, and you know nothing." She held up the page. "With typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time."

"That number is fake."

"It's the real-world number. The box number assumes people are perfect, and you, Marcus, once put a metal fork in the microwave to make it 'cook faster.'"

He laughed, which broke something open in the room, and after that it stopped being a performance. She walked him through consent, how it has to be ongoing and can be withdrawn, how silence isn't it. She showed him the clinic's walk-in testing hours and explained that testing was free, confidential, and did not require a parent. He asked real questions, one of them so basic she nearly teased him for it and then didn't, because she remembered being eighteen and pretending she already knew.

By the end Marcus was quiet in a new way. "Nobody ever told me any of that," he said. "Not the numbers, not the consent part. Nothing." He took one of each pamphlet, which Ella found funny, and then he took a second copy of the testing one, and she decided not to find that part funny.

On Friday the teen center group was six girls and one boy who had been dragged by his sister. Ella's hands shook through the first minute, and then a girl asked about the condom statistic before Ella even reached it, because the girl had seen a TikTok and wanted to know if it was true that "they basically don't work." Ella said the number, the whole number, thirteen in a hundred with typical use, and added, "Mostly because they're not used correctly every time, so the method isn't the problem, the everything-around-the-method is." A hand went up asking how to get tested, and Ella found herself explaining the walk-in hours with the calm of someone who had done this before, once, in a room with a microwave-fork guy.

Afterward, while she stacked chairs, the center's director came over. The director was perhaps sixty, wore a cardigan the color of a moribund houseplant, and had spent the session in the corner doing paperwork with visible skepticism.

"Dear," the director said, holding out her hand, "do you have one more of those pamphlets? The one about testing." She looked at the door, then back at Ella. "It's not for me, exactly. It's for my daughter. She's thirty-four, and I've never once managed to say any of it out loud."

Cohen had read the chapter twice before English, and the second time he had done it with a pencil, which meant the margins were now crowded with arrows that pointed at each other. The narrator, a woman named Mrs. Keeling, kept insisting she had married for love, while every detail she offered suggested she had married for the house. Mrs. Abara wanted them to notice how point of view worked on a reader, how the first person invited you in and then quietly picked your pocket. "So is she lying," Cohen asked, "or does she just not know?" Mrs. Abara said that was the question he should bring to his essay, which felt like being handed a box with no bottom.

He wanted the essay to be good, and not only for the grade. His older sister was home from college and had taken to asking what he was reading, and Cohen wanted an answer that wasn't a shrug. The problem was that he could see both sides of Mrs. Keeling. She was either a calculating liar or a sincere woman whose sincerities had been installed by someone else, and he could not tell which essay to write, because each one seemed to cancel the other.

The book club met on Thursdays in the library's back room, an arrangement Ms. Dover had started and then mostly abandoned, so it belonged to the students now. Six of them sat around a table with a scratched surface, arguing about whether Mrs. Keeling's choice at the end, giving up the house to follow a man she barely knew, was courage or something else. Priya said it was obviously freedom, the first real decision in the whole book. Marcus said it was axiomatic that a person can only want what she's been taught to want, and Priya said that was the most depressing sentence she'd heard all year.

"It's not my sentence," Marcus said, and began to gesticulate with both hands, as if the argument were something he could shape in the air. "Simone de Beauvoir. The Second Sex, 1949. She wrote that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Meaning society does the becoming to you. It's on my mom's shelf."

"Fine," Priya said, "but de Beauvoir isn't in this novel."

"That's the point," Marcus said. "She's in the water. She's in every heroine who thinks she chose."

Cohen, who had been peeling the label off his water bottle, stopped peeling. The line Marcus had quoted rearranged the whole problem in his head. If Mrs. Keeling had been made into a certain kind of woman by her society, then her sincerity and her unreliability weren't opposites at all. She could be telling the truth about her feelings and lying about their origin, without knowing either way. The narrator was unreliable not because she deceived but because she reported faithfully from inside a distorted room.

He tried to say this out loud and it came out in three false starts, which Priya let him have, and Marcus interrupted once, and then Cohen got it out whole: "She's not lying to us. She's lying to herself about where her wanting came from, and the book is honest about her dishonesty, if you read the gaps instead of the sentences." The room went quiet in the way that meant people were either thinking or embarrassed for him. Priya said, slowly, that the ending still bothered her, because if everything Mrs. Keeling wants is trained into her, then giving up the house isn't freedom either, it's just new training. Marcus said maybe some wants are more hers than others, and couldn't say how you'd tell.

That was the part Cohen couldn't resolve, and he didn't try to in the essay he wrote that night at the kitchen table. He argued that Mrs. Keeling was a reliable witness and an unreliable guide, and that de Beauvoir's line, which he looked up to make sure Marcus had gotten it right, gave him a way to hold both claims at once. In the last paragraph he admitted the boundary stayed unclear: where the self ended and the shaping began was a question the novel refused to settle, and he had decided to trust the novel's refusal more than his own need for a verdict.

Walking to school the next morning he passed the economics room, where Mr. Vashti was writing "stagflation" on the board for the seniors, a word that meant, as far as Cohen could gather from the grumbling through the door, everything going wrong at the same time. He thought briefly that Mrs. Keeling's world was like that, stagnant and inflating at once, then decided the comparison was clever rather than true and let it go. At lunch he put his essay in Priya's hands and waited while she read the final page. She looked up and said, "You left it open." Cohen said, "Yeah." She handed it back and said, "Good," and went to get in line for the microwave.

The placement exam was on Saturday, and Chase had until then to prove he belonged in the fall chemistry section instead of the semester-long remedial one. He sat at the kitchen table with the practice booklet open to a problem about heating limestone: given the mass of calcium carbonate, calculate the moles of calcium oxide formed. His mother kept the house quiet for him, and she'd left a plate of cut mango by his elbow without saying anything, which was her way of saying plenty.

He copied the problem onto a fresh sheet. Fifty grams of calcium carbonate. He knew the molar mass was supposed to be on the periodic table, that you added the atomic masses, and he did that part slowly, writing 40.08 plus 12.01 plus three times 16.00, checking the columns twice the way his chemistry teacher had drilled into him back when he still showed up. Then divide the mass by the molar mass to get moles of the reactant. That was the conversion he could do. What he kept losing was the next step, the bridge between the moles of what he started with and the moles of what he ended up with.

Maya let herself in through the back door at four, the way she had since they were nine. She smelled like espresso and the lemon cleaner they made her wipe the counters with at the café on Miller Street. She pulled out the chair across from him and sat down without asking, which was also the way since they were nine.

"How's the prison sentence," she said.

"Three more days." He turned the sheet toward her. "I can get the moles of reactant. Then there's supposed to be a ratio, one to one or whatever it is, and I keep guessing instead of knowing why."

She picked up the mango and ate a piece, watching him. "You need the balanced equation. The coefficients tell you the ratio. If it's one to one, then the moles of product equal the moles of reactant, and that's it, you're done."

He pulled the booklet closer. The equation was there at the bottom of the problem, and he'd skipped over it, hunting for something more complicated. One calcium carbonate made one calcium oxide, so the moles came straight across, 0.499, and he wrote it and immediately doubted it because it had felt too easy. He'd spent forty minutes on something that took four once he knew where to look.

"Is that all it is? Finding the door instead of the wall?"

"That's a lot of things," Maya said. She was quiet a second, then laughed a little. "It's like the shop today. Same number of people inside all afternoon, seriously, the counter clock said forty-one at two and forty-one at five. But it wasn't the same people. They kept coming in the front and leaving through the side door, just at the same rate, so the count never moved."

"Okay," Chase said. He was only half listening, checking his division again.

"That's what my boss said equilibrium is," she said. "He took chemistry at the community college. Both reactions keep happening, forward and reverse, but at equal rates, so the amounts stay constant. I thought about it all shift."

He set his pencil down. "The amounts stay constant even though nothing stops."

"That's what he said. Dynamic, he called it. Moving and still at the same time."

He looked at his problem, the little balanced equation with its ones, and at her, still in her apron, mango juice on her thumb. He had been treating the chemistry like a locked box, something that either opened or didn't, and she was describing a door that people passed through both ways forever while the room stayed the same size. He wasn't sure yet what the two ideas had to do with each other, whether the mole problem and the equilibrium thing were neighbors or strangers, and he was honest enough with himself to sit in that not-knowing instead of papering over it with confidence.

"I might be doing that," he said. "Learning like nothing's moving so the answer stays put."

"Or you could stop letting yourself off the hook," Maya said. "You did that all through junior year. It's not casuistry when you do it, it's just excuses."

He laughed, caught. "Same thing, though. dressed up or dressed down."

"Dressed up it's worse." She slid the mango plate closer to him and stood, rinsing her hands at the sink, because she knew he'd forget to eat otherwise. "I have a closing shift tomorrow. Text me when you finish a practice exam and I'll bring you the day-old scones."

That evening his mother came through on her way to bed and found him still at the table, three more problems deep, the sheet of conversions now running in a neat column. She read over his shoulder, not understanding any of it, and he preempted the question by telling her the limestone one anyway: fifty grams in, half a mole out, the ratio doing the quiet work between them. She touched his shoulder and left the mango plate a little nearer his hand.

On Saturday morning, waiting outside the testing room with his admission slip, he did a last judicious review of the steps, not everything, just the ones he'd gotten wrong twice: molar mass, then divide, then the ratio, then stop. Somewhere in the middle of it Maya's café came back to him, the forty-one customers, the front door and the side door, and he thought about how a number could hold perfectly still while everything inside it kept moving. He didn't know if he'd pass. He knew how to find out. The proctor opened the door and said, "Phones off, find a seat," and Chase went in.

Brandon had shared the video at 11:42 on a Tuesday night, and by Wednesday afternoon two hundred people had seen it through him alone. It showed a warehouse fire, a wall of orange rolling toward a camera, someone screaming behind the lens. His cousin Dex had texted him a single question mark an hour later, then a link to a fact-checking site, then nothing, which was somehow worse than anything he could have typed. Brandon walked to the public library because his room had bad lighting and worse associations, and because Mrs. Okafor, who ran the media literacy workshop on Thursdays, had once told him the computers there had bigger screens and no history anyone at school could subpoena.

The video had come with a caption claiming the fire happened that morning in a city four states away, which explained why his aunt had called his mother in a panic about an uncle who lived there. That part still made his stomach drop. He had forwarded it to the family group chat, where it had multiplied like something biological. Brandon sat down at a terminal, created a folder in his drive called Never Again, and opened a tab.

Mrs. Okafor drifted past with a cart of returns. "You look like a man doing penance," she said.

"I shared a fire video that wasn't a fire video," Brandon said. "It's from 2017. Some guy just proved it to me with a screenshot, but I want to know how he did it."

She set the cart down. "Reverse image search. Take a frame, feed it to the search engine, and it finds where the picture has been before. You want the source and the date before you believe anything, let alone forward it to eleven relatives."

He paused the video on its clearest frame, the one where the smoke made a shape like a fist, and saved it. Then he dragged it into the search bar the way she'd indicated, with a small flourish he immediately regretted, and waited. The results bloomed slowly, like something thinking. There it was: a news article from another country entirely, dated four years back, about a fire that had already happened, already been counted, already been grieved by people who were not his relatives.

"Okay," Brandon said quietly. "Okay, that's actually magic."

"That's indexing," Mrs. Okafor said. "Learn the difference and you'll go far."

Dex arrived at four with a slushie and no apology, which was his way of apologizing. He dropped into the chair beside Brandon's and peered at the screen. "So you're the arsonist's accomplice turned detective. My mom thinks you personally set the fire."

"I didn't denigrate the family name," Brandon said. "I just laundered a lie through it."

"You forwarded a 2017 video to twelve adults with phones. That's not laundering, that's arson." Dex slurped his drink with intent. "How'd you check it?"

Brandon showed him the frame, the drag, the results. Dex watched with the expression of someone seeing a card trick he suspected he could learn. "Wait, so the search engine knows every picture that's ever been on the internet?"

"No," Brandon said, and then, realizing he didn't actually know what the answer was, "Sort of? Give me a second." He typed how does the search engine store all those images and got a descending spiral of forum posts, then a scanned chapter from a database textbook the library had digitized, its pages yellow at the margins on screen.

The chapter opened with a sentence he read three times: that the relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." He turned to Dex. "This is why everything's tables. This guy Codd, in 1970, some IBM researcher, wrote a paper called 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks,' and now the whole internet is rows and columns."

"Fifty years and we're still doing homework off one guy's paper," Dex said. "Hope he got paid."

Brandon scrolled on, half reading, half marveling. He had assumed the internet was chaos all the way down, and it was, in a way, but underneath the chaos someone had decided things would sit in tables, and that decision was older than his parents. What he still couldn't figure out was whether that made the video easier to catch or just made him feel like it was catchable, a distinction he suspected mattered. The fact-checking site had found the original in under a minute; his cousin's friend had needed an hour; the twelve adults in the group chat had needed a night of worry. Same tables, different searchers.

Dex leaned back and balanced his slushie on his knee. "So is it fixed? The group chat?"

"Nothing's fixed. Aunt Rosa's still texting my mom about Uncle Theo, who lives nowhere near any of it." Brandon copied the fact-check link, pasted it into the family chat, and typed an apology he rewrote twice before sending, shorter the second time. Then he opened his Never Again folder and, after a pause, renamed it something less dramatic: Before Sharing.

The reply came in fast, from Aunt Rosa: a thumbs-up, then a photo of Uncle Theo at a grill, entirely unharmed, giving the camera a look of profound insolvency, as though the fire had spent something he could never recover. Dex laughed so hard the slushie nearly went over. Brandon screenshotted it, ran the frame through a reverse image search out of pure habit, and found nothing but the family chat itself, dated today. "First original photo in the group," he said, and sent it back with the caption, verified.

The library at half past three had the crepuscular hush of a place that had given up on the day, its long windows letting in a light the color of weak tea. Xavier spread his materials across the table with the ceremony of someone who had read about ritual but never practiced it: the photocopied pages of Jane Eyre, his notebook, a pencil he had sharpened into a weapon. His assignment, due Friday, was to read the passage where Mr. Rochester interrogates Jane about her feelings and then to explain it through either a feminist or a Marxist lens. He had chosen both, mostly because choosing felt like commitment and commitment felt like a trap.

"You look like a man defusing something," said Priya, dropping into the chair opposite him with a paperback held at arm's length, as though it had bitten her.

"I'm applying critical lenses," Xavier said. "It's a whole process."

"It's a whole scam, is what it is." She set the book down. Gone Girl, the cover said, 2012 stamped in the corner of her book club flyer tucked inside. "The book club pick. It alternates between two narrators, the husband and the wife, so you get his chapter, then hers, all the way through. I trusted her half. I believed every word." She jabbed the cover. "Amy. Her name's Amy. She wrote a false diary, and she planted it so it would mislead the police. I spent a hundred pages inside that diary feeling sorry for her."

Xavier considered this. "So the book lied to you on purpose."

"The book did its job. I did mine badly. How did she get me, though? That's what I want to know. What's the trick?"

He didn't have an answer, but the question sat down next to his own problem like an unwanted sibling. He looked at his Jane Eyre pages, at the paragraphs he had already marked, and began to titrate his argument, adding one piece of evidence at a time and watching for the moment the whole solution changed color. Jane says she is poor, obscure, plain, and little; Rochester calls her elf, sprite, fairy. A feminist reading noticed that he never quite lets her be a woman with wages. A Marxist reading noticed that she is, in fact, an employee, and that his flattery arrives at the exact moment she might otherwise ask for a reference and leave. The two readings, he was starting to suspect, were not rivals. They were describing the same cage from two sides.

"That's actually it," he said aloud, mostly to himself.

"What's it?"

"The diary. Amy had to sound like a real person, so Flynn gave her the small true things, the boring things, and slid the lie in underneath." He turned back to Jane Eyre. "Rochester does the same thing. He sounds like a man in love because half of it is true, and the untrue half is about ownership. The lens doesn't tell you the book is bad. It tells you where the author's thumb is on the scale."

Priya squinted at him. "You just solved my problem and your problem at the same time, which is deeply annoying."

He copied a sentence into his notebook, feeling briefly like a scholar of antiquity deciphering a coin, certain the emperor on it had a name and certain he would never know it. Then he got to the fourth page of the photocopy, the paragraph where Rochester laments that Jane will ruin him, and stopped. The prose had gone strange. There was a joke about a Tesla. There was the phrase "emotionally unavailable, which is literally his whole brand." Xavier read it three times, the way you reread a floor you are about to fall through.

"Priya," he said. "Look at this paragraph."

She read it. Her face did something complicated. "This is from the internet. Someone pasted a parody paragraph into the copy. Your whole Marxist thing is built on a fake."

He sat back. Half his margin notes lived in that paragraph. The other half lived in paragraphs that were, as far as he could now prove, real, though he could not prove it from where he sat. He thought about Amy's diary again, about how a lie needs a carpet of truth to stand on, and then about how he would explain to his teacher that his essay was mostly sound, provisionally, pending verification against an actual edition.

"So what do you write?" Priya asked.

Xavier picked up his pencil. "I write it anyway," he said. "And I footnote the Tesla."

Mr. Okafor had written one thing in red at the top of Jade's paper, and she had been staring at it for ten minutes without touching her tea. Use the right system, it said, and under it: author-date? She sat at the kitchen table with the paper flat in front of her, the ceiling light buzzing, her little brother's shoes drying on the radiator and smelling faintly of pond. She had thought Chicago was Chicago. She had footnoted everything, numbered everything, built a bibliography that looked, to her, like a small city.

Her mother came through with a bag of groceries and set it down. "You look like somebody died."

"It's fine," Jade said. "It's just a citation thing."

Her mother peeled an orange, unimpressed, and left the segments in a bowl beside the teapot, which was her way of staying.

The assignment, the one that mattered, was still due Friday: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, in this case whether standardized testing narrowed achievement gaps or merely measured them. Article one, by a sociologist named Reinhardt, ran forty pages of regression tables and ended in a hushed, statistical kind of defeat. Article two, by a historian named Amaya, was almost lugubrious in its prose, moving through a century of testing policy like someone walking through a graveyard reading names. They disagreed, and they disagreed in a way that seemed to Jade deeper than evidence, deeper than who had the better data. They disagreed about what kind of question it was.

She had highlighted a sentence of Reinhardt's: The gap is not a fact about children but a fact about measurement. She had highlighted a sentence of Amaya's: A test is an argument about what a society has decided to count. Those two sentences sat in her notebook, side by side, and she could not make them stop contradicting each other, or maybe they didn't contradict, maybe they were two halves of something, and that possibility palpitated in her chest whenever she looked at them, quick and irregular, like something alive under a cloth.

First, though, the returned paper. She opened her laptop and typed Chicago citation systems and read, and read again. There were two. One was called notes and bibliography, and it was common in history and the humanities. The other was called author-date, and it was common in the sciences. She looked at Mr. Okafor's question, author-date, and at her neat numbered footnotes, and understood, slowly, that she had used the historian's system for a paper in a class that ran like a science. Amaya would have loved her footnotes. Reinhardt would have wanted parentheses.

Her friend Priya called at nine. "Did you fix it?"

"There's nothing to fix, exactly," Jade said, holding the phone with her shoulder while she reformatted. "There are two systems. Notes and bibliography, or author-date. I used the wrong one for his class." She was typing as she spoke, pulling dates out of footnotes and pushing them into parentheses, and the paper changed shape under her hands, became leaner, less ceremonious, a different kind of argument dressed differently. "It's the same sources. It's just two ways of saying where they came from."

"That's insane," Priya said.

"It's kind of not," Jade said, and found she meant it.

She went back to the two articles after Priya hung up, and here the withheld thing surfaced, the thing she had been circling all week without naming. Amaya's article, the one whose system she had used, whose sentences she had loved, had a flaw, and it was in footnote eleven. Amaya cited a study there, and the study was Reinhardt's, from years earlier, and Amaya described its findings in a way the findings did not support. Reinhardt had found no effect. Amaya's footnote said the study showed modest gains. Jade checked it three times, tea gone cold, orange segments brown at the edges. The historian she admired had bent the scientist's numbers, and the scientist's whole argument rested on the premise that numbers did not bend.

She wrote until one in the morning. Her review argued that Reinhardt's rigor and Amaya's context were both necessary, that a test was a measurement and a decision, and that where they conflicted was in footnote eleven, where the two systems of knowing touched and one of them gave way. She ended with what she could not resolve: whether Amaya had misread carelessly or hopefully, and whether it mattered which. She cited everything in author-date, parentheses like small doors.

At school on Friday she slid the pages under Mr. Okafor's door before the bell, and at lunch he found her in the hallway and held the review up, already dog-eared, one page turned down at the corner.

"Footnote eleven," he said. "You caught that?"

"I think so," Jade said. "I'm not sure she meant it."

"That's in here too," he said, tapping the last page. "Good. That's the part most people leave out."

Elijah had agreed to tutor his little cousin Nadia in biology partly as a favor and partly as subterfuge, because if he taught the material out loud he might finally understand it himself before Monday's exam. The community garden on Saturdays was where their mothers volunteered, so that was where the tutoring happened, wedged between the compost bins and a bed of somebody's ambitious kohlrabi. Nadia was ten and wanted only to know why her peas were dying, which Elijah felt was a fair question and not one the textbook answered.

"Okay," he said, laying a pea vine on the bench between them. "Every cell in this plant has a book of instructions in it. DNA. And the book never leaves the library." He paused, checking his own memory. "So when the cell needs to make something, it copies one page."

"Photosynthesis makes sugar," Nadia said immediately, because she had been told this at school and considered it her best fact.

"Sure, but that's the kitchen. I'm talking about the copying part." He traced a line down the pea leaf with his finger. "The copy is called mRNA. It carries the recipe out to the machinery, and the machinery reads it three letters at a time and builds a protein. Copying is transcription. Building is translation."

Nadia squinted at him. "You're just transliterating the textbook. Sounding out words you can't read."

That stung precisely because it was true. He could recite the sequence, RNA polymerase to ribosome to amino acid chain, the way he could recite song lyrics, and it meant about as much. He decided to prove her wrong, which was as good a motivation as any.

Mr. Okafor, who ran the tomato rows and had a saturnine way of watching the world as if it had disappointed him before and would again, came over to refill his watering can. "You two arguing over those peas?"

"Nadia wants to know where the mass comes from," Elijah said. "The plant gets bigger every week. Where does the new stuff come from?"

"Air," said Mr. Okafor, and walked off before explaining, which Elijah found deeply unsporting.

"Air is nothing," Nadia said.

They carried the pea vine to the little pond at the garden's edge to water it properly, and Nadia, being ten and therefore incapable of sitting still, blew bubbles across the surface through a reed. Between bubbles she breathed on a cold stone and drew in the condensation with her fingertip. "Is carbon in my breath? We breathe out carbon dioxide, we did it in class."

Elijah opened his mouth to say something vague and found that the vague thing had a shape now. "Yeah, CO2. Six of them, actually, if you burn one sugar molecule all the way down." He picked up a dead leaf from the pond's edge. "So a sugar is C6H12O6. Glucose. Six carbons. And it burns with six oxygens, and out come six CO2 and six water, plus energy. That's respiration. In, out. Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water."

"So the carbon in my breath was in a sugar," Nadia said slowly. "Was the sugar in my toast this morning?"

"Was in the wheat, which got the carbon out of the air, which is where Mr. Okafor's tomatoes are getting their new stuff." Elijah sat back on his heels, feeling the loop close with an almost audible click. "So the plant builds protein from the recipe in its DNA, but the atoms, the actual stuff, half of it drifted in as gas."

Nadia blew one more bubble and watched it pop. "So the library writes the recipe, but the kitchen is made of air."

He wrote that down in the margin of his notebook, because it was better than anything his textbook had said. On Monday the exam question asked him to explain transcription and translation, and he wrote about a library and a copy and a kitchen, and got the order right. What he still could not have said, even under oath, was how a string of letters became a protein that folded into exactly the shape it needed, how the kitchen knew what shape a tomato was. He suspected nobody fully knew, which he found comforting rather than alarming.

The next Saturday the peas had perked up, having objected to drainage rather than to philosophy, and Nadia demanded a new topic. Elijah looked at the pond, at the reed still lying in the grass where she had dropped it.

"Photosynthesis," he said. "It's the equation backwards. Bet you can't guess what the plant breathes in."

Seth had been staring at Dana's laptop for twenty minutes, and the empty result grid was starting to feel personal. The kitchen table was littered with her mother's mail, a bowl of pistachio shells, and two glasses of lemonade gone warm, and on the screen, patient and blank, sat the query.

"Run it again," Dana said.

"It's going to be empty again."

"Run it anyway."

He clicked the button. The grid stayed empty, zero rows returned, and Dana leaned back in her chair with the pugnacious satisfaction of somebody who had been right about a mystery before it was even a mystery. She worked the summer shift at her uncle's landscaping office, entering orders into a database she had mostly taught herself, and she had promised Seth she would teach him too, because he had said, once, at the edge of a conversation about their futures, that he wanted to understand how information was stored. He hadn't expected the learning to involve so much failure first.

The assignment she had invented for him was simple to say. Two tables, one of customers, one of orders. Find the customers who had never ordered anything. Seth had assumed this would take five minutes. Instead he had typed a query that said, in effect, give me every customer whose ID is not in the list of IDs found in the orders table, and the database had answered him with silence.

"Maybe the query's wrong," he said.

"Or maybe it's right and something's hiding." Dana spun her finger in the air, the universal sign for try it a different way, and Seth retyped the whole thing by hand, slowly, the way his father had taught him to change a tire: no shortcuts, name every step out loud. Still nothing. He felt the particular itch of being close to an answer, that sensation he loved and hated in equal measure, the one that had kept him up past two in the morning last spring converting his grandmother's recipe cards into a spreadsheet, just to see whether it could be done.

She reached over and pulled the laptop toward herself. "Watch this," she said, and she ran a small query against the orders table alone, counting rows. Then she filtered for something, and Seth watched the count drop by one.

"One order has a blank customer," Dana said. "My uncle's shop guy, he types the plant list first and forgets to pick a name. The system saves it anyway. So that row is sitting in there with nothing in the customer column."

Seth looked at the single offending row, a Saturday order for forty boxwood shrubs attached to no one at all. A suspicion arrived, not fully formed, more like weather moving in. He scrolled back up to his query, the one with NOT IN, and read it again as if meeting a stranger who had been standing in the room the whole time.

"Wait," he said. "So the list my subquery builds, the list of customer IDs from the orders table. That list has a blank in it now."

"Say more."

"Last week, when you showed me this on Tuesday, it worked. It listed three customers. Then Saturday happened, the boxwoods, the blank." He heard himself say it and stopped, because the rest of it assembled itself without narration: the query that had returned three rows on Tuesday returned nothing at all today, and the only thing that had changed was that one empty value. The list his NOT IN was checking against contained a single blank, and the whole result had gone dark because of it.

He tested it the only way he could think of, which was to sequester the blank row, setting it aside in its own temporary table where it couldn't touch anything, and then run his original query against everything else. Three customers appeared, instantly, the same three from Tuesday: a dentist, a school, and a woman named R. Okafor who had signed up at a garden fair and never bought a thing.

"So it's not that the query was wrong," Seth said slowly. "It's that one blank poisons the whole list. A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL."

"That's what it looks like," Dana said. "I didn't know it had a name for why. I just knew to dodge it."

They sat with that for a second. Outside, Dana's little brother was failing to land a skateboard trick in the driveway, the clatter and the scrape of it arriving through the screen door at irregular intervals, a counterpoint to the hum of the laptop. Seth thought of his father again, changing that tire, saying that a car can refuse to start for one bad wire and a mechanic who only checks the battery will call it haunted. He wondered how many other things worked this way, whole systems falling silent over one empty value nobody meant to create.

"Is there a way to write it so it can't happen?" he asked.

"There's a different join that handles it," Dana said. "I'll show you. But first."

She pushed the laptop back toward him and pointed at the screen, at the Saturday row with its missing name. "Fix it."

Seth cracked his knuckles, typed UPDATE, and paused, cursor blinking beside the word SET.

The laundromat on Fenwick Street had two broken dryers and a vending machine that ate quarters, and Audrey had claimed the folding table by the window because from there she could watch the parking spaces along the curb. Her father called them practice bays. She called them torture devices with bumpers. Every Saturday they did three loads of wash and one load of parallel parking, because the car had to be somewhere while the clothes tumbled, and her test was in eleven days.

"Again," her father said, standing on the sidewalk with his coffee, steam fermenting in the cold air like the whole morning was quietly going sour. Audrey pulled forward past the orange hatchback, reversed until her rear wheel was level with its bumper, and turned the wheel. She ended up a foot and a half from the curb, angled like something that had given up halfway through a decision.

"Twenty-five centimeters or less," her father said, tapping the roof. "You're generous with your distance."

"I'm generous with everything. It's my whole personality." She straightened the car, tried again, and this time heard the tire kiss the curb with a sound like a knuckle cracking. She let the brake off an inch. The car settled. When she got out and looked, she was close, actually close, and she stood there in the cold feeling something she didn't have a word for yet, a small triumph that she immediately distrusted because she'd done nothing but the same thing six times until it worked once.

The highway came later, after the laundromat, because the dryer took forty minutes and the on-ramp to Route 9 was four blocks away. Audrey's father believed in the round trip: wash, drive, merge, come back, fold. "Use the time," he said, which was his answer to most things, including grief, including her mother having left in September, including money, which they didn't discuss in numbers anymore. The laundromat itself was a kind of confession. Everyone there was washing somewhere else because they couldn't wash at home, and Audrey had started to recognize the regulars: the man with the work jackets, the woman who read court documents, the teenager who slept against the wall with headphones on.

On the ramp, Audrey accelerated and looked over her shoulder. A delivery truck sat in the right lane, close, its grille filling her side mirror like a wall. She waited for it to slide left, to open a door for her, the way she'd seen cars do for her mother a hundred times. It didn't move. She ran out of ramp, braked hard at the gore point, and sat there with her hazard lights ticking while her father set down his coffee.

"Who has to yield here?" he asked. Not angry. That was worse, in a way, because it meant he'd known this was coming.

"The truck," she said. "It should move over."

"Traffic already on the highway has the right of way," he said, and that was all he said. Audrey looked at the mirror again, at the stream of cars behind the truck, and understood that nobody was going to make room, that the road was not a meritocracy where good intentions earned you a gap, that she had to find the space herself. She watched the pattern of vehicles come at her, a school of them, and picked out a hole two cars back, adjusted her speed to shrink toward it rather than demanding it shrink toward her, and merged. The car settled into the lane like a word finding its place in a sentence.

They drove in silence for a while. Audrey was thinking that her mother had always been the one who moved over, who made room, and that maybe that was a way of being good or maybe it was a way of disappearing, and she couldn't decide, and the not-deciding was itself a kind of answer she didn't like. At the laundromat they folded towels side by side, her father pairing socks with a penurious exactness, refusing to lose even one. The teenager by the wall had woken up and was watching the dryers spin as if they held something of his. Audrey laid her palms flat on a stack of warm towels, still carrying the shape of the steering wheel, and thought of the test, eleven days out, no promises attached.

"Next week the highway first," her father said, handing her the keys to lock up.

"Fine," she said. "But I pick the music."

Nicole pushed the coffee table to the wall and set nine coins across the rug: a quarter for Priya, a nickel for Marcus, pennies for the others. Her mother had asked, twice, why the living room smelled like dust and basement, and Nicole had answered both times that the drama room was booked until six and the performance was Friday.

The one-act was thirty pages long and hers to direct, which still felt like a mistake the drama teacher would eventually correct. She knelt over the coins and moved the quarter two inches left, then back. "You stand here when he says the thing about the river," she said to Priya, tapping the carpet, "and you cross on 'impecunious,' because it's the ugliest word in the play and the crossing makes it funny." Priya walked the path once, stiff-armed, waiting.

Marcus refused to move at all. He stood by the bookshelf with his script rolled in his fist and said that his character wouldn't cross, that his character would stay planted, and that actors found those things by trying them, not by being told. "That's what blocking is for," Nicole said. "It's the plan for where everyone stands and moves." Marcus said plans were for people who didn't trust their actors, and Priya laughed in a way that suggested she had picked a side.

That night, after everyone had gone, Nicole sat on the couch with her laptop and looked up where the word came from. Nineteenth-century directors, she read, including W. S. Gilbert, planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. She read it twice, then got a wooden block from her little brother's shelf and set it on the coffee table where Marcus refused to stand. It was a plain square of maple, and it did exactly what she told it to do.

She was not sure which of them was right, and she tried to introspect on it honestly, which mostly meant sitting still and watching herself not decide. Last year she had assistant-directed under a boy who choreographed every gesture, and the play had been precise and dead. The year before that she had acted in a production where nobody planned anything, and by opening night the cast had been blocking each other in the literal sense, colliding around a doorway in the second scene like strangers in a stairwell. Two failures, two opposite reasons. Somewhere between them was the thing she actually wanted, and she could describe it only as control that left room.

Her friend Dee came over Thursday with her chemistry flashcards, because Dee studied everywhere, even on Nicole's floor during a break. "Monomer," Dee said, flipping a card. "It's one unit on its own. Then a bunch of them link up and you get a polymer." Nicole looked at the coins still scattered across the rug, each one a separate small decision, and thought that a blocking plan might work the same way, except that actors were units that argued back.

At the final run-through, she tried it. "Marcus," she said, "I'm giving you the spot by the shelf as yours. Planted, like you wanted. But when Priya crosses on 'impecunious,' you turn your head and follow her, and that's not negotiable, because the audience needs to know you noticed." Marcus turned his head, once, experimentally, as if checking whether his neck agreed. "And everyone else," Nicole said, kneeling to slide the pennies along the carpet, "you follow this, but if something true happens in the moment, take it, and tell me after so I can change the map."

The run-through was not clean. Priya went up on a line and covered it with a cough, and one of the pennies, standing in for a boy named Elliot, ended up on the sofa while Elliot himself was still by the window. But the crossing landed, and Marcus's head turn landed harder than any of her choreography had, because it cost him something to do it. Afterward, while the others gathered scripts and shoes, Marcus stopped at the door. "Gilbert guy used blocks," he said. "I looked it up too. Whole model stage, one block per actor." Nicole held up the maple square she had left on the coffee table. "Then this is you," she said, and set it down on the shelf spot, and left it there.

The garage smelled of WD-40 and the ghost of every lawn mower Nolan's father had ever abandoned there, and at its center, balanced on two sawhorses and an upturned milk crate, stood the ramp. It was a length of vinyl gutter with one end propped on a stack of physics textbooks, which Nolan considered a nice touch, like a snake eating its own tail. At the bottom of the ramp the gutter curved into a short horizontal lip, so that a marble rolling down it would leave the edge moving purely sideways, purely horizontally, and then fall, and then, if Nolan had anything to say about it, land exactly where he predicted.

He had predicted the desk. The marble had just landed in a coffee can he had put there on a whim, which was worse, somehow, than missing entirely, because now the can was acting smug.

"You're grinning at a can," said Priya from the workbench, where she sat with her knees pulled up on a stool, a printout in her lap. She had come over under the pretense of helping, which so far had meant watching him chase marbles and eating the crackers he'd set out for himself. She was phlegmatic about most things, Nolan had decided long ago, the kind of person who could receive a failing grade or a free car with the same mild blink. "That's not a good sign for either of us."

"It landed where I said. Approximately. Within the can's radius plus the desk's width." He crouched and picked up his notebook, where he had split the marble's launch into two halves that had nothing to do with each other, which was the part that still felt like a magic trick. Sideways, the marble kept its speed forever, unbothered, seven meters a second from now until the end of time. Downward, it started from nothing and got faster, dragged into acceleration like everyone else. Two lives, lived simultaneously, only meeting again when he combined them to find where the thing came down. "The whole point is you don't mix them up. Horizontal doesn't know about gravity. Gravity doesn't care about horizontal. They're strangers on the same train."

"That's almost poetic."

"It's the only poetry I'm getting this semester." He rolled the marble back up to the top of the ramp and let it go. It clicked down the gutter, whispered across the lip, dropped, and this time missed the can by a full hand-width. Nolan stared at the wet mark it left on the concrete, transfixed, as though the marble might apologize and shuffle over. It did not. He measured the distance anyway and wrote it in the column marked should have been.

Priya slid off the stool and came to crouch beside him, holding out the printout. "Okay, since you're the local genius. My lab from the college thing. Two plates, twelve millimeters apart, hooked to the supply, and we were supposed to move the probe around and check the field against the formula. E equals V over d. Mine matched in the middle, more or less. Then I moved the probe near the edge of the plates and my number went weird. Too small. Like way too small. And my write-up is due Monday and the TA wrote, in actual red pen, 'explain this discrepancy.'" She said the last two words with the flat dread of someone reading a prophecy.

Nolan took the paper. The numbers marched down the page, well-behaved in the middle rows and then, near the end, sagging like the end of a week. "What did you write?"

"That I think I held the probe wrong." She shrugged. "Which is possible. I hold most things wrong."

He was quiet for a moment, not because he knew, but because the shape of her bad numbers reminded him of something, the same way the marble's miss had a shape to it. His mind drifted briefly into a reverie of all the perfect drawings in his textbook: neat parallel arrows, field lines marching in formation between two plates, straight as soldiers, straight as the marble's imaginary sideways life. And then his actual marble, curving off its appointed path the instant it left the ramp, because the ramp's guidance stopped at the edge and the world's sloppiness began. He got up, stepped over the crate, and dug through the milk crate of books until he found the chapter on capacitors, its edges already soft from his grandmother's habit of reading while cooking.

He flipped pages. There it was, a diagram of two plates, and at the plates' edges the once-orderly lines bowed outward, escaping into open air like prisoners gone over a wall. He read the caption aloud, slowly, following it with his finger. "Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, so E equals V over d holds best near the centre." He looked up. "There's a name for it. Fringing."

"Fringing," Priya repeated, testing the word like a marble on her tongue. "So the edges of my plates are fringing, and my probe wasn't wrong, it was just standing in the wrong part of the field."

"That's the good part. Your measurement isn't the mistake. The formula is the thing with the boundary." Nolan set the book down on the workbench, open to the diagram, and Priya leaned over it, her ponytail hanging into the space between the drawn plates, which he chose not to point out because he was, at this moment, generous. She copied the caption into her notebook, then added three exclamation points and a small drawing of her TA's red pen being snapped in half.

"So the middle of the field is tidy," she said, "and the edges are where everything bends out and leaks away."

"Which is why my marble's late, probably. It's fringing." Nolan pointed at the wet mark on the concrete, three centimeters from where physics said it should be, and Priya laughed the way she always did, quietly and mostly through her nose. He picked up the marble again, weighed it in his palm, and walked it back to the top of the ramp.

The kitchen smelled like burnt toast and solder, which meant Marcus had commandeer the entire first floor for his interview prep. Jason set his backpack down by the door and found his friend at the table with his grandfather, both of them adjusting their grips on each other's hands like they were tuning an instrument.

"Again," the old man said. "You're giving me a dead fish."

"It's a handshake, Grandpa. Not a hostage exchange."

"It's the first thing they'll judge you on. Jason, tell him."

Jason hesitated, because the thing he actually knew was more specific than that. "There was a study," he said. "Two thousand, led by a psychologist named William Chaplin. He found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. That's it. That's the whole finding."

"There," the grandfather said. "Firm handshakes, favorable impressions. Science agrees with me."

"Correlation," Marcus muttered. "Not destiny."

Upstairs, the real work was waiting. Their robotics team had regionals in eleven days, and Marcus was the presenter, the one who had to explain their water-quality sensor to the judges in four minutes. He ran the demo for Jason and his grandfather, who had followed them up to reclaim his reading glasses, and Jason watched him lose the room in the first thirty seconds. He fiddled with the sample vial. He said "um" the way other people breathe. He ended with "so, yeah," which was the verbal equivalent of the dead fish.

"Well?" Marcus said, after. He was still holding the vial, and his knuckles had gone pale around it.

Jason knew what he was supposed to say, because Coach Ramirez kept saying it: be honest with your teammates. He also knew that last month, when he'd told Marcus the old arm design was "kind of a mess," Marcus hadn't spoken to him for two days. Those two approaches sat in him like two incompatible things, honesty on one side, the friendship on the other, and he could not find the hinge between them.

"It was fine," he said.

"Fine means bad," Marcus said. "You do this face."

"I don't do a face."

"You're doing it right now."

Marcus's grandfather, from the doorway, did not help by being facetious about it. "Perhaps the machine could shake hands with the judges," he offered. "Since it appears to be the only one here with a firm grip." Marcus threw a pillow at him and he retreated, laughing, down the stairs.

Jason pulled out his biology flashcards, mostly as something to do with his hands. Antigen, read the top one, and he stared at the word while he tried to think. An antigen was a thing the body recognized as foreign and responded to. That was the problem, he realized. His feedback kept arriving looking like an attack, so Marcus's whole system treated it as something to fight off. "Kind of a mess" wasn't information. It was a shapeless insult with no handle on it.

"Run it again," Jason said. "I want to time the opening."

"Seriously?"

"Thirty seconds to the demo, then you're talking. Go."

Marcus ran it again. Jason counted the filler words on his fingers, marked where the vial-fiddling started, watched where the explanation of the sensor's calibration actually landed, because it was good, sharper than anything the other teams would bring. When Marcus finished, Jason made himself start there.

"The calibration part, the ninety seconds in the middle, is the best thing you've done all season. It's clear, it's confident, and it's the part the judges will remember." Marcus's shoulders came down an inch. "The problem is everything before it. You said 'um' nine times in the first thirty seconds, and you picked up the vial before you told us what it was for, so we watched your hands instead of listening. If you just stand still for the first ten seconds, the 'um's stop."

Marcus looked at the vial in his hand, then set it deliberately on the desk. "Nine?"

"I counted."

"Creepy, but okay." He rubbed his palms on his jeans. "Again?"

They ran it four more times. By the third, the opening was clean, and by the fourth Marcus had stopped reaching for the vial entirely. His grandfather reappeared at the door with two glasses of lemonade and made them both shake his hand before he would surrender the drinks, and Marcus gripped hard enough to make the old man's eyebrows go up in approval.

"See," the grandfather said. "Favorable first impression."

"Correlation," Marcus said, but he was grinning. He turned back to the desk and squared his shoulders toward the imaginary judges. "Thirty seconds. Time me."

Jason raised his phone, thumb on the stopwatch. "Go."

The assignment was on the board in Ms. Okafor's handwriting: a ten-minute play, one moment from your own life, staged by Friday. Matthew sat in the third row of the classroom and wrote nothing for most of the period. He had a moment. He simply did not want it performed by a boy from his fourth period in front of thirty acquaintances.

The moment was this: two Januaries ago, his father had missed his regional swim final, and afterward, in the parking lot, Matthew had said the sentence he could not stop hearing. "You were at work when it mattered." His father had not answered. He had unlocked the car, and they had driven home with the radio on, and that was all. Matthew wrote four other ideas that week, about a lost wallet, about a fistfight he had never actually been in, about a made-up summer job. Ms. Okafor read them in conference and slid them back across the desk. "These are costumes," she said. "Write the parking lot." She was not doctrinaire about much, but she held this line against every draft he brought her, and by Wednesday he gave in.

He cast Dev Raghunathan as himself, which was a mistake he would understand later. Dev was tall and confident and had never once, as far as Matthew knew, been ashamed of anything. Priya Nair, who had stage-managed the winter one-acts, agreed to run the rehearsal because she owed Ms. Okafor a favor and because, as she put it, she liked watching people rehearse badly and then stop. They got the black box theater on Thursday after school, one folding table for the car, two chairs.

The first run-through collapsed in ninety seconds. Dev delivered the line facing the empty chair where his scene partner, a girl named Carmen playing the silent father, sat. From the house, Matthew watched the back of Dev's head. Priya stood up from her booth stool. "You're losing your face," she said. "Cheat out. It means you turn your body partly toward the audience even while you're talking to another character, so your face and voice carry." Dev tried it, angled maybe thirty degrees toward the empty seats, and suddenly Matthew could see his mouth moving, could hear the words land instead of dying against the back wall.

Matthew had his AP Bio textbook with him, because the midterm was Monday, and during a break he sat on the stage edge reading about antigens, the molecules your immune system learns to recognize and then attacks on sight. He looked up at Dev and Carmen running the scene again, and he thought that the line he had written was like that, something in him that had been recognized once and could not now be passed over without a reaction. He did not say this out loud. Priya would have called it trying to reify a feeling into a fact, which was something she said about bad plays, plays that took something moving and made it into a statue.

The second problem was worse than staging. Dev played the argument with style, with a kind of swagger, and Matthew sat in the house getting angrier with each run. "That's not how it went," he finally said, walking up onto the stage. "I wasn't winning. I was seventeen seconds too late to take it back." Dev folded his arms. "So what do you want, man? Sad kid yells at dad, dad's silent, drive home. That's the whole play?" Matthew stood there between the folding table and the chairs. "Yes," he said. "That's the whole play. I've been trying to make it something else all week and it isn't." Dev looked at him for a moment, and then something in his posture loosened, and he said, "Okay. Run it."

On Friday afternoon the class filed in. Carmen had been given one direction only: she never cheated out. She faced Dev fully, the whole time, so the audience saw her profile and Dev's face, which meant that the silence belonged to Matthew's father while the sentence belonged to Matthew. Whether that was fair, Matthew did not know. He suspected it was not. He had put it that way anyway, and he sat in the back row with his arms crossed, honest at least about the uncertainty, because the play asserted a judgment about that parking lot that he had never actually settled in two years of thinking about it.

The scene ran ten minutes and four seconds. Nobody laughed where he had feared laughter. At the line, Dev cheated out toward the audience, the words carrying into the dark, his face open and slightly turned, and in the silence afterward Carmen stared straight ahead at him and said nothing, and the folding table held the imaginary car keys, and the lights came up.

Ms. Okafor asked afterward whether he wanted to talk about it, and Matthew said no, and she nodded and moved on to the next play. After class, in the hallway, Dev caught up with him at the water fountain. "Hey," Dev said. "That thing where I turn toward the audience. Your dad. That's you doing that to everyone, right? Facing them partly so they can hear you?" Matthew drank, wiped his mouth on his sleeve, and walked the other way down the hall, keeping his back to him.

Mr. Okafor had said the words twice, and both times they had slid off Robert like rain off waxed paper: DNA to RNA to protein, transcription, translation. Then he had said the thing that mattered. "If you can teach it to someone who doesn't know it, Robert, then you know it. Otherwise you've memorized it." The test was Friday. Robert had until then to find somebody to teach.

The garden on Delancey Street had forty plots and a shed with a rusted roof, and on Saturday mornings Robert worked his mother's plot because she worked doubles at the hospital and because last summer he'd let the tomatoes die. This Saturday he brought his notebook anyway, propped open between the stakes of the bean trellis, and read his cramped notes while he pulled crabgrass. Nucleotide. Base pairing. RNA polymerase. The words sat on the page like strangers at a bus stop.

"That's the weirdest weeding I've ever seen," said Priya, from the plot beside theirs. She was a sophomore at the community college, garrulous in the early way of someone still delighted to have opinions, and she was forever talking across the fence about her biology class. "You're going to plant a textbook."

"I have to learn this stuff by Friday," Robert said. "And apparently the only way to learn it is to teach it. You want to be my victim?"

Priya dusted soil off her hands and leaned on the fence. "I literally just had a test on it. I failed it. So I'm a great victim, I won't accidentally know things."

He started badly. He said DNA was a template, and she asked what a template was, and he discovered he didn't know, not in a way he could say out loud. He turned back to the beans, and the turning helped. The vines climbed the strings by twining, each cell along the way reading something and becoming something. "Okay," he said slowly. "The DNA is like the master copy. It stays in the nucleus, it never leaves. But the cell needs instructions out at the ribosomes, where protein gets built. So it makes a copy of the part it needs. That's transcription. RNA polymerase unzips the DNA and builds a matching strand of RNA, one monomer at a time, matching base to base."

"Like writing down a recipe instead of carrying the whole cookbook to the kitchen."

"That's it. Exactly that." He felt something click into place that hadn't clicked in class, where the diagrams had all been arrows and nobody had said cookbook.

"And then translation is the cooking part?"

"Then translation is the cooking part." He crouched and drew in the dirt with a stick, three letters at a time. "The RNA gets read in threes, and each three is a codon, and each codon calls for one amino acid. The ribosome strings them together. Amino acid after amino acid, and the chain folds up and it's a protein. It's how the instructions become a thing that actually does work in the cell."

Priya was quiet for a second, which for Priya was remarkable. Then she pointed her trowel at the water barrel by the shed, the one that collected rain off the roof through a pipe. "You know what I got wrong on the test? Not this part. The energy part. There was this guy, Mitchell, he proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane. It's called chemiosmosis." She said the word carefully, the way she said new words, tasting it. "He won the Nobel Prize for it in 1978. That part I remember, because it was on the study sheet like four times. What I couldn't get was the gradient itself."

Robert looked at the barrel. The water behind it, pressing to get out through the pipe. Then he looked past the fence to the far end of the lot, where the Alvarez family had a little dirt dam across the drainage ditch to slow the rainwater for their peppers. "Like that," he said. "Like water behind a dam. The protons pile up on one side of the membrane and they want to get across, and that wanting is the energy. The cell lets them through a gate and uses the push."

Priya stared at the little dam across the ditch, water backed up and shimmering behind it, trickling through the one gap Mr. Alvarez had left. "A farm dam," she said. "He proposed it in 1961 and everybody laughed at him? And then seventeen years later they hand him the Nobel?"

"Seventeen years," Robert said. He thought about that. He thought about Mr. Okafor saying you know it when you can teach it, and about Priya failing her test anyway, and about how neither of those things had turned out to be the whole truth. Priya had known the fact cold, the name and the dates, and still hadn't been able to picture it until a pile of dirt across a drainage ditch did the work. Maybe knowing was layers, and you never got to the bottom one. He could explain transcription now, he was almost sure, but the why of it, why threes, why this monomer and not that one, was still dark water.

On Friday Robert got an A minus. He missed one question, about the energy, and he thought of Priya and almost laughed into his scantron. After school he walked to the garden. The Alvarez dam had been leveled by the storm Wednesday night, the peppers standing in mud, and Priya was already there with a shovel, and she handed him a second one without being asked.

"They said it couldn't hold," she said. "It held for three weeks."

He set his feet in the mud and drove the blade in.

The community centre smelled of floor wax and instant coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged into something the coach called a courtroom, though it looked more like a wake. Tyson sat at the respondents' table with a binder full of tabs he had labelled himself: Facts, Precedent, Rebuttal, Panic. He was eighteen and had never argued anything in public except with his mother about curfew, and now he was supposed to stand up in twenty minutes and defend a newspaper that had printed something wrong about a mayor.

He had drawn the harder side first. Tomorrow he would argue for the mayor; tonight he had to explain why an inaccurate story should not cost the paper anything. The error was small and human: the paper had reported that the mayor missed a council vote, when in fact he had left early and cast his ballot by proxy. Nobody disputed the mistake. What Tyson had to dispute was the punishment, and until three days ago he had assumed the paper would simply lose.

His discovery had happened by accident, scrolling in the centre's computer room while the seniors played euchre behind him. He found the case, New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964, and read the holding twice, then a third time with his finger under the words. A public official suing for libel had to prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth. He wrote it on his palm in ballpoint, then thought better of that and wrote it on an index card, which he now turned over and over between his fingers like a small dry piece of bread.

"They're ready for you," said Priya, who had drawn the judges' bench and was wearing her mother's black blazer for authority. She sat above him on a stacked table, flanked by two other students who had promised to ask hard questions.

Tyson stood. "Your honours, the paper made a mistake. But the plaintiff is a public official, and under New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964, he must prove actual malice. He has to show the statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth. There's no evidence of either. The reporter called the clerk's office twice. She wrote what she was told."

One of the judges, a boy named Marcus who took debate far too seriously, leaned forward. "So the mayor just has to absorb it? He did nothing wrong and his name is wrong in the paper?"

"No," Tyson said, and heard his own voice steady, which surprised him. "He can absorb a correction. That's what the paper ran, page two, and it exonerates him for anyone who reads it. What he can't do is collect damages without showing the paper didn't care whether it was true. That's the line. It's there so a paper that honestly gets it wrong isn't bankrupted, and honestly getting it wrong is what happened here."

Priya tapped her pen. "Suppose the paper hated the mayor. Suppose it wanted him gone."

"Then it's still not enough to hate him. Hating isn't knowing. They'd have to show the paper knew, or didn't care at all, and that's a hard thing to prove on purpose. It's supposed to be hard." Tyson paused, aware he was arguing something he half doubted. "I think it should be hard. If it were easy to sue, papers would only print what was safe, and a mayor could act like a little despot with a lawyer on retainer. Silence is cheaper than defence."

"But the wall can't be impermeable," Marcus said. "Somebody who lies on purpose has to pay."

"Somebody who lies on purpose fails the test," Tyson said. "Knowing falsehood is exactly what the rule catches. The rule is not a wall against everything. It's a wall against punishing error." He heard the metaphor and winced internally; Marcus had said impermeable, not him, but the borrowed word sat in the room anyway.

Priya looked at her colleagues, then down at her notes, then made a show of deliberation. "We'll rule for the paper," she said. "Insufficient showing of actual malice."

Tyson exhaled and sat down, and Marcus slid a folded paper across the aisle. Inside was the schedule for tomorrow's round. Tyson saw his name first, at the top, arguing for the mayor, and beneath it, in Priya's handwriting, the judges' roster for that session. Marcus had been reassigned to the bench. Tyson's best questioner was now his judge, and the first note on Marcus's pad, already written, read simply: "Ask him if he still believes the wall."

Tyson folded the schedule back along its crease and started crossing out tonight's closing argument.

Maxime's phone buzzed at 9:40 on a Tuesday night with a message from Yusra: the robotics club's roster program was due to Mr. Halvorsen by eight the next morning, and it was broken. He read it twice, then carried his laptop down to the kitchen, where his mother was sealing leftovers into containers with the methodical attention she gave everything after ten.

The program was supposed to look up whether a name was on the club roster, which had grown to four hundred members after the fall recruitment drive.
