Yusra had written the lookup herself, and she was proud of it; she'd called it a binary search in the meeting last week and sketched it on the whiteboard while Theo nodded along. But since Monday, three members had been told they weren't registered when they plainly were, and one had been locked out of the parts cabinet over it. Yusra had sent Maxime the code, the roster file, and a single line: "Fix it or I lose my mind."

He ran it with the name "Priya Raman." Not found. He ran it with "Priya Raman" again and got the same answer, which at least meant the program was consistent. He opened the roster file next and scrolled. Alvarez, Bhatt, Chen, then out of nowhere Ozdemir, then back to Dubois. The list was alphabetical only in patches, like a shelf where someone had shoved books in wherever they fit. He scrolled to the bottom and found a block of names added after recruitment, unsorted, pasted in by whoever had handled the sign-up sheet.

In his own code, Maxime tended to compartmentalize: rendering went in one file, input in another, and never did the two acknowledge each other. He had learned this from his father, who kept the pharmacy's taxes and the pharmacy's gossip in entirely separate drawers of his head. But this problem refused to stay separated. The program and the data were wrong together, and fixing one meant understanding the other.

He remembered, then, the afternoon in September when Yusra had first shown him what she was building. They were in the club room with the window open and the fan turning the smell of solder around, and she had explained it with a deck of cards. "You look at the middle card," she'd said, laying out a row face up, ordered lowest to highest. "If what you want is smaller, you throw away the whole right half, because it can't be there. Then you do it again on what's left." She'd snapped half the cards off the table each time, and the target turned up in three steps. It had seemed, that afternoon, like a trick with no catch.

Now he saw the catch. He typed a small test: he sorted a copy of the roster, ran the lookup on it, and Priya Raman appeared instantly, with a checkmark Yusra had added. He ran it on the original file and she vanished. So the program wasn't broken. It was doing exactly what it had been designed to do, and the middle item it kept landing on was Ozdemir, and everything it threw away after that was a half of the list that might have held Priya Raman but, as far as the program could tell, could not.

Yusra, at her desk across town, had reached the stage of debugging where she read her own code aloud as if interrogating a hostage. Her mother had gone to bed and left the hall light on, which meant she was allowed to keep working but was expected to whisper. She had tested the loop bounds. She had tested the comparison operator. She had drawn the indices on graph paper with her good pen. Nothing was wrong anywhere she looked, which was itself a kind of clue she didn't yet know how to read. Her somnolence kept arriving in waves; she fought it with mint tea and the conviction that Maxime would message soon, because Maxime, whatever his other faults, was perspicacious about things being wrong in places nobody checked.

Her phone lit up. "your list isn't sorted," Maxime had written. "the code is fine." She stared at the sentence and felt something between relief and insult. She opened the roster file, scrolled, and saw the September names, all eighty-two of them, sitting at the bottom in the order they'd been signed, which was the order of whoever had elbowed to the front of the line.

She called him. "So it just looks at the middle name?"

"And throws out the half that can't have your name in it," Maxime said. "But only if it's sorted. That's the whole rule. It wasn't fair of the list to lie about being alphabetical."

She laughed once, a short exhale. "The list didn't lie. I assumed."

"Same thing, at two in the morning."

It was eleven. They sorted a copy of the roster together while still on the call, Yusra reading names and Maxime running a script that merged the September block into place, and then she pasted it back into the club directory and ran every name that had failed. All found. She mailed the file to Mr. Halvorsen at 11:52 with a note about sorting the data on import, and he would read it at seven with his coffee and add it, without comment, to the list of things the club had learned this semester.

What neither of them wrote in the note, because neither could say it cleanly, was what they still weren't sure of. Maxime believed now that the fast way and the reliable way weren't opposites, that the fast way was simply a promise with conditions attached, and that you had to check the conditions the way you checked anything, by running the ugly test and watching it fail. But he couldn't decide whether the person who pasted in eighty-two unsorted names had been careless or whether carelessness was too small a word for a thing nobody had thought to ask about. He closed his laptop and sat in the kitchen light a while, and his mother put a container of rice in front of him without a word.

Yusra stayed at her desk. Before shutting everything down she opened a new file and typed, at the top, in a comment meant for whoever came after her: "The list must be sorted before this runs. Ask me how I know." Then she capped the good pen and turned off the lamp.

The printer in the library annex took four minutes to produce Chloe's graph, and it jammed twice on the way there, so by the time she carried the warm page back to the table, Devon had already eaten half the pretzels and rearranged her note cards into a fan.

"Your part's the graph," he said. "Mine's the stuff about gases trapping heat. I figured you'd want the hard half."

She spread the page out. It showed carbon dioxide climbing across a century, and across the climb, a fine sawtooth, up and down, up and down, thousands of tiny teeth. She had chosen it because it looked scientific, and now, printed, it looked like the machine had hiccuped the whole time. "I think there's something wrong with the data," she said. "Look at the wiggles. Maybe the sensor was broken. I'll say that in the presentation."

"You're going to stand up in front of Mr. Ruiz and tell him the most famous graph in climate science is broken."

"I'm going to say it cautiously. I'll preempt the question before anyone asks." She wrote on a card: possible instrument error. Devon took the card, read it, and slid it back with the flat expression of someone deciding not to be bellicose about it.

Mr. Ruiz's rule was that presentations could not be read off cards, which Chloe considered a form of clemency he extended to the audience and no one else. Third period, she stood at the front with the graph projected behind her, ten feet wide, her supposed error rendered in glorious detail. She got through the greenhouse part. Molecules absorb heat radiating from the surface and re-emit it, some of it back downward, so the atmosphere holds warmth it would otherwise lose. That part she could say in her sleep. Then the sawtooth filled the screen, and she heard herself say, "The small oscillations here may reflect measurement noise," and Ruth Okonkwo, who sat by the window and never spoke except when she was right, raised her hand.

"Chloe," Ruth said, not unkindly, "what happens to trees in spring?"

The room was quiet in the way rooms are quiet when someone has just moved a piece on a board nobody knew was set up. Chloe looked at the graph. "They grow."

"And in fall?"

"They lose their leaves." She said it slowly, because something was assembling itself. "There's, what, most of the land in the Northern Hemisphere. All those plants. So in spring and summer they're taking carbon dioxide in, and in fall and winter the leaves die and decay and it goes back out." She traced one tooth with her finger, the drop, the rise. "That's the wiggle. The whole planet breathing."

"So the zigzags are real," Devon said from the second row, with the satisfaction of a person whose suspicion about her note card had been vindicated in public.

"Yes. They're the Northern Hemisphere's seasons. It's not noise." She stood there a second longer than she needed to. The climb was still there too, the long slope under all the teeth, the part that didn't breathe, and she pointed at that, and said the oceans and the burning of fossil fuels had put it there, and then she sat down, and Mr. Ruiz wrote something in his book that she chose to believe was positive.

Afterward Ruth caught her at the lockers. "You got there yourself," Ruth said. "I only asked about trees."

"You asked the exact right question. That's not nothing." Chloe shut her locker. "I'm still not sure I could explain why the line keeps going up even while everything breathes. The breathing doesn't cancel it. I don't fully get why not, and I'm not going to pretend I do."

"Ruiz likes that," Ruth said. "The pretending, he hates."

The presentations ran through Friday, and on Friday afternoon the grades went up, and Chloe got an A minus, the minus apparently for the word "oscillations," which Mr. Ruiz had circled and annotated with "when you mean zigzags, say zigzags." She photographed the page and sent it to Devon, who replied with a single thumbs up, and then, a minute later, a photograph of his own grade, which was also an A minus, his minus earned for telling the class that greenhouse gases work like a blanket, an analogy Mr. Ruiz had circled twice and marked "partially true, ask Chloe."

She was still looking at that when her mother texted to ask whether she'd finished her college essay, the one about a time she changed her mind. Chloe typed out a paragraph about the graph, about standing in front of a room and being wrong in the exact direction of assuming the world was noisier than it was. She read it over, decided it made her sound reflective, which she was not, and deleted it. Then she wrote the truth instead, which was that Ruth Okonkwo had asked her one question about trees and she had spent the rest of the period feeling like the floor had tilted an inch. At the bottom she added a line she liked, about how the planet had been keeping careful records all along, and the only error was hers.

She pressed send, then opened the fridge and stood in its light, thinking about leaves.

"Close the door," her mother called from the other room. "You're letting the heat out."

Austin had promised Ms. Ferrante he would come to the summer book club with something to say about chapters twelve through sixteen, and he had read them twice, but he still had nothing except the feeling that Huck and Jim drifting down the river on a raft was the freest thing he had ever read. He found the group already assembled in the corner by the microfilm machines: Priya, Desmond, and Lorna, who was a retired nurse and the only one who ever brought her own coffee mug.

"Okay," Priya said, opening her paperback. "Mr. Alvarez wants us to try a lens this time. I picked Marxist. Property, labor, who owns the raft."

Desmond groaned. "Can't we just talk about the book?"

"That is talking about the book," Lorna said. "Go on, Austin. You had your hand up before you even sat down."

He hadn't, exactly, but he let it stand. "The part where Huck describes the fog," he said. "He wakes up and Jim is crying because he thought he'd lost him, and Huck pretends it was all a dream, and Jim figures out he's been played." He turned to the page. "And then Jim says, when he finds out, that trash is what people is that puts dirt on the head of dey fren's."

There was a quiet moment while everyone found the passage. Priya was frowning at it the way she frowned at a math problem, which Austin had learned meant she was interested.

"Huck doesn't get it," he said slowly, hearing himself arrive at the thought as he said it. "Not really. He says he was so sorry he could almost kiss Jim's foot, but a minute later he's complimenting himself for humbling himself to a black man. The joke is on Huck, and Huck is the one telling the story."

"A naive narrator," Lorna said, tapping her mug against the table.

"Yeah. That's it exactly. He reports everything honestly, he doesn't lie to us, but he misunderstands what he's seeing. So we see more than he does." Austin looked around the table, checking whether they were with him. "Every scene I laughed at, that's why. The duke and the king, the feuding families, all of it. The comedy is Huck not getting the joke he's telling."

Desmond, who had been slouched with his arms crossed, sat forward a little. "So it's like an unreliable narrator, but the opposite. He's reliable and clueless."

"Reliable and clueless," Priya repeated, writing it in the margin. "Okay, but here's my problem with the whole Marxist angle. If we're reading through the lens of class and labor, Twain owns the joke, Huck doesn't. Huck's down in the lowest white stratum of that whole river society, barefoot and beaten, and he still thinks he's above Jim. The hierarchy doesn't just exist out there, people carry it around inside them and it gets reified, made into this thing that seems solid and natural, like it's furniture."

"But Jim works," Desmond said. "He's the only one on that raft who actually does labor. He cooks, he watches the raft at night while Huck sleeps. And the reward money, that's the sickest part. Miss Watson is going to sell him for eight hundred dollars and everyone on shore treats him like walking cash. The whole economy of the town treats a person as property."

"That's the noxious part," Lorna said. "Not just slavery itself, which is obviously monstrous, but how casual it is. The ordinary people, the churchgoers, they've all made peace with it. It's in the wallpaper."

Austin had come in with an argument prepared against the lens assignment, something about how forcing a theory onto a book was like wearing someone else's glasses, and now he couldn't find the argument anywhere. He had expected the lens to flatten the book and instead the book kept opening. "Here's what I keep wondering," he said. "Does Huck change? He apologizes to Jim in the fog scene, and it costs him something, he says so. But then later he tears up the letter and says he'll go to hell, and that's not him understanding slavery is wrong. He still thinks he's doing a bad thing. He never figures out the thing we've figured out."

"Maybe that's the point," Priya said. "Twain trusts us to do what Huck can't. The reader has to finish the moral work."

"Or maybe," Desmond said, "Twain couldn't finish it either. He brings Tom Sawyer back at the end and turns Jim into a game, a plaything, for two hundred pages of the worst chapters in the book."

"That's true," Lorna said, and no one argued with her.

Austin looked at his notes, at the margin where he'd written it's just a story about a raft, and he understood that he'd been wrong about that an hour ago, sitting in his room, so certain. He wasn't certain now, and it felt less like losing something than like the difference between a photograph of the river and the river. He raised his pen.

"One more question before we break," he said. "If Huck never sees what we see, then somewhere out there, right now, there's a book where we're the naive narrator."

Priya looked up sharply. Lorna set down her mug. "Write that one down," she said.

The trail behind the reservoir looped for two miles through pine and birch, and Leo had chosen it because nobody walked it on weekday afternoons. He carried his phone in one hand, stopwatch running, and spoke to the trees.

"DNA is the master copy, right, and it stays in the nucleus like a reference book you can't check out. So the cell makes a photocopy of the one page it needs. That's transcription. An enzyme unzips the double helix, reads one strand, and builds a single strand of messenger RNA off it, letter by letter." He stumbled on a root and kept talking. "Then the messenger leaves the nucleus, and translation happens. A ribosome locks onto it and reads three letters at a time, and each three-letter word codes for one amino acid, and the amino acids get chained together, and the chain folds up, and that folded chain is a protein. That's it. That's the whole thing."

Eight minutes, and the trees had asked no follow-up questions. On Friday he would stand in front of a review panel for a summer fellowship and do this for real, and if he rambled or hedged, the fellowship would go to someone else. He stopped at the overlook where the water opened gray and flat, and that was where he found Dana, sitting on the guardrail with her backpack beside her, a blue ribbon of paper crushed in her fist.

"You're the guy who talks to trees," she said. She was a junior; he knew her from the science fair in the spring, where her model of enzyme kinetics had taken second place behind his presentation on gene expression. "I heard you from the switchback."

"I'm practicing an explanation. Transcription and translation."

"Of course you are." She smoothed the paper against her knee, and he could see it was a rejection letter, county-level competition, her fall research entry turned down. "They said my design lacked clarity of purpose. Whatever that means. I'm never doing it again."

Leo sat down on the rail a few feet from her. His heart had begun to palpitate, the way it did before he had to speak in front of anyone, and he was honest enough with himself to notice that talking to Dana counted. "Can I try the explanation on you? You already know most of it."

"I don't want a lesson."

"It's not a lesson. It's practice. You tell me if it makes sense." He waited until she shrugged, that minimal permission, and then he started over, slower this time, and Dana interrupted twice, once to say the photocopy image was confusing because a photocopy isn't single-stranded, and once to ask how the ribosome knew where to start. He had answers, but the answers changed as he gave them, and he found himself saying "I think" and "probably" and then correcting himself, because hedging in front of a panel was death, but pretending certainty where he hadn't earned it was worse. Somewhere in the middle of this he understood that the two things he was holding, clarity and honesty, were not the same value, and that every sentence was a small arbitration between them.

"You say 'the cell wants' a lot," Dana said. "Cells don't want anything."

"You're right. That's anthropomorphism. But it helps people follow."

"So use it, and then say you're using it."

He looked at her. That was it exactly, and it had taken a sixteen-year-old on a guardrail to say it. "Where'd you learn that?"

"From getting rejected." She held up the letter. "Clarity of purpose. I finally figured out what they meant. I never said what the project was for. I just showed that I could do it." She looked at the water instead of at him. "My mom said Krebs had a paper turned down once. I looked it up last night so I'd have something to be smug about."

"What paper?"

"The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle. He published it in Enzymologia instead." She said the names flatly, like reciting a spell. "He got the Nobel later, so, you know. Whatever."

Leo laughed, and it came out harsher than he meant. "That's supposed to comfort you? Nature is the journal. Everyone in the field reads it."

"That's the point. The people whose whole job is judging science got that one wrong. The system isn't an oracle, it's a panel. Panels are obdurate and panels are sometimes wrong and you go back to work anyway."

He turned that over while a merganser lifted off the reservoir, wings slapping the surface like applause from someone who didn't mean it. He had been treating Friday as a verdict on whether he was a scientist, and Dana had been treating her letter as a verdict on whether she was finished, and both of them, he thought, were confusing the judges for the truth. Though he couldn't prove the truth part. Maybe the panels were right about both of them. He held that possibility open the way he was learning to hold an uncertain step in an argument, not closing his hand around the nearest comfortable conclusion.

"Do the explanation again," Dana said. "From the top. But this time tell me what it's for."

"For?"

"You said it yourself. Clarity of purpose. Why should I care how DNA gets copied?"

He set the phone face down on the rail, took a breath, and began. "Every cell in your body carries the same two meters of DNA, and almost none of it is being read at any moment, and what gets read, and when, is the difference between a nerve cell and a skin cell. So the interesting question isn't the copying. It's the choosing." He heard his own voice change on the last sentence, and Dana was writing something on the back of her rejection letter.

"What are you writing?"

"An idea for spring," she said, and folded the paper into her pocket.

The cafe smelled of burnt espresso and wet umbrellas, and Victor spread his materials across the corner table as if laying out evidence for a trial nobody had asked to attend. There was his grandfather's copy of a style guide, its spine cracked and its margins penciled in a hand he almost recognized, and there was his rough draft, returned Thursday with three red circles around the same word. On the draft, Ms. Andaya had written "outdated, check current manual" beside each circle, and the circled word, three times, was "ibid."

"Grandpa's book says it's fine," Victor had told his mother that morning, and she had said, in the tone she used for weather, that manuals change, that his grandfather had typed his dissertation on a machine you had to hit. Victor had carried the old book to the cafe anyway, out of something between loyalty and stubbornness, because his grandfather had pressed it on him the last visit, saying the rules in it were the rules, that scholarship meant consistency. He had also carried his laptop, because he was seventeen and knew that consistency was not the same as being current, though he could not yet have said why both felt true.

His friend Devon slid into the opposite chair with a hot chocolate and no intention of working. "What's the word?"

"Ibid." Victor turned the draft around. "It means, like, same as the source right above it. My grandpa uses it everywhere."

"So what's the problem?"

"The problem is Ms. Andaya circled it like it was a typo." Victor opened the old guide to the tabbed page, where his grandfather had underlined a passage in blue pencil gone violet with age. The page prescribed "ibid." for repeated references. He read it twice, then closed the book and opened his laptop and typed, with the slight shame of a betrayal, "Chicago Manual of Style ibid."

What he found rearranged something in him, a small seismic shift, less an earthquake than the settling of a floor he'd thought was level. The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, had begun discouraging "ibid." in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title. Not because "ibid." was wrong, exactly; it was old, and it broke easily, and the new way repeated the author and a short title so a reader never had to hunt backward. He sat with that for a moment. His grandfather had not been careless. His grandfather had been careful in 1974.

"So is your grandpa's book garbage?" Devon asked, stirring his chocolate.

"No," Victor said, and heard how quickly it came out. "It's right about where to put the commas. It's right about footnotes going at the bottom. It's just wrong about this one thing, and only because the seventeenth edition came out in 2017 and started discouraging ibid. Now you're supposed to repeat the author and a short title instead." Saying it aloud like that, with the edition and the year and the direction of the change, made it solid, a fact he could stand on.

He began to collate the pieces: the draft, the old guide, the library's online copy of the current manual, his notes on the Ludlow Massacre, which was his actual argument, that the Colorado National Guard's actions in 1914 had been less a spontaneous escalation than a planned operation. That was the paper underneath the paper, the thing the citations existed to serve, and for an hour the footnote question had threatened to swallow it. Now he worked through the pages and replaced each "ibid." with Turco, The Ludlow Massacre, 112, and Klamforth, "Company Towns," 58, watching the draft become both more correct and more his. Somewhere in the middle of that his phone buzzed with a photograph from his mother: his grandfather asleep in his armchair, the twin of the style guide still on his shelf.

Victor looked at the photo for a while. He would call the old man on Sunday, and he did not know what he would say. That the guide had been the beginning of the trail, not the end of it? That learning the new rule had made him trust the old ones more, because a rule that admits of revision is a rule you can actually think with? He couldn't say any of that without it sounding like a speech, and anyway part of it was still uncertain to him, whether authority lives in the book or in the edition, whether his grandfather would feel retired or merely superseded. He marked the question in the margin of his notebook, next to a doodle of a footnote number climbing a page.

"Breaking news," Devon said. "Nerd finishes homework at nine p.m. on a Friday."

"Nearly." Victor was on the bibliography now, alphabetical, hanging indents, the author's name reversed and then given straight, and he typed his grandfather's old guide into the list of works consulted without deciding whether it belonged there. Under "additional sources," with a note beside it in his own shorthand: 17th ed., 2017, no more ibid. Then he closed the laptop, left the old book open on the table to the page his grandfather had underlined, and took a photograph of that, too, to send with the phone call he had not yet figured out how to make.

Sophie had three bars of dark chocolate, a thermometer she'd borrowed from the chemistry classroom without asking, and a marble slab that was actually the underside of a serving tray from Dani's mother's kitchen. She laid them out on the counter like surgical instruments.

"You know this is just chocolate," Dani said, leaning on the fridge. "People eat it. They don't perform rituals on it."

"People eat bad chocolate," Sophie said. "Chocolate that's gray and streaky and bends instead of breaking. That's what happens if you don't temper it." She was repeating this like an aphorism she'd decided to live by, though she'd learned it from a video at midnight two days ago, and she didn't fully understand it yet. Something about crystals. Something about temperature windows, 115 degrees down to 80 and back up to 88, precise as a landing approach.

She chopped the chocolate into even pieces, which took longer than expected because her knife skills were theoretical, and melted two-thirds of it in a bowl over simmering water. The chocolate went glossy and loose. She stirred in the remaining third, the "seed," watching the thermometer creep down.

"Hand me the tray." She poured a puddle onto the cold marble and began working it with a spatula, spreading and scraping, spreading and scraping. Her wrist ached. The chocolate thickened by degrees, and just when it seemed on the verge of calcifying into a dull lump, she scraped it back into the warm bowl and stirred. The thermometer read 88. She dipped a knife blade and waited.

"Why are we whispering?" Dani whispered.

"I'm not whispering."

"You are. You've been whispering since the thermometer hit 90."

The chocolate on the knife set in about ninety seconds, and when Sophie bent it, it snapped, cleanly, with a sound like a small dry branch. It was shiny as a beetle's back. She actually bounced on her toes, which she would deny later. "Okay. Okay. Now we dip things." There were strawberries, and some pretzels, and one Oreo Dani had designated the test subject.

From Dani's perspective, the whole enterprise looked like a friend briefly possessed by a very calm demon. Sophie dipped with the focus of someone defusing something, coating each strawberry in a thin even sheet and setting it on waxed paper. The Oreo went under completely. It was a good afternoon, is what Dani would have said, until her older brother Marco came home from his shift at the garden center and opened the cupboard.

He pulled down a bag of orange candy melts, the kind he used for coating pretzels at Halloween, and stood eating them by the fistful while he watched Sophie work. "Why's yours so complicated?" he said. "I just melt these and dip. They harden right up on the counter. No thermometer, no slab, none of this."

Sophie stopped with a strawberry suspended over the bowl. "What are those?"

"Candy melts."

She took one from the bag and read the label, frowning. Palm kernel oil. Vegetable oil. She looked up palm kernel oil on her phone with chocolate-sticky fingers, then read for a while, then laughed, one short surprised note.

"What," Marco said.

"They're not really chocolate. That's compound, or coating chocolate. It replaces some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats, so it sets without tempering." She set the bag down between them like evidence. "But it doesn't have the same snap." She took one of his melts, broke it. It gave with a soft, slightly waxy bend, no sound at all. Then she took a shard of her own tempered shell and broke it next to his ear, so he could hear the crack.

"So mine's better," she said, and immediately felt the ground shift under her, because that wasn't the whole truth and she knew it. Marco's melts had cost four dollars and taken ten minutes. Sophie had spent an hour, used her mother's good chocolate, and seized a batch an hour ago when a drop of water got in the bowl and the whole thing went grainy and ruined. She held both broken pieces in her palm, hers bright and brittle, his matte and pliable, and could not rank them honestly. Ease was worth something. So was the snap. She didn't know yet how to weigh one against the other, and she suspected she'd be finding out for years, and not only about chocolate.

"Yours is prettier," Marco conceded, eating another melt. "Mine's done already, though."

"Mine's better," Sophie said again, but quieter, testing it.

Dani picked up the fully drowned Oreo, cracked it open, and offered half. "Test subject survived," she said. "Barely."

The bus shelter on Carling Avenue smelled like wet gravel and old coffee, and Jackson stood under it with a folded page of G-test notes in his back pocket, running through the steps for the third time. Mirror, signal, shoulder check. Full stop at the line. His road test was at two o'clock, and his mother had left the Corolla in the lot by the pharmacy so he could practice parallel parking between two traffic cones she'd bought with the last of her patience. He had knocked one over four times that morning and cleared it twice, and both of those times he'd sat in the idling car with his hands on the wheel, grinning at nobody.

His grandfather was at the stop too, waiting for the 16 to his own appointment, and he was muttering at a letter he'd taken out of his jacket. "Petrov wants me to come in and sign," the old man said. "A new lease. One whole year, he says, or he can't promise the unit."

"Aren't you moving?" Jackson asked.

"Nowhere to move to. But I don't like signing things when I don't know what I'm agreeing to." He folded the letter along its worn creases. "Maybe I should take it to that woman at the church who reads contracts for people. Last time she did it, they gave her an honorarium, forty dollars in an envelope, and she tried to give it back."

Jackson had his phone out already, half for the transit app and half out of habit, and he typed his grandfather's situation into the search bar without deciding to. He expected a maze of landlord-tenant forms. Instead the answer surfaced plainly, on an official page, in a sentence he read twice: in Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms. He read it aloud, slowly, holding the phone where his grandfather could see the blue-and-white page over his shoulder.

"So I say nothing," his grandfather said, "and it just keeps going?"

"That's what it says. Month to month, same terms. You don't have to sign anything."

The old man was quiet for a moment, refolding the letter into a smaller square. "Forty years I've been signing papers because someone with a desk told me to." Then he laughed, short and surprised, and put the letter back in his jacket. "You're useful today. What's all this driving you're doing, then? Cones in the parking lot?"

"Road test at two." Jackson showed him the notes, the cramped handwriting about merging. "That's the part that scares me. The on-ramp. Everyone says you have to get up to speed fast, but the ramp near the test centre is short and there's always a transport truck in the right lane."

His grandfather had driven trucks for thirty years and offered no wisdom at all, which Jackson understood to be its own kind of wisdom. "The highway doesn't care that you're nervous," the old man said finally. "You acclimate to it or you stay in the right lane forever." He watched the 16 appear at the far corner, its sign lit through the drizzle. "Both of those are allowed, mind you. But you already put down the cones in the lot, so I know which one you picked."

On the ride out, Jackson sat by the window and thought about the two things he was doing that day, giving his grandfather a fact that meant the man didn't have to sign, and taking a test that would put his own name on a licence. One was refusing a signature; the other was earning one. He couldn't make them line up cleanly. Maybe independence was just deciding case by case, and maybe he'd get the merge wrong anyway. The bus ran its diurnal route past the mall and the test centre, the same stops it made every day regardless of who was aboard, and he got off two blocks early so he could walk past the on-ramp and look at it.

From the sidewalk he watched the cars merging, how each one chose its gap, some smoothly, some with a wobble that straightened out. He walked to the pharmacy lot, moved the cones to the exact width the examiner would use, and got into the Corolla. He adjusted the mirror, and pulled out of the space to begin again.

The market opened at seven, and by half past, the tent behind the peach stand already smelled of warm cocoa. Charlotte had asked for the job two weeks earlier, after spending her savings on a thermometer and a slab of marble she could not really afford. Marisol, who ran the chocolate stall, had looked at the marble, then at her, and said Saturdays, be early, don't touch the tempering machine until you can do it by hand.

That was the arrangement: learn the old way first. The old way meant melting the chocolate to fifty degrees Celsius, cooling it on the marble with a scraper until it thickened and lost its shine, then warming it gently back to thirty-one, where it would set glossy and hard and snap when broken. Charlotte had done it four times now. Four times it had worked, more or less, though her snaps were still duller than Marisol's.

The problem that morning was the weather. Rain had come through overnight and left the air thick, and the tent's canvas held the dampness like a held breath. Marsol frowned at the hygrometer hanging from the center pole and moved the finished bonbons away from the open side. Charlotte, meanwhile, had a box of sample squares she had made the night before and kept in her refrigerator at home, because her mother's kitchen was the only cool place in their apartment. She had carried the box to the market in her backpack, packed against a cold gel pack, and she set it on the table between the cash box and the sign that said SAMPLES, TAKE ONE.

"Those were in the fridge," Marisol said. Not a question.

"For three hours. They were fine when I closed the box."

Marisol picked one up and turned it over. Where the night before there had been a shine like polished stone, there was now a dry, pale film, gritty when she dragged a fingertip across it. Charlotte felt something drop in her stomach. She took another square from the box and rubbed it with her thumb. The coating came away as a powder, and underneath the chocolate was still firm, still good, only gray.

She had wanted to show off. She had wanted Marisol to taste one and say something that acknowledged the snap, the shine, the weeks of scorched batches and gritty failures. Instead she stood there while a customer reached toward the samples and Marisol moved the box out of reach with one hand.

"The heat, right?" Charlotte said. "They got too warm in the bag?"

"No. Heat gives you fat bloom, streaky, oily-looking. This is different."

Charlotte looked at the powdered square again. Her mother had once left a chocolate bar in the fridge door for months and it had come out wearing the same dull white, and her mother had said it had gone bad and thrown it away, and Charlotte had said nothing because at twelve she had not known there was anything to know. Now she turned the fact over the way Marisol turned the bonbon. The fridge was cold. The market air was wet. The chocolate had come out of one into the other, and the wet air had touched its cold surface, and something on that surface had dissolved and then dried out again into rough little crystals. She held the square close to her mouth.

"Sugar bloom," she said.

Marisol nodded once and went back to piping.

Charlotte stood by the table and thought about her two weeks of work, which now looked like two different projects. There was the chocolate itself, which behaved according to rules you could learn and then trust: temperatures, seed crystals, the precise moment when the cooling mass stopped flowing like liquid and started moving like tar. And there was the air, which followed no schedule and owed her nothing, which could undo in an hour of humidity what five degrees of careful heating had built. She had been treating the craft as if precision alone were enough, and this morning it plainly was not, and she could not yet say where the line fell between controlling conditions and simply choosing better ones. She only knew the box should have stayed home, or come dry, or not come at all.

She threw the samples away behind the peach stand, where the pit bucket was, and came back and washed her hands. Marisol was scraping the tempered chocolate off the marble, folding it over itself, and she did not look up when she spoke.

"You want to watch or you want to do it?"

Charlotte took the scraper. The chocolate moved under it in a wide, even ribbon, cooling as it spread, and she kept her eyes on the surface, waiting for the shine to go flat.

The house smelled of cardamom and old paper, as it always had, and Alexis stood in the hallway holding the folded newspaper like a summons he had been waiting all summer to ignore. His grandfather had left it on the kitchen table that morning with a pencil resting across it, which in this house meant something. It had meant something for three weeks now, ever since Alexis arrived, and he had learned to read the small signals: the coffee set out at nine, the dictionary pulled from the shelf and left open, the chair turned toward the window where the light was best.

Today he could not pretend not to see it. He carried the paper to the porch, where his grandfather sat with his hat on his lap, and sat down across from him without asking permission, because asking would have made it a thing that could be refused.

"Vorwärts," his grandfather said, nodding at the front page. "One article. You read it, then you tell me what it says. In German or English, I don't care which."

"I don't speak German."

"You speak ten words and you have a dictionary. That is how everyone starts."

Alexis unfolded the paper. The article was short, maybe four paragraphs, about a bridge somewhere in the north, and the first thing he noticed, before he understood a single sentence, was the strangeness of the page itself. Half the words seemed to begin with capitals, not just the ones at the start of sentences or the names of towns. Words sat in the middle of lines with their first letters raised like flags. He counted them in the opening sentence and found five capitals in a stretch of text that should have had one.

"Why does everything start with a big letter?" he asked, and immediately regretted it, because his grandfather's face closed the way a drawer closes.

"Figure it out," his grandfather said. "You have the dictionary. You have the pencil."

So Alexis bent over the page and worked, and the morning went by. He looked up Brücke and found it meant bridge, and it was capitalized; he looked up the words around it and found that the ones in lowercase were doing things, going, standing, costing, while the capitalized ones were things themselves: the bridge, the city, the river, the year. He wrote the words in the margin in two columns, capitals in one, lowercase in the other, and sat back and looked at it. He tested it against the names, Hamburg, the minister's name, and against every small word he knew, und, in, der. The pattern held. German capitalized every noun, not only names, so that a reader's eye could pick the nouns out of a sentence at a glance, and the whole strange page suddenly made sense as a design, a system someone had built on purpose, like the grid of the garden behind the house.

"It's the nouns," he said. "They're all capitalized. Every single one. That's why the page looked like that."

His grandfather's expression was equivocal, half approval and half something Alexis could not name, and he said only, "So read."

Alexis read, slowly, halting over the second paragraph, where the article turned to a dispute about whether the bridge should be repaired or torn down, and the word Abbruch kept sliding away from him. The pace of the reading slowed until each sentence felt like wading. His grandfather sat perfectly still, hat still on his lap, and Alexis became aware, in the way you become aware of a sound only after it has gone on too long, that the old man was watching him with unusual concentration, more concentration than a bad reading of a newspaper article could possibly warrant.

He reached the third paragraph and stopped. There, beside a column of text, was a name in the byline that he had skimmed past at the top and now saw properly for the first time. It was his grandmother's name. His grandmother, who had died in March, who had written for newspapers in Hamburg for forty years, whose desk was still locked upstairs.

"That's Oma," Alexis said.

His grandfather looked out at the garden for a long moment. "Her last piece," he said. "They printed it in April. I have been trying to read it since. My eyes, they don't..." He set his hat down on the table, carefully, brim aligned with the edge. "I wanted to know what she said. The German is easy for me. The eyes are not. So you read it, and you tell me."

The porch was quiet enough that Alexis could hear the wasps in the eaves. He understood, then, the coffee at nine and the dictionary left open and all the folded newspapers, and he understood that his grandfather had not been teaching him German at all, or not only that, and the distinction mattered, though he could not have said exactly how. He thought of his mother saying that his grandfather was too proud to ask for anything, as if pride were a wall rather than a door, and of his own school arguments about whether anything could be true for one person and not another, the relativism his philosophy teacher kept pulling them back to. Sitting here, he felt that pull weaken. The article said what it said, in a language with rules, and a reader either got it right or didn't, and it was in no one's power to make the words mean something easier. Yet what the article meant to his grandfather would not be what it meant to him; that much stayed uncertain, and he decided he could hold both ideas at once without dropping either.

He read the last two paragraphs aloud, translating as he went, stumbling and correcting himself, and the article turned out to be short and dry, a small matter of a small bridge, and his grandmother had used it to write about the things a city owes its river. When Alexis finished, his grandfather took off his glasses and pressed the heel of his hand to one eye, and then the other, and was silent.

"That's what she said," he said at last. "That is exactly what she would say." He put his glasses back on and squared the newspaper on the table, folding it along its old creases. "Tomorrow, the second page. Bring the dictionary."

He stood, put on his hat, and walked down the porch steps toward the garden, and Alexis stayed where he was with his two columns of nouns still penciled in the margin, listening to the wasps in the eaves.

Olivier sat at the kitchen table with the assignment sheet in front of him and the laptop open to a blank document. Ten minutes, one scene, drawn from his own life, staged for the class in two weeks. He had tried to parametrize the thing at first, listing possible subjects in columns, rating each for stakes and feasibility, but the list kept collapsing toward one entry he did not want to use. His sister Camille, who had come home from her first semester in November and now spent most afternoons in her room with the blinds tilted so the light fell in a single stripe across the floor.

Margot, fourteen, came in and put her chin on the back of his chair. "Is it about Camille?"

"It's not about anything yet."

"You should make it about Camille. And I should be in it." She pulled out the other chair and sat, which was her way of claiming territory. "I can cry on command. Watch."

"I'm not watching."

She dried her eyes with her wrist anyway. "If you put her in it and it's mean, that's chicanery. You'd be stealing her to get a grade."

He told her the assignment was autobiographical, not theft, and she said that was exactly what a thief would say, and then she went to the refrigerator and stood there with the door open, radiating grievance, until he told her to close it.

Later that night he typed a scene about the day Camille came home, then deleted it, then typed a version where the sister was called Bridget and had a different reason for everything, and that version was worse because it was vague where his memory was exact. The teacher had put The Glass Menagerie on the list of models, so he found the script online and read it straight through at the table, and when he went looking for why the play felt so sure of itself, one page after another, he found what he hadn't known. Tennessee Williams had based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose. He read the sentence twice, then said it out loud to the empty kitchen, just to hear it. "Laura is Rose." The stage had a door and his family had a door and the same person had walked through both.

He sat with that for a while. It didn't tell him whether it was permitted. Williams had done it, and Williams's sister had spent her life in hospitals, and Olivier didn't know what Rose had thought of the play or whether anyone had asked her. What he had was the fact that the version people trusted most was the version closest to the real girl, glass animals and all, and the fact that he was afraid of the same closeness. He could keep hiding behind a renamed sister, and the scene would stay thin, a story about a girl shaped generally like grief. Or he could write Camille and let the class see her, which felt less like writing than like opening her door while she slept.

In the morning Margot found him at the table again, surrounded by printed pages with lines struck through. "Did you do it?" she asked.

"I started it. It's about her. The real her, not a fake sister with a fake problem."

Margot picked up a page and read the first lines with her lips moving. Her shoulders settled. "It's not mean," she said. "It's just sad."

"That's the same thing to some people."

"It's not, though." She put the page down and squared it against the edge of the table. "Can I still be in it? There could be a little sister. I wouldn't even have to cry. I could just stand in the doorway like I do."

He looked at her standing there in the actual doorway, hand on the frame, and then at the page where he had written the doorway in. "Fine," he said. "But you say the lines the way they're written."

"I always say lines the way they're written," said Margot, and came and sat down across from him to hear the whole thing.

Jake's mother had declared an amnesty on the refrigerator. Anything left in it by Sunday night would be thrown out without comment, without blame, and, she said, without a funeral. This was her way of telling him that if he wanted to eat next week, he had to figure out how, because she was working the night shift and his father still believed pasta was a food group.

So on Saturday morning he stood at the entrance of the farmers' market with a list he had written the night before, half in his handwriting and half in his friend Priya's. She had walked him through it over the phone: pick four dinners, make each one twice, cook everything on Sunday in one long stretch so the week took care of itself. Rice on Monday means rice on Thursday. Roast the squash, save half, buy the greens loose. He had argued with her about whether a person could actually eat the same soup twice in five days. She said he could and that she had receipts, metaphorically, and also that he should exhume whatever was at the bottom of his crisper drawer before he bought anything, because he was the sort of person who owned three bags of carrots without knowing it.

He did, in fact, own two bags of carrots, softened into something like regret, plus a lime and a bulb of garlic that had begun to sprout. He threw them out at home before coming, which felt like progress.

The market ran along the waterfront, and the stalls closest to the water sold what the vendor called littoral greens, kelp and sea beans and a salty spinach that grew where the tide reached. Jake bought a bag of the sea beans because Priya had put them on the list with a question mark, and because the vendor's dog was lying across the bags of arugula in a way that suggested the dog, at least, had strong feelings about the sea beans.

He was carrying a flat of eggs, the sea beans, three squash, and a lump of honeycomb he had not planned on when he found Priya at the chocolate stall. She lived above the bakery two streets over, and the chocolate vendor was her mother's friend, and Priya had an apartment with a kitchen and, more importantly, a broad stone counter by the window that stayed cold even in August.

"Come up," she said. "I'm tempering. You can watch. Or help. Or eat the failures."

"The failures are the best part," the vendor said, and sold Jake a slab of dark chocolate at what he suspected was not the real price.

Upstairs, Priya chopped the chocolate into small pieces and melted some of it in a bowl over a pot of water, and then she did something Jake did not expect. She poured the melted chocolate directly onto the cold stone counter and spread it flat with a scraper, working it back and forth, pushing it out and gathering it in, over and over.

"It's called tabling," she said, when he asked why she was bullying the chocolate. "You spread it on the stone and work it to cool it down."

"For how long?"

"Until it thickens a little and it's right. Then it goes back into the bowl with the rest."

She tested it by dabbing a bit on her lower lip, which Jake thought was unscientific and possibly the most scientific thing he had ever seen, since her lip was exactly the temperature a human was. Then she folded the cooled chocolate into the warm, and poured it into molds, and set them on the windowsill.

"You're doing your batch thing too, right?" she said. "That's why you're carrying a squash like a football."

He laid out his plan on her table while the chocolate set. Sunday he would roast all three squash at once and cook a pot of rice and the lentils, and the sea beans would go with the eggs on Tuesday, and the soup would happen Wednesday and also Friday, and Thursday was the wildcard, which in his system meant whatever he could make from whatever remained. He had learned this from two directions, he realized. His mother cooked by improvising from whatever the fridge offered, and it never lasted the week; Priya cooked like a general planning a campaign, and hers did. He was trying to hold both, to plan hard enough that the improvising had something to improvise with. What he could not figure out, even on paper, was whether Thursday-as-wildcard was freedom or just a failure he had scheduled in advance.

"The thing about Thursday," Priya said, "is you're going to buy something on the way home anyway. Nobody's wildcards stay empty."

"I could be disciplined."

"You brought honeycomb you didn't plan on."

"That was the dog," Jake said. "The dog made a case for it."

The molds on the windowsill had gone glossy and hard. Priya turned one out and broke it along the lines, and the pieces snapped clean, with a sound like a small dry branch. She handed him the end piece and kept the one with the little defect, the shallow bubble near the corner, which had always been her favorite and which she claimed tasted different, though they both knew it didn't.

The chocolate had the snap of something that had set up exactly right, and Jake ate it slowly, looking at his bags of squash and eggs and sea beans by the door, and at the stone counter with its faint brown residue of the work. He took out his phone and photographed the counter, in case it mattered later, in case his own kitchen and his own week turned out to need something like it.

"Same time next Saturday?" Priya said, already scraping the stone clean.

"Same time," he said, and picked up the squash like a football, and tucked it under his arm.

Sadie spread the photocopy across the kitchen table and weighted its corners with a mug and a jar of pens. The passage was from Jane Eyre, the scene where Mr. Rochester dresses as a gypsy fortune-teller to trick his guests, and the assignment, due at the end of her college's summer bridge program, required her to read it through a critical lens of her choosing. She had chosen feminism at eleven o'clock that morning, switched to Marxism by noon, and by two in the afternoon had written nothing except her name and a thesis she had crossed out so hard the paper tore.

Her younger brother, Owen, slid into the opposite chair with a peanut butter sandwich and no apparent awareness that she was working. He was fourteen and loud, but he also refilled her water glass without being asked whenever he got up, which was a kind of courtesy he would have denied under torture.

"Who's the gypsy," he said, chewing.

"A disguise. A man puts it on so he can manipulate a young woman into confessing her feelings."

"That's creepy."

"I know it's creepy. That's not the paper. The paper is about why it's creepy and to whom." She tapped her pen against the mug. "If I read it as a feminist, it's about Rochester controlling what Jane is allowed to know and feel. If I read it as a Marxist, it's about a rich man playing at being poor and exotic, borrowing a lower class like a costume, then going home to his estate. Both of them fit. That's the problem. They both fit so well I can't tell which one is the reading."

Owen considered this with the seriousness of someone who had recently discovered that teachers sometimes argue with each other about books. "Can't you do both?"

"That's called having no thesis." She pulled her laptop closer and opened her notes, which were a trenchant mess of quotations and accusations, every line capitalized at the guilty party: HE ALREADY KNOWS. HE ASKS ANYWAY. "Or it's called synthesis, which is what Dr. Okafor keeps saying she wants. A considered position. Honestly about what stays uncertain."

The screen door banged and their grandmother came in from the garden with a colander of tomatoes, her hands stained at the knuckles. She set one, small and split, beside Sadie's papers without comment, the way she always did, and Sadie ate it without comment, the way she always did, because it was how they told each other things.

"Whose idea was the cross-out," her grandmother asked, nodding at the torn page.

"Mine. All of it's mine. That's the whole problem with this assignment. There's no answer to check."

Her grandmother laughed and started sorting tomatoes by ripeness, discarding the ones the sun had begun to desiccate into a bowl for sauce. "In my day we were told what the book meant and we wrote it down. You get to mean it yourself. Harder."

It was Owen, surprisingly, who broke the logjam. He had gone quiet over the second half of his sandwich, reading the margins of her notes where she had scribbled comparisons to unreliable narrators, and he pointed at a line she'd copied from somewhere.

"What's this one? The Poe thing?"

"That's from discussion on Tuesday. We were on 'The Tell-Tale Heart,' Poe's story from 1843. The whole time he's describing how he murdered an old man, the narrator keeps insisting he is not mad. And this guy in my seminar, Danny, said the protests are the problem. The more he says he's sane, the more you doubt him. Nobody made him say it. He just keeps saying it." She realized she was talking faster. "What you claim about yourself can be the evidence against you."

"So what does Rochester claim about himself?"

Sadie looked at the passage. Rochester, in his fortune-teller costume, claims to read minds, claims to be outside the social order, claims it's all a game. "He says he's only playing," she said slowly. "He says it's harmless. He says he'll tell her the truth about another woman afterward, as if that cancels it." She started writing before she finished speaking, the sentences arriving in an order she hadn't planned. The feminist lens and the Marxist lens weren't competing explanations; they were two ways of naming the same confidence, the rich man's certainty that he is entitled to know a poor woman's secrets and that his performance, including his performance of harmlessness, will be forgiven.

She wrote for twenty minutes without stopping. When she surfaced, Owen had cleared his plate and her grandmother had left three more tomatoes by her elbow, and there was a paragraph at the end she was genuinely unsure about, about whether Jane's silence in the scene was submission or strategy, and she underlined a question mark beside it instead of pretending to be certain.

"Dinner's at six," her grandmother called from the stove. "Write your revolution, but leave room for soup."

Sadie saved the file twice, copied it to a thumb drive, and then, feeling like either a savant or a fraud and unable to decide which, read the uncertain paragraph aloud to the empty kitchen to hear how it sounded.

"It might be both," she told the tomatoes. "I'm allowed to say it might be both."

Owen, passing through with his headphones half on, said, "Then say it," and kept walking.

The bookshop had a back table reserved on Tuesdays for the summer reading circle, and Brianna had claimed the corner chair three weeks running before Mrs. Amaro finally asked her what she was doing there with a single paperback and a fistful of orange sticky notes. Brianna had shown her the cover, The Great Gatsby, and explained, with more confidence than she felt, that she was preparing for a first-year seminar that expected her to read the novel through a feminist or Marxist critical lens, whichever she could defend by September. Mrs. Amaro had squinted at the book, then at Brianna, and offered her a small honorarium, ten dollars a session plus trade credit, if she would lead an informal discussion for the shop's high school summer staff. Brianna had accepted before she understood what she had agreed to.

Now, on the first Tuesday of July, she sat with the novel open to the scene where Nick first visits the Buchanans' house, and across from her sat two teenagers who worked the register, Priya and Marcus, both holding copies they had clearly not opened. "So we just talk about it?" Marcus asked, spinning a pencil on its point. "We just talk about it," Brianna said, and realized as she said it that she had no idea how to make that true.

She had tried, the night before, to parametrize the problem, breaking the chapter into questions she could actually answer: who speaks, who is described, who gets money and who spends it, whose marriage is praised and whose is merely endured. But every question kept snagging on the same knot. Nick, the narrator, kept insisting on his own judgment, that he was inclined to reserve all judgments, that he was one of the few honest people he had ever known, and yet everything he described seemed to quarrel with everything he concluded. She had begun, almost superstitiously, to mark the spots.

"Here," she said, turning the book toward them. "Nick tells us Daisy's voice is full of money, like he's figured her out. But listen to what Daisy actually says on this page." Priya leaned over. Daisy tells the story of her daughter's birth, says she woke up and asked the nurse whether it was a boy or a girl, and that when the nurse said a girl Daisy turned her head away and wept, and said she hoped the girl would be a beautiful little fool. "That's not what a person full of money sounds like," Brianna said. "That's someone who knows exactly what being a girl in that house costs, and Nick walks right past it because her voice is prettier than her complaint."

Marcus had stopped spinning the pencil. "So the narrator's lying?"

"Not lying," Brianna said, though she was working this out as she spoke, watching her own hands arrange the sticky notes into a loose line down the table's edge. "Wrong, maybe, or motivated. Look what happens when I put these in order." She had marked, over the weekend, every place where another character contradicted Nick directly: Jordan catching him in a claim about being engaged back home; Gatsby correcting his own biography that Nick had repeated as fact; Tom, of all people, accurately naming Nick's pretense. And beneath those, the events themselves refusing to cooperate, the party guests behaving nothing like Nick's summary of them, the marriage neither charmed nor broken in the way he kept insisting. Readers usually catch an unreliable narrator exactly this way, she had read somewhere and now watched prove itself on her table, through contradictions, other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims. Stacked in orange, the pattern was almost embarrassingly visible.

"It's like tectonic plates," Priya said, and Brianna looked up, grateful. "Two things sliding against each other, and you only see the pressure where they catch."

"Exactly. So a feminist reading and a Marxist reading aren't different books," Brianna said, sliding one stack of notes on top of another. "They're two ways of measuring the same fault line. Nick keeps telling us the women are careless, the workers are invisible, and the story keeps showing us the opposite, that Daisy is calculating because calculation is all she's been given, that Wilson matters precisely because everyone, including Nick, declines to see him. The contradictions aren't noise. They're the argument."

They worked for another hour, and it stopped being her session at all. Priya argued that Daisy's fool line was a Marxist critique disguised as a mother's wish, that she understood her daughter's value would be assigned, not earned. Marcus argued back that this let Daisy off too easily, that plenty of people in that book saw clearly and chose comfort anyway, and that Nick's real unreliability was that he never chose anything. Brianna took notes on both and found she could not fully side with either, and said so, and was surprised that saying so felt less like defeat than like the beginning of an essay she might actually write.

When the shop emptied, Mrs. Amaro came back with two cups of tea and set one in front of Brianna. "Good crowd," she said. "You'll come back next week?"

"I'll come back," Brianna said. She began collecting the sticky notes, peeling them off the table one at a time, and Mrs. Amaro watched her with something that was almost a smile.

"You know," Mrs. Amaro said, "that book you were quoting from, the study guide with the yellow cover you had on your lap? I sold the last three copies in June. It was written by my daughter." She straightened the tea cups. "She never actually finished college."

Brianna looked down at the yellow book in her lap, with its confident margins, and slowly ran her thumb along the page where it had told her, in calm and certain prose, exactly how to spot a narrator who couldn't be trusted.

The assignment sheet said seven days, and Clara had filled all seven. Sprints Monday, throws Tuesday, plyometrics Wednesday, and so on until Sunday, which she had labeled "active recovery" in handwriting that looked, even to her, like an apology. Coach Renner tapped the paper twice and slid it back across the desk. "Where's the rest?"

"That is the rest," Clara said. "I planned every day."

"Rest isn't what you do when you're not planning. It's what you plan so the planning works." He wrote nothing on the sheet, which was worse than a grade. "Warm-ups, too. Revise it. Thursday."

She took the sheet to the bleachers behind the gym, where Priya was sitting with a bag of frozen peas pressed to her elbow. Priya had been the best thrower in ninth grade and was now, by her own account, disaffected, a word she had started using after quitting the competitive squad. She still came to practices, still threw, but only for Clara's ragtag rec team, the one that existed because Ms. Okafor had signed the gym request out of pity.

"He maligns rest days," Priya said, nodding at the sheet. "He used to make us do ladders on Sundays."

"He's making me redo the whole plan."

"Let me see." Priya read it, peas shifting against her arm. "You have throws the day after plyometrics. You threw last Thursday, remember? Your elbow was wrecked and every javelin went flat."

Clara remembered differently, or wanted to. She remembered her wrist. Coach Renner had spent the whole session circling her saying "bend your wrist, bend your wrist," and she had bent it so conscientiously that she'd forgotten the field existed. The javelin had landed like something dropped from a window.

"Thursday," Priya said, "Nadia's sister ran the drills. She's doing a sports science degree. She kept saying the same thing until I wanted to throw a cone at her."

"What thing?"

"Something about a researcher. Wulf. She said Wulf found that learners improve faster focusing on the effect of a movement, the target, instead of their own body parts." Priya shrugged. "Sounds like fortune-cookie coaching."

Clara wrote it down anyway, on the back of the training plan, under an arrow that pointed nowhere yet.

Thursday she was on the track at six, before Renner even arrived, with Priya and two others from the rec team. She had taped paper plates to the fence at throwing height. "Don't think about your arm," she told Marcus, who had the worst elbow flare on the team and knew it. "Just hit the plate."

"Hit the plate," Marcus repeated, in the voice of someone humoring a person with a clipboard.

His first throw sailed wide. His second clipped the fence post. The third hit the plate dead center, and when he turned around his face was doing something complicated, half delight and half suspicion, as if he'd been tricked into competence. He didn't flare his elbow at all, Priya said, and Priya had spent three years watching his elbow flare like a settling pigeon.

"Say the Wulf thing again," Clara called to Priya. "For the plan."

"Learners improve faster with an external focus, the effect on the target, not the body parts." Priya delivered it flat, then ruined it by grinning. "Revisionist history. Next you'll tell me warm-ups matter."

But Renner had arrived somewhere during Marcus's third throw, and he was standing at the edge of the track with his coffee, watching. When Clara gathered her pages he came over and read the revised plan without asking. Tuesday and Friday were blank now except for the words REST, deliberate, capitalized, and a Monday warm-up block with dynamic mobility written as an actual progression, not a line item. He read it twice.

"The plates," he said.

"For external focus. The target, not the wrist."

"I know what it is." He handed the sheet back. "I coach the way I was coached." He said it like a confession that had cost him something, and then, more quietly, "My senior year my coach had me thinking about my shoulder so hard I couldn't feel the field."

He walked off toward the equipment shed. Priya raised the bag of peas in a small salute.

Clara sat on the low wall with her plan and a pen. She still didn't know how much of Thursday belonged to the plates and how much belonged to Marcus simply being tired of failing, or whether rest days were medicine or just permission, and the honest part of her suspected the answer changed by the person. She underlined REST twice, then wrote beside it: ask Marcus how the arm feels before deciding.

He was still at the fence, collecting the paper plates. She jogged over. "Same time Saturday?"

He folded a plate into quarters and put it in his pocket, like he intended to keep it. "Hit the fence post by the third flag?" he said. "I want to try something."

The kennel room smelled of disinfectant and something faintly animal beneath it, and Logan had learned in three weeks of volunteering that this was the smell of a slow Saturday. He set his biology binder on the counter beside the scale, opened it to the diagram of a mitochondrion, and began filling the water dishes in the run while Dr. Patel's voice carried from exam room two, telling someone that the dog would be fine.

"You're studying cellular respiration," said Marisol, the technician, glancing at the binder as she passed with a stack of clean towels. She was the one who had shown him, on his first day, how to fold a towel so it stayed put under a cat's chin. "Glycolysis and all that."

"Glycolysis, then the Krebs cycle, then the electron transport chain," Logan said, mostly to himself, the way tracing the steps aloud made them stick. "Glucose gets broken down, and the mitochondria make ATP." He crouched to slide a bowl under the chain-link gate of run four, where a beagle named Gus lifted his head, decided Logan was not worth standing up for, and lowered it again.

"You say that like a recipe," Marisol said. "Glucose in, energy out."

"That's the problem. It's a recipe I can recite and not cook." He turned the page to his homework, which the red pen had marked wrong, and there it was: the example problem. A sequence of DNA bases, one letter changed from the textbook's original, and the question asked what would happen to the resulting protein. Logan had written that the protein would be damaged, or at least different, because a changed letter should change something. His answer had a slash through it and the word "recheck" beside it, and the recheck had only deepened the puzzle, because when he'd looked up the amino acid each codon specified, the changed letter gave the exact same amino acid as before.

Marisol set the towels down and looked at the page for a long moment. "What are they called again?" she said. "My niece had this last year." She frowned, then snapped her fingers. "Silent mutations," she said. "That's the word. Her whole class had to memorize it."

Logan copied the phrase into his margin, but the word didn't settle anything; it only named the strangeness. "So the DNA changed and nothing changed," he said. "The protein comes out exactly the same." He thought of his own life in the past year, his father's move to Phoenix, the way everyone kept telling him nothing essential had changed when everything visible had, and he set that thought aside because it was the kind of thing his English teacher would call a metaphor and he didn't need a metaphor, he needed the mechanism. Except the mechanism, or at least the part he was allowed to know, was just this: several codons could code for the same amino acid, so some single-base mutations changed nothing in the finished protein. The cell went on. The lineage of cells descended from it went on. Somewhere in Gus the beagle, Logan supposed, entire ancestries of cells carried altered letters and produced their proteins anyway, undamaged, indifferent.

"Bring the beagle," Dr. Patel called from the doorway, and Logan closed the binder, clipped the leash to Gus's collar, and walked him down the hall with the dog's shoulder brushing his knee at every second step. In exam room one, a woman sat with her hands folded too tightly in her lap, and Logan recognized the posture before he recognized her, the mother of the cat who'd been in two weeks ago with the lump.

"Good news," Dr. Patel was saying. "The biopsy came back, and it's benign. It's not what we feared." The woman's hands came apart, and she pressed one of them flat against her chest, and Logan stood very still by the door with Gus leaning warm against his leg. He was not sure what the biopsy had tested, exactly, but he understood the shape of what had happened: something had looked like an error, looked like damage, and the test had exonerated it. The cells were doing what cells were supposed to do.

He thought, and then tried to stop thinking, that it was like the homework problem. A change that changed nothing. Except that it wasn't, or wasn't quite, or he couldn't tell whether it was, and that distinction seemed suddenly to matter more than glycolysis. The mutation in his textbook was harmless because the protein was the same either way. The lump had been harmless because it was the same kind of tissue behaving the same way it always had. But a change could also be harmful while looking like nothing, or be harmless and still change something he had no test for, and Logan had no way, standing there with a borrowed beagle, to sort those cases into columns.

"Logan, Gus needs his weight recorded," Dr. Patel said, and Logan guided the dog onto the scale, steadied him with a hand on his ribs, and read the number out loud while the woman smiled at both of them with her hand still resting over her heart.

After the appointment, Marisol brought him a cup of coffee from the lobby machine, although she must have known from his age that she wasn't supposed to, and they stood at the counter while he wrote Gus's weight on the chart. "So did you figure out your homework?" she asked.

"I figured out the answer," Logan said. "I haven't figured out whether the answer is reassuring or terrifying." He looked at the binder, still open to the mitochondrion, the little folded inner membrane like a maze with glucose entering one end and ATP coming out the other, and he tapped the diagram with two fingers. "Every step in here goes one direction. Glucose to pyruvate, pyruvate to the cycle, electrons down the chain. Everything in the cell has to follow the steps." He paused. "Except apparently sometimes the instructions change and the cell can't even tell."

Marisol drank her coffee and considered that. "And you think that's terrifying."

"I think it's both," Logan said. "I think it's both and I can't make it be just one." He closed the binder, and Gus, hearing the sound, thumped his tail once against the floor of the run.

Mr. Alvarez handed back the first drafts with the expression of a man returning borrowed umbrellas. "Daniel," he said, pausing at Daniel's desk, "you've summarized two articles. I asked you to weigh them. What do you actually think?" Daniel looked at his paper, at the two neat paragraphs, one on each article, and realized he did not know. Both concerned the same question, whether a school reading program raised comprehension scores, and both claimed to answer it. That was the assignment: compare, evaluate, decide which argument held more water. He had described both buckets and never touched the water.

At lunch he spread the articles across the table in the corner of the cafeteria, near the window where the radiator clanked like a small imprisoned animal. Article A, from a glossy education journal, reported a clear improvement across twelve schools. Article B, denser, from a smaller journal, found nothing at all, no effect, and spent its last section listing every way the first study might have gotten lucky. Priya slid into the seat across from him and stole a fry.

"Which one's right?" she asked, chewing.

"That's the whole problem. I found eleven other studies this weekend. Eleven. Every single one found the program worked."

Priya gesticulated at the pile with her stolen fry, as though the papers themselves were being unreasonable. "So it works. Write that."

But it bothered him, the way a word repeated too many times begins to sound invented. He said so, and she rolled her eyes with an insouciance that suggested she had never in her life been bothered by anything at eleven in the morning. "Everything agrees with everything," he said. "Since when does that happen?"

After last period he went to the library, which smelled of old laminate and the lemon cleaner the custodian used on the tables at three o'clock. He did not go looking for more studies. He went looking for the null one, Article B, because it was the only dissenting voice he had, and dissenting voices, his father liked to say at dinner, usually know something. He read its bibliography, which ran three pages, and noticed something odd: the authors kept citing themselves, earlier papers reporting failures to find effects. Failure after failure, in print, going back a decade. If they had a drawer full of these, where were everyone else's?

He followed one citation to a 1979 paper by a psychologist named Robert Rosenthal, found it in a database, and sat very still while the abstract loaded. The screen was slow; somewhere behind him a printer groaned through someone's chemistry lab. Rosenthal had given the thing a name. Studies with null results, the ones finding nothing, go unpublished, sitting in researchers' files, and so the published record ends up looking more positive than the actual evidence. Daniel read it twice. It was like being told that the parking lot outside was only the cars that hadn't broken down.

The next morning he found Priya at her locker, which she was decorating with a laminated photo of a capybara for reasons she declined to explain. "It's called the file drawer problem," he said. "Nineteen seventy-nine. This psychologist Rosenthal. The studies that find nothing never get published, so the record only shows the winners."

"So your eleven studies are the survivors."

"Which means I can't just count them. I have to count what's missing, and I can't, because it's missing." He heard how absurd it sounded and said it anyway.

Mr. Alvarez's fifth period was warm and smelled of whiteboard marker. When Daniel asked, during work time, whether he could write part of the review about the studies he couldn't find, Mr. Alvarez leaned back and said only, "Interesting instinct. What would you put in that section?" which was the teaching equivalent of handing someone a flashlight and pointing at a cave.
