Tuesday it rained, and only Ibrahim and Fergus came, the three of them under the floodlights with cones Mathis had to beg off the caretaker. They walked the triangles in the wet, passing, checking shoulders, and when Fergus played a first-time ball through a gate that Mathis hadn't even set up yet, just into space where Ibrahim would be, Mathis crouched by the cone and thought about how much of coaching was accident wearing the costume of intent. "Again," he said. "Same one."

Antoine found the book on the third shelf of his grandfather's study, wedged between a water-damaged atlas and a box of pipe cleaners no one had touched in decades. The French Revolution: A History, by Thomas Carlyle, published in 1837, if the title page could be believed. He had come to the house for a quiet weekend to draft his essay on how views of the Revolution had changed since 1800, and his laptop bag held six PDFs, two library books, and a stack of notes that read, dispiritingly, like the outlines of other people's arguments.

He should have left the volume alone. Instead he carried it to the kitchen table, where his grandfather was sorting mail with the concentration of a man defusing something.

"Is this yours?" Antoine asked.

"It was my father's." His grandfather squinted at the spine. "He was a connoisseur of gloom, Carlyle especially. Read passages aloud at dinner until my mother left the room." He went back to the mail, but Antoine noticed he kept glancing over, wanting, Antoine suspected, to be asked more than he was being asked.

The problem emerged within three pages. Carlyle did not write like the historians in Antoine's PDFs. He wrote like a man narrating a storm from inside it, giving whole chapters to single figures, to Mirabeau's face, to a coach arriving at Versailles. Where Antoine's modern sources discussed fiscal crises, class structures, and long-term forces, Carlyle seemed to care about whether particular people had chosen well or badly, as though the Revolution had turned on conscience. Antoine underlined a sentence, then another, then stopped underlining because he was underlining everything.

"You look querulous," his grandfather said at lunch. "That's the face your grandmother used to make at my father."

"I can't tell if this book is good history or just good writing."

"Read me some."

Antoine read a passage about the King's flight to Varennes, all thunder and moral weight. His grandfather listened with his fork down, which he never did, and when it ended he said, "He thinks people matter more than forces. That was his whole quarrel, I think. Individuals and their choices." He said it lightly, as if recalling a rival's position rather than reciting a fact, and then he ruined the moment by asking whether Antoine wanted the pipe cleaners.

That night Antoine sat with the essay outline on one side of the laptop and Carlyle on the other, and the two sides refused to ferment into anything. He tried drafting a paragraph claiming Carlyle was simply outdated, a pre-scientific dramatist superseded by structural analysis, and it came out smug. He tried the reverse, that Carlyle had grasped something the forces-people had lost, and that came out sentimental. Around midnight he deleted both and typed a single sentence at the top of a blank page: the question is not whether individuals or forces explain the Revolution, but what each way of explaining is for. He looked at it for a long time. It was not an answer. It might have been a hinge.

In the morning he found his grandfather in the study with a dust cloth, rearranging the shelf where the Carlyle had been, an activity that clearly required an audience. Antoine said he wanted to keep the book for the essay, and also, possibly, after.

"After the essay."

"After the essay. It's the first source I've actually wanted to read twice."

His grandfather straightened a row of atlases that did not need straightening. "You could quote him where he's wrong," he said. "My father hated that. Do that." He pulled a second book from the shelf, one Antoine hadn't noticed, a thin English edition of Tocqueville, and set it on the desk without comment, then stood there a moment as if deciding whether to say something further about his father, the dinners, the room his grandmother used to leave.

Antoine took the Tocqueville, sat down, and opened the Carlyle to the first page again.

Kyle had been staring at the same diagram for eleven minutes when Marisol leaned across the lab bench and tapped the mitochondrion with her pencil.

"You're supposed to be labeling the inner membrane," she said. "Not having a religious experience."

He was having something, though he wouldn't have called it that. The worksheet showed glucose being broken down step by step, arrows shrinking it through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, until what remained poured into a spiral of proteins embedded in the folded membrane. At the end of the spiral sat a small mushroom-shaped structure, and the label read ATP synthase. Their teacher, Ms. Okafor, had drawn it on the board that morning and said only, "By Friday, each of you will be able to trace this pathway from start to finish and explain the last step. The last step is where most of you will stumble." The quiz was Friday. It was Tuesday, fifth period, and the radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock.

"The arrows go in a circle," Kyle said. "Look at it. Hydrogen ions come back through this thing, this synthase, and it turns, and then it makes ATP. But the worksheet doesn't say how turning makes anything."

"Maybe it just does," Marisol said. She was already filling in her own sheet, her handwriting small and certain. "Write what the diagram says and move on."

That was the difference between them, and Kyle knew it. Marisol wanted the right answer; Kyle wanted the reason underneath it. He used to think of his own habit as the better one, maybe even a grandiose way of thinking, as if he were the kind of person who saw deeper than everyone else. Lately it felt more like an indictment, something to be read aloud against him: Kyle cannot accept what he is given. His father said it at dinner last month, after Kyle had argued with an uncle about a news story for twenty minutes. "You can't just trust anything," his father had said. "Not a diagram, not an article, nothing."

He hadn't come back with an answer then. He was trying to come back with one now.

Ms. Okafor was at her desk grading quizzes from another class, a mug of tea cooling beside her. Kyle walked over with the worksheet and the classroom's battered laptop, which he'd carried back from the cart without asking, because the cart was open and asking took time. "Can I look something up?" he said. "The last step. The ATP synthase."

"Look it up," she said, not looking up. "That's what the internet is for. Cite it if you use it."

He typed the name into the search bar at the third lab table, near the window, where the afternoon light came through dusty and made the screen hard to read until he angled it away. The first results were diagrams like his. Then a headline caught him: two men, Paul Boyer and John Walker, had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.

"They won a Nobel for this," he said out loud. Marisol looked over. "The last step. The part Ms. Okafor said we'd stumble on. Two guys worked it out and they gave them a Nobel Prize for it. Nineteen ninety-seven."

"So it's hard," Marisol said. "That's not news."

But it was news to Kyle, and it rearranged something in his thinking. He had assumed the worksheet left out the mechanism because the mechanism was simple, something a sentence could cover and the printer had skipped. Instead people had spent years on it, and a committee in Stockholm had judged the answer worth one of the highest honors there was. That meant the diagram wasn't withholding something small. It was withholding something enormous, simplified down to a mushroom shape and three arrows. His instinct to distrust the diagram had been right, and wrong at the same time: right that something was missing, wrong to think the missing thing was easy.

He read a little further, careful now, the way Marisuol would have been careful, checking the name and the year against a second page before writing anything down. Then he carried the laptop back to his own bench and picked up his pencil.

"Okay," he said. "Here's what I've got. Glucose gets broken down, the ions pile up on one side of the membrane, and they come back through ATP synthase, and that's what makes the ATP. The turning part, how the enzyme actually does it, that took decades. Boyer and Walker got the Nobel in 1997 for explaining it." He paused. "I don't fully get how it works. But I get what it does, and I get that the part I don't get is real and huge."

Marisol had stopped writing. "So for the quiz on Friday, we write the part we know."

"And I ask Ms. Okafor about the rest after class," Kyle said. "Not to argue with her. Just to ask."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere down the hall a door closed. Kyle wrote "ATP synthase, last step, Nobel Prize 1997, Boyer and Walker" in the margin of his worksheet, then drew a careful box around it, the pencil whispering against the paper.

The physics demonstration room on the second floor of the museum smelled like floor wax and old electricity, and Rose had claimed the ballistic table before anyone else could. It was a long metal runway with a launcher at one end and a carbon-paper sheet laid out on the floor beyond the edge, so that a marble fired off the end would land and leave a smudged gray mark wherever physics had decided to put it. Beside the table, a volunteer in a museum polo shirt watched with the expression of someone who had seen a hundred teenagers discover gravity that afternoon.

"You're supposed to predict first," he said. He was taciturn in the way of people who preferred machines to conversation, and he slid a clipboard toward her with the printed grid already on it. There was a girl from another school there too, a boy with a lanyard, a scatter of parents. Rose had come alone, on the bus, because the placement exam for the engineering program was in eleven days and she could not make the marble land where the equations said it should.

The problem was the launcher fired at an angle, and Rose kept treating the speed as one thing, firing it at herself, so to speak. She wrote and crossed out, wrote and crossed out. The other girl leaned over her shoulder.

"You split it," the girl said. "The sideways part never changes. It just goes straight at whatever speed it has sideways. Only the up-and-down part feels gravity." She tapped the grid. "Two problems wearing one coat."

Rose looked at the marble, the angle stamped on the launcher's protractor, and something rearranged itself behind her eyes. She multiplied by the cosine, wrote the horizontal speed as a constant, gave the vertical its own little equation with a minus sign in front of half of nine point eight. She marked the landing spot on the carbon paper with a pencil X. The volunteer released the spring. The marble struck two centimeters from her X, close enough that the boy with the lanyard said "whoa" without irony, and Rose felt a thin, almost embarrassing warmth climb her neck.

Eleven days, and a scholarship that would allay the part of the tuition her mother's job at the deposition office of the county courthouse could not cover, transcribing testimony eight hours a day with her wrists braced. Rose remembered being nine, sitting under her mother's desk among the boxes of taped statements, thinking that every word spoken in that building eventually lay down flat on paper, in lines, like the smudges on the carbon sheet. Her mother had wanted her to be a stenographer too. Steady, she had said. Numbers don't go to college, she had said, in the spring, before Rose's physics mark came back and she stopped saying it.

The volunteer was resetting the launcher when the other girl, whose name was Priya, asked about the next exhibit over, a glass case where a small metal ball hung between two brass plates and drifted sideways instead of falling straight. A placard gave the numbers. "Two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, 100 volts across them," Priya read aloud. "Five thousand volts per metre between them."

"That's it?" the boy said. "A hundred volts doesn't sound like much."

"Per metre," Rose said slowly. She was doing it on the clipboard margin, dividing, and the number that came out was the number on the placard, exactly. Then she thought of something and frowned. "Wait. If somebody put the distance in centimetres." She wrote it the wrong way, dividing 100 by 2 instead of 0.02, and got 50. Fifty against five thousand. "They'd get an answer a hundred times too small. Two centimetres instead of two hundredths of a metre." She looked up. "That's all it takes. You could do the whole method perfectly and still be off by a hundred."

Priya laughed, but not unkindly. "That's physics," she said. "Right and wrong at the same time."

The volunteer cleared his throat and pointed at the placard, which was already turning back toward the ball between the plates, but Rose wasn't really looking at it. She was thinking about the marble, the X in pencil, the two centimeters of miss. She had done the method right and still not hit the mark, and the two centimeters could have been air resistance or a stretched spring or her own handwriting, and she would not know which. The new way of splitting the motion had given her an answer that was almost true, and she found she could not decide whether that was a comfort or a warning. Eleven days from now there would be no carbon paper, no second launch, only the one answer she wrote down.

The room was emptying. Priya gathered her bag, asked which bus Rose took, and seemed pleased when the answer was the 14. They stood a moment by the ballistic table, where the fired marble had rolled into the corner and sat gleaming among its own gray smudges, a whole afternoon of attempts laid out flat.

"The vertical one," Rose said, mostly to herself, picking up the marble and weighing it in her palm. "That's the part that always comes back down."

Priya held the door, and the marble was cool and heavy in Rose's hand as she walked out still carrying it.

The community centre on Ashfield Road kept its pianos in a room that had once been a gymnasium, and the parquet still showed the ghost lines of a basketball key under the legs of the upright. Joseph arrived early on Tuesdays because the bus schedule left him no choice, and for twenty minutes he had the room to himself. He would sit at the piano with his workbook open to a page of blank staves and write nothing, which had become its own ritual.

The assignment was plain enough on paper: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation. Ms. Okafor had said the chords did not have to be adventurous, only honest, and Joseph liked that word applied to harmony, as though a C major triad could be a liar. He had a melody in his head, four notes that rose and then dropped a sixth, and he could hum it, but when he tried to write it down the rhythm kept dissolving, the way a dream does when you describe it out loud.

Marisol came at half past six, shaking rain off her jacket, and found him staring at the staves. She set down her coffee and pulled a pencil from her bag without being asked, the eraser chewed to a soft grey nub. "Bar lines first," she said. "Sixteen boxes. Draw the fences, then fill the field." He acceded, because arguing with her about method was a thing he had given up in September, and because the fences did help: within the boxes, his four notes found a home on beat one of bar one, whole and definite.

Ms. Okafor played recordings while they worked, and that evening it was a sonata with a first section that repeated its tunes politely, almost sweetly, and then a middle section that turned stormy. Joseph stopped writing. Something in the churn sounded familiar, three notes buried in the bass, then the same shape upside down in the treble. He leaned toward the speaker. "That's the opening tune," he said. "It's in there, isn't it? Broken up."

She looked at him over the rim of her coffee. "That's the development."

The word opened a door and Joseph walked through it alone, because she had already turned back to Marisol's workbook, and he liked it better that way. He listened again and again in his head, and then on his phone on the bus home, earbuds in, window streaked. The development took the exposition's themes and broke them into short fragments, and moved those fragments quickly through several keys, and that was why the section sounded restless, like someone pacing a small room. He tested the idea: he hummed his own four notes, chopped off the last one, and shoved the remaining three into a key he'd never written in, G minor, which made them sound melancholic and a little desperate, like relatives of the original who had fallen on hard times. There was a consanguinity between the two versions, a blood relation he could hear even when he could barely recognize the face.

The following Tuesday he brought in his sixteen bars, and they were no longer one melody but a family of them. Bars one through eight stated the tune over simple chords, F major with a D minor turn. Bars nine through twelve took the first three notes and ran them through three different keys, one bar each, no time to settle. Bars thirteen through sixteen brought the whole tune back, changed by the journey. Marisol read it over his shoulder while Ms. Okafor was helping Deni with his ledger lines. "Nine and ten feel like falling," Marisol said. "Is that on purpose?"

"Sort of," Joseph said. "I stole it from the sonata. The stormy part. The tune's in there if you listen for it, just cut into pieces and shoved around." He played bars nine and ten for her, then the original, then nine and ten again, and watched her face do the same thing his had done on the bus: confusion, then recognition, then a small laugh at herself for not hearing it sooner.

Ms. Okafor sat down at the upright and sight-read his page, pedal down, and the room filled. The fragments in the middle keys went by like fence posts from a train window. When she finished she did not say it was good or bad. She said, "Bar twelve, you never resolved the D minor. You land the return on the weak beat. Was that a choice?"

Joseph looked at bar twelve. He had written it at eleven at night, tired, and he honestly could not remember whether it was a choice or an accident, and he knew those were not the same thing even when they sounded identical. "I don't know yet," he said. "Can I leave it and find out next week?"

She handed back the page. Marisol was already playing bar twelve herself, then changing it, then playing his version again, her chewed pencil hovering over the staff.

Julia spread the two leases across the kitchen table the way her mother used to spread tarot cards, corners squared, everything visible at once. She had told Dana she was good at this, had said it more than once, and Dana had believed her, which was the problem with being believed.

"Garfield Street is nine hundred a month," Dana said, tapping the first page. "Which is a hundred and ten less than the one on Willow."

"That's just rent." Julia pulled a legal pad toward her and wrote the number down anyway, because it felt like an accomplishment. Outside, the sprinkler next door chattered through its arc, and somewhere in the house her father was on a call, his voice rising and falling behind his office door.

The Garfield lease mentioned heat was not included. The Willow lease said it was. Julia sat back. She was eighteen and had never paid a utility bill in her life, though she had watched her mother do it, every Sunday night, a ritual of envelopes and small disbursements that Julia had pretended to find boring. Her mother had died in March, obdurate about the bills until the end, refusing help, refusing to explain. Julia had found the checkbook after, balanced to the penny, and had cried over the arithmetic of it, the neat carried digits.

"So what do we do?" Dana asked. "Just pick Garfield? A hundred and ten is a hundred and ten."

"We add it all up first." Julia was drawing columns now, and something in her chest loosened as the columns grew. "Rent, and then every recurring cost the tenant pays. Heat, electricity, water, internet, insurance. Everything that comes every month. Total monthly cost. That's how you compare them fairly."

"Where'd you learn that?"

"A book my mom left on the shelf. Personal finance, 1998. It smelled like her." Julia did not say that she had found the book in June and read it three times as if it were a letter. She did not say that last year she had advised her mother to renew a lease based on rent alone, that the building had switched to tenant-paid heat in the spring, that her mother had never once mentioned what the change cost. Julia had found the bills. She knew the number. She had not told anyone, not even Dana, that the advice had been hers.

They worked through it together, Dana reading figures off the lease riders while Julia wrote. Garfield: nine hundred rent, plus heat in winter that the current tenants estimated high, plus electricity, water, internet, renter's insurance. Willow: a thousand and ten, but heat was in the rent, water was in the rent, and only electricity, internet, and insurance landed on the tenant. When Julia added each column top to bottom, twice, the way her mother had taught her without either of them noticing it was teaching, the totals came out nearly even, and then, on the third check, Garfield came out higher. Fourteen dollars higher, and that was before winter.

"You're sure?" Dana leaned over the pad, and Julia could smell the chlorine still in her hair from the pool.

"I did it three times."

"Because you said you were bad at math in eleventh grade. You told Mr. Ferro you were bad at math."

"I was bad at math. This isn't math." It was true and it wasn't, and Julia held both of those in her mouth at once. What she had been bad at was being looked at while she worked. What she was good at, alone at this table, was numbers that underpinned a decision, columns that would hold weight. She turned the pad so Dana could see the arithmetic, every line visible, nothing squared away in a drawer.

"Then Willow," Dana said slowly, testing it. "The place that looked expensive is the cheap one."

"Cheaper. Not cheap." Julia looked at the two totals, fourteen dollars apart, and thought of winter in her mother's building, the radiator that clanked, the bill her mother had paid without comment while Julia advised her about rents. Fourteen dollars could reverse itself in a warm January or a cold one. She wrote both totals on the pad and did not cross either out. "There's a margin here we can't see yet. Utilities move. So we pick with that in the open."

Dana picked up the Garfield lease and folded it in half, then in half again, undecided, the paper thick in her hand. "Can we sleep on it?"

"We can sleep on it." Julia gathered the Willow pages but left the pad on the table, columns facing up, the two totals side by side, fourteen dollars apart. Behind the office door her father's call ended, and she heard his chair push back. He came out drying his hands on a dish towel and stopped at the table, reading the pad upside down the way he read everything.

"Which one's she leaning toward?" he asked Dana, nodding at Julia, and Dana said, "The one that costs more," and her father laughed once, short, before he saw Julia's face.

"What?" he said. "What is it?"

"Nothing," Julia said. "Read the columns."

He read them, right side up now, silent, his finger moving down each line the way her mother's had. When he finished he didn't laugh again. He sat down in her mother's chair and said, "Okay," and then, after a moment, "Which one was yours?"

"The Willow," Dana said. "But she says we should sleep on it."

I never cared about the tempering unit, which is why I signed up for it twice. That was a joke I told people, and like most of my jokes it worked because it was almost a lie. The truth was that last spring I had bombed the practical, left the room before the chocolate set, and never gone back to look at the dull, streaky results. Ms. Okoye had left them on the counter with my name card beside them for two days. I told everyone I'd forgotten. I told myself that too, and mostly it held.

The second time around, we had marble slabs, bench scrapers, thermometers, and a room that smelled like warm cocoa butter. I was paired with Nadia, who was morose that week over a rejected college application and stirred her chocolate like she was punishing it. What we were doing was called tabling: pouring two thirds of the chocolate onto cold marble, working it back and forth until it cooled and thickened, then returning it to the warm bowl. Ms. Okoye demonstrated once, said the words "form V crystals" without further comment, and left us to it. She believed, or claimed to believe, that we learned more from failure than from instruction, a philosophy I privately thought was convenient for someone paid to walk around with a clipboard.

My chocolate bloomed anyway. Gray stripes spread across my sample like weather. Nadia's, despite the punitive stirring, snapped clean and glossy, and she had the grace not to gloat, which somehow made it worse. I scraped my batch into the discard bowl and started over with the last of our couverture, and halfway through the tabling Nadia abandoned her slab to text someone, and I was alone with a thermometer reading a degree too high and a spoon going nowhere.

Here is where I have to be honest, since you'll hear it from Devi anyway. Devi had sent me a message that morning, and I hadn't answered it. She'd read it over my shoulder later and I let her believe I'd only just seen it, which is its own small accounting. The message said: "No marble slab at my house. I used the seeding method instead. Chopped up some leftover store-bought chocolate that was still tempered and stirred it into my melted chocolate. The melted part copies the crystals from the chopped part, form V, and sets shiny. Cheap Easter bunny, technically a hero."

So then there was Nadia, leaning over my shoulder, morose and curious at once, and there was Devi's message glowing on the counter. The choice in front of me was not really chocolate. I had spent a year dividing the world into people who followed the hard technique and people who took shortcuts, and I had put Devi in the second pile and myself in the first, and the whole dichotomy had been doing me no favors. It was, if I'm honest, less a way of thinking than a way of losing with dignity. My chocolate was currently demonstrating the dignity part.

I chopped a bar from the pantry shelf, checked the label, checked that it was glossy and snapped clean, and stirred the pieces into my too-warm bowl a few at a time until the thermometer came down. Nadia watched me do it. "Is that cheating?" she asked. "It's seeding," I said. "Tempered chocolate in, and the rest copies it." She said that seemed like less work, which from Nadia was litotes for admiration.

What I hadn't told Devi, and what I'd told Ms. Okoye at the start of term, was that I'd never even attempted the retest I'd promised myself. I'd said I forgot the practical, forgot the results, forgot the whole unit. Unreliable, my brother would say, meaning me. When the seeded chocolate came down to temperature, I dipped a knife tip and laid the strip on parchment, and we both stood there while Nadia's timer counted and my heart did something embarrassing.

The strip set in five minutes and snapped when I broke it, and the break was glossy at the edge, clean as anything off Nadia's slab. Devi texted again while I was holding the two pieces side by side: "Did you try it or are you still being a snob about your marble." I typed "maybe" and then deleted it and typed "it worked" and then deleted that too, because both were true and neither was the whole of it. Whether the tabling mattered more than the seeding, whether the technique was worth the year I'd spent guarding it, whether Devi would still want to talk to me if she knew how long I'd waited to answer her message, all of that stayed open on the counter with the parchment and the thermometer.

I put the two chocolate pieces in my pocket instead of eating them, which Nadia noticed and mercifully didn't comment on. Then I wrote "worked, sorry, call you tonight" and pressed send.

The bookshop on Miller Street held its Thursday night club in the back corner, between the poetry shelves and a radiator that clanked every few minutes. Nolan had been coming for two months, since his senior year English teacher announced she was leaving and he wanted somewhere to keep arguing about books. Tonight the group was six people and the novel was Jane Eyre, and Nolan had promised himself he would say something that mattered.

He had marked a passage on page 271, where Jane returns to Thornfield and Rochester reminds her that he pays her wages, thirty pounds a year, and that she depends on him for everything. He had underlined it three times in pencil and then, ashamed of the pencil, tried to erase the extra lines. He wanted to say something about it. He had spent the weekend reading a photocopy of a critical essay that Ms. Andaya had left in his mailbox at school, and the essay's vocabulary sat in his head like borrowed furniture.

When Priya, who ran the shop, opened the floor, Nolan cleared his throat too loudly. "I want to try something," he said. "Not like an opinion exactly. More like a lens." He read the passage aloud, the wages, the dependence, the line where Rochester says he has bought her. "If you look at it through a Marxist lens," he said, "the romance is also a transaction. She's selling her labor. He owns the house."

"Sure," said Marcus, who was fifty and read everything with a pencil behind his ear. "But it's a love story. That's not nothing."

"I'm not saying it's nothing. I'm saying it's both." Nolan turned the essay over in his mind, trying to find a way to hold the two claims at once without dropping either.

Then Priya pulled a slim paperback off the shelf behind her, an old Penguin edition of The Communist Manifesto, its spine cracked white. "This might be your lens in its original form," she said, and found the page with her thumb. She read aloud: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. That's how the first section opens. Marx and Engels, 1848." She looked up. "Does it fit the novel? Victorian England, a governess and her employer?"

The radiator clanked. Nolan thought about it. "Jane's not a factory worker," he said slowly. "She's educated, sort of gentry without money. So the class struggle in her case isn't barricades. It's that she can't marry Rochester without becoming his dependent, because her wages are nothing and his property is everything. The whole plot turns on that imbalance." He paused, aware that everyone was looking at him. "But here's what I can't settle. When she inherits money and comes back to him as an equal, is that the book fixing the class problem or just hiding it? One character getting lucky doesn't change the structure."

"That governess," Marcus said. "She's one woman, standing in for a whole class of them."

"Synecdoche," Nolan said, and was pleased that the word arrived on time. "The one standing for the many. The essay called it that." He had not expected to enjoy saying it. He had expected to feel like an impostor, the way he felt in the college writing sample he was supposed to mail by Friday. Instead the word did work that "symbol" would not have done.

Priya set the Manifesto on the table between the teacups. "The trouble with that lens," she said, "is it can flatten things. Love becomes wages, the person becomes a position. You reify them, turn living relations into dead objects, and then you've explained the book by killing it."

"Maybe that's the honest answer, though," Nolan said. "The lens shows you something real and it costs you something. Jane Eyre as a transaction, Jane Eyre as a love story. I can hold both. What I can't do is pick one and pretend the other isn't there." He heard his own voice go up at the end, like a question, and let it.

Marcus wrote something in his margin. Priya poured more tea. Outside the front window a bus went by, and its light crossed the poetry shelves and the faces around the table, and Nolan turned back to page 271 and read the passage aloud a second time, slower, listening for what he had missed the first time.

The quarry filled with pale light by mid-afternoon, the cut walls of limestone catching the sun the way a bowl catches water. Sofia spread her notes on the flat top of a boulder and weighted the pages with smaller stones, because the wind off the water was insouciant about other people's work, flipping whatever it pleased. Dex sat cross-legged beside her with his laptop balanced on his knees, its screen dulled by the glare.

"Run it again," she said.

He pressed play on the animation she'd built for their Earth science presentation. Molecules drifted across the screen, and little arrows of infrared radiation rose from a cartoon ground, bounced off the drifting shapes, and came back down. She had drawn every frame herself in a notebook over three nights, then photographed and sequenced them. The point she wanted to make was simple in her head and impossible in her mouth: sunlight comes through, heat tries to leave, gases like carbon dioxide send part of it back. "It's not a wall," she kept saying to Dex. "It's more like the air remembers the warmth a little longer than it should."

Then he showed her the graph. It was the real one, the carbon dioxide record measured on a Hawaiian volcano across the last century, and she had seen it before in the textbook but never alone, never with time to run her finger along it. The line began low and level, wobbling faintly each year like something breathing. Then it bent. Then it climbed. The bend came in the same decades her grandmother was born, then her mother, then her, three generations stacked along a curve that did not care about any of them. She copied the shape onto a fresh page so she could carry it without a screen.

"So I found something," Dex said, and he hesitated, which was unlike him. In her draft, the one she'd already printed for the teacher, she had written a confident sentence: the Gulf Stream alone keeps Europe's winters mild. It had sounded authoritative. She had liked how it sounded. Dex turned the laptop toward her and read aloud from a study led by a researcher named Richard Seager, published in 2002. "He argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters."

"That can't be right," Sofia said. "Everyone says the Gulf Stream."

"I know. That's why I checked twice."

She sat with it. The quarry was quiet except for water dripping somewhere below the ledge, patient attrition wearing the rock down into something smoother, grain by grain, on a schedule no one kept. She thought about how a thing everyone says gets repeated until it hardens into fact, and how a graph does the opposite, keeps its soft shape, admits its wobble. Two ways of knowing, and she had been trusting the wrong one, or maybe trusting both and never checking where they disagreed.

"Say the Seager line again," she said. "Slowly." He said it, and she wrote it down word for word, then crossed out the sentence in her draft and wrote a new one with his pen, which was better than hers and she told him so. He shrugged, pleased.

That evening her grandmother sent her a message, the kind she typed with one finger on a phone with enormous letters:

Sofia, your mother says you are doing a talk about the air. When I was a girl in February the canal froze thick enough to walk on and the men played football on it. I have not seen it freeze like that again. I don't know if that means anything. But you like the numbers, so maybe you can tell me. Come Sunday if the bus is running. There is cake and it is the kind you like.

Sofia read it three times. Her grandmother's canal and the Hawaiian volcano had never met, and yet the wobbling line on the graph, that faint yearly breath, was winter and summer, was ice and thaw, was somewhere a canal freezing or not freezing. She could not say how much of the warming curve was the canal. She could say the curve was real, and that the old sentence about Europe needed correcting, and that correcting it felt less like losing than like being let in on something.

On Sunday she took the bus. She brought the page where she'd copied the graph by hand, and she set it on the kitchen table between the teapot and the cake, and put her finger on the low, level beginning. "This is your canal," she said.

Her grandmother leaned close, glasses down on her nose, and touched the climbing end of the line. "And this?"

"That's me," Sofia said, and cut her a slice of cake first.

Eli had been meaning to give Marcus the note for two days, and practice on Thursday was the last chance before the relay trial. He had commandeered the corner of the bleachers where the gym bags lived, sitting with his phone out, rereading a screenshot his older sister had sent him from a college psych course. In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise their essays when the teacher's critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. His sister had added, "Works on roommates too." Eli didn't know if it worked on best friends you'd known since fourth grade, friends whose flyaway left elbow you'd watched ten thousand times.

The problem was simple and not simple. Marcus had started rushing his second exchange, and at the last meet it had cost them nearly half a second, which in a relay is an ocean. Half a second was the difference between qualifying and watching the sectional final from the folding chairs. Coach had said something vague about "cleaning up transitions," which told Marcus nothing and let him pretend the fault belonged to daylight or the official's whistle. Eli was the one who stood next to Marcus on the line. Eli was the one who could actually see it.

He tried it out in his head during the warmup laps. You're dropping your elbow early. True, specific, useless, because Marcus heard any correction the way he heard his mother about homework: something to be survived. Last season Eli had told him his start angle was off and Marcus had gone petulant for a week, doing the corrected angle with exaggerated slowness whenever he caught Eli watching, a performance of obedience that made them both feel small.

But Eli had also watched Coach Delgado fix a girl on the junior varsity, Priya, whose handoffs had been worse than Marcus's. Coach hadn't softened the criticism. She'd been blunt about the timing, and then she'd said, "I'm telling you because I think you can run with the varsity squad by October." Priya had stopped rolling her eyes at corrections after that. She'd started asking for them. Eli had assumed it was just Priya being mature, but the screenshot made him wonder if the sentence had done something, if belief wasn't a garnish but an ingredient.

Practice divided itself the way it always did, varsity on the near lane, everyone else drifting to the far one, a kind of speciation by stopwatch that Eli usually found funny and tonight found a little sad. He and Marcus were on the same side of it, for now. That was the whole point of telling him. If the elbow kept drifting, they'd end up on opposite sides of the gym, and Marcus would never believe it hadn't been said out of cruelty.

They ran the exchange four times before water break. On the fourth, Marcus rushed it again, the baton slapping into Eli's palm late and crooked, and Marcus's face did the thing it did, the wince he disguised as squinting at the scoreboard clock. Eli walked over with his bottle and made himself start before the silence got too heavy to cross.

"Your left elbow's flying open on the second exchange," Eli said. "You're losing the baton angle, and it's costing us like half a second." Marcus's jaw set, and Eli kept going, faster than he'd planned. "And I'm only saying it because I know you can run a clean exchange. You've done it. I think you're the best sprinter on this team when your form holds."

Marcus unscrewed his cap and drank for a long time. "Half a second," he said finally.

"Half a second."

"Fine. Watch the next one, then. Tell me if it's still ugly." They ran it again, and the elbow stayed tucked, and the baton landed in Eli's palm like it had been aimed there. It could have been the rest between reps. It could have been that Marcus was already tired of rushing. Eli didn't know, and he wasn't going to pretend he did; one clean pass wasn't a study. But at the end of practice Marcus lingered by the door instead of leaving first, and said, "Tomorrow, same thing. If I screw it up, tell me. Don't just tell Coach."

"Deal," Eli said, and picked up both their bags to carry them out.

The video had been sitting in Brayden's camera roll for forty minutes, and every minute he didn't post it felt like money draining out of a pocket with a hole in it. It showed a pundit, mid-rant on some cable panel, jabbing a finger at footage of a flooded street while text over the top claimed it had happened that morning, two states over. Brayden's group chat had seven people in it, and Marcus in particular had a habit of posting first and being wrong loudest. If Brayden sent it now, he'd be the one who knew things.

He was at Priya's house, which complicated the timing. Her kitchen table was covered in the sprawl of her laptop, a tangle of charger, two mugs going cold, and a notebook with SQL scrawled across half the pages. Priya had a paid internship interview on Monday, and the take-home task was due Sunday night, and she'd been at the table since ten that morning saying almost nothing.

"Two minutes," Brayden said. "You have to see this."

"I'm in the middle of something that's killing my laptop."

"Two minutes."

She angled the screen toward him anyway, because Priya never could resist being the one with the interesting problem. The cursor was a spinning wheel. Her database homework had a query window open, half a wall of text, and the fan under the machine was running like something trying to take off.

"I ran it and it just froze," she said. "It's been like this for two minutes. The sample data's tiny. It should be instant."

Brayden leaned in, thumb still hovering over the share button on his phone. He read the query top to bottom even though most of it was a foreign country to him. He knew what SELECT meant and what FROM meant and not much past that. Near the bottom there was a JOIN between two tables, customers and orders, and below it a WHERE clause, but between them, where it seemed like something should connect the two tables, there was nothing. Just whitespace.

"Is this part supposed to be blank?"

Priya pulled the laptop back and looked. Her mouth opened, then closed, and she pushed both hands into her hair.

"I forgot the ON clause," she said. "A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows. So 100 customers and 1,000 orders, that's 100,000 rows."

Brayden was already doing it on his phone's calculator, because the number sounded too big and too round at the same time. A hundred times a thousand. The display said 100000. He looked at the frozen cursor, the fan howling, the little progress bar that had crept maybe a fifth of the way across, and something about it rearranged how he was sitting. Every customer matched with every order. Every row shaking hands with every other row, a party where nobody knew which conversation they belonged to.

"So it's not broken," he said. "It's just doing something enormous and stupid."

"It's doing exactly what I told it to." She held the power button until the machine went dark, which felt, to Brayden, a little like putting a horse down.

While she waited for it to reboot, she took his phone and watched the flood video. He watched her face instead of the screen, because he'd already watched it four times and had metabolized the whole thing into certainty, the certainty you get from footage that makes you feel something before you have time to think. She handed it back.

"Post it," she said. "That's going everywhere."

His thumb found the share icon again. The group chat was open, Marcus's name at the top of a conversation about weekend plans, nothing since. First. He'd be first.

And then, the way the missing ON clause kept snagging at him, another thought snagged the same way. The footage was doing something enormous with nothing connecting it to anything. A street, water, a claim in bold text. Two rows from two different tables, side by side, because somebody forgot to say whether they actually matched.

"Does your laptop still work enough to open a browser?" he asked.

"It's rebooting. Use the desktop. Why?"

He was already at the family computer in the corner of the kitchen, taking a screenshot of a frame from the video, dragging it into the image search. "One sec."

Priya came to stand behind him, arms crossed, the way she stood when she thought someone was wasting time she could be spending on her own rescue. The search loaded. The same flooded street, the same brown water at the same height against the same pharmacy sign. Four years old. A different state, a different storm, a hundred shared posts with a hundred different captions, each one evanescent, gone within a week, replaced by the next outrage, none of them ever checking where the water actually was.

"Huh," Priya said.

"It's not from this week." Brayden put the phone face-down on the table. "It's not even from this decade, basically."

"So don't post it."

"I'm not going to post it."

She went back to her laptop, which had come back up, and typed the ON clause into her query with the focus of someone who intended to finish her assignment before dinner and rehearse interview answers before bed. She wanted Monday the way Brayden had wanted to hit send, and he sat at the counter watching her work, feeling the strange lightness of a disaster that hadn't happened to him.

Around nine, after the query ran in under a second and she'd exported her results, Priya picked up her own phone and stretched. "What's Marcus doing," she said, mostly to herself, and opened the chat. Brayden saw her stop. She read for a while.

"What?" he said.

"Nothing. Marcus posted that flood video an hour ago. It's got like forty likes already."

He came around the counter. There it was, at the top of the chat, Marcus's caption in all caps: THIS IS INSANE. And below it, a reply from Priya that she must have typed while he was reading over her shoulder, one word, wrong.

"Haha I know," she'd written. "Crazy."

"Priya."

She locked the phone and set it down, face-up, and looked at her finished assignment on the screen.

"Brayden, I have an interview on Monday."

"Take it back."

"It's forty likes," she said, and picked the phone up again.

Logan spread the data table across the kitchen table, pushing the fruit bowl aside to make room. The table listed the equilibrium constant for the same reaction at four temperatures, and he had been staring at it for ten minutes because the numbers were going the wrong way. He had expected them to climb as the temperature climbed. Instead, from 300 kelvin to 500, the K values fell, steadily, like a stairway descending into a basement he hadn't known was there.

His sister Delia came in with a mixing bowl under one arm and a bag of chocolate chips in her fist. "I need the oven at six," she said. "I'm making cookies for Kayla's going-away thing, and I need you to not be weird about the kitchen for one hour."

"I'm not even using the oven." He tapped his pencil against the table. "I'm using this table. Different appliance entirely."

"You're going to be sitting there muttering for an hour. You always mutter." She set the bowl down on the counter and began measuring flour with the concentration of someone defusing something. Delia was sixteen and treated every departure, every going-away party, every ending, as a seismic event that required baked goods to propitiate it. Logan had watched her do it for years, churning out brownies and lemon bars as if sugar could hold people in place.

He returned to the table. The assignment asked him to predict, using Le Chatelier's principle, which way the reaction would shift if he heated it. He knew the rule everyone recited: heat the system and the equilibrium shifts to use the heat up. What he kept missing was what that did to the constant itself. He copied the K values into his notebook in a column and looked at them until his eyes watered. Then he drew an arrow beside the column, pointing down, and wrote beside it: exothermic, so heat is like a product. He stopped. That was the part he'd had backwards all week.

"Move your elbow," Delia said, reaching past him for the vanilla. She cracked an egg one-handed, a move she had practiced until it worked.

"Say you have a reaction that gives off heat," Logan said, not looking up. "Exothermic. You raise the temperature."

"Is this going to be one of your lecture things?"

"You raise the temperature and the K actually drops." He turned the notebook so she could see the column. "Look. Four temperatures, and every time the temperature goes up, the constant goes down. And it's the opposite for a reaction that takes in heat. Endothermic. Raise the temperature and the K goes up. That's the whole thing I had wrong. I kept thinking K was fixed, like it was a property of the reaction. It moves."

Delia looked at the numbers for longer than he expected. "So the reaction changes its mind depending on how hot it is."

"Something like that." He pulled the sheet back toward himself. "For this one, heating it makes less product at equilibrium. If I wanted more product, I'd have to cool it, and even then I don't know how far, because the table doesn't tell me." That part bothered him, a low hum under the rest: the principle told him the direction, and the table told him the constants, and neither told him everything. He wrote that in the margin too, because it seemed honest.

Delia preheated the oven and began dropping dough onto a sheet, spacing the balls with a ruler's precision. "Kayla leaves Saturday," she said. "I keep thinking if I make the right thing, she'll come back more."

Logan watched her level off a scoop of dough, then looked down at his column of shrinking numbers. "Cooling helps," he said, "but it doesn't get you all the way."

"Everything all right at three fifty?" Delia asked, squinting at the oven display.

"Three fifty's fine," he said, and set his pencil across the page to hold his place.

The last seat in the lab was by the window, and Camille had habituated to it over six weeks of sitting there, enough that when Mrs. Okafor reassigned the bench groups for the stoichiometry practical, she felt the rearrangement like a small ordinance, something decreed from above and not open to appeal. Her new bench had Priya, who annotated everything in three colors, and Marcus, who had a trenchant opinion on every topic and no patience for anyone else's. Camille wanted one thing from the practical: to leave with a grade good enough to hold her application to the summer research program, which required a B or better in the second semester. Her grade was sitting at a hair above a C.

The task sheet gave them a mass of reactant and asked for the moles of product. Camille read it twice, then a third time, the way you reread a text message hoping it will rearrange itself into sense. Marcus reached for the balance first. "You get the mass. I'll get the mass," he said, though the mass was already printed on the sheet, 4.90 grams of the reactant, and the weighing was only for verification.

"You have to go through the molar mass," Priya said, uncapping a blue pen. "Grams divided by grams per mole, then across the coefficients."

"I know what a mole is," Camille said, and discovered, saying it, that this was only half true. She knew it the way she knew the word for a country she had never visited. She wrote the molar mass of the reactant, 98.09, at the top of her page, then divided 4.90 by it, and the number that came out, 0.0500, sat on her paper looking back at her, small and exact, and she felt something loosen in her chest. One fiftieth of a mole. A countable thing, almost. She looked up the molar mass of the product, 100.46, multiplied, and got a theoretical yield, and then it was Priya's turn with the balance and the filtering flask, and the room filled with the smell of the hot plate warming.

It was while their precipitate was drying that Marcus, flipping ahead in his binder, started the argument. "Next unit," he said. "Equilibrium. Question. If the forward reaction is endothermic, and you warm it up, which way does it shift?"

"Toward the reactants," Priya said. "Heat's on the products' side, so adding it pushes back."

"That's backwards. Endothermic means the forward reaction absorbs heat. So heat it and it goes forward, toward the products."

Priya's pen stopped. "You're treating heat like a reactant. That's not what the question says."

"That's exactly what it says."

They both looked at Camille, the way people look at a third judge, and she wished they wouldn't, because she did not know. What she knew was the small clean chain she had just built, grams to moles, moles to moles, moles back to grams, and it annoyed her that the chain gave her nothing here. She thought about the hot plate in front of them, about their own reaction which had to be kept warm, and she thought about how the teacher had set out two sealed tubes at the front station with a sign that said observe, do not touch, one in an ice bath and one in warm water, both the same reaction, both changing color before their eyes.

"I don't know," she said. "But there's a way to find out that isn't arguing."

The tubes were at the front, and Camille was the one who walked up to them, Priya and Marcus trailing behind. The cold tube held a pale, nearly colorless liquid. The warm tube, the same reaction pushed only by temperature, held a deep, unmistakable blue, the blue of product. Mrs. Okafor had a card beside them with the balanced equation and a single phrase, forward reaction is endothermic, and Camille read it and read the two colors again, the cold faint and the warm saturated, and let the observation settle into the place where Marcus's claim had been standing.

"The products," she said. "If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. The warm tube's the one that went blue."

Marcus made a small sound of vindication. Priya crossed her arms, then uncrossed them, then leaned in to look, and Camille watched her do the thing that honest people do, which is to keep looking after they have stopped wanting the answer to be different. "Fine," Priya said. "But I still think my way of reasoning about it works for exothermic ones. There has to be some version where both framings agree."

"There probably is," Camille said. "I haven't gotten that far." She was aware of how much she hadn't gotten that far on, how the mole calculation had been the first thing all semester to feel like it belonged to her, and how the summer program committee would not care about tubes of blue liquid or about the moment Priya conceded. But when they got back to their bench, the precipitate had dried, and Camille put the filter paper on the balance and read the mass aloud, and Priya wrote it down, and Marcus divided it by the molar mass to compare against her theoretical yield. Their number was low, by about six percent, wet product or lost crystals, and Priya said they should note that, and Camille noted it.

At the end of the period she stayed behind to copy the two tubes into her notebook, the pale one and the blue one, drawing them side by side and writing underneath, warm goes toward the products, endothermic, forward. Mrs. Okafor passed behind her on her way to the ice bath and said, "Next week we do it with numbers."

"Good," Camille said, and kept writing.

Evan had come to his grandfather's house for the weekend with a laptop and no plans, which was how his grandfather liked him: available. On Saturday morning the old man set a black stone paperweight on the kitchen table, igneous and glassy, as if it were the subject of the meeting, and slid a printed spreadsheet beside it.

"I have customers," his grandfather said. "Two hundred and six of them, if the list is honest, which I begin to doubt. And I have orders, a stack of them, three years deep. I want to know who has never ordered anything. Not the ones who stopped. The ones who wrote their name down at the nursery open day and then vanished into silence like ghosts."

"You want me to find the ghosts," Evan said.

"I beseech you to find the ghosts. Then I will write to them, or shame them, I haven't decided which."

The problem was simple to describe and, for the first hour, impossible to do. Evan had one table of customers and one table of orders, and every way he joined them, he got only the people who had ordered, because that was what a join did, and because he had learned SQL from a course that assumed everyone eventually bought something. His grandfather sat across from him eating a tangerine with the concentration of an epicure at a tasting menu, peeling it in one unbroken spiral, and offering commentary that was no commentary at all.

"Also," his grandfather said, midway through the spiral, "look at this. Dora sent it to me. She thinks it is me."

He turned his phone around. A clip, grainy, a man in a greenhouse yanking a seedling out of its pot and throwing it into a bin while someone off camera laughed. The caption said a local nursery owner had been caught destroying stock rather than sell it at a discount. Evan watched it twice. The man had his grandfather's slouch and his grandfather's hat, which was the trouble, because his grandfather owned one hat and so did half the men in the county.

"Is it you?" Evan asked.

"It is not me. My greenhouse has a wooden bench. This one is metal. But Dora has four hundred friends and they believe captions." His grandfather set the phone down. "Can you prove a thing like that? You are the technical one."

Evan took the phone and tried the clip in an image search first, pasting the link, and got nothing useful, and then, in a quiet hour of trying things, discovered the method himself. A video could not be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so the way in was to take screenshots of the key frames and search those images instead. He scrubbed to the clearest moment, the turn of the man's face, caught the frame, and searched it. Nothing. He caught the moment the hat came off. A result surfaced, older, from a garden supplier two counties over, same man, different caption, filmed years back as a joke about culling weak stock. He captured two more frames to be sure, and the frames kept pointing at the same original upload, and the local caption turned out to be stitched on afterward by an account that posted a great many captions.

"So you can show that Dora's version is a cut and paste," his grandfather said, reading over his shoulder. "You prove it with the picture, not the video."

"That's the trick. The video itself won't search. You have to pull stills from it, the important moments, and search those." Evan screenshotted the greenhouse bench in the background too, metal where his grandfather's was wood, and sent the whole set to Dora, who replied with a sheepish thumbs-up and no apology, which Evan decided was probably the standard currency.

Then he went back to the ghosts, because the two problems sat side by side in his head and one kept shedding light on the other. The clip had failed because he was searching the wrong shape of thing, expecting the search to see a whole video when it could only see a picture. The join kept failing the same way. He had been asking it to match customers to orders, and it answered with matches, and the ghosts were precisely the ones with nothing to match. What he needed was a join that kept every customer whether or not an order existed, left every customer in, and then he could keep only the rows where the order came back empty. He typed it, ran it, and thirty-one names appeared, ghosts at last, ranked by how long ago they had signed the open day sheet.

His grandfather put on his glasses and read the list slowly, twice. "The Hendersons," he said. "They came for the free cider, I always suspected it." He carried the page to the desk by the window and began copying names onto notecards in his upright, formal hand.

Evan left the query on screen, the empty order column showing its nulls like breath on cold glass, and wondered whether finding the ghosts and clearing his grandfather's name were the same kind of truth or only felt like it, and whether Dora's four hundred friends would even look at stills. He took a screenshot of the results, just in case, and pasted it into the message thread.

"There," his grandfather said, sealing the first notecard. "Now we write to the Hendersons."

Levi claimed the table beside the folding counter the way other people claimed barstools, spreading both leases across it while the washers filled, because the laundromat on Fern Street was the only place left where nobody asked him questions. He was fine. He had said so at dinner, said it again in the car, and he meant it, mostly, the way you mean anything you repeat. Apartment A sat on Halden Road, five hundred dollars a month plus utilities. Apartment B sat above the vacuum repair shop, four sixty plus utilities, and its landlord had written "utilities reasonable" in handwriting that Levi distrusted on principle. His mother had offered to look at both leases and he had said no too quickly, and now here he was doing the thing alone, which was obviously a victory and not a retreat.

He had one utility bill, a photocopy the Halden landlord had given him, marked August. Gas and electric, forty-one dollars. He wrote that number on a napkin and felt the small pleasure of arithmetic behaving itself. Four sixty plus forty-one was five hundred and one. B was cheaper by nothing. He sat back and waited for the dryer's warmth to make the conclusion feel final.

A woman at the next table was folding towels with the efficiency of someone who had done this a thousand times and resented all of them. "You commandeered the whole table," she said, not unkindly. "College?"

"Moving out," Levi said. "Comparing places." He did not say that his mother had cried in the kitchen on Tuesday, because she hadn't, exactly; her eyes had been wet but that could have been the onion, and anyway he was the one leaving, which was a decision and not an abandonment.

The woman introduced herself as Dee, said her son had done the same thing two years ago, said the boy above the vacuum shop was probably an aesthete who'd painted the walls some fashionable gray and called it character. Levi laughed and then caught himself laughing, because it was true, the listing had said "designer tones," and he had liked the look of it in the photos more than he liked any number he'd written down. He turned the napkin over so she couldn't see how little was on it.

"You've got an August bill," Dee said, nodding at the photocopy when he didn't move fast enough to hide that either. "My mother-in-law warned my son about that. August bill looks friendly, she told him, but heating in the cold months will eat you, and cooling in summer too if the place has air conditioning. She said average a whole year of bills, summer and winter both, and that'll give you the true monthly cost. One month lies to you. That's what she said." Levi said nothing, because he had been about to defend his napkin, and there was nothing on his napkin worth defending.

He found the landlord's phone number on the B lease and called right there, coins of dryer noise around him. The landlord, sounding as if Levi had woken him at noon, admitted he had twelve months of bills for the vacuum shop unit, from the last tenant, and read them out while Levi wrote on the back of the Halden lease. High numbers for the winter months, higher than Levi expected, higher than the rent difference, then dropping through spring and climbing again in summer with the cooling. He added all twelve and divided, and the answer sat on the page looking nothing like forty-one. The unit's true monthly cost was far past five hundred, past the Halden apartment even before he knew Halden's own winter numbers. He asked the Halden landlord for a year of bills too, and the man promised to text them by Friday, and Levi understood that the comparison wasn't finished, that a single August bill had nearly decided his whole year.

Dee had been listening while she folded. "So the cheap one's the expensive one," she said.

"Probably," Levi said. "I don't know yet what the other one costs in January." Saying it out loud felt strange, like admitting the napkin had been a costume. He thought about calling his mother from the car, walking her through the twelve numbers, and then thought about how he'd told her he didn't need help, and how both of those things could be true at once. He texted her anyway, just the question: do you still have our utility bills from last year. The reply came before the dryers finished: a whole folder, come by whenever. He looked at it for a long moment, then at the two leases, the true one and the one he'd wanted to be true.

He folded his clothes badly, the way he always did, shirts becoming shapes no aesthete would claim. Dee left with a wave, taking her opinions with her, and the laundromat went back to its hum. Levi gathered the leases, both of them, the folder text still unread on his screen, and carried everything out into the cold.

The screen door announced Hailey with its usual shriek, and her grandfather looked up from his crossword long enough to say, "Lemonade's in the fridge, glasses are where glasses have always been." He was a taciturn man, but the lemonade was always cold and there was always a glass with her name scratched into it, so she had learned years ago to translate. She set her laptop on the kitchen table between his newspaper and a bowl of peaches going soft, and opened the video her teammate Priya had sent at midnight: their robotics club's first build walkthrough, four minutes of Priya explaining the arm mechanism to the camera.

Hailey watched it twice. The mechanism was clever, genuinely clever, but the explanation eviscerated it. Priya jumped to the third step before the first, mumbled through the pivot joint, and ended with "so yeah, it basically works," which told the judges nothing. At their last practice, when Hailey had tried to say this, it had come out as "it's kind of confusing," which was the feedback equivalent of patting someone on the head. Priya had smiled, said thanks, and changed nothing. Regionals were in eleven days. Hailey wanted to say something that would actually help, and she was beginning to suspect that wanting it kindly and wanting it usefully were two different hungers.

Her grandmother drifted in from the garden with tomato leaves stuck to her sleeve and read the situation off Hailey's face in about two seconds. "Who are you figuring out how to be honest with?" she asked, which was unfair, like being x-rayed by someone in an apron. Before Hailey could answer, the back door banged again and her cousin Marcus came in, still smelling of the deli where he worked, waving his phone.

"Big news. Diego quit, so Rick offered me his Sunday shift. Time and a half, running the slicer." He did a little dance with a peach in each hand. "Seventeen-year-olds can work unlimited hours, you know. I could basically live there."

"Can you run the slicer, though?" Hailey asked, and then, because the question had a shape she recognized, she pulled out her phone. She typed "16 and 17 year olds work rules slicer" and watched the results assemble themselves. "Wait. Hold on. Marcus. It says there's no limit on hours for sixteen and seventeen-year-olds, that part's true, but the Department of Labor has a list of jobs it's declared hazardous, and minors can't do those. Meat slicers are on it."

Marcus set down the peaches. "That can't be right. Rick says everybody starts on the slicer."

"Rick wants everybody on the slicer," Grandma said mildly, rinsing a tomato.

Hailey scrolled, chasing the thought down the page the way she used to chase frogs in the creek behind this house. Last summer, when she was fifteen, Marcus had dared her to hold a frog and she had lectured him for ten minutes about amphibian skin, and he had listened, actually listened, because she had laid out the facts like stepping stones instead of dropping them on his head like bricks. She remembered that now with a small internal click. "Look," she said, turning the phone toward him, "you can work every hour Rick will give you. What you can't do is the hazardous stuff. The slicer's hazardous. So the shift as offered isn't legal, but that doesn't mean the shift is dead."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning ask Rick what else the shift includes. Prep, register, dishes. Maybe he just means Sunday busy work and you're picturing the slicer because Diego always had it."

Marcus frowned at the phone as if it had personally insulted his paycheck. Grandpa, without looking up from the crossword, said, "Boy who worked the counter before you lost a thumb tip. Ask your Rick about that too." Marcus left to call from the porch, and Hailey sat back down at her laptop feeling, for the first time all week, like a thought had actually finished itself.

She watched Priya's video a third time, and this time she wrote while she watched. Not "it's confusing." Instead: the pivot joint explanation starts at 0:47 and it's the best part, do that first. Instead: you say "it basically works" at the end; tell them the one thing you'd fix if you had another week. She drafted the message twice, deleted the opening apology, deleted the exclamation points, and kept the part where she said the mechanism itself was better than anything at last year's regionals, because that was specific too, and it was true.

Grandma set a glass of lemonade beside her and peered at the screen. "That's kinder than what you said before?"

"It's the same thing," Hailey said, then stopped. "No. It's more specific. The kindness is that she can actually use it." She hovered over send, aware that she was still not sure where the line was, whether the line was even one line, whether Priya would hear it as help or as Hailey deciding she was in charge. There was only one way to find out which version of the truth this was. She pressed send, and out on the porch, Marcus was saying, "No, Rick, all the other stuff, just not the slicer part."

The debate packet landed on Violet's desk with a slap that carried through the last rows of Room 214. Mr. Okafor had typed the resolution across the top in bold: the student council should be reorganized as a parliamentary system, its president chosen by and removable by the council's majority vote. Violet's partner, Devon, slid his packet across the aisle and tapped the margin. "We're affirmative," he said. "Easy win. Popularity contest out, accountability in." Violet had learned not to trust Devon's assessments of ease.

The real problem surfaced at lunch. Nia, the student council president, had spent the fall pushing a policy that let students distribute an independent newspaper in the front hall, and Principal Ames had suspended the paper after one issue lambasted the new dress code in language he called inflammatory. Nia had defended the paper publicly, twice, at assemblies. Now three council members were circulating a petition to remove her, claiming she had "lost the confidence of the council." Violet watched Nia across the cafeteria, eating slowly, keeping her face still. "That's a no-confidence vote," Violet said. "That's literally our debate topic." Devon shrugged. "Coincidence. We're affirmative. Use it."

They met Thursday after school in the library's back corner, where the radiators clanked and the windows fogged from the rain. Devon spread his notes: in a parliamentary system, he said, the head of government emerges from and serves at the pleasure of the legislature; a majority can withdraw support and the leader falls. In a presidential system, the chief executive is elected separately, for a fixed term, and can only be removed through impeachment, which is deliberate and rare. He wanted to argue that the first model kept leaders responsive. "So Nia should fall the moment the votes tip," he said. "That's responsiveness." Violet turned her pen over and over. "Or that's a popularity meter. The principal is the one who should be answerable, and he's not even in the equation."

The mock court was the other half of Friday's government grade. Each pair had to argue whether the school could suspend the paper, and Mr. Okafor required them to read the governing text aloud before choosing sides. Devon picked up the handout and read flatly, "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." He looked up. "That's the First Amendment. Ratified in 1791." He said it like a box being ticked, then went back to his notes on Tinker and school publications, building a case that schools could regulate student speech when it disrupted learning.

Violet stopped writing. She read the sentence again to herself, then aloud, slowly, as if the order of the words mattered: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." "You already read it," Devon said. "Yeah, but you argued from it without hearing it. It says Congress. It doesn't say Principal Ames, and it doesn't say anybody may not abridge speech through pressure, or through a dress code, or through a student council petition." Devon leaned back. "So what, we concede?" "No. We argue the principle and admit the gap. The amendment restrains Congress, ratified in 1791, and everything since has been people fighting over how far it reaches past that one sentence. We can be honest about that and still make our case."

The honesty made Devon uneasy, but Violet pressed him through it. On the walk to the council meeting that evening, the rain gone and the pavement steaming, they drafted the debate position together: parliamentary removal by majority vote makes a leader accountable continuously but vulnerable to faction; presidential impeachment makes removal difficult, which protects independence but can shield a leader from genuine accountability. Violet said the words "I'm not sure which one is better" out loud, and Devon winced, but she kept it in the case. She had stopped being sanguine about easy resolutions; the assignment deserved her actual uncertainty, stated plainly.

The council meeting ran long under the gym's fluorescent glare, folding chairs scraping the varnish. The petitioners moved for a vote on removing Nia. Before the vote, Nia stood and read aloud, from the suspended newspaper's next issue, proofed and printed, the sentence she intended to distribute in the hall regardless of consequence: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." The room went quiet enough that the radiators could be heard ticking. She said the amendment had been ratified in 1791 and that she was not Congress, and neither was anyone sitting there, and that was exactly why the sentence had to be spoken aloud, over and over, by whoever would speak it.

The vote was eight to seven to keep her. Violet found Devon by the doors afterward. "You still think we should argue she's removable at will?" Devon zipped his bag slowly. "I think we argue both and let the judges squirm." Violet laughed once, short, and folded the handout with the amendment on it into her back pocket. Nia was taping the newspaper to the front hall doors, one strip of tape at a time.

The art shack at Camp Wenonah smelled of turpentine and bug spray, and by four o'clock on the last full day, Elijah had spread his portfolio across two picnic tables pushed together, sixteen pieces he'd made over three summers, drying in the heat like evidence at a trial he was losing. He had until the evening showcase to submit his AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio, or rather to submit what he could of it, because the deadline the College Board would not extend was the same deadline the camp bus would not delay, and the cabin wifi reached only as far as the picnic tables, barely.

"You're doing the Selected Works section?" said Priya, dropping onto the bench across from him with her own stack of charcoal drawings. "How many do you need?"

"Five," Elijah said. "And the whole section's only worth forty percent of the score." He said it flatly, the way you report a sentence you've already served.

Priya whistled. "So which five?"

That was the problem. He had a still life with a broken mirror, two self-portraits, a color study of his mother's kitchen, a copy exercise of Hopper's light, and half a dozen others, and no principle for choosing among them beyond liking them, which he distrusted, because liking was how he'd chosen everything so far, including this camp.

The art instructor, a taciturn man named Mr. Okonkwo who mostly painted watercolors of the lake and spoke maybe forty words a day, had left a single book on the table that morning: a monograph of Frida Kahlo, with a sticky note on the self-portrait with thorn necklace and hummingbird. "For the written part," was all he'd said.

Elijah opened it now, mostly to avoid his own work. The hummingbird, black and dead, hung at the throat. The thorns drew a line of blood down the neck and chest. Background leaves pressed forward, flat and crowded, closing in, while the face stayed perfectly still, composed, almost serene. He'd seen the painting before, in a textbook, and had done the thing he suspected everyone did: felt something large and vague and moved on. But the written portion of his portfolio asked for analysis, not feeling, and he didn't know the difference yet, or whether there was one.

"She looks calm and it's a lie," Priya said, leaning over.

"Or she looks calm and it's the truest thing in it," Elijah said. He turned the page and back. The leaves were the same green as the parrot in the background foliage, almost the same green as her shawl wasn't. The blood was red, precise, small. Nothing in the painting was accidental; every color had been placed, which meant every color could be discussed. "Look at the composition. Everything pushes in on her. The animals, the plants. But she's the vertical. She holds."

"Is that analysis or is that you liking it?"

He didn't answer, because the question was a good one. He took out the notebook where he'd been drafting his portfolio statement and started writing instead: the saturated greens compress the space; the hummingbird, a symbol of fallen warriors in Aztec tradition, hangs dead at the throat like a pendant; the symmetry of the face against the asymmetry of the blood. He wrote fast, and the sentences came out more certain than he felt, which bothered him, and then didn't, because he was running out of afternoon.
