If she didn't test into the calculus section, she couldn't take the astronomy elective in spring, and astronomy was the only thing she had ever wanted unambiguously, stars being the one subject that had never lied to her.

"Expand it," Theo said. "Then tell me what you have."

"A polynomial. Twenty x minus two x squared." She looked at it. Somewhere under the toddler noise, a thought surfaced: the derivative of a polynomial is easy, it's just bringing the power down. She brought the power down. Twenty minus four x. She set it equal to zero, and it fell apart in her hands, x equals five, area one hundred, and she sat back as if the table had stopped wobbling.

"A square," Theo said, tapping her answer. "The best rectangle is always a square. The universe is lazy and fair at the same time."

"That's not fair, that's just pretty."

The sweetness of it reminded her of something, and she was gone from the room for a second. Her grandmother's kitchen, two summers ago, graph paper taped to the table, a pot of tea going cold. Gran had drawn a curve, smooth and steepening, and told her to count the squares under it from zero to one. Sienna had counted and counted, shading little strata of half-squares and quarter-squares like layers of a cake, and got something close to a third but never exactly, and Gran had laughed and said the answer was exactly a third, that a whole branch of mathematics existed to prove what a girl with a pencil could only approach. Sienna had thought that was the saddest thing she'd ever heard, all that machinery for a number she could almost see.

"Hello," Theo said, waving a hand. "You left."

"Sorry. My grandmother used to make me count squares." She pulled a fresh sheet toward herself and drew the curve, y equals x squared, from zero to one, quick and sure. "We counted the area under this with graph paper. It comes out to one third exactly, she said, but you can't get there by counting. You can only get close."

"Sounds like a wise woman."

"She cheats at cards, but yes." Sienna shaded under her curve in light strokes, the shaded region narrowing to a point at the top of the parabola. There was something here she couldn't quite say, and she tried anyway. "It's like, today I found a maximum by climbing down a slope that the function itself couldn't see. And Gran's one third is the same thing from the other direction. The curve knows things. It's just not telling."

"The curve is keeping secrets from you personally," Theo said, capping and uncapping his marker, which was as close as he got to enthusiasm.

"Don't mock me before I finish mocking myself." But she was still looking at the shaded region, because there was a question underneath the question, and it was this: if the exact answer was always inside the picture, patient, waiting for the right tool, did that mean the counting had been pointless, or did it mean the counting was the reason she believed the answer at all? She could do the procedure now. She was less sure she understood what the procedure knew.

The dinosaur on Theo's lanyard spun once on its clip. "Do problem thirteen," he said. "It's about a rain gutter, and it's even more of a liar than problem twelve."

"A gutter." She squared the paper. "Fine. Slander it with me."

Jasmine spread the printout of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas" on the picnic table and weighed its corners with river stones from the flowerbed, because the August wind kept lifting the paper like something trying to escape. Her laptop sat open beside it, cursor blinking in a document titled Final Draft (2), which was a lie, since it was her fifth draft and the essay was due at eight the next morning.

The assignment had seemed simple a week ago: critique the painting using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism. She had chosen Kahlo herself, feeling clever about it, and now every sentence she wrote sounded like a museum pamphlet. The blue dress suggests sadness. The heart suggests pain. She read her last paragraph back and heard her own voice flatline.

Her little brother Danny came out through the screen door with a popsicle and no shirt, as usual, and draped himself across the hammock. "You're still doing that?"

"I'm stuck."

"You wrote stuff. I saw you writing stuff at dinner."

"I wrote stuff that's wrong." She turned the laptop so he could see the comment her professor had left in the margin, three sentences of red: You keep calling Kahlo "the artist" at arm's length, as though you're describing a stranger's work from across a room. Who is speaking in this essay? Jasmine hadn't answered, because she didn't know. She had been taught never to say I in a school paper, and the habit felt sedimentary, layer upon layer of teachers circling it in red the way this one was circling its absence.

Danny licked his popsicle and studied the painting over her shoulder. "Why are there two of her?"

"That's part of what I have to figure out." And that was the actual problem, she admitted to herself as Danny swung his feet. The left Frida wore European dress, the right Frida traditional Tehuana dress; the two hearts were joined by a single vein, and the European Frida's heart had been cut, the vein dripping onto her white skirt. Two selves, one bleeding out. She could see all of that. She just couldn't seem to say it as though she were the one seeing it.

She typed a sentence, deleted it, and then, out of desperation more than inspiration, opened her search history to the museum page she'd skimmed for facts. Scrolling past it this time, she stopped at a section she'd skipped before, small print under a heading she now read twice: Artist's Statement. Below the heading was Kahlo's own voice, first person, explaining why she painted, what she intended, the context she worked in. Jasmine read the little explanatory line beneath the heading, the kind of gloss museums put for visitors like her: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.

First person. Ideas, methods, context. She sat with that for a moment, the wind moving the stones slightly on the paper. The statement wasn't a confession or a press release; it was the artist saying I about her own choices, and maybe a critique could stand on the same ground. Not I feel sad looking at this, which was what she'd been afraid of, but I see Kahlo dividing her own body across the canvas and connecting the halves with a vein, and I think the composition argues that the two selves survive only in symbiosis, each keeping the other's heart beating. She was reaching with that last word, she knew. She underlined it in her notebook anyway.

"Was Kahlo saying one of them is fake?" Danny asked, squinting at the torn heart.

"Maybe. Or maybe the fake one is the one that's dying, and she's showing us that." Jasmine pulled the laptop closer and cut her first paragraph apart. She wrote: Kahlo splits the canvas between warm tones on the right and colder ones on the left, and the composition makes the viewer's eye travel the vein like a road between two countries. She stopped, read it aloud quietly, and heard, for the first time in five drafts, a person talking. It didn't exhilarate her the way finishing usually did; it was quieter than that, more like setting down something heavy she hadn't noticed carrying.

She kept writing until the light went amber and Danny went inside and the stones looked like dark heads bowed over the table. Some things stayed unresolved, and she let them. She couldn't prove what the hummingbird meant, whether it stood for freedom or for the weight of hovering, and she wrote that uncertainty straight into the essay: The symbol resists a single reading, and that resistance may be the point. Her professor might hate it. She left it in.

At full dark she read the whole draft once through by the light of the laptop screen, the painting beside her flattened into greys, all its colour stripped away, just composition remaining: the two figures, the joined hands, the small cancelled heart. She wrote one more sentence, saved the file, and closed the lid. Then she picked up the river stones one at a time and carried them back to the flowerbed, setting each one down where it had been.

The community garden had a bulletin board held together by binder clips and optimism, and in June it announced the first annual Interfaith Garden Science Fair, entries due by August. Noemie had signed her name mostly because thesignup sheet had a blank line and she disliked blank lines. Her grandmother, who had pushed for the plot of tomatoes in the first place, asked her what she would enter. "Something about mitochondria," Noemie said, and her grandmother nodded as though this were a reasonable crop.

The trouble was that Noemie's relationship with biology was a truce, not an alliance. She had passed the exam on cellular respiration by memorizing a route she could recite but not inhabit: glucose in, a little ATP up front, then the long haul through the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, the mitochondria churning out the rest. It had felt like directions to a city she had never visited. The garden, she thought, might be a way to visit it. She wanted, though she would not have said this aloud even to the tomatoes, to actually understand it before she had to stand at a folding table in August and pretend she did.

Her grandmother's plot sat between a bed of collards tended by Mr. Okafor, who had opinions about soil pH, and a patch of artichokes belonging to a woman everyone called Professor Danzig, though nobody could confirm the title. The garden itself was a cosmopolitan place by any standard, which Noemie appreciated in the abstract and occasionally resented in the particular, since everyone felt entitled to comment on her tomatoes. She had learned to titrate attention the way Mr. Okafor titrated lime into his beds: a little at a time, checking for a change.

For the fair she built a walking tour. Stakes in the ground marked glucose at the gate, glycolysis along the gravel path, the Krebs cycle curling around the compost bin, and the mitochondria, represented by an old washtub, at the center of the plot. Visitors would walk the path and end at the tub holding thirty-odd pennies, each penny an ATP, which was the point she kept losing: not the pennies themselves but how the cell squeezed them out of sugar and air. She walked the route every evening after watering, saying it under her breath, and the neighbors got used to a girl muttering about electron carriers while she weeded.

Professor Danzig's contribution to the fair was a decoding puzzle, laid out on a card table under the artichokes: a strip of paper printed with the letters A, U, G, C, and a chart of codons. "Figure out what it says," she told anyone who paused. "It's a message in the cell's own language." Noemie, taking a break from muttering, picked it up. She found the beginning of the strip where it looked tidy, lined up the codons, and got methionine, then isoleucine, then a nonsense tangle that produced amino acids in an order that spelled nothing, no protein a cell would recognize. She assumed the puzzle was broken and told Professor Danzig so, with some satisfaction.

Professor Danzig looked at her over her glasses and said, "You started in the wrong place. Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine." Noemie went back, ran her finger along the strip until she found an A followed by a U followed by a G, started there, and the message resolved into a short, sensible chain. She felt the specific humiliation of having blamed the puzzle, and then the more interesting feeling underneath it, which was that she had just watched a cell's grammar work. A sequence was meaningless until you began where the cell began.

She sat on the edge of the washtub with the strip in her hand and thought about how much of her truce with biology had been a problem of entrances. She had started respiration at glucose because glucose came first on the page, and the whole thing had stayed a list. Walking it, starting where it started, had made it a place. Both were true, she supposed; the diagram was true and the path was true, and she had spent a year mistaking one for the whole. She could not decide whether that counted as learning something or as having been obtuse for twelve months, and she filed the question under things to think about on the bus to campus in September.

The fair itself, in August, was a modest triumph of folding tables and zucchini. Mr. Okafor demonstrated pH strips. A boy from the mosque down the street explained nitrogen fixation with beans in jars. Noemie walked her route fourteen times, for children, for a skeptical retired chemist, for her grandmother, who took the pennies out of the washtub at the end and counted them as though auditing her. A few people asked questions she could not answer, and she said so, plainly, and found that saying "I don't know, but I know where it starts" sounded better than a bluff.

Professor Danzig came by late, when the tables were folding. She asked Noemie what she had concluded. Noemie considered inventing something quotable about science and gardens and roots, then decided against it. "That you can know the whole sequence and still start reading at the wrong end," she said. "And that it's not the same as not knowing anything. It just feels the same until you find the start codon."

Professor Danzig nodded slowly, the way her grandmother nodded, as though the answer were a crop that had come in late but usable. She pocketed her codon chart, patted the rim of the washtub like the flank of a horse, and said, "Methionine's a funny thing to begin with. Every protein, the same first word." Then she gathered her artichokes and went home through the gate, past the stake marked glucose, into the ordinary evening.

The deadline was Friday, and Luca had eleven days of nothing to show for it. The gallery on Cass Street was showing a survey of self-portraiture that term because his teacher, Ms. Adeyemi, believed you could not build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme until you had stood in front of art long enough to be bored by it, and then interested again. He had requisitioned the corner bench by the south wall, spreading his sketchbook and two pencils across it like a man claiming territory, and had so far produced forty minutes of small cars and an outline of his own left hand.

His friend Priya arrived at noon with a sandwich she split without being asked, which was the kind of thing that made her easy to be around and hard to say no to. "What's your theme," she said, not as a question but as a diagnosis.

"That's the problem. Ms. Adeyemi rejected my first three. She said hands are a subject, not a theme. Then I said isolation, and she said every eighteen-year-old says isolation, and then I said, fine, doors, and she looked at me like I'd brought her a dead bird."

"Maybe you should bring her a dead bird," Priya said, and stood up. "Come on. She said bored first, interested after. You're only at bored."

The Kahlo self-portrait hung in the third room, and Priya planted herself in front of it with the air of someone conducting an inventory. "Okay. Monkey on her shoulder. Hummingbird on a thorn necklace. A butterfly, I think, near her hair. And a black cat peeking over her other shoulder like it wants to know what she's writing." She pointed at each one in turn. "What are they all doing there? Is there a key?"

There was a laminated card on the rail beside the painting, and Luca read it while she talked over him, which was their usual arrangement. The cat, the card said, is usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death. He read the line twice, because something about it snagged. "The cat's the bad omen," he said. "It peers over her shoulder. Everything else in the painting is alive and busy and hers, and the cat is just watching, like it's waiting."

"That's morbid."

"It's honest. She put the death in the corner of her own portrait and kept painting herself anyway." He looked at his sketchbook, at the forty minutes of cars and the outlined hand, and felt the idea arrive not as lightning but as permission. "Ten self-portraits. Not faces. Self-portraits with the thing watching from the corner. The cat stays the same in every one and everything around it changes."

"Your theme is a cat?"

"My theme is, I don't know, keeping going while something watches." He said it and immediately heard how it sounded, like a slogan on a mug. Priya was kind enough not to laugh and honest enough not to nod.

They spent the afternoon in the room. Priya, who wanted to study biology and had once described herself, bitterly, as "a failed polymath, decent at everything, spectacular at nothing," argued that the animals had to mean something biological too, that the monkey was her fertility and the hummingbird, suspended on thorns, was freedom caught. Luca argued back that you couldn't diagram a painting like a frog. "It's not germane what the monkey meant to her biographically if what it does in the painting is hold her," he said, and Priya said that was the most useful thing he'd said all day, which he suspected was an insult, and accepted it anyway.

By five o'clock he had filled six pages: himself at his desk with the cat on the bookshelf, himself on the bus with the cat in the window reflection, himself at his grandmother's kitchen table with the cat under the chair where the dog should have been. Some of it was terrible. The bus one looked like an ad for public transit. But two of them, the desk and the kitchen, had something in them that made him keep turning back to the pages, and he knew enough now to trust that turning back.

Ms. Adeyemi's email required the artist's statement by Friday along with sketches of all ten, and Luca sat on the bench after the gallery announced closing, drafting it in the back of the sketchbook. He wrote that the series was about what it was like to make anything while a part of you watched and predicted failure. He wrote that he did not know yet whether the watching thing was fear or grief or just attention, and that he thought the not knowing was part of the subject. He read it over and didn't cross any of it out.

Priya gathered the sandwich wrappers while the guard unlocked the front doors. "Statement done?"

"Done enough. Nine more drawings by Friday."

"That's impossible."

"It's extremely possible," Luca said, zipping his pencil case, and then, more quietly, because the room was almost empty and the cat in the painting was still peering over Kahlo's shoulder the way it had been all afternoon, "It's just going to be a long week." He stood, tucked the sketchbook under his arm, and walked out backwards, looking at the painting until the door swung shut between them.

I am, by my own account, the most honest person on the robotics team, which is why it stung so much when Dev told me I had let everyone down. I've been turning that over all summer, through the last weeks of senior year and into this party at Marisol's house, where her cousin's playlist is too loud and somebody's little brother keeps opening the screen door to let mosquitoes in. The party is for Marisol's eighteenth, and half the team is here, and of course Sami is here too, which is the whole problem, or the whole solution, depending on which version of me you believe.

Here is what I tell people happened: at regionals in March, Sami's wiring harness failed twice during inspection, and I said something, because I always say something. Here is what actually happened: I said nothing either time. I stood by the pit table with my arms crossed and watched her re-solder the same bad joint, and when she looked up at me for confirmation I gave her a thumbs up, because she'd been having a hard month and I didn't want to be the one who made it harder. We missed the alliance picks by one match. Dev, our driver, didn't speak to me on the bus home.

At the party I find him by the cooler, fishing out a cream soda that is definitely not for him since it's Marisol's dad's. "You're still mad," I say, which is a generous framing, as though his anger were an overreaction I've patiently tolerated.

"I'm not mad," Dev says. "I'm done being surprised by you." He cracks the can. "Priya told me you told her the intake arm design was 'fine.' She spent two weeks on it. It wasn't fine, and she told me she would have fixed it in a day if you'd said one specific thing."

One specific thing. That phrase has been following me around like a stray. My sister, who reads management books for fun, an amalgam of ambition and self-help she consumes the way I consume chips, threw one at me in June. She said, "In her 2017 book Radical Candor, Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly." I'd rolled my eyes at the time, some atavistic male reflex against anything with the word "radical" on the cover, but the sentence stayed. It stayed because I recognized myself in its failure, in the gap between its two halves. I had cared personally, fine. I had cared so much it made me useless.

Across the room Sami is teaching Marisol's little brother to juggle with limes, dropping them, laughing, picking them up again. She's not fragile. She never was. I'd decided she was, and then dressed my cowardice up as gentleness, told myself I was being kind when I was really being absent. There's a way of pathologizing other people's hard months, treating sadness like a diagnosis that means they can't hear the truth, and I'd done that to her without ever asking what she actually wanted.

"You should tell her," Dev says, following my eyes. "Not for me. Not for the team, we're all graduating. For you, man, because you're going to be somebody's roommate in August, somebody's lab partner, and they're going to need you to say real things."

I take my drink and cross the room, and it takes approximately forever, maybe eight seconds. Sami catches me mid-approach and grins. "Cole! Marisol said you're going to that engineering program, the big one. You deserve it."

"Thanks. Sami, hey." I put my cup down on the counter so my hands have nothing to hide behind. "At regionals, the wiring harness. I saw the cold joint before inspection, both times, and I didn't tell you because I thought you couldn't handle it that week. That was wrong of me, and it cost us a match, and I'm sorry." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. "If it happens again, tell me to shut up and check the joint."

She's quiet long enough for the playlist to change songs. Then she says, "You watched me solder that thing twice and said nothing?"

"I gave you a thumbs up."

"I know. I thought it looked good because you gave me a thumbs up." She laughs, but it isn't entirely a laugh. "I failed my driving test that month and my grandmother was in the hospital and I still would have rather you just said, Sami, redo the joint, it looks like a cold one. I'm not made of sugar."

I start to apologize again and she waves it off, juggling her three limes, tossing me the fourth. "So how was the party for you," she says, "before you came over here to confess?"

"Honestly? Terrible until about a minute ago."

"Good," she says, and drops all the limes on purpose, and Marisol's little brother cheers like something has been won.

Gavin locked the bathroom door at his grandfather's house, set his phone on the edge of the sink, and faced the mirror. He had eleven minutes before lunch, and on Monday he had to stand in front of his health class and explain three things: what consent actually means, how contraception works, and where a person goes to get tested for infections. Mr. Ruiz had called it a "wellness briefing," which made it sound like a report on stretching, but Gavin knew the room would go quiet the second he said the word condom.

He started with consent, because it was the part everyone assumed they already understood. "Consent isn't the absence of a no," he said to the mirror, watching his own mouth shape the words. "It's the presence of a yes. Freely given, reversible, informed." He had read those words so many times they'd begun to feel like someone else's, and he wondered whether that was how it worked with anything you learned, whether saying a thing over and over gradually handed it from you to the room and back again. His elocution was stiff. He tried again, slower, and this time he heard a version of himself that sounded like he might actually believe what he was saying.

There was a knock. "Gavin? Lunch in ten. Soup and sandwiches." His grandfather's voice came through the door like it was traveling a long way. Gavin opened the medicine cabinet for a drink of water and found, inexplicably, three cans of soup stacked beside the toothpaste. His grandfather stored things wherever there was room, the house having filled up over decades the way a river silts.

Gavin picked up a can. Cream of mushroom, serving size one cup, sodium 890 milligrams. He turned it over, then checked the second can, chicken and rice, 940 milligrams. Somewhere in his health folder, half-memorized for the same presentation, was a fact from the World Health Organization, and now it surfaced with the odd clarity of something finally useful. "Grandpa," he called through the door, "did you know the World Health Organization says adults should eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day? That's less than 5 grams of salt. Two cans of this stuff and you're already most of the way there." There was a pause, then a grunt, then footsteps retreating toward the kitchen, and Gavin stood there holding the can, feeling the strange satisfaction of having caught the world in a small, countable act.

He got back to it. Contraception next: he laid out the options in plain language, condoms, the pill, IUDs, and the one point he wanted to land, that no method was a personality or a promise, just a tool with a failure rate, and that doubling up methods was how careful people actually lived. Then testing: the county clinic on Delmore Street, walk-in hours on Tuesdays, no insurance required, results by phone. He'd called them himself last week, just to be sure the number was real, and the woman who answered had said "Thanks for asking," in a tone that made him feel briefly enfranchised, like a citizen of something he hadn't known he belonged to.

The hard part, he thought, rinsing his hands, wasn't the facts. The facts sat still. The hard part was that his class contained Dana Okafor, who asked sharp questions, and Ty, who joked about everything, and probably someone who had already needed the clinic and never told anyone. How did you say "get tested" in a way that didn't make that person feel seen in a way they hadn't consented to? He tried a sentence aloud, abandoned it, tried another. The mirror gave him nothing back except his own uncertain face, which was at least honest.

There was a second knock. "Soup's on. And Gavin, I checked the label like you said. You want the low-sodium one, it's in the pantry, but your grandmother bought that mushroom kind in 1997 and it's fine, so choose."

Gavin looked at the cans in the cabinet, at his phone with its eleven bullet points, at the door between him and lunch. He could keep rehearsing through the interminable afternoon his grandfather would otherwise fill with stories about the hardware store, or he could go out and eat soup with too much sodium in it and let the presentation arrive on Monday the way most true things arrived, slightly unrehearsed. He pocketed the phone, opened the door, and followed the smell of mushrooms down the hall. At the table he picked up his spoon, looked at the bowl, and said, "So, low sodium. Who came up with that, anyway?"

The walk-in door swung shut behind Oliver and the cold pressed against his neck like a hand. Saturday mornings he arrived at Rocco's before the delivery trucks, and Chef Deshi had decided that this month Oliver would learn what she called the whole arc: plan a week of meals, write one list, shop it once, cook in batches on Sunday. Oliver wanted this for reasons he hadn't said out loud. His mother had started working nights at the hospital, his father was gone until spring, and the refrigerator at home held mustard, half a lemon, and a science of takeout containers. Last week she had fallen asleep with her shoes on at the kitchen table, and Oliver had stood in the doorway holding a bowl of cereal he'd made her, unable to decide whether to wake her.

"Six dinners, two lunches," Chef said, slapping a clipboard down beside a crate of onions. "Braise one thing that improves overnight. Cook a grain that holds. Roast a tray that becomes three different plates." She demonstrated rather than lectured, and Oliver wrote in the margins of his list: chili, then chili over baked potatoes, then chili with cornbread. She watched him portion chicken thighs into labeled bags, and when his knife wandered crooked she adjusted his grip without comment, then quietly cut the last two breasts herself so he could catch up.

The week's plan needed a dessert, because Wednesday was his mother's birthday and she would be awake for it only between four and six in the afternoon. On his break he drove his own car, the old hatchback, to the restaurant's supplier and bought chocolate: two dark bars for the frosting he'd planned. He set the bars on the passenger seat, went back inside to carry in a produce order, and by the time he returned the car had been sitting in the sun for an hour. The wrappers were slack and warm, and when he peeled one back, the chocolate wore a dull grey film, streaky, white in places, like frost that had grown from the inside. He turned the bar under the fluorescent light of the kitchen doorway, transfixed by the pattern, and felt his whole birthday plan tilt.

Chef Deshi was in the office reconciling invoices when Oliver carried the bars in and laid them on the steel counter. She had seen a hundred teenagers panic over ruined ingredients, and she watched now as he hunched over the chocolate, running a thumbnail along a grey streak. He took out his phone, typed with his thumbs, frowned, typed again. "Fat bloom," he said at last, half to himself. "That dull grey or white streaky film. It's what happens to chocolate that wasn't tempered right, or that melted and reset." He looked up. "My car melted them. So they reset like this." She kept her face still, though she wanted to grin; the supplier stocked a lesser couverture and she'd suspected as much. "So what's your plan," she said, "now that your frosting is grey?"

He stood there a long moment. His first theory, that the bars were spoiled and had to be thrown out, no longer seemed tenable; the websites disagreed about that, and the chocolate smelled like chocolate. He wanted the etiology right before he decided anything, the way Chef talked about diagnosing a broken hollandaise before fixing it. Melted and reset. That was the key phrase. Whatever had gone wrong had happened in his car, in heat, and if heat had done it, then more heat might undo the shape of it, if not the streaks. "I can't frost a cake with it," he said slowly. "But if I melt it all the way into brownies, the streaks don't matter. Nobody sees the surface. It just becomes chocolate."

Chef Deshi nodded once and pulled a sheet pan from the rack. "Bake them here today, take them home Wednesday morning," she said. "And write this down in your plan, because this is the real lesson. A weekly plan isn't a promise the week can't break. It's a net." She measured sugar into a bowl for him, then set the eggs in warm water to take the chill off, small courtesies she performed for every cook and no one ever mentioned.

At home that Sunday, Oliver braised the chili, cooked a pot of barley, roasted squash and onions, and labeled everything with masking tape and a marker. His mother woke at three in the afternoon, padded into the kitchen, and stood in front of the open refrigerator without speaking. Shelf after shelf of containers, dated, stacked, deliberate. "You did all this," she said. He shrugged and told her about the chocolate, about the car and the grey streaks, and she laughed until she had to sit down on a stool.

On Wednesday he baked the brownies at four, while she showered for her night shift, and by the time she was dressed the kitchen smelled like the restaurant's. She took one bite with her coffee and closed her eyes. "Happy birthday to me," she said, and reached for a second piece before her coat was even on.

The article was twelve lines long, in Portuguese, and Sydney had read it four times before her grandmother set a kitchen timer on the table between them. "Five minutes," Vovó said, tapping the timer's red face. "Then you tell me what it says. Out loud, in Portuguese, your own words. No reading to me like a robot."

Sydney had wanted this summer at her grandmother's house in Fall River for reasons she hadn't fully admitted even to herself: the good bread, the hydrangeas, the radio playing fado while Vovó cooked. What she had not wanted was the deal they'd struck before her parents' car pulled away, that she would spend forty minutes a day on Portuguese, her grandmother's language, the one Sydney had only ever absorbed in fragments at holidays. She wanted to know it properly before college, before it was too late to claim something that had always hovered at the edges of her family. But wanting and being able, she was learning, lived in different rooms of the same house.

Reading had gone well all month. She could work through a paragraph with a dictionary, silently, at her own pace. Yesterday she had even read a whole article about rising ferry fares and felt a small, private triumph. So this morning, when Vovó had slid the newspaper across the table, an item about a library losing its funding, Sydney had thought the task would be the same thing with a clock on it.

The timer ticked. She began, "O artigo fala sobre..." and then stopped. The library, she had. The funding, she had, sort of. What she did not have was the verb for what the town council had done, the word for "cuts," the way to say the library would close by autumn. She knew the facts of the article cold. What she couldn't do was say them. It was like reaching for a light switch in a familiar room and finding the wall smooth. "Eu não sei como dizer," she said finally, feeling her face go hot, and pushed the paper away.

"There," Vovó said, not unkindly. She poured more coffee, because she had noticed Sydney's cup was empty, and set it closer to the girl's hand. "Now you know exactly what to look up."

That night Sydney lay on the foldout couch cogitating on the strange satisfaction underneath her embarrassment. In her duffel bag was a book her aunt had given her, a linguistics text bought secondhand for a college course, and she got up and found it, angling the lamp so as not to wake the house. Flipping through, past diagrams and dense paragraphs, she stopped at a page with a heading that named what had happened to her at the kitchen table. Merrill Swain, the book said, had proposed the output hypothesis: that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn. Sydney read the sentence twice. Reading, she had believed all month, was where learning happened. But the gaps had stayed invisible until she opened her mouth.

She tested it, because she distrusted anything that convenient. The next morning she asked Vovó for another article, and this time she didn't just read it first; she tried, out loud, alone in the bathroom mirror, to say what it was about before she looked anything up. The holes announced themselves immediately: "flood," gone; "volunteers," gone; "evacuate," gone, though she could have recognized all three on a page. Her nemesis, she decided, was not vocabulary but the difference between recognizing and producing, and it had been hiding behind her own competence the way a deleterious habit hides behind an otherwise good one, quiet until the moment it costs her something in front of someone.

By the fourth morning they had a routine. Sydney would read the article, attempt a summary aloud, fail in specific places, and then dig for exactly those words while Vovó washed dishes and pretended not to listen. On Friday the article was about a farmer's market expanding, and when the timer went off Sydney said, haltingly but completely, what it was about: the market, the new stalls, the Saturdays through October. Her grammar was crooked in at least two places and she could hear it, and let it stand, and finished anyway.

Vovó dried her hands and sat down across from her. She didn't correct anything. She looked at the newspaper, then at Sydney, and something in her face had gone soft and proud at once.

"Say it again," she said. "I want to hear it twice."

The party was for Dana's seventeenth, and Dana's mother had put out a bowl of punch so large it suggested she expected the whole street. Camille stood near it with her phone in her pocket, not checking it, which took effort, because in her notes app was a video she had watched four times that week. A man in a blazer had stood in front of a whiteboard and said that seven percent of communication was words, thirty-eight percent was tone, and fifty-five percent was your face. Which meant, as far as Camille could tell, that what you actually said barely counted at all. She had an interview on Tuesday for the frame shop on Delancey, her first real interview, and she intended to walk in smiling.

"You look like you're planning something," Dana said, arriving with two cups of punch and giving her one.

"I'm rehearsing a face."

"That's the saddest sentence anyone has said to me all year."

Camille explained the video, gesturing at her own features as though they were a presentation. Words, seven percent. Tone, thirty-eight. Face, fifty-five. "So I'm just going to make eye contact and smile a lot and let the percentages do the work."

Dana's cousin Theo, who was nineteen and home from his first year at college, had drifted over during the explanation, eating chips with the patience of someone waiting for a bus. "Who did the study?" he asked.

"Some guy. Mehrabian, I think."

"Albert Mehrabian," Theo said. "We covered him in psych. Those numbers came from experiments about conveying feelings, and he said himself it doesn't apply to all communication."

Camille felt something in her plan lose structural integrity. "He said that? Where?"

"In basically every clarification anyone's ever asked him for. People quote the numbers like they're a law of physics. They were about feelings, not everything."

She took a long drink of punch to avoid answering immediately. She had spent three days not writing out answers to interview questions, on the theory that words were a rounding error, and now she was standing at a birthday party doing arithmetic in reverse. If the numbers only covered feelings, then the actual content of "why do you want this job" was back on her plate, unrefrigerated, going stale. She tried to ruminate on this quietly, but Dana's other friend Priya had arrived, and Priya worked at the coffee place and had opinions.

"Honestly the words are half of it," Priya said. "My manager rejected a girl because she said 'whatever' about the schedule."

"That's tone," Camille said.

"She said the word 'whatever,' in words."

Across the room, Dana's mother, Mrs. Okonjo, was lighting candles on a secondary cake, for the vegetarians, and calling out that anyone who wanted a job at her new location should talk to her before she got busy. This was directed at nobody and everybody. Camille's mother had mentioned, twice, that Mrs. Okonjo was hiring, in the tone mothers use for things they consider destiny.

Camille set down her cup. "Mrs. Okonjo, could I ask about the job?"

They sat at the far end of the table, between the vegans and the presents. Mrs. Okonjo asked the standard questions, and Camille answered them watching the woman's face, which was impossible to read, a smooth professional mask that gave back nothing, and Camille thought, not for the first time, that any statistic about faces fell apart against a face like this. She caught herself starting to smile her rehearsed smile and let it go. "I'm careful with detail," she said instead, and gave the example of the two weeks she'd spent reorganizing the art room supply closet by medium and then by color, which nobody had asked her to do.

"You did that voluntarily?"

"Our art teacher cried. She's not a detractor of mine, is what I'm saying."

Mrs. Okonjo laughed, a real one, briefly. "Tuesday, four o'clock. Bring the closet story."

On the walk home, Camille thought about what remained uncertain, which was most of it. She didn't know what the smile had contributed, or whether the closet story had carried the day, or whether Tuesday would need a different Camille entirely. She only knew that the words had mattered, that the face had probably mattered some, and that nobody had ever run an experiment on a frame shop on Delancey. She took out her phone, opened her notes, and typed "why do you want this job," then, after a pause, "in actual words."

She was still typing when the streetlight came on.

Raphael spread his homework across his grandfather's kitchen table, which smelled faintly of cedar and decades of coffee. The problem was a polynomial, some expression in x with a coefficient he kept dropping, and beneath it the instruction: find the derivative, then locate the maximum. His grandfather, Louis, set down two mugs and looked at the page the way he looked at a faulty fence, with a patience that implied the fault was temporary.

"Exam in August," Raphael said. "Placement. If I do well I skip first-semester calculus." He did not add that Nadia had texted him at midnight, her message still glowing in his phone: "i know you said the summer was for your grandfather. i'm not asking you to come home early. i'm asking you to admit you're hiding." He had typed three replies and deleted each one, because each one was true in a way that made him flinch, and he had chosen instead to photograph the lake and send nothing.

Louis did not proselytize about work the way some grandparents did, but he held convictions about attention. He believed a boy could learn anything if he sat still long enough in the right room. He believed this room, facing the boreal treeline with its wall of black spruce, was the right one. He pulled a chair beside Raphael and read the problem over his shoulder without touching the paper.

"What is a derivative, to you?" Louis asked. "Before the rule."

"A slope," Raphael said. "How fast something changes." He wrote it out anyway, the mechanical descent of the exponent, the x cubed becoming three x squared, because the mechanical part was what he trusted. The maximum, when he set the derivative to zero and solved, came out to x equals four, and he sat back as though the number were a fish he had landed.

"Good. Now tell me why you believe it's a maximum and not a minimum." Louis was peeling an apple in one unbroken ribbon, the knife moving without his eyes. Raphael looked again. The parabola of the derivative opened upward, which meant the zero was a low point, not a high one. He had answered the question before understanding it, a habit he recognized from elsewhere in his life, and he crossed out his conclusion without being told to.

The next morning Louis needed to drive to the mill office, forty minutes along the gravel road, and Raphael went along with his notebook. At Louis's suggestion, one Raphael suspected was not entirely spontaneous, he read the speedometer every minute and wrote the number down. Sixty, fifty-eight, fifty-five where the road dipped past the creek, back up to sixty-two on the straight stretch. By the time they reached the office he had a column of thirty-some velocities, and the ride had felt, from inside it, like nothing at all, just gravel and dust and Louis humming something in French.

That evening he graphed the numbers, velocity against time, and connected the dots into a ragged rising and falling line. He had learned areas in school, rectangles under curves, and he sat with his pencil making bars until the page looked like a piano. When he added them up, each minute's height multiplied by its one-minute width, he got a distance. He checked it against the odometer, which Louis had read aloud at both ends of the trip, and his estimate was within a few hundred metres of the truth. He felt something shift in him that he did not have a word for, the sense that a whole scattered hour of changing speeds could be captured and summed.

"Displacement," Louis said, tasting the word the way he tasted wine. "That is what you found. The area under the velocity-time graph." He said it as a man confirms a rumor he has long believed, not as a lesson. He had gone only to the eighth grade in a school whose roof leaked, and he had learned this idea hauling logs, counting loads, knowing in his hands how the day's throughput of wood depended on speeds and times he never wrote down. Raphael looked at his grandfather differently for a moment, then looked again at the page, where the sum of all those narrow rectangles stood beside its number.

It occurred to him, taping the graph into his notebook, that the derivative and this adding-up were facing in opposite directions, one unrolling a function into its changes and the other rolling the changes back into a total, and he could not yet prove this or even state it cleanly. He wrote it in the margin as a question and left it there, honest about its roughness. He thought about Nadia's message again, about how he had spent the summer believing he was doing one thing, keeping a vigil at his grandfather's table, when the numbers suggested he might be doing another. A derivative, he thought, tells you where you are rising or falling, but it does not tell you which you chose.

He finally answered her that night, typing slowly: "You're right that I'm hiding. But I'm also here, and the here is real. The maximum of this summer might be behind me or ahead of me, and I genuinely can't tell. I found the derivative of a cubic today and got it wrong first." He pressed send before he could revise it into something safer, and the reply came before he slept: "come home when the box is a box, not before." He read it four times, uncertain whether it was forgiveness or a test, and decided it was probably both, and that this was allowed.

On the last morning, Louis drove him to the bus stop, and Raphael read the speedometer every minute out of habit, the numbers rising to seventy on the last straight stretch where the spruce opened onto the lake. At the stop, Louis reached over and turned off the ignition, then pointed at the dashboard. "Eighty-one thousand, two hundred and six kilometres," he said. "I put on forty since yesterday, driving you to the mill office and back twice." Raphael looked at the odometer, then at his notebook, then at his grandfather's mild and unhelpful face, and realized the old man had driven the same route an extra time, alone, purely so the number would not match, purely so the boy would have to decide whether to trust his own graph. Raphael laughed, zipped the notebook into his bag, and stepped up into the bus.

Jason's grandfather had a Nova from 1979 with a bench seat and a column shifter, and he let Jason practice in the empty church lot on Saturdays, provided Jason was home by the time the deacons arrived at nine. The lot had one advantage over the driving school's course: two faded yellow lines, painted years ago for a basketball hoop that no longer existed, that sat almost exactly a car length apart. Jason used them as his curb. Back in, cut the wheel, watch the mirror, straighten. He clipped the imaginary curb eleven times the first morning.

The test was in three weeks, and the test included parallel parking and a short stretch of Route 9, where traffic came off the overpass at highway speed. His grandfather rode in the passenger seat with a folded newspaper he never opened. "You prevaricate at the merge," he said once, after Jason had slowed to forty and waited for a gap the size of a football field. "You're not deciding. You're stalling while pretending to decide. Signal, pick your hole, commit."

At the house afterward, they drank coffee, his grandfather's thick enough to stand a spoon in, Jason's mostly milk. The kitchen table had a stack of envelopes, and Jason noticed one from the county housing office on top. His grandfather pushed it aside without comment. On the fridge, held by a magnet shaped like a trout, was a page torn from a spiral notebook in his grandfather's square handwriting: a column of rents, a column of hours, a division problem half finished at the bottom.

"Can I look?" Jason asked. His grandfather waved a hand, which was permission the way his generation gave it. The page listed five apartments in the county, their monthly rents, and beneath each one a fraction. At the bottom his grandfather had written 30 percent and circled it, then written the word "burdened" beside it without punctuation, like a note to himself he no longer trusted.

Jason took out his phone and opened the calculator. He typed the rent from the listing on Delancey Street, divided it by what he made at the hardware store in a good month, and got 44. He did the one on Fenwick, the studio behind the laundromat, and got 31. "Grandpa," he said. "Forty-four. That's more than thirty percent of what I make."

"I know what it is," his grandfather said. He poured more coffee, sat down, and tapped the circled figure with one finger. "The Department of Housing and Urban Development calls a household cost-burdened if it spends more than thirty percent of its income on housing. I learned that last spring, when your uncle was looking." He said it flatly, the way he read box scores, and turned the newspaper so the crossword faced Jason. "Four letters. Flightless bird."

Jason filled in emu and kept calculating. The apartment over the hardware store itself came out to 28, and he sat with that number for a while, because 28 was under the line and under the line meant something, apparently, meant not burdened, though the place had a hot plate instead of a stove and a radiator that banged like a dropped wrench all winter. He thought about the driving manual too, which he had been reading on his own since the instructor moved too slowly, an autodidact's approach his mother called stubborn and his grandfather called sensible. The manual said a safe following distance was three seconds, and three seconds at sixty-five was different from three seconds at thirty, the same number meaning different things at different speeds. Thirty percent of one income was not thirty percent of another. He wrote 28 on the notebook page, under his grandfather's division problem, and neither of them said anything about what the margin of two points was worth.

The next Saturday they went to Route 9 at eight, before traffic thickened. Jason signaled a quarter mile out, watched the mirror, and when a pickup passed with a Saturn three lengths behind it he pressed the accelerator and slid into the gap without lifting, without braking, without the petulant little stab of the horn that one driver gave him anyway. His grandfather folded the newspaper. "Better," he said. "That was a decision."

They did parallel parking after, in the church lot, and Jason cleared the faded yellow lines on the first try, wheels within a foot of the imaginary curb, though when he pulled forward to straighten he ended up crooked again and had to back up once more. He sat with the engine running, looking at the lines, at the space between them, at the way the Nova sat in it not quite centered. His grandfather got out, walked around the car once, and knocked twice on the roof.

"You'd pass," he said through the open window. "Question is whether you'd park like that on Delancey, where there's a hydrant and a guy in a wheelchair who watches everything." Jason put the car in reverse and tried it again, slower, and this time the rear tire kissed the line he was using for a curb, and he held the wheel still and felt the car settle, and his grandfather stood by the basketball pole with his hands in his pockets, not saying whether it was better or not.

Austin had wanted the directing slot since sophomore year, when he watched a senior move two chairs three feet apart and turn a dull argument into something unbearable to sit through. Now the slot was his, a one-act about two brothers fighting over their dead mother's record collection, and he stood in the black box theatre with a roll of spike tape and four actors who were all older than he was.

His first instinct was to plan everything. He spent a Sunday night drawing the stage on graph paper, plotting every crossing, every turn, so that by Monday's rehearsal he could hand out the blocking like a subpoena, each actor served with their required movements. Devon, who played the older brother, took one look at the diagram and laughed. "You want me to walk away on that line? That's the line where I finally admit I need him."

"But it looks good," Austin said. "The diagonal. It opens up the stage."

Devon looked at him for a long moment, then walked the diagonal anyway, nonchalant, hands in his pockets, and Austin saw immediately that it was wrong. The admission happened while the actor's body was already leaving. It looked like he didn't care. That night Austin sat with the graph paper and wondered how much of directing was geometry and how much was something the graph paper couldn't hold. Was a stage picture a picture of bodies, or a picture of what the bodies were hiding?

The next rehearsal, Priya, who played the younger brother's girlfriend, asked to try something. She'd rewritten her scene, the one where she tells the younger brother to stop idolizing his dead mother. In Priya's version, nobody said what they meant. The girlfriend talked about the weather in the car, about a parking ticket, about whether they should get food after, and the younger brother answered in the same flat coinage, and the scene ended with both of them still sitting there, saying nothing true.

"It's better this way," Priya said. "Nobody actually says it. In real life nobody says it."

"It's like subtext," Devon said, leaning against the record shelf. "The meaning underneath what they actually say. Anger, love, whatever. The line never names it out loud."

Austin had heard the word in English class, applied to Chekhov, and had filed it under things that belonged to essays. Now he watched Priya and Marcus run the rewritten scene and felt the floor of the play shift under him. When the girlfriend said, "There's a good burrito place on Fifth," her voice caught on the word good, and Marcus went still, and the whole audience-less room understood that she was asking him to stay, and that he understood, and that he would not answer. The graph paper could not have predicted the catch in her voice. Blocking was what you could plan. This was what you had to catch.

So he changed how he worked. Instead of announcing the moves, he asked questions. "Where do you want to be when you lie to him?" he asked Devon, and Devon thought about it, honestly thought, then walked to the record shelf and picked up an album and held it wrong, like a man who had never played a record in his life, holding his mother's thing as if it meant nothing. Austin's chest went tight. He burnedish nothing, arranged nothing; he just said, "Stay there," and wrote it down, and the note in his binder read only: holds it wrong on purpose?

He wasn't sure it would survive an audience. That was the part he couldn't test. Some of the quietest choices might read as nothing from twenty rows back, and some of the loud ones, the slammed doors and upturned chairs, might be the only things that landed. He thought about the senior from sophomore year, the two chairs moved three feet apart, and wondered whether she had known it would work or had simply believed it and been right. Maybe there was no way to know the difference beforehand. Maybe directing was making the bet anyway.

On Thursday his faculty advisor, Ms. Ro, watched a run-through from the back and afterward said only, "Tighter scene changes," and left, which Austin decided to take as a kind of victory.

Friday night, the small audience came. During Priya's burrito line, someone in the third row made a sound, half laugh, half something else. Austin stood at the tech table in the dark with his headset on, watching Devon hold the record wrong under a single blue light, and did not move his hands from the board. He didn't know yet if any of it had worked, only that the sound in the third row had been real, and Devon turned the album over slowly, and read the back of the sleeve, and said his next line to it rather than to Marcus.

The kitchen of the Marlowe had gone quiet after the lunch rush, and Owen stood at the steel counter with a slab of dark chocolate, a thermometer, and the fear that he was about to ruin thirty dollars of couverture. Chef Ruiz, who was taciturn on his best days and had said exactly nine words to Owen since hiring him, had assigned him the weekend bonbons and then walked away, which Owen understood to mean that asking for help would count against him.

He chopped the chocolate into uneven pieces and set two thirds of it in a bowl over the simmering water. His phone lay on the dry shelf beside the peppers, playing a podcast he'd downloaded for his environmental science class, the one assignment he actually cared about. The chocolate began to melt as a voice on the phone said, almost casually, that a UN Environment Programme report had found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, and that about 60 percent of that waste happened in households. Owen wrote the numbers on a scrap of receipt paper because he had a habit of exhuming facts like that later, dragging them up from the bottom of his backpack the night before they were due.

He thought of his mother's refrigerator at home, the drawer of softened carrots, the half-loaf gone fuzzy in its bag. He'd always assumed waste was a restaurant problem, an industry problem, something that happened in the back of places like this one. Apparently it was mostly a kitchen like his mother's. The chocolate reached 118 degrees and he pulled the bowl off the heat, then dumped in the reserved third, the seed, stirring so the cool pieces would drag the temperature down. His chemistry teacher would have called it nucleation. Ruiz would have called it nothing, just watched to see if it snapped.

The phone voice moved on to cocoa farming, and Owen found himself listening with half his attention while the other half followed the thermometer's slow fall. He had wanted this job because of a documentary about pastry chefs, all glossy glazes and composed plating, and because his friend Dara had said, with the air of a sycophant praising a king, that he'd be famous by twenty. He was beginning to suspect the documentary had left things out. What it had not shown was a boy alone at a steel counter, waiting for a number to drop, hoping the dull brown liquid would turn itself into something with a shine.

At 82 degrees the chocolate thickened on him, going pasty, and he panicked and set it back over the water for three seconds too long. The thermometer climbed past 90. Ruiz drifted past the doorway, looked at the bowl, and said nothing at all, which was somehow worse than shouting. Owen stirred and waited, and the temperature settled at 88, the range the internet had promised him, and he dipped the edge of a spatula and let it set on the counter beside the receipt paper with the numbers on it.

While it set, Dara texted him a photo of the school parking lot with the caption "last year of this." Owen looked at it, then at the bowl, then back. He had been telling people for months that he wanted culinary school, that this summer was the first step, that he'd work in a kitchen like this one and then a better one. But standing here he realized he'd been running two ideas side by side without ever letting them touch: the dream of making beautiful things, and the fact he'd just written down about a billion tonnes of food going to waste, most of it in ordinary kitchens, ordinary houses. Chefs made beautiful things out of what people had. His mother threw away carrots.

He didn't know yet what to do with that. Maybe nothing. Maybe culinary school and a good kitchen and, someday, thinking harder about portions and ordering and what people actually ate. He tested the spatula's edge. The chocolate had set firm, and when he bent it, it broke with a sound like a small, clean crack, and the surface caught the overhead light. He held the piece up so Ruiz could see it through the doorway. Ruiz looked at the shine, looked at Owen, and nodded once, then went back to the office.

Owen pocketed the receipt paper with the numbers, 1.05 billion and 60 percent, and lined up the molds. He filled the first one carefully, tapping out the bubbles, listening to the kitchen's refrigerator hum behind him. Somewhere in it were crates of fruit that would be used or not used, and he filed that away with everything else he hadn't solved. He poured the next mold, and the chocolate ran off the spatula in a smooth, glossy ribbon.

Arianna arrived at Priya's house with her phone in her hand, which was how she arrived most places now, and found the dining table commandeered by Priya's laptop, two notebooks, and a tangle of charging cables. Priya's father had claimed the kitchen, so the two of them had settled into the dining room, beside the aquarium in the corner that Priya maintained like a small biome, testing the water every Sunday, trimming the plants with nail scissors. On the wall above it hung a shelf of DVDs that nobody had watched in years, vestigial now that everything streamed, but Priya's mother wouldn't take it down.

"I have a bug I can't find," Priya said, sliding over to make room. "It's for the shop project. I need every customer with no orders, the ones who signed up and never bought anything. I got the list yesterday. Then I added one filter this morning and half of them vanished."

Arianna put her phone face down on the table, a gesture she'd been practicing lately, and pulled her chair closer. The screen showed a query joining customers to orders, and Priya pointed to the last line. "I only added orders.total > 0. I wanted to exclude refunds. But now every customer with zero orders is gone from the results, and they're the entire point of the report."

"Maybe the filter runs before the join?" Arianna said. "Or after? Which order does it go in?"

"I don't know. That's the problem." Priya opened a forum thread she'd found, scrolling past three wrong answers and someone asking about a completely different database. Near the bottom, a reply laid it out plainly, and Priya read it aloud: "In a LEFT JOIN, putting a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total > 0, removes the NULL rows and makes it act like an inner join." She sat back. "So that's it. My filter belongs in the join itself, not down there."

Arianna stared at the sentence for a moment. "So you asked a question that assumed two kinds of customers existed, and then your filter quietly deleted one whole kind before you could see them." Priya was already moving the condition, rerunning the query, watching the missing names reappear, so she didn't answer, but she reached over and squeezed Arianna's wrist without looking up, the way she did when something worked.

Arianna turned her phone over. On it was a video a girl from her school, Dana, had sent to their group chat an hour ago: brown water swallowing a street, a man carrying a dog on his shoulders, text across the top reading THIS IS HAPPENING RIGHT NOW, forty miles from us. She had typed half a message to her mother, who would want to know, who would call her grandmother, who lived in the direction the video claimed the water was moving. "Hey," she said. "Can I borrow your laptop for one second? There's a thing I want to check before I send something." Priya pushed the computer across without a word, still reading her query results, then thought better of it and leaned in, because leaning in was her way of offering company.

Arianna paused the video on a clear frame, the dog's face and a crooked street sign behind it, and searched the image. The results filled the screen slowly, and then all at once. The same footage, posted five years ago by a regional news channel, in a town on a different river in a different part of the country. Below that, reposts. Dozens of reposts, each claiming a new disaster, some with donation links. And the account that had posted it most recently, captioned with a town forty miles from Arianna's grandmother, was one she recognized. She'd followed it for two years. It belonged to Dana.

"She sent it to us like it was breaking news," Arianna said. "It's hers. She runs the account."

Priya looked from the screen to Arianna's face and waited, hands folded now, not touching the keyboard. "So what do you want to do?"

"I don't know yet." Arianna pulled the phone toward her, opened the group chat, and typed, then deleted it, then typed again. The dog's face stared up from the paused frame, patient, five years old, being carried out of a flood that had already ended long before either of them ever saw it. She pasted the link to the original news report underneath Dana's video and pressed send.

The screen in his grandfather's study was older than Owen was, a thick monitor pushed back on a desk crowded with seed catalogs and a magnifying glass. Owen had brought his own laptop, but the study was the quietest room in the house, and he liked the smell of it, pencil shavings and the faint dust of newspapers that had dried out years ago. His assignment was due Sunday night: build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. He had written the class in an hour. The testing was where he had stalled.

He called the class Playlist, because that felt more honest than SongCollection, and gave it a private field called songs, an ArrayList, with methods to add a song and to get the list back. In the test class, in a different file, he wrote the usual things. He created a Playlist, added three songs, printed the size to prove it worked. It printed three. So far so good.

His grandfather came through with a watering can, paused at the door, and read the screen upside down, a habit from decades of insurance work where, he liked to say, he had been a fiduciary for people who trusted him with their savings and expected him to deserve it. "What's private mean in there?" he asked.

"Nobody outside the class can touch it," Owen said. "The field's locked."

"Locked doors," his grandfather said. "I've known a few of those." He went on down the hall with the watering can.

Owen ran the rest of his tests. In the second one, he wanted to prove the field really was protected, so from the test class he fetched the list with the getter, called clear on it, and then checked the playlist's size, expecting three. It printed zero. He sat back. He cleared his own head the way you clear a smudged lens and ran it again. Zero. He added the songs again, got the list, removed one item from it, and the playlist reported two.

He got up and stood at the window, where the garden was doing its slow August work, tomatoes swelling on stakes his grandfather had tied in June. The field was private, he had typed the word himself, and yet code in another file had emptied it as easily as if he had handed over the keys. The problem, he began to suspect, was not the word private but what the getter handed back. It wasn't handing back the list's contents, safe behind their lock. It was handing back a reference, the same reference his own class held. Outside code could change it. He remembered a forum thread he had skimmed and half denigrated at the time as overcautious, something about mutable objects. A list could be changed after you gave it away. Strings couldn't. A list could.

He sat down and tried the fix that seemed obvious only after it had stopped being invisible: in the getter, return a copy instead. He wrote return new ArrayList, passed songs, rebuilt, ran the test. He cleared the returned list, checked the playlist, and it printed three. He removed a song from the returned list; the playlist still had all three. He pushed the laptop back an inch and looked at the two lines that had failed and the one line that now succeeded, wanting to feel finished and finding the feeling wouldn't settle all the way. The copy fixed his test. Whether it was the right choice everywhere, whether some future caller would be annoyed that removing a song through the getter did nothing, was a question he could see the shape of without seeing the bottom of.

His grandfather returned, empty watering can in one hand, and stood beside him again. Owen showed him the failing test and then the passing one, pointing at the getter.

"So the lock was on the door," his grandfather said slowly, "and you were passing things out the window."

"Basically, yes. Now I pass out a photocopy."

"And the real thing stays inside."

"The real thing stays inside," Owen said. He ran the whole test file once more, all green, and saved it. Outside, the garden hose dripped onto the stones, and his grandfather set down the can to watch the last line print.

The clipboard felt heavier than it should have, three pages of Samuel's own handwriting under his thumb. Coach Reyes had given the under-sixteens a week to bring him a training program, their own, with rest days marked in and warm-ups written out minute by minute, and had said he would read every one. Samuel wanted his to be the one taped to the noticeboard by Friday.

He started by watching Dev Okoro. Dev was seventeen, a sprinter the younger boys eulogized in the changing room the way people talk about someone who has already left, even though he was still there, lacing his spikes at the far bench. Dev's warm-up was famous. He would lower himself into a hamstring stretch against the fence and hold it, perfectly still, for what looked like a full minute, sometimes longer, then fold into a quad pull with the same patience, breathing like a man praying. Samuel timed him from the touchline: sixty, seventy seconds per muscle. When Dev stood up he rolled his shoulders once and walked to the blocks as if the race were already his.

"You copy him?" Nnamdi asked, catching Samuel with his phone out, stopwatch running.

"He's the fastest person I've ever met in real life."

Nnamdi shrugged. "My cousin does jumping jacks and high knees. Leg swings. She says stretching long makes you slower."

"That's not stretching, though. That's just moving around."

Samuel wrote Dev's routine into his program anyway, word for word, hold each stretch sixty seconds or more, then wrote hard sessions on six of seven days because Dev trained six days. Rest day: Sunday, in small letters, almost an apology.

Saturday was the time trials. Samuel went through the copied ritual on the sideline before his forty meters, folding into the long holds, one minute, sometimes more, feeling solemn and prepared. At the gun his legs had nothing in them. He ran the distance like a boy carrying luggage, and Nnamdi beat him by three body lengths. The grand build-up, the minute-long ceremony, and then the bathos of jogging in behind everyone else, was almost funny, except that his time was on the whiteboard in permanent marker.

Afterward he sat on the ball bag while the pitch emptied. He watched the under-twelves warm up at the far end, their coach sending them through lunges and skips and leg swings, everything moving, nothing held. Then he watched Dev, who was stretching again, unconnected to any race, taking an almost epicurean pleasure in it, eyes closed, unhurried. It occurred to Samuel that Dev's long holds came after his runs, in the cool-down, and always had. He scrolled back through his video from Tuesday to check, and it was true: the famous stretching was an afterward, not a before.

He rewrote the program that night at the kitchen table. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hard, Thursday off entirely, a whole blank day, which still looked like laziness to him even as he typed it. And for the warm-up he put down eight minutes of dynamic work, jogging to lunges to high knees to leg swings, each one moving, none of it held, and beside the old static section he wrote, cool-down only, sixty seconds per muscle, after.

Nnamdi read it over his shoulder the next morning. "So the long holds belong after?"

"That's what I've got. Held a minute or more, right before you sprint, and you can feel flat in the race itself. Moving stuff before, holding stuff after."

"Where'd you read that?"

"Nowhere. I ran it." Samuel looked at the page. "It might be different for other people. Dev's Dev. I don't actually know why it works, if it works."

Reyes read the program in his office with the door open, pen tapping. He paused at the blank Thursday, then at the two warm-up columns. He did not eulogize it, did not praise it; he circled the rest day and wrote one word, good, then handed the pages back.

"Time trial next Saturday," he said. "Same forty meters. Run it your way and see."

On the touchline that Saturday, Samuel jogged the width of the field, then swung his legs at the fence, forward and back, never stopping in one place. Dev watched him from the bench with mild interest, still folded into his own long, unhurried hold.

"New religion?" Dev called out.

Samuel kept swinging. "After the race," he said. "You can have the old one after."

The trail switchbacked up through pines above the river, and Daniel's uncle Ray walked ahead with the folded house listing jammed in his back pocket, where it had been all morning. Daniel carried the weight of a textbook in his pack that he hadn't opened since June, a geography text with a cracked spine, borrowed from the community college library because his deposit on the fall semester was due in three weeks and he was trying to test out of the intro course. He had told his mother he was hiking to clear his head. He had told himself the same thing, and it was mostly true, except that the chapter he couldn't stop thinking about was the one on population pyramids, the shapes of countries drawn as stacked bars, wide at the bottom or wide at the top, each shape whispering a different future.

"You quiet up there?" Ray called back, slowing so they fell into step. He was fifty-four and walked like a man negotiating with his knees. "You sulking about the house?"

"I'm not sulking." Daniel watched the river through the trees, gray-green and fast from the spring melt. "I'm thinking about the listing."

"The listing's perfect. Three bedrooms, big yard, and it's twenty grand under everything else in that neighborhood." Ray wiped his forehead with the heel of his hand. "The agent says the only catch is paperwork. Some flood zone thing. Hundred-year flood zone, she called it."

They stopped at an overlook where the river bent below them, and Daniel took the listing out of Ray's pocket himself, uninvited, and read the fine print at the bottom of the page while Ray drank from his water bottle and pointed out a hawk. The phrase was there in the disclosure: located within a 100-year flood zone. Daniel had seen a version of it two nights ago, in the textbook's chapter on hazard maps, and something about it had snagged then, too, some phrasing that didn't sit right.

"She said it's safe for a century," Ray said. "One flood in a hundred years. I can live with those odds. My grandfather's house stood eighty years and never took water."

"Wait." Daniel held up a hand, the way his statistics teacher used to, though the teacher had never explained this, had only put the hazard map on the projector and moved on. Daniel sat down on a flat rock and worked it through out loud, because that was how he did it, suturing one idea to the next and testing the seam. "I don't think that's what it means. I read this. It's not one flood every hundred years. It means there's a one percent chance of flooding in any given year."

Ray lowered the water bottle. "Every year? One percent every year?"

"That's what the book said. It doesn't mean you get a hundred years off after a flood." Daniel picked up a pinecone and turned it over. "It's like, the map is drawn from probability, not from a schedule. Nobody's counting. Nobody knows when the last one was." He heard his own uncertainty and let it stand. "I think that's right. I don't know everything about how they draw the zones, but I'm sure about the one percent part."

Ray sat down heavily beside him and was quiet for a while, which was unusual, and Daniel noticed the way his uncle's shoulders dropped, and offered him the last of the trail mix even though he wanted it himself. Below them the river ran high against its banks, brown at the edges where it had chewed the soil.

"Twenty grand under asking," Ray said finally. "That's not a discount, then. That's the price of the risk, spread out over everyone who's looked at it and walked away."

Daniel thought of the pyramids again, the way a wide base of young people meant a country would need schools, and a top-heavy shape meant nursing homes, and how neither reading told you when, only that the need was coming, a probability you could plan for but not schedule. He had been treating the whole subject as abstract, something for exams. It felt different sitting next to a man about to spend his savings. "Maybe," he said. "Or maybe you buy it and carry flood insurance and it never takes water in your lifetime. Both things are true. I can't tell you which one happens."

"You sound like your mother." Ray laughed, but he took out his phone and photographed the listing, zoomed in on the disclosure line. "I'm calling the insurance office Monday. Before I sign anything."

They climbed the last mile in easier conversation, about Daniel's roommate assignment and the hawk, which had come back and was riding the updraft above the ridge. At the trailhead Ray stopped by his truck and put a hand on Daniel's shoulder, brief, the way he did things.

"You still want to test out of that class?"

"I think I might actually take it," Daniel said. He slung his pack into the bed of the truck and got in, and Ray turned the key.

Sophie spread the current map across the flat top of the cooler and weighted its corners with four shells, because the wind at Crane Beach had already flipped it twice. She had sprained her ankle two weeks earlier playing football, and the doctor had said three more days of resting it, so she sat with the leg stretched out and told herself the beach counted as recuperating as long as she did not walk on the sand. This was not entirely true. She had walked from the parking lot on it, and it ached now in a low, persistent way she preferred not to examine.

The map showed the North Atlantic in blues and oranges, arrows thickening along the eastern edge of the United States and swinging northeast toward Europe. Her brother Theo had brought it home from the planetarium where he worked weekends at the front desk, and he had told her one thing before handing it over: the test on Tuesday would ask her to explain how warm water carried north by the Gulf Stream keeps northern Europe milder than other places at the same latitude.
