The original example. Which countries, which goods?" He said England and France, wool and wine, with more confidence than he owned. She demurred, tilting her head, and said, "I think there's Portugal in it somewhere." He had laughed it off, bought the peaches, and gone home, where the itch of it followed him to the bookshelf. The book was in the house, an old fat paperback of Ricardo's, and he found the example printed there in 1817, in a book whose full title took three lines to say, England and Portugal trading cloth and wine. He had been wrong on every count but England. He'd copied the whole thing onto an index card and then, out of some private shame, carried the card in his back pocket for two days.

"I still don't see the connection to inflation," his grandmother said now, brushing crumbs toward the edge of the table.

"Right. The connection," he said, and turned the card over in his pocket. He laid his hands flat on the table. "When the bank raises rates, borrowing costs more, so people and businesses take out fewer loans and spend a bit less, and saving pays a bit more, so money moves slower, and prices stop climbing so fast. It's like the whole economy is a party and the central bank is turning the music down. Nobody leaves. Everybody just stops shouting." He paused. "That might be a terrible analogy."

"It's the first thing you've said that I understood," she said. "Although who decides when the music is too loud?"

"That," Riley admitted, "is the part I actually can't answer. Whether they turn it down too hard and stop the party entirely, or too softly and nobody even notices. My textbook has four different economists disagreeing about it, and the chapter doesn't pick a winner. I have to present on Monday and my honest position is that the mechanism is clear and the timing is a guess."

His grandmother considered this while eating what remained of her cake in small, deliberate bites. "So you'll say that."

"I'll say I'm sure about the direction and unsure about the measure," he said. "Apparently that's allowed."

Izzy came thumping down the stairs with her earbuds around her neck, drawn, as always, by the sound of food. "Are you rehearsing again? Use the Ricardo one, that one's good." She took a corner of his cake without asking. "England and Portugal, cloth and wine, 1817. That book with the title that's longer than the chapter."

Riley stared at her. "How do you know that?"

"I was behind you at the honey stall. The whole conversation." She pointed a fork at him. "You were so confident about France, I almost felt bad for you."

He looked at his grandmother, who was smiling at the ceiling. On Monday, he decided, he would lead with the part he'd gotten wrong, and the card went into the drawer with the pencils. Izzy took the last of the cake and went back upstairs, calling down, "You owe me a peach."

Morgan laid out twelve cones in the grass, six and six, spaced exactly as far apart as the gap between her team's midfielders when they lost the ball. Again. Three times in the last match, a pass had trickled out of bounds because the girls sent it blind, without looking, without checking their shoulders first. She was seventeen and had been made assistant coach of the under-fourteens mostly because she was the only one who volunteered, but she had decided that if she was going to do it, she would do it like it mattered.

Her little brother Eli sat on the porch steps with his economics homework, radiating gloom. "I have to write a paragraph on stagflation," he announced, "and I don't care about the economy, and the economy doesn't care about me."

"Tragic," Morgan said. "Hold this clipboard."

"Who am I, your intern?"

"Yes. Unpaid. Like a real job." She handed him the clipboard anyway, and he held it with the sullen dignity of a boy who had nowhere better to be, which he did not, and knew it.

The first drill she tried was the obvious one: pass, move, receive, pass again, down the line of cones. Eli rolled balls to her and she rolled them back, feet turning, weighting each pass soft enough that a thirteen-year-old could control it. But when she imagined her girls running it, she could see the flaw. They would get good at passing when nobody pressured them, and then Saturday would come and some opposing midfielder would stand exactly where the drill had pretended no one ever stands. She sat down on the grass and thought about her own coach, Mr. Ruiz, who believed in repetition above all things, and about her club coach, Dana, who believed that nothing counted until it was chaotic. For years Morgan had assumed she had to pick one of them, the way you pick a side in a family argument.

Eli's phone buzzed. "Podcast," he said. "It's for my paragraph."

"Speaker," she said, mostly to be annoying, and he turned it up out of laziness. The voice talked about prices and wages for a while, and then, in a segment that had nothing to do with Eli's homework, mentioned a trial done in Norway in 2008, young female soccer players aged thirteen to seventeen, and something called the FIFA 11+ warm-up. Players who did it had about a third fewer injuries overall. Morgan made Eli replay it twice. "A third," she said. "That's like taking three injuries and getting rid of one."

"That's literally what a third means," Eli said. "That's why the word exists."

"Shut up, that's why you exist." But she was writing on the clipboard now, fast. Her girls spent about ninety seconds warming up, jogging in a loose circle, stretching whatever hurt, and then moaning when she asked them to do more. If she had numbers, an actual Norwegian trial with actual thirteen-to-seventeen-year-old girls, that was different from Coach Says So. Teenagers ignored authority but they respected evidence, mostly, when it suited them, which was often enough to be useful.

Here was where the two coaches met in her head, and she felt a small, unreasonably pleasant click: keep the warm-up structured, like Ruiz would, but keep it short and honest, like Dana would, ten minutes, the whole 11+, every session, and let the drills themselves carry the chaos. She redrew the cone drill with a defender added, a chaser who started three steps behind the passer, so the girls had to look up or lose the ball. Pressure built in. Repeats stayed. Both coaches, one practice plan.

Saturday morning, the girls stood in their loose circle, yawning. Priya, the captain, had already objected twice on the group chat.

"We're going to lose ten minutes of actual soccer," Priya said.

"There was a trial in Norway in 2008," Morgan said. "Girls our age, thirteen to seventeen, who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall. A third."

"In Norway," said Nia, "everything works. They have fjords."

"They have fewer injuries," Morgan said. "We have cone drills. Ten minutes."

Priya looked at the cones, then at the sky, weighing ten minutes against a season, and Morgan could see her doing the arithmetic, and could also see that she wasn't finished doing it, that some part of her was holding the number up against her own aching hip from last spring. She didn't say yes. She said, "If it's boring, I'm walking to the fence," and jogged to the front of the line.

"Then you'll be doing burpees by the fence," Morgan called, and Priya flipped her a peace sign without turning around, and the first ball rolled, and Nia's pass skipped straight past the second cone, out of bounds, into the hedge, exactly on schedule.

Lea arrived at the Saturday market before the sun had cleared the rooftops, dragging two crates of strawberry preserves and a folded canopy that refused to cooperate with anyone. She had until noon. At noon, in the air-conditioned office of a community foundation two blocks away, a panel would ask her one question about economics, the discipline she had declared on her scholarship application with more confidence than she actually possessed, and she intended to have an answer that did not sound like the first paragraph of a textbook she had skimmed at two in the morning.

The question, according to a friend who had interviewed last year, was almost always the same. Why does raising interest rates slow inflation? Lea could repeat the words. Prices rise too fast, so the central bank makes borrowing more expensive, so people spend less. But when she said it aloud in her car it had the hollow ring of artifice, a structure she could inhabit without believing in, and she suspected the panel could hear that hollowness the way customers could taste sugar that was hiding something.

She set up her table between a beekeeper and a woman selling alluvial soil, rich black loam bagged from the river bottom, or so the sign claimed. Lea had inherited the preserve stand from her grandmother and run it herself since junior year, which was the entire basis of her application essay: small business, real customers, actual arithmetic. Her brother Marcus, fourteen, arrived twenty minutes later with a clipboard and his headphones around his neck, and slid onto the folding stool behind the cash box without being asked.

Marcus handled the schedule now. He had handled it since April, taking the custom orders by text, telling Lea when the restaurant wanted forty jars of apricot and when the church fair needed her Saturday. He was slower at it than she was. He misread one order in May and they had made thirty jars of the wrong thing, and Lea had spent an evening furious, scrubbing the kitchen, until she did the month's accounts and found they had still earned more than before he started. Every hour she spent answering texts about delivery times was an hour she wasn't cooking, and her cooking, not her scheduling, was what the restaurants paid for. She could type faster and organize better and it still paid to hand it over, because the hour she gave up was worth more than the hour he gave up. She'd written a paragraph about this in her essay, the one thing in it she was sure of, though she couldn't have named it.

At ten the market filled. A man in a linen shirt sampled the blackberry, bought two jars, and asked, idly, whether she worried about prices, since sugar had gone up twice this year. "Everything's gone up," Lea said, and found herself actually thinking about it instead of just agreeing. Her jars cost more to make. Her customers had less to spend. Somewhere, someone had decided that making money more expensive would fix it, and she had never once stopped to ask how that could possibly work.

She worked it out the way she worked out the stand, hands moving, talking to Marcus between customers. If borrowing cost more, she wouldn't take the loan for the bigger kitchen she'd been imagining. If she didn't take it, she wouldn't buy the additional fruit, the additional jars, the part-time help. Multiply her by every stand here, every shop on the street, and the spending slowed, and the people selling to all of them felt it slow, and rising prices without rising spending couldn't keep rising, or at least that was as far as she got before a woman with a stroller wanted to know whether the peach had less sugar than the apricot.

"It's like Marcus," she said to him during a lull, wiping down the tasting spoons. "Everyone doing the thing that costs them least to do, and the whole thing runs cheaper. Except backwards. The bank makes everything cost more so people stop doing so much of it." Marcus looked up from his clipboard. "That's the dumbest economics I've ever heard," he said, not unkindly. "No," Lea said slowly, "I think it's the honest kind. It hurts somebody on purpose because the hurting is supposed to be smaller than the alternative. That's the part I don't know. Who decides that, and whether they're the ones who feel it." The beekeeper, overhearing, laughed and said the answer to that was nobody and everybody, and offered them a damaged jar of honey for a dollar.

At eleven forty she counted the register, signed the clipboard Marcus pushed toward her, and left him the keys with instructions he had heard a hundred times. She walked the two blocks with jam under her nails and the argument suturing itself together in her head, the parts she believed joined now to the part she didn't, and decided she would say both out loud, including where her understanding stopped, because an honest seam was better than a smooth fake. At the office door she checked the time, took a breath, and knocked.

Hannah arrived at the diamond early enough that the dew hadn't burned off the infield grass, and she stood at home plate with her clipboard, waiting for eleven twelve-year-olds who did not yet know she had a plan. The plan was the problem. Coach Ruiz had handed her the passing drills two weeks ago, the same drills he had run for three seasons, and she had watched the girls run them in a flat, dutiful line, tossing the ball the same short distances at the same unhurried pace, and she could not stop thinking that something about it was wrong. Not dangerously wrong. Just quietly, structurally wrong, the way a shoe can fit badly without ever falling off.

She had said as much to her friend Dex on the phone, and he had countered with his father's favorite aphorism, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it," delivered in his father's exact cadence, which Dex could do scarily well. Hannah had pointed out that the team had lost five games in a row, every one of them on throws that sailed or died in the dirt between second and third. It was broke. The question was where.

The girls trickled in, cleats clicking on the concrete lip of the dugout. Marisol came first, as always, glove already oiled and buckled, and behind her the twins arguing about something Hannah couldn't hear, and then Priya, who had made three throwing errors in the last game and hadn't looked at anyone on the field since. Hannah marked attendance and thought about Priya's arm, how it was strong and how it didn't seem to be getting stronger, and how the drills never once asked it to do more than it had already done.

They started with grounders, then passing lines, the same exercise as always: ten feet, partner toss, back and forth. The girls did it competently, the way you brush your teeth. Hannah stood at the foul line watching the ball travel its small, familiar arc, and the wrongness she had felt pressed closer to the front of her mind. She thought of her own winter in the weight room, sophomore year, when she had benched the same weight every session for months and then stood in front of the mirror in March unable to see any difference, and how a senior on the team had laughed at her and said one sentence that had rearranged something in her head. "That's not progressive overload," the senior had said. "You keep adding a little weight, or a little distance, a little intensity, so your body actually has a reason to adapt." Hannah had changed her routine the next week. She had never thought about applying it here, to twelve-year-olds, to a passing drill, until this exact moment on the foul line with the dew gone and the ball still traveling ten feet.

"Bring it in," she called.

The girls gathered, and Hannah crouched in the dirt with her clipboard, drawing two lines farther apart than the old ones, then farther still. She explained it simply: today the passing lines would start at their usual distance, and every few minutes they would step back a pace. Not far. One pace. The throw would get a little harder each time, and they would miss some, and that was the point. Priya looked at the diagram like it was written in a language she had almost learned.

"You're changing the drill," Marisol said. Not a question, and not friendly.

"It's the same drill," Hannah said. "It just grows."

"Coach Ruiz does it the other way."

"I know." Hannah let that sit. She had prepared, the night before, a whole speech about why this was justified, and she had cut it down and cut it down until what remained was almost nothing, the most parsimonious argument she could make: the old drill worked until it stopped working, and the team was losing games on throws it never trained. Marisol held her gaze a beat longer, then jogged to the first cone, and the others followed her, and Hannah understood that she had won something small and might lose something larger later, when Ruiz heard about it.

The drill began at the old distance, easy, ordinary. Then she called the first step back, and the ball had to travel farther, and the girls leaned into it. The second step back, and Priya's throws started to hum. The third step back, and Marisol overthrew her partner twice, swore under her breath in a way Hannah pretended not to hear, and then adjusted, shortened up, found the throw again. At the fourth step back Hannah watched Priya release a ball that crossed the whole gap on a line, no arc, and the girl catching it, the younger twin, had to stab for it and still almost dropped it, and the whole line made a sound, a small collective "oh" that Hannah would have paid to hear again.

But by the fifth step back, the drill began to come apart. Arms were tiring. Throws sailed. The younger twin started flinching before the ball even left the thrower's hand, and Hannah felt the moment stretch and slow, the whole diamond suddenly quiet except for leather smacking palms and missing them. She had pushed too far, or too fast, or both, and she did not know which, and there was no diagram on the clipboard for this. She could beseech her own brain for the right call, and her brain offered nothing.

"Water," she called, and the girls broke apart gasping, and Hannah walked to the fence where Dex sat on the bottom rail, having shown up mid-drill the way he did.

"So you changed it," he said.

"A little. Then too much, I think." She looked at the field, at the cones she had placed by feel rather than by any real knowledge, and admitted the thing she had been circling all afternoon. "I don't know exactly where the line is. Where it stops making them better and starts just making them tired and scared of the ball."

Dex was quiet for a second. "That's a coaching problem, not a drill problem."

She turned that over. It was both, she thought, or it was the same problem seen twice: she had taken the old way, which never asked for more, and the new way, which had asked for too much too soon, and somewhere between them was a version that asked for a little more each practice, at a pace she would have to find by watching, not by decree. She still wasn't sure she could find it. She walked back to the infield.

"Same drill," she called out, moving the cones in, but not all the way back to the start. "From here."

Priya picked up the ball, wiped it on her hip, and set her feet.

The courthouse steps were already warm at nine in the morning, and Kevin climbed them with his notes folded into quarters inside his jacket pocket, where he kept checking that they were still there. He had been assigned to the respondent side of a showcase debate staged in Judge Marín's ceremonial courtroom, part of a civics program that bused in students from three districts. The resolution, printed on the agenda he'd received two weeks ago, was that flag burning should be criminalized. He was arguing for it.

His older sister Priya worked in the county clerk's office on the second floor, and he'd promised to stop by before the session started. She slid a visitor badge across the counter and asked what the debate was about. When he told her, she laughed, not unkindly. "You know that's settled, right?" she said. "There's a case."

"I know there's a case," Kevin said, though at that moment he knew only that there was a case, that his government teacher had circled a citation on his rough draft and written find this in red ink. He had not found it yet. He'd spent his evenings drafting arguments about respect for sacrifice, about cohesion, about deterrence, the idea that a penalty might stop people from doing something that tears at the community. It had seemed axiomatic to him that a nation could delimit its own symbols, could draw a line around the flag and say: not this.

"There's a law library down the hall from my office," Priya said. "Third floor. You've got forty minutes."

The library smelled like old carpet and warm toner. A woman with reading glasses on a chain pointed him to a shelf of fat red volumes, and he ran a finger along the spines until he found the year he needed, 1989, and the name his teacher had circled: Texas v. Johnson. He carried it to a carrel and turned pages, skimming past other cases, until the syllabus appeared and then the first lines of the majority opinion. He read the vote line twice. Five to four. The Court had ruled, five justices to four, that burning the American flag as a political protest was protected symbolic speech.

He sat back. Five to four. He had assumed, without ever having put the assumption into words, that the important cases were unanimous, or near it, that they arrived like laws of physics. This one had passed by a single vote, one person's reasoning standing between the position he'd been hired, in effect, to attack and the position that now controlled the country. In a parliamentary system, he thought, writing nothing, just thinking it, a government that lost by one vote on a matter like this could fall entirely; a vote of no confidence and the prime minister would be out, the whole cabinet dissolved into back benches. Here the ruling stood regardless, insulated, and the only way to change it was to outlast it. He turned that over for a while, the way a head of government is chosen by the confidence of the legislature in one place and by a separate national election in the other, and how removal follows from the choosing. It was the first time the comparison had felt like something he could hold in his hands instead of a diagram from a textbook.

Downstairs, the ceremonial courtroom filled. Judge Marín sat at the bench in her robe but said little; two seniors from the other district took the opposing side, and a girl named Adaeze opened against him with exactly the arguments he had drafted and now no longer trusted. Kevin stood for his rebuttal with his notes still folded in quarters and barely opened them.

"I want to concede something first," he said. "The Supreme Court decided this in 1989. Five to four. Burning the flag as political protest is protected symbolic speech. That's the law, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't." He heard a shuffle in the gallery, someone shifting in a pew-like seat. "So my argument isn't that the Court was lawless. It's that the margin matters. One vote. In a parliament, a one-vote loss on a question this hot could bring down a government, and the people could judge the whole ministry at the next election. Here we wait, sometimes for decades, for one seat to change. I'm asking whether that patience is wisdom or just slowness wearing a robe."

Adaeze was given the last word, and she used it to say that patience and slowness were the same thing when you were the one being asked to be patient. Kevin wanted to answer and could not; the format did not allow it.

Afterward, in the corridor, Judge Marín caught him by the elbow near the water fountain. "You found Johnson yourself?" she asked.

"Third floor," Kevin said. "My sister pointed me to the library."

"Good," she said. "Now tell me the part you left out. Which side would you have voted, if it had been you instead of Brennan?"

Kevin looked past her at the door to the steps, where the morning light had gone hard and white. "I don't know yet," he said. "Ask me again in October."

The music room smelled of valve oil and old radiators, and Maria had claimed the piano bench like territory, two pencils behind one ear and the score of Mozart's K. 545 open on the stand. Her quiz was Thursday. Mr. Okafor had said, cheerfully and without mercy, that anyone who could not find the second theme by Friday would be "musically lost in the woods until December."

The trouble was the woods kept moving. She had taped blank staff paper above the score, ruled it into columns, and labeled the first column Exposition with the confidence of someone drawing a map of a country she had never visited. Somewhere around measure twelve the map stopped agreeing with the territory. She counted bars, and the fourth one came out wrong: three beats where four should have been, a hole in the floor of the phrase.

"Your bar's one beat short," said Thea from the door, holding a grape juice that had already stained two fingers purple. Thea played clarinet and had failed this same quiz last year, which made her either the worst possible tutor or the best one, depending on the hour.

"I know it's short. I don't know why it's short." Maria pointed at the note with her pencil. Thea leaned over her shoulder, gesticulating with the juice box in a way that threatened the score, and tapped the long note at the end of the bar.

"That's half a beat short of what he wrote," Maria said. "No, wait. It's two beats, and then he owes me one more."

"Look at it again."

She looked. There was a dot after the note, small and smug as a freckle, and she had been ignoring it for ten minutes because in her head a dot was decoration. She plunked the note on the piano, held it, and counted. Then she held it longer and counted again, and the bar closed itself like a door. A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so this dotted half note lasted three beats, and three beats plus the quarter note beside it made four, and the bar was whole. She wrote a fat exclamation point in the margin, then crossed it out in case Okafor graded margins.

"You're welcome," said Thea, settling onto the bench beside her with the gravity of a person about to gesticulate a lot.

The Exposition, once the floor stopped having holes in it, turned out to be almost polite. First theme in C, chatty, all scales and curtsies. Second theme in G, quieter, wearing what Maria privately called its traveling clothes. Then a repeat sign, which was Mozart saying, in case you missed it. She drew her double bar line and wrote Development and felt extremely intelligent for about ninety seconds.

The Development was where the woods moved. Mozart took the themes apart the way her brother took apart pens and never reassembled them, fragments drifting through keys she could not name, minor creeping in like weather. Maria listened with her eyes shut, pencil hovering, and marked where the first theme splintered. Then she marked where something new started, and Thea said, "That's not new, that's the first theme in disguise," and Maria said, "Then why does it sound like a stranger?" and they argued about it in whispers, as though Mozart were asleep in the next room.

"He's showing off," Thea said. "The whole development is showing off. It's a contrivance, it's a machine for making you think the music got lost."

"It's not lost. He knows exactly where he's going." Maria rewound the recording, and this time she heard it: the fragments circling, tightening, and then the first theme walking back in, unhurt, in the home key, as though it had merely stepped out for air. Recapitulation, she wrote, and underlined it twice. Second theme came back too, but it stayed in C this time, home instead of traveling, and she drew a small house above it, which she would definitely erase before Thursday.

"See, the map works," Thea said, sucking the last of the juice. "Exposition, development, recapitulation. Lost in the woods, come home."

But Maria was staring at her columns. The second theme in the recapitulation wasn't quite the same as the second theme in the exposition, and she could not decide whether the difference was important or whether she was being intransigent about a detail Mozart had changed the way you change your grip on a pen. She wrote a question mark in the margin and left it there, un-erased, a small admission to future Maria that some things were still open.

"That mark will annoy Okafor," Thea said.

"Good."

Thea laughed, capped her dead juice box, and flicked the Exposition column with one purple finger. Maria played the opening theme once, slowly, with the dotted note held out full and rich, three whole beats, and did not stop at the double bar line.

Claire spread the two folders on her grandmother's dining room table, side by side, the way her coach had shown her. The left folder held her arguments for the petitioner, a student suspended over a banner the school called disruptive; the right folder held the school district's case, which she would argue twenty minutes later in the same round, as the rules of the competition required. Her grandmother's house smelled of coffee and old paper, and the long table, sedimentary with decades of holiday tablecloths pressed one atop another, gave off a faint creak whenever Claire leaned on it.

"You have made an altar to your own confusion," her grandmother said from the kitchen doorway, drying her hands on a towel. Her English still carried the shape of Lyon, though she had lived in Ohio for fifty years.

"It's called arguing both sides," Claire said. "It's the whole point. If you can win with the school's position, you have to be able to win against it too." She pulled the petitioner's folder toward her. "My problem is I believe this side. The kid hung up a dumb banner, and the school freaked out, and now it's at the Supreme Court, or the fake one, anyway."

Her grandmother set down the towel and sat across from her, which was how Claire knew the afternoon had changed shape. Her grandmother did not sit at this table for anything less than a genuine quarrel or a genuine confidence.

"In France," her grandmother said, "when I was a girl, we argued about everything at dinner. Speech, governments. It was a sport." She tapped the table. "Do you know how our republic works, over there?"

"Separate powers," Claire said carefully. "Like ours. President, parliament."

"Partly like yours. The president is elected directly by the people, and he appoints the prime minister." Her grandmother paused, letting the weight settle. "But the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion. The president chooses, and the Assembly can unchoose."

Claire wrote it down in the margin of her folder before she fully understood why. "That's a censure motion," she repeated. "So it's not really separate at all."

"It is not purely one thing or the other. It is a mixture, and the mixture is the point." Her grandmother stood to refill her coffee but kept talking toward the window. "You keep saying you believe one side. When I was seventeen, I believed speech should never be restricted, and I said so at a dinner where a man had lost his brother to certain newspapers, certain slogans. I was right in principle and unbearable in that room."

Claire looked down at her notes. The school district's folder sat there with its tidy arguments about educational mission and disruption, arguments she had assembled with a certain contempt and now regarded differently, the way you regard a person once you have spent an hour defending them.

"That's what I'm scared of," she said. "Not that I'll lose. That I'll argue the school's side and it'll be better than my real side, and I won't know anymore which one I actually believe." She said it to the table, because it was easier than saying it to her grandmother's face.

Her grandmother carried her cup back and moved the school district's folder three inches to the left, squaring it with the table's edge. "Then argue it better. If the school's case wins, let it win honestly. You do not owe your first opinion your loyalty forever. Opinions are not flags planted in the ground." She thought a moment. "The French system taught me that. Everyone wants a constitution to be one clean idea. The subtlety is that it never is. Something in it will always answer to something else, and that answering is not a flaw. It is the design."

Claire turned back to the petitioner's folder and read her opening line silently, the one she had rehearsed in the car, and found she no longer liked its certainty. She crossed out a sentence and wrote a smaller one above it, a concession she had been avoiding all week: the school had a real duty, and the banner had caused a real disruption, and still the suspension could not survive. She had never let the two thoughts sit in the same paragraph before.

"Better," her grandmother said, reading upside down, which she could do and Claire could not.

"It might lose me the round," Claire said.

"It might. Or the judges will believe you precisely because you did not tidy it up first." Her grandmother gathered the coffee cups, then paused with her hand on Claire's chair. "When it is your turn for the school, remember you are not betraying the boy. You are stress-testing his case. If it cannot survive you, it does not deserve to survive the Court."

At the high school gymnasium that had been dressed up as a courtroom, Claire stood at the podium for her first rebuttal and heard herself make the school's strongest argument cleanly, without apology, and watched the judge in the middle lean forward and write something down. Twenty minutes later, standing again for the petitioner, she opened with the concession, and the room went quiet in the particular way rooms do when someone stops performing. She did not know yet whether she had won. The judge's pen was still moving when she said, "And with the Court's permission, I'd like to reserve my last two minutes."

Simon had three days to learn to read a blood pressure number, and his study method so far had been staring at a photocopied chart while eating cheese puffs, which even he could tell was a kind of oxymoron.

"You know the cuff thing squeezes your arm," said Priya, dropping into the seat beside him in the library. "You know the top number is when the heart beats and the bottom is between beats. That's most of it. Now tell me what's too high."

"Too high is, uh." He turned the chart sideways, as though the numbers might behave differently in another orientation. "Priya, my grandfather thinks blood pressure is a mood. He texts me things like 'pressure is good today, ate a lemon.'"

Priya laughed so loudly the librarian materialized, capricious as weather, sometimes merciful, sometimes confiscating an entire bag of chips. They lowered their voices.

"Fine," Priya said. "Quiz me, and then I'll quiz you, and Thursday we will both walk into Ms. Okafor's quiz like professionals."

He read the practice cases aloud. A runner whose numbers were low and steady. A man whose reading had crept up over years. Simon was surprised by how much story lived in two numbers, how the chart was less like math and more like reading a face. "High but he says he feels great," Simon read, and paused. "Wait, that's my grandfather. That's literally his whole file."

"What do you mean?"

"He says he feels fine, so his pressure must be fine. He hasn't measured it in two years because he feels good."

Priya tapped the case sheet. "And what does the case say about the man who feels great?"

Simon read it, then read it again. "It says high blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all." He looked up. "None? That can't be right. Something being wrong and you feeling nothing, that's like the definition of a problem you can't sense."

"There's a name for it in there," Priya said. "Second page."

Simon found it, and something about the phrase made the library feel slightly colder. "They call it the silent killer," he said. "That's why they find it mainly by measuring it. Because otherwise there's nothing to find." He sat back. "That's a terrible name. It's also a completely accurate name. I hate how accurate it is."

He wrote to his grandfather that night, because Grandpa refused phone calls after eight, believing radiation, believing also in the healing power of lemons, holding both positions with total serenity. The text Simon sent was short: "Pop, quiz Thursday. Homework question. If you feel fine, is your blood pressure fine? Answer honestly, this is graded."

The reply came while Simon was brushing his teeth: "Feel excellent. Pressure therefore excellent. Tell teacher I said so. Full marks."

Simon stood in the bathroom holding the phone, foam in his mouth, and understood that he was now the only person in this particular family who knew the thing he knew. That was an odd weight to carry at seventeen. He typed back: "Pop. The whole point is that it doesn't announce itself. It's called the silent killer because it doesn't feel like anything. You measure it or you don't know. Can you measure it? Pharmacy machines are free."

Three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared. "The lemon is not enough?"

"The lemon was never enough. Please. Thursday, when I've passed my quiz, I'll call and walk you through it."

"Fine," his grandfather wrote, which in his dialect meant a negotiation had opened, not closed. "If you pass. If you fail, the lemon theory stands."

Thursday morning, Priya quizzed him on the walk to school, and Simon explained the diet and exercise part the way Ms. Okafor had framed it, not as a punishment but as an adjustment, the way you'd lower a volume that had crept up so slowly nobody in the room had noticed. Regular movement and a plate with less salt and more vegetables could bring the numbers down, could be, over time, the difference between a reading that was fine and one that wasn't. He even used the word atrophy, correctly he hoped, to describe what happened to habits you didn't use, and Priya said, "Show-off," which meant he'd used it correctly.

The quiz had a case study at the end. A man, sixty-eight, no symptoms, no measurement in years, feels wonderful. What should be done and why. Simon wrote for ten minutes, and at the bottom of his answer, where the space ran out, he added a line about how feeling fine proved nothing either way, that only the cuff could tell you, and that a person could be honest and still be wrong about his own body.

That evening he called his grandfather, who answered on the sixth ring, sounding wounded.

"Did you pass?" his grandfather asked.

"Ninety-two. Now sit near the phone. I got a pharmacy three blocks from you. Saturday, ten o'clock, you and me and the machine."

"The machine that strangles my arm?"

"The machine that tells the truth," Simon said. "Bring a lemon if it makes you feel better. But Pop, put your arm in the cuff."

Charlotte would like it recorded, for the sake of her future biographers, that she came into Hartnell's Secondhand Books on a Saturday to buy a birthday present for her mother, and not at all because Theo from her seminar worked the till on Saturdays. Anyone who claims otherwise is a liar and, worse, is probably right. She had been circling the feminist criticism shelf for ten minutes, holding a slim volume she had no intention of buying, when Theo materialized beside her with a stack of returns.

"You're hiding," he said. "You hide by standing very still, like a heron. It doesn't work, by the way."

"I'm browsing. Browsing is a normal activity in a bookshop, which is where we are." She held up the book so he could see she was being academic. The cover said, in assertive yellow letters, Patriarchy and the Plot. "Essay's due Monday. I have to read a chapter of Jane Eyre through a feminist lens and then some other lens, and I keep picking up the books and putting them down like they're hot."

Theo set the returns on the counter and pulled a stool over for her, which she took as an invitation to colonize the space behind the till, which it was. "Which chapter?"

"Ten-ish. The one where Jane gets sent to Lowood and everything is cold." She flipped her paperback open. "For the feminist part I've actually got something. Mr. Brocklehurst starves the girls to keep their souls humble while his own daughters parade through in velvet and feathers. That's practically gift-wrapped for an essay."

"And the second lens?"

"Marxist, which is where it all goes wobbly, because I understand it in theory and then I sit down at my laptop and my brain makes the sound of a kettle that never boils." She said this with dignity, as though it were a common scholarly phenomenon. Theo said it was, in his case, more of a toaster.

She read for a while, chewing a thumbnail, and then something snagged. "Hang on." She pulled a pencil from her bag and started making small tick marks in the margin, which Theo said was vandalism of shop stock, and she said it was her own copy, and he said he knew that, he just liked objecting on principle. "In this chapter the servants are everywhere. Someone carries her trunk, someone opens gates, Bessie cries over her. Let me count. Named servants, and then how many times any of them actually speaks."

She counted twice, because the first time she lost track when Theo asked whether she wanted tea, and losing count over tea felt like a failure of character. Then she counted again, lips moving, which Theo mercifully did not photograph. "So they're named a handful of times, and they speak once. Maybe twice if you count Bessie's goodbye, which I do, because I like her." She sat back. "They do all the carrying and cooking and gate-opening that makes Jane's whole journey possible, and they get about one line between them."

"That's the reading, isn't it?" Theo leaned on the counter. "A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing."

Charlotte looked at him with genuine resentment. "You can't just say the thing. I wanted to say the thing. I was about to say the thing."

"You were about to say something about a kettle."

"It was going to develop into the thing." But she was already writing, fast, in the gap between two paragraphs of her notebook: who carries the trunk, who lights the fires, who is invisible while doing it. Then she stopped, pencil hovering. "Here's what I can't make fit, though. Jane isn't comfortable. Jane's a governess, she's one wage packet above the servants herself. So is it still the same argument, or does the lens bend? And does the feminist part and the Marxist part fight each other, since Brocklehurst's daughters are also trapped in velvet? I keep trying to titrate the two, like there's exactly the right amount of each and I'll know when the mixture goes pink."

"Maybe it doesn't go pink."

"Unhelpful. Genuinely unhelpful." She pulled the feminist book closer anyway and skimmed the index for anything about class, then put it back, because the argument in her notebook had already outrun it. She could hold both ideas, she decided, the way you hold two full cups: carefully, and with a certain acceptance about the carpet. Some of it would stay unresolved, and she wrote that down too, because it felt more honest than pretending she'd solved it, and because, if she was very lucky, the unresolved bit was where the good marks lived.

She packed up at closing, accepted the tea she had never been offered, and left the notebook on the counter by accident, which Theo discovered after she'd gone, and which meant he had to run half a street in the rain to catch her, waving it over his head like a small square flag.

"You forgot your whole brain," he said, dripping.

"Give it here," said Charlotte. "Monday needs me."

The laptop refused to cooperate, and the clock on Grandpa's mantel struck seven with the solid certainty of a clock that had never once cared about anyone's deadlines. Victoria had until midnight to submit the database assignment, and she was spending her evening in a riparian cottage two buses from campus, watching her grandfather's phone screen instead of her own.

"Look at this," Grandpa said, lowering himself into the chair beside her. "From the neighbours. They say the mill race burst this morning and the lower fields are underwater. Karim wants me to post it to the village group before bed, so people move their animals." The video showed brown water sliding over a fence, a shed door flapping, a street she almost recognized. "I don't like it. Something about it doesn't sit right. But I can't say what, and I can't very well accuse a neighbour of machinations without proof."

Victoria had seen something at her mother's office last spring that she hadn't thought about since. A colleague had been checking a clip on his screen and she'd asked what he was doing. "InVID-WeVerify," he'd said, not looking up. She remembered because the name sounded like a plumbing fixture. She had watched him work for a minute before her mother called her away, and what she remembered was a row of images, like film stills, each with search buttons beneath it.

"I might be able to check it," she said. "Wait." She installed the plugin on Grandpa's old browser, chewing the inside of her cheek while it loaded, and when the tab opened she read the small print aloud so they could both hear it. "InVID-WeVerify, a project funded by the European Union." The extension let her drop the video in, and then it did what she remembered: it split the video into key frames, a strip of stills, each one ready to be reverse-searched.

"Those are like fingerprints," she murmured, dragging the first frame, the fence and the flapping door, into the search bar. While it worked, her assignment sat open behind the tab, half a query abandoned on the screen. She'd been at it since four, trying to join a customer table to an orders table and surface the customers who never ordered anything, and every version she wrote either returned everyone or no one. The trick, she was almost sure, was in the join itself, in asking the question from the empty side of it.

The search results came back, and there was the fence. There was the flapping door. The matching page was three years old, from a flood in a river town two valleys over, and the street she'd almost recognized was one she'd seen in a photograph on Grandpa's hallway wall, from a trip before she was born. "It's not our river," she said. "It's an old video wearing our river's clothes."

Grandpa put the phone face down on the table, exhaling through his nose. "So I post nothing. Karim will grumble, but half the village would have been awake all night for nothing." He watched her switch back to the assignment window. "Go on, then. Don't let an old man's flood eat your future."

She went at it differently now. Instead of starting from the customers and asking who had orders, she started from the join itself and let it keep every customer whether or not anything matched, then kept only the rows where the order side came back empty. When she ran it, the result table filled with names, customers with no orders at all, each one surfaced precisely because the other table had nothing to say about them. 11:54 glowed in the corner of the screen. She checked the output twice, attached the file, and pressed submit at 11:58, then sat back with her hands still hovering over the keys, not quite believing the names would still be there when she looked again.

"You look like a woman who won something," Grandpa said.

"Maybe," she said. "Ask me tomorrow." She was already less certain than she sounded; the query was right for tonight's tables, and she had a feeling that the empty side of a join could hide things too, that absence was easier to find than to interpret. She was reaching to close the laptop when his phone buzzed on the table. He squinted at the message and turned it toward her, half laughing. It was the seed catalogue, confirming the twelve packets of sweet peas he had sworn, for weeks, he would never order.

Robert found the tube on Monday morning, propped between two books on the shelf his grandfather still called the chemistry shelf, though nothing else in the house suggested a laboratory. His grandfather had taught chemistry for thirty-one years, and then the stroke had come in March, and now the words arrived late or not at all, like buses in a town Robert had never been to. Robert had a test on Thursday. He was staying the week because his mother thought the company would be good for both of them, and because the apartment was empty otherwise.

The tube was sealed glass, the length of his forearm, and inside it the gas was the brown of old tea. A label in his grandfather's cramped hand read NO2. Robert knew the notation from class. He knew, in the flat way of things memorized the night before, that nitrogen dioxide could run both directions, pairing off into a colorless compound and unpairing again, an equilibrium. Knowing the sentence and having any sense of what it meant were, he was beginning to understand, different projects.

He carried the tube downstairs. His grandfather sat at the kitchen table with the crossword he no longer finished, pencil moving in slow, stubborn circles around one square.

"What's this for?" Robert held the tube up to the window. The brown looked denser at the bottom, though his grandfather had told him once, back when telling was easy, that gases don't settle like that. It was probably the light.

His grandfather looked at it for a long moment. Then he pointed at the kettle.

"Hot?" Robert said.

His grandfather nodded once, a small precise motion, and Robert, who had planned to spend the morning on his phone, felt something shift toward an actual morning. He filled a bowl from the kettle and lowered the sealed tube into the warm water the way he'd lower anything he suspected of being fragile and important at once. The brown deepened, slowly, then unmistakably, like weather coming in over a field. He moved the tube into a bowl of water and ice from the freezer, and the color thinned, faded toward pale, though it never vanished.

He sat with it. Heat made it darker, which meant heat made more of the brown gas, which meant the reaction ran toward the brown side when he added heat, and away from it when he took heat away. The system leaned against whatever he did to it. He checked the impulse to write this down as a rule, because rules were how you equivocated with yourself, deciding a thing was understood when it was only filed. He didn't want to file it. He wanted it in his hands.

His grandfather was watching him. Then he rapped the table twice, pointed at Robert, pointed at the pantry, and made a shape in the air with both hands: a box.

"You want a box?"

His grandfather nodded and mimed pumping something up.

Robert went to the pantry and found a cardboard box from the garage, and a ruler, and he measured it, multiplying out the sides with the pencil from the crossword. It came to about twenty-two litres, close enough, and he stood there doing the arithmetic he half remembered from a Tuesday in September until the shape of it assembled itself. One mole of an ideal gas, at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, would take up about twenty-two point four litres. A mole of gas would fill this box, roughly, if the box were full to the brim and freezing. The whole idea he'd been copying off the board for weeks, that abstract and unphotographable quantity, had a size you could stand next to. He picked the box up and turned it over, looked inside its plain brown emptiness, and felt the fact settle in with the warmth of something discovered rather than delivered.

"Twenty-two point four," he said. "Per mole. At zero Celsius. One atmosphere."

His grandfather's mouth worked. Then, clearly, with effort, like a man lifting something with a bad arm: "Fill it."

They couldn't, of course, not exactly, not with a mole of anything in the kitchen, and not at zero degrees. That was the part Robert refused to paper over. The box was a picture of the fact, an approximation standing in for a truth he couldn't hold. He thought about telling his grandfather this, about the difference between a demonstration and the thing itself, and then decided his grandfather had spent three decades being the kind of man who knew that difference better than anyone alive.

He carried the tube back to the bowl of ice water. The brown had gone faint again, the reaction pressed toward its colorless side, waiting, patient, ready to lean back the other way the moment he warmed it. He kept his hand in the water a moment longer than he needed to.

"When it warms up," he said, "it goes brown again. That's the whole test, isn't it. That's every question they can ask."

His grandfather smiled, picked up the pencil, and drew one slow line through the empty square.

The trail switchbacked up through pines that still smelled of last night's rain, and Luke kept one hand on his phone, scrolling through a search page he had already read three times. His presentation was at nine the next morning. Eighteen minutes long, graded, the first real grade of his first semester, and he had the science down cold except for the part he didn't, which was the part everyone would actually remember.

"I still don't have the station," he said. "I have the scientist. Keeling. I have the institution, sort of, Scripps something, in California. I have the year. But my slides say 'a remote station' and Mr. Farrell wrote 'where?' in the margin of my outline like it was a personal insult."

Beside him, Marisol stepped over a root without looking up from her granola bar. "So look it up."

"I've been looking it up. The internet has decided I need a summary of the entire Industrial Revolution instead." He pocketed the phone, then took it out again. The deadline had a way of reaching him even through granite and pine litter, a subterranean hum under the nicer sounds of the afternoon.

They had planned this hike weeks ago, before the assignment existed, and Luke had refused to cancel it on the grounds that a person could think while walking. Marisol had agreed on the grounds that she wanted to see whether that was true. Now she said, "Explain it to me. The greenhouse thing. You're always saying if you can explain it to me, you can explain it to anyone."

"I said that about my Spanish oral."

"Transferable skill. Go."

He waited until the trail leveled and he could gesture without falling. "Okay. Sunlight comes in, that's visible light, it warms the ground, the ground sends heat back up as infrared. Certain gases let the sunlight through but catch some of the outgoing heat. More of those gases, more heat caught. That's the whole engine of it. The trick in the presentation is the graph, because the graph is the receipt. It shows carbon dioxide climbing, decade after decade, this sawtooth line going up and up, and you can't argue with a line."

"You can argue with anything," Marisol said. "People argue with the moon landing."

The trail bent around an outcrop, and below them the valley opened, hazy, the town a smear of roofs. Luke stopped and pulled up the graph itself, the one he'd printed and taped inside his notebook, the one whose station he could not name. The sawtooth was there, the little annual rise and fall, and over it all the long climb. He had learned to read it the way you learn to read anything: first the shape, then the axes, then what the shape was doing to you.

"You know what the sawtooth is?" Marisol asked, leaning in.

"Seasons. Plants breathing." He turned the notebook sideways as if that would help. "That's not my problem. My problem is I'm going to stand up there and say this line comes from some mountain somewhere and someone's going to ask which one, and I'll say I don't know, and that'll be the moment the whole thing collapses. It'll look like a veneer. Like I found the picture on some blog and never asked where it came from."

Marisol took the notebook from him and looked at it longer than she'd looked at anything all day. "There's a name in the corner. Tiny. Is that a K?"

He took it back and held it at the angle where the light caught the gloss of the tape. It was a name, partly smeared, and the full phrase was almost certainly there in the original file if he could find the original file. He sat down on the outcrop, opened the search again, and this time typed the half-legible word first, before anything else. The results came back in a rush. Charles David Keeling, of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, who had begun regular carbon dioxide measurements in March 1958, on Mauna Loa, Hawaii. A volcano, of all things, chosen for its clean air. And the graph, which Luke had been staring at for a week without knowing it had a name people actually used.

"It's called the Keeling Curve," he said.

"Named after him?"

"Named after him. Keeling Curve. It sounds like a road in Scotland." He copied the words into his notes, all of it, station and date and the full institution, then read the sentence back twice to make sure he had it exactly. The hum under the afternoon went quiet. He could already see slide eleven, the sawtooth line with Mauna Loa printed underneath in the small confident font of things verified.

Marisol offered him the last piece of the granola bar, which was mostly oats and pretense. He took it anyway. They stood at the overlook a while longer, the town going gold at its edges, and she said, "So tomorrow you're going to explain to thirty tired people how the air holds heat."

"Eighteen minutes."

"You're going to point at a line on a screen and tell them it started on a volcano in 1958 and never stopped." She shouldered her pack. "Better you than me. Race you to the creek."

The video arrived at 9:40 on a Tuesday morning, while Liam was still sweeping the glass crumbs out of the back workroom of Ferreira's Phone Repair. His cousin Dree had sent it to the family thread and then to him directly, twice, which meant she wanted something. He watched it standing between the shelving of cracked-screen donors and the heat gun: a grainy clip of a man in a parking lot yanking a phone out of a woman's hand, then running. Text over the top said it had happened at the Milford Plaza lot, two streets from the shop. Dree's message read, This is literally by us, share it, everyone needs to know.

Liam had worked at the shop for six weeks, long enough to have replaced eleven screens, two batteries, and one charging port that a toddler had filled with raisins. Mr. Ferreira trusted him with the register now, which underpinned a small pride in him, though he hadn't yet earned trust with anything that required judgment. This felt like it might require judgment. The video had forty thousand views already, and Dree was not a careless person, exactly, but she was fast, and speed was contagious. His thumb hovered over the share arrow.

Before he could decide, the bell over the door rang and Mr. Ferreira came in carrying coffee and his ancient laptop, the one he used for the customer database and refused to replace despite its many idiosyncrasies, including a power cord that had to be held at a specific angle. "Liam, I need the list of customers who haven't ordered anything this year," he said, setting the laptop on the counter. "For the mailing. We want them back."

Liam had watched Mr. Ferreira run queries before but never written one himself, and Mr. Ferreira, it turned out, had a dentist appointment in twenty minutes. "You know the file," he said. "Customers in one table, orders in another. Join them. My nephew showed me once." Then he was gone, and Liam was alone with the laptop, the video still open on his phone, and a task he only half understood.

He found the query software and, with the wary concentration of someone defusing something, built a join between the customers table and the orders table. He ran it. A tidy list appeared: every customer, each with their order history attached. He scrolled, feeling competent, and then he scrolled again, slower. Mrs. Okonkwo, who had bought one screen protector in 2021 and nothing since, was not on the list. Neither was the man with the raisin toddler, who had paid cash and never come back. He tried a search inside the results to be sure. Gone, all of them, every customer with no orders at all.

He called Mr. Ferreira's nephew, Deshawn, who answered on the fourth ring with the truculent patience of a college sophomore interrupted during something. "It's an INNER JOIN," Deshawn said, around chewing. "That's the default. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely." Liam wrote this down on a receipt slip. "So the people I most want," he said slowly, "the ones with nothing in the orders table, are the exact ones it's erasing." Deshawn said, "Yep," and asked if that was all, because he was eating.

Liam changed the join to the other kind, the one that said LEFT, and ran it again, and there they all were, Mrs. Okonkwo and the raisin man and dozens more, with empty spaces where their orders would have been. He stared at the blank cells for a moment. It bothered him, in a way he couldn't immediately name, that the default setting had quietly decided the missing people didn't count, and that he'd almost mailed a list built on that decision without ever noticing a deletion had occurred.

Then he looked at his phone, still open to the parking lot video, and the two problems touched each other somewhere behind his sternum. He didn't know how to reverse image search, but Mrs. Okonkwo's daughter came in most Thursdays and was, according to Dree, " terminally online." She was due for a charger pickup at eleven. When she arrived, Liam asked, feeling his ears go warm, whether there was a way to find out where a video actually came from. "Reverse image search," she said, like it was obvious. "Screenshot a frame, drop it in. Takes ten seconds." She did it for him, right there on her own phone, tapping through the frames until she found one clear enough.

The oldest result was from three years ago, from a city four hundred miles away, attached to a local news story about a phone theft outside a different plaza entirely. Somebody had re-uploaded the clip, written new text over it, and given it a new parking lot. Liam sat with that for a second, the way he'd sat with the empty cells in the spreadsheet. In both cases the missing thing had been invisible until he'd gone looking, and in both cases the default, the easy path, the INNER JOIN of ordinary scrolling, would have hidden it forever. Though he also knew, honestly, that this wasn't a perfect parallel; a missing customer was a fact of a database, and a viral video was something murkier, a thing with motives behind it, and he couldn't fully see those motives from here. Maybe whoever re-uploaded it wanted clicks. Maybe they wanted Milford Plaza to look dangerous. He couldn't prove which, and he didn't try.

He texted Dree the news link with the three-year-old date and wrote, Not our parking lot, and please don't share it. Then he printed the corrected customer list for Mr. Ferreira, with every zero-order customer restored, and clipped it to the register. When Mr. Ferreira came back from the dentist and read the video story off Liam's phone, holding the cord at its necessary angle, he scrolled the old news article twice and said, "Good," and then, pointing at the printed list with his chin, "Both of those, today. Not bad for a Tuesday." He tapped the screen of the laptop, and the cursor blinked in the query box, waiting for whatever Liam wanted to ask it next.

The laundromat on Delancey had a parking lot with exactly four spaces, two of them always taken by the shop van, and Sara had claimed the remaining corner as her personal driving school. Her mother sat inside behind the window with a paperback, one eye on the dryer and one on the lot, while Sara practiced parallel parking between a traffic cone and a folding chair she had wedged where the curb would be. She was failing at it with a regularity that had begun to feel almost scientific.

"You're crooked again," her mother called through the propped door, not unkindly. "Like a car parking itself sideways out of spite."

Sara got out and looked. The nose of the Honda pointed toward the folding chair at an angle that would have earned her an automatic fail, the kind of angle that made other drivers pity you. She had been turning the wheel the wrong way, she realized, or at the wrong moment, though she could not yet say which. That was the infuriating part: the error was somewhere in the sequence, invisible until it bloomed into crookedness.

She had her reasons for wanting the license by August, and they were not the ones her friends assumed. Not concerts, not freedom in the abstract. Her grandmother's dialysis was Tuesdays and Fridays, and her uncle, who normally drove her, had taken a job in Hartford. Nobody had said the words "you should learn," because nobody in her family said things like that directly; they reified obligation into silences and calendar gaps and the sudden appearance, on the kitchen table, of a practice test booklet. Her mother's maxim, delivered once while folding towels, had been: "We don't ask people to be grateful in this house, we just show up." Sara had found, over the years, that this sounded simpler than it was.

A boy from her school, Marcus, came into the laundromat that afternoon with a garbage bag of laundry and no detergent, having forgotten his, a fact he announced to the room with the cheerfulness of the truly disaffected. He watched Sara from the window while his socks tumbled.

"You're doing it backwards," he said through the screen.

"Thank you, Marcus. Extremely helpful."

"No, I mean the wheel. My sister taught me last summer. You pull up next to the car in front, right, alongside it, and then you back in. You turn the wheel toward the curb first." He mimed it, hands rotating an invisible wheel left. "Then when the car swings into the space, you turn back the other way to straighten out. That's the part you're skipping. You're turning away the whole time, so you just end up diagonal."

Sara sat with that for a second. Toward the curb first, then away. It felt counterintuitive, like being told to lean into a fall, but she had spent forty minutes doing the intuitive thing and it had produced nothing but geometry of shame.

She got back in, pulled forward until she was alongside the folding chair, checked her mirrors, and reversed, turning the wheel toward the curb. When the car had swung partway into the space, she turned the wheel away, and the Honda, obedient for the first time all afternoon, straightened itself against the curb like a sentence ending in a period. She sat there with the engine idling, surprised by how small the correction had been.

"See," Marcus said, mildly.

The highway was the other half of the test, and the harder half for her, though not for the reasons on the checklist. Merging required her to commit: to accelerate down a ramp toward a gap in moving traffic and trust that the gap would hold. Parking, at least, was a negotiation with stationary objects. She thought of her uncle, who had once admitted over Christmas dinner that he had taken the Hartford job partly because he was tired, and she had not known whether to be angry at him for the honesty or grateful for it, and had settled, as usual, on neither. Perhaps commitment was like the wheel: you could not tell, until you were inside the maneuver, whether you had turned too early or too late.

She practiced the merge that evening on Route 9 with her mother in the passenger seat, hands rigid on the armrest. The ramp, the acceleration, the glance over her shoulder, the slide into the lane between a pickup and a bakery van. Her mother exhaled.

"That was fine," her mother said. "That was actually fine."

"Say it like you mean it."

"I mean it like I mean it. Tuesday, you drive your grandmother."

Tuesday was four days away, and the test itself was not until September, which meant one of them would have to sit in the dialysis parking lot for three hours, and Sara understood that this was the family's way of asking her to choose. She signaled, checked her mirror, and eased into the right lane.

The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, but Amelia had not come for the food trucks or the dancers. She had come for the blue tent at the far end, where the Spanish debate table was folded, with a sign-up sheet and a kitchen timer, five minutes per speaker, entirely in Spanish. Her mother had signed the permission slip without reading it carefully, assuming it was the folk-dance workshop. Amelia had not corrected her.

Her topic was whether phones should be allowed in schools, which she had argued twice already in English, once for and once against. Her coach believed in picking a side and holding it until the timer ran out. Her grandmother, who had raised three children without a single device in the house, believed phones were rotting attention spans outright, that the mind would atrophy if you fed it nothing but screens. Amelia had spent two weeks trying to get underneath both positions, writing phrases on index cards at the kitchen table while her grandmother stirred soup and muttered.

She was third on the list. The first speaker, a college boy with a lanyard, spoke fluidly about digital literacy, and the second, a girl from Amelia's own school named Rosa, argued the grandmother's side with real fire. Then came the fourth slot, a boy everyone called Teo, who was visibly nervous and spoke faster as the timer went on. He was describing a school policy, and Amelia caught most of it, until he said, leaning forward, "Los estudiantes se sienten muy embarazados," and the small audience broke into laughter, a ripple of it, and a woman near the front hid her mouth with her hand.

Teo stopped dead. His face went red and he sat down without using his last minute, folding his arms like a child told to wait outside. Amelia leaned toward Rosa, who was still smirking. "What did he say?"

"Embarazado. He meant embarrassed. But embarazada means pregnant. He told everyone the students feel very pregnant."

"That's cruel, kind of," Amelia said, but she wrote it down on the back of an index card, because her own notes had the word in them too, circled twice, and her stomach turned at how close she had come.

The moderator called her name. The woman who had laughed caught Amelia's sleeve as she stood. "False friends," the woman said, tapping Amelia's card without reading it, as if she'd guessed. "Words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning. They get everyone eventually." She let go and turned back to the table.

Amelia stood at the podium and the timer clicked, and she began in Spanish, slower than she had practiced, each sentence placed rather than thrown. She argued that phones in schools were neither poison nor freedom, that her grandmother was right that attention could be lost and her coach was right that banning things taught nothing, that the real question was who taught students to use the tool, and that she did not yet know how schools could do this at scale. She said the last part plainly, "no sé todavía," and noticed that saying it in Spanish made the uncertainty feel less like defeat than like a door left open. She used her final thirty seconds to concede a counterargument she could not answer, because it seemed more honest than pretending.

When the timer buzzed, there was scattered applause and no laughter. Teo was watching her from across the tent, arms still folded, though less tightly now. Rosa came over afterward. "You said you didn't know. In a debate."

"I didn't," Amelia said. "I still don't."

They gave out ribbons at four o'clock, blue ones, and Amelia did not win one; a graduate student with the manner of an aesthete, praising the music of Teo's broken sentence before Teo's own turn, took first place. Amelia found Teo at the empanada stand instead, holding a plate he hadn't touched. She showed him her index card, embarazado crossed out, embarazada written above it, and said, in her careful, slow Spanish, "I almost said it too."

He looked at the card, then at her, and something in his shoulders let go. "Next year," he said, "I'm saying it on purpose. First sentence."

"First sentence," Amelia agreed, and tore the card in half and dropped it in the bin between them.

Vanessa had claimed the economics room for last period, and she stood at the whiteboard with the marker capped in her fist, rehearsing the argument she would have to deliver tomorrow morning. Raise the policy rate, she said to the empty desks, and borrowing costs more, so households and firms spend less, and spending that slows drags on price increases, which is how the central bank gets inflation to ease. She said it three times, and each time it sounded more like something copied from the back of the chapter. What she wanted was to make the class feel the mechanism, to watch it click behind their eyes the way it had finally clicked behind hers at midnight, but the sentence kept coming out flat, a bromide recited at a podium.

Marcus found her there because he had signed up for the same presentation slot and needed somewhere to panic. He dropped into a front-row seat and pulled out a stack of index cards, and when she tested him, asking why higher rates cool prices at all, he gave the textbook line and then ruined it with a joke about his overdraft. He expostulated with the whiteboard itself, as though the supply curve had personally wronged him, and Vanessa laughed, and for a while they traded the argument back and forth, sharpening each other's phrasing until hers was leaner, almost incisive, and she thought the presentation might survive after all.

Mr. Ferrante's rule, announced that morning and still hanging over all of them, was that the question period after each presentation would be unscripted, graded, and random. A name drawn from the attendance tin. Whoever's name came up had to answer a question from the audience about anything in the unit, trade as well as money, and Vanessa had not yet opened the trade chapters. She told herself she would study them that night. She told Marcus the same thing, twice, in a voice that made her sound more certain than she was, and he seemed to accept it, which made the lie easier to keep sitting inside her.

Marcus, on his side, noticed more than he said. He had watched Vanessa skip lunch, had seen the trade chapters still sealed in shrink-wrap when she dug for a calculator, and he assumed she was simply overloaded, the way she got before auditions. What he did not know, what nobody at school knew, was that her mother had spent the evening at the kitchen table with a refinancing letter, running her finger down a column of numbers that had moved against them, and that Vanessa had sat opposite her, mute, recognizing the very mechanism she was supposed to teach. He only knew that when he asked, half-teasing, whether the rate hikes her presentation praised might also be squeezing somebody, she snapped a no that sounded like a yes.

She studied anyway, in the library after dinner, because the tin did not care about refinancing letters. Somewhere past midnight she hit a passage about a country with vast farmland, a place that shipped out grain by the megaton and yet imported every phone and circuit board it used, and the puzzle stopped her. It seemed backwards. Rich land, and it bought its electronics from somewhere else. She read the next paragraph twice, then once more aloud under her breath, and copied the shape of it onto a card.

The next morning Ferrante drew a folded slip from the tin before her presentation had even cooled, and the name he read out was Vanessa's own. A boy in the second row, the one who asked questions to show off, leaned back and delivered his: if a country has all that farmland, why does it export grain and import electronics instead of making the electronics itself?

The room waited. Marcus watched her turn the marker over in her hands once, twice, and he could see the card in her mind, the one copied at midnight, and he could also see something else in her face that he couldn't name. Time stretched. Someone coughed. Ferrante's pen hovered.

"It's about what a country has a lot of," Vanessa said slowly. "Land, labor, capital. That's the Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after two Swedish economists, Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin. It explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of those things. A country with vast farmland is rich in land, so that's where its advantage sits. Grain uses what it has the most of. Electronics need other things it has less of."

The boy nodded as though he had known that all along. Ferrante made a note, and Vanessa sat down, her hands steady now, and found that the two halves of the night had joined somewhere without her permission: the model on the card and the letter on the kitchen table, both true at once, neither canceling the other. She could defend the mechanism. She could not say, yet, whether slowing inflation was worth what it was costing, and tomorrow she would try to say that out loud too, without a card.

After class Marcus caught her at the door. "You went quiet up there. Longer than you had to."

"I was deciding how much of the truth fits in a graded answer."

He hoisted his bag. "And?"

She pushed the door open into the corridor's noise. "I'll tell you at lunch."

The repair shop smelled of solder and lemon wipes, and Mackenzie was behind the counter because Deshawn had called in sick, which meant she handled customers alone until noon. She was eighteen and saving for a laptop before September, and so far the morning had produced one cracked screen, one waterlogged tablet, and a boy named Percy from her old statistics class who came in every Tuesday with his Chromebook and sat by the register doing homework while his mother worked two doors down at the dental office.

Today Percy had his database assignment open, and his report said something wrong. The shop's owner, Mr. Okonkwo, kept a whiteboard behind the counter for tracking repairs, and Percy kept glancing at it like it might help. "It says every customer ordered at least once," he said. "The teacher gave us a sample database. Thirty customers. I got thirty."

Mackenzie looked up from the tray of screws she was sorting. "Every one?"

"Every one." He turned the Chromebook toward her. She saw two tables, Customers and Orders, and a query with LEFT JOIN in it, which she recognized because she'd spent the whole previous week teaching herself SQL from a library book, in preparation for a class she was taking in the fall. "You're counting wrong," she said.

"I'm counting with COUNT," Percy said. "That's the whole point of the function."

She wiped her hands on her jeans and came around the counter. The screen had his query in a plain text editor, and beneath it the result grid with its single number, thirty. She read it twice. He had selected the customer names and counted them, and he had used COUNT with the star, which she remembered from the library book had a specific behavior she had never fully believed until she tested it herself one night at the public library terminal.

"Run it again," she said. "But instead of the star, count the order ID column. The one from the Orders table."

Percy typed it. The number came back twenty-six. He stared at it. He counted the rows by hand on the screen, tapping each name with his finger, and got to four customers whose order column was empty, blank in every row the join had produced.

"They're the same join," Percy said. "I didn't change the join. I only changed what I counted."

"I know," Mackenzie said.

"Then which number is real?"

She pulled a stool over next to his. Behind them the door chimed and a woman came in holding a phone with a spiderweb crack across its face, diaphanous as frost on a window, and Mackenzie took it, wrote a ticket, told her ninety minutes, and came back. She did not sit down yet.
