She picked up the shop's demo tablet and a screen protector and began to suture the two together with the smoothing card, working the bubbles out from the center, because the morning's repairs did not pause for Percy's grade.

"Here's what I think happens," she said, working the card. "When you LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still gets a row. The row just gets filled in with NULLs where the order data would go. The row exists. It's one row."

"So counting rows counts them."

"COUNT with the star counts rows," she said. "So a customer with no orders gets counted once, because of that NULL-filled row. But if you count the order column itself, the column is empty, and you get zero for that customer." She set the tablet down. "That's why your thirty said everyone ordered. And why the twenty-six is the customers who actually did."

Percy looked at the screen for a long time. "So which one did the assignment want?"

"Both, probably. It depends what question you're asking. Do you want to know how many customers exist, or how many ordered?"

"That's not fair. Both questions sound the same out loud."

"They only sound the same until you decide what a customer with nothing counts as." She said it and then heard how it sounded, and Percy laughed, and she let it go. She went back to the counter, rang up a man buying a charging cable, and answered a call about a battery replacement. When she hung up, Percy had written both queries side by side and was running them over and over, thirty, twenty-six, thirty, twenty-six, like checking a door he knew was locked.

"My mom says computers are either right or wrong," he said. "She works at a dentist's office and thinks everything is like that, one answer, like a theocracy where there's a single truth and you just obey it. But this is two true answers that don't match."

Mackenzie finished with the screen protector and held the tablet up to the light to check her work. "Then the assignment is probably asking which truth you meant," she said. "Write down why you picked the one you picked."

Percy closed the Chromebook and stood, and at the door he turned around. "The four who never ordered. Should I feel bad for them?"

She hadn't thought about it. She looked at the ticket rack, at the cracked phone waiting in its sleeve with its promised ninety minutes, and said she didn't know, and Percy pushed through the door into the heat.

Victoria stopped at the third trail marker because the ink on her flashcards had begun to blur, and because the sugar maples were doing that thing in October where the light comes through them like stained glass, and she wanted to memorize something that wasn't glycolysis. Her backpack held a peanut butter sandwich, a half-charged phone, and a biology worksheet due Monday: trace glucose through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, down to ATP in the mitochondria. She had drawn the whole pathway twice at the kitchen table and both times it had come out looking like a subway map drawn by someone who had never ridden a train.

The real problem was Thursday's quiz. She had gotten a 62 on transcription, the lowest grade she had ever received in a science class, and the teacher had circled the same error four times before writing "see me" in red. Victoria had not gone to see her. Instead she had walked out the school doors, past the bus loop, past the impecunious little produce stand where the farmer sold dented apples by the bag, and all the way to the trailhead, because she thought better while moving, and because a person who fails at sitting still has to turn walking into a method.

She recited the pathway aloud as she climbed. Glucose splits in the cytoplasm, two molecules of pyruvate, a shuttle into the mitochondria, the cycle that strips carbons and loads electron carriers, the chain that uses those electrons to pump protons, the protons flooding back through a spinning enzyme to make ATP. She could say it. She could not yet feel it, and she suspected the gap between saying and feeling was exactly the gap between a 62 and an A.

At the overlook she sat on a flat rock and unfolded the worksheet again, and it was there, in the margin, that she found her old quiz, folded into quarters and forgotten. She smoothed it out against her knee. The question had given a stretch of DNA, adenine and guanine and thymine and cytosine in their pairs, and asked her to transcribe it into RNA. She had copied the sequence faithfully, letter for letter, and that was the disaster. Somewhere in her copying, a thymine had kept sneaking in where it did not belong.

The memory of Thursday came back whole. She remembered the classroom smelling like pencil shavings, remembered her friend Dara leaning over from the next desk. "You're writing T again," Dara had whispered. "In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine." Victoria had nodded and then written a T in the very next line, because her hand had its own habits. Adenine pairs with thymine in the DNA, she now understood, and guanine with cytosine; but when the message got copied into RNA, the T became a U, pairing with adenine. It was as if the language changed one letter in translation, and she had spent the whole quiz writing in the wrong alphabet.

She took out her phone and opened the photo of the worksheet. She would contextualize the pathway, she decided, by walking it: glucose at the trailhead, glycolysis at the first bridge, the Krebs cycle at the overlook where she sat, the electron transport chain at the far end where the trail looped back. She walked the loop twice, pointing at ferns and saying the steps to them, and the second time through the sequence stopped feeling like words and started feeling like a route, something her feet could keep.

A man came down the trail with a golden retriever on a green rope leash, and he watched the girl point at a fern and say "and that's where the protons go back through," to nobody, with total seriousness. He had walked this trail every morning for nine years and had seen weepers and joggers and one man who believed the trees were recording him. The girl looked up as he passed. "Sorry," she said. "I'm studying out loud. It works better if the trail has some verisimilitude, like the pathway is actually going somewhere."

"It goes to the parking lot," the man said, and the dog pulled him on.

Victoria laughed, alone again, and took the loop a third time, faster now, reciting the whole sweep from glucose to ATP without stopping, no thymine where a uracil belonged, no gaps. At the far end the trail did curve back toward the lot, toward Monday, toward the desk with the teacher's red pen and the door she had not yet walked through. She stopped where the path forked, one way down to the creek and one way up, and stood there breathing hard with the worksheet crushed warm in her hand. She could go see her teacher Tuesday, or she could keep walking. The creek was loud below her. She turned toward the water.

The math club met on Tuesdays in Room 214, where the radiator clanked like a metronome nobody had asked for, and where Alexis had claimed the seat by the window since September. Today Mr. Ferreira had put a problem on the board that looked, at first glance, like a joke: find the area under the curve of some cubic between zero and four. She had assumed calculus was a semester away, something for college, and now here it was demanding to be understood by Thursday.

"You're integrating," said Priya, sliding into the next seat and immediately stealing Alexis's pretzels, which was their arrangement. "Sort of. Ferreira wants us to see it before he ruins it with notation." Priya's actual want, never quite hidden, was to be the first one in the room to solve anything, and she had already uncapped her green pen like a fencer saluting.

Ferreira had drawn the curve freehand, a lopsided hill rising out of the origin and dropping again somewhere past the middle of the graph. "A company's profit," he said, tapping the hilltop. "Sketch me where it peaks, and I'll show you why the area tells you total earnings." He refused to say more, which was his method, and which Priya had once excoriated in a letter to the school paper as "pedagogical withholding," a phrase Alexis still found funnier than the letter itself.

Alexis drew her own copy. She had spent the weekend on her grandmother's couch helping sort receipts for the little bakery, the one surviving on Fridays and holidays, and a profit curve was not an abstraction to her; it was her grandmother's face in March, doing arithmetic on the back of an envelope and going quiet. She shaded the region under the hill with the side of her pencil, light strokes, and thought: that shaded space is everything the bakery earns over time. The height is how fast. The area is how much.

"Your peak is wrong," Priya said, leaning over, sardonic and cheerful at once. "You put the top where it looks tallest, but look, it's still climbing there." She tapped the point Alexis had marked, where the curve was unmistakably still going up. Down the table, Marcus was arguing with his calculator, and Theo, who wanted only to finish early so he could get to orchestra rehearsal, kept checking the clock with the resignation of a man watching a bus leave without him. Theo passed Alexis a fresh pencil without being asked, because her point had gone flat, and he had noticed, and that was Theo.

She erased the dot and slid it right, toward where the hill leveled. Then she slid it too far, past the moment when the curve had already begun to fall, and Priya laughed at her. Alexis sat back and looked at the shape itself. At the very top of the peak the curve wasn't climbing and wasn't falling. It was, for one instant, flat. The tangent line up there, she said slowly, touching the summit with her pencil tip, would be horizontal. Slope of zero. She wrote "slope = 0" beside the dot and heard Priya stop laughing.

"At a local maximum the derivative equals zero," Priya said, mostly to the room, mostly to claim it, and Ferreira, from his desk, made the small gratified noise he made when someone said a true thing unprompted. Alexis didn't mind that Priya said it first out loud. What mattered was that Alexis had put her finger on the actual point, the exact spot where the tangent line went flat, and it was hers; she had found it by drawing and erasing, not by remembering.

"Now the area," Ferreira said, and the room groaned, and Theo's chin lifted off his hand. Ferreira showed them rectangles, thin ones under the curve, more of them, thinner, until the shaded region Alexis had drawn in pencil seemed to be built from countless slices. The area was the sum of the slices; the integral was what you got when the slices became infinitely thin. Alexis copied the rectangle sketch twice, once for her notebook and once, without deciding to, on a separate sheet she folded and put in her pocket. Her grandmother did not know calculus. Her grandmother knew envelopes.

What Alexis could not yet reconcile, and did not pretend to, was the tension she felt sitting there: the peak said where profit was greatest in a single moment, and the area said what accumulated over all the moments, and the bakery's March had been a month with a low peak but a long, decent area, while some Saturdays spiked beautifully and then gave back everything by Sunday. Which mattered more depended on a question mathematics could state but not answer, which was what the bakery was for.

Ferreira assigned the actual computation, the antiderivative, the constants, for Thursday. Priya had already finished and was reading a lemma in the textbook with the green pen parked behind her ear, but she moved her bag so Alexis could spread out her graph, and slid the pretzels back across the table, half of them, which for Priya was practically a sacrament. Alexis ruled a clean tangent line through the peak, made it as horizontal as her unsteady hand allowed, and began slicing the hill into rectangles thin as pages.

Emile found the tube in the bottom drawer of his grandfather's desk, wrapped in a dishcloth and lodged between a slide rule and a tin of drawing pins. It was sealed at both ends with black wax, and inside it the gas sat brown as strong tea. He held it up to the window of the study, where the late light came through the fig tree and printed shifting leaves on the wall, and he remembered the museum in Lyon, the summer he turned sixteen, when a demonstrator had plunged a tube just like this one into a beaker of ice water and the brown had drained out of it like a stain being rinsed. Warm the tube again and the colour came back, deepened, darkened. He had stood at that display for twenty minutes while his classmates moved on to the Tesla coil.

That was two years ago. Now he was supposed to be revising for the entrance exam, and the principle behind the tube was on the syllabus, listed in the revision guide his grandfather had lent him with a dry remark about how the binding had outlasted three governments. Emile had read the chapter twice on the train down and understood it the way he understood a colloquialism he had never actually heard anyone use: he could define it, but he did not own it. His own notes said that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change imposed on it, and the words lay on the page like borrowed clothes.

He carried the tube to the kitchen, where his grandfather was extruding dough through the old brass machine bolted to the counter, the handle turning with a sound like a slow clock. "There's ice in the freezer," his grandfather said without looking up. "And the kettle is still warm from my coffee. If you are going to do what I think you are going to do, do it over the sink."

"You knew I'd find it."

"I left the drawer open. That is not the same thing."

Emile filled a bowl from the ice tray, added water from the tap, and lowered the tube in. He crouched with his phone ready to film it, feeling faintly ridiculous, a grown boy filming a tube of gas in his grandfather's kitchen while tagliatelle piled up on a tea towel behind him. But the brown began to fade almost at once, from the bottom of the tube upward, until the gas above the waterline was pale, nearly colourless, and the part still in his fingers stayed stubbornly brown. He turned the tube, and the warmth of his hand left a smudge of darker colour on the glass where his fingers had been.

Henri watched the boy from the counter, and the sight worked on him slowly, the way the ice worked on the gas. Forty-one years since he had sealed that tube himself, over a burner in a school laboratory in Roubaix, wax dripping on his knuckles, and he had chosen that year not to take the research post in Strasbourg. He had told himself it was for the children, for the stability, and he had told himself so often that the sentence had worn smooth and stopped meaning anything in particular. He had never regretted it in a way he could point to. But watching the brown bloom back into the tube as Emile held it under the running hot tap, watching the colour return exactly as it had gone, he understood that his own life had never been sealed like that. Nothing ran backward in a man. You could not cool him down and get the earlier colour out of him again.

"Darker when it's warm," Emile said, mostly to himself. "Paler when it's cold." He said the reaction running forward, the brown gas folding into the colourless one, must give off heat, because the cold was pushing it that way, toward the pale side, and the heat was pushing it back. He did not say it confidently. He said it the way you offer a coin to a machine, waiting to see whether it will be taken.

"That is the direction I would argue," Henri said, and left it there. He was not going to hand the boy a lecture; the boy had the tube, and the tube was better than any sentence Henri could construct. The boy's father, Emile's father, had wanted every answer finished and signed, and look what that had made of him. Henri lifted the pasta sheet and draped it over the back of a chair.

Emile wrote the observation in his notebook without the mechanism, just what he had seen: brown, colourless, brown again, heat one way, cold the other. He sat back on his heels and looked at the tube, at his grandfather, at the bowl of melting ice, and knew that he half understood it and could not have said which half. The exam would want more than that. The exam would want it closed.

"You'll stay for dinner," Henri said. It was not a question. He fed a sheet of dough into the machine and turned the handle, and the brass extruded a pale, even ribbon through its gap, and the kitchen filled with the smell of flour and the small persistence of the crank going round.

Sienna had claimed the corner computer by the window because it was the only one where the screen did not glare, and because from there she could see the whole second floor of the library, including the table where her grandfather sat waiting for the printer. She was working through a tutorial on a folded sheet of paper Mr. Alvarez had given her after third period: two tables, one called customers and one called orders, and a question in his cramped handwriting, "Which customers have never ordered anything?" She had written her first attempt an hour ago and it had returned the entire customer list, which she knew was wrong, because she could see order rows sitting right there in the second table, eight of them belonging to people whose names were now on her screen as if they had done nothing at all.

Her grandfather had come along because the printer at his apartment still refused to cooperate, and because he liked to be where she was, though he would not have said it that way. He had printed a photograph, a dramatic one, a soldier carrying a child through floodwater, and he had it in a plastic sleeve, and he had already told two people at the next table that it was from the news and that nobody was reporting it. He leaned over her shoulder now, smelling of coffee and the cold outside. "Look at this," he said. "They're hiding it."

She had seen the photo before. Not this exact one, but photos shaped like it, forwarded to her by a friend's cousin in a group chat with the caption "why isn't the media covering this," and she had scrolled past. She took the printout from him and turned it over. The paper was thin, the kind her grandfather bought because he was impecunious and refused to admit it, twenty sheets for a dollar at the surplus store, and the ink had bled at the soldier's boots.

"Grandpa, let me check it," she said.

He sat down in the chair beside her, which was not his chair, which belonged to whoever was waiting for a computer, and a man in a gray coat gave him a look and then did not do anything about it. Sienna lifted the photo out of the sleeve, laid it flat on the desk, and, because the library scanner was broken, took a picture of the picture with her phone. She had learned the method from a girl in her civics class who proselytized about it constantly, before every current events discussion, checking sources the way other people checked their hair. Google had added search by image back in 2011, the girl had said, so you could upload a picture, or paste its link, and find where else it appeared on the web. Sienna had nodded at the time without really listening. Now she uploaded the image and waited for the little spinning circle.

The results came back as a list of pages, and the photograph was on all of them. The oldest entry she could find dated it years before the flood her grandfather had described. One page called it a reenactment. Another said it was from a movie. She scrolled slowly, not to hide anything from him, but because she wanted to get it right before she said anything, and that was the habit she could not trace the lineage of, whether it came from her mother, who read every contract twice, or from Mr. Alvarez, who made them show their work. She turned the screen toward her grandfather.

"So it's fake," he said.

"It's from before. It's not from last week." She showed him the page with the date. He pulled the screen closer with two fingers, the way he handled his own phone, and read for a while.

"That's a different picture," he said finally. "They look alike."

"It's the same one, Grandpa. See the shadow on the stairs."

He was quiet. Across the room the printer finished and nobody went to it. He was quiet in the way he got when he was deciding whether to argue, and she watched him decide, watched his hand move toward the plastic sleeve and stop.

Here is what her grandfather would tell her mother that evening: that Sienna had found the picture was real, only misdated, that the whole web was unreliable and had corrected itself wrongly, that a thing could be true and a machine could still call it false. He believed some version of this while he sat beside her. He was not lying when he retold it; he was remembering in the direction he preferred, the way he remembered his own father's store as thriving until the city took it, though her mother had once shown Sienna the tax records in a shoebox, and the store had been failing for years. He remembered forward, toward the version where he was not fooled.

Sienna did not know any of that yet. What she knew was the screen, and the tutorial still open behind the browser tab, her broken query with its join returning everyone, the question of which customers ordered nothing still unanswered. She looked at her code again. The join matched customers to orders, so every customer with an order got a row, and the ones with nothing got nothing, and then she had asked for the customers, and gotten them all. She needed the ones the join could not find. She needed to ask for absence, which was a strange thing to type, a request for the shape of what was not there.

She wrote it a second way, joining and filtering for the empty side, and ran it, and got two names out of the whole list. Two customers, silent in the orders table, invisible unless you asked the question exactly right. She thought of the photo then, the way it had sat in the database of the web with its true date attached, waiting for someone to join it to the question. It could be found. That was the part she was sure of. Whether her grandfather would keep the answer was the part she was not.

"They printed my thing," her grandfather said, standing, pulling the plastic sleeve toward him across the desk. "Which one's yours?"

"That one," she said. "Third from the top."

He picked up both pages, his photograph and her query, folded together, and held them up to the window light as if comparing watermarks.

Isabelle locked the bathroom door and spread her note cards along the edge of the tub, because it was the only room in the apartment with a lock and the only place her mother's friends wouldn't drift in with questions. She was seventeen and had volunteered, somewhat against her own better judgment, to co-lead the peer health session on Friday: consent, contraception, how to actually walk into a clinic and ask to be tested. She had the facts. What she didn't have was a way of saying them out loud to thirty classmates without her voice going thin.

She practiced at the mirror. "Consent is a yes you can take back," she said, and winced, because it sounded like a poster. She tried again, softer, the way the nurse at the Riverside clinic had said it last month, when Isabelle had gone for her own appointment and stayed to ask how a person her age could get tested without a parent in the room. The nurse hadn't blinked. You book it yourself, she'd said. At your age, in this state, you don't need permission for that. Isabelle had written it on her wrist in pen before it washed off.

She was midway through the contraception cards, jogging her memory between IUDs and implants, when someone knocked. "Belle. It's me." Marcus, her cousin, sixteen and a senior of nothing much. He'd been in the living room all afternoon being quiet, which for Marcus was like a kettle deciding not to whistle.

"One second." She slid the cards under a towel and opened the door. Marcus came in anyway, sat on the tub's edge, and looked at the faucet rather than at her.

He got there eventually. There was a girl, Dara, and Dara had said maybe, and then later she had said nothing at all, and Marcus didn't know if maybe was a yes or if nothing was a no or if he was supposed to ask again or if asking again was the bad thing. It came out of him in one long breath, like a confession of theft.

Isabelle pulled the towel off the cards, not to show him, just to have her hands busy. Her mother would have said this was not a conversation for a bathroom, or really for anyone under thirty, and that girls especially should keep their knowledge quiet so as not to seem, in her mother's word, effusive. The nurse at Riverside had held the opposite view, handing Isabelle pamphlets like a woman giving out water in a drought. Between those two positions Isabelle had been circling all week, and now, with Marcus watching the faucet, she settled where she actually stood: you say the true thing plainly, and you let the other person be as knowledgeable as they want to be.

"Maybe isn't yes," she said. "And nothing isn't yes either. You ask once, and you listen to the whole answer, and if it's not a yes, that's the answer." Marcus nodded slowly, then asked what you did about the rest of it, the pregnancy worry, the other worry, the one boys at his school joked about and clearly didn't understand. She told him what the nurse had told her: that condoms were at the drugstore with no questions asked, that the clinic tested you for infections for free, that you could walk in alone. He asked what it was like there, and she described the waiting room, the fish tank, the folded magazines, an older man across from her reading a review of restaurants with the devotion of a true epicure, mouthing the word "uni" to himself while everyone around him worried.

"Also," Marcus said, as she was gathering her cards, "when Grandma took me for my physical, the nurse said her blood pressure was stage 2, and Grandma got mad about it. She said the top number was only 142 and the bottom was 88, so how could it be stage 2 if the bottom one was fine." He looked at Isabelle like she was the family's designated decoder of medical things, which, since the Riverside visit, she more or less was.

Isabelle turned that over. Her cards had a page on blood pressure, and she found it, and read it twice. "It's either number," she said. "Stage 2 hypertension means the top number is 140 or higher, or the bottom one is 90 or higher. Grandma's 142 was over the line all by itself. The bottom number doesn't have to be high too. Either one does it." Marcus said, quietly, "So she's actually stage 2," and Isabelle said yes, and thought about calling her grandmother tonight, not to lecture, just to say she'd looked it up, and would come along next appointment if Grandma wanted company.

Marcus stood, hand on the doorknob, then paused. "Friday. Your talk. Is it okay if I sit in back?" He was already turning the knob before she could answer, so she said it to the closing door: "Sit wherever you want." She picked up the cards, squared them, and started over at the mirror, saying the first line the plain way this time.

The gym had been divided in half with folding screens, and the stage was a rectangle of tape on the parquet floor where the free-throw line used to matter. Ashton stood at the edge of it with a binder under his arm, watching Priya and Marcus run the second scene for the fourth time. They kept crossing too early, both of them drawn to the tape marks like iron filings, and their lines arrived in the right order but with nothing behind them, letters read off a page.

He had taken the directing slot because no one else wanted it, and for the first two weeks he had treated it like an assignment, moving people the way Mrs. Okonkwo's handouts suggested, keeping his notes in the margin of the script. Then he had watched a senior's production the year before and understood that blocking was not traffic control. Where a person stood decided what the audience believed about what they said. He had started over with index cards, one per beat, and now the floor of his bedroom was covered with them like a vestigial model of the play, a paper stage he could rehearse in his head.

"Off-book on Thursday," he had told the cast at the start of the week, and Priya had nodded while Marcus looked at his shoes. "Off-book means no scripts in your hands. You perform from memory, the whole act, no calling for lines." Marcus had said fine. Priya had said fine twice.

Thursday came, and Priya came off book. Marcus did not. He walked onto the taped stage holding his script closed against his chest, like a hymnal, and when the scene began he opened it and read his first line off the page. The line was about leaving. He delivered it to the floor.

"Stop," Ashton said. He said it quietly, which was worse than shouting, and both actors stopped. "We said off-book today."

"I've been busy," Marcus said. "I had two tests. I know most of it."

"Do the scene without the book."

"I said most." Marcus held the script tighter. "I'm not going to stand up here and dry every thirty seconds in front of everyone."

There it was. Ashton had a rule and a Thursday and a performance in eleven days, and he had an actor who would rather defend the script than be seen failing with it. Priya sat on the bleacher step they were using as a bench and waited, arms crossed, in character even now, which Ashton noticed and filed away.

He had been reading a borrowed book on directing, the kind that liked big words, and one chapter argued that a director's real job was to historicize the moment, to set each scene at a specific time and place so the actors stopped playing ideas and started playing people in a room. Another chapter went on about phenomenology, about how the audience experiences the body in space before it understands a single word. He had underlined both passages and suspected both writers of overdoing it. But standing there, he could see the shape of what they meant. Marcus was not afraid of forgetting. He was afraid of being a person without the object, alone in the space, and every argument Ashton might make about fairness or deadlines would only make the script more precious to him.

"Give me the script," Ashton said.

"Why?"

"Because it's not a script anymore. It's a shield. Hand it to Priya."

Priya held out her hand without a word, still half in character, and Marcus looked at her, and after a moment he gave it to her. She set it behind her on the bleacher step, face down.

"Run it," Ashton said. "If you blank, stand there. Stay in the scene. The other person keeps talking, and you find your way back in. Nobody laughs."

Marcus ran it. He blanked twice, once for a long time, long enough that Priya shifted her weight and looked at the door as her character would, and that small movement gave Marcus something to answer, and he came back in with a line Ashton had never heard him say like that, quiet and late, as if it had just occurred to him. The rest of the scene was rough, was full of gaps, and it was the first time the play had looked like people instead of a reading.

Ashton called places again, and Marcus stepped to his tape mark, empty-handed, flexing his fingers once at his sides.

"Same scene," Ashton said. "And this time, when she crosses, don't follow her. Let her go."

The rehearsal room at the far end of the arts building had been locked all summer, and on Tuesday somebody finally opened it. Victor walked in carrying his binder for the one-act and stopped in the doorway. The chairs were not in rows facing the front wall. They were arranged in a ring, four deep on every side, with a square of bare floor in the middle.

"Moved you," said Priya from the snack table. "The black box got double-booked. Choreography."

Victor set the binder on a chair and stood in the center of the square. He had spent a week blocking the play against an imaginary front wall. The mother sat downstage left; the son crossed to the window; the confrontation happened center, both actors facing the same direction, the way faces face in every film he had ever studied. He walked through the old blocking alone, saying the lines under his breath, and from where he stood he could see only his own imagined back.

"Your play," Priya said. He turned. She was eating pretzels and watching him with the flat patience she used on people she found interesting for reasons they hadn't earned. "You going to just stand there or rehearse?"

He got the cast together after lunch. Marcus played the son; Dana played the mother; a quiet sophomore named Elias had one scene as the neighbor. They ran the first half in the new room exactly as Victor had staged it in the old one, and it took him thirty seconds to see the problem. During the long argument, Marcus and Dana planted themselves upstage, facing away from the chairs behind them, and stayed there. An entire quarter of the audience, if the chairs had been full, would have watched two backs for four minutes.

"Rotate it," Victor said, stopping the scene. "Keep moving. If you stand still too long, someone's staring at your shoulder blades."

"Every line?" Marcus said. "That'll look random."

"Then we find where the turns go. In the arguments, probably. You shift when you shift tactics." Victor said it before he had fully thought it through, and he could feel it was half right. On a stage in the round the audience sat on all sides, so the people watching were divided, and fairness to them was a physical problem, a geometry, not a matter of one lucky front row. The whole space had to be used, and used continuously, or some section of chairs only ever saw the backs of the actors.

They worked the argument for an hour. Dana kept offering solutions that sounded reasonable and weren't: what if she faced one way for the whole scene and Marcus faced the other, splitting the difference. "Each side gets half a play," Victor said. "That's not the same as a play." She called that sophistry, which it wasn't, but he let it go because the clock was running and because she was partly right that his counterexample about windows was irrelevant. In the old room the window had been an imaginary rectangle of air on the front wall. Here it couldn't live on any wall, so it had to live on nothing, and he had to find a way to make an audience believe in an object that pointed in no direction.

He taped an X in the center of the floor with a broken corner of chalk instead, and told Elias to treat the X as the window. Elias stood at the X in his one scene, delivering the neighbor's awkward speech about borrowed tools, and turned slowly the whole time, like a man reluctant to be anywhere. It looked accidental. It looked, Victor thought, better than anything he had staged on purpose all week.

At five o'clock Priya came back through with her water bottle and watched the last run from behind the chairs on the north side. Afterward she was effusive, more than the run deserved, and Victor suspected she was being kind because she had watched him fail in that room at two o'clock. He didn't mind. He sat on the arm of a chair with his binder open and crossed out three pages of blocking diagrams, the ones that assumed a front.

"There's still the ending," Marcus said, toweling his neck. "They reconcile standing still. That's the whole point, they finally stop moving."

Victor looked at the ring of empty chairs. He hadn't solved it, and he was tired enough to admit that out loud. "I don't know yet," he said. He capped his pen. "Tomorrow. Everyone in the center, we'll turn the stillness itself." He snapped the binder shut and started stacking chairs against the wall.

The assignment was taped to the back of the auditorium seats in case anyone forgot: one ten-minute play, drawn from your own life, staged by Friday. Mason had forgotten, in the sense that he had known about it and done nothing, and now it was Tuesday and Ms. Ruiz was walking the aisles collecting first drafts.

His draft was fourteen pages. It followed an entire summer, the one after his grandfather died, and it moved from the hospital waiting room to the funeral home to his aunt's kitchen to the lake where his cousins tried to teach him to fish, and then somehow to a bus station, and then to his own bedroom, where the last scene took place in September. Six locations in total. He had counted them twice on the bus that morning, hoping the number would shrink.

"Fourteen pages," said Devon, who sat behind him and read over shoulders as a matter of policy. "Ten minutes is about ten pages, max. And you've got a whole road show here."

"It's one summer," Mason said. "It's one thing."

"It's a genealogy of one summer," Devon said. "Every relative, every room. You're writing a family tree with scenery."

Ms. Ruiz reached their row. She read Mason's pages standing, flipping through them the way a doctor flips through a chart when the news is already obvious to her. "A ten-minute play usually has one setting," she said, "and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." She handed the pages back. "You have a summer. I need a moment. Pick one."

"Which one?"

"That's not my summer." She moved on to the next row.

The auditorium emptied for lunch except for the stage crew kids hauling the spring musical's flats into the wings, and Mason stayed in his seat because going to the cafeteria with fourteen useless pages seemed worse than sitting alone with them. He spread the scenes across three seats like tarot cards. Hospital. Funeral home. Kitchen. Lake. Bus station. Bedroom. Six little worlds, and he had maybe two days to keep one and bury five.

He tried to prognosticate, the way his grandfather had prognosticated weather off the lake, reading a sky nobody else could read, and he understood now that the old man had mostly been guessing with confidence. Which scene would survive? He couldn't tell. He liked the lake scene because his cousins were funny in it, but the cousins were auxiliary, really, three extra people who came on, cracked jokes about the fish, and left. Few characters, Ruiz had said. He had nine.

The hospital waiting room had only two people in it, him and his mother, and it never changed location. By the play's own arithmetic, that was the scene. But it was the one he least wanted to stage, because in it he had told his mother he was fine and gone to the vending machines and stayed there for forty minutes, and a person sitting in an audience would watch him do that and know exactly what it meant.

Devon came back from lunch with chips and no shame. "Kill your darlings," he offered, having read this somewhere.

"Which darlings?"

"The funny ones. The cousins."

"That's what I was thinking."

"Then why do you look like you're at the funeral home scene?"

Mason laughed, or something adjacent to laughing. He gathered five of the scene descriptions and folded them into his pocket, which was not deleting but was close enough for a first draft. The waiting room stayed on the seat in front of him. He read it over. His mother's one line was "He's still sleeping," delivered three times to three different relatives, but the relatives were offstage now, voices in a hall, which meant he could keep the line and lose the people, and he wrote that down in the margin: voices, no bodies. Two characters. One room. He did not know yet whether the forty minutes at the vending machines was honesty or just an excuse for a second scene, and he decided, provisionally, to write it and see.

By Friday he had eleven pages, and Ruiz read them in the front row while the crew kids rigged a work light to stand in for the fluorescent glare of a hospital corridor. She read without expression, which Devon claimed was her highest rating.

"Who's the voice on the paging system?" she asked.

"Nobody. It's a voice."

"Good. Stage it."

Mason stood at the edge of the stage while Devon, drafted as his mother with a scarf over his head, sat in a folding chair and said, "He's still sleeping." The work light buzzed. Offstage, one of the crew kids read the paging voice off a cue card, and Mason walked slowly toward the imaginary vending machines, slowly enough that an audience might watch him not turn around.

The bathroom was the quietest room in the house, and that was why Grandpa did his blood pressure there, sitting on the edge of the tub with his sleeve rolled up, the cuff wheezing tight around his arm. Kaylee stood in the doorway with the notebook her mother had left on the counter, the one with "help him keep track" written across the top in her mother's urgent, slanted hand.

"Read it to me," Grandpa said. "The top number and the bottom."

The screen showed 148 over 94. Kaylee copied it down, then looked at the folded paper the doctor had given him at his appointment, the one he'd been carrying around unfolded and refolded until the creases went soft. There were numbers on it, ranges with lines drawn between them, and a word he hadn't wanted to say out loud in the car.

"What's hypertension mean?" she asked, because he'd gone quiet when the doctor said it, and quiet was not like him.

"High blood pressure," he said. "Same thing, fancier coat."

Kaylee sat down on the edge of the tub beside him, the porcelain cold through her jeans. Below the ranges on the doctor's paper was a single underlined word, DASH, and after it, "diet." She'd assumed it meant cutting something out, fast, the way her aunt had cauterized sugar from her kitchen after her own diagnosis, throwing away half a pantry in one Saturday. Grandpa was already bracing for that version. He'd been bellicose about it all week, grumbling that if the doctor wanted him eating rabbit food he should say so plainly.

"Can I look it up?" she asked. He waved a hand, which meant yes.

Her phone worked even in the bathroom, one bar flickering by the window. She found the letters spelled out. DASH stood for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It wasn't a diet of denial at all; it was a plan that had been tested, an actual trial, funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997, back when she wasn't even born. She read the line twice. Somebody had done this on purpose, with real people, and written it down.

"It's not what you think," she said. "It's not taking things away. There's fruit, vegetables, whole grains. You can still have chicken."

"Chicken," Grandpa repeated, as if she'd offered him a peace treaty. "And the salt?"

"Less salt. But there's still, like, food in it."

He watched her write it down, the way she always wrote things, half printing and half cursive, ink smudged along the side of her hand. She drew a line down the middle of the page and put the reading on the left, 148 over 94, and on the right she started a list of what he'd eaten that day. She was guessing at how the two connected. The website said the diet mattered and exercise mattered, and she could see that the numbers were supposed to come down, but how much, and how fast, and whether the reading on any single Tuesday meant anything at all, the website didn't say. The more she read, the more she understood that one number was a snapshot and the pattern was the story.

"So which number is the bad one?" Grandpa asked.

"They both matter," she said. "The top one is when your heart beats. The bottom is between beats." She pointed at the doctor's ranges, the lines drawn between them. "You want them under the line."

"And this food gets them under the line."

"That's the idea. That's what the trial was for. They tested it before they told people to do it." She liked that. She liked that somebody had checked. Most of what she'd been told to believe in school had arrived the same way, she realized, conclusions handed over already finished, and she had never once asked who had done the checking.

Her mother appeared in the doorway then, still in her work coat, holding grocery bags. "Is he doing the cuff?"

"He's doing the cuff," Kaylee said. "And we're doing the diet." She held up the notebook. "I made a plan. Sort of a plan."

Her mother came in and stood behind them both, reading over Kaylee's shoulder, and Kaylee felt her mother's hand rest briefly on the top of her head, the way she used to when Kaylee was small and brushing her teeth at this same sink. "You looked it up?"

"It stands for something. Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. There was a whole trial. Nineteen ninety-seven."

"Better than I did," her mother said quietly. "I just bought the chicken."

That night Kaylee taped the notebook page to the bathroom mirror, next to the reading, and under it wrote Monday, walk, 20 minutes, if he'll go. She knew the ending wasn't going to arrive all at once, the way it did in books, some clean denouement where the numbers dropped and everyone was safe. It would arrive, if it arrived, in small entries on different days, a graph she'd have to draw slowly. Grandpa came in to brush his teeth, saw the page, and read it with his mouth full of foam.

"Twenty minutes," he said.

"We'll walk to the mailbox and back. Twice."

He spat, rinsed, and looked at her in the mirror. "Get your shoes on, then. I'm not waiting till Monday."

Sarah had agreed to the presentation on a Tuesday in March, when the health teacher asked for a student co-leader and nobody else raised a hand, and she had spent every evening since regretting it in small, manageable installments. The topic was reproductive health: consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections at the clinic on Ames Street. She was seventeen, which meant she was qualified to say the words out loud only if she could also make them sound like facts rather than confessions.

The clinic had agreed to let her observe the testing process, so on Thursday she took the bus downtown and filled out the forms and sat in a plastic chair while a nurse wrapped the cuff around her arm. When the nurse peeled off the printout, it read 118 over 76, and next to it the nurse wrote a single word: normal. Sarah looked at the numbers for longer than she probably should have. "Is that good?" she asked, and the nurse didn't lecture, just tapped a poster on the wall, the kind with plain text and no cartoons, and moved on to the next question on her clipboard.

Sarah read the poster twice while the nurse asked about symptoms she didn't have. Normal adult blood pressure, the poster said, is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. She sat with that. Her numbers were under both lines, 118 under 120, 76 under 80, and she understood that she had passed something without knowing the test had started. It occurred to her that this was most of what health was: thresholds you crossed or didn't, quietly, in rooms that smelled like hand sanitizer.

At home that night, she spread her notes across the kitchen table and tried to assemble them into something she could say to a room of her classmates without her voice going thin. Priya, who was fifteen and had been circling the kitchen for an hour with the particular patience of someone who wanted something, finally sat down across from her.

"You're doing the sex thing at school," Priya said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm doing a health presentation," Sarah said. "And you're not helping."

"I wasn't offering to help. I was offering to listen." Priya pulled one of the pages toward her, a diagram of the clinic's walk-in hours. "Danny's sister said you have to tell your parents. Is that true?"

"No," Sarah said. "In this state you don't, for testing." She heard the certainty in her own voice and checked it against her notes, and the notes agreed with her, and she felt something loosen slightly in her chest.

Priya had been reading about it anyway, Sarah discovered, in the fragmentary way of someone with an older sister and a phone: consent meant yes, but Priya had heard it explained as a cup of tea, and she thought that was stupid, and Sarah, who had also seen the tea video, privately agreed that it made something serious sound like a nursery lesson. "You can say the same true thing badly," Sarah said, "and then people laugh and stop listening." She was writing that down when she realized she had just, for the first time, articulated why the presentation scared her. It wasn't the subject. It was the laughing.

She practiced on Priya for an hour, and Priya, whose actual want surfaced only gradually, interrupted near the end. "If I asked Mom to go with me," she said, "would they let her in the room?" Sarah said she didn't know, that it probably depended, that Priya could call and ask without giving her name. Priya nodded and didn't look up, and Sarah understood that the question had not been hypothetical, and that she was not going to ask which part of it wasn't. This was the price of being the sister who knew things: you got the questions, and you rarely got the story behind them.

Their mother came home at nine with takeout and the interminable retelling of a staff meeting, and somewhere in it she began to excoriate a colleague, a man named Rick who had apparently taken credit for the quarterly numbers, and Sarah listened with half an ear while highlighting her contraception cards. Her mother's frustration had a familiar shape, the shape of someone whose competence was treated as ambient, and Sarah thought about disincentives the health teacher had mentioned, the ways fear of judgment kept people from clinics, and how both her mother and a scared sixteen-year-old at Ames Street were governed by the same arithmetic: if speaking up costs more than staying quiet pays, people stay quiet. She filed the thought for her closing slide and then deleted it from the closing slide, because it was too true for a Friday afternoon audience.

The night before the presentation, Sarah rehearsed alone in her room. She said the word consent eleven times until it stopped sounding strange. She rehearsed the clinic part with the most care, the part about walk-in hours and what the nurse would ask and how long results took, because that was the part that was actually a set of stairs someone could climb. When she got to the end she stood in front of her mirror and realized she still had the clinic printout folded in her jacket pocket, 118 over 76, the word normal in blue ink. Below 120, below 80. She had walked in healthy and had not known it, and half the people she'd be talking to tomorrow would walk in scared and not know that either.

The next afternoon she stood at the front of the room with her cards, and the first slide came up, and Tommy Wilcox in the second row said something about the tea video that she couldn't quite hear, and a laugh moved through the room like weather. Sarah looked down at her cards, then back up.

"This part takes four minutes," she said. "Then you can go back to whatever you were doing." She turned to the next card, and began.

The chocolate had failed twice before Zoey understood that failure was the whole curriculum. Her first batch, poured onto waxed paper in her grandmother's kitchen, had set overnight into something gray and dusty, bending like an eraser when she tried to break it, and the second had bloomed with pale streaks while she slept, as though winter had gotten into the pantry. She was eighteen and had two weeks at her grandmother's house before orientation, and she had promised herself she would leave with one skill that had nothing to do with anything she would study.

She found the answer in a battered paperback, "Chocolate Science for the Serious Amateur," shelved between a canning manual and a book of florid inscriptions her grandmother had collected from old greeting cards. Cocoa butter, the book said, could crystallize in six different forms. Zoey read the sentence three times, then read it aloud to the empty kitchen. Six. And only one of them, form V, gave chocolate its shine and its clean snap. Every other form was dull, or soft, or streaked, or all three. Tempering was the art of coaxing most of the cocoa butter into that single form and keeping it there.

"Six forms," she told her grandmother at lunch, spreading butter on toast. "And only form V gives you shine and snap." Her grandmother nodded and asked whether Zoey had eaten, though the toast was in Zoey's hand. It had been like this since spring. The doctors used words like progression, and Zoey had stopped flinching at them; the summer had desensitized her to small wrongness, the repeated asking, the keys in the refrigerator. What she had not gotten used to was the kitchen itself, which still worked perfectly, still smelled of her grandmother's old precision, the copper bowl hanging on its hook like a retired instrument.

The method she pieced together from the book was simple to state and merciless in practice. She chopped a bar of dark chocolate into pieces the size of thumbnails, set two thirds of it in a steel bowl over simmering water, and stirred until it melted entirely, erasing every crystal the chocolate had ever known. Then she pulled the bowl off the heat and beat in the remaining third, cold from the pantry, chopped fine. The seed chocolate, the book called it, and she liked that; it sounded like something you could believe in. She stirred and stirred with the thermometer lying in the bowl like a lazy fish, watching the numbers fall through the range where form V could survive and the other forms could not.

Her grandmother drifted in while the chocolate was at ninety-one degrees, sat down at the table in her pink cardigan, and watched. "You used to read recipes like scripture," Zoey said, stirring. "I remember you saying that." Her grandmother frowned, working at the memory the way she worked at names now, patiently, with her fingers laced. "A recipe is a text," she said finally, with the careful dignity of someone reciting something she trusted, "and a text wants interpreting." Zoey laughed, surprised. In her grandmother's good years she had taught a seminar on interpretation, on hermeneutics, and had treated a béchamel the way she treated a poem: as something with a history that had to be honored and then changed.

"It wants interpreting and it wants obedience," Zoey said. "Both at once. That's the terrible part." The thermometer read eighty-nine. She dipped a knife tip and waited, and this time, when the smear set, it set in under two minutes, glossy as wet stone. She almost shouted. She poured the tempered chocolate into the bar molds she had bought with her last paycheck, tapped out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry, and her grandmother said, "You always did have cold hands. Like your mother."

The bars set for an hour. When Zoey turned one out of its mold, it came free with a click, and the surface was so dark and even it looked like a pane of night. She broke a corner off and the break was audible, a hard, dry, decisive sound, and the broken face showed a clean grain. She carried a piece to her grandmother, who held it and studied it as though it were a small mirror. "Beautiful," her grandmother said, and put it in her mouth, and chewed, and for a moment her whole face was young. Then she said, "What is this?" and swallowed, and the moment closed like water over a dropped stone.

Zoey wrapped the rest of the bars in foil. There were six of them, and she labeled each with a strip of masking tape: FOR MOM, FOR DAD, FOR THE ROOMMATE I HAVEN'T MET. She would take them to campus in a cooler pack, three hundred miles, and hand them out during that first week when everyone was performing themselves. It had cost her something to make them, the whole afternoon, and the last of her certainty that her grandmother was only tired. She knew now, and knowing sat in her like the seed chocolate had sat in the bowl, hard and necessary, melting slowly.

On the last morning, she tempered one more batch, smaller, and poured it into the mold shaped like a maple leaf, her grandmother's favorite. She worked without the thermometer this time, testing by the cooling on her lip, because she had learned the numbers and then learned to leave them behind, which felt like the only kind of mastery worth having. The leaf set perfectly. She set it on a saucer in front of her grandmother with a cup of coffee, and her grandmother picked it up and turned it over and smiled.

"I made these," her grandmother said. "Years ago. I never could get them shiny like this." She broke the leaf in half with a snap that rang in the quiet kitchen, and ate her own chocolate, and did not offer any back.

The kitchen table had been Sophia's desk for three days, and by now it held the shape of her thinking: two pencils, one snapped near the eraser, a printed score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, and a phone face down beside the sugar bowl. The assignment was due Friday. Mark the first movement's form, her professor had said, as though form were a thing you could outline in pencil, when really it moved under her hands like water.

She had begun, as everyone began, with the obvious. The theme stated itself in the first six measures, plainly, almost childishly. Then came the variations, and her certainty dissolved. Her textbook insisted that sonata form meant an exposition, a development, a recapitulation, and that these sections could be found, bracketed, labeled. The textbook made it sound like sorting mail. But measure by measure, the melody kept transmuting itself, ornament folding into ornament, until Sophia could not say where the theme ended and its disguise began. She drew a bracket, erased it, drew it shorter, erased it again.

Her phone buzzed at half past seven. A message from Danny, who played piano in the jazz ensemble and had never once, in four years of friendship, asked her for anything academic.

"Big favor," the message read. "Playing a thing Saturday for my cousin's engagement party. Somebody gave me the melody only, no accompaniment, and I can't build anything from a bare tune. You know theory. Could you write the chords in for me? Just put them over the notes, the way you'd want them. I'll pay you in samosas."

Sophia typed back, "Over the notes how?" because she genuinely did not know what he meant. She had spent two years reading scores from the bottom up, bass to soprano, harmony as something latent in the counterpoint.

"Like a lead sheet," he answered. "Chord symbols above the staff. C, Am, G7, whatever fits, written over the spot in the melody where the chord goes with it. That's how it works. Then I can see what to play under the tune at a glance." Then, a few seconds later: "Please. My cousin already paid the deposit on the hall."

She looked at the message for a long moment. It was such a backwards way of thinking. In Mozart, the harmony was the melody's shadow, inseparable from it, implied in every leap and resolution. In Danny's world, the melody stood alone on the staff and the chords floated above it like weather markers, C over this bar, G7 over that, the accompaniment reducible to a handful of letters. She wrote back that she would try, and pulled the simple tune he had photographed toward her, a folk-ish thing in C major with no accidentals to trouble anyone.

The work was easier than she wanted it to admit to being. She hummed the melody, felt where it rested on G and wanted to go home, and wrote G7 above that measure. Where it sank toward the third of the chord, she wrote C. An Am appeared over the phrase that darkened, briefly, like a cloud crossing a lawn. The letters accumulated above the staff in her small, judicious handwriting, and the strange thing was that the tune became clearer to her, not less mysterious but more legible, its phrases suddenly visible as harmonic decisions rather than as a ribbon of sound.

She photographed the page and sent it, then sat back down at Mozart with the two ways of thinking still running in her at once. On the lead sheet, structure was written above the music, explicit, a row of signs. In the sonata, structure had to be inferred from below, from the grain of the thing. She picked up her pencil again and, instead of asking where the exposition ended, asked what the music itself was doing when it left home. The moment the harmony pulled away from the tonic, the moment a small restlessness entered, she marked a double bar. Her hand was nearly steady.

The phone rang. Not a message this time, an actual call, and Danny's voice came through tinny and too fast. "It's perfect, thank you, but listen, the real reason I asked you." A pause long enough for her to hear a television somewhere behind him. "My cousin's fiancé is a conservatory guy. He's going to be watching me play. I didn't want to tell you that before because you'd have said no, you always say no when it matters to someone's reputation."

"You're my reputation now?"

"Saturday night. Eight o'clock. The samosas are already ordered." He hung up before she could answer, which was his way of preventing refusal.

Sophia set the phone back beside the sugar bowl, face down again. The room had gone quiet enough that she could hear the refrigerator's hum, and she recognized, with some irritation, the particular ennui of a Friday evening spent indoors, the feeling that everyone else was already somewhere else. She looked at her score. Her brackets stood now where the harmony said they should: an exposition that ended when the music reached its second key, a development she had traced through the wandering, a recapitulation that began, quietly, exactly where the theme returned home. Whether her professor would agree, whether the labels were truth or merely her best guess, she could not yet say, and she let that uncertainty sit on the table beside her without sweeping it away.

She copied the page in ink, folded it, and wrote on the outer sheet, in letters as small as chord symbols: Sophia, third floor, if the fiancé hates it. Then she carried it out to the mailbox at the curb, and the lid of the blue box clanged shut behind it.

Henry kept telling himself he understood interest rates, which was easier than actually understanding them. He had the index cards spread across the kitchen table like a hand of solitaire, each one holding a sentence he'd copied from a website whose authority he had never checked, and he had been staring at them long enough that the words had begun to dissolve into shapes. It was the last week of August, the particular summer ennui that settles in after the graduation parties end and before college begins, and he was trying to sublimate all his restlessness into preparation, because tomorrow his grandfather was coming to dinner and would ask.

He had told his mother he knew the material cold. "Grandpa's irascible, but I can handle him," Henry had said, and she had given him a look he chose not to interpret. All he knew for certain was that the old man had opinions about the central bank, loud ones, and that at some point during dinner he would say something like "raising rates just strangles people," and Henry, who had appointed himself the family's defender of economic literacy, intended to explain how raising rates actually slows inflation. He just needed, first, to understand how raising rates actually slowed inflation.

The cards were no help. They used words like "demand" and "cooling" that themselves needed cards.

Through the window he saw the neighbors' lemonade stand, folded card table and crooked sign, run by Priya, who was twelve, and her brother Sam, who was nine and mostly decorative. What he heard next stopped him. They were arguing. Priya wanted to raise the price from fifty cents to a dollar, and Sam, gripping the pitcher with both hands, was objecting on the grounds of fairness. Henry drifted out onto the porch, ostensibly to check the mail, and let their argument reach him.

"Everything's going to cost more next month," Priya said. "Mom says the cups alone went up. So we have to charge more now, before it happens."

"So charge like sixty cents," Sam said.

"If everything's going up, sixty won't cover it later. You have to get ahead of it." She said it with the flat certainty of someone quoting an adult, probably their mother, and Henry felt the strange vertigo of watching his index cards come to life in a nine-year-old's hands.

He came down off the porch. "Can I ask you something? Why do you think everything's going to cost more?"

"Because it always does," Priya said, as if he were the child.

"But what if you didn't think that? What if you were sure the cups would cost the same next month as they do now?"

Priya considered this with the seriousness the question deserved. "Then I wouldn't charge a dollar. I'd maybe go to sixty, like Sam said. Or keep it fifty." Behind her, Sam was already revising the sign with a stub of pencil, hedging his bets at seventy-five.

Henry stood very still on the hot sidewalk. He was not, he realized, the person he had been describing to his mother all week, the one who knew this cold. He had been reciting. But here it was, happening in front of him with a pitcher and a pencil: what people expect changes what they ask for. If Priya expected higher prices, she demanded a bigger increase now, a whole extra fifty cents, and her raising the price made the price higher, actually higher, for every kid on this street. If she trusted that prices would stay low, she'd ask for less, a dime, nothing, and the smaller increase would keep things low, which was, he understood suddenly, the same thing the central bank was after. Not magic, not strangling. Trust, manufactured on purpose. The whole country was a lemonade stand, and people's expectations were doing half the work. He felt the thought click into place and also felt its edges, the parts that didn't click, the distance between a card table and an economy, and he let that stay open rather than paper over it.

At dinner his grandfather set down his fork and said, "So. Your mother tells me you've got opinions about the rate hikes."

"I think I can explain it now," Henry said. "Want to hear about a lemonade stand?"

His grandfather's expression changed into something Henry had never seen on him before, and he reached into his jacket, which still hung on the back of his chair, and produced a worn business card, sliding it across the tablecloth. Henry picked it up. The name was his grandfather's. Below it, in small type he had to squint at, were the words he had somehow never been told in eighteen years of family dinners: Central Bank, Research Division.

"Priya," his grandfather said, "the one running the stand. What did she decide?"

"Seventy-five cents," Henry said. "Sam talked her down."

The party had thinned to the kitchen by eleven: Leah, her robotics teammate Priya, three boys arguing about a card game, and a bowl of punch going warm. Priya sat on the counter with her phone, and every so often Leah caught her scrolling back through the team chat, to the message Leah had sent two days before. Five lines of compliments about the arm mechanism Priya had designed, then one sentence about the wiring, which was, honestly, a hazard. Priya had not spoken to her since.

Leah's mother had a phrase for parties like this, the late hour when everything went soft with somnolence and people said what they meant. Nothing good is decided after ten, she liked to say, but Leah was seventeen and had decided plenty after ten, and tonight she intended to decide something else.

She took two plastic cups of punch and crossed the kitchen.

"You're hiding," she said.

"I'm recharging." Priya took the cup anyway. "Also I'm rereading your message. The wiring thing."

"I said your arm design was the best thing on the robot."

"You said five nice things." Priya set the cup down without drinking. "I counted. And then you said the wiring could burn out the board, and that's all I've heard in my head for two days. Five against one, and the one wins."

Leah had read something about this, late one night in the spring, chasing a citation for a psych paper she'd half written and never finished. A review from 2001, led by a researcher named Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good." It had found that negative events and remarks usually affected people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. She'd underlined it at the time because it seemed obvious and also unbearable, the way gravity was obvious and unbearable, and then she had gone and lived it without noticing.

"There's this thing," she said. "A review. 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good,' 2001, Roy Baumeister ran it. Bad stuff hits harder than good stuff the same size."

"So I'm statistically normal."

"So I did it wrong." The boys at the far end of the table erupted over the card game, someone adjudicating a dispute about whether a jack could be played on a nine, and Leah waited for the noise to settle. She had spent two days drafting apologies and burning them, because an apology would have taken back the true part, and the wiring was genuinely dangerous. What she wanted, she realized, standing there with punch sweating in her hand, was to be believed twice: once when she praised, and once when she criticized, and the two beliefs kept trying to cancel each other out.

"Here's what I should have said," Leah told her. "Your arm mechanism is the best thing on the robot. That's not a warm-up, that's the whole review. And the wiring is a fire risk, and I should have asked to fix it with you instead of handing you a sentence and leaving."

Priya's face was mercurial, quick to storm and quick to clear, and now it did neither; it just held still, which was worse to wait through than either.

"You think I can't hear criticism."

"I think I gave you a bundle and let you sort it alone. And the bad part was heavier. Not because you're weak. Because that's just how it weighs."

Priya slid off the counter. For a moment Leah thought she was leaving, and she began rehearsing the walk home, the cold block to the bus stop, the whole conversation replaying with the bad parts outweighing the good, because of course they would. Instead Priya opened the team chat and held the phone out.

"Rewrite it, then. Right now. The wiring part. Specific, and like you're talking to me and not to a document."

Leah typed slowly, deleting twice. She wrote that the gauge was too thin for the current draw, that it had heated up in the last test run, and that she wanted to reroute it together on Saturday before the qualifier. She read it aloud. Priya listened all the way to the end, then took the phone back, and looked at the message, and then at her.

"Saturday," Priya said. "Bring snacks. The good kind, not the kind you bring."

The appointment was for eleven, and Maxime arrived at the bank at ten forty with two printed emails in his jacket pocket, both from landlords in the city where he would start school in September. The first offered a studio at the edge of campus: six hundred and eighty a month, heat included, electricity and internet extra. The second was a shared flat closer to the river: five hundred and fifty, but everything separate, water, hydro, wifi, and a laundry machine that took coins. He had come to open his first account, alone, and to ask someone in a gray vest whether the numbers he had scribbled on the backs of the pages were actually arithmetic or just anxiety dressed up as arithmetic.

While he waited on the padded bench by the tellers, he took out his phone and reread the message his mother had sent that morning. "Your father says use the two-second rule no matter what, and longer if it's raining or snowing or dark. He says city drivers don't leave room, so you have to leave it for them. Call me after the bank." It was a short message, the kind she sent instead of the long ones, and he understood that she was practicing for the autumn, when short messages would be all they had.

The two-second rule had a history for him. Last winter, in the months before his test, his father had driven him out past the water tower on the old highway and made him count. When the truck ahead passed a mile marker, Maxime was to say one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand under his breath, and if he reached the sign before the two was finished, he was too close. In the snow that day his father had made him hang back even farther, watching the marker come and go with the wipers keeping their slow time, and Maxime had felt something close to exhilaration, the car seeming to belong to him at last, the road unspooling under his own decisions. He had passed the test in February. His father had said only, well, all right, and shaken his hand as though at the acquittal of a defendant neither of them had been sure of.

"Maxime?" The account manager's name tag said Sylvie. She had a small office with a plant that was dying politely in the corner, and she spread his two leases across the desk without asking why an eighteen-year-old wanted a financial opinion. "So let's be honest about the studio first. Heat included is real money here, that's maybe eighty a month you don't pay in January. Electricity, call it forty. Internet, fifty, but you'd split nothing." He watched her underline his own scribbles and add figures he hadn't thought of, a bus pass for the far one, laundry for the near one, renter's insurance for both.

"Wait," he said. "The shared one. Hydro isn't the same as heat?" She smiled the way people smile when they remember not knowing. "Hydro can be the heat, depending on the building. Here it says baseboard, so the electric bill climbs in winter. Your friend in the other bedroom uses the shower, uses the kitchen, and you pay half of all of it." He wrote winter in the margin of the river flat, then drew a box around it, and the box began to look like a cell.

The totals came out closer than he had expected. The studio at eight hundred and change, the share at seven sixty, and Sylvie pointed out that the difference was one Friday night a month, which made him laugh and then feel caught, because he knew which of his future selves she meant, the one already planning a hedonistic first term with people whose names he'd learned in a group chat. "That self also needs the bus," she said. "That self also wants the room with the door that locks."

He opened the account with the money from two summers at the garden centre, and Sylvie printed a debit agreement and slid a pen across the desk. While he signed, he thought about the drive home, forty minutes on the highway, and how he would pick a sign, any sign, and count one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand behind whatever car was ahead of him, and how in the dusk it would be longer than that, because his father had been right about the dark, and his mother's message had said so, and he was still checking.

He hadn't decided between the leases when he left. In the parking lot he sat in his car with the engine off, the two pages on the passenger seat, the studio with its included heat and its isolation, the flat with its split bills and its stranger who might become a friend or might leave his dishes. His mother's text sat unanswered on the phone in his hand. He typed, "Studio is 40 more but closer to everything, flat is cheaper if the guy is normal," and then, before he could second-guess it, he started the car, signalled, and pulled out toward the road.

Jacob had the graph half drawn when the power flickered, and for a second he thought the outage had come early, that the storm the radio had promised all afternoon had finally arrived to ruin his night. The lights steadied. He sharpened his pencil with his thumb against the blade of a pair of scissors, because the sharpener had been dead since March, and went back to the two axes labeled wheat and cloth.

The assignment was due first period, eight hours away, and the textbook's example sat in front of him like a locked door. Country A could make forty bushels of wheat or twenty bolts of cloth if it pushed all its labor one way or the other, and the homework asked him to show what happened when A traded with Country B, which was worse at both. He had drawn the frontier for A, a straight line sloping down, and then the answer key in the back of the book had marked a point outside it. He checked it twice. The point was beyond the curve, in the blank space where the graph said nothing could exist.

His sister Ruth came through the kitchen with her soccer bag over one shoulder and her cleats dripping rain onto the linoleum. She wanted the table, because she had a project of her own, a poster about volcanoes that was due Friday and that she had left until now, and the table was the only surface in the house big enough for it.

"I'm using this," Jacob said, without looking up.

"You're using half of it." She spread her poster board along the far edge and started cutting red paper into lava. Their mother was working the late shift, and the note on the fridge said leftovers, oven, three fifty, which meant Jacob was also responsible for dinner.

He tried to resuscitate his understanding from the class notes, but his notes were mostly a drawing of Mr. Okafor's tie and the phrase "comparative advantage" boxed twice, which was the name of the concept and, at the moment, the whole of his knowledge of it. He remembered Okafor saying the word, and he remembered not writing down anything after it because the bell had rung. Now the outside-the-curve point sat there like an accusation.

Ruth leaned over his paper, chin propped on her fist, rain still in her hair. "Why is that dot in the middle of nowhere?"

"That's the problem." He tapped the frontier. "Everything on this line is what Country A can make itself. The dot's past it. The book says that's where they end up after trading, but that's impossible. You can't be outside your own line."

"Then erase the dot."

"It's the answer."

"So the book's wrong." She went back to her lava with the serene confidence of a fourteen-year-old who had never once been punished by an answer key.

Jacob sat with the presentiment that the book was not wrong, that the error was in him somewhere, and the feeling was close to the one he'd had sophomore year when he'd argued with a geometry proof for an hour before realizing he'd assumed what he was supposed to show. He set the oven, put the leftovers in, and stood at the counter eating crackers while he stared at the two frontiers side by side, A's and B's, B's line squat and low, worse at wheat and worse at cloth both.

He tried it with actual numbers, because numbers could not be argued with. If A made only wheat and B made only cloth, and then they swapped some of each, Jacob could pick the swap himself, any swap, and see where each country landed. He chose an exchange that sounded fair to nobody, ten bushels for six bolts, wrote it out, and plotted the result. A's new point sat outside its line. He plotted B's. Also outside. He did it again with different amounts, and again, and the points kept landing in the impossible region, in the blank space, as if the graph's own arithmetic had turned bellicose and decided to overrun its borders.

"Ruth. Come here."

"I'm doing lava."

"Two minutes. Look." He held the pencil at the point. "This line is everything A can make alone. Right? Alone, no trade, all the combinations are on this line or under it. But if A makes just wheat and trades some of it for cloth from B, A ends up right here." He tapped the outside point. "Same for B, over on its graph. By specializing and trading, both of them end up with combinations they could never have produced on their own. They're past the line. That's the whole point of the dot."
