Ruth frowned at it, chewing the cap of a marker. "So the line is only the line if you're by yourself."

"That's it. That's exactly it." He wrote the sentence in his notebook, near enough to the boxed phrase that the two ideas now touched. Whether it would survive being said out loud in class tomorrow, whether he really understood it or had only followed the numbers to a place he couldn't defend, he couldn't tell yet. He had a feeling the teacher would ask why it worked, and Jacob did not yet have a why, only a that.

The oven timer went off. He pulled the tray out with a dish towel, burned his thumb, ran it under the tap, and divided the food onto two plates while Ruth rolled her poster to one side to make room. They ate at the half-cleared table, and she told him the volcano poster was now going to have a graph on it, a graph of something, she hadn't decided what, because graphs looked scientific and she needed the extra credit.

"Put it outside the lines," Jacob said.

"Eruptions don't have lines."

"Everything has lines. That's what today taught me."

The cuff hissed, tightened around her mother's arm, and then the numbers appeared on the little screen: 152 over 96. Annabelle wrote them in the notebook she had started that morning, the one with BLOOD PRESSURE written on the cover in letters that looked more official than she felt.

Her mother was in the garden pulling bindweed, which was her way of not thinking about the appointment she had on Thursday. Annabelle carried the monitor out to the porch and held it up. "It did it again," she said. "Over 150."

Her mother sat back on her heels. "The nurse said one high reading isn't the end of the world."

"I know. But it's the third one this week." Annabelle turned the notebook toward her. She had made a chart, because charts were something she could do. "The top number is when your heart beats. The bottom is between beats. High means the blood's pushing too hard on the vessel walls, and the nurse at the pharmacy said that has to do with the salt we eat, because salt makes you hold water, and more fluid means more pressure. And exercise makes the heart stronger so it doesn't have to push as hard at rest." She said it all in one breath, the way she had rehearsed it, and her mother laughed.

"Listen to you."

"I'm going to explain it to Grandma on Saturday so she stops telling you it's just nerves." Annabelle had decided this in the night, lying awake. If she could understand the numbers, she could stand between her mother and Grandma's bellicose certainty that doctors were inventing problems to bill for. Grandma had taken their grandfather off his pills years ago and considered it a victory. Annabelle wanted ammunition that wasn't a fight.

Inside, her phone buzzed. A message from her sister Dee, who was nineteen and had an appointment at the campus clinic that afternoon, an appointment she had not told their mother about. Annabelle leaned against the kitchen counter to read it.

"Okay so. Update from the clinic," Dee wrote. "You were right that I should ask instead of panicking. The nurse went through everything with me. She said the pill is fine if you take it every single day, but nobody's perfect, and real life happens. Then she said the IUD and the implant fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use. Fewer than 1 in 100, Annie. A YEAR. I practically demanded the implant on the spot." Then, a minute later: "Don't tell Mom. I mean it. I'm paying for it myself with my job money, it's my business. But I wanted you to know first."

Annabelle read it twice. She had been the one who suggested the clinic, mostly because Dee had spent two weeks wild-eyed and snapping at everyone, externalizing a fear she wouldn't name. Now the fear had a shape and a number, and the number was small, and Dee was calling it her business. Annabelle understood that. She also understood that their mother would be hurt to find out later, the way she had been hurt about the tattoo, and that keeping this secret would mean sitting at dinner holding it under her tongue like a coin.

She typed, "Your business. My mouth is a vault," and then, because she was sixteen and couldn't help it, "does it hurt."

"A sting, then nothing. I'll be at dinner Sunday. Tell Mom I'm buying the good bread."

Annabelle set the phone face down and looked at her notebook. Two things she was keeping track of now: her mother's pressure, and her sister's privacy. In biology they had just started genetics, and the teacher had shown them a family pedigree the way you'd show a map of landmines. Heart disease on one side, diabetes on the other. Your genotype wasn't a verdict, the teacher said, it was more like a hand of cards, and how you played it mattered. Annabelle thought of the salt shaker on the table, of her mother skipping her walks when she was tired, of Dee riding a bus across town to handle her own body without asking anyone's permission. The cards were dealt, but the playing went on and on, in choices the size of a dinner.

That evening Annabelle cooked, which she almost never did. She found a recipe with no added salt, used lemon and garlic instead, and set out the monitor beside her mother's plate. "After we eat, and after you sit for five minutes with your feet on the floor," she said. "That's how you're supposed to do it. Not right after gardening."

"Since when do you know how I'm supposed to do anything?"

"Since Thursday's coming and Grandma's coming Saturday and somebody in this house has to be calm about it." She slid the lemon chicken across the table. "Also, we're walking tomorrow morning. Slow is fine. The nurse at the pharmacy said even walking makes the heart stronger over time, and then it doesn't have to work so hard, and the numbers come down."

Her mother cut a piece of chicken, tasted it, raised an eyebrow. "There's no salt in this."

"There's lemon in this."

After dinner her mother sat with her feet flat on the floor, arm resting on the table, and let the cuff do its work. Annabelle watched the screen the way she'd watch a pot about to boil. 148 over 92. She wrote it down without saying anything, and her mother watched her write it, and neither of them called it good or bad. It was a number in a column, the second-lowest of the week.

On Sunday, Dee arrived with the good bread and a small bruise on the inside of her arm that she kept her sleeve over, and their mother said, "Sit, sit, before it gets cold," and Dee caught Annabelle's eye across the table and tipped her chin, half a nod, half a question. Annabelle cut the bread and passed it, and outside the window the garden went dark, and the notebook lay closed on the counter with its chart waiting for Monday.

Alexander taped the floor of the black box theater on a Tuesday afternoon, three long strips of spike mark forming a doorway that didn't exist yet, and understood for the first time how much of directing was pretending a room into being. Ms. Ruiz had handed him the one-act without ceremony, a script called "The Alluvial Fan" about two brothers fighting over a river that kept changing course, and said only, "It's yours to ruin or not." The stage manager, Priya, watched him measure the diagonals twice because she'd seen freshman carpenters trust a single measurement and recuperate from the mistake for a week. The actors arrived at four, and the older brother, Marcus, clapped Alexander on the shoulder as if they were equals, which they were not yet.

He had planned the opening blocking in his notebook all weekend, little arrows and x's marching across a diagram that made sense from above. "Start downstage center," he said, "then cross to your left when she enters." Marcus took two steps toward the wings on the audience's left, the wrong side, and Priya called a halt before Alexander could find words. Everyone waited. He was seventeen and had never told anyone older than a dog what to do.

"Sorry," Marcus said, not sorry, just efficient. "Which left?"

Alexander looked at his diagram, then at the stage, and felt the two orientations slide apart like overlaid transparencies. "Stage left," he said. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience." He heard his own voice go flat with the effort of not sounding like a textbook, and Priya wrote it on the running sheet anyway: director means stage directions, always. The correction cost him something he couldn't name yet, a small tax on every future instruction.

The second rehearsal went worse in a different way. He had blocked the brothers' final argument as two long parallel crosses, mirrored and geometric, because the diagram was beautiful, and Priya had to point out, gently, that the actors were now spending the climax as far from each other as the stage allowed. Marcus and Danny, playing the younger brother, stood at their marks like alluvial deposits the river had abandoned, and the scene's heat drained out through the distance. Alexander had drawn pictures instead of asking what the people needed. That was the harder lesson, and it didn't fit in a notebook margin.

He tried again on Thursday with the diagram closed on the floor. "Stand wherever the fight starts," he said, "and move when you have a reason." Danny moved immediately, small shifts, weight from foot to foot, circling; Marcus stayed planted and let Danny orbit him, and suddenly the river in the script had a shape. Alexander felt the gain arrive and recognized its price at the same moment: the scene was better and it was less his. He had made a map, and the territory had walked away from it.

On Friday the disbursement forms for the regional festival came back with their small budget halved, which meant no rented risers and, therefore, no elevated platform for the flood monologue. Priya laid out the numbers on the props table like a hand of losing cards. Alexander stared at the taped floor and remembered that the spike marks were only tape, that a doorway could be moved with a utility knife, that a flood could happen at floor level if Danny gave it everything from his knees.

"Can you do it down?" he asked Danny. "The monologue, flat on the boards?"

"From my knees," Danny said. "Like the water's already won."

They ran it. Marcus, upstage, kept his back turned through the whole speech, and Alexander almost corrected him, almost said turn around, face him, and then held it, because the turned back was saying something about brothers that his blocking never would have found. He watched the speech end in silence and did not call places again, letting the quiet run four seconds, five, until the lights in the booth clicked off and on, Priya's signal that someone in the dark had cried.

Afterward Marcus found him coiling cable by the taped doorway. "Saturday, the wrong-left thing," Marcus said. "You knew before you said it. I saw you figure out whether to tell me like a person or like a director."

"Which did I pick?"

"Neither, both." Marcus took the other end of the cable and looped it, matching him. "Keep doing that."

Alexander drove home with the windows down, the diagram of the final blocking half-abandoned in his head, half of it still the mirror-world arrows, half of it now Danny on his knees and a brother's turned back. He did not know which version he would choose at dress rehearsal, and he noticed that the not-knowing had stopped feeling like a failure. In the passenger seat lay the script, already dog-eared, already less his than it had been on Tuesday, and under it the roll of tape.

Paige had taped her note cards to the kitchen cabinet in the order of her argument, and by Sunday afternoon she could recite them without looking, which was exactly the problem. Her economics teacher had assigned each student one question to answer in front of the class, and hers was this: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She could say the words. She just could not make anyone believe them.

"It's like a disincentive," she told her mother, who was sorting mail at the counter and not really listening. "Borrowing costs more, so people do less of it." Her mother made a sound of acknowledgment. Paige knew the sentence was true the way the capital of a state is true, a fact with no weight, nothing you could drop on a table.

Uncle Ray arrived at four to fix the garbage disposal, which had been making a sound like a small animal trapped in the pipes. He came every few weeks lately, since the plant where he had worked for twenty-two years closed and he started taking whatever jobs people offered. He knelt under the sink with a wrench and a flashlight, and Paige, restless, read her note cards to him while he worked.

"Interest rates go up, people spend less, prices stop climbing," she said. "The whole economy cools down."

"Whose whole economy?" Ray asked from inside the cabinet. He emerged with a piece of something black and unidentifiable and set it on the counter like evidence. "You're writing an essay about trade too, aren't you. I saw your book on the table."

"It's the same unit," Paige said. "Comparative advantage. Countries specialize in what they're best at, and trade raises the total income of the whole country. It's one of the few things economists actually agree on."

Ray wiped his hands slowly on a towel, the way he did when he was deciding whether something was worth saying. "I made radiators for two decades," he said. "Then the imports came in cheaper, and the plant shut, and the country's income went up. So somebody gained. It just wasn't anybody I worked with."

Paige opened her mouth to argue and found she had nothing. She looked at her note cards, all seventeen of them, and not one of them had a place for her uncle. The textbooks had explained the gains so confidently that she had never thought to exhume the losses, to dig down past the aggregate number and see who was underneath it. Her cards said the country. Her uncle said the people.

She sat down on the floor next to him and they took the trap apart together, black water spilling into the bucket, a corroded washer at the bottom of everything. "So both things are true," she said slowly. "The total income rises, and the workers in the industries that face the cheaper imports still lose their jobs or their wages. It's not a contradiction. It's just two different levels."

"That's a trenchant observation," Ray said, deadpan, and Paige laughed, because he had once told her the only economics he trusted was the price of gas. He held up the washer. "This is the whole problem, by the way. One piece worth forty cents."

That night she rewrote the speech. She kept the mechanics, the higher rates, the costlier borrowing, the cooling demand, but she added a section at the end that her teacher had not asked for. The medicine works on the whole, she wrote, and the whole is real, but a whole is made of parts, and some parts pay more than others. She could not promise the speech would win anything. She only knew that when she said it aloud in the kitchen, her own voice sounded different, less like a recitation and more like someone who had been under the sink.

On Monday she stood at the front of the class and delivered it, and when she finished, a boy in the second row raised his hand and asked the exact question she had been afraid of: so who actually pays when the central bank does this? Paige said she wasn't sure yet, and she watched the class lean forward instead of back.

After school her phone buzzed. It was Uncle Ray: the disposal stopped working again, bring your cards. She texted back that she had a new question for him, about what happened to the workers at a bank when the bank raised rates. He replied with a single wrench emoji, and then: the mechanic is on his way, parts included.

The restaurant was called La Casuela and it smelled of cumin and scorched onions, and Maya had chosen it because the owner, Señora Reyes, had agreed to let her practice Spanish there every Thursday afternoon, before the dinner rush, in exchange for bussing tables. Maya sat at the corner table by the window with her phone flat on the white tablecloth, a short article from El País open on the screen, and a water glass she kept forgetting she wasn't supposed to touch because her hands were supposed to be free for gesturing.

The article was about a city in Spain banning cars from its center, and Maya could read most of it, slowly, the way she could pick her way across a rocky stream. Her problem was not vocabulary, exactly. Her problem was that every time she tried to summarize it aloud, it came out like a grocery list. "The city banned cars. The air is better. The shops lost money. Some residents are angry." Four true sentences standing in a row like strangers in an elevator, refusing to look at each other.

Señora Reyes came over with a rag and wiped the table next to Maya's even though it was already clean, which Maya understood was her way of listening without hovering. Maya tried again, out loud, feeling the syllables clunk. "The city banned cars. The air is better." She stopped. "It sounds like I don't think the two things have anything to do with each other."

"What is the article actually saying?" Señora Reyes asked, leaning on her mop.

Maya looked at the screen. "That it's complicated. The air got better, but, the shops, they lost money." And then she saw the word sitting there in the third paragraph, a word she had skimmed past three times because she didn't know it: sin embargo. "What does sin embargo mean?"

"However," Señora Reyes said, wringing out the rag.

Maya wrote it in the margin of her notebook, and something small shifted in her head, the way a key turns before the bolt actually moves. She went back through the article and found more of them: pero, por lo tanto, aunque. She had been treating them like decoration, little words she could skip on the way to the nouns and verbs, the way she skimmed ads at the top of a webpage. But they weren't decoration. They were doing something her grocery list couldn't do. However said: I know what I just told you, and here is the thing that pushes back against it. Every one of her arguments could stay grammatically simple, subject verb object, and still sound like an argument, as long as the hinge words were there.

She tried it. "The city banned cars, and the air is better. However, the shops lost money. Therefore, some residents want a change." It was clumsy. Her accent made embargo into something with too many syllables. But the sentences turned to face each other now, like people at a party who had finally been introduced. Maya sat back, amazed that one small word could reorganize everything around it.

"Better," Señora Reyes said, and went to greet a couple coming in from the cold.

Maya started to internalize it, not the dictionary meaning, which she could have recited all afternoon, but the move itself: state, then counterstate. She wondered whether English worked the same way for her without her noticing, whether every "but" she had ever spoken had been quietly holding two ideas in tension while she took the credit. She thought about her history teacher, Mr. Okafor, who could make a paragraph of short declarative sentences feel like a debate, and realized he was doing it with hinges, not with fancy verbs. It was almost disappointing, like learning a magician's trick was a mirror and some thread. Almost, but not quite. The trick still worked.

There was a boy, Diego, who bussed tables with her, sixteen like her, whose grandmother was the cook, and who took a gratuitous pleasure in correcting her vowels, drawing them out like taffy whenever she got one wrong, even when no one had asked him. He came over now, carrying a tub of dishes. "You're doing the robot," he said. "Ehm. The air. Ehm. Is better."

"I'm doing the robot in a new language," Maya said. "What's your excuse?"

He laughed, and she liked him for it, and she tried her summary again, this time on him, watching his face the way you watch a litmus test. When she got to sin embargo, she saw his eyebrows lift slightly, some involuntary recognition, and she knew the word had landed where she aimed it. He argued back, in English because he was lazy, that the article was biased, that the shop owners were exaggerating, and she caught herself reaching for sin embargo in English form, "however," and then pushing further, "but even if they're exaggerating, someone has to," and she stopped, because that wasn't the point she meant, or maybe it was, she wasn't sure yet.

That was the part she couldn't resolve. The hinges let her say that two things were in tension, but they didn't tell her which thing was true. She could connect any claim to any counterclaim and sound thoughtful doing it. Did the connective words make her smarter, or just more fluent-sounding? She could hear Mr. Okafor saying that a well-signaled bad argument was still a bad argument. But Señora Reyes, wiping down the bar, had said only "better," and she meant the whole thing, the breathing and the grammar together.

A family of four came in, shaking rain off their coats, and Maya got up to clear the corner table. She slipped her phone into her apron pocket, and her thumb, without her quite deciding it, found the article again under the cloth. Por lo tanto. Therefore, the city will expand the ban. She mouthed the words once, silently, watching the family settle into their seats, and then she stacked the plates two high and carried them toward the kitchen, already drafting, under her breath, "sin embargo" at the door.

The waiting room had one wall of windows and a rack of pamphlets, and Jordan stood in front of it like a man choosing a career. He had agreed, two weeks earlier, to train as a peer health educator for the sophomore wellness class, and Ms. Adeyemi had told him to show up at the clinic on Thursday to practice with real materials before he stood in front of thirty fifteen-year-olds. The rack offered him laminated options: contraception, condom use, STI testing, consent. He took one of each and sat down beside his mother, who was folding and unfolding the appointment slip.

"You're staring at those like they're final exams," she said.

"They kind of are." He spread the pamphlets across his knee. "I have to explain this stuff to people my age. Out loud. In a room." What he did not say was that the health class at his school had spent exactly one period on any of it, a period in which the teacher read a slide in a monotone and the boys in the back laughed at the word condom, and that Jordan suspected half of what he'd absorbed came from the internet, in pieces, some of it wrong. Ms. Adeyemi had used the phrase "media hegemony" about online misinformation, the way certain voices dominate a subject until everyone else just repeats them, and Jordan had written it down because he wanted to be the voice that interrupted.

When the nurse called his mother's name, Jordan gathered the pamphlets and followed her back. His mother sat on the crinkling paper of the exam table while the cuff tightened around her arm, and the nurse looked at the number on the screen and looked at it again.

"It's a little high today," the nurse said. "Not an emergency. But let's have the doctor talk with you."

The doctor came in with a laptop and a unhurried manner, and she asked about salt, sleep, stress, and then exercise, and his mother said, honestly, that she drove to work, sat at work, and drove home. "The good news," the doctor said, "is that regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including people who already have hypertension." She turned the screen so they could see the number. "Most days. Not weekends of heroics. Consistency."

"Hypertension," his mother repeated, tasting the word like something she'd been accused of.

"High blood pressure," the doctor said. "That's the name for it."

While his mother made small talk with the doctor about her sister's heart pills, Jordan sat by the window and worked something out on the back of a pamphlet. He wrote brisk walking, most days, then drew seven boxes and began filling them: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, a gap on Thursday for his training, Thursday again, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. When the doctor left, he showed his mother the boxes. "There's a loop through the park behind the school," he said. "It's about a mile. If I come home and we walk it before dinner, that's most days right there. I'll be coming back from practice anyway."

"You want to walk with your old mother," she said, but she was looking at the boxes, and her finger touched the Thursday gap. "You can miss a day," she said. "Most days isn't every day."

"That's what the doctor said. Exactly that." He folded the paper and put it in his jacket, and it occurred to him that this was the first fact he'd collected all morning that he actually trusted, because it had come with a number on a screen and a doctor's unhurried voice and not from a comment section.

The practice session with Nurse Practitioner Okafor happened in a small consult room with two chairs and a box of sample kits. She played a sixteen-year-old named Sam who wanted to know things, and Jordan, sweating through his shirt, explained condoms and the pill and the ring and the shot, stumbling only when he got the effectiveness numbers tangled, and Okafor corrected him with a look rather than a lecture. Then she asked the hard one. "Say Sam didn't want to stop and the other person did. What do you tell Sam?"

Jordan was quiet long enough that the clock on the wall became loud. "Consent isn't a form you get signed once," he said finally. "It's continuous. You check in, you pay attention, and silence or freezing isn't a yes. And if you're unsure whether you have a yes, you stop and ask, because being profligate with someone's trust is worse than an awkward pause." He hadn't planned the sentence; it arrived whole, and Okafor nodded once, which felt like being handed a diploma.

"Testing," she said. "Sam asks where."

"Here, or the county clinic. It's confidential. You can walk in, ask to be tested for infections, and they take a urine sample or a blood draw depending on what they're screening for. Results come back in about a week, and if anything shows up, most of it's treatable." He'd rehearsed this part in the shower that morning, externalize the fear, his brother had told him once, meaning put it outside yourself where you can look at it, and it had worked: the sentences came out level.

Walking out through the waiting room, pamphlets under his arm, Jordan saw his mother still at the front desk scheduling her follow-up. He held up the folded paper with the seven boxes. "Monday," he said. "The park loop. Six o'clock."

"Six," she said. "Bring a jacket."

The whiteboard in lab 2C still held the ghosts of fourth period: a half-erased list of numbers, a bracket, and in the corner, in green marker, the notation O(log n). Sarah copied it into her notebook before Mr. Reyes could wipe it away, then opened her laptop and stared at the empty file.

The assignment was due at the end of the period. Build a class in Java called Playlist, with private fields for the song titles, getter methods to read them, and a test that proved the getters worked. Mr. Reyes had inculcated the rule since September with the patience of a man who had watched too many students lose points to it: no field left public, no getter forgotten. Sarah had absorbed it the way she absorbed most rules, by writing them until they became the vernacular of her thinking, words she used without translating them first.

The problem was her test kept failing. She had written getTitle expecting the first song and gotten null, and the red bar in the test runner sat there like an accusation. Across the table, Devon leaned over, chewing his pen.

"You never initialized the array," he said.

"I did." She scrolled up. She hadn't, exactly. She had declared the private field and written the getter, and somewhere between the two she had assumed the list into existence. Devon didn't say anything, which was worse than gloating, and she fixed it in six keystrokes and ran the test again. Green. She let out a breath she'd been holding since second period.

"Sarah." Mr. Reyes was at the board now, marker uncapped. "Before we vote on which search the class implements next week, tell us what that means." He tapped the green notation. "You wrote half of it down before I even erased."

She stood, and her mouth went dry. She knew this, she realized; she knew it because last night she had read the chapter twice, arguing with it in the margins the way she argued with her mother, which was to say carefully, without raising her voice. "Linear search is O(n)," she said. "The work grows in step with the list. Twice the songs, twice the looking." Devon's pen had stopped. "Binary search is O(log n), so the work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. The list can get huge and the work barely keeps up."

"Which do we use?" Mr. Reyes asked.

"That depends," Sarah said, and Mr. Reyes's dour expression flickered, the way it did when a student refused to hand him a clean answer. "Linear search doesn't need the list sorted. Binary search does. So if the list changes all the time, sorting it might cost more than you save."

"So which one?"

"I'd want to know how often it changes before I vote." She sat down. Her hands were shaking slightly, and she pressed them flat against the desk.

The vote went to binary search anyway, eleven to six. Devon voted for it and shrugged at her afterward, as if to say the class had chosen the smarter-sounding word, and maybe it had. Sarah wasn't sure she'd been wrong to hedge, and she wasn't sure she'd been right either, and that uncertainty sat with her through lunch like a stone in her pocket that she kept reaching in to touch.

After school she stayed in the lab. Her Playlist class was done, getters tested and passing, but she added a search method anyway, linear first, because it was honest: it worked on any list, sorted or not. Then she sorted the list and wrote the binary version beside it. She wrote a test with ten thousand song titles and timed both, watching the numbers print. The linear one climbed with the list, step for step. The binary one barely moved.

She looked at the two timings for a long moment, then opened her notebook to the page where she'd copied the green notation from the board. Underneath it she wrote: both are true. Use the one the situation earns. Then she closed the notebook, shut the laptop, and carried both out into the hallway, where the lights were already clicking off behind her, room by room.

The wifi in the cafeteria of Northgate High was down again, which meant Eric had forty minutes between rounds, a dead laptop battery, and a scholarship application open on his phone that he had been avoiding since August. The prompt wanted a ten-minute play about a moment from his own life, and the deadline was Monday. He had assumed he would never apply, and had been quietly amortizing the cost of that decision across the whole semester, a little regret each week, manageable, like a payment plan. Now the tournament schedule had trapped him in a folding chair with nothing else to do.

"Is this about losing?" Priya dropped into the seat across from him, still wearing her Extemp blazer, and read over his shoulder before he could lock the screen. She was his partner in Public Forum and, as of this year, a drama kid, which Eric privately considered a betrayal. "Because if you're writing a play, you can't write it like a case. Nobody gives a constructive speech in a kitchen."

"It's not a play yet. It's a panic." He turned the phone toward her anyway. He trusted Priya more than he trusted most people, which is to say he trusted her to be honest in a way that stung slightly. "I don't even know where it starts. The moment I want to write about is the day my dad taught me to drive and we didn't talk the whole time, and then at the end he said, good, like I'd passed some test nobody explained."

Priya stole a napkin from the stack by the pretzels and flattened it against the table. "Okay. So at drama camp this summer, this girl drew me this." She sketched fast: a triangle, cut into slices by horizontal lines. She labeled the bottom slab, then worked upward with her pen. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid in his 1863 book on drama technique. Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, bottom to top."

"That's a triangle, not a pyramid," Eric said, because it was easier to argue about geometry than to think about his father.

"Freytag called it a pyramid, take it up with Freytag." She jabbed the pen at the top slice. "The question is where your climax goes. Driving with your dad, silence, then 'good.' Where's the peak?"

Before he could answer, a kid from another school leaned over from the next table, wearing a Harvard sweatshirt three sizes too big. "Are you two doing Dramatic Interp? Because I have the best DI piece about a lighthouse keeper, it made a judge cry in Ohio."

"Nobody's crying in Ohio," Priya said. "That's the state motto." The kid wandered off, wounded, and Eric realized he was laughing, which felt like the first non-debate thing he'd done all day.

He took the napkin and drew the drive onto it, placing scenes along the pyramid the way he'd place contentions along a case: backing out of the driveway as exposition, the near-miss with the mailbox as rising action. Then he stopped. In debate, structure was armor; you knew every rebuttal before it arrived. But the drive hadn't felt like that. The drive had felt like determinism, honestly, like every silent minute had been decided before the engine started, and the strange part, the part worth writing, was that his dad had felt it too. Eric had seen it in his hands on the wheel. He wrote in the margin of the napkin: the climax is not the mailbox. The climax is his knuckles when the turn signal clicks.

"Wait, that's good," Priya said, reading it upside down, an annoying talent of hers. "But now you need falling action. What happens after the knuckles?"

"Nothing happens after the knuckles. That's the problem. He says good and we go inside." Eric looked at the pyramid, at the neat slice labeled resolution sitting at the bottom like it was owed to somebody. "What if I just don't resolve it? What if the play ends on good?"

Priya considered this the way she considered a risky framework in round, which meant she pursed her lips and stole another pretzel. "Freytag's pyramid is a description, not a law. You could end on the climax. Judges might hate it."

"Judges aren't my dad." He heard how it came out, more bitter than he meant, and Priya didn't flinch, just slid the napkin back toward him.

"Your next round's in twelve minutes," she said. "Write the falling action tonight. Even if it's just them standing in the garage." She stood, straightened her blazer, and then, because she was Priya, added, "Also you have an incipient mustard situation on your tie."

Eric looked down. He dabbed at it with the corner of the Freytag napkin, smearing exposition across the silk, and the Harvard sweatshirt kid passed by again and said, sincerely, "It adds character." Eric folded the napkin into his pocket, pyramid inward, and went to find his room.

The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of dust and radiator heat, and Faith had spread her score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C across the folding table usually reserved for coffee hour. She was there because the church was quiet on weekday afternoons and because her grandmother kept the key. Music theory was the one class she had chosen against her mother's advice, her mother being of the opinion that AP scores were a kind of currency and that electives were for people with money to spare. Faith's household had never been penurious, not exactly, but it had been careful, and careful households did not spend their savings on paper printed with notes.

She had a pencil with a good eraser and three colors of sticky tabs, and her assignment was to mark the form of the first movement: exposition, development, recapitulation. She had listened to the piece eleven times on the bus, and she had a theory about where the exposition ended, at the repeat sign, obviously, but also a smaller theory about the second theme, whether it arrived at the measure she thought or six bars later when the left hand changed. Between theories, she was learning to hold both of them at once, which was not something she had been taught to do anywhere.

Her grandmother came in at four with two thermoses and a hymnal under her arm, sat down across the table, and began folding the leftover bulletins from Sunday into fans. "You're still on that Mozart," she said. It wasn't a question. She had sung in this choir for forty years, had directed it for twelve, and had retired the year Faith was born, which Faith sometimes thought of as a door closing just before she reached it.

"Listen to this," Faith said, and played the recording through the small speaker she'd brought. When it reached the end, her grandmother made a small sound, almost a hum of approval, and then, without asking, hummed the final phrase herself, adding two notes that weren't in Mozart at all, notes that fell like a soft descent.

"What did you just sing?" Faith stopped the recording.

"Amen," her grandmother said. "You end the hymn and you land the Amen. That's how it goes." She hummed it again, slower, and this time Faith heard it: the chord underneath the word shifted once, a single step, and settled.

Faith pulled her theory workbook toward her and flipped until she found the page, and there it was in the margin of her own notes from Tuesday, half asleep in third period. "That's the four chord going to the one chord," she said. "We have a name for it. The Amen cadence." She checked the diagram against the sound still ringing in her memory. "People in class laughed, but it's literally because that's where hymns sing the Amen."

"Imagine," her grandmother said, dry as the radiator air. "Church had it first." She said it lightly, but Faith caught something underneath, the particular steadiness her grandmother wore when the world had rearranged something she'd assumed was hers. Faith's mother had that same steadiness, worn the same way, whenever Faith mentioned the college application that was not a pre-med track.

Faith went back to the score with the new chord in her ear. She placed a tab at the double bar and wrote exposition in the margin, then played the recording again from the beginning, listening now for how Mozart ended the whole movement, how the final chords differed from that plagal step her grandmother had hummed. It did not match, and she felt an odd disappointment, as though the two kinds of ending should have agreed. The sonata closed in a way that was firmer, more final, and she understood that the Amen was something else, an ending that leaned on what came before it rather than declaring itself.

An epicure of arguments, her uncle called himself, meaning he liked them well made, and Faith had inherited the taste; she wanted the form of the movement to be a structure she could defend line by line. So she defended it aloud, to her grandmother, over the bulletins: first theme in C, transition, second theme in G, exposition closes, development wanders through the minor, recapitulation brings the second theme home to C instead of G. Her grandmother listened with her head tilted, then interposed a hand over the score. "You said the middle part wanders. Does he not know where he's going?"

"He knows," Faith said. "He just doesn't tell us yet." She lifted her grandmother's hand, gently, and marked the development with the blue tab.

What she could not decide, and said so, was whether the second theme began at the measure with the trill or the measure after, and she wrote both numbers in the margin with a question mark, because pretending to be sure would have been a kind of lying and she was tired of that particular kind. Her grandmother packed up the thermoses and stood in the doorway with the hymnal under her arm, and paused there, humming the Amen again, the four chord falling to the one, and Faith, alone with the open score, hummed the last note with her.

The sea oats bent all one way, and Laura walked under them with her flashcards sweating in her back pocket. Tomorrow morning she would stand in front of the honors seminar and explain, in eight minutes, how greenhouse gases trap heat, and then read aloud the meaning of a graph she had only half understood when she'd copied it from the library printer. She had come to the beach because her apartment was too quiet and the beach was the opposite of quiet, which somehow helped her think.

Her younger brother, Dev, was already at the waterline, standing where each wave died in a run of foam. He was supposed to be helping her drill the material. Instead he was drawing in the wet sand with a stick, a long wobbling line that curved north along a shape he'd scratched out, a shape with a tail like Florida.

"That's not a beach thing," she said. "That's a museum thing."

"Field trip Tuesday," Dev said, not looking up. "There's a current map on the wall, glass, with arrows. The teacher let us touch it." He put his finger at the wide part of his drawing. "It's called the Gulf Stream. It's a warm current. It comes out of the Gulf of Mexico, goes through the Florida Straits, then runs north along the east coast of the United States." He traced it again, slowly, like he was memorizing it for a quiz. "That's why the water's warm here even in October. Sort of. I think."

Laura crouched beside the drawing. In her flashcards, sunlight passed through the atmosphere and the Earth absorbed it and re-emitted it as infrared, and molecules like carbon dioxide absorbed the infrared and sent part of it back down, so the surface kept more heat than it would otherwise. She could recite that in her sleep. The graph was the problem: a line crawling sideways for decades, then bending upward like something deciding to stand. She had printed it at eleven the night before, and the bend had looked small, and she had thought, that's it? That little bend is what everyone is shouting about?

"Quiz me," she said.

Dev flicked water off his stick. "I don't know any of it."

"You know the Gulf Stream."

"Quiz me on that, then."

So she did, and he got it right, all of it, the Gulf of Mexico and the Florida Straits and the direction, north along the east coast, and she made him say it twice because she wanted to hear the order of it. Then she made him hold the flashcards while she explained absorption and re-emission to the horizon, and the waves came in behind her voice like a diminuendo, each breaker softer than the last as the tide eased off.

"Here's the part I can't do," she said finally. She sat down in the dry sand above his drawing and smoothed a patch flat. With her finger she drew the graph, axis by axis, the flat creep and then the bend. "Tomorrow they'll ask me what it means. And I keep saying, carbon dioxide over the last century, rising, and everyone nods, but the graph doesn't say rising. It says faster. The bend is the sentence. The bend says whatever was happening before, more of it is happening now."

Dev studied her sand-graph. "So tell them that."

"They want a prognostication. What happens next. The teacher literally said, so what does the future hold." She pulled a knee up. "And I don't know. I can say if the line keeps its bend, more trapped heat, warmer water. I can't say what the Gulf Stream does. Nobody at my level can."

"Then say that."

"Say what, I don't know?"

"Say what you do know first, then say what you don't." He tapped the flat part of her graph, then the bend. "Even I can see there's two different things there. The flat thing and the standing-up thing. That's two facts, not one."

A jogger passed behind them, headphones in, indifferent. Laura looked at his sand map of the current and her sand copy of the curve, both already softening where the groundwater seeped up through the beach. She thought about her father, who drove an hour each way for the job that paid for her tuition deposit and who called the whole subject a religion for indigent pessimists, and she thought about Dev's teacher letting eleven-year-olds touch the glass over the arrows, and she understood that she had been trying to make the graph into an argument, a weapon for one side or the other, when it was more like the Gulf Stream itself: a thing flowing through, warm where it passed, and chartable only so far.

"Draw the Straits again," she said. "The narrow part. I want to see if the warm line narrows there."

He crouched and redrew it, the current squeezing through between the land, widening again as it headed north. "If they ask you about the future," he said, "you could just draw it. Like this. And stop where you stop."

Laura took the stick from him and pressed a short line into the sand beyond the last of his arrows, then set the stick down. "There. That's as far as it goes."

Justin sat on the swing at the far end of the playground, knees apart, a folded copy of his application in one hand. His cousin Dara stood in the wood chips in front of him holding a printed list of questions and a phone to record the time. The job was at the garden center by the river, twenty hours a week, and the interview was Monday.

"Question one," Dara read. "Tell me about yourself."

"I'm Justin, I just graduated, I worked the cash register at my uncle's store, I can lift fifty pounds." He said it to the fence behind Dara's head.

"That's the answer your dad made you memorize," Dara said. "Look at me when you say it. You're interviewing with the manager, not the fence."

That was the problem, and both of them knew it before anyone said it out loud. His father had drilled him for two evenings in the kitchen: steady eye contact, hold it through the answer, that's what confidence looks like in an interview here. Then his grandmother had watched one of the practice sessions from the doorway, and when he held his father's gaze for a full question and answer she had remonstrated with him, sharp and quiet at the same time, saying that staring straight at a senior person that long was rude, that a young man should lower his eyes and show respect. His father said she was talking about the old country. She said he was talking about television. Justin had gone to bed with both instructions in his head and no way to follow them at once.

He tried it now. He looked at Dara's eyes and began the answer again, and four words in he dropped his gaze to the wood chips, then dragged it back up, then away again. Dara stopped the timer.

"You look like you're flinching."

"I'm not flinching. I'm deciding."

"Decide before Monday."

He stood up off the swing and walked to the water fountain by the slide, which had been dry since spring, and pressed the button anyway out of habit. He was thinking about which of them was actually right, and he noticed he had been framing it that way, as though one of them had to be wrong. But his grandmother had spent forty years in offices in Seoul before she retired here, and his father had been interviewing and hiring people in this city for fifteen. It was possible they were both describing something real, in different rooms, and the difference was the rooms.

"Ask me the question again," he called back. "Don't tell me when you're going to."

Dara folded his arms. "Tell me about yourself."

Justin walked back toward him and answered the whole thing, forty seconds, watching Dara's face the entire time, and this time it held, because he had stopped trying to do both things at once and had chosen. The manager at the garden center was local. Her name was on the email, a name like half the names in his graduating class. Whatever was true of prolonged gaze in a room in Seoul, this interview was in the room it was in, and Justin decided he would meet her eyes and not count the seconds while he did it.

"I don't know if it's respectful," he said. "I don't actually know what she'll think. Maybe she'll find it too much."

"Too much?"

"Some people do. That's the part I can't know from here." He picked the application off the swing and folded it along its original creases. The paper had his grandmother's handwriting in the margin from the night she'd watched, three small characters he couldn't read, next to the line about customer service. He had assumed she was correcting him. Now he looked at it longer and thought she might have been correcting his father.

The afternoon was cooling and the playground had emptied except for a man reading on a bench near the riparian walk that ran behind the equipment, the strip of mown grass between the fence and the river. The days after graduation had felt like an interregnum, school over and the job not yet begun, and Justin had been filling them with forms and practice and this swing. He put the application in his back pocket.

"Monday, ten o'clock," Dara said, gathering the list of questions. "You want one more run-through?"

"One more," Justin said, and sat back down on the swing. "Ask me why I want to work at a garden center."

Jade spread the two articles across the library table like cards she didn't trust, the way her grandmother used to lay out a hand of solitaire before admitting it was lost. The first, printed from a database and curling at the edges, was by a researcher named Okafor, who had surveyed thirty students at a rural school about whether part-time jobs hurt their grades. The second, on her laptop screen, came from a team who had surveyed thirty thousand students across four counties and asked almost the same question. Both had found the same thing: students who worked fewer than fifteen hours a week did slightly better, not worse. Jade had underlined the two conclusions in different colors and then sat there, stalled, because her assignment demanded a critical review, not a summary, and she could not yet see what separated them.

"You look like you're divorcing somebody," said Marcus, dropping into the chair opposite with his own stack of books. He was applying to eight colleges and had been living in the library since September, surviving on vending machine crackers and the impecunious pride of refusing his mother's lunch money.

"I'm supposed to compare them. But they agree. How do I critique two things that agree?"

"Then the critique is why one of them shouldn't be trusted as much." He stole a cracker of his own from his pocket, which defeated the whole point of refusing hers.

She almost dismissed him, and then she looked again at the methods sections she had skimmed the night before, half asleep. Okafor: thirty students, one school, one semester. The other team: thirty thousand, four counties, three years. She remembered her statistics unit in the spring, the unit she had survived by memorizing formulas the night before. There had been a line in the textbook she'd photographed and never reread, something about how much you could lean on a number depending on how many people it came from. She pulled the photo up on her phone. Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one. She read it twice, and the two articles rearranged themselves in her head without her permission. Okafor's finding and the big team's finding were the same finding, but they were not the same evidence. One of them was a whisper; the other was a chorus.

A memory surfaced, uninvited. Eighth grade, her cousin DeShaun at the kitchen table, telling the family he was dropping out of his community college survey course because he'd concluded statistics was just a way to make lies sound official. Her aunt had laughed and poured him more tea. Jade, thirteen, had laughed too, and had carried that joke for four years like a coin in her pocket, pulling it out whenever a number was cited at her. Now she sat in the library feeling the coin go thin in her fingers. DeShaun had been wrong, but not entirely; the numbers weren't lies, they were just wearing different amounts of armor, and only one of these articles had bothered to say so out loud.

"Wait," she said to Marcus. "Okafor's the small one, right? Thirty kids?" He leaned over. She showed him the two methods sections, side by side. "So if I'm reviewing these, I can't treat the conclusions as equal. The thirty-thousand study's result is more precise. Okafor's same result has a wider margin of error. That's actually the whole hinge of my paper."

Marcus squinted at her laptop. "Couldn't you argue Okafor's is richer? Thirty interviews versus a survey form."

"I could." She meant it. The small study had quoted students at length, had followed them through a semester, had noticed things a checkbox never would. The large one had flattened thirty thousand lives into percentages. That was its own kind of loss, and she found she wasn't willing to pretend otherwise.

By last period she had a page and a half. She wrote that the large study should anchor the claim, then allowed that Okafor's work usefully problematized the tidy picture, raising questions the big survey's design couldn't hear. In the margin of her notebook she drafted the sentence she suspected was the most honest thing she'd written all year: the review could weigh the two against each other, but it could not fully reconcile them, and she did not think anyone could. She thought of adding DeShaun's line about lies sounding official, then flipped it, testing it, decided the truth was worse and better at once: numbers could be honest and still not settle anything. She deleted the draft sentence and let the uncertainty stand in the body of the paper, unexplained.

At the circulation desk on her way out, the librarian, Ms. Ferreira, stamped her interlibrary loan, a book Okafor had cited about the historiography of student labor research, how each generation of scholars had asked the question according to its own worries. Jade balanced it on top of the articles, one hand on the strap of her bag. Marcus was still at the table in the window, four crackers deep, waving her over to look at something on his screen. She stood a moment in the doorway between the stacks and the hall, then walked back and set her bag down beside his.

The cuff hissed, and Parker counted the ticks as the needle settled, the way the nurse had shown him in the hospital room two weeks after his father came home. His father sat at the kitchen table with his sleeve rolled up, reading the sports section, his forearm dusted with the fine gray hair that Parker somehow had never noticed before. One fortyy-six over ninety. Parker wrote it in the notebook, then slid the notebook out of sight when his father glanced over.

The first number had been higher. At the follow-up appointment on Tuesday, the machine in the exam room had flashed something in the sixteens over the high nineties, and Parker had watched his father's face go still and formal, the way it did at funerals. But the doctor had only leaned back on his stool and asked, before prescribing anything, whether they could measure at home instead. "Sometimes it reads high just from being in here," she said. "It's called white coat hypertension." Then she'd handed Parker a cuff and a pamphlet, as if he were the patient's secretary rather than his son.

Parker had spent three evenings with the pamphlet and then with the laptop, past his old habit of stopping at the first result. He learned that the top number was the pressure when the heart pushed, the bottom when it rested, and that the numbers answered to slow things: salt pulling water into the blood, walking widening the vessels over time, weight easing the work of the pump. It was less like chemistry than like argument. Everything negotiated. Nothing decided in a single reading.

His father had spent thirty years deciding otherwise. Parker remembered the summers his father had driven to job sites on two hours of sleep, the birthday he'd waved off chest pain as "garbage from the drive-through," the capricious way he'd take the stairs one month and refuse them the next. Now he was supposed to convalesce, a word the discharge papers used and nobody in the house said aloud, and he treated it as a foreign occupation, some temporary hegemony of doctors and pill organizers that would eventually be overthrown.

"Dad. Arm."

His father folded the paper. "You're enjoying this."

"Somebody has to write the numbers down." Parker wrapped the cuff, aligned the marker over the artery the way the diagram showed, and pressed the button. While the machine inflated, his father studied the window over the sink, where the tomato plants had gone leggy and brown. When it finished, the screen read one thirty-two over eighty-four.

"Better," Parker said, and logged it, and then sat back. Better than Tuesday at the hospital, anyway. But Thursday it had been one thirty-eight, and Saturday morning, after pancakes, one fortyy-two, and he still couldn't say which of those was the real one, or whether the real one was a single thing at all. The doctor had said she'd want a fuller picture before deciding about medicine, maybe even a monitor that read all day, and Parker understood now that she wasn't being cautious. She was refusing to let one frightened number in one bright room speak for his father's whole life.

"So what's it mean," his father said. It wasn't really a question. He was looking at the notebook now, at the column of figures in Parker's careful print.

"It means the machine at the clinic was scared of you." Parker tapped the page. "Here, at home, you're lower. Not perfect. The walk Dr. Reyes wants you doing, the salt thing, that's what moves it over weeks. It doesn't jump in a day."

His father was quiet long enough that Parker heard the refrigerator cycle on, a low hum under the room. Parker thought of asking him, finally, about those years of drive-throughs and skipped physicals, whether he'd known, whether knowing would have changed anything. He didn't ask. He wasn't sure he wanted the answer more than he wanted the afternoon.

"We walking tonight or not?" his father said. He rolled his sleeve down, but slowly, and left the paper folded on the table.

Parker closed the notebook. "After dinner. And I'm cooking."

"No salt."

"Some salt," Parker said, and got up to see what was left in the crisper.

The trail switchbacked up through pines that smelled like heat given up reluctantly, and Laurence kept the folded graph in her back pocket like a confession she had not yet made. Tomorrow morning she was supposed to stand in front of eleven middle schoolers at the library's summer program and explain why carbon dioxide matters, and she had promised the coordinator, Mrs. Okafor, that she "knew the material." She did not. She knew the graph existed. She knew the line went up. That was the extent of her expertise, and the extent of her lie.

"I still don't get why you didn't just say no," Priya said, two steps behind her, breathing harder than she let on.

"Because I need the service hours. Because it felt like an easy yes at the time." Laurence stopped where the trail opened onto granite, the lake below them flat and bright as a coin. "You can titrate a good decision, you know. Add the commitment drop by drop until you find the exact point where it turns into a disaster. I skipped straight to the disaster."

"So un-titrate it. Learn it today. You have until nine tomorrow."

Laurence pulled out the graph, a printout she'd made at the library, and flattened it against a boulder. The line began low and level, a patient almost-flat stretch through the fifties and sixties, then bent upward and climbed in a sawtooth scribble, up and up, small drops and recoveries, a staircase of seasons. She had looked at it the night before and understood nothing except that the shape frightened her in a way she couldn't articulate to anyone, least of all a room of twelve-year-olds.

"Read it to me," Priya said, dropping onto the rock with her water bottle. "Like I'm one of your middle schoolers."

"Okay. So this is carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The little dips every year are summer in the northern hemisphere, when plants are growing and pulling it back out. And the overall line climbs." She traced it with her finger, and something shifted as she did, the way a sentence in a foreign language suddenly parses. "It's not climbing evenly. It's accelerating. The last decades are steeper than the first ones."

"That's it? That's your whole talk?"

"No, that's the graph. The mechanism is different. The sun sends light in, and the Earth sends heat back out, and carbon dioxide lets the light through but catches some of the heat on the way out. Like a blanket that only traps the outgoing stuff." She paused. "I think. I need to say it better than that."

Priya was already typing on her phone, thumbs moving with the sure speed of someone who had never once doubted that answers were findable. "Last night at the planetarium someone asked whether climate predictions only started with computers, and the speaker said no, but she didn't give details. Hold on." She squinted. "Okay, here. In 1896, a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled."

"Eighteen ninety-six?" Laurence took the phone. "Before cars were common. Before anyone was even measuring CO2 in the air. He calculated it by hand?"

"That's what it says. First calculation, doubled carbon dioxide, how much Earth would warm."

Laurence sat down slowly on the warm granite. She had been thinking of the graph as a modern thing, a product of satellites and supercomputers, and the knowledge that the central question had been asked in the nineteenth century rearranged something. It was like the moment in her historiography seminar, the one day she'd been allowed to sit in with her mother's college class, when she'd understood that history isn't what happened but the argument about what happened, layer after layer of retelling. Arrhenius had asked the question before the evidence existed to answer it. The graph was only the answer arriving, a century late, in a language of rising lines.

"I should lead with him," she said. "Start with the person, not the science. Twelve-year-olds don't care about parts per million. They might care about a guy in Sweden in 1896 doing math by hand about a future he'd never see."

"See, you're already teaching. Try the mechanism again, for real this time."

Laurence held up her hands, palms out. "Light comes in. It passes through. The Earth warms up and tries to send heat back out, and the carbon dioxide stops some of it. More carbon dioxide, more heat kept." She dropped her hands. "Is that too simple? Is it wrong? I can't tell the difference between simple and wrong."

"That's not simple and wrong," Priya said. "That's simple and true. Those aren't the same thing, and you keep acting like they are." She took a long drink and looked at the lake, where a pelagic cormorant, far from open water for some reason of its own, cut across the glare and vanished behind a point. "The stuff you're unsure about, leave room for it. Kids can smell a fake answer anyway."

They walked back down through the pines with the sun low and orange behind the trunks, and Laurence rehearsed the opening under her breath, twice, then a third time, changing the order of the sentences each time. At the trailhead she stopped, took out the graph one last time, and folded it along the steep final decade, so that when she opened it tomorrow in front of the class, the first thing they would see was the climb.

"Arrhenius," she said to Priya, zipping the paper into her pack. "I'm going to write his name on the whiteboard and let them try to pronounce it."

Alexandre pushed the coffee table against the wall and dragged two kitchen chairs to opposite sides of the living room, which was all the stage he had. The play was a one-act about two brothers dividing their dead father's tools, nineteen pages he had found in a library anthology, and his actors were arriving in forty minutes. He had taped an X on the floorboards where the imaginary workbench stood. That was the extent of his directing so far, and it did not feel like enough.

His mother's book club had been cajoled into moving to Thursday by the promise of a lemon cake he had not yet started, and his little sister had been bribed with screen time to stay upstairs, though she was already leaning on the banister, watching him measure the distance between the chairs with his feet.

The actors were two boys from his grade, Tomas and Felix. Tomas was tall and deliberate and had been in every school production since seventh grade. Felix was newer, quick-moving, and famously irascible when corrected, so Alexandre had spent the morning deciding which notes to give him and in what order, softening each one in his head like sanding a rough edge.

They ran the first scene on their feet almost immediately, because Alexandre had read somewhere that talking about a scene before doing it was a kind of artifice, a way of seeming productive while avoiding the actual risk. So they stood, and he sat on the stairs with the script, and they began.

The trouble arrived by the fourth page. Felix crossed toward the workbench, which the script required, and each time he crossed, he ended up directly between Tomas and the taped X, and the audience, which was the staircase, lost Tomas entirely. Alexandre could see only Felix's shoulders and the flicker of Tomas's hand gestures behind them. They finished the scene anyway, because he had not learned yet how to stop a run without feeling rude.

"Did it look all right?" Felix asked, hopeful, still standing in Tomas's light.

Alexandre considered several answers. "Part of it vanished," he said. "Tomas, you were gone whenever he moved."

"I kept moving over," Tomas said, stepping sideways with the weary patience of someone who had done this for years. "He follows the same track every time. I'd shift, then he'd land right in front of me again."

They ran it again, and Alexandre watched not the actors but the shape they made together, the negative space of the room. When Felix crossed, Tomas drifted a step to his left, unhurried, almost unconscious, and Alexandre noticed that afterward the two of them framed the space more evenly, both of them held in view. It looked, for a moment, composed rather than accidental.

"What did you just do?" Alexandre asked.

"Countering," Tomas said, as if naming a town he passed through often. "You move to balance it out."

Alexandre wrote the word in the margin of his script, then underlined it, and beneath it he wrote the whole thing out plainly: one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, so both stay visible. It was not a line of dialogue, not a feeling, not even really acting, and yet the scene had become suddenly watchable the moment it happened. He had spent two weeks thinking directing meant having opinions about tone and pauses. This was something else, closer to geometry, and he liked the way the two kinds of thinking sat beside each other without settling which mattered more.

"Felix," he said, "when you cross, go ahead and cross, but slower on the last two steps. Tomas will adjust. Tomas, counter earlier, before you're walled in, not after."

They ran it four more times. On the third, Felix snapped that he was being told to walk like a funeral procession, and Alexandre let the moment sit until Felix tried it again on his own. On the fourth run, the crossing and the counter arrived together so smoothly that Alexandre forgot to watch for them and simply watched the brothers argue over a hacksaw that was not there.

From the banister his sister said, "That one was good. Do that one again."

"Go upstairs," Alexandre said, but he said it while already reaching for his pencil, because there was something in the margin he wanted to fix.

Savannah had come to her grandparents' house to study, on the theory that a screen door and a ceiling fan made better company than her phone. In eleven days she would take the economics placement exam that decided whether she started college in the intro lecture hall or skipped ahead, and she had promised her mother she would know the material cold. She did not know it cold. She knew it the way she knew the route to the pool, well enough to arrive, not well enough to draw it.

Her grandfather found her on the porch with her notes spread across the wicker table, and he set down a jar of his clover honey beside her textbook like an offering. Saturday was the farmers' market, where he sold honey and Mrs. Okafor, two stalls over, sold apples, and the two of them had been circling each other all week about a trade. He did not ask what she was reading. He said, "When you've finished pretending to study, I need a judge."

"I'm not pretending," Savannah said, though she had read the same paragraph on inflation four times without feeling it attach to anything.

"Then explain it to me while we walk the rows," he said. "If I can understand it, anyone can."

The market occupied the gravel lot behind the fire hall, white canopies snapping in the wind. Her grandmother had come along only for the blood draw at the mobile clinic parked at the edge of the lot; she was arguing with a nurse about whether her last antigen panel had really justified a second vial. Savannah left them to it and followed her grandfather past tables of bread and cut dahlias, rehearsing in her head.

"Interest rates," she began, and then made herself start over, slower. "When the central bank raises them, borrowing gets more expensive, so people and companies take out fewer loans, so they spend less and build less. There's less money chasing the same goods. Prices stop climbing so fast. That's how raising rates slows inflation." It came out flat the first time, a recitation, and she knew it. She tried again at Mrs. Okafor's stall, using the dahlias as an example, and then the apples themselves, and by the third telling it had a shape to it, an actual argument with joints in it. Her grandfather listened with his hands in his pockets and gave nothing away.

Then Mrs. Okafor turned to her grandfather and said, "All right, Frank. Three jars of honey for one basket of my apples, and we shake on it now."

"Two jars," her grandfather said. "Three's robbery."

"You'd give up three jars to grow that basket yourself," Mrs. Okafor said, sardonic, tapping the wooden rim. "You told me last autumn. Your bees and your apple trees share the same hour of your day."

"And you'd give up one jar," he said. "You told me your apple rows are so thick you barely notice a basket gone, but you'd have to buy a hive to make a single jar."

Savannah, standing between them with her notes still under her arm, felt the placement exam materialize in the gravel lot like a mirage. Both of them made both goods; both of them had said out loud what it cost them, in jars, to produce a basket of apples. Her grandfather's cost was three jars. Mrs. Okafor's was one. Somewhere in her notes was a rule about exactly this, and for a moment she could not find it, and the two of them were still haggling, four jars, two and a half, the deal drifting toward collapse.

"Wait," she said. "The trade only works for both of you if the rate is between your costs. Between one jar and three. She can't go below one, you can't go above three. Anything inside that, you both come out ahead. Anything outside, one of you loses." She heard herself say it and understood it at the same instant, the way you sometimes feel a stair with your foot. Two jars was inside. Three was the edge itself. She looked from one face to the other.

Mrs. Okafor studied her for a long moment, the wind snapping the canopy overhead, a dahlia petal coming loose and skidding between the stalls. "Whose child is this," she said, not really a question, and then she picked up the basket and set it in Savannah's grandfather's hands. "Two and a half jars, then, since you raised a judge. And I want the clover, not that buckwheat you palm off on tourists."

They shook on it. Her grandmother came back pressing cotton to the crook of her elbow, complaining that the nurse had emancipated her from her own opinion about her own veins, and the four of them walked the rows while the light went long and gold across the gravel.

That evening, back at the house, Savannah went looking for a book to prop the porch door and opened the wrong shelf. The spine she pulled out was thin and gray, stamped with a seal she recognized from her textbook's chapter on monetary policy, and inside the cover, in faded ink, was her grandfather's name and a date thirty years before she was born. She stood in the hallway holding it, and she did not yet know what she would say to him about it, or whether she would say anything at all.

She carried the book out to the porch, where he was wiping down empty jars in the last of the light, and she set it on the table between them, cover up.

"Well," he said, not looking at it, and not looking away from her either. "You were explaining interest rates. You stopped just where it gets interesting. Go on."

Gabriella set her fork down before she started talking, which her mother noticed, because her mother noticed everything. "I have to tell Marcus his practice interview was bad," she said. "He asked me to watch it, and it was bad, and he's going to want to know."

"Marcus from robotics?" her brother Theo asked, not looking up from his phone. "The one who talks for ten minutes before he gets to any point at all?"

"That one." The roast chicken sat in the middle of the table between the candles, and her grandmother's good plates were out because it was Sunday, and Sunday meant everyone came, even Theo, who spent most Sundays being querulous about having to come. "He's interviewing for that summer internship Friday. He filmed himself answering questions and sent it to me. He wants feedback before he goes in."

Her father carved a second piece of chicken for her grandmother. "Feedback is a kindness," he said. "Withheld criticism isn't tact, it's just cowardice wearing a nicer shirt." This was how her father talked, as though every dinner were a courtroom where he might have to litigate the ethics of passing the green beans. Usually Gabriella found it funny. Tonight it just pressed on the bruise she was already carrying.

"The problem is he'll argue," she said. "He'll say I don't know what I'm talking about, or that rambling shows enthusiasm, or something. And then I'll soften everything until I've said nothing at all." She pushed a piece of potato around her plate. She had watched Marcus's video three times, once at her desk and twice on the bus, and each time the same thing happened: the interviewer asked him to describe a time he'd solved a problem, and Marcus began with the founding of the robotics team, and by the four-minute mark she had lost the thread entirely and, she suspected, so had he. Nothing landed. Nothing ended anywhere.

Her mother passed the water pitcher. "Here's a postulate for you," she said. "People can hear a hard thing if they can see the shape of it first. Tell him the shape, then fill it in." Her mother did this, offered ideas the way she offered the pitcher, without insisting anyone take one.

Later, in her room, Gabriella found the sheet her college counselor had given the juniors in the spring, still folded in the front pocket of her binder. It was about interview answers. It said to use the STAR method, which structures an answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened. She read it twice. Marcus's answers had Situation and then more Situation and then a kind of fog. They never arrived at a Result. And she saw, with an odd flattening sensation, that her feedback could take the same shape. Here's the situation, Marcus. Here's what I was trying to do watching your video. Here's what I actually did, sat and watched and lost the thread. Here's the result, which is that you should try it this way. Even kindness, she thought, could ramble.

On Monday after practice, she sat across from him in the empty lab, the video pulled up on her laptop between them. "Before I say anything," she said, "I'm going to tell you the shape of it, so you know where I'm going. One thing that worked, one thing that didn't, one thing to try. That's all." Marcus nodded, arms crossed, already a little defended. "The robot demo part was great, you were specific and I could see it. The long story at the beginning, about how the team started, it loses the interviewer. You never say what happened in the end. Try Situation, Task, Action, Result, and stop when you get to the Result. Pick the sensor failure story and end on the fact that you fixed it."

Marcus was quiet long enough that she could hear the custodian's cart squeaking down the hall. Then he scrubbed the video back to the beginning. "Play it again," he said. "Count how long I go before anything happens." She counted. Two minutes and forty seconds of preamble. He winced at his own voice on the recording, then winced again, then laughed, and asked her to film a second take right there on her phone.

At Sunday dinner the following week, Theo asked, without irony, whether she'd do the same thing for him before his interview at the hardware store, because his practice answers, he admitted, went on forever. "You could use the STAR method too," Gabriella said. "Situation, Task, Action, Result." Theo frowned at his plate. "My result," he said, "is that I've never had a job, so I have no results."

The library smelled like radiator dust and old glue, and John had claimed the carrel by the window because it was the only one with an outlet. He spread his sources across the spartan desk: four articles, a book, a printout of a database search, and the assignment sheet on which Mr. Reyes had written, in red, "An argument, not a report." Three weeks. His topic, vaccination rates in rural counties, had seemed solid until he'd found two articles that disagreed completely, and he had no idea how to choose between them.

Marcus found him at lunch, slid into the opposite chair, and picked up the first article. "Which journal is this?"

"American Journal of Public Health. Why?"

"Throw it out." Marcus held up the other one, the one from the journal with the glossy cover John had found through a search engine. "This one's way better. Everybody knows."

"Knows what?"

"Knows it's more important. My cousin's at State, she says you check the number." Marcus tapped the corner of the page. "See, higher number, better journal. Better journal, better article. Basic."

John looked at the number. Then at his other article, whose page he turned until he found a different, smaller one. "It's not that simple."

"It's exactly that simple."

They left it there, but John couldn't leave it. After last period he went back to the database and typed in the phrase Marcus had used. The screen filled with results, and the third one down contained a definition he read three times. The impact factor, it said, devised by Eugene Garfield, was the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
