He copied it into his notebook word for word, because it felt like the kind of thing that could slip away from him if he paraphrased it badly.

He sat with it. The glossy journal had a big number; the public health journal, a smaller one. But the number counted citations, averages, two years, not quality. His article in the glossy journal was an opinion piece, he realized, when he looked again, written by a think tank fellow with no data. The other one was a study, with methods and tables and a section admitting its own limits. The number told him something about the journals, not about these two articles, and Marcus had skipped the middle step entirely.

At the writing club on Thursday, Marcus brought it up again, louder this time, leaning across the circle of chairs. "John's using the weak source because he won't admit the good journal beat it."

"It's called an impact factor," John said. "Average citations in one year to articles from the previous two years."

"So I'm right."

"You're half right. It measures citations. It doesn't measure this article." He held up the opinion piece. "This could be garbage in a journal people cite a lot. That's not the same as good."

Delia, a senior who never spoke at club, looked up from her notebook. "So what's the counterpoint? Why use the number at all?"

"Because a journal nobody cites, ever, might be publishing things nobody could verify," John said. "It's evidence. Just not the evidence Marcus thinks it is."

Marcus folded his arms. "You're just scared to pick a side."

That stung because it was half true. John went home and drafted the paper that night, and by Friday morning he had six paragraphs and a thesis: that rural vaccination rates fell not because of access alone but because of trust, and that the opinion piece, read against the study, revealed exactly where the trust argument was thin. He used the opinion piece. He used it as the position he was arguing against. In the margin of his draft he wrote a note to himself: the study's data was from four counties, and whether it generalized, he could not say.

The footnotes took him two hours in the library on Saturday, hunched over the style guide, counting periods and commas like a man defusing something. The bibliography took another hour. He kept both articles in it, listed evenly, side by side, and the evenness of the list pleased him, two perspectives given equal weight on the page before the argument itself chose between them.

Marcus appeared at the window of the carrel, backpack over one shoulder. "Finished?"

"Footnotes done." John turned the page so he could see. "You still think the number settles it?"

Marcus looked at the bibliography for a long moment. "I think you like losing arguments in slow motion."

"Hand me that style guide," John said, and held his pen over page nine.

The attic smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and Olivia had to duck under the sloped beam her grandmother had duct-taped with foam years ago. She had spread her ten sketchbooks across the floor like evidence at a trial, and none of them agreed with each other. Six landscapes from the lake, two portraits of her ex-best friend Dana, one charcoal of the broken greenhouse, and a watercolor of a bus station that she'd done at two in the morning and could not explain. The application wanted ten works around a single theme plus a statement of purpose, due in nine days, and she had arrived at her grandmother's house with a duffel bag and the beginnings of a headache.

"You're hiding up here," her grandmother said from the ladder, holding two mugs of tea. She was seventy-six and still painted every morning in the converted garage, though she sold almost nothing now, which Olivia had once thought was sad and now suspected was something else.

"I'm working."

"You're staring."

"That's part of working." But she took the tea. The mug was warm in her hands, and through the round window she could see the wind moving the birches, their leaves flashing silver then green then silver again, like the whole trees couldn't decide what color to be.

Her grandmother lowered herself onto the floor with a grunt, crossing her legs like a teenager, and thumbed through the sketchbooks without asking. She lingered on the greenhouse. "You drew the glass twice," she said. "Once broken, once whole. Same angle."

"That was an accident."

"It's the best accident you have."

Downstairs, in the hallway between the kitchen and the guest room, hung the print her grandmother had bought in Mexico City in 1971, before Olivia was born, before Olivia's mother was even married. Olivia had walked past it maybe forty times in her life. She stopped now because the hallway was cold and she had gotten up for more tea, and because a portfolio needs a thesis and she had none. The painting showed two women sitting side by side, holding hands, one in a white European dress with a clipped artery bleeding onto her skirt, one in Tehuana dress holding a small portrait of someone absent. She put her hand flat against the wall beside it, measuring by instinct, and then went back upstairs and got a tape measure from her grandfather's old toolbox.

Her grandmother found her on a kitchen chair with the tape measure extended along the wall, the metal trembling and kinking at arm's length.

"What on earth."

"It's huge," Olivia said. "The real one. I looked it up on my phone. It's oil, from 1939, and it's nearly square, about 173 centimeters each side. Both of them, the two of them together, filling almost six feet of canvas." She climbed down. "I always thought of it as a small thing. Something you lean in to see. But you'd have to stand way back. You'd have to give it the whole room."

Her grandmother sipped her tea and said nothing, which was how she said the most.

That night Olivia couldn't sleep, so she sat in the kitchen with the hallway light on, and she found herself trying to verbalize what she'd been circling all day without words: that a theme wasn't a subject, it was a wound you were willing to show from more than one side. The greenhouse drawn broken and whole. Dana laughing and Dana looking away. Maybe the theme was doubleness itself, the two versions of every person and place she couldn't choose between. She started a list of ten on a paper napkin, crossed out four, kept six, and understood with a small cold drop in her stomach that she'd have to discard some pieces she loved. The profligate ones, the bus station, the pretty lake at sunset, would have to go. It felt like a betrayal and also like the first honest decision she'd made about her own work.

The next morning she found the twist. She was looking for the guest room's spare blanket, which her grandmother kept in a trunk at the foot of the bed, and under the blanket, wrapped in a pillowcase, was a portfolio. A real one, old, the cardboard softened at the corners. Inside were ten drawings, all of the same woman: standing, reading, sleeping, at a window, laughing at something off-frame. They were beautiful and they were not her grandmother's style, and when Olivia turned the last one over, the paper was dated 1968 and initialed with her grandmother's maiden initials.

"You went to art school." Olivia stood in the doorway of the garage holding the portfolio, and her grandmother, who was mid-brushstroke on a hillside, set the brush across the jar and looked at it for a long time.

"I was accepted," her grandmother said. "I didn't go. Your grandfather got the job in Ohio, and it seemed, at the time, like the sensible thing." She wiped her hands on her apron, leaving a green streak. "Mine was all one woman. My mother. I thought that was a weakness, that I couldn't paint anything else. Now I think it was the only thing I knew how to do right, and I abandoned it for range."

Olivia wanted to say something wise and found she had nothing. All her planned words about sacrifice and risk sounded, in her head, like statements from college pamphlets. Her grandmother's sagacity had always worked this way, delivered sideways, and Olivia suspected the woman knew exactly how the story would land and had chosen today anyway.

They sat on the porch with the portfolio open between them, and the birches went on flashing, and Olivia showed her grandmother the napkin with the surviving list. Six pieces about doubleness, four to make new. "The statement's the worst part," Olivia said. "I can draw it. I can't write what it means without sounding like I'm lying."

"Then write what you're not sure of," her grandmother said. "Put that in. Nobody trusts a nineteen-year-old who's certain."

The wind came up and lifted the corner of the napkin, and Olivia caught it and turned it over, where the ink of her crossed-out titles had bled through from the other side, so that the lost pieces showed as pale ghosts behind the kept ones. She looked at that for a while. Then she got her phone, opened the notes app, and typed the first sentence, showing the screen to her grandmother, who read it and handed it back without comment, which was enough.

The museum's biology wing smelled like floor wax and vending machine coffee, and Maxime had it mostly to himself on a Tuesday afternoon in July. He stood in front of a wall-sized diagram of a cell, the mitochondrion blown up to the size of a small car, its folded inner membrane rendered in cross-section like a topographic map of some country he'd never visited. His biology final was behind him. He had passed, barely, and the deal with his mother was that he would come here once a week and actually learn what he had memorized, because memorizing and learning were, in her vocabulary, opposites. He wasn't sure he agreed. Memorizing had gotten him through the exam. Whether anything had gotten through him was the open question.

He had a worksheet from the museum's front desk, printed on blue paper, with questions in a font that tried too hard to be friendly. Trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP, it said, and he had honestly meant to do it at home, but home had Ana's messages stacked on his phone like unpaid bills, and the museum at least had the dignity of being nobody's.

He traced the outer edge of the diagram with his finger, not touching the wall, hovering an inch away like his mother had taught him around paintings. Glucose got broken down first, in the cytoplasm, that part he remembered. Then the fragments moved into the mitochondrion, into that maze of folded membrane, and here the worksheet got cagey. It asked him to place the steps in order and offered a touchscreen beside the diagram where he could drag little labeled blocks: glucose, pyruvate, electron transport chain, ATP, water. He dragged water to the end and the screen buzzed, red. Wrong, or not yet.

At that moment his phone vibrated in his pocket. It was Ana, message number four since morning: Are you seriously at the science museum again. I need an answer by Friday about the debate team. You said maybe and maybe is eating me alive. She had wanted the two of them to co-captain in the fall, her final year, her one grandiose plan for a senior season that would, in her telling, catalyze the whole club into something people actually watched. He had said maybe in June. Maybe had felt kind at the time. Now it felt like a coin he kept refusing to flip.

He typed back, At the museum, learning what I actually failed to learn, and put the phone face down on the touchscreen ledge. Then he looked at the word he'd dragged wrong. Water. The block had a small caption under it, written for someone younger than him: Oxygen you breathe in ends up here. He read it three times. His hand went up, absently, toward his own chest, and he felt slightly ridiculous, standing in an empty museum wing touching his sternum like a man in a play.

He worked the screen again, slower. Glucose, then pyruvate, then the middle steps whose names he'd crammed and half-forgotten, and then the block labeled electron transport chain, which he placed along the inner membrane on the diagram, and the screen finally accepted it, turning the folded membrane green. A kid of maybe nine wandered over, chin at ledge height, watching the colors change. "What's that one?" the kid asked, pointing at the green. "The electron transport chain," Maxime said. "It sits in the inner membrane. That's where the oxygen goes." The screen, patient, walked him the last step: oxygen waited at the end of the chain as the final electron acceptor, taking on protons, becoming water. Not metaphorically. In his own cells, presumably at this second, the air he'd pulled in at the door was being turned into water inside him. He thought of the water bottle in his backpack and could not decide if drinking felt different now or only seemed to.

He picked up the phone. Ana's message sat there with its deadline, and he thought about the way she said maybe is eating me alive, which was Ana all over, wanting an answer more than a particular answer. He had been treating his maybe as a way of keeping both doors open, and standing here he recognized, unwillingly, that he did the same thing with biology, with the exam, with most things: he kept the fact at arm's length so it could never be wrong in his mouth.

He typed, You can put me down as yes for debate. Then, before sending, he looked at it. The chain on the screen was still green, the water block still waiting at the end, oxygen becoming something quieter than anyone would guess. He deleted the yes and typed, Can I give you a real answer Thursday, in person. Not a maybe. A real one by Friday. He sent it and put the phone in his pocket, and the kid tugged his sleeve and said, "So the air turns into water," and Maxime said, "Yeah. The air turns into water," and dragged the last block into place.

The portfolio deadline was Friday at three, and by Tuesday Ella had nine finished pieces and no statement, which meant she had no theme, only nine paintings that happened to live in the same folder. Ms. Okafor had been clear on the first day: ten artworks around one idea, plus a page of writing that explained why the idea was hers. The art room stayed open until five on Tuesdays, so Ella spread the nine across two tables and stood back with her arms crossed, trying to see what a stranger would see.

Dana and Marcus came in arguing, the way they usually did, carrying their own portfolios like luggage. They dropped into the stools at the next table and Dana slapped a printout of The Two Fridas between them, a reproduction small enough to lose the brushwork but big enough to show the double figure seated hand in hand, hearts exposed.

"The one in the Tehuana dress is the real Frida," Dana said. "The Mexican one. The other one's basically a costume."

"That's backwards," Marcus said. "The European dress is who she actually was half the time, married to Diego, living in that world. The white Victorian one. You can't just pick the dress you like better."

"The white one's the one with the cut heart, though," Dana said, tapping the figure on the left. "That's the one being abandoned."

"That doesn't make her more real. That makes her sadder."

Ella came over, mostly to stop the argument before it got loud enough to bring Ms. Okafor out of the kiln room. She looked at the printout for a long moment. "Maybe neither one's the costume," she said. "Maybe the whole point is that she's both, sitting there holding her own hand." Dana and Marcus both started talking at once, and Ella held up a palm. "I don't mean that as a compromise. I mean both dresses are hers. That's why there are two of her."

Marcus turned sardonic, the way he did when he thought someone was dodging. "So nothing's the real anything. Convenient."

"Fine, then the real one is the pair," Ella said. "One Frida in the Tehuana dress, one in the European one, and the real subject is the space between them." She was mostly saying it to end the argument, but the sentence kept going in her head after she stopped saying it out loud.

She walked back to her nine paintings and laid them out again in a different order. There was her grandmother's kitchen table with the plastic tablecloth; there was the school parking lot at dusk; there was the self-portrait she'd done holding her mother's rosary even though she didn't pray. She had been telling herself these were separate things, one for home and one for school, the way she was one person in Spanish at the dinner table and another in English in the hallway, and she had thought of that split as a problem the portfolio needed to route around. Dana and Marcus had wanted to know which Frida was real, and the painting refused to choose, and Ella understood suddenly that her folder had been refusing to choose all semester. Ten pieces about standing in two places at once, holding her own hand. It wasn't a dodge, or not only a dodge. It was a position, and positions could include a claim about what stayed uncertain. In her sketchbook she wrote a possible first line: I keep two dresses in the same closet, and the question of which one I really wear is the work.

She spent the last hour before five painting the tenth piece, small, on a scrap of good paper: two chairs at one table, one holding a plastic tablecloth, one holding a chemistry textbook, a single pair of hands in the middle shared between them. It was rough. It might reify the idea too neatly, pinning it like a butterfly before it had finished moving, and she noted in the margin to try it looser tomorrow. At five o'clock Ms. Okafor's keys jingled in the doorway and Dana leaned over Ella's table on her way out.

"That's your tenth?" Dana asked.

"That's my tenth."

Dana looked at it, then at the printout still lying facedown on the other table. "She should have painted them holding hands," she said, gathering her portfolio. "The two Fridas. Not just the one vein."

"She kind of did," Ella said, and turned off the light.

The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the tangerine Priya always peeled at four o'clock sharp, as though the meeting could not officially begin without citrus. Maika sat near the window with her notebook open to a page she had ruled into two columns, derivatives on the left, antiderivatives on the right, because Mrs. Okafor had once told her that the surest way to understand an operation was to run it backward. That had been two years ago, in a hallway, and Maika had ascribed her whole decision to join math club to that sentence, though she suspected the real reason was smaller and more embarrassing: she liked being the one who wrote neatly on the board.

Today's problem came from Danny, who ran the club like a man collecting evidence. "A farmer has sixty meters of fence," he read from his phone, "and wants to build a rectangular pen against a river, so only three sides need fencing. What dimensions give the maximum area?" He looked up. "Who wants it?"

Maika raised her hand before she decided to. At the board she let the width be x along the river, so the two other sides took the rest: sixty minus two x, split evenly, meaning the area was x times thirty minus x. She wrote A of x equals thirty x minus x squared. Then she remembered what Danny had taught them the week before, that the derivative of x to the n was n times x to the n minus one, and she worked it down the left side of her brain and the right side of the board: thirty minus two x. She set it to zero. Fifteen. The pen should be fifteen meters along the river and fifteen deep, a square pretending not to be one, and the maximum area, if she multiplied it out, was two hundred twenty-five.

"Check it with the antiderivative," Danny said from the back, arms crossed, impervious to the tangerine peel Priya had lobbed at his head. "Go backward."

Maika knew the backward rule too, or thought she did. The antiderivative of x to the n was x to the n plus one over n plus one. She ran thirty x back to fifteen x squared and x squared back to x cubed over three, and there it was, fifteen x squared minus x cubed over three, whose derivative was exactly what she'd started with. She turned, satisfied, and found Theo already at the second board, chewing his pen.

Theo was the kind of student who trusted a rule further than it deserved. He had written one over x on the board, then one over two x squared, and was now standing very still. "It gives me division by zero," he said. "The rule says n plus one on the bottom, and my n is minus one."

Maika came to stand beside him. She had been here before, in a sense. There was a memory she carried from eighth grade, a test on which she had used a formula for the area of a trapezoid on a shape that only looked like one, and Mrs. Okafor had written in red that a rule was a promise about where it applied, not about the whole world. Maika had cried about the grade, but what stayed with her, uncomfortably, was the thought that she had liked the formula precisely because it spared her from looking at the shape itself. She had never told anyone she ascribed that small dishonesty to herself, and she didn't intend to tell the club now. But she looked at Theo's board the way she wished she had looked at that trapezoid.

"The rule just doesn't cover n equals minus one," she said slowly. "Every other n, fine. But minus one is where it breaks. You'd get x to the zero over zero."

"So the antiderivative of one over x is nothing? It doesn't exist?"

Maika didn't answer right away. She drew the curve of one over x on the board with its two arms reaching for the axes, and she pointed at the vertical line the curve fell toward and never touched. "That's an asymptote," she said. "It's not that nothing exists there. It's that we've walked off the edge of what this rule knows." She suspected, from something she'd glimpsed in Priya's older brother's calculus book, that a different function entirely, one with a name she couldn't recall, lived on the other side of that edge. But she didn't say so. She wasn't sure enough, and she had learned, somewhere between the trapezoid and this board, the difference between what she knew and what she wanted to have known.

"What do we do, then?" Theo asked.

"We say what's true. The rule is x to the n plus one over n plus one for every n except negative one. Minus one is the hole in it." She capped the marker. "And the farmer still gets his two hundred twenty-five square meters, because polynomials never give us trouble like this."

Danny snorted. "The farmer doesn't exist, Maika."

"The fence exists," she said. "Somebody measured sixty meters of something." She went back to her seat and, in the right-hand column of her page, under her neat antiderivatives, wrote a single question mark next to the words n equals negative one. Then she underlined it.

Priya leaned over. "You're going to look it up tonight, aren't you."

Maika closed the notebook on the marker still in her hand. "I'm going to look it up tonight."

The debate workshop met on Thursday nights in the community hall, in the room with the folding chairs and the smell of floor wax, while the bigger room next door filled with folding tables for the synagogue's Seder practice. Gavin had signed up because Ms. Okafor's flyer promised they would learn to argue an ancient rule using the text itself, no shortcuts, no appeals to how things made people feel. His first attempt, two weeks ago, had collapsed in ninety seconds when he'd said a rule was outdated because "obviously" it was, and a girl named Priya had asked him, mildly, which verse he was reading.

Tonight's assignment was the afikoman passage, or the closest thing to one, the Mishnah line about no dessert after the paschal lamb. He sat in the corner with the photocopied pages and his annotated copy of the Haggadah, and Priya sat across from him because she always sat across from him, and they were meant to argue opposite sides: whether a rule laid down when the Temple stood could still bind people who would never see it.

"You're treating the text like a museum piece," Priya said, tapping his page. "It either applies or it doesn't. That's not how it works and you know it."

"That's exactly how debate works," Gavin said, though he wasn't sure anymore. He'd spent four days with the passage and it kept shifting under him. In the original setting the rule had a logic he could almost touch: the lamb was the last thing eaten, the taste that stayed. But the text itself, when the Temple fell, had been reread, and somewhere in that rereading the middle matzah got pulled into the rule's orbit.

Their argument was interrupted by a commotion through the sliding partition. In the big room, Mr. Adler, who was running the practice Seder for families who'd never hosted one, was standing at the head table with his hands flat on the cloth, saying something urgent to his wife. Gavin caught fragments. He'd broken the matzot, he'd set aside the pieces, and then in the scramble of getting forty people seated he had left the afikoman on the tray under a napkin instead of hiding it, and now the children, primed all evening for a hunt, were already circling.

"It's called the afikoman," Mr. Adler was saying to the room, holding up the wrapped piece. "The middle matzah, broken and set aside. It gets hidden, usually, for the children to find, and it's eaten at the very end, the last food of the meal." He looked at his wife. He looked at the napkin. "It can't be the last food if I hand it to them now."

Priya leaned toward the partition, and Gavin realized he was already on his feet. He didn't decide it; it was closer to remembering something he'd read at two in the morning. He slid the partition back and said, "Hide it now. It doesn't matter that they watched. The rule isn't about the children not seeing where. The rule is the meal can't end without it, and nothing comes after it."

Mr. Adler looked at him. "You want me to hide it in front of them."

"The text doesn't care about surprise," Gavin said. "It cares that this is last. That's the whole weight of it. Someone decided a taste had to be preserved, and everything else grew around that." It came out faster than he intended, and he could feel Priya behind him cataloguing every word for the rebuttal she'd deliver in the car.

Mr. Adler walked the length of the head table, past the front door, and wedged the wrapped piece behind the umbrella stand, unhurried, theatrical, while the younger children shrieked and the older ones pretended not to watch. Then he came back and resumed the Seder as though nothing had happened, though something had: the room was looser, and a boy of about six was guarding the umbrella stand with his whole body.

Later, in the parking lot, Priya wouldn't let it go. "You argued my side," she said. "An ancient rule surviving by bending, by being reread. That was my thesis."

"I didn't argue your side," Gavin said, but he stopped, because she was right and it cost him something to admit it. He'd gone into the hall an intransigent literalist and come out with a position he couldn't fully claim: the rule was real, the text was binding, and the binding had metastasized into games and umbrella stands and children who would grow up thinking the hiding was the point. Whether that was the rule living or the rule dissolving into custom, he genuinely didn't know, and he found he preferred not knowing to the clean positions they'd been assigned.

"You could write it up like that," Priya said, unlocking her bike. "Both readings. The one you can't decide between."

"Ms. Okafor will say it's a dodge."

"Ms. Okafor will say it's honest." She swung onto the bike, then paused, one foot on the pavement. "Existentialism would say the rule is whatever the people at the table decide it is. You'd hate that."

Through the hall's back window, the light still on, Mr. Adler's table was visible, and a small shape was crouched by the umbrella stand, reaching. Gavin watched the boy's hand close around the wrapped matzah and lift it over his head like a trophy, and inside, someone started to laugh.

The kitchen clock at Grandma Ruth's read 4:52, and the science fair upload portal closed at midnight, which meant Emma had seven hours to fix an experiment that had already failed once. She spread her notebook across the table between the sugar bowl and a dish of peppermints, and her grandmother, drying a roasting pan at the sink, watched her do it without saying anything. Grandma Ruth had taught chemistry for thirty-one years and almost never talked about it, which Emma had always found strange, the way a retired pilot might be reticent about the sky.

"It went wrong," Emma said. "The numbers, I mean. Not the numbers I calculated, those were fine. I took fifteen grams of the reactant, and the molar mass is one hundred, so that's zero point one five moles, and the ratio is one to one, so I predicted zero point one five moles of product. I weighed what I actually got and it was less. A lot less. Like a third less."

Grandma Ruth set the pan down. She pulled out the chair opposite Emma and sat, and reached for the notebook, tilting her glasses to read the page. "What was the reaction?"

"It's in the write-up." Emma flipped pages for her. "Nobel prize stuff, I know. Baking soda and vinegar, but I did it with a scale and stoichiometry because the fair wants rigor this year."

"Rigor," her grandmother repeated, as if tasting the word. "And how did you run it?"

"In a jar on the windowsill, because it was warm there. The first trial I did in the garage and the numbers came out closer, but the photos were bad, so I redid it in the sun." Emma stopped. She looked at the window, where the afternoon light was still hot on the sill, and then at her own notebook, and something turned over slowly in her mind, the way a key turns before the bolt actually moves. "Wait. Is it the temperature?"

"Tell me what you think happens when a reaction gives off heat," Grandma Ruth said, which was not an answer, and Emma had learned by now that with her grandmother it never would be.

Emma pressed her pencil against her lip. "It gives off heat. So heat is like a product, almost. It's on that side." She drew it, an arrow with the word heat written after the products, then stared at her own handwriting. "So if I add heat, if I warm it up, then it's like I added more product. And adding more product pushes it backward. Toward the reactants." Her pencil hovered. "So if the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants. The system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse. That's why my sunny window trial gave me less product. I fed it the one thing that makes it retreat."

"Run the trial again tonight," Grandma Ruth said, "in the garage, and take your photos with the good lamp. You'll want both sets of numbers in the write-up. A failed prediction that gets corrected honestly reads better than a perfect result nobody had to fight for."

"It's more than that," Emma said, already writing. "My whole write-up pretended the chemistry was arithmetic. Mass to moles to mass, like a recipe. But it's not a recipe, it's a negotiation. There's a conversation happening in that jar about heat and direction, and I was only listening to half of it." She paused, uncertain how to say the next part, and said it anyway. "I think I like it better this way, honestly. The math was satisfying because it was clean. This is satisfying because it's true."

Her grandmother smiled at that, briefly, and stood to fill the kettle. "You'll want tea for a long night." While the water ran, Emma copied the corrected prediction into a fresh section: zero point one five moles available, temperature-dependent yield, forward reaction exothermic, elevated temperature shifting equilibrium back toward reactants and lowering the measured product. She could hear the garage door from the kitchen if she left it open, and the clock gave her till midnight, and somewhere between the kettle and the second page of writing she realized she had subsumed the failed trial into the project rather than hiding it, the mistake becoming part of the method instead of an embarrassment beside it.

At 10:40, in the cold garage with the door cracked for air, Emma weighed the new product and the number came within a gram of prediction. She photographed the scale twice, the jar once, and the thermometer once, because Mr. Delgado at the fair loved a thermometer in frame; he called it verisimilitude, and she'd had to look the word up, and now she used it herself, quietly, to mean the thing that made data believable. She typed the last paragraph of her conclusion at 11:31 on her laptop at the kitchen table, and hovered the cursor over Submit.

"Should I say the equilibrium thing more plainly?" she asked. "In the conclusion? Like I'm sure of it?"

"You ran it once in the cold and once in the sun," Grandma Ruth said from the doorway, arms folded, still in her slippers. "How sure does one cold trial make you?"

Emma looked at the screen. "Not as sure as I sound," she admitted. "I want to run it three more times at three temperatures before I'd claim it. But I have twenty-nine minutes." She typed a sentence she could defend: further trials at controlled temperatures needed to confirm the shift, then pressed Submit, and the confirmation banner came up green. She sat back. Outside, in the jar she'd left on the sill as a control, the last of the afternoon's warmth was still working on the reaction, invisibly, patiently, undoing what it could.

The community centre had booked the mock court into the same room as the seniors' card afternoon, so Nicolas set up his folders at a folding table between a rack of folding chairs and a table where four old men were sorting a deck. He was eighteen and had agreed to argue both sides of a fictional Supreme Court case about a student suspended for a speech posted online, and he had three evenings to learn how to hold two positions at once.

His grandfather, Walter, sat near the window doing the crossword and pretending not to listen. Nicolas read his petitioner's outline aloud, then his respondent's, and stopped because the two voices in his mouth sounded identical, equally flat, equally convinced of nothing.

"You're arguing like a pundit," Walter said, not looking up. "Both of him. Pick a fight with yourself."

Nicolas tried. He built the petitioner's case: the school had punished speech off campus, speech that never disrupted a class, and the First Amendment did not stop at the school's chain-link fence. Then he stood, moved two chairs to face each other, and sat in one as the respondent: schools act in loco parentis, the post had named students, the harm had walked into the building on Monday morning with everyone else. He argued back and forth across the gap, raising his voice at his own objections, while the card players watched him with an amusement he pretended not to notice.

One of the old men, Mr. Okafor, folded his hand and came over. "Who told you the First Amendment decides this?" he asked. "It's a mock Supreme Court. You keep talking like the judges were elected to please a crowd."

"They're appointed. For life. That's the point."

"Is it," Mr. Okafor said. "So who do they answer to?" He went back to his cards without waiting for an answer, and Nicolas sat there transfixed by the question, not because it was deep but because it dismantled something he had assumed was load-bearing. If the judges answered to nobody, then his whole strategy of appealing to them as if they were voters was wrong. He had been arguing to an audience that did not exist.

He took it to Walter, who was at his own table now, at his granddaughter Priya's house the following Sunday, where Nicolas had come to borrow a law dictionary he never opened. Priya, sixteen, was arguing with her mother about the news, some parliamentary country where the government had nearly fallen, and she turned to Nicolas in the crepuscular kitchen, the light going amber behind her, and said, "Nobody even voted for that guy. How is he in charge if nobody voted for him?"

"They voted for his party," Nicolas said. "In a parliamentary system the prime minister keeps office by holding the confidence of the legislature. Nobody wins a separate popular election for it. So the confidence is the whole job."

"That's worse," Priya said. "Or better. I can't tell."

Nicolas could not tell either, and that was what he took back to the community centre on the last evening before the mock court. He set the chairs facing each other again. On the left he put the petitioner's argument, which treated the judges as guardians of a principle that stood outside any majority. On the right he put the respondent's, which treated them as part of an institution that exists only because other institutions, somewhere, answer to voters. Neither argument could be the whole case. He wrote across the top of his outline: the judges answer to the law, the law answers to something, and I do not know what.

At the mock court the next afternoon, the panel was three volunteers from a local law firm and a retired civics teacher who kept score on a clipboard. Nicolas argued the petitioner first, and when the retired teacher asked whether a school could ever reach past its gates, he said yes, and gave the conditions, and conceded the edge of the case honestly instead of defending it. Then he crossed the room, took the respondent's chair, and argued the opposite: that the gates had never been the real boundary, that the boundary was harm, and that harm had entered the building.

The judges conferred longer than they had for any other student. When they came back, the retired teacher said the votes were split, two to one, and that they had split over Nicolas's cases rather than over his errors. On the walk out, Walter asked him which side he actually believed. Nicolas turned his key ring over in his pocket, once, twice.

"Ask me tomorrow," he said.

The paper was due Monday, and Victoria had brought it to her grandmother's house because the house was quiet in a way her own apartment never managed, the kind of quiet that let her think in straight lines. She spread her notes across the kitchen table, between the sugar bowl and a dish of peppermints. The assignment was a short report on the history of the integral, and she had already built the demonstration herself: a curve drawn on graph paper, rectangles fitted underneath it, the areas of the rectangles added up. Thin rectangles gave a better answer than fat ones. Infinitely thin ones, she was almost sure, would give the exact answer. The almost was what kept her at the table.

Her grandmother set down a cup of tea at her elbow without being asked. "What are the little boxes for?"

"They're for measuring the part under the curve," Victoria said. "The area. You add up all the boxes and you get close to it."

"Close to it." Her grandmother lowered herself into the opposite chair, knees popping, and reached for the graph paper. "And this is what you're writing your report on. The history of it. Not the doing of it."

"Both, kind of. I have to say whose idea it was." She slid the library book across the table, a fat blue volume called A History of the Calculus, its spine cracked at the chapter she needed. She had already looked through it twice, once last night and once on the bus, and she had found the name she wanted but not yet copied the sentence she needed. "The rectangle method has somebody's name on it. I just have to get the details right."

Her grandmother turned the book toward herself and put on the reading glasses that hung from a chain around her neck. "Riemann," she read. "There's a whole section. Bernhard Riemann." She pronounced it Ree-mann, soft and certain.

Victoria wrote the name at the top of a fresh page. Then she found the paragraph and read it aloud, slowly, the way she read anything she meant to keep: "Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen." She wrote it down word for word and checked it twice, because her chemistry teacher had failed a whole set of reports last spring for sloppy citation, and because something about the sentence pleased her, its smallness, the way a whole way of thinking could be tied to one man handing over one paper.

Her grandmother was quiet for a moment, turning her cup in its saucer. "I knew a man from Göttingen," she said at last. "When I was a girl. He taught me to waltz at my sister's wedding."

Victoria looked up. "Grandma. You grew up in Ohio."

"He was visiting. Universities send people all over." Her grandmother's face was perfectly composed. "He spoke about mathematics the way some men speak about horses. He said the numbers circumscribe the world, if you let them. He said that exact thing."

Victoria wrote circumscribe in the margin of her notes, liked it, and underlined it. She did not write down anything about the waltzing man, because her mother had told her once, gently, that her grandmother's memories had begun to arrange themselves according to their own wishes. A cousin who had drowned young was sometimes alive at dinner. A house they had rented for one summer was sometimes the house they had owned for thirty years. Nothing alarming. Just a slow tide, her mother said, moving things a few inches this way and that.

Later that afternoon Victoria took the graph paper out to the porch, where the light was better, and worked the rectangles again with a finer pencil. Her grandmother followed with her own tea and sat in the wicker chair, watching the pencil move. Victoria tried a curve that dipped below the axis and found her rectangles going negative, which startled her, and she sat with the surprise instead of erasing it. The method had an opinion about which areas counted and which didn't. She hadn't expected a pile of boxes to have opinions.

"Your grandfather was an autodidact," her grandmother said from the wicker chair. "He taught himself to fix radios. He never trusted anything he hadn't taken apart."

"Is that true?" Victoria asked it before she could stop herself.

"It's true enough." Her grandmother smiled at the yard, at the maple dropping its early leaves. "I know what you're doing. Your mother told you. It's all right." She said it without hurt, the way you'd report that rain was coming, and Victoria felt something shift in her chest, small and seismic at once, a fault line she hadn't known was there going quietly about its work. "The waltzing man might be from a film. It might be my sister's story. I keep him anyway."

Victoria looked at her rectangles, at the sums marching up the margin. The method was honest in one direction only. It said: here is the area, here is how close we are, here is the error shrinking toward nothing. It did not say anything about the parts of the past that had been rounded off, the slivers under the curve that no rectangle would ever exactly cover. Both of the people she had spent the day with, the man in the blue book and the woman in the wicker chair, were in the business of fitting shapes to the truth, and both of them left gaps, and both of them seemed to think the gaps were worth the trouble.

She wrote the report on the porch as the light went long and yellow across the boards. She used the sentence about 1854 and the lecturer's paper exactly as the book gave it. She described her rectangles and her negative areas, and she left in the part she still couldn't decide, whether an answer you only approach is an answer or a promise of one. Her grandmother read over her shoulder, peppermint clicking against her teeth.

"Put the waltzing man in," her grandmother said. "Just a sentence. Footnote him."

"Grandma. I can't footnote a waltz."

"Everyone else footnotes everything." She tapped the blue book with one finger, right on the name. "He's got his name on all of it, and he's been gone a hundred years. I only want one line."

Victoria laughed, and pulled the page back toward her, and after a while she wrote, at the very bottom, in smaller letters than the rest: other sources exist.

Wyatt spread the two leases side by side on the bench, weighted against the wind with his phone and a water bottle. The 4:40 bus was late, which gave him forty minutes he had not planned on, and the deposit for one of these places was due to Dev at five o'clock, no later, because someone else was coming to look at the Henderson Street unit at six.

The leases did not make the choice easy. Henderson Street was six hundred and eighty a month, plus electricity, plus gas, plus water, and the list said "tenant pays all utilities." The place on Corliss was eight hundred and twenty, and heat and water were included, only electricity separate. Wyatt had a pen and the back of an envelope from his mother, which had arrived containing forty dollars and nothing else.

He started a column for Henderson. Electricity, his cousin Amara had told him, ran her about sixty a month in a one-bedroom, though she kept the place warm as a greenhouse. Gas, if the stove was gas, maybe thirty. Water, maybe twenty-five, maybe forty, no one seemed to know. He wrote the numbers and disliked how much guessing held them up. Under that he started the Corliss column: eight twenty plus electric, call it fifty. The totals sat close together, close enough that the choice was not really about money. Henderson's lease was month to month. Corliss wanted twelve months, and Wyatt had a slot in the welding program at FortAllen that began in January, a two-year commitment, and twelve months would fit inside it if nothing changed, and nothing ever stayed the same.

Behind him, in the parking lot of the strip mall, a car with a student driver top light eased out between the nail salon and the dollar store. A woman sat in the passenger seat, one hand on the dash. The boy at the wheel looked younger than Wyatt, sixteen maybe, and the car crept toward the road and stopped at the edge of the lane.

The signal clicked on at the same moment the car began moving left into traffic. A hatchback braked behind it, horn short and sharp. The woman said, "You signalled as you started to turn. Signal before you change lanes, before you move, so the other drivers know what you're about to do and have time to adjust. If you signal too late, or not at all, they get no warning at all." The boy sat still for a second. Then he pulled the lever back and waited, engine idling, signal ticking, while two more cars passed. The third car slowed, made a gap, and the boy merged into it, slow and deliberate, and the woman said, "Better."

Wyatt looked at his envelope. The line between the columns ran crooked where the pen had slipped.

He thought about Dev, the Henderson landlord, who had shown him the unit on Tuesday and talked for an hour, an honest raconteur, telling stories about the building's old furnace and the tenant who'd kept a piano in the kitchen. Dev had been ebullient about everything, including the cracks in the plaster. Amara had warned him that charm was not a lease term. The Corliss landlord was a management company; she had answered exactly two emails and both had said the same thing in different fonts.

Wyatt took out his phone and pulled up his texts. His mother was still convalescing at his aunt's house after the surgery, and she had told him last week that he should decide by himself, that she could not get down to see either place before fall. He typed, then deleted, then typed again: If I take Henderson I can leave in the spring if the program moves me to the campus site. He did not send it. He wrote, instead, on the envelope, under the Henderson column, a new line: ask Dev, in writing, what utilities ran last year. Anything else was guessing stacked on guessing.

The bus came around the corner. The driver, an ebullient man named Roosevelt whom Wyatt had ridden with all summer, called out, "You look like a man doing taxes, Wyatt."

"Sort of," Wyatt said. He folded the envelope and put it in his pocket, leases stacked on top of each other, Henderson on the outside. At the top of the steps he stopped, one foot on the platform, and typed one more message, to Dev this time: Can you send me the utility totals for last year at the Henderson unit before 5?

He sat down by the window. The phone buzzed once against his thigh before the bus had even pulled back into traffic, and he turned it over in his hand without opening it yet, watching the strip mall slide past the glass.

Tyson had agreed to spend the Saturday at his grandfather's, which meant agreeing to spend it in the customs house, a low stone building by the harbor where his grandfather volunteered as a guide and where, according to a laminated sign, nothing of consequence had happened since 1798. He sat on a bench in the counting room with his laptop balanced on his knees, a half-formed document open, and his grandfather upstairs arguing with the gutter contractor. The essay was due Tuesday. The teacher had called it a historiographical essay, which Tyson had gathered meant you were not supposed to write about the French Revolution at all. You were supposed to write about what historians had said about it, and how that had changed since 1800, and then, apparently, you were supposed to have an opinion about the historians. This felt like being handed a menu and told the kitchen was closed.

The public library copy of the 1978 book had been sitting on his nightstand for a week, spine cracked by some earlier student whose marginalia stopped abruptly at page forty. Tyson had read page forty a few times. He typed a sentence, deleted it, and went to find the drinking fountain, which was in the room with the ship manifests. His grandfather's friend Ruth was in there, cataloguing, a pencil behind her ear.

"You're the grandson," she said. "You look like a person losing an argument." She nodded at the laptop. "With whom?"

"An essay. On how people's ideas about the French Revolution changed. Since 1800." He said it the way you say a thing you don't yet own. "It's not even about the Revolution. It's about the arguing."

"Ah," Ruth said, and left a silence he could fall into or not.

He fell into it. "I get that for a long time everybody basically told the same story, like the Revolution was the beginning of everything, all of modern France came out of it. And then in the seventies that fell apart, and I found this book that's kind of the moment it fell apart, but I don't know how to say what changed without just picking a side, and my teacher said picking a side is the least interesting thing I could do."

Ruth pulled a box toward her and began sorting bills of lading by date, which seemed to be her way of listening. "So what did the man with the book say?"

Tyson closed the laptop lid halfway, the way his grandfather did when a tour group asked a question worth thinking about. "François Furet. Nineteen seventy-eight. It got translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, which is basically the whole argument right there, it's about the interpreting." He was assembling it as he spoke, and could feel the assembly happening. "He said the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history. Not that it didn't matter. That it wasn't the key. Like everybody had been using one door for two hundred years and pretending the building had no other doors."

"And is he right?" Ruth asked, mildly, because she was the kind of person who asked that the way you'd ask about the weather.

"I don't know yet. That's the problem. He's arguing against people who thought 1789 explained everything after it, and they weren't stupid, they had reasons, and he had reasons. And I have four pages." He paused. "Also I have to preempt the obvious move, which is making my whole essay 'and then Furet fixed everything,' because that's just the same mistake with a new key."

Upstairs the gutter contractor called something down about flashing, and his grandfather answered at a volume that suggested the building's acoustics were being tested. Ruth laughed without looking up.

Tyson went back to the bench. He wrote for an hour, the harbor going from grey to gold outside the salt-streaked window, and the sentences came out in a shape he recognized as his own. He laid the two views side by side without flattening either. When his grandfather came down at closing, smelling of sawdust and old arguments, he read the last paragraph over Tyson's shoulder.

"Seismic," his grandfather said, tapping a word on the screen. "Big word."

"It was, though. That's the one place it fits." Tyson looked at the paragraph. "Everything else I cut."

His grandfather read on. "You say here you can't tell whose right."

"Can't tell yet. Maybe can't tell at all. The sources don't agree, and I don't know enough about where they came from. Provenance, Ruth calls it. Where a thing started before it got to you." He saved the file twice, out of habit. "It's due Tuesday. I might know more by Tuesday. I might not."

His grandfather turned off the lamp in the counting room, and the three of them went out through the manifest room, past the shelf where Ruth had left the box half-sorted, dates squared to dates, the work of the afternoon waiting for Monday.

"Come back Sunday," his grandfather said. "The gutters are an ongoing situation."

The screen door banged behind Nicolas before anyone could tell him not to let it, and he carried his chemistry book and a wrinkled practice sheet out to the kitchen table where his grandfather sat with the newspaper folded to the business section.

"Quiz Friday," Nicolas said, dropping into the chair across from him. "Equilibrium. If I don't pass it, my grade is done for the semester." He smoothed the paper flat against the oilcloth. The problems were about Le Chatelier's principle, predicting which way a reaction would shift when you heated it or cooled it, and the first one wanted him to figure out how many grams of carbon dioxide were involved before he could say anything else.

His grandfather lowered the paper an inch. "When I was your age, we had a teacher who would lambaste you in front of the whole class for forgetting to carry a digit. Called it mathematical illiteracy. I never forgot a digit again."

"I'll try to remember that." Nicolas pulled a pencil from his backpack and wrote the formula at the top of the page. He remembered the atomic masses from the table he'd copied in class: carbon was 12.01, oxygen was 16.00. He added them and wrote the answer in the margin.

His grandmother came through with a dish towel over her shoulder and set a glass of iced tea beside his elbow without asking whether he wanted it. "How is the studying?" she said, and then, to her husband, "Did you take your pills?"

"I took them," his grandfather said, in a tone Nicolas recognized as not entirely reliable. He was eighty-one now, and last month he had told the same story about the 1970s twice in one dinner, first as a story about stagflation and then, forty minutes later, as a story about a man he used to work with, as though the two versions had nothing to do with each other. Nicolas's mother had pulled him aside afterward and said, gently, that it was going to be like this more and more.

Nicolas worked through the calculation. The problem asked how many moles of carbon dioxide were in 88 grams of it, and he divided by what he'd written in the margin and got a little over three, which then fed into the equilibrium question about whether heating the system would push it toward the products or back toward the reactants. He wrote that heating shifted it toward the side that absorbed energy, crossed out the reactants, circled the products, and moved on to the second problem feeling almost steady.

At the second problem, the numbers stopped working. The grams wouldn't divide evenly, the moles came out ugly, and when he tried to fix it by adjusting the equilibrium shift too, the whole answer fell apart. He sat back and stared at the margin where he'd done the simple part, the part that couldn't be wrong. Carbon, 12.01. Oxygen, 16.00. He added them again on a fresh corner of the page and got the same thing he'd gotten before.

Then he looked at his own formula, the CO2 with its small subscript two, and he saw it. Two oxygens. The molar mass of a compound was the sum of the masses of the atoms in its formula, all of them, which meant for carbon dioxide it was 12.01 plus 16.00 plus 16.00 again. 44.01, not 28.01. He had cut the oxygen in half, and everything downstream had been quietly wrong while feeling completely right. He erased the margin, rewrote it, and did the division again with the correct number; the moles came out clean, and the equilibrium answer that had wobbled now sat still.

"I forgot to double the oxygen," he said out loud, half to the table.

His grandfather folded the paper the rest of the way down. His face had that phlegmatic calm it got these days, unhurried, hard to read. "Twice sixteen is thirty-two," he said. "Plus twelve. Forty-four." He tapped the margin with one finger. "My teacher would have loved you today."

"It's not that funny."

"It's a little funny." But he was looking at the page with something more serious underneath, and Nicolas understood, without either of them saying it, that his grandfather had followed the arithmetic perfectly and would maybe not remember, by Sunday, that the conversation had happened at all. Nicolas thought about how the wrong answer had felt just as solid as the right one, and how he would have written it on the quiz with total confidence, and how nothing in the feeling of it would have told him. You just had to go back and count the atoms again, both of them, every time, and even then you couldn't be sure you'd caught everything.

He copied the corrected number onto a clean sheet so it would be the first thing he saw Friday morning. His grandmother took his empty glass and put her hand briefly on his grandfather's shoulder as she passed, and his grandfather covered it with his own hand without looking up from the newspaper.

James had won his first two rounds of the tournament, which was, he told himself, exactly according to plan, and so the free hour before round three belonged entirely to the one-act. He had the script in the side pocket of his blazer, three copies, because the cast numbered three, and he had reserved the empty classroom at the end of the humanities hall at eleven, which was a thing he had definitely done rather than a thing he had walked past and found conveniently unlocked.

Priya was already there, sitting on a desk with her heels hooked on the chair rung, and Devon came in late, still carrying his flowpad from the previous round. James arranged the copies on the desk. "We're going to sit and read it first," he said. "No standing, no moving. Just the words."

"A table read," Priya said. "My cousin does community theater. You sit around and read the script through before anybody stages anything, so you can hear how the dialogue actually sounds."

"I was going to say that," James said, and opened his copy, and to be fair to himself he had been going to say something adjacent to it. The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the hallway beyond it roared with tab room chaos, forensics kids arguing about speaker points, and here in this pocket of quiet the play began. Priya read the mother. Devon read the son. James read the stage directions in a level voice, unbothered, a director in full command of an incipient production that did not yet exist.

The trouble, in James's private accounting, was small. There was a line on page four where the son tells the mother he never wanted the lake house sold, and when Devon said it aloud it landed with a thud, formal and stagey, nothing like the way any eighteen-year-old on earth would say it to his mother. James had read that line perhaps forty times on his own and it had sounded fine, which was itself informative, since apparently a script sounds one way alone in a bedroom at one in the morning and an entirely different way in a room with other bodies in it. He had believed, before this, that writing was enough, that the page contained the thing. The page did not contain the thing. The thing happened between people, or it did not happen.

"That line's wrong," Devon said, before James could gently arrive at the same conclusion through a series of Socratic questions he had been composing since breakfast. "Nobody talks like that. 'I never consented to the divestment of the property.' Who says that."

"I say that," James said. "In rounds. That's debate. That's the whole problem, actually." And he heard himself say it and understood that it was true, that he had spent four years learning to interpolate evidence into arguments the way a mason slots bricks, and somewhere along the way the mortar had gotten into his ear. He could not tell yet whether the play was an escape from that or just debate wearing civilian clothes. His coach would have said there was a teleology to it, that everything in forensics bends toward the ballot, and James wanted the play to bend toward nothing, but he did not know how to make something bend toward nothing, or even whether that was coherent, whether a story needs a target the way a case needs one.

"We could change it," Priya said.

"I wrote it for the sound of it, not the truth of it," James said. "Or I thought I wrote it for the sound. Let's do the line again." He had them read the scene twice more, seated, scripts flat on the desks, and on the third pass Devon dropped the formal version and said, quietly, "Mom, you sold the lake without asking me," and Priya let the silence run four full seconds before her answer, and the silence did more than either of their lines. James wrote nothing down. He just listened. That was a new instrument and he was not yet sure how to hold it.

Then, because he was who he was, he tried to hold it anyway. He cleared the desks to the wall and stood Devon at the door and Priya at the window, eleven feet apart, which he measured by eye and later described as twelve, and ran the scene again with bodies in it. Blocking, he explained, was the term for where actors move and when, and he had read two chapters about it in a book he would, in later retellings, have studied exhaustively. In fact Devon refused to stand at the door. Devon wanted to sit on the floor with his back against the wall, and James's first instinct was to overrule him, and his second instinct, arriving late but arriving, was to let the actor's body vote. The seated version was worse for the geometry he had imagined and better for everything else.

A girl from another school put her head in the door and said pairing for round three was posting, and Devon left at a run, and Priya folded her copy of the script and put it in her bag and paused at the desk where James was still standing.

"So is the line changing or not?"

"I'll know when I hear it again," James said. "Saturday. My house. Kitchen table, obviously."

"Obviously," Priya said, and knocked twice on the doorframe on her way out, which he chose to take as applause.

The training room behind the planetarium dome smelled of dust and projector oil, and Brayden sat at the end of a table of folding chairs, copying a graph onto his notepad. The graph showed carbon dioxide rising across a century in a sawtooth line, small dips and recoveries riding a long, steep climb. He was there because the planetarium had accepted him as a weekend explainer, and because his grandfather, convalescing after the surgery in March, had said it would look good on an application and keep him out of the house where every conversation turned to illness. His real want was smaller and stranger: he wanted to be the kind of person who could stand under the dome and answer anything.

Mrs. Okafor, the volunteer coordinator, gave them worksheets and left the room, which was her way of testing them. The worksheet asked how greenhouse gases trap heat, and Brayden wrote that they absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it, some of it back toward the surface, so the atmosphere holds energy the way the glass of a greenhouse does. He knew that much from physics. The graph was harder. The sawtooth bothered him. He traced the little dips with his pen and could not say what they were.

The girl across the table, Priya, watched him. "You've been staring at that for ten minutes."

"The teeth. They go down every year and then back up."

"Plants," she said. "Northern summer. The hemisphere breathes in." She turned her sheet over. "That's not the one I'm stuck on."

Hers was a different sheet, the one on ocean heat. A boy of about eleven, there for a birthday party that had drifted away from the supervised group, had stopped at their table and pointed at her diagram of the North Atlantic. He asked why the wind direction mattered for a warm current, whether the warmth just sat where it was. Priya started to say something and stopped, and the boy looked at Brayden instead, because Brayden was the one wearing the volunteer lanyard.

Brayden's first answer was wrong. "The wind cools the water," he said, "so the heat sinks." The boy frowned, and Priya mouthed no. Brayden felt his face go warm, the projector fan suddenly loud in the quiet room. He took the diagram and turned it so the boy could see, and he made himself slow down, the way he had learned to do when a proof collapsed in calculus. He put his finger on the ocean.

"Okay, forget the wind for a second. In summer, the ocean takes in heat and stores it. All that warmth is sitting in the water. Then in winter, the ocean releases that stored heat into the air above it." He moved his finger east. "And the prevailing winds over that part of the ocean are westerlies, which means they blow from west to east. They pick up that warmed air and carry it onto northwestern Europe." He tapped the coastline. "So the wind direction matters because it decides where the released heat goes. If the winds blew the other way, the warmth wouldn't land there."

The boy read the diagram again, lips moving. "So the ocean is like a battery."

"Charging in summer, discharging in winter," Brayden said, and the boy nodded slowly and wandered back toward the party, already looking at the ceiling as if the stars might also be a battery.

Priya slid her sheet across. "You just explained my worksheet."

"I got it wrong first."

"I know. That's why I let you." She tapped the sawtooth graph on his pad. "The breathing, and the storage. They're the same idea at different scales. The ocean holds heat seasonally, the atmosphere holds it continuously. That's your greenhouse, actually. The gases raise the enthalpy of the whole system, the total heat content, and the graph is the receipt." She said it flatly, not showing off, and Brayden wrote enthalpy in his margin because he wanted to look it up properly later, not because he would admit not knowing it now.

They were called into the dome after that for a rehearsal, and Brayden stood at the console while the projector woke, the room going torpid and dark around the slow wheel of stars. Mrs. Okafor asked him to present the carbon dioxide graph to the group as if they were visitors. He held the laser pointer on the sawtooth, said the hemisphere breathes in every summer, and followed the long climb upward with the red dot, and found that his hand was steady. Afterward Priya caught his eye across the dome and tilted her head at the boy from the birthday party, who was standing at the exit, waiting, holding a folded page of his own diagram.

"You dropped this," the boy said, holding it out to Brayden, though Brayden had not dropped anything. At the top of the page, in pencil, the boy had written a battery, discharging.

The library's second floor smelled of carpet glue and old bindings, and Laura had claimed the corner table by the window since four o'clock, three legal pads fanned in front of her like cards she was refusing to show anyone. In two weeks she would stand before a panel of local judges at the regional mock court tournament and argue a free speech case, and the tournament's particular cruelty was that each advocate had to argue both sides: petitioners in the morning round, respondents in the afternoon. She had written until the two positions began to bleed into each other, until she could no longer tell which argument she actually believed.

Priya arrived at six with a milkshake and the truculent expression she wore whenever she'd been thinking about something all day and had decided everyone else was behind. "You're doing it wrong," she said, dropping into the chair across from Laura.

"I haven't said anything yet."

"Your face said it. You're trying to pick a side. That's not the assignment. The assignment is to be good enough that the side picks itself for you, both times."

Before Laura could answer, a boy from the study carrels drifted over, backpack straps bunched in one fist. Derek, from her government class, the one who never spoke unless something was actually bothering him. "Can I ask you guys something? You do the mock court thing, right? This morning in first period, Ms. Harrowwell told Marisol she had to stand for the pledge. Not say it, just stand. Marisol said no. She got a referral. So can they make you stand, or not?"

Priya set down her milkshake. "No. West Virginia versus Barnette, 1943. The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Marisol should take the referral to the principal and cite it."

Derek repeated the case name back slowly, writing it on his hand. "Nineteen forty-three. Six to three. Okay." He went back toward the carrels, and Laura watched him write it again on a sheet of paper, more carefully, as though his skin might smudge the law.

"That," Priya said, "is your problem in one referral slip."

"What do you mean?"

"You just watched a rule protect somebody. Feels good. Feels like the case is settled, speech wins, done. Then this afternoon you argue the other side, and you'll hate yourself unless you understand why the three dissenters weren't monsters." She tapped Laura's legal pads. "So tell me why a school might want everyone standing. Steelman it. I'll be the judges."

Laura looked at the window, at the parking lot lights coming on. She had been raised in a house where certain words did double duty, where her mother said "community" and meant "obedience," and she'd spent two years at debate learning to call that coercion out loud. Now Priya was asking her to build the case for it. "A school is a small public," she began, halting. "If a public can't ask anything of its members, not even standing, then it isn't a public. It's just a room full of individuals. The three in the majority had utilitarianism on their side and still lost, I mean the dissent, the dissent said the country needed unity more than it needed to protect one conscience."

"Careful," Priya said. "Which three?"

"The three dissenters. In Barnette." Laura heard the words leave her mouth and felt the floor tilt, because she'd had it backward for a week. She'd been telling herself the dissent was about safety in wartime, about order, and that the majority's logic was the utilitarian one, the counting of harms. She grabbed the casebook and turned pages until Justice Jackson's opinion lay open under the desk lamp. She read the line about no official orthodoxy being prescribed by the Supreme Court, then read it again, and something in the argument she'd built for the respondent side, the side defending compelled speech, quietly collapsed and rebuilt itself in a different shape.

"Say what you figured out," Priya said. "Out loud. That's the whole tournament, saying it out loud before a stranger makes you."

Laura closed the book on her thumb. "I had the values reversed. I thought standing together was the practical argument and freedom was the principle. It's not. Compelled unity is the principle, a real one, a whole way of thinking about what a country is, and freedom is the practical one, the thing that actually works, that lets a nation hold people who don't agree. I can argue both now. I understand both now. What I can't do is tell you which one I'd vote for, because I keep switching, and I think switching might be the honest condition."

"That's the answer nobody wants," Priya said, "and the only one worth hearing." She gathered her keys. "Ten tomorrow. Bring the Harwell thing, we can work Marisol into a hypothetical."

Laura stayed after the lights dimmed to the yellow of the night section, copying the case citation onto a fresh card, and she was still there at nine when Derek came back through on his way out. He stopped at her table, and instead of the question she expected, he said, "Marisol stood today. Fourth period, before she even went to the principal. She said the fight was exhausting her more than the pledge did, so she just stood up." He shrugged into his backpack. "Funny, right? You spend all that time learning she doesn't have to, and she goes and does it anyway."

Laura looked down at the card in her hand, Barnette, 1943, six to three, and realized she could not decide whether Marisol had lost something or found it. She slid the card into her pocket next to her speech, where both sides of her argument sat folded together, and started stacking the legal pads to go home.

The biology classroom stayed open until five on Thursdays, and by four o'clock the smell of whiteboard marker had soaked into everything. Eva had claimed the far table because it had the good model kit, the one with plastic nucleotides that actually clicked together, and she spread her notes across it like a hand of cards she was losing. Her presentation was in two days: explain how DNA is copied and then turned into protein. She could say the words, transcription and translation, but when she tried to say them in order, out loud, the whole thing came apart like wet paper.

Devon arrived first, dropping his bag on the chair beside her. Then Priya, who had brought two granola bars and ate both. Marcus came last, still holding his phone, and the four of them were supposed to be Eva's audience for a practice run. She stood at the whiteboard, drew a rectangle, labeled it DNA, and said, "Then RNA polymerase makes a copy, called mRNA, and that's transcription." So far, so good. Then Marcus said, "You forgot the part where the code gets read in the cytoplasm," and Priya said he was wrong, and the practice run ended before it started.

"Translation happens at the ribosome," Devon said. "That's where amino acids get strung together." He said it slowly, the way he said everything, as though the sentence might break if rushed. Marcus waved his phone at them. "That's not even the fight. The fight is carbon dioxide. Where does the first CO2 come from? I said glycolysis. Priya said the Krebs cycle."

Eva wrote CO2 on the board and underlined it twice, which was more attention than it deserved from her. Glycolysis, she thought, breaks glucose into pyruvate, and she could not remember a gas being released there. But she had not read that chapter carefully, and she knew it. She said so. "I actually don't know. Don't let me guess out loud, I'll just make something up." Marcus looked personally wounded. "You're the one presenting." "I'm presenting DNA to protein," she said. "Cellular respiration is a different day of my life."

Priya took the marker and drew a box. "The mitochondrion. There's an inner part, the matrix." "Like the movie," Marcus said. "Like the movie," Priya agreed, and for a second everyone was quiet, respecting the movie. She drew pyruvate moving into the matrix and then, beside it, a small arrow and the label CO2. Devon leaned in and read aloud from his own notes, which were better than everyone else's because Devon wrote things down. "In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide." He read it a second time, slower.

"So not glycolysis," Eva said. Marcus put his phone face down on the table, which for him was a kind of surrender. "Not the Krebs cycle either, then," Priya said, though nobody had fully claimed the Krebs cycle, and Eva decided not to point this out, because being right in the tone she would have used was a travesty of being right. She let it go and picked up the model kit instead.

She clicked nucleotides together while they argued about whether she should say "the first CO2 of respiration comes before the Krebs cycle even begins," which was accurate but sounded like a dodge. What she was actually doing was thinking about her own presentation, because the pyruvate argument had loosened something. DNA to RNA was a copying step, one alphabet to a near-identical one. Then translation changed alphabets entirely, nucleotides into amino acids, the way pyruvate became something else in the matrix and gave off a gas on the way. She did not say this comparison out loud, because it was nascent and half-wrong and she was not going to decorate her presentation with a metaphor she could not defend. But it ordered her thinking.

She stood up and gave the practice run, start to finish, and it went better than it augured, since she dropped the marker twice and called the ribosome a "ribosomething" on the first try. Marcus clapped with his granola-wrapped hands. "You still didn't say where the first carbon dioxide comes from," he said. "It's not my topic," Eva said, and then, because he had waited all afternoon: "It's the pyruvate, in the matrix. One CO2 per pyruvate." She packed the model kit, snapping the last nucleotide into its slot, and left the whiteboard covered in arrows for the janitor to judge.

The parking spot in front of the Foodway sloped downhill, and Nevaeh took it anyway, easing the car in beside a cart corral while her sister Dee held her coffee and said nothing, which was its own kind of commentary. It was only Nevaeh's third time driving without their mother, and the slope made the parallel park crooked, so she pulled forward and tried again, straighter, and then sat with her hands still on the wheel.

"Which way do the wheels go?" Dee asked, because Dee had been in the car for the lesson last month and remembered everything, even the things Nevaeh would rather she forgot.

"Into the curb." Nevaeh turned the steering wheel until the front tires pointed toward it. "Downhill, facing downhill next to a curb, toward the curb. That way if the brakes ever fail, the car rolls into the curb instead of out into traffic." She had gotten that question wrong on the first try, in a strip mall parking lot with the instructor tapping the window, and she'd repeated it to herself so many times since that it had lost all meaning except as rhythm, pure phonetics, four syllables and then four more.

Inside, the Foodway was cold and bright, and Dee steered them past the produce toward the little seating area by the deli, where two laminated folders came out of her tote bag like something contraband. Two apartment leases. Dee had toured both buildings on Saturday while Nevaeh was at work, and now she slid the pages across the table and said, "Tell me which one."

"I don't know how."

"You know math. That's the whole skill."

The first lease was for a one bedroom on Calder Street, six hundred and eighty a month, but the listing said tenant pays all utilities. The second was a studio above the dry cleaner on Pine, seven hundred and forty, with water and trash included, only electric and internet on the tenant. Nevaeh got out her phone and opened the calculator app, and then the notes app, because the calculator didn't hold enough numbers at once.
