"See," Noor said, not looking up from her bees. "Even the air has rules."

Maria spread the notebook across her knees on the third bench from the fountain, the one with the best view of the ball field, and wrote "Week 1" at the top of a fresh page. In eight weeks the college club softball team held open tryouts, and every plan she'd drafted so far had collapsed by Wednesday, because she had written in seven days of throwing with no rest and no warm-ups, and her shoulder had answered by aching through her night classes. Below the heading she drew seven boxes. Two of them she crossed out before writing anything, which felt almost criminal, like leaving two questions blank on an exam on purpose.

Priya arrived with a paper bag of pistachios and dropped onto the far end of the bench. "You're doing homework at the park on a Sunday. That's genuinely sad." She leaned over, saw the boxes, and softened. "Two crossed out?"

"Rest days," Maria said. "Coach Ruiz says a training week without them is just an injury schedule." She wrote Monday's plan anyway: warm-up, thirty minutes of long toss, cool-down. The words "warm-up" still struck her as time stolen from actual practice, though Ruiz had made the whole summer league jog laps before touching a ball, all season, without exception.

Priya cracked a pistachio and studied the field, where the twelve-year-olds Ruiz coached were scattering into pairs. "Is he still doing that weird thing where he never tells anyone how to move?"

They both watched. Ruiz stood between two girls tossing a ball back and forth, and where most coaches would have said bend your elbow, or keep your wrist firm, he said, "Don't think about your arm. Hit her hands. Just hit her hands." The younger girl's throw, wobbly for ten minutes, suddenly arced clean and flat into her partner's glove. She laughed, surprised at herself, and did it again.

Maria had assumed it was a style, a quirk. Then, scrolling later while Priya hunted a trash can, she found she'd saved a screenshot weeks ago and forgotten it, a page from a sports science text Priya had sent during finals. "Listen to this," Maria said, and read aloud: "Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts."

"That's what he's doing," Priya said. "The hands. He's the hands."

Maria wrote it in the margin of Week 1, then thought better of the margin and gave it its own line at the bottom of the page, small and deliberate: focus on the target, not the arm. It reframed things she'd done all summer without naming them. Every time she'd thrown at a chalk circle on the backstop, she'd improved by the end of the session. Every time she'd stood in the mirror and tried to fix her elbow, she'd gotten worse and finished in a worse mood, too, watching herself fail at herself.

She tried it on her own body right there, standing at the edge of the grass while Priya held up her palms as a target. The first throw she caught herself thinking about her shoulder and pulled it into the dirt. The second she aimed only at Priya's hands, and the ball arrived with a satisfying smack that seemed, for a moment, to enrapture even the toddlers by the fountain, who stopped chasing pigeons to applaud. Priya bowed. Maria felt the pleasure of it and also, faintly, the melancholic edge of understanding something at eighteen that she would have paid anything to know at twelve, during all those wasted seasons in front of the mirror.

The light was going amber by the time she finished the week. Monday, Wednesday, Friday: warm-up, long toss, target work. Tuesday and Saturday: sprints, no throwing, because legs recovered on their own schedule. Thursday and Sunday: crossed out, nothing but the walk to this park and back. She had learned to plan a week, and she had learned where to put her attention, and the two lessons kept circling each other in her head, something she could have written a whole essay on for her biology class, the way an animal's phylogeny and its daily habits each explain part of it and neither explains it alone. But an essay would have been guessing. What stayed uncertain was whether a week on paper would survive contact with an actual September, and whether she could hold a target in her mind for eight straight weeks when her whole instinct was to check her own machinery, her arm, her schedule, her boxes, all of it.

Priya packed up the pistachio shells and stood. "Same bench next Sunday? I want to see if the crossed-out boxes survived."

Maria closed the notebook and held it against her chest. "Hit my hands," she said, and tossed her the empty pen.

Victoria spread the briefs across her grandmother's kitchen table, the good table, the one that smelled faintly of lemon wax and held a framed photograph of her grandfather standing in some montane landscape, boots laced, squinting into an altitude of light. Two stacks: petitioners on the left, respondents on the right. On Thursday she would argue for a student's right to wear an armband in a public school. On Friday she would argue the school's side, against herself, and the whole point, her coach kept saying, was that she had to mean both.

The trouble was that she did mean both, and it felt less like a skill than like a defect. In practice rounds she kept conceding mid-sentence. "Speech is not absolute," she would begin, robust and confident, and then hear herself add, "though of course the school suspended her for a silent, non-disruptive symbol, which is hard to defend." Her partner Zoe had started keeping a tally on her wrist.

Her grandmother set down two mugs of tea and lowered herself into the chair at the head of the table, where she sat every afternoon with the radio on, waiting for the four o'clock news even though she complained about every item in it. "Who's winning?" Gran asked.

"I don't know yet. That's the assignment. Both sides."

"Ridiculous," Gran said, but she said it fondly, and she pulled the petitioner's brief toward her and put on her reading glasses, which she wore on a chain like a medal.

Victoria had chosen this house for the quiet, but the quiet kept filling up. Her phone buzzed: Zoe, who had relatives in Manchester, had sent a voice note from the library. "Okay, random but listen. I've been telling my cousins about your case, freedom of speech, all of it, and they said, you realize in 2022 the UK had three prime ministers without a general election. Boris Johnson, then Liz Truss, then Rishi Sunak, all in one year, and nobody voted except the governing party changing its own leader. I didn't believe them. I looked it up. It's real. Three, in one year." Victoria played it twice. She thought about the school board in her case, appointed and then acting, and how much of what governed anybody arrived without a ballot. The fact sat strangely in her, useful and not useful at once, a coin from a country she wasn't visiting.

"Something funny?" Gran asked.

"Zoe's cousins. Three prime ministers in one year and nobody got to vote on it."

"Mad year," Gran said, and sipped her tea, and Victoria understood that to Gran this was not trivia but weather, something lived through.

She went back to the briefs. Arguing for the school, she had learned to build the genus first: all school-speech cases, then the subset of cases involving minors in compulsory settings, then the narrower subset where the symbol functioned as speech directed at other children who could not leave. Classify, then rule. It was elegant. Arguing for the student, she had learned to attack the classification itself: the armband was silent, the disruption was fear of disruption, and a school that could punish fear could invent it whenever it wanted. Two grammars for the same sentence.

What she could not do was pretend the school had acted in bad faith. The principal believed the armband would exculpate nobody and inflame plenty; his record showed he had suspended students for far worse with far less ceremony. So on Friday she would stand up and argue for a man she partly believed in, against a girl she entirely believed in, and the only honest way through, she decided at the table while Gran murmured corrections to the radio, was to stop trying to win and start trying to be right about what each side saw.

Thursday night she argued the student's side and won on points. Friday morning, in the borrowed courtroom of the county annex, she stood at the respondent's podium and said, "The school asks this court to believe that a fourteen-year-old's silence is not harmless," and she made herself believe it, for nine minutes, and the judges leaned in. She lost that round, narrowly, on rebuttal, and her coach wrote one word on the scoresheet and turned it so Victoria could read it: finally.

That evening she drove back to Gran's, tea and toast and the four o'clock news, Gran triumphant over her crossword, one clue left. "Nine letters," Gran read. "'Worth considering.'"

"Debatable," Victoria said.

Gran filled it in without asking her.

The notebook was open to a page that said, in Devi's handwriting, "You can't test what doesn't exist. Unless." Victoria had found it in her backpack that morning, shoved between the camp T-shirt she never washed and a stick of deodorant, and she had been turning the sentence over all day like a coin she couldn't decide to spend. Now it was almost nine, the kitchen table had been cleared of dinner, and her laptop hummed in front of an empty file called Student.java.

Devi had issued the challenge on the last night of camp, sitting cross-legged on a bunk while everyone else packed. Victoria remembered the mosquito coil smoldering by the door, the way Devi kept clicking a pen against her knee. "You write the class first," Devi had said, "because that's what everyone does. I'm telling you to write the test first. For something that doesn't exist yet." Victoria had laughed, and Devi had not, and the silence after that had felt like the beginning of an argument they never got to finish, because lights-out came and then buses came and then summer ended.

So here she was, at home, alone with the idea. The assignment from the online course was simple: build a Student class in Java with private fields, name and grade, and getter methods to read them. The ordinary path was obvious. Declare the fields, write getName, write getGrade, and only then, if you felt virtuous, write a little test to prove it all worked. She had done it that way a dozen times. The test was like a stamp at the end, a formality, and a green check mark could almost absolve her of ever having doubted the code in the first place. Almost. That was the word that had started to bother her at camp. Almost.

She opened a new file instead, StudentTest.java, and typed a test that called new Student("Victoria", 11) and then asserted that getName returned "Victoria". The class didn't exist. She had written a test for a ghost. When she ran it, the screen filled with red: compilation errors, cannot find symbol, the whole cascade of the compiler telling her, in its blunt way, that she had written a lie. She sat back. It was strange how satisfying the failure was, how it felt less like an error and more like a map. The red told her exactly what the world lacked.

Her mother wandered through for a glass of water and paused at the screen. "Your grandmother used to say the perspicacious ones ask before they know enough to be embarrassed. What's all the red?" "It's on purpose," Victoria said. "Supposedly. It's a thing called red, green, refactor. You write a failing test first, then make it pass, then clean up the code." Her mother sipped her water. "Who dreamed that up?" "Somebody named Kent Beck. He popularized it, Devi says. It's called test-driven development." Her mother nodded slowly, the way she nodded at Victoria's grandmother's opinions about soup, and carried her glass back down the hall.

Alone again, Victoria built the class the red demanded: private fields, name and grade, hidden away where nobody could reach in and change them, then two small getter methods that handed the values back. When she ran the test, everything went green. She caught herself grinning at a check mark, which was absurd, and grinned anyway. The green meant only that her code did what she had thought to ask of it. She began to see how someone could mistake that for proof, and how the mistake would be a quiet one, the kind you'd never notice until a name came back wrong six months later.

She scrolled a programming forum while she waited for nothing in particular and found a diagram someone had labeled the phylogeny of programming languages, Java branching off C++, C++ off C, the whole family tree drawn like a naturalist's sketch. She liked that. Ideas inherited traits the same way beetles did, small mutations passed down until someone gave them a name. Maybe that was all Beck had done, she thought, noticed a mutation that had been drifting through the population and pinned it to a board. Or maybe he'd built it from nothing. She didn't know, and the not-knowing felt okay, even interesting, like a door she could see but hadn't opened yet.

Then she did the last part, the refactor. The getter for grade was fine but ugly, cluttered with a comment she'd written to reassure herself. She deleted the comment, straightened the spacing, ran the test again. Green held. She leaned forward and started a second test, this one for a student with an empty name, just to see what the red would say about that. The cursor blinked at the end of the line, patient, waiting to be proved wrong.

Claire had promised Marcus forty minutes of calculus for fifteen dollars, and she had promised her mother the money by Friday, and both promises were sitting on the kitchen table at nine at night beside a bag of corn chips neither of them touched. Marcus was in her grade but in the slower section, and his worksheet had one problem left, the one with a fraction whose numerator was just the number one.

"So you use the power rule," Marcus said. He was already writing. "One over x is x to the minus one, so you add one to the exponent and divide by the new exponent."

Claire watched him do it. Add one and you get zero. Divide by zero. He sat back and looked at the undefined expression like it had insulted him.

"That's not it," she said.

"You said the power rule works for everything."

"I said it works for what we've done." She pulled the worksheet toward her. Her own class was two weeks ahead, and she remembered the day her teacher had drawn a curve on the board and said there was a hole in the method, a single case where the rule collapsed, and then had moved on to homework collection before Claire finished copying it down. She had told herself she would look it up. She hadn't. Fifteen dollars and Marcus's quiz tomorrow were what it took to finally make her care.

"Try it on your calculator," she said. "Graph one over x and tell me what you see."

While he tapped at it, she texted Priya, whose notes were always complete, whose whole system of colored tabs seemed to underpin her GPA the way rebar underpins concrete. Priya answered in fragments, the way she answered everything. The power rule fails there. Special case. It's the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x.

"Okay," Claire said, and turned the phone face down before Marcus could see she'd needed it. "The power rule has a gap. One function falls through it, and it's this one. The antiderivative of one over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x."

"Logarithms." Marcus said the word like a diagnosis. "Why would a log just appear? That's random."

"It's not random, it's the one case that fills the gap." She wrote ln, then the absolute value bars, then x, and the bars bothered him more than the log did, so she said, "The absolute value just handles negative numbers, don't worry about it tonight." He copied it three times, the way he copied everything, as if handwriting could substitute for understanding, and she let him, because for tomorrow it probably would.

He did the last two problems alone and got them right. His mother's car pulled into the driveway and he shoved fifteen dollars at her, crumpled, still warm from his pocket. "You should be a tutor for real," he said at the door. "My cousin pays thirty."

After he left she sat with the worksheet. Marcus's cousin, thirty dollars an hour, and behind that, the tuition letter her father had left open on the counter for a week like a test he was waiting for someone else to pass. He wanted her to study something with a clear lane, had said "epidemiology" twice at dinner with the confidence of a man who had read one article, and she had said nothing, because what she wanted didn't have a name that satisfied him yet.

She picked up her pen and did the problem herself, slowly, from the graph up. One over x, the curve swooping along its asymptotes, and underneath it an area you could actually compute now, area that had been unmeasurable to her an hour ago and was only a logarithm away. She checked it against Priya's note, then closed the phone and did it again from memory. There was a question still sitting underneath the mathematics, the same one under the tuition letter, which was whether knowing the special case meant you understood the rule, or only that you'd memorized the patch. She didn't have that yet. She wrote the fact on an index card anyway, both sides, and left it propped against the sugar bowl where she would see it at breakfast.

Sadie had carried the sealed tubes in a shoebox lined with a towel for eleven blocks, and now they sat on the folding table between her trifold poster and a colorimeter she had borrowed from the chemistry storeroom, a squat obsolescent thing with a dial instead of a screen. The tubes held nitrogen dioxide, brown, in equilibrium with its colorless dimer, and her whole project was the sentence she had lettered across the top of the poster: a system at equilibrium, when disturbed, shifts to oppose the change. She had written it in September, when it was just something to put on a poster. She had not yet met Mr. Okonkwo's question.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and someone else's vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano. Her friend Priya had been placed two tables down, between a boy with a homemade wind turbine and a girl who had sensitized a webcam to track pollen drift for her project about allergies. Sadie envied the webcam. Her tubes just sat there, brown, doing nothing observable, the forward and reverse reactions canceling each other out at a rate no eye could catch.

The first judge was kind and hurried. She dipped one tube into the ice bath Sadie had brought in a cooler, watched the brown fade toward pale gold as the equilibrium absorbed the cold by shifting toward the dimer, nodded, signed her sheet, and moved on. The second judge was Mr. Okonkwo, who taught AP Chem at the school across town and had a habit of tilting his head like a bird before he spoke.

"Show me the hot water," he said. Sadie lowered the second tube into the beaker on the hotplate. The brown deepened within seconds, dark as strong tea, and she began her rehearsed line about how the system shifted to use up the added heat. He tilted his head. "Heat speeds up reactions," he said. "Both directions. Why doesn't it just run faster in both directions and stay where it is?"

Sadie opened her mouth and found nothing in it. She looked at the tube, darkening still, and said, honestly, "I don't know. That's a good question." He smiled at that, which she suspected was the point of the question, and told her he would come back before the end of the hour, and then he was gone toward the wind turbine.

She sat down on the folding chair and wrote it out in her notebook the way she did when a problem refused to be stared down. Heat speeds up both reactions, she wrote. Forward and reverse. And yet the color changes, so something must be unequal. She drew two arrows, one above the other, and looked at them for a long time. If both got faster and the mixture still changed, then one of them must be getting faster by more. Which one? The mixture had gone darker when she added heat. Darker meant more of the brown gas. More of the brown gas meant the shift was toward the reaction that made it, which meant that was the direction the heat favored, which meant, she wrote slowly, that making the brown gas must take in heat, must be the direction that consumes it. Raising the temperature sped up both reactions, but it sped up the endothermic direction more, and that was the whole reason the equilibrium moved. She underlined it, then felt the familiar doubt arrive on schedule: she had reasoned her way to something that felt true, and she had no way in this gymnasium to check it.

She took out her phone and, because Priya's older sister was a chemistry major at the state university and had answered Sadie's questions before, she typed a message. "Question. If you heat a reaction at equilibrium, both directions speed up, right? So why does it shift at all instead of just running faster both ways?" She sent it, then rearranged the tubes in the shoebox so the pale one and the dark one sat side by side, before and after, the whole argument in glass.

The reply came while a middle schooler was photographing her poster. "You're close to something big. Both speed up, but not equally. The endothermic direction speeds up more, so the equilibrium shifts that way. Check Le Chatelier again. Gotta run, lab." Sadie read it twice. It matched what she had written, sentence for sentence, direction for direction, and the match did not feel like luck. It felt like the way the pale tube and the ice bath matched: something real, held steady from two sides.

Mr. Okonkwo came back at quarter to noon, as promised. "Any thoughts on my question?" he asked, and she stood up so fast the table rattled.

"Heat speeds up both reactions, but not by the same amount," she said. "It speeds up the endothermic direction more. So the equilibrium shifts that way. That's why the tube goes darker when I heat it, because forming the brown gas is the endothermic direction, so it's the one that wins." She heard her own voice, too fast, and made herself slow down. "I got it wrong in my head this morning. I had it as the system just resisting me. It's more like a race where both runners speed up, but one speeds up more."

Mr. Okonkwo tilted his head the other way. Priya had drifted over from her table and was listening with her arms crossed. "Last year," Priya said, "you called my idea about redesigning the poster board reactionary."

"I said the format was obsolescent," Sadie said. "I said you were being reactionary about keeping it. Those are different complaints." Priya laughed, and Mr. Okonkwo wrote something on his clipboard that Sadie could not read, and the dark tube sat in its beaker of cooling water, its brown already beginning, imperceptibly, to fade.

Coralie had been given the auditorium for two weeks, a photocopied script, and four actors who were older than she was, which was the whole problem and also, she kept telling herself, the whole point. The one-act was called The Ferryman's Daughter, and the third act took place on the banks of a river, which was why everybody in the cast had started calling stage left the riparian side, and had somehow made the phrase sound like a joke that was also a fact.

The first rehearsal, she had planned everything. She had drawn the stage in her notebook in pencil, every entrance a clean diagonal, the sofa exactly where the argument was supposed to happen. Ten minutes in, the sofa had moved. Devin and Nasra carried it between scenes and set it down slightly differently each time, and by the third run-through the argument was happening three feet from where it was supposed to live, and the whole shape of the scene had gone soft, like a word repeated too often.

"You keep putting it back differently," she said, feeling the complaint sound smaller out loud than it had in her head at one in the morning.

"It's heavy," Devin said, not unkindly. "We're estimating."

The problem was that Coralie didn't want estimation. She had learned, over two years of running lights for other people's shows, that a stage only means something if it's deliberate; causality up there is manufactured, a chair placed so that a person has to pass it and remember. If the furniture wandered, the memory wandered. But she also knew that the actors hated being treated as furniture, positioned and carried, and Nasra had already said, quietly, in the parking lot, "You're directing us like we're marks on a graph."

That was the word that sent her to the drama room's supply cabinet after school on Thursday. She had seen the roll a hundred times without seeing it: bright fluorescent pink, half-used, shoved behind the gaffer tape. She peeled a strip and pressed it to the stage floor at the exact coordinates from her notebook, then a second strip at the sofa's other foot, and then, because she was there anyway, small T's of green at each actor's opening position, a different color for each scene.

"What is that stuff?" asked Priya, who played the ferryman's daughter and had arrived early to run lines alone, which Coralie found quietly moving.

"It's called spike tape," Coralie said. "It marks where furniture and actors go."

Priya crouched and touched the green T with one finger. "So I stand here."

"Opening position. You can move wherever after."

She expected resistance, but Priya seemed, if anything, relieved, and when the others arrived and the sofa slid perfectly onto its pink marks for the first time all week, Nasra laughed out loud. "It actually lands in the same place," she said. "That's so satisfying." Devin ran the scene twice just to watch it work.

Coralie had been prepared to defend the tape as a compromise between her pencil diagrams and their improvisation, and instead she found the compromise was stranger than that. The marks did not make the actors mechanical; they made them freer, the way the riverbank makes the water. Because Priya knew exactly where she began, she could take a different route each night to the sofa, and the route she took on the second run was better than anything in Coralie's notebook, a small detour past the window as if she'd heard something on the water. Coralie did not pencil it in. She just watched it, and let it stay unrecorded.

The two ways of thinking did not resolve into one clean philosophy by Friday. She still believed the blocking was hers to shape, and Nasra still believed a director should problematize her own diagrams out loud instead of presenting them as settled, and they had a short, careful argument about the second scene in which neither of them gave ground. But at the end of it, Nasra tore a strip of pink tape and knelt and marked the ferryman's chair herself, asking Coralie only, "Here? Or further from the water?"

Coralie crouched beside her on the boards, both of them looking at the empty floor where a river was going to be. "Further," she said. "I think."

Jade folded her arms against the cold of the boathouse and watched Priya shake hands with a fence post. Not the post itself, technically, but the handrail of the dock stairs, which Priya had wrapped in a spare sock to make it feel, she said, more like a person. On Monday Priya had an interview for a rowing scholarship at a college upstate, and the night before, her grandfather had drilled her on it over video call, timing her grip with a stopwatch and pronouncing each attempt dead, dying, or alive.

"My grandfather says a psychologist proved this," Priya said, pumping the sock. "A 2000 study, some guy named William Chaplin. People with firm handshakes made better first impressions."

Jade had been stretching her hamstrings on the bench beside the dock, half listening, the way you half listen to a teammate's nerves before a hard piece. But the name caught her. Chaplin. She had read the study two summers ago, in a library book about first impressions she'd picked up because she was, at fourteen, terrified of being perceived. She remembered the year because she'd thought it was old then, and it was older now, and yet here it was, dressed in a sock, on the boathouse dock.

"Firmer than that," she said, before she could decide whether to say anything at all.

Priya stopped and looked at her. "That's the problem with you, you know. You never say anything during practice and then you say one thing like you've been keeping score the whole time."

That stung because it was accurate. Jade had spent two seasons as the quietest oarswoman in the boat, the one whose judgments lived entirely inside her own skull. The coach had tried to codify honest feedback into the team culture at the start of the fall, posting a rule on the corkboard: praise in public, critique in private, both in specifics. Jade had read it and understood it the way you understand a grammar rule, which is to say not at all until you have to speak the sentence.

"Priya," she said. "Do it on me."

Priya turned, wiped her palm on her spandex, and took Jade's hand. The grip arrived and then hesitated, the way a novice's catch does at the water, arriving and checking in the same instant. Jade held it for three seconds and let go.

"Here's what happens," Jade said. "You grab, and then you go soft halfway through, like you're afraid of hurting me. You won't hurt me. You've seen my hands." She held them up, the blisters gone to callus, the callus gone to something like leather. "Also your wrist is limp, so it's not really your arm doing it. And you look at the handshake instead of at my face."

Priya's mouth did something complicated. "My grandfather said I have a moribund handshake. He uses words like that. He said it's the weakest part of my whole application."

"That's the thing," Jade said, and then she stopped, because the thing she wanted to say was large and she hadn't finished assembling it. She sat down on the dock stairs, and Priya sat down next to her, and out on the river the novice eight went by, their blades splashing in the ragged way that Jade, six months ago, would have watched in silence.

"My grandfather thinks the handshake is everything," Jade said slowly. "Yours, I mean. Like it stands for your whole self, like it's a synecdoche. One part meaning all of you. And my coach thinks no single thing means anything, it's all just the sum of the work." She looked at the sock on the handrail. "I think they're both sort of right and I can't make them into one clean idea. A firm handshake makes a better first impression, that's what the study found. But I don't actually know if first impressions are what an interview is, or if it's more like a season, where you can start badly and fix it by the end."

Priya was quiet for a moment. "So which do I practice?"

"Both, obviously. The handshake and everything after it." Jade stood and offered her hand, palm dry, wrist straight. "Again. Firm the whole way through. Look at me, not at it."

Priya took the hand and gripped, and this time the grip arrived and stayed, certain all the way to the release. Her eyes came up to Jade's and held. For a second, Jade thought, she would have believed this was a person who had never been afraid of anything.

"That one," Jade said. "Do exactly that on Monday."

Priya grinned and peeled the sock off the handrail, wadding it into her pocket like a trophy. From the boathouse the coach's voice rang out across the water, calling the varsity women to the stretchers, and Jade went to get her oar.

Sienna spread the poster board across the picnic table in the backyard, weighting its corners with a soccer ball, a cleat, a rock, and her water bottle, because the wind in October had opinions. On the board she had drawn a grid: seven columns for the days of the week, rows for warm-up, drills, scrimmage, rest. She was applying to be a junior counselor at the rec league next summer, and the application asked for a sample weekly training program, with rest days built in and a proper warm-up protocol. She had assumed the hard part would be filling the boxes. It turned out the hard part was deciding what belonged in them.

Her brother Marcus was in the far corner of the yard with his own ball, working on receiving a pass against the fence and turning. He was twelve and freshly cut from the travel team, a fact he mentioned roughly every forty minutes. "Watch this," he said, and miscontrolled it off his shin into the hydrangeas.

"Inside foot," Sienna called. "You're reaching for it. Let it come across your body." He tried again, better. "Good, but you peeked up too late." The next one clanked off the fence and rolled under the table. She corrected the next one, and the one after that, and for a while the corrections felt like the whole point of having an older sister in the yard. Then he had to take the trash out, and when he came back she had gone inside for a granola bar, and from the kitchen window she watched him play against the fence alone. He fell apart. He was reaching again, rushing the turn, and he knew it, and it was making him worse, and finally he sat down on the grass and put his face in his cleats.

She brought him half the granola bar and ate the other half herself. "You were fine when I was out here," she said.

"That's the problem."

That night she went looking for an answer, not to exculpate herself exactly, though the thought crossed her mind that her sideline commentary might not have been the pure charity she'd imagined. She found a page about motor learning, about how feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, and how less frequent feedback often helps retention. "It's called the guidance hypothesis," she read aloud to Marcus, who was lying across her doorway with a controller. "Like a handrail."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning I talk too much."

The next afternoon she tested it, because a page on the internet wasn't the same as a fence and a twelve-year-old. Marcus set up his receiving drill and she announced the rules with mock solemnity: no comments for ten attempts, then one. He scored her solemnity a three out of ten but agreed. The first ten were ragged, and she bit down on roughly four hundred sentences about inside feet. The eleventh, he struck cleanly, and she said only, "That one," and let the silence resume. By the time the light went amber he was picking out his own errors before the ball had finished rolling. "Nobody told me that one was bad," he said, delighted and slightly betrayed by his own brain.

She sat back down at the picnic table and looked at her grid with new suspicion. Her first draft had been maximal: technical drills Monday through Friday, two hard sessions back to back, a warm-up listed in four bullet points like a legal document. She had treated rest days as empty boxes, failures of ambition. But her legs had been heavy since Thursday, and her first touch had gone sloppy in exactly the way Marcus's did when he was overloaded, and she began to see that the plan's whole morphology was wrong, that the shape of it needed holes the way the fence needed gaps. She crossed out Wednesday's session and wrote REST in letters large enough to be a small act of defiance. She trimmed the warm-up to eight minutes, joint by joint, and moved the hard days apart so the days between them could do their quiet, unmeasurable work.

Her dad came out with two mugs of tea and looked over her shoulder at the grid. "Rest on Wednesday," he said. "Bold."

"Less is apparently more."

"Since when?"

"Since last night," she said, and did not elaborate, because she was still working out how much of it she believed. The page had been about learners like Marcus, beginners with embryonic skills and a fence to play against. Whether it held for her, for a seventeen-year-old with four years of habits already grooved in, she couldn't say. Maybe her version of too much feedback was a training plan that graded every single day, every touch, every ache, and never let anything settle unsupervised. Maybe that was a different problem entirely. She wrote a question mark in the corner of the board, small enough that she could pretend it was punctuation.

Marcus called from the fence, "Ten more, then one thing, right?" She nodded, put the cap on the marker, and carried her tea to the grass, where she sat down and watched him play badly, then adequately, then well, saying nothing at all.

The skate park was mostly empty by five, the September light going long and gold across the concrete bowls, and Charlotte had the picnic table by the fence to herself, which was the only reason she'd brought her physics homework here at all. Her brother Theo had cajoled her into coming with the promise of a ride and the threat of telling their mother she was failing, and she had brought the textbook as a kind of shield, something to hold between herself and the afternoon. Now he was somewhere below in the shallow bowl, dropping in again and again, and she was stuck on a problem about a charged ball launched between two metal plates, one with an angle and a speed and no obvious mercy.

She understood the launch part better than she'd expected to. You took the velocity and split it, horizontal piece and vertical piece, and then the two directions went their separate ways, one coasting steadily like a stone skipped across still water, the other rising and falling under gravity's ledger. She'd gotten that far at the kitchen table last night, drawing little arrows until her pen ran dry. What she couldn't figure out was the plates. The problem said the ball was launched somewhere between two large parallel plates, and it asked for the force on it, and Charlotte had spent twenty minutes with her ruler trying to work out how far the ball was from each plate, because surely that distance mattered, surely a point close to one plate felt something different from a point in the middle. She'd measured the diagram so many times the numbers had gone soft in her head.

A boy about her age coasted up to the table to retrieve his water bottle, which someone had set on the far end, and paused when he saw the page. "Physics," he said. "I did that unit last year. You look like you're about to burn the book."

"I'm trying to find where the ball is between the plates," Charlotte said. "Like how close to each one."

He tipped his head, considering, in no hurry to leave. "Between big parallel plates it's basically the same everywhere in the middle," he said. "Away from the edges, a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point halfway between them. My teacher made us test it and then told us we'd wasted a class proving we could have skipped it." He shrugged, grabbed his bottle, and rolled off toward the bowl, leaving her staring at a diagram she'd covered in pencil measurements that meant nothing.

She erased them slowly, all the little tick marks, and the erasure felt like both a loss and a door swinging open. All that arithmetic, discarded. But if position didn't matter, then the field was just the field, uniform as a held breath, and the force came out in two lines instead of twenty. She checked her result twice because a thing that easy seemed like it must be hiding something, and the second check agreed with the first, and she wrote her answer small, as if to apologize for its size.

"Who's the nerd whisperer?" Theo asked, climbing the fence a few minutes later, hair stuck to his forehead. He nodded at the departing boy, who was now attempting something on the coping of the bowl with a small crowd of younger skaters watching him like acolytes.

"He told me the answer to my homework," Charlotte said. "More or less."

"That's cheating."

"It's not cheating. He told me what kind of problem it is. I still had to do it." She turned the notebook toward Theo, who looked at it with the polite blankness he saved for her schoolwork, and then, because he was her brother and knew her too well, said, "You're going to spend all night checking whether he was right, aren't you."

"Probably," she admitted. That was the part she couldn't explain to him, that trusting a stranger's sentence felt different from trusting her own pencil, and that tomorrow she would go to the physics room before first bell and find out one way or the other, and either way the certainty she had right now was borrowed, equivocal, a coin she hadn't bitten yet. She looked at her answer again. It sat there in her small handwriting, plausible and unproven.

The younger skaters had gone quiet because the boy was dropping in from the highest edge now, and Charlotte watched him go down the curve and up the far side, the board leaving his feet for half a second, and she thought, without meaning to, that he was all one velocity at the top of the arc, his horizontal and vertical selves crossed at a single instant before gravity started its collecting. He landed it. The little crowd thumped their boards against the concrete, that hollow applause skate parks make instead of clapping.

"Again," one of the small kids said, and the boy climbed the ramp to try it a second time, because once was luck and twice was knowing, and Charlotte closed her notebook on her two-line answer and slid off the bench to watch.

The fellowship hall of Grace Covenant smelled like steam and ginger by four in the afternoon, and James stood at the folding table with a clipboard he was supposed to be using for the reunion dinner menu. His aunt Vivian had put him in charge of ordering, which mostly meant writing down whatever his grandmother said. He had written rice, noodles, dumplings, a tray of chicken, and then his pencil stopped.

"No fish?" his grandmother asked, looking over his shoulder. She tapped the clipboard twice, the way she did when a wrong answer could still be fixed.

"I was going to skip it," James said. "It's the most expensive thing on the list, and half the kids won't touch it anyway."

She took the clipboard out of his hands and added a line herself, in characters he couldn't read, then translated for the order form: whole steamed fish. "At New Year's Eve, fish cannot be left off," she said. "The word for fish, yu, sounds like the word for surplus. You leave it off, and what are you wishing us?"

He hadn't known that. He wrote it down, because it seemed like the kind of thing a person should know about his own family, and then he had to run, because the debate workshop started at five in the chapel and he was already late.

Pastor Liu ran the workshop for the older youth group, six of them in a circle of mismatched chairs. This year's tournament topic was whether ancient religious rules still bind people now, and the pastor's one rule of preparation was that every argument had to come from the text itself, quote by quote, no hand-waving about what everybody knew. That afternoon they were working through the dietary laws in Leviticus, and James found himself holding the fish question in his head like a coin he kept turning over.

"James," Pastor Liu said, "you've been quiet. Adjudicate this for us. Verse fourteen lists the creatures you may eat. Does the verse answer our question or not?"

"It answers what they ate then," James said slowly. "It doesn't answer whether we have to. But it also doesn't say it expires. That's the problem. The text just sits there."

"That's not a problem," said Priya, across the circle. "That's the whole debate."

He thought of his grandmother's pencil moving across the clipboard, of the fish she refused to leave off, and he raised his hand even though the pastor didn't require hands. "What if the rule isn't really the rule? Like, what if the point was never the fish?"

Pastor Liu tilted his head. "Then what would the point be?"

James didn't have the sentence yet. He had an embryonic version of it, half-formed, and he let it come out crooked: "At my grandmother's dinner, you have to serve fish, but not because anyone wants fish. The fish is standing in for a wish, for abundance. So maybe the rule is the wish, and the fish is just how it got carried around."

The room was quiet a moment. Priya wrote something in her notebook, and Marcus, who usually argued for the sake of arguing, only nodded.

Later that evening, back in the hall, James found his grandmother alone by the steam tables, testing the burner with a small pot of water. He set down the boxes of napkins he'd carried in and sat on the stool beside her.

He remembered being nine, the year his grandfather had still been alive, standing in this same kitchen on New Year's Eve while his grandfather lifted the lid off the steamer and told him to look at the fish before anyone served themselves, and James had asked why he had to look, and his grandfather had only said, "So you remember there's more coming," and put the lid back. James had forgotten that for years, and it returned to him now whole, the hiss of the steam, the shape of his grandfather's hand on the lid.

"Yeye never explained it either," James said. "The fish thing. He just made me look at it."

His grandmother smiled without turning from the burner. "Some things you explain. Some things you keep doing, and the explanation catches up later."

"I have to argue both sides for the tournament," James said. "Whether an old rule still counts. I kept wanting to say it obviously doesn't, because who needs it. But I don't think that's honest. It's doing something. I just don't know exactly what, or whether that makes it binding, or just good."

"That sounds like a problem for your side of the table," she said, and patted his wrist. "Mine is just to make sure the fish arrives on time. Speaking of which, go check whether the order went through, and if the boy at the market tries to say they're out of whole fish, you tell him your grandmother will come down there herself."

James stood, clipboard in hand, and paused at the door. "If I argue that the rule is the wish and not the fish," he said, "does that mean the fish is optional?"

His grandmother turned the flame down to a simmer and looked at him the way she looked at a pot that wasn't boiling yet. "That depends," she said. "Are you ordering it or not?"

The handicap stall in the humanities building basement was the only private space at the Ridgemont Invitational, so Kaylee and Priya had claimed it as a green room. Priya sat on the sink counter with the rules sheet for the exhibition event, which nobody took seriously, folded into her fist. "Original performance," she read. "Ten minutes. A moment from your own life. Staged, not read."

"My life doesn't have moments," Kaylee said. "It has rounds."

"Then stage a round." Priya kicked the stall door with her heel. "You have until the assembly slot at four."

Kaylee's debate partner, Dev, had dropped debate for the spring to direct a one-act at the community theatre, so she texted him between semifinals and finals. He showed up at the basement with a messenger bag of scripts and the specific confidence of someone who had recently learned what things were called. "Ten minutes is nothing," he said. "You write one moment and you block it."

"Block it?"

"Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals." He said it the way people recite the first sentence of something they read two weeks ago. "I found out the hard way. My two leads bumped chests in scene two like fighting pigeons, opening night, because I never set where anyone stood."

Priya volunteered to act. The problem was the material. Kaylee had written, in her legal pad, four false starts: one about nationals, one about her extemp file, one about the time a judge called her "perspicacious" on a ballot and she'd had to look it up in the hallway, which was funny but wasn't a moment. The real one came out sideways, while she was moving Priya from the door of the handicap stall to the counter: the fall of junior year, when her father explained at dinner that he was selling the annuity his mother had left him, because her care had eaten everything else, and Kaylee had understood only one word of the whole speech and had kept eating so nobody would ask her anything. She hadn't told anyone at school. The school counselor had a form, and the form had a word on it, and she'd refused to be the girl the word was for. Kids who took the free lunch were stigmatized enough without her adding a family that was quietly broke.

"Okay," Dev said, when she'd said it out loud, flat, as a fact. "Who plays you?"

"I'll play me. Priya can be my dad."

They blocked it in the basement. Dev set Priya at the sink, standing, one hand flat on the counter, and set Kaylee at the door with a cafeteria tray they'd borrowed from the concessions table. The blocking was simple: Kaylee crossed to the table, sat, and did not look up, while Priya delivered the dinner speech in pieces, moving one step forward each time, until she was directly across from Kaylee, who kept arranging and rearranging the same three meatballs. Dev watched them bump at the doorway twice and re-set the cross so it curved. "You have to decide," he said, "whether she looks up at the end or not."

"That's the whole question," Kaylee said. "I didn't look up. Not that night."

"So you don't look up, and the audience decides what that costs." He checked his phone. "Or you look up and it's a different play. Forgiveness play. Cheaper ticket."

She thought about it through the final round of the tournament, where she lost on a two-one decision because she spent her last rebuttal thinking about meatballs. She'd been trained her whole debate career to state both sides and choose, loudly, on a timer. The play wanted the other thing: to stand in the true position and admit what she still didn't know, which was whether her silence that night had protected her father or simply spared her.

At four, in the assembly hall, with maybe thirty tired competitors scattered in the seats, she and Priya ran it exactly as blocked. Priya crossed the stage in her five steps. Kaylee arranged the meatballs, which were actually rolled-up socks from the emergency kit, and did not look up. The lights were just the auditorium lights, nobody ran a board, and when Priya stopped speaking, the silence went on longer than silence was supposed to, and some boy in the third row laughed, quietly, at the socks, and then stopped himself.

Afterward Dev found her by the doors. "So which play was it?"

"I don't know yet," she said. "Ask me at the next tournament."

He wrote something in his script margin. "You're blocking it again either way," he said, and held out the pen.

Sierra had claimed the window seat before anyone else was awake, her copy of Pride and Prejudice wedged against the radiator and her notebook open to a page headed with two words in careful capitals: FEMINIST. MARXIST. The assignment was due Monday: choose a lens, apply it to one passage, and be prepared to defend the choice in seminar. She had underlined the scene where Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth, and then, in the margin, written nothing, because she could not decide what she actually thought.

Her cousin Priya came over at eleven with a thermos and her own battered paperback, because Priya's first-year seminar was doing the same novel and their mothers had decided the cousins should study together whether or not the cousins agreed. Priya dropped onto the floor, poured coffee into the thermos lid, and read the two capitalized words upside down.

"You can't do both," she said. "Pick one and get on with it."

"The professor said we could combine them if we could justify it."

"Then justify it." Priya flipped her book open to a page dog-eared in three places. "My book club argued about Mrs Bennet for forty minutes on Tuesday. Marcus called her a gold-digging caricature. Vulgar, grasping, all of it."

Sierra turned her own book to the early chapters, where Mrs Bennet nags and flutters and mortifies her daughters. "She's written to be laughed at," she said. "Austen keeps letting her embarrass everyone."

"Except," Priya said, and she slid a finger down her page, "Marcus's mother started the meeting by asking whether he'd read the legal background. He hadn't. I hadn't either." She found the passage and turned the book so Sierra could see it was the same paragraph in both editions. "The Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home."

Sierra read the line twice. "None of them. Not even a share?"

"Not a share. When Mr Bennet dies, the house goes to a cousin they've never met. Mrs Bennet and all five girls are out."

Sierra set her coffee down on the windowsill and pulled the notebook onto her knees. She wrote the word entail and boxed it. "So her matchmaking," she said slowly, "isn't greed. It's the only pension plan she has. If the daughters don't marry, there's nothing."

"There's marrying Mr Collins," Priya said. "That's the offer on the table. He's going to own their house."

They sat with that for a moment. Outside, a delivery truck reversed up the street with its warning beep, and the cat pushed between them and settled on Priya's ankle.

Sierra drew two columns. Under the first she wrote property is the trap: the estate is the family's whole solvency, and the law that protects the estate is the same law that disinherits the daughters. Under the second she wrote marriage is the labor market: for women with no inheritance, a husband is an employer, and Elizabeth is refusing the only job offer that guarantees survival. She looked at the columns and thought they belonged together, that separating them would be a lie, that the money and the marriage in this novel were the same machine seen from two sides.

"Here's my problem," she said. "The feminist reading makes Elizabeth the hero for refusing Collins. The Marxist reading makes her refusal a luxury. Charlotte Lucas takes Collins and the reading says she's pragmatic, or compromised, or both, and I can't tell which."

"Maybe she's both," Priya said. "She's twenty-seven and plain and she takes the house."

"That's not an answer, though. That's a shrug."

Priya drank her coffee and considered the notebook. "Your professor really allows combined lenses?"

"If it's a considered position. Not a mush."

"Then don't mush it. Say what each lens sees, and say where they collide, and say you don't know which is truer."

Sierra wrote collision in the margin between the columns and circled it. She read back over her lines about property and labor and thought the phrasing sounded borrowed, like something a textbook would presage with the phrase as we have seen. She crossed out both column headings and started again in plainer words: the law hands the house to a man none of them chose. Charlotte takes the man because she cannot take the house. Elizabeth refuses both and Austen rewards her with Darcy, which is the part Sierra could not make fit any lens at all, because Darcy's ten thousand a year forgives everything the argument has just exposed.

She said this out loud, more or less, and Priya laughed.

"So your conclusion is that Austen cheats?"

"My conclusion is that I have a conclusion for Collins and Charlotte and Mrs Bennet, and Darcy is a separate problem." Sierra closed the notebook and looked at the window, where her own reflection sat ghosted over the street. The seminar was Monday. She had a thesis, two columns, one circle, and a hole shaped like a man with ten thousand a year.

"Start with the entail," Priya said, standing, gathering her thermos. "Lead with the fact. Let them fight about Mrs Bennet after."

Sierra opened the notebook again and, at the top of the first column, wrote: Begin with the house.

Oliver had spread the topographic map across the picnic table so completely that there was no room for anyone's dinner, and he knew this, and he still didn't move it. Around him the campsite was settling into evening: his father coaxing the stove to light, his little sister stacking kindling with the solemnity of a priest, and, two sites over, Dana Okoye from his geography class, who had materialized on the same bus to the same trailhead and whose family's tent glowed diaphanous against the darkening pines. Oliver's phone lay face down beside the map. He had forty percent battery, one bar of signal that came and went like a guilty conscience, and an assignment due Monday that he had promised his teacher would be finished before the trip.

The assignment asked him to look at a population pyramid, that stacked pair of bar graphs with males on one side and females on the other, and decide what a country would need more of in twenty years, schools or nursing homes. He had chosen two countries almost at random. One pyramid looked like an actual pyramid, wide at the bottom, tapering to almost nothing at the top. The other looked like a barrel, bulging in the middle, thin where the children should have been. He could see that they were different. What he couldn't see was what the difference meant, and the essay he'd drafted that afternoon in the car read like someone describing two paintings by listing their colors.

His map wouldn't help either. Before the trip, as a warm-up exercise, he'd tried to overlay the city's housing layer with the flood zone layer on the school's GIS software, and the result had baffled him: every house in the city appeared on his screen, red dots spilling across neighborhoods that sat on hills, nowhere near any water. He'd screenshotted it and saved it to his phone, meaning to ask his teacher, and now there was no teacher, only trees.

He heard footsteps on gravel. Dana stood at the edge of the firelight holding a mug.

"Mr. Halvorsen says you're the only one who did the flood map," she said. "He told my whole period. In his lecture voice."

"His oratory," Oliver said. "He does that when he's disappointed. Did you hear him do the one about plate boundaries?"

"Twice." She set the mug down and looked at his phone screen, which he'd turned over out of some instinct he couldn't name. "Is that the overlay? Can I see?"

He handed it to her. She studied the red dots, tilting the screen away from the fire's glare.

"That's every house in the city," she said. "An intersect overlay keeps only the areas that appear in both layers. Intersect the housing with the flood zone, and you'd see just the homes inside the zone."

Oliver took the phone back and stared at it. The dots he'd spent an hour generating, and been quietly proud of, were worse than useless; they showed everything, which meant they showed nothing. He had used the wrong tool and mistaken its noise for a result. And then, standing there with the smell of his father's burning rice drifting over, he felt something shift, the way a word you've been mispronouncing suddenly corrects itself in your mouth.

"Wait," he said. He pulled the map toward him and grabbed his pencil. "The pyramid is the same problem. I was reading the whole shape, all the bars, everything at once. But it's an intersect. The bottom bars are the children who will be the parents, and the middle bars are the people who will be old in twenty years. I don't need the whole country. I need the part where the two things overlap."

Dana sat down on the bench across from him. "Overlap how?"

"Like, the wide bottom means lots of kids now means lots of parents later means more kids after that, so schools. The barrel shape means fewer kids and a heavy middle, so by the time that middle reaches the top, nursing homes." He drew two quick shapes on the map's margin, a triangle and a barrel, and bracketed the bottom of one and the middle of the other. "The tool isn't software. It's just asking which group falls inside which future."

"That's actually not bad," Dana said, and then, more quietly, "which countries did you pick?"

He told her. She was quiet for long enough that the fire popped twice.

"The second one," she said. "That's where I was born. I always figured it would need more schools, because that's what everyone says about it, young country, bright future." She turned her mug in her hands. "The pyramid you're looking at is five years old. Things changed fast."

Oliver looked at his pencil marks, which now seemed less like an answer and more like a question with better grammar. He had a method, finally, but the method needed data he didn't have, on a phone with one flickering bar.

"So it could still go either way," he said.

"It could still go either way," Dana agreed. She looked up at him through the firelight. "Show me the software in the morning. I want to see the intersect one work."

Behind them, Oliver's father announced, with genuine despair, that the rice had burned, and his sister dropped the whole stack of kindling into the flames at once, sending a column of sparks up through the black pines.

Dominic had never minded history until the essays started requiring him to have an opinion. On Tuesday Ms. Achterberg handed back his paragraph on the origins of the Cold War with a single note in the margin: "You have summarized two historians. Now weigh them." The two historians were Aldrich, who put the blame on Soviet expansion after 1945, and a revisionist named Korenblyum, who argued that Western capitalism needed an enemy and manufactured one. Dominic had assumed one of them was simply correct, the way a math answer is correct, and that Ms. Achterberg knew which and was withholding it out of some pedagogical cruelty. He wanted the key. Priya, who sat in front of him and underlined her books in three colors, seemed to have it.

On Thursday his class walked to the town square for the remembrance assembly, and while the head teacher droned at the war memorial, Dominic drifted along the low stone wall reading the plaques the twin-town association had bolted to it over the years. One small brass plate listed names of French mayors and deputies the association had honored, and at the bottom, weathered nearly smooth, stood the name Jean Jaurès. "That's a street," said Marcus, leaning over his shoulder. "There's a Rue Jaurès near my cousin's flat in Lyon. I thought it was, like, a cheese." Dominic traced the letters with his thumb and felt the small itch he got when a fact refused to fit its shelf. The plaque said nothing else about the man. It didn't even say what he'd done, only that the twin town had sent the plaque in 1962.

That night he looked Jaurès up, half for the essay and half because Marcus had made him promise to find out whether the cheese thing was real. Jaurès had been a socialist politician, and he had been assassinated in 1914, shot in a café months before the war began. But the part that stopped Dominic was further down the page: in the early 1900s, Jaurès had written a socialist history of the French Revolution, a multivolume work, and that history had shaped how people understood the Revolution for most of the twentieth century. The class-conflict interpretation, the textbook's phrase, the one that framed the Revolution as the bourgeoisie toppling a feudal order, had a single author with a political program behind it. Dominic sat with that for a while. A politician had written the past, and the past had stayed written that way for decades.

He started seeing the pattern everywhere, which was probably dangerous. Korenblyum, the revisionist, kept describing the Cold War as a struggle of economic classes wearing national costumes, the United States acting as the executive committee of capital, the Soviet Union as a besieged workers' state. Dominic couldn't prove Korenblyum had ever read Jaurès, and he wasn't going to claim it, but the lens had a lineage, and lineages were not neutral. Aldrich, though, was no cleaner. Aldrich called Stalin an autocrat in the first paragraph, ascribed every crisis from Berlin to Korea to one man's paranoia, and wrote as if institutions, evidence, and ordinary caution played no part, as if a whole country's foreign policy were the mood of a single patient. Dominic found a footnote in a library copy where Aldrich dismissed Soviet fears of invasion as "atavistic," which was a word Dominic had to look up and then distrusted immediately, because calling a fear primitive is a way of not answering it.

In Friday's seminar Ms. Achterberg put them in pairs, and of course Dominic drew Priya. "Korenblyum is obviously closer," she said, arranging her three pens. "The documents support him." "Which documents," Dominic said. "The ones he chose to read. The Soviet archives opened in the nineties and both of them kept their conclusions, which is a little strange, isn't it, if evidence is supposed to settle things." Priya looked at him with something that was not quite respect, more the recalibration you'd give a vending machine that suddenly produced the right snack. "So you're saying nobody can know anything." "I'm saying a historian is a person first," Dominic said, and heard how it sounded, like a fortune cookie, and said it anyway.

He wrote the essay that weekend, hating most of it and keeping one page. The page said that Aldrich explained the Cold War better when the question was who decided, and Korenblyum explained it better when the question was who benefited, and that a reader who wanted a single answer should probably ask which question she actually cared about, and why. He admitted that he couldn't weigh the two men against the evidence until he admitted the evidence had already been weighed once by whoever gathered it, and probably twice by whoever taught him to read. He handed it in feeling like he'd built half a bridge and charged people to cross it.

Ms. Achterberg returned the essays on Wednesday with grades but no comments until you asked. Dominic got the highest mark he'd received all year, and beneath it one line: "Finally an argument. Though you never say whose explanation you'd trust with your own country." He stared at that for the whole period, because he'd thought the honest part was the not knowing, and she seemed to be saying the honesty was a place to stand, not a place to live. After the bell he walked back to the square, ostensibly for the bus, actually for the plaque. He crouched, ran his thumb over Jaurès's name again, and noticed for the first time the smaller engraved line beneath it, which Marcus had been blocking with his elbow on Thursday. "Un hommage de la ville jumelle à tous les historiens engagés," it read. A tribute from the twin town, he translated slowly, to all committed historians. "Ha," he said out loud, alone on the war memorial steps. "You too, huh."

Florence had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, and around her lay the evidence of a stalled campaign: three highlighters, a paperback of Jane Eyre swollen with torn paper strips, and a blank document titled, optimistically, "Essay Draft 1." The prompt on her phone read, "Identify an unreliable narrator in your chosen novel and analyse how point of view shapes the reader's trust." She had read the novel twice. She still did not trust herself to write about trust.

Her grandmother's copy sat beside the school's edition, and that was the problem, or at least the beginning of it. She had found it last Sunday in the house on Perry Street, in a box of books her mother wanted taken to the charity shop. The cover was cloth, gone soft at the corners, and the title page said Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell, Esq. Florence had assumed the editor was the author until she opened her school copy and found no Currer Bell anywhere in it.

"It's not an editor," her grandmother had said from the armchair, not looking up from her crossword. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell. It didn't tell anyone the author was a woman."

"Why not?"

"That's a different question from what you asked me." Her grandmother had filled in a word, seven letters, and Florence had spent the drive home deciding whether the deflection was evasion or an invitation.

In the library now, Priya dropped into the opposite chair without asking, the way only Priya could. "You look like your essay murdered you."

"Sort of the reverse. I can't decide who's lying." Florence turned the old book toward her. "Rochester tells Jane his whole history, and he leaves out one fairly significant wife in the attic. Jane narrates the book, and she narrates him sympathetically, so we half forgive him before we even know. It's like the lying happens two layers down."

"An unreliable narrator through a reliable one," Priya said, chewing the cap of her own pen. "That's actually a decent thesis."

"It's a decent sentence. A thesis needs to go somewhere." Florence pulled the old copy back. "And then this. The whole book is Jane telling us her autobiography, except the real woman who wrote it signed it with a man's name and called it an autobiography anyway. I keep thinking that's part of the same problem, and then I keep thinking I'm reaching."

Priya leaned over the page. "Who's Currer Bell?"

"Charlotte Brontë. Nobody reading it in 1847 knew the author was a woman." Florence heard her grandmother's phrasing come out of her mouth almost intact, like a coat borrowed and worn the same way.

Priya sat back. "Okay, but is that unreliable narration? She didn't lie about anything in the story. She just didn't tell the truth about herself."

"That's exactly what Rochester does." Florence said it faster than she meant to, and then more slowly, testing it. "He doesn't lie to Jane, mostly. He just doesn't tell her the truth about himself, and the not-telling is shaped so she'll trust him. Brontë shapes the reader's trust the same direction. Every choice about what to withhold is a choice about who you're letting the reader be." She wrote two lines in the margin before she could lose them, then crossed one out.

The crossing-out felt familiar. Two years ago, in the debate club semifinal, she had done the same thing, cut an argument she privately believed because the judge would find it anachronistic, judging a Victorian novelist by modern expectations. She had won that round and had thought about it maybe once a month since. Whether that was principle or cowardice she had never fully settled, and the crossed-out line brought it back with the peculiar recidivism of old doubts, the way they return no matter how many times you've answered them. She uncrossed it. Then she crossed it out again and left both marks visible, which Priya noticed and mercifully did not mention.

"Here's my problem, though," Florence said. "If I say the pseudonym counts as narrative unreliability, I'm claiming Brontë deceived her readers, and I don't think that's fair to her. She was preempting something, not lying. And if I say it doesn't count, I'm pretending the name on the title page doesn't shape how the whole book gets read, and it obviously does. So I have to hold both, and I don't know if that's insight or just indecision with better vocabulary."

"That's the most honest thing anyone's said about an essay in this library," Priya said, "including the library."

Florence laughed, and under the laugh something assembled itself. She opened the blank document and typed a first sentence she almost liked: The most important liar in Jane Eyre may be the name on its cover. She would probably cut it tomorrow. She kept typing anyway.

At the circulation desk on her way out, the librarian, Mrs. Adeyemi, stopped her. "You left the cloth edition on the scanner bed," she said, holding out the old book. "Lovely. Where did you get it?" Florence explained the box, the charity shop run that hadn't happened yet. Mrs. Adeyemi turned to the title page and went still.

"Florence," she said. "Open the back cover." Inside, in faded brown ink, someone had written: To Harriet, who lent me the courage to send it out under my own name at last. Christmas, 1864. Below it, in the same hand, a different signature: C. Brontë was never here, but Harriet Bell was, and this was her shelf.

Florence read it twice. "Bell," she said. "Currer Bell. Harriet Bell."

"Your grandmother's family name," Mrs. Adeyemi said, "before the marriage. You'd have to ask her about the rest. I only shelved her donations for thirty years." She slid the book back across the desk. "Some narrators you have to interrogate in person, while you still can."

Florence looked at the inscription, then at the door, then at her phone, and dialed the Perry Street number as she pushed out into the cold.

Mackenzie had until Friday, and it was already Tuesday evening, and the essay was supposed to be about how historians' views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, a topic she had chosen in a fit of ambition she no longer remembered fondly. She spread her books across the table by the library's tall windows, where the late light came down in dusty columns, and opened her notebook to a page that said only, in her handwriting from Sunday: figure out what historiography even is.

She had figured that much out by now. Historiography, as far as she could tell, meant arguing about the arguers. It meant reading Carlyle and finding a great man thundering across the pages, then reading a Marxist historian who saw no men at all, only classes shifting like tectonic plates. What she could not figure out was how to organize any of it, how to make the pile of quotations into a shape. Her teacher, Ms. Adeyemi, had written one comment on her proposal: "Good topic. Now take a position. You can hold two ideas and still choose." Mackenzie had underlined it twice and understood it not at all.

The boy at the next table kept glancing at her stack of books. He had a chemistry textbook open and a look of genuine despair. "You're doing the French Revolution thing," he said, not a question. "The historiography one. Half the class is doing it."

"And you're doing chemistry, apparently."

"Due Friday," he said. "Yours too?"

"Friday," she said, and the word landed between them like a shared sentence.

His name was Theo, and it turned out he worked at the library shelving returns, which was why he knew where everything was, including the things nobody asked for anymore. When she told him her problem, that she needed older sources, he led her back into the stacks, past the bright new displays, to a section that smelled faintly of dust and glue. "Nobody comes here," he said. "This whole area's kind of moribund." He pulled a slim volume off the shelf, a survey of modern European history printed decades ago, its jacket gone soft. "Old books say old things. Might help."

She took it to a carrel and read, at first only skimming for the Revolution chapter. But on the way there, a heading caught her: a few pages on the Cold War, written in a voice of settled certainty. The book laid the outbreak of the Cold War chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, one side blamed, the other side absolved, the whole thing delivered as though it were simply what had happened. Mackenzie sat back. She had never thought of a textbook as having an opinion before. It was like discovering that a mirror could choose what to show you.

There was a flashback then, unbidden: her grandfather's apartment two winters ago, the radiator clanking, a documentary about the Cold War on his small television. She had been fifteen and half watching while scrolling her phone. Her grandfather had said, "That's not how it was," at the screen, and when she asked what he meant, he'd only said, "Depends who's telling it," and she had gone back to her phone, and he had died that spring. She hadn't introspect on it much since; there had been no reason to. Now, at the carrel, she felt the cost of that, the conversation she hadn't bothered to have, sitting right next to the strange gain of finally understanding what he meant.

She went back to the Revolution sources with new eyes. She reread Carlyle and the Marxist and a revisionist who blamed the whole upheaval on a nobility too rigid to reform, and this time she saw them not as competitors for the truth but as a sequence, each answering the anxieties of its own decade. She began to write fast, filling a page, then stopping. The trouble was that taking a position felt like betraying someone. If she argued that each generation rewrote the Revolution to suit itself, didn't she still have to say which reading was best? Ms. Adeyemi's comment surfaced again: you can hold two ideas and still choose. Maybe the choice wasn't between Carlyle and the Marxists. Maybe the choice was between pretending certainty was possible and admitting it wasn't, and choosing the second was itself a position, an honest one, though it left a hollow place where conviction was supposed to live.

At nine o'clock the overhead lights dimmed once, the library's way of saying thirty minutes remained. Theo appeared at the end of the aisle, coat already on. "Any of it useful?" he asked. "The moribund section, I mean."

"Useful," she said, and surprised herself by laughing a little. "Did you know people who wrote about the Cold War back in the fifties were called orthodox or traditionalist historians? That's what the book called them. They mostly blamed the whole thing on the Soviets." She held up the volume. "The author was one of them, I think. He didn't say so. He just wrote it like weather."

"Like weather," Theo repeated, weighing it. "So the book's wrong?"

"No," she said slowly, closing it and running her thumb along the soft edge of the cover. "That's the part I can't get to the bottom of. Wrong isn't the right word. It's just that a fact from one decade isn't the same fact in another." She slid the book into her bag next to her notes, half a draft, three days left, her grandfather's unhad conversation folded somewhere into all of it. She zipped the bag and stood. "I'm going to say that, I think. That I can't tell the difference between what they knew and what they believed. And that maybe neither can I."

Theo held the door, and the cold outside hit her face as she stepped through it, the streetlights already on, the essay unfinished and finally, somehow, begun.

Olivier sat on the closed lid of the toilet with his father's blood pressure cuff open on his knees like a stubborn book. The instruction sheet had fallen behind the radiator, so he was working from memory: arm at heart level, feet flat, still. He had told his father he would figure the thing out before Friday, when the visiting nurse came, and his father had laughed in that dry way of his and said, "You're the college man now, go on." The bathroom was the only room with a door that locked and a chair at the right height, so the bathroom it was.

He wrapped the cuff above his own elbow, pressed start, and watched his arm squeeze until his fingers tingled. The numbers came up: 122 over 78. He wrote them on the mirror in dry-erase marker, the way he kept his formulas for exams, and sat with them a while. Systolic, the top number, was the heart pushing; diastolic was the resting between. He understood the mechanics well enough from the diagrams, but what he wanted was to know what the numbers meant when they moved, which ones mattered, and how a person could actually change them instead of just worrying about them.

His phone buzzed against the sink. It was Danny from his orientation group, who had gone to the campus clinic that morning for a sports form and come back quiet. "They asked if I wanted STI testing while I was there," Danny texted. "I said no thanks. I feel completely fine, so what's the point, right?"
