She stood very still, because thirty and sixty added up to ninety, and somewhere in the back of her mind a teacher's voice had said something about complementary angles, something she had filed away as a trivia item and never touched. "Do it at forty and fifty," she said. It felt like a test she was setting for herself as much as for them.

They did it at forty and fifty, same spring, same ball, level concrete, and the two landing marks sat close enough that the bottle cap covered both. Dev whooped. The saturnine boy sat down on the launcher, which was probably not good for it, and said, "Nobody threw the ball different. Same speed. It just... lands there either way." He said it the way people say things they don't yet believe.

Anais walked back to the fence, but she was walking differently now, the way she walked when a problem had stopped being flat. She sat down and looked at her two charged plates and thought about what a field between them might actually be like. If the plates were two walls and you stood in the middle, the field would push you, every point between them, the same push at every point. She'd been treating the field as something that varied, that had interesting geography, and the homework number kept coming out wrong. But if the push was the same everywhere inside, then the point in the question didn't matter at all. The whole space between the plates was one uniform thing.

She divided the voltage by the distance between the plates, wrote the answer, and then, because the boys were still firing, wrote it a second time in the margin to see if it would dare come out different. It didn't. She wondered whether that sameness was a real property of the world or a convenience of the diagram, whether real plates out here in the air, with wind and dust and crooked edges, would keep that promise the way the concrete had kept its promise about thirty and sixty degrees. The concrete had ignored the air, mostly, and been honest anyway. Or honest enough. She couldn't say where the line was, and she left a small question mark next to her answer, not because she doubted the arithmetic but because she wanted to remember that she didn't know everything the number was standing for.

"Hey," she called to the boys, holding up the notebook. "You want to see something weird that's not weird at all?" Dev jogged over, and she turned the page toward the dying light, her pencil still in her hand, the question mark visible at the edge.

The waiting room smelled like spearmint and carpet cleaner, and Hunter had been sitting under the fluorescent light long enough to memorize the poster about gum disease. His father's blood pressure was the reason they were both here, in a way. Dad's physical last week had come back with a number the doctor called borderline, and Dad had shrugged it off, so Hunter had decided, without exactly saying so to anyone, that he would learn what the number meant and explain it in a way his father could not shrug off.

The hygienist, a woman named Carol with reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, wrapped the cuff around Hunter's arm without asking. "New machine," she said. "We take everyone's now. You'd be surprised how many people find out they have a problem in a dental chair." The cuff tightened, hugged, released. Carol tilted the screen toward him. "One twenty-four over seventy-eight. That's a good one."

"What do the numbers actually measure?" Hunter asked.

"Top one's the pressure when your heart beats. Bottom one's between beats, when it rests." Carol stripped the cuff off and folded it. "Your dad got a high one somewhere, didn't he. I can tell by the question."

"That obvious?"

"Only to people who ask it that way." She pointed her pen at the poster. "Salt makes you hold fluid, more volume in the same pipes, more pressure. Exercise widens the pipes over time, kind of, makes the whole system run lower. It's plumbing plus habits. Nobody's born with their final number."

Hunter turned that over while Carol printed his chart. Plumbing plus habits. Not a verdict, a reading. That distinction felt important, and he held onto it the way he held onto a locker combination, testing it twice.

His grandmother, in the chair beside him waiting for her own appointment, was scrolling her phone with one finger, the way she did everything, deliberately. "Listen to this," she said. "A country in Europe, they're raising the age of consent to seventeen. Seventeen. There's a whole argument about it in their parliament."

Hunter leaned over. He had never thought about it having an age at all, or rather he had assumed it was simply eighteen everywhere, the way eighteen was the age for everything he'd been told about. "It's not the same everywhere?"

"Goodness, no. It differs by country. And your cousin Denzel was telling me it's not even the same across our own states, that it falls between sixteen and eighteen depending on where you are." She set the phone face-down on her purse. "I suppose lines on a map decide things we think are just true."

He looked it up himself, quietly, while Carol called his grandmother back. Country to country, state to state, sixteen to eighteen, a patchwork he had never noticed. He thought of the blood pressure numbers, how the same body could read differently depending on what had been done to it, and how the same fact could be legal in one place and not another, and how neither system was as fixed as it looked from the outside. He did not fully know what to do with that yet. It sat beside his locker combination, unfinished.

A man across the room was flipping through a local paper with unnecessary violence, and every page he turned he seemed to shake, like the paper had personally offended him. Beside him, his son, maybe ten, read over his shoulder and asked why they kept writing about the aquifer, and the man said, "Because we drink out of it, that's why," and Hunter understood from the words alone: water under the ground, drawn up, argued over. It was a gratuitous amount of anger for a waiting room, though maybe the man was angry about other things and the newspaper was just the nearest target. Hunter's father did that too, anger misplaced onto objects, onto the lawnmower, onto the salt shaker Carol would have confiscated.

When his own name was finally called, Hunter sat back in the chair and let the dentist look at his molars, and when the chair came up he asked, before he lost his nerve, "My dad's pressure was high. If he walks every day and cuts salt, how fast does it change?"

"Weeks to months, if he actually does it," the dentist said. "The body's not instant. But it responds." He looked at Hunter more carefully then. "You want to tell him that?"

"I want to tell him why, not just that."

"Good luck," the dentist said. "I've been telling patients the why for thirty years. Some of them hear it. Some of them just hear a number."

On the drive home, his grandmother asked him to beseech the pharmacist to fill her prescription before five, using the word the way she always did, as if asking were a formal ceremony, and Hunter said he would. At the pharmacy, while the labels printed, he texted his father: Numbers move. Walking and less salt, that's the actual mechanism, not a lecture. He stared at the message for a long moment, thumb over send, thinking that he knew what the numbers meant and did not yet know whether his father would care, and then he sent it anyway and picked up the white bag with his grandmother's name on it.

His phone buzzed against the counter before they reached the car. "Fine," it said. "Walk with me tomorrow. Six a.m."

"Six," Hunter said out loud, to nobody, to the bag, to the whole plumbed and shifting world. "Okay. Six."

The textbook fit on the counter between the register and the lottery scratch-offs, which struck Makayla as the most hopeful arrangement in the store. She had six weeks until the placement exam at Middlesex County College, six weeks to learn enough calculus to skip the remedial course that would cost her a semester and nine hundred dollars she did not have. Between customers she worked the practice problems, and when the bell over the door chimed she covered the page with the flyer for Dev's cold brew special, as though the derivatives were something she'd be embarrassed to be caught wanting.

Dev wanted the cold brew special to work more than he let on. He had raised the price twice since June, and each time he watched the cooler like a man waiting for a verdict. "Nobody vilifies a dollar-fifty increase," he said, tapping the handwritten sign. "But nobody buys it either. There's a number out there, the right price, and I don't know it and the guy who delivers the cups doesn't know it."

Makayla, restocking the day-old pastries whose edges had gone friable enough to shed crumbs down the whole front of the case, said she thought the right price might be a maximum. Not a guess, a point. She had just spent an hour on a page headed Locating Maxima, and the idea had begun to feel less like math and more like a claim about the world: that somewhere between too cheap and too expensive there was exactly one best spot, and the derivative would put her finger on it.

That was the part she couldn't yet hold onto. She could run the rules, bring the exponent down, subtract one, set the whole thing equal to zero. She could do it the way she'd learned to do everything, which was to memorize the motion and trust it. But when she tried to say why setting the slope to zero found the top of a hill, the explanation went friable in her hands too, crumbling before she could hand it to anyone. She had two ways of thinking and no bridge between them.

Ana came in at four-thirty with her book bag and her tutoring money rolled in a rubber band. She was fourteen and preparing for the same placement track two years early, and she installed herself at the ice cream freezer's lid, using it as a desk. Makayla had started helping her on Tuesdays, informally, in exchange for Ana's mother sending over samosas. Today Ana pointed at Makayla's open book, at the tall thin symbol, and asked why the integral sign looked like a stretched-out letter.

Makayla opened her mouth and then closed it, because she didn't know. She flipped to the back of the chapter and found a sidebar boxed in gray, a paragraph about notation, and read it quietly first and then aloud. Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s, because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum. "An infinite sum," Ana repeated, as if tasting it. She looked at the symbol again and decided it was better than the other notation, the scrawny prime marks, which to her looked like a cat had scratched the page. Makayla didn't argue. Something about the long s settled her anyway, the thought of a man in 1675 deciding that a shape should carry a meaning, that a curve's area was a sum of slices too thin to see.

She turned back to Dev's problem while Ana worked her own page. She wrote a revenue function on the back of the cold brew flyer, something she made up out of the numbers he kept mutbling about: p dollars per cup, cups sold falling as the price rose. She chose R equals 200p minus p squared, because she could differentiate it without hesitating, and then she made herself slow down. The derivative, she said to Ana more than to Dev, is the rate of change. At the top of the hill the rate is zero for one instant, neither climbing nor falling. She brought down the two, set 200 minus 2p to zero, and got p equals one hundred, which made Dev laugh so hard he had to lean on the cigarette rack, because nobody in this neighborhood would pay a hundred dollars for coffee. The function was wrong; the method, she thought, was not.

What she couldn't decide, walking Ana out past the friable donuts and the indemnity notice Dev kept taped inside the register in case the cooler ever died, was whether understanding had to come before the rules or could arrive after them, quietly, the way the meaning of the long s had arrived three hundred years after the man who drew it. She stood in the doorway with the exam book under her arm and Ana already halfway down the block, and Dev called out from behind the counter, "So what's my price, math girl?"

"Lower it," she called back, "and watch the cooler for a week." She held the door open, letting the evening air in, the flyer still in her hand with the hill and its single perfect top drawn on the back.

Madeline arrived at the community art studio twenty minutes early, which she told herself was diligence, though she suspected it was fear dressed up in better clothes. The Thursday evening class was called Looking Harder, and the instructor, a quiet woman named Reva, had pinned a print of Frida Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace to the corkboard at the front. Madeline had chosen the class because her college application essay had been due, and she had needed, urgently, to be a person who did things like this. She had gotten in. The essay was submitted, the acceptance letter folded into her desk drawer at home, and yet here she still was, sitting on a stool with a notebook, unsure why she had come except that quitting after the payoff felt like a small fraud she didn't want to commit.

There were five other students, most of them older, and one boy about her age named Tobias who was eating sunflower seeds out of his jacket pocket and spitting the shells into a paper cup with startling accuracy. He had set up an easel in the corner, which was odd, because the class was about looking, not painting. On his easel were two small canvases of the same tree: one at dawn, the branches rinsed in pale blue, and one at dusk, everything amber and heavy. He kept standing back from them, frowning, as if distance might reveal something proximity withheld.

Reva began with the Kahlo. "Tell me what you see," she said, and Madeline's hand rose before she had decided anything. "The hummingbird is black," Madeline said, "which is wrong, hummingbirds aren't black, so the wrongness has to mean something. And the thorns come from the monkey, not from her, like someone else's cruelty that she's wearing." A woman in a green cardigan nodded slowly. Reva wrote colour, composition, symbolism on the whiteboard and said only, "Keep going. Formal analysis means you stay with what's in front of you."

Madeline kept going, but she found herself drifting toward Tobias's corner, because his frown had deepened into something that looked like despair. During the break he stood beside his two trees with his arms crossed, and when she came near he said, "It's the same tree twice. That's all it is. Two times of day. Is that enough?" He said he had thought repetition would make the paintings feel like studies, serious, the way artists' repetitions were supposed to feel, but looking at them now he thought they might just be the same idea twice, which was worse than one bad idea.

Madeline said, without planning to, "Monet painted the facade of Rouen Cathedral more than thirty times, in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year." She had read it in a library book the summer she was fifteen, the summer her grandmother was dying and Madeline spent whole afternoons in the art section because it was quiet there and nobody asked her how she was doing. Tobias looked at her. "Thirty," he said. "More than thirty views," she said. "Different light, different times of day and year." He turned back to his canvases as if she had handed him something heavy.

She had not told him the rest, which was that she had once believed she understood the Monets completely, and now suspected she had understood them not at all. At fifteen she had thought the cathedral series proved that attention itself was enough, that if you looked hard enough at one thing, truth accumulated like sediment. Now, at eighteen, standing in a studio that smelled of turpentine and someone's microwaved soup, she thought the series might presage something harder: that the object dissolves under attention, that thirty views give you thirty cathedrals and no solid one, that the tree Tobias had painted at dawn and the tree at dusk might not agree with each other about being the same tree. She had applied to college as an art history major partly on the strength of that fifteen-year-old certainty. She wondered whether the admissions office would want it back.

"Paint it at noon," she told Tobias. "And in rain. And in January, when it's bare." He was already sketching, the pencil moving fast, and she felt a small complicity with him, as though they had agreed on something neither of them could fully state. Or perhaps, she admitted to herself, she had simply needed someone to practice her half-knowledge on, someone who wouldn't know that the confidence in her voice was borrowed from a dead summer.

When the class regathered around the Kahlo, Reva asked Madeline to finish her analysis. Madeline looked at the print: the parrot, the dark leaves, the necklace of thorns drawing a thin line of red, the face that gave nothing away, impermeable to the viewer's wish for an easy reading. She said, "I think the colours are doing what the thorns are doing. The green of the leaves and the green of the background are almost the same green, so the beauty is continuous with the hurt, and I can't find a place where one stops being the other. But I don't know if that's what she intended, or what I'm imposing." The woman in the green cardigan said, "Does it matter which?" and Madeline said, "I genuinely don't know," and was surprised, saying it, by how much the not knowing felt like a position rather than a failure.

Later, gathering her notebook, she saw Tobias had taped a scrap of paper to his easel. On it he had written thirty times, and under that, noon, rain, January. He was packing up his seeds, the paper cup full of shells, and he caught her looking at the note and grinned, embarrassed. "More than thirty," he corrected himself, crossing it out and writing it again. He lifted the two tree paintings off the easel and slid them into his portfolio, one over the other, dawn hidden inside dusk. "Same tree," he said, "but I'm keeping both."

Nevaeh had promised herself she would finish the summer reading before August, and now August was three days away, and she was sitting on her grandmother's porch with the novel open on her knees and a legal pad full of crossed-out sentences. The assignment asked one question: is the narrator trustworthy, and how does the point of view shape what the reader is allowed to know? She had written four attempts at an answer. All four sounded like a person quoting a textbook she hadn't read.

"Still fighting that book?" her grandmother asked, coming out with two glasses of lemonade and a plate of saltines with peanut butter, which she considered a complete snack.

"It's not the book, it's the narrator. He keeps saying he's the reasonable one, but every time something happens he's the only one who saw it." Nevaeh flipped to a dog-eared page. "Like here, he says the neighbor slammed the door on him, but there's no one else to ask. It's all first person. Him, him, him."

Her grandmother settled into the other rocking chair and put her feet up on a milk crate she had owned since before Nevaeh's father was born. "When I was in school we had to memorize a speech from Julius Caesar. My elocution teacher would smack the desk with a ruler if we mumbled." She said this with obvious nostalgia, as if the ruler had been the fun part.

"You're saying my problem is diction?"

"I'm saying you've been reading with your elbows." Her grandmother sipped her lemonade. "Read me a piece. Out loud. Sometimes the thing tells on itself when it has to go through the air."

Nevaeh read the scene where the narrator described the neighbor slamming the door, doing a voice for him that made him sound faintly like a martyr. Her grandmother laughed into her glass. "That man is lying," she said immediately. "Or at least editing. Nobody slams a door that politely."

But polite or not, the book gave Nevaeh no way to check. She sat with that for a minute, rocking. The whole novel was locked inside one skull, and the skull had opinions. Then she turned to a blank page on the legal pad. "Grandma, help me try something. What do you think the neighbor was actually doing in her kitchen right before she closed the door?"

"Cooking something with onions, I'd guess. And probably deciding this man was the kind who'd stand on a porch until you agreed with him."

Nevaeh wrote it out, the scene again, but from across the street, through the neighbor's window. The neighbor could hear the narrator talking, could not hear what he said, could see him smile in a way she found rehearsed. It took ten minutes and it exhilarate her more than any page she'd written all summer, though when she read it back it was rough, inchoate in places, more of a sketch than a scene. Still. Something had shifted. In her version, the reader learned what the neighbor thought, and what the narrator looked like from outside, and how wrong his account of his own charm had been. She held up the two pages side by side like a woman comparing paint samples.

"So you fixed him," her grandmother said.

"Not fixed. Saw him. The first version, the one in the book, all we get is what he sees and what he decides to tell us. He's the only window." She tapped the second page. "And this one, I'm basically pretending to be somewhere else entirely, some narrator who can go into anyone's head, hers, his, the dog's if I wanted. That's the difference. That's the whole assignment, maybe."

"Then write that down before you lose it."

Nevaeh thought of Mr. Okafor's classroom in the spring, the day he'd assigned the book. He had drawn a stick figure on the board with a speech bubble and said, "Remember, this is a person, not a camera," and she had written it down without understanding it, the way she wrote down most things that year, hoarding sentences the way her grandmother hoarded buttons in a coffee tin, certain they'd matter later and unsure how. It had been a rough year for certainty generally. She had applied to six colleges and gotten into her safety and been deferred by her first choice and told everyone she didn't care, which was itself, she now suspected, a first-person account with editing.

She started a fifth draft on the legal pad. "The narrator reports only what he sees, knows, or chooses to say," she wrote, then paused, because that wasn't quite the whole of it either. She still couldn't prove he lied about the door. Maybe the neighbor really had slammed it, onions or no onions, and Nevaeh's rewrite was just a different bias wearing a nicer dress. She wrote that down too, in the margin, with a question mark.

Her grandmother leaned over to look. "You're putting your doubts in the actual paper?"

"He said we could. He said the smart answer to an unreliable narrator is not 'he lies,' it's 'here is exactly how much we can know and no more.'"

Her grandmother considered this, then stole a saltine off Nevaeh's plate. "In my day we just said the man was no gentleman and got on with it."

"Your day had rulers, Grandma. You had resources." Nevaeh laughed, underlined the question mark twice, and reached for the last saltine at the same moment her grandmother did.

The polling station occupied the gymnasium of Roosevelt Middle School, and Charlie had claimed a folding table near the door where the line couldn't help but pass her. She was there for a civics project, an exit poll with a clipboard and a stack of questionnaires, due by email at nine o'clock that night. Her teacher had asked for one page on a question Charlie had circled twice before deciding to take it seriously: whether it should be harder or easier to remove a head of government. She had until the polls closed at eight to collect responses, and after that her page would have to stand on whatever she had gathered.

The project had started as an argument with her debate partner, Marcus, who insisted the American way was obviously superior because a president couldn't be toppled by a tantrum in the legislature. Charlie had countered, half remembering something from a documentary, that in a parliamentary system the prime minister simply loses a vote of confidence and is gone, no trial, no drama. Marcus wanted to win the regional tournament in November, and he wanted their case airtight, which was why he'd texted her four times before noon demanding citations. She'd promised him an answer by tonight. That was her first deadline, and it pressed harder than the one from her teacher.

The line moved in stops and starts, voters shuffling past the bake sale table that the PTA ran every election with a devotion that mesmerized Charlie, so orderly and so persistent, like a stratum of bedrock under the whole noisy surface of the day. A woman in a green coat stopped at Charlie's table, took a questionnaire, and answered the last question in careful pencil: "Too hard to remove them now. Write that down." A man behind her said the opposite without being asked, something about chaos and snap elections, and the two of them traded half-smiling sentences all the way to the check-in desk.

The oldest voter of the afternoon came in around five, a retired history teacher named Mr. Okafor who walked with a cane and declined a questionnaire but stayed to talk when he learned what Charlie was studying. He wanted something too, she realized gradually: an audience. His wife had died in the spring, and he had come to vote because she always had, and because the poll workers knew his name, and because the gymnasium was warm and full of strangers he could tell things to. He asked Charlie what she knew about Andrew Johnson, and when she admitted she knew almost nothing, he looked quietly delighted, the way a man looks when he has found the one person in the room who hasn't heard his best story.

"In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote," he said. "Thirty-five senators voted to convict. One short of the two-thirds needed." He let that sit for a moment, watching her face the way a chess player watches an opponent consider a blunder. Charlie wrote it down, and then wrote it again in the margin of her draft, and something in the shape of her whole question changed. One vote. A president had come that close to removal and survived, and the country had gone on. Whether that meant the bar was exactly right or catastrophically wrong, she couldn't yet say, and Mr. Okafor refused to say it for her. "You're the one writing the page," he told her. "I'm just the one remembering it."

Between voters she worked the arithmetic on the back of a flyer. In a parliamentary system, she thought, a prime minister clinging to office by one vote would already be finished; a simple majority against and out. A president in this country needed enemies amounting to two-thirds of the Senate, which meant the system was built to absorb ordinary political hatred and act only on something rarer. Marcus would love that part; it was practically his case already. But the woman in the green coat was still in her mind, along with a dozen other voters who had written, in various handwritings, that a government nobody could remove was a government nobody could reach. Charlie couldn't make those two feelings into one clean position, and she noticed that she didn't entirely want to.

At seven forty the line thinned and a poll worker named Denise began unlocking the machine seals for the close, calling out the time in a voice that stayed level but carried. Charlie typed fast on her phone with her thumbs while Mr. Okafor held her clipboard steady, unasked, as if it were the most natural service in the world. She told Marcus, in the message, that the tournament case could keep his half of the argument, but her page was going to hold both halves open at once. The 1868 numbers went in exact, the way Mr. Okafor had given them, and underneath them she wrote her actual position: that she found the high bar defensible in principle and frightening in practice, and that she could not yet collapse those two judgments into one, and would not pretend to.

Marcus replied as the last voters went through: "That's not a position, that's a shrug." Charlie looked up from the screen. Mr. Okafor was at the door now, thanking Denise, and Denise was telling him she'd save him a cinnamon roll from the leftovers, and he was saying, in a voice suddenly bellicose for a man with a cane, that he would take two and she knew it perfectly well. He raised the cane in a small salute toward Charlie's table on his way out. She wrote back to Marcus one more line before the polls closed. "Then it's a shrug with footnotes," she said, and pressed send.

Annabelle sat on top of the climbing dome with her physics workbook wedged against her knees, because the playground was the only place her little brother would agree to spend the afternoon and the homework was due tomorrow. The problem was a soccer ball kicked at fourteen metres per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal, and for three days she had been treating the motion as one thing, one arc, the way a ball in flight looks like one thing. The textbook kept insisting it was two. Split the velocity, the margin note said in her own handwriting from Tuesday, when she had copied the phrase without believing it.

Below her, Marcus was negotiating with a four-year-old over a dump truck, so she had maybe ten minutes. She drew the kick again: a horizontal arrow, a vertical arrow, a slanted arrow between them. The horizontal part carried the ball forward at a constant rate, untouched by gravity; the vertical part rose, slowed, stopped, fell. Two stories about one ball, running side by side. She tested it on the swing set across the sand, a girl pumping her legs, and found she could not look at the swing the old way anymore.

Her phone buzzed. It was Deshawn from her lab table, and the message was a photo of his homework with the caption: check question six, I got something different. His answer and hers matched to two decimal places, but his units said newtons per coulomb and hers said volts per metre. They had been fighting about units all semester, actually, ever since he had called her method sloppy on the electric fields quiz and she had stopped sitting near him. His note under the photo said: mine has to be right, force over charge makes sense. Yours is just voltage divided by distance.

Annabelle typed back that voltage over distance made perfect sense, then deleted it, because it didn't yet, not perfectly, and she had learned something in the last hour about claiming certainty she hadn't earned. She sat with the two answers. Same number, different words. On the dome, her brother had moved on to the slide, and she watched him climb the ladder, rung by rung, each rung a separate decision about height, while the slide did all the horizontal work at once.

It occurred to her that the fight with Deshawn depended on a taxonomy she had never questioned, the idea that different units must name different quantities, that force-over-charge and voltage-over-distance belonged to separate drawers in some cabinet of physics. The ball had broken her of that once already today. The arc looked like one motion and was two; the two unit expressions looked like different quantities and might be one. She couldn't prove it from where she was sitting. All she had was the coincidence of the matching number, and coincidence was a thing Mr. Okafor warned them about, tangential evidence, he called it, evidence that touched the conclusion without supporting it.

She texted Deshawn: same number, same question, maybe same thing. He replied with a screenshot of the inside back cover of the textbook, the unit equivalence table she had never once opened, and there it was in small print, volts per metre and newtons per coulomb listed as equals. Neither of them had been wrong. That was the part that unsettled her, sitting there in the late sun while a toddler dropped sand out of a bucket in a thin, even stream, like a very small demonstration of constant flow. She had spent a week predicating her opinion of Deshawn on the assumption that one of them had to be the sloppy one, and the assumption had turned out to be the sloppy part.

She thought about telling him she was sorry, and did not type it, and then thought about how last month she would have sent something sharp instead, something about him checking his facts before he insulted her methods, and how the table in the back of the book would have let her be right and alone at the same time. Marcus fell off the bottom of the slide and looked around to see whether anyone had witnessed it. She raised a hand so he would know that she had, and that it was fine.

She finished the soccer ball problem on the walk home, holding the workbook against her hip, working the vertical half first because gravity was the part she trusted, then using the time it gave her to carry the horizontal half across. At the corner she stopped under the streetlight and sent Deshawn one more message: the ball thing and the units thing are kind of the same thing, I think. Two ways of looking that don't fight each other. Then, after a pause: I'm still not sure I'd predicate a whole grade on that. He started typing, stopped, started again. The message, when it came, was only: want to split the reading for Friday? Marcus pulled her sleeve toward the crosswalk, and she put the phone in her pocket and followed him.

The pit was louder than Mathis had expected, a turbid roar of drills and cheering that seemed to have no single source, and he stood behind Team 4021's table holding their robot's driver station like it might go off. Their first match of the day had gone badly in a small, humiliating way: the scouting app on his laptop, the one he'd written in Java over three weekends, had printed a blank line where an opponent's robot name should have been. "Team 5809, null, 62 points," the screen had said, and the scout beside him had asked if 5809 was fielding a ghost.

He hadn't known what to tell her. Between matches he sat on the floor behind the pit banner and opened the code, scrolling past the part where he parsed the schedule CSV and built each entry. He found the constructor, the one that took a team number and a score, and saw that it never set the name at all. He'd meant to fill it in later, then forgot. So where had the app gotten the idea that there was a name to print? He ran it again and watched the same line appear, null sitting there in the output like a word the program had invented.

"You look like you found something," said Priya, dropping onto the floor beside him with a granola bar. She was their programmer, a senior, and he'd been careful all season not to ask her too many questions, in case the questions calcified into a reputation.

"Why does it print null instead of crashing?" he asked. "I never set the name."

"So you left it alone," Priya said, "and Java didn't."

He tried it. He made a tiny test class with a number field, a boolean, and a String, set none of them in the constructor, and printed all three. The number came out 0, the boolean came out false, the String came out null. It wasn't an error. It was a policy. Numbers started at zero, booleans at false, object references at null, whether you touched them or not. He sat with that for a second, oddly comforted. The language had an opinion about emptiness. "I sort of assumed it would just yell at me," he said, and Priya laughed and said that was exactly what C would do, which opened a door he made a note to walk through later.

But the schedule was still wrong, and the next qualification match was in forty minutes. The real problem, he realized, was the find method. He'd written it to look up a team by stepping through the whole list from the front, comparing each entry, and with the list now sorted by team number the stepping felt clumsy, like walking down a hallway checking every door when you already knew the rooms were numbered. He'd read something once about halving. He sketched it on the back of the schedule sheet: check the middle entry; if the team number you want is smaller, throw away the top half; if it's bigger, throw away the bottom half; repeat. Each look cut the remaining possibilities in half. On a list of a hundred and twenty teams, the linear way could take a hundred and twenty comparisons, and this took, what, seven? He counted on his fingers, halving a hundred and twenty over and over until it fell to one, and got seven and a small electric feeling in his chest.

He rewrote the method in eleven minutes, and the mistake he made was an old one from his notes: computing the midpoint as low + high instead of low + (high - low) / 2, which worked fine here because the list was short, and he knew from a forum post it wouldn't on lists long enough to overflow, though he didn't fully understand overflow yet and wrote TODO beside it in pencil. When he ran it, the lookup found Team 5809 in five comparisons. The name still printed null, because that was a different bug, the one about the untouched field, and he fixed it by finally setting the name in the constructor the way he'd always meant to.

"Alliance selection's in an hour," Priya said, peering at his screen. "Is the ghost gone?"

"Gone. And the lookups are faster now, on sorted data." He started explaining it to her, the middle, the halves, why it beat checking every entry, and halfway through he noticed she wasn't the one he was really explaining it to. He was rehearsing. Their drive coach had said the judges might come by the pit and ask what each person contributed, and Mathis had contributed, for most of the season, attendance. Now he had something, and he kept talking, straightening the explanation the way you straighten a tool on a bench, until he could say it in two sentences without his voice going up at the end.

The pit announcer called their match. Priya stood and offered him a hand up, and as he took it he saw two people in polos with clipboards pause at the end of their row, looking from table to table. He closed the laptop halfway, not all the way, and pushed through the crowd toward the field.

The print of The Broken Column hung crooked on the art room wall, held up by two pins that some senior class had bent out of shape years ago. Carson sat in the second row with his notebook open to a page he had titled, then crossed out, then titled again. His problem was simple and annoying: everything he wanted to say about the painting sounded like the first three results of a search, words like "suffering" and "resilience" stacked into sentences that could have been written by anyone. He wanted to write something only he could have written, and he had until Thursday.

Beside him, Priya was already three paragraphs in, her pen moving without pauses. "You're staring at it like it owes you money," she said.

"I'm doing formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Mr. Okafor said no biography."

"So look at it."

He looked. The desert behind the figure was a warm, cracked umber, the sky a pale band, the whole background almost empty, so that nothing competed with the body at the centre. The figure stood frontally, symmetrically, cut open down the middle to show a broken stone column where her spine should be. A white surgical corset held her together, dotted with straps and buckles. And then there was the part he kept circling back to: nails pierce her face and body, a whole field of them, small and black and evenly spaced, while tears run down her cheeks. He wrote that down as an observation, not yet a claim.

What he could not write was the thing that happened when he sat with the image for longer than a minute. She looks straight at the viewer. He felt it now, in the bright room with the smell of turpentine and the radiator ticking, that discomfort of meeting painted eyes, and he tried to explain it to himself in the margins. If she looked away, or down, he would pity her. Because she doesn't, he is forced to stand where he is, in front of the damage, and be seen seeing it. The nails are directed at her body; the gaze is directed at him.

Priya leaned over. "What's 'amalgam' doing in your margin?"

"It's a note to myself. Her face is an amalgam, sort of. The tears and the nails and the direct stare all on one face at once. They don't blend." He tapped the page. "That's the composition problem. Everything vertical, everything frontal, nothing softening it."

On the wall near the window, someone's old poster of a littoral landscape, grey sea meeting grey sand, had faded almost to one tone. Carson noticed it for the first time and thought that Kahlo's desert did the opposite: the dryness made the tears louder. A little formal point, but it was his. He wrote it down.

In the critique circle on Thursday, he read his paragraph aloud, his voice steadier than he expected. He described the umber ground, the frontal symmetry, the corset as a compositional axis, and then the face. "Nails pierce her face and body, and tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer," he said, and paused, because that was where his argument had to earn itself. "The discomfort isn't in the gore. It's in being watched while you look. My first draft wanted to call it brave. I don't actually know if that word belongs to a painting or to a person, and I can't get there from colour and composition alone. What I can say is that the gaze transmutes the viewer's role. You stop being an audience and become a witness, and a witness can't claim to be innocent of looking."

Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. Priya raised her hand. "But couldn't the straight look just be convention? Portraits look at you. Lots of them do."

"That's fair," Carson said. "That's the part I'm least sure of. Convention would explain the direction. It doesn't explain why the tears still work when the eyes are dry." He looked at the print again, the crooked pins, the small black nails, the face that would keep looking at whoever sat in the second row after he was gone. "I'd rather leave that open than close it with a word I can't defend."

Priya was quiet a second, then turned her notebook to a fresh page. "Say the witness thing again. Slower."

The gym had been requisitioned for the drama festival three weeks before the performance, which meant Claire's one-act shared the space with folded volleyball standards and a climbing rope that hung from the ceiling like a hung jury. She had taped a rectangle on the floorboards to mark her stage, and inside it stood Priya and Marcus, holding their scripts, waiting for her to say something. Claire had wanted to direct for a year, ever since she'd watched the fall play fall apart because nobody told the actors where to go, and now she had her chance and a clipboard and a problem she hadn't expected: the play she'd chosen, which her friend Dev had written about a family argument, didn't seem to end.

"Take it from the top," she said. "Priya, you come in from the kitchen side. Marcus, you stay at the table until she says the line about the car keys."

They ran it. Priya crossed the taped line with her chin lifted, doing the elocution exercises the drama teacher had made everyone learn in September, every consonant crisp even when the words were ugly. Marcus stayed put, gripped the back of the metal folding chair, and delivered his monologue about the money. Then Priya shouted, and Marcus shouted, and then the script ran out and they both looked at Claire, breathing hard, the silence after the last line as blank as the wall behind them.

"It just stops," Dev said from the bleachers. He'd come to watch the rehearsal even though Claire hadn't asked him to. "What changed?"

"I don't know," Claire admitted. "Something's missing. It feels like the middle of something."

Dev came down off the bleachers and stood at the edge of her taped rectangle. He was disaffected about most things, school spirit, the cafeteria, the festival itself, but not about this play, and that was why his question landed so hard. "It's a whole fight," he said. "It doesn't go anywhere."

Claire looked at her clipboard, at the blocking notes she'd been making all week, arrows and X's that moved the actors around the rectangle without ever moving them through anything. She had been so focused on where people stood that she hadn't asked what the story was for. She'd been treating the play like a picture instead of a shape. The night before, unable to sleep, she had read a chapter of her brother's old theater textbook for ideas about staging, and one line had snagged in her mind. She hadn't understood why until now.

"In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end," she said, mostly to herself, then louder. "That's what's wrong. Yours has a beginning and a middle. There's no end, so nothing that happens in it matters to anything else."

Dev frowned at his own pages. "So it's not whole."

"It's not whole."

For the next hour they worked differently. Claire stopped blocking and started asking questions. What does Priya's character want by the last page? What does Marcus lose? Dev sat on the floor with a pencil and crossed things out, and twice he argued that the argument shouldn't resolve, that families don't resolve, and Claire agreed, cautiously, that an ending didn't have to mean a settlement, only that something had to change and be seen to change. What she couldn't figure out was whether the ending Dev finally wrote, where Priya puts the car keys on the table and walks out, was an ending or just a bigger stop. She said so. Dev said he didn't know either. She put a note on her clipboard to decide by Thursday.

On the day of the festival, the gym smelled like floor wax and nerves. The volleyball standards had been pushed against the wall, and folding chairs faced Claire's taped rectangle, which the janitor had half scrubbed away overnight so that the stage now had one fuzzy corner. Claire stood at the sound table with her script, and when the lights came up, Priya entered from the kitchen side exactly as blocked, and Marcus held his chair exactly as blocked, and the audience went quiet at the shouting. Priya set the keys down on the table with a small click that carried across the whole gym. She walked out through the fuzzy corner, off the tape, into the part of the floor that wasn't the play anymore, and the lights went down on Marcus alone, staring at the keys.

Afterward Dev found her by the water fountain. People were telling him his ending was the best part, and he kept saying thanks, thanks, and then he leaned close to Claire and whispered, "I cut your note. The one you gave me Thursday, about her coming back for the keys at the end. I never wrote it."

"You cut it?"

"You said you didn't know if it was an ending or a stop. So I made it a stop." He shrugged, almost smiling. "You decide. Is it?"

Claire looked back at the gym, where the janitor was already peeling up the rest of her tape.

Nolan locked the bathroom door at his grandmother's house and unfolded the index cards on the sink counter, arranging them in a fan like a poker hand no one would ever bet on. Thursday he had to stand in front of a room of ninth graders and explain, in five minutes, consent, contraception, and how to get tested at a clinic, and the health teacher had said the only rule was that he sound like a person and not a pamphlet. He pressed record on his phone, faced the mirror, and began.

"Consent means the other person says yes, out loud, without being pushed, and they can change their mind," he said, watching his own mouth shape the words. "Condoms are free at the county clinic on Meridian, and so is testing. You walk in, you don't need a parent, you give a name, it doesn't have to be your real one."

His voice sounded thinner than he'd expected, like a stranger doing an impression of confidence. He tried again, slower, and it was on the third attempt, reaching for the tap, that he knocked the phone off the counter. It skidded under the lip of the cabinet, and when he crouched to fish it out, his hand found instead a spiral notebook wedged behind the pipe.

It was his grandmother's handwriting, small and upright, a column of dates and numbers. 138 over 84. 132 over 81. 135 over 86. Beside each entry a note in the margin: felt fine, gardened, slept well. There was a folded sheet of paper clipped to the back cover, some photocopy from the doctor's office, and he read it twice by the light under the sink.

Three summers ago he had found a different notebook in a different room of this house, his grandfather's, full of bird sightings logged months after the funeral, the last pages blank. He had put it back and never said anything, and he had thought about that silence a hundred times since, the way it had felt like protection and also like a locked door. He sat down on the bathroom floor with the new notebook and did not put it back.

At dinner his grandmother talked about the neighbor's fence and a cousin who was trying to monetize her baking videos, selling the recipes as a digital download, and Grandma said the word monetize like it was a species of rodent she had identified but declined to chase. Nolan pushed his potatoes around and thought about how a person could build a whole artifice of being fine, a beautiful one, hand-stitched in a column of small upright numbers, and how impermeable it could be, and how he had stood outside it before with his grandfather's notebook and let it hold.

"Grandma," he said when the plates were cleared. He set her notebook on the table, open to the last month of entries. "I found this when my phone fell behind the sink. I'm sorry. But I read the sheet that was clipped to it."

She looked at the page for a long time, then at him, and her jaw set in the way he recognized from arguments about her driving at night.

"Those numbers," he said. "The guideline sheet says stage 1 hypertension starts at 130 over 80. Yours are in that range. That's stage 1 hypertension."

"I know what my numbers are," she said. "I write them down every morning before the coffee, like Dr. Okafor asked. That's the whole point of writing them down, so I know." She closed the notebook with one hand and kept her palm flat on the cover.

"Have you shown them to her? To Dr. Okafor?"

"They're for me to keep track. I don't need to run in every time a number wobbles. Your grandfather turned every ache into a production, appointments and waiting rooms, and I sat in those chairs for forty years. I am not doing that."

"That's not what I'm saying. You don't have to do what he did. Just show her the page. One page." He slid the clinic card out of his pocket, the one he'd grabbed for his presentation, the county clinic on Meridian, and then felt how absurd it was, a card about condoms and testing sitting on her tablecloth. He picked it back up and put it away.

She turned the notebook over, then over again, as if the answer might be printed on the back. Outside, the neighbor's dog started at something along the fence line.

"Thursday, after your little speech," she said. "You can drive me."

The courthouse smelled of floor wax and old paper, and Simon had been standing in its lobby for forty minutes with a paperback in his back pocket that he had not opened. His mother was upstairs in the ceremonial courtroom, waiting to be sworn in as a citizen, and the elevator kept arriving full of people who were not her. In the lobby, between the metal detectors and the stairs, the county had set up an early voting station, a folding table, two laptops, a banner that drooped on one side. A boy about Simon's age stood at the table, holding a sample ballot like it was written in a language he half remembered.

"Why does the ballot only have the president on it?" the boy asked the poll worker. "I watched this thing last night about England, and they had a king and a prime minister. Why do they get two and we get one?"

The poll worker, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, said she only did the laptops. Simon, who had a comparative politics placement essay due in nine days and had been chewing on exactly this question for most of the summer, felt the answer assemble itself in his mouth before he decided to say it. "Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state from the head of government," he said. "The king, or in some countries a ceremonial president, is the head of state. The prime minister runs the government. Here, the president is both."

The boy looked at him. "Both?"

"Both. One person, two jobs." Simon heard how it sounded, like a slogan, and he disliked that, because the slogan was the easy part and the essay was supposed to be about the hard part, which was how each system gets rid of its head of government when things go wrong. He had drafted three pages arguing that a parliament could withdraw confidence and force a prime minister out between elections, which seemed tidier than impeachment, and his professor's only comment had been a single underlined sentence: whose hands are on which levers, and does that make them safer or just colder?

"Do you go to State?" the boy asked. "You talk like a syllabus."

"Starting in the fall." Simon sat down on the lobby bench across from the voting table, and the boy sat down too, which surprised him, and unfolded the sample ballot on his knee. He said his name was Danny, that he had turned eighteen in June, that this was his first election and he had expected it to feel like something and so far it felt like the DMV. Simon understood that. He had voted the week before at this same table, in this same lobby, and had walked out holding his sticker and ruminating on the fact that he had felt nothing until he saw his own signature in the register, small and provisional-looking, under eighteen years of his mother's rent checks and night shifts.

They fell into it, the two of them, low-voiced, while a guard by the stairs watched them without interest. Danny wanted to know who you fire when the country goes wrong, and Simon worked it out aloud, which was not how he usually worked, and he kept noticing that the sentences came out better spoken than they ever had on the page. He said that in a parliamentary system you could bring a government down without waiting years for a fixed term, and Danny said that sounded like the politicians firing each other, the way a bad boss protects himself, and Simon stopped, because he had written the opposite in his draft and had not once questioned it.

"Maybe," Simon said slowly, "the two systems don't differ in who has power, only in how far apart the power is spread before you have to grab it." He said that the head of state in a parliamentary country was almost ancillary to the daily fighting, a figure who opened bridges and signed things, and that the American president carried both roles in one body, which made the office enormous and the removal of it enormous too. Danny said, "So when we're mad, we're really mad at one guy," and Simon said, "When they're mad, they have to decide which guy they're mad at," and then they were both quiet for a second, because upstairs, on the third floor, Simon's mother was taking an oath to one of them.

The elevator opened and she came out with nine other people, all holding small flags, and she saw Simon and did not wave, just lifted the flag an inch, which was their private signal, inherited from a game they played when he was small and she wanted him to wait without looking like he was waiting. He stood up. Danny stood up too, out of some instinct, and then looked unsure why he had.

"So who wins?" Danny asked. "Your essay. Which system is better?"

"I don't know yet," Simon said, and found that saying it in a courthouse, with his mother crossing the lobby toward him holding a flag she had waited eleven years to be handed, did not feel like failure. It felt like the honest version of the sentence he had been circling all summer. He had started the summer certain that cleaner removal meant better government, and now he suspected the question of removal was only the doorway, and the actual question was whether a country wanted its dignity and its decisions in one pair of hands or two, and he could argue it either way and had, out loud, twenty minutes ago, to a stranger who voted for the first time today.

His mother reached him. She smelled like the elevator's hand sanitizer and she was crying without changing her face, the way she did. She put the flag in his hand as if handing him evidence. "There was a judge," she said. "He made an injunction against nobody, he just talked, for twenty minutes, about what you can do now that you couldn't do this morning." She straightened his collar. "You still have the sticker?"

"Still on my jacket," Simon said, and turned it toward her so she could see.

The basement belonged to Priya, whose father had converted it into something he called a lab and everyone else called a room with three monitors and a dehumidifier. Hannah had come with her laptop and a problem, which was that her Java class was due at midnight and every time she tested it, the program hung. Not crashed. Hung, patiently, like a customer waiting at a closed register.

"Show me the class first," Priya said, pulling a beanbag chair over with her foot. "Fields private?"

"They're private. I did that part right." Hannah turned the laptop so Priya could see. She had written a Student class with a name field marked private, and a getter called getName that returned it, and a small test in main that built three students and printed their names. That part ran. The trouble started after, when she read a file of four hundred names into an array and searched it.

Priya read the search method with her chin propped on one hand. She was the sort of person who could prognosticate a bug from across the room, though she claimed she couldn't and merely had a good memory for her own disasters. "Run it," she said. "Search for someone who's in the file."

Hannah typed a name from the middle of the file and hit enter. The answer came back instantly, found at index 211. "See? It works."

"Now search for someone who isn't."

Hannah typed a name she made up on the spot, Marta Okafor, which sounded plausible enough that both of them half believed in her. She hit enter. The cursor sat at the start of an empty line and stayed there. One second. Three. The dehumidifier hummed in the corner like it was taking a side.

"It's not frozen," Hannah said, watching the fan on her laptop spin up. "It's doing something."

"It's doing everything," Priya said. "That's a linear search. It checks the names one by one from the start of the array, all the way through. So if the name is at the end, or if it isn't there at all, it has to look at every single item before it can give up." She reached over and tapped the loop in Hannah's code, the one that ran from zero to the array's length. "Your found names in the middle finish fast. Marta has to be checked against all four hundred."

Hannah sat with that. Four hundred didn't sound like much, and it wasn't, but her actual assignment file, the one due at midnight, had nine thousand entries, and her test harness searched it once for every student in her class of thirty. She did the arithmetic on the back of a receipt and did not like the number she got. "So the program's not broken. It's just doing exactly what I told it to."

"Welcome to the whole thing," Priya said, and opened a bag of chips she had apparently been saving for a moment like this.

Hannah had spent the semester defending this major to her mother, whose detractors, if she kept a list, would have included anyone who thought coding was a job for other people's children. Her mother was not impervious to argument, exactly, but she was very good at redirecting it toward nursing school. And Hannah had never had a clean answer for her, because half the time the work felt like following a recipe where the recipe fights back. This was different. Tonight she could see the two things she'd been carrying around side by side: the machine did only what it was told, and what it was told could still surprise her. Both were true at once, and she wasn't sure yet which one she was supposed to love.

She fixed the small version first, the one in the basement. Then she changed the test so it searched for a name she knew was last in the file, and then a name she knew was missing, and watched the counter she'd added tick up to the full length of the array both times. Every item, exactly as Priya had said. Somewhere past eleven, with the file trimmed and the searches returning before she could blink, she leaned back and looked at the getter methods lined up in their tidy rows, each one guarding its private field like a small, overpaid doorman.

"So is it done?" Priya asked, crumbs on her sleeve.

"It passes every test I have," Hannah said. "Which might just mean I don't have enough tests."

Priya considered this, then closed the chip bag. "Submit it anyway. Then come help me figure out why my dad's dehumidifier is running when it's dry down here."

Lea spread the printout on the picnic table and weighted its corners with two tomatoes and a jar of screws, because the backyard wind in August treated paper like a personal grievance. Her grandfather came out with his coffee, moving carefully on the bad knee, and lowered himself onto the bench across from her.

"You're studying out here now," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"Practice for my roommate," Lea said. "First-year seminar. We have to explain something scientific to somebody who doesn't know it, and I picked you."

"Flattered, I'm sure." He squinted at the graph. "That looks like somebody's heartbeat on a monitor."

"It kind of is. Sort of." She traced the jagged line with her finger, the small sawtooth rises and falls stacked on a steady climb. "This is carbon dioxide in the air, measured at a place called Mauna Loa, in Hawaii. Every year it wiggles up and down because of the seasons, but underneath that it keeps going up. Like stairs."

He leaned in. She had rehearsed this part in her bedroom and again walking to the bus stop, and now, in the actual air, with an actual person, the words came out slower than she wanted but truer. Sunlight comes in, she said, and the Earth sends heat back out toward space, but carbon dioxide and other gases hold some of that heat in the atmosphere, the way the glass of a greenhouse lets light through and keeps warmth from leaving. It was not a perfect comparison and she said so. The gases don't form a lid; they're mixed through the whole sky, absorbing and re-emitting, and the extra warmth is spread thin everywhere rather than pooled in one place.

"Then the graph," her grandfather said, tapping the paper with one finger. "What's this line crossing here, where you drew the arrow?"

"That's the part I'm trying to pin down." She had circled the point where the scribble of the line finally lifted above a horizontal line she'd drawn and labeled 400. "The daily average passing 400 parts per million for the first time in the record. It matters because it's a number nobody alive has ever seen before, but I can't remember what year it happened, and if I tell you wrong on Tuesday, my whole presentation is suspect."

"So look it up."

"My phone's dead. The charger's inside and it takes forever." She said this with the querulous tone she'd been trying to shed all summer, and she heard it and laughed at herself. "See, that's why I need the practice."

Her grandfather drank his coffee and looked at the garden, where the zucchini had gone feral again. "You said Mauna Loa. There used to be a fellow on the news who talked about Mauna Loa, back when your mother was small. Keeling, maybe." He set the cup down. "I remember the news saying four hundred, and I remember it felt like a number you were supposed to flinch at, and I remember it was before your mother finished college. She finished in 2014."

Lea sat with that. Her mother had graduated in May of 2014, so the crossing had happened before that, which put it somewhere in 2014 or earlier. She looked at the graph again, at the arrow, and thought about how to adjudicate between her grandfather's memory and her own blank. Memory was a witness, not a record; but a graph without a date was a record with no address. She needed one more fact, and the only place to get one was inside.

She left the tomatoes on the corners and went in through the screen door, found the charger, waited by the outlet while the phone took its first sip of power, then searched with what charge it had. When she came back out, the wind had moved one tomato and the paper had shifted but held.

"May ninth," she said, sitting down. "Twenty thirteen. The daily average at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record. May 9, 2013."

"Before your mother walked," he said.

"A year before." She wrote the date beside her arrow in small print. "So your memory was right, just not exact."

He studied the graph a while longer, and she let him, because she understood that he was doing something she hadn't planned for the presentation: he was taking it personally, matching a jagged line against a daughter's graduation and a granddaughter's first semester. She would not put that in the slides. But she thought she might keep it, the way he'd once told her that a person who notices where he was standing when the world shifts has a kind of sentience about his own life, an awareness of being present for something.

"Okay," she said, squaring the paper. "From the top. You're my roommate, you're from a family that thinks climate science is a scam, and you just asked me why the graph matters."

"Then answer her this," her grandfather said, folding his hands on the table. "If the heat is spread thin everywhere, how does anybody measure it at all?"

Lea looked at the sawtooth line, and the wind lifted the paper's edge under the tomato, and she started to answer.

The basement of St. Brigid's smelled like burnt sugar and folding chairs, and Lucas stood at the counter with his grandmother's recipe box open in front of him, trying to remember whether the blessing came before the soup or after. For thirty-one years his grandfather had led the Christmas Eve supper, the whole extended family crammed between the radiator and the nativity mural, twelve dishes carried down the church steps in dish towels. This year Grandpa Ray was in room 412 of County General with a wire in his chest, and he had told Lucas, on the phone, in a voice like gravel being poured slowly, "You know the order. I wrote it down." The notebook was on the counter. Lucas had not opened it yet.

He opened it. Inside was a schedule in pencil: candles, blessing, soup, readings, the honeyed bread, the carol his mother always mangled, the toast at the end. Underneath, in the margin, his grandfather had written Lucas practices Sundays and boxed it twice, hard enough to tear the paper a little. Lucas set the notebook down flat and went to find the ladles.

His uncle Denny arrived early to set up tables, which he did loudly, clacking metal legs like a man aggrandizing a small task into a public works project. "So you're running it," he said. "You know what you're doing?"

"I have the notebook."

"Ray's a hard act. People expect the full performance, the Latin bit and everything."

"I'm not doing a performance."

"Good luck telling Mom that."

The family came in a slow flood, coats and casseroles and the little cousins who went straight for the mural to argue about whether the donkey was the same donkey from last year. Lucas's mother set down her dish, hugged him too hard, and asked him three questions about the soup he could not answer. Then she lowered her voice. "Your grandfather's on the phone. He wants to talk to you before you start."

Lucas took the phone into the stairwell, where the plaster was cold against his shoulder.

"You're doing the whole thing," his grandfather said. Not a question.

"Yes."

"I heard you had practice this morning. Coach called it for Christmas Eve morning, seven a.m."

Lucas looked at the linoleum. "I went. I got back by ten."

There was a long breath on the other end, the mechanical lift of the hospital bed. "Sundays," his grandfather said. "All season you've been gone on Sundays. That used to mean something in this family."

"Grandpa." Lucas had the argument ready; he'd been carrying it for a week like a stone in his pocket. "In Mark, chapter two, verse twenty-seven, Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath. He says it to people criticizing his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath. Picking grain. On the day of rest. And he took their side."

Silence, except for a monitor somewhere beeping in its patient rhythm. Lucas waited, listening to his own heartbeat doing something similar.

"Second chapter," his grandfather finally said. "You memorized it to beat me with."

"I memorized it because it's true. The day is for us. Not the other way around. I went to practice and then I came here to do this, and I'm going to do it right, and both of those things are the point."

Another silence, and Lucas understood that what he was hearing was not surrender but something closer to a detente, two positions agreeing to stop firing across the same ground they would still argue about at Easter. His grandfather said, "The blessing goes before the soup. Readings after the bread. Don't let your mother sing the second verse alone, she'll flat on 'dispersed.'"

"I know."

"You don't know. You think you know." A wheeze that might have been a laugh. "Start with the candles. Nobody expects much from a beginner."

"Is that a compliment?"

"It's the notebook talking, not me. Go feed them."

Lucas carried the phone back in and lit the candles with the long match from the utility drawer, the kind that always smelled faintly of sulfur and of every year before this one. Twelve dishes steamed on the counter in an order that mostly matched the pencil schedule. His cousins were seated. His mother had the hymnal open to the wrong page and did not know it. Uncle Denny raised his glass early, out of turn, and Lucas touched his arm and shook his head, and Denny, for once, put it down.

He stood at the head of the table, notebook open, and said, "The Sabbath was made for man," and looked up at all of them. "So let's eat."

His mother started the carol anyway, half a beat early, and flat on 'dispersed,' and everyone came in behind her.

Luca had come to Camp Abernathy for the sailing, and it was therefore a personal injustice that his favorite hour of the day was now the one spent in a basement lab with eleven other teenagers and forty laptops that smelled like warm dust.

"You signed up for Competitive Programming," said Priya, without looking up from her screen. "It's on your lanyard. It's practically tattooed on you."

"I signed up because my mother said I couldn't convalesce on a couch all summer. Her word. She looked it up so she could use it in the argument."

The project that week was to build a class in Java. Not just a program, a class, with private fields the outside world couldn't touch and getter methods standing politely at the door, and then to test it until it confessed everything. Luca had named his class Catalog, a thing that held a sorted array of item codes and answered whether a given code existed. Priya had named hers DragonHorde. "Because the fields are private," she said. "Like treasure. Nobody touches the hoard without a getter."

He liked that more than he wanted to admit. He'd been raised on his grandfather's cooking, all patient layering, nothing measured, and on his father's spreadsheets, where every cell was audited and every column had a rule. He'd never decided which way of thinking was his. The Catalog felt like both: a warm middle with a fence around it, and Luca sat there at his keyboard enjoying the impossible idea that he had invented a small, orderly country.

Then Friday came, and the competition dataset. Eight million item codes, sorted, waiting to be searched. The camp leaderboard, projected on the wall, ranked every team by speed. Luca's tests had all passed in the lab, small arrays, dozens of cases, green checkmarks like a lawn. He ran the big dataset and his program crashed with an error about a number that couldn't fit where he'd put it.

"That's not a speed problem," said Marcus from two seats over, leaning back in his chair with the serene confidence of a boy who had once eaten an entire lemon on a dare. "That's an arithmetic problem. Look at your midpoint line."

Luca looked. His binary search computed its middle as low plus high, then divided by two. On the test data it was fine. On the huge array, he was told, adding those two numbers could overflow, could go past what an int could hold, and the whole search came apart. Marcus pointed at the screen with a pencil. "Try low plus, in parentheses, high minus low, then divide by two. Same middle. No overflow."

Luca changed one line. The program ran the entire eight-million-code dataset and finished so fast the leaderboard had to blink twice to believe it. He spent the rest of the hour half triumphant, half annoyed, because the fix was small and the difference between his way and Marcus's way was a thing he hadn't known existed. He had trusted his tests, and his tests had trusted small numbers. It occurred to him that being right in the lab and being right in the world were two different jobs.

"You're doing the face," Priya said. She saved her file with a dramatic click. "The face of a boy discovering that the universe has fine print."

"Everyone thinks they're the main character until an int overflows," Luca said, and Marcus snorted so hard he knocked over his water bottle, which missed every laptop, a miracle the whole lab agreed to never report to the counselors.

The next morning, Saturday, was sailing, and Luca convalesced on the dock in the sun while the wind took a day off. Priya sat beside him with her laptop, which she had carried to the dock like a pet. "The autocrat has a bug," she announced. By the autocrat she meant the head counselor, Dennis, who had decreed that the leaderboard be wiped and the competition rerun that afternoon, since he refused to believe Luca's Catalog had beaten his favorite team. Dennis's rerun, it turned out, ran on an old machine in the boathouse, and Dennis's own sample search program, which he had written himself years ago and never once changed, crashed on the huge dataset in front of everyone.

"Let me guess his midpoint," Luca said.

"Low plus high, divided by two," said Priya, grinning. "Endemic. It's everywhere. Half the code on that machine has it."

Luca thought about walking up to Dennis and telling him about the one line. He thought about the two ways he knew of being in the world: his grandfather's, where you'd say nothing and quietly fix the man's soup, and his father's, where you'd present the audit in writing. He honestly did not know which was kinder, or which would work, or whether knowing the answer to an overflow question had anything to do with knowing the answer to a people question. He suspected it didn't. He suspected it might.

He ended up doing neither, exactly. He printed the fixed line on a scrap of paper, folded it once, and left it on the boathouse bench where Dennis kept his sunglasses. Then he went back to the dock.

Priya watched him do it and said nothing for a while. Then she said, "You know he's going to think it's a note from a secret admirer."

"It's a note from a secret admirer," Luca said. "I admire people who fix one line instead of arguing about the whole program."

Down the lake, a sail finally caught some wind, and a small orange boat tipped, righted itself, and kept going.

The party was in Derek's backyard, and Brooklyn had until midnight to fix the thing she'd been avoiding for nine days. His mother had strung lights between the fence posts and set out a cake that said DEREK 17 in icing already melting sideways, and somewhere behind the speakers Brooklyn's phone sat with the notification she kept half-reading: Marisol had sent the final draft of their history essay, the one Brooklyn was supposed to edit, the one due at 11:59.

"You're doing the face," Derek said, dropping onto the cooler beside her. "The essay face. You look like you're being followed."

"Marisol wrote six paragraphs on urban renewal and only one on the resistance movement, which was the actual assignment. And she keeps saying 'thus.' Thus, thus, thus. It's like being yelled at by a thesaurus."

"So tell her."

"It's not that simple."

"It's exactly that simple."

Derek was canny about most things, but he had never been the weaker half of a partnership, and Brooklyn didn't expect him to understand what it was like to be the one whose feedback could flatten somebody. Last year, when she'd told a lab partner his data tables were "a mess," he'd stopped contributing for the rest of the semester, and she had spent those months doing the work of two people while pretending that was a victory of standards. Marisol was her best friend on the team, fragile in the specific way of someone who had transferred schools twice and was still auditioning for every room she entered. Brooklyn had already typed three drafts of a comment, and every one of them was a lie of politeness, a lot of "really strong start!" that would codify, over time, into Marisol believing Brooklyn thought she was fine, when Brooklyn actually thought she was talented and off course, which was worse to leave uncorrected.

She scrolled through her saved articles while Derek blew out a rumor of candles on the half-melted cake. In the fall she'd bookmarked a write-up of a 2014 study led by David Yeager, because her older sister had mentioned it during a fight about Brooklyn's "brutal honesty." Students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. One sentence of belief attached to the hard feedback. Brooklyn had filed it away as an excuse for her sister's side of the argument and never used it, and now here it was, suddenly operational, at a birthday party, with two hours on the clock.

The flaw in her plan was that Marisol was at the party, leaning against the fence with a paper cup of sparkling cider, which meant Brooklyn couldn't hide behind a screen. She considered texting the feedback and driving home. She considered softening everything into mush. Then Derek's cousin turned the music up, someone's little brother stepped in the cake, and in the general disruption Marisol wandered over and asked the question Brooklyn had been dreading: "Did you read it? Be honest."

There it was. The invitation, which was also a trap, which was also, possibly, a door.

"Can I try something weird?" Brooklyn said. "I read this thing. A study, 2014, David Yeager. Students revised their essays way more often when the criticism came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. So here's my note." She took a breath that tasted like sugar and someone's grape vape. "I think you're the best writer on our team, and I think this essay is underneath what you can do, and I'm saying that because I believe you can fix it, not to be nice. You have six paragraphs on renewal and one on the resistance, and the resistance was the assignment. Also, please stop saying thus."
