He looked where she was looking. The line was his constructor, the one that was supposed to set the name and the balance. In front of it, small and ordinary and fatal, he had typed void. He had done it because every other method in his files had void in front of it, and because his hands had learned the rhythm, and because nothing had told him otherwise. Anselm's napkin, he realized now, showed a constructor with no return type at all. He had assumed the napkin was sloppy, a cousin's shorthand. He found the napkin in the front pocket of his backpack, soft from handling, and smoothed it on the desk beside the keyboard. There it was. No void. No int, no String, nothing where a return type would go.

He didn't delete the word immediately. He sat with his finger over the backspace key and thought about what he had actually been doing all afternoon, which was carrying a rule from one place into another where it didn't apply. Then he erased the void, letter by letter, v-o-i-d, and ran the test.

The output appeared at the bottom of the screen, and it was exactly what he had typed into the constructor, the name and the balance, arriving in the world at last. Dara had leaned in without his noticing. "So that word was the whole problem?"

"Java's like that," he said. "Everything's exactly what it says, nothing more." He copied the corrected file to his flash drive, then, after a moment's thought, copied the broken version too, and titled it mistake.java, and the cursor blinked at the end of the name while he decided whether to keep it.

The test streaks on parchment adumbrated the finished bars Hannah hoped for, faint hints of gloss that would either deepen into shine or dull into bloom, and she could not stop checking them against the side of the tray. Behind the folding table at the farmers' market, under a canopy the color of dry lavender, she held the bowl of melted chocolate at thirty-one degrees and waited the way Dara had taught her, which was to say not passively but with attention, watching for the moment the surface stopped looking wet and started looking alive.

"You're hovering," Dara said. She was restocking the truffle case and did not look up. "Hovering changes nothing. Either you seeded enough stable crystals or you didn't."

Hannah stirred anyway, slow figure eights, because her hands wanted something to do. She had been coming to this stall since the first Saturday in June, when she'd admitted to herself that the summer her mother had imagined, a hospital volunteering schedule and a head start on prerequisites, was not the summer she wanted at all. Dara had hired her on the condition that she learn tempering before she was allowed near a mold. "Snap is honesty," Dara had told her. "A bar that snaps clean tells you someone paid attention. A bendy bar tells you they didn't."

Theo appeared at four minutes to ten, before the market officially opened, carrying a cooler that looked older than either of them. He set it on the ground by the honey stall next door, where the keeper was arranging jars of a wildflower strain she described, to anyone who paused, as autochthonous to the valley, native to these hills and nowhere else. "Salvage operation," Theo said, lifting the cooler lid to show Hannah a brick of frozen soup wrapped in a grocery bag. "From the dorm kitchen. Everything got tossed at move-out, so I took it. Been in the freezer at my uncle's all month."

"Your uncle's freezer."

"Deep freeze. The big chest kind." He looked proud of this, the way he used to look proud of finishing a problem set an hour before it was due. "I figured I'd thaw it tonight and we'd eat it before my shift. Freezing kills everything anyway, right? It's like sterilizing."

Hannah kept stirring. She had spent the winter reading whatever she could find about food, first out of guilt about abandoning the medical track and then out of something that had stopped being guilt, and one of the things she'd read had stuck with her the way certain facts do, complete and portable, a stone in the pocket. "It doesn't kill them," she said. "Freezing food at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, which is zero Fahrenheit, stops bacteria from growing, but it doesn't kill most of them. Thawed food can spoil again."

"So it's fine and then it's not fine."

"It was never fine. It was paused." She said it and heard, with a small internal wince, how much it sounded like her mother, who had said a version of it about her deferral, about the year Hannah wanted to take before committing to anything. Everything is paused, nothing is decided, and meanwhile time spoils. Hannah had argued then that deciding too fast was its own kind of failure, that a choice made under pressure was a snapshot, not a portrait. She still believed it. She also, at ten in the morning at a folding table, with soup thawing in a cooler a meter away, felt the pull of the opposing claim, and could not say which one was truer.

Theo squatted by the cooler, hand resting on the lid. In his first-year philosophy seminar he had discovered nihilism and worn it like a jacket for about six weeks, claiming nothing mattered, not grades, not the deadening logistics of adulthood his father laid out for him over dinner. Then he'd spent a spring weekend caring for a friend's sourdough starter and quietly stopped making the claim. He looked at the soup the way he'd once looked at the starter. "The move-out fridge was unplugged for a day before I got there," he said. "Maybe two."

"Then don't eat it."

"It smells okay."

"You can't smell okay. Okay is invisible." She tapped the side of her bowl. The chocolate had thickened to the right working consistency, and Dara was watching now over the top of the truffle case, saying nothing, which Hannah understood as permission or as a test, probably both. She spooned a cap of chocolate onto parchment and watched it set in the breeze coming off the river. When she peeled it up and snapped it in half, the sound was clean, a bright small crack, and the broken edges showed a surface with a depth to it, like the shell of something that had decided what it was. Tempered. She held out the two halves, one to Theo and one to the honey keeper, who took hers with a nod of professional respect.

"It's the crystals," Hannah said, mostly to Theo, though she was careful not to lecture. "You have to get the right ones to form, and then they recruit the rest. It's order spreading through the whole batch." She was aware that she was talking about more than chocolate and also that she did not want to say so out loud, because saying so would make it a speech, and some things survive being said and some things don't, and she didn't yet know which kind of thing this was.

Theo ate his half slowly, which for Theo was remarkable. Then he closed the cooler, carried it past the compost bins near the port-a-johns, and came back with empty hands and the grocery bag gone. He stood at the end of the table while the ten o'clock bell rang and the first customers came down the row, a woman with a canvas bag already asking about the dark bars, and Hannah reached for a sheet of molds, and Theo picked up the tasting knife without being asked and began slicing samples, laying them out in a fan.

The restaurant smelled of burnt coffee and onions, and Zoe had chosen it because it was loud enough that no one would listen to her stumble through Portuguese. She spread the newspaper on the table between two water glasses, smoothing the fold flat with the heel of her hand. In forty minutes she would call her placement examiner, read a short article aloud, and summarize it in her own words. If she passed, she could register for the intermediate seminar in the spring instead of spending another semester in a room where they conjugated verbs she had already conquered in middle school.

The article was three paragraphs about a city council vote on bike lanes. Three paragraphs, and she was still on the first sentence, dragging her finger under each word like someone crossing a river stone by stone. "Depois," she read, "de, das, das discussões." She said it again, slower, as though the sentence might pity her and rearrange itself. The waitress came by twice. The second time she refilled the water and said, "You're doing homework on a Friday night," not unkindly, and Zoe said, "Something like that," and put her palm over the page so it wouldn't look like homework.

The problem was not the vocabulary. She could look up words; her phone was right there. The problem was time. When she read this way, every sentence cost her a minute, and by the time she reached the end she had already forgotten the beginning. She had tried to summarize the article twice on the ride over, and both times she had produced a list of fragments, like the turbid water at the bottom of a glass: when the vote happened, that a man named something had objected, that there was a number, three hundred or three thousand, she honestly could not have said which.

At the next booth, two college-aged guys were arguing about a study guide. "You skipped the whole chapter," one said. The other held up his highlighter like a piece of evidence. "I wasn't reading it, I was scanning it. Scanning is when you hunt for one detail, like a name or a number. I just needed the date." His friend rolled his eyes. "That's why you missed the point. Skimming gets you the general idea, fast. You skipped everything that mattered." Zoe's hand stopped moving over her page.

She turned the words over while the waitress set down a plate of fries she had ordered to justify the table. Skimming, reading quickly for the general idea. Scanning, hunting through the text for one specific detail. All semester she had been doing neither; she had been reading like a defendant signing a contract, terrified of missing a clause. But the examiner was not going to quiz her on clause eleven. The examiner wanted to know what the article was about.

She flipped the newspaper over, then back, as though the page itself were responsible for her method. Then she gave herself one pass, fast, no dictionary, letting the unfamiliar words blur past like telephone poles from a car window. Her eyes snagged on numbers, on the capital letters of names, on words she recognized: votação, ciclovias, orçamento. Vote, bike lanes, budget. When she reached the end she was breathing hard, which was ridiculous, because she was sitting in a restaurant eating fries. Still, something about the speed exhilarated her, the way letting go of the handlebars had when she was nine, the ground rushing by under a self she hadn't known she could trust.

Second pass. This time she scanned, deliberately, hunting for the one detail she had already forgotten, the figure that kept sliding between three hundred and three thousand. Her eyes moved in a pattern, rejecting whole lines, snagging only where a numeral stood out against the type. There it was: três mil, three thousand, the cost in some currency she would have to fudge as "the budget amount" if asked. She looked up at the ceiling and laughed once, quietly. She had spent half an hour on paragraph one and four minutes on the whole article.

The waitress collected the ketchup and said, "Whatever that was, it looked like a win." Zoe, warmed and reckless, explained: a test, a phone call, a summary in a language she had been studying for six years and still could not read like a normal person. The waitress said her nephew was bilingual, said it like a bromide, the kind of comforting thing people say about other people's struggles, and Zoe nodded and thanked her and privately disagreed. Bilingual was a place she had not arrived at. She was, at best, a competent tourist with a decent map.

At 7:40 she dialed. A recorded voice gave instructions in Portuguese, and she understood them, which felt like being handed a gift she hadn't paid for. She read the article aloud, tripping only twice, and then the examiner asked her to summarize it in her own words. Zoe heard herself say that the council had approved new bike lanes after a long debate, that a councilman had opposed the cost, and that the project would take a share of the annual budget, roughly three thousand, though she hedged on the unit and the examiner did not press.

There was a pause on the line, long enough that Zoe's stomach dropped. Then the voice said, in careful, accented English, "Your reading is very precise. Almost too precise. You read like someone who is afraid of the words. Next time, read like someone who is curious about them."

Zoe said she would. She hung up, sat back, and pushed the newspaper to the edge of the table. After four minutes of skimming she could say what the article meant; after forty minutes of crawling she could only recite it. So which one had she failed at, exactly, and which one counted? She picked up a cold fry, wrote the words "skimming" and "scanning" on the napkin so she wouldn't lose them, and then, hearing herself, laughed and turned the napkin over. "It's not a cheat sheet," she told the empty booth. "It's just the rules of the road."

She left the napkin on the table, face up, for the waitress to clear or the next Friday-night student to find.

Mrs. Okafor's studio smelled of rosin and the lemon polish she applied to her piano bench every Friday, as though preparing it for surgery. Juliette spread the score of Mozart's K. 332 across the music stand, a photocopy already bruised with three colors of pencil, none of which she trusted anymore.

"Again," said Mrs. Okafor, and played the opening eight bars. "Tell me where your first theme ends."

Juliette put her finger on the page and then took it off, as if the paper had asked for an acquittal she could not grant. "Measure twelve. Or nineteen. It keeps depending on which side I argue from."

"You sound pugnacious about it."

"I sound like a lawyer, is what I sound like." She leaned closer to the staves. The trouble was that Mozart, being Mozart, refused to stop singing. The tune at the beginning spilled onward so graciously that she could not point to the bar where it finished being itself and started being something else, and her markings kept sliding around like furniture in a dream.

Mrs. Okafor folded her hands. "Instead of hunting the end of the tune, hunt the change of key. In the exposition there's a passage that moves you from the home key to the second key. It's called the bridge."

Juliette wrote bridge? in the margin and played from measure twelve with her right hand alone, following the harmony under her left. Somewhere around measure twenty-two the music stopped being tuneful and got busy, scales and figures hurrying somewhere, and then, with a small click she could feel in her teeth, the notes settled into a new key. She sat back. "There. That's where it modulates. So the busier stuff before it, that's the bridge, which means the first theme has to end before the bridge starts, which means it was measure nineteen all along and my blue pencil was right and my red pencil owes my blue pencil an apology."

"Your pencils have a legal system now?"

"They've acclimated to the firm. It's very hierarchical."

They marked the exposition together after that, second theme bracketed in green, codetta in a color Juliette improvised by scribbling blue over red, which produced something like a bruise. When she got to the development, though, she slowed down. The development did what it wanted. It took her bridge material, her busy un-tuneful scales, and made them the main event, tumbling through keys she could not name, and she thought: so the passage that merely carries you from here to there becomes the whole conversation elsewhere. She did not say this out loud, because Mrs. Okafor had a policy about epiphanies announced in lesson time, but she marked a question mark next to it.

"The recapitulation," said Mrs. Okafor, "you'll find on your own for Thursday. And bring the Beethoven, the little one, op. 49."

"Is that a test?"

"It's a present. It's easier."

Juliette began gathering her pencils, and then stopped, because she had noticed something she had been noticing for three weeks and refusing to examine: Mrs. Okafor kept saying Thursday, and giving her extra repertoire, and mentioning, in the offhand voice of someone mentioning weather, that the conservatory audition deadline was in November. Juliette had said, at Christmas, in front of her mother, that she was going to study biology and keep the piano for herself, for pleasure, ungraded. Mrs. Okafor had said "of course." Now here was Beethoven arriving like a subpoena.

"Mrs. Okafor. Opus 49. The audition deadline."

"Mm," said Mrs. Okafor, polishing the fallboard with her sleeve, an elaborate innocence. "Lovly piece, opus 49."

"You think I should audition."

"I think you found the bridge in twenty minutes after hunting the theme's ending for a week. You find things. That's all I think." She closed the piano lid. "Whether you want to be found is a separate question, and not mine."

Juliette looked down at her score, at the bruise-colored codetta, at her question mark in the development. She was good at questions with answers, at expositions that modulated where the book said they would; what she was not good at yet was deciding things that stayed decided. On the empty staff paper beneath the last system she wrote, in very small letters, biology?, and beneath it, also small, november, and then, because the moment seemed to require honesty, she drew a fermata over both of them, a hold, unmeasured.

She closed the score. "For Thursday, then. The Beethoven."

"And the recapitulation."

"And the recapitulation," said Juliette, and at the door she turned back and pointed her blue pencil at the piano like a small pugnacious baton. "If the bridge shows up in the Beethoven disguised as a second theme, I'm calling you about it."

"I'd expect nothing less," said Mrs. Okafor, and lifted the lid again.

The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered shoe repair, and on the Tuesday of her spring break Kaitlyn arrived at nine with a laptop bag and a printed sheet of instructions from her geography teacher. Mrs. Okonjo had arranged the placement through a cousin who owned the agency, and the assignment was due Friday: study two countries the agency books trips to, and use their population pyramids to argue which would need more schools and which would need more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Kaitlyn wanted the argument to be good enough that Mrs. Okonjo would read it to the class instead of filing it.

The cousin, Ms. Adeyemi, put her at the desk by the window between the printer and the rack of brochures. "Kenya and Japan," she said. "We send a student group to Nakuru every summer and a retirees' tour to Kyoto in autumn. You can use the booking maps, but don't touch the till." Then she went to the counter to help a man who wanted to change a flight to Lagos.

Kaitlyn opened the pyramids first. Kenya's was a triangle, wide at the bottom, each bar for children longer than the bar above it. Japan's looked like a top spinning on a thin stem, the widest bars in the sixties and seventies. She wrote in her notebook that a country with a broad base is young, so its spending would run toward classrooms and teachers, and a country whose bulge sits near the top will build wards and hire caregivers. She underlined it, then stopped underlining, because the sentence felt like something copied rather than concluded.

She pulled up the agency's file of trip maps to see whether the argument changed depending on which part of each country you looked at. The Nakuru map had a shaded strip along the lake, riparian zones marked in green, but the flood-risk layer covered other streets too, blocks that sat well back from any water. That bothered her. She had assumed flooding meant living beside a river, and if that assumption was wrong, her pyramid argument might rest on the same kind of guess.

She clicked through the map's layer list. Underneath the flood shading was a layer labeled DEM, and she turned it on alone. The town appeared as a grid of tiny squares, each one carrying a number. She moved the cursor along a street three kilometres from the lake and watched the values drop, square by square, toward a low pocket where the numbers clustered in the thirties while the surrounding blocks read in the hundreds. The flood layer's shaded blocks sat exactly over that pocket.

"You found the elevation data," Ms. Adeyemi said, coming over with two cups of tea. She set one down at Kaitlyn's elbow.

"It's called a digital elevation model?" Kaitlyn asked, reading the layer's full name from the panel.

"That's the one. Every cell stores the ground height, and the software uses it to say where water will flow and collect." Ms. Adeyemi tapped the low pocket on the screen. "That street floods because it's a bowl, not because it's near anything." She went back to the counter, where a woman had begun asking about visa fees.

Kaitlyn sat with that for a while. The map had exculpated the river, in a way; the water's arrival at those far streets was no longer the river's doing but the ground's shape, gravity reading the landscape square by square. She thought about the etymology lesson from the term before, how "population" came from a word for a place being peopled, as though the people were a layer laid over the land the way the numbers were laid over the map. You could read a country stacked like that: elevation underneath, ages on top.

She went back to the pyramids with the same caution. She zoomed the Kenyan map to a district whose population data she found in a government table, and its base was even wider than the national one. In Japan she found a prefecture where the bars in the eighties exceeded the bars in the twenties by more than the national shape showed. So the answer was not simply Kenya schools, Japan nursing homes; it was which region, which decade. She wrote three paragraphs, then cut the third because it claimed more than her tables supported. What stayed uncertain she marked plainly: she could not say how fast migration would move young workers into the old prefectures, and no pyramid told her that.

At five Ms. Adeyemi checked the printer, found a test page Kaitlyn had run of the Nakuru map with the elevation layer on, and pinned it above the brochures for the summer bookings. "Useful," she said. "Families ask about the rain." Kaitlyn packed her laptop, folded the map into the side pocket of her bag, and paused at the door with it half open, looking back at the pin.

The video arrived during fourth period, passed from phone to phone like contraband: grainy footage of a fire at a food processing plant, a caption claiming it had happened that morning in a town two hours away, that the smoke was toxic, that everyone downwind should be evacuated. Rose watched it twice on Priya's cracked screen, feeling the particular jolt that such clips were designed to produce, the way three seconds of fire could desensitize you to the fact that somewhere real people might be running. Priya had already sent it to forty people in the marching band group chat. Rose told her to wait, and Priya said wait for what, and Rose didn't have an answer yet.

She had an answer of a different kind waiting in the computer lab. The class was doing a database unit, and Rose and her partner Marco had written a query that was supposed to list every customer in one table alongside their orders from another. When the results came up, half the rows were fine and the other half showed the word NULL, printed in gray, where the order information should have been. Marco leaned back and declared the database broken. "We broke it," he said. "Or the software broke it."

Rose stared at the gray words, then at their SQL, which had the phrase LEFT JOIN in it. She opened the unit's reference sheet, then a tutorial page, then ran the query both ways, once with LEFT JOIN and once with an INNER JOIN, and compared what appeared. With the inner join, the NULL rows vanished entirely; with the left join, they came back. She turned the screen toward Marco. "It's not broken," she said. "A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, and fills the right table's columns with NULL wherever there's no matching row." Marco frowned at the words as if they were personally insulting him, then counted the rows, then counted the customers, and the numbers agreed.

That evening, at the auxiliary campus library annex where the main building's renovation had chased everyone, Rose sat with the fire video open on her laptop. The idea that had worked on the NULL rows kept nagging at her: the thing wasn't broken, it was behaving according to a rule she hadn't known. So what rule governed a video like this? She remembered a segment from a media literacy assembly, half-attended, something about checking where an image had come from before trusting where it was going. She took a screenshot of the video's clearest frame, opened a reverse image search, and dropped it in.

The results stacked up quietly. The same frame appeared in a news article from four years ago, a fire in an entirely different province, with no toxic smoke and no evacuations. The caption in the viral post was a costume draped over old footage. Rose felt the jolt drain out of her and leave something colder behind, and also something like the small triumph of the NULL rows: not broken, just misunderstood. She screenshotted the article and its date and closed her laptop.

Priya was harder than the query. Rose found her before first period by the lockers, where the morning crowd thinned around them without quite leaving. "It's real fire," Priya said. "I saw it burn." Rose held out her phone with the search results, and Priya looked, and her face did something complicated, moving from defense to confusion to a flush that Rose recognized as embarrassment on behalf of the forty people in the band chat. "So I panicked everyone for nothing."

"You did what anybody would," Rose said. "It's built to make you do that." She was aware of her own uncertainty as she said it, because the video being old didn't prove the new caption was entirely false, only that its evidence was, and because Priya forwarding a correction meant admitting she'd been fooled, which cost something. There was also the question of the chat itself: whether to send the correction as Priya, publicly, or quietly, as an anonymous courtesy, letting the rumor die of starvation rather than confrontation. Priya chewed her thumbnail through a long pause.

"Send it from you," Priya finally said. "People like you. You're the person who knows things." She said it without bitterness, which surprised Rose, who had been braced for the opposite. In the lab that afternoon, the teacher returned their graded query with a check mark and a note about the NULL rows reading exactly as expected, and Rose found herself smiling at the gray word, which had gone from looking like an error to looking like information: a record of the absence of a match, which was, after all, still a fact worth listing.

Priya's message went out at 2:14, from her own phone, with the old article attached and a single line of text: "I shared this without checking it. Here's the source and the date. Sorry for the scare." The replies came in slowly at first, one trumpet player sending back a thumbs up, then a long silence, then someone asking, half joking, whether anybody could teach them that reverse image thing before finals season. Priya turned her phone toward Rose across the cafeteria table, the question glowing on the screen, and Rose pulled out a chair and said, "Sit down, bring your laptop."

Lucas arrived at the farmers' market at seven with a folding table, a double boiler, and three kilograms of couverture chocolate he had bought with his last paycheck. He had secured the corner spot near the honey vendor by promising her ten percent of whatever he sold, and he set up the table under the one canvas awning that still had all its grommets. His plan was modest: tempered chocolate bark with pistachios and dried cherries, sold in paper sleeves for four dollars each. The night before, he had watched the same eleven-minute video four times, and the maxim from it had stuck in his head: the chocolate must be heated, cooled, and heated again just slightly, or it would never set with shine.

The morning was already warm. By nine the thermometer zip-tied to the market's information booth read 34 degrees Celsius, and the canvas over his table did little except make a patch of shade the color of weak tea. He melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, poured two thirds of it onto the marble slab he had borrowed from his mother's kitchen, and worked it with a spatula, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, until it thickened and began to hold a ridge when he dragged the edge through. That part felt like something he could learn with his hands.

The seed method was what undid him. He returned the slab chocolate to the bowl and added the reserved third to bring the temperature down to thirty-one, but his thermometer had been sitting in the sun and read high, and by the time he trusted it, the bowl had cooled past the point of no return. A test streak on parchment dried dull and bent when he tried to break it. The second batch went the other direction: too warm, and the streak never set at all, staying wet under his fingertip like paint.

He was scraping the failed batch back into the boiler when Priya from the tamale stall came over with a plate. "Lunch leftovers," she said. "Half a plate of rice and whatever you want off it. My eyes were too big." She set it on his table, and they ate standing up, and then she left the remainder, wrapped in foil, next to his burner. "I'll be back around one," she said. "We'll finish it for dinner."

She did not come back at one. At two, Lucas noticed the foil packet still sitting on the table's sunny edge, warm as a stone from the grill. He thought about their old family rule at home, the one his father repeated, that food was fine as long as it smelled fine, and then he thought about the six hours the rice would have sat out by the time Priya returned for dinner. He pulled out his phone and searched, standing between his marble slab and the honey jars.

The result was from the USDA, plain as a road sign: refrigerate cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius. Ninety Fahrenheit, the page said, for anyone who thought that way. He looked at the thermometer on the information booth, which still read 34, and looked at his own watch, which said the rice had been out since noon. He picked up the foil packet, walked it to Priya's cooler, and set it on the ice. When she wandered back at three with a bag of limes, he pointed at the cooler. "It's been over ninety all day," he said. "You've got one hour, not two. It went in at twelve fifty." She thanked him and did not argue, which he noted with some surprise.

The fact sat in his mind while he worked the third batch of chocolate. His father's maxim about smell was not exactly wrong, he decided, just built for a different world, a kitchen where the same hands cooked and ate. The USDA number was a rule for strangers and heat, a way of commodifying safety itself into something a vendor could quote at a market. It was not tangential to what he was doing with the chocolate either. Both were about temperature and time, about a narrow window in which a thing stayed good, and both were learned by ruining a batch.

The third batch behaved. He brought the chocolate down on the slab, seeded the bowl, and when he streaked a line of it on parchment, it set in under two minutes with a surface like a dark window. He broke off a corner and it snapped, a clean sound with no bend under it. He poured the rest onto parchment, scattered pistachios and cherries, and cut it into rough rectangles before it fully hardened, scoring lines that would break straight later.

Priya came by at closing with two dollars and a slice of watermelon. She took a sleeve of bark, broke a piece, and listened to it snap. "So you figured it out," she said. Lucas took the money, folded the table's legs, and put the last sleeve of chocolate in his own cooler, on top of the ice.

The first time Eva's grandfather lost the number game, he blamed the kitchen noise. The second time, he blamed his coffee. By the fourth time, he set down his mug, folded his hands, and said, "All right, Tinkerbell. What are you doing to me?" He was the one who had proposed the game, an old standby from his dispatch days: think of a whole number from 1 to 100, and the other person guesses, with only higher or lower for an answer. He had beaten her aunt with it for thirty years. Eva had simply started in the middle, at fifty, and then picked the middle of whatever remained. Higher, so sixty-five. Higher, so eighty-two. She never needed more than a handful of guesses, never fumbled, never once went back over ground she'd already covered. "You're cutting the field in half every time," he said slowly, tapping the table. "Every single time." He demanded a rematch after dinner and lost that one too.

That was over spring break. Now it was Monday, third period, Computer Science II, and Mr. Okafor had put a sorted list of a hundred names on the board with a single name circled. "Find Vasquez," he said. "Write me a function. You have the period." He sat back down at his desk, which was his way; he assigned and waited, and if you wanted help you had to come to him, which Eva never did because asking felt like admitting the problem had beaten her before she'd fought it.

She started the obvious way, looping from the first index and checking each name against Vasquez. It worked. She ran it and the counter said she had checked forty-one names. It worked, and it was slow, the way walking every block of a city to find one address works. Beside her, Dooriya was doing the same thing, chewing the end of her pen and muttering, "Forty-something, I bet. Watch, it'll be like fifty." Their friendship had a rhythm: Dooriya talked, Eva listened, and on Thursdays Dooriya saved her a seat at lunch without being asked, because she knew Eva's bus ran late on Thursdays.

Eva sat very still with her hands off the keyboard. The kitchen table came back to her, her grandfather's face going from smug to suspicious to delighted. Fifty, then the middle of the half, then the middle of that. She had never known what it was called. She had just known that it won.

She opened a new file and wrote it carefully: find the middle of the range, compare, and if the target is higher, keep the upper half; if lower, the lower half. She tracked it on paper first, drawing brackets around shrinking sections of the list, because she didn't trust herself with the boundaries yet, the off-by-one places where the halves met. The first version looped forever. The second skipped Vasquez entirely and landed on the name after it. On the third try the counter read six. Six comparisons. She turned her screen slightly toward Dooriya without a word.

"Six?" Dooriya leaned over. "Mine's at forty-one. What is that, some trick?"

"It's called binary search," Eva said. "It only works on sorted data."

"Why only sorted?"

Eva started to answer and stopped, because the honest reply was that she could feel the shape of it, the way halving only helped if higher and lower actually meant something, but she couldn't yet say it in a sentence she trusted. "I'll show you at lunch," she said. "I want to get the words right first." Dooriya nodded and copied down the middle-finding line, and when Mr. Okafor wandered past and glanced at Eva's counter, he looked at it for a long moment, then at her, and wrote a small check in his grade book without saying anything at all.

At lunch she laid it out for Dooriya using napkins, one hundred of nothing in her head, guessing games, higher, lower, keep halving. Dooriya caught on fast and then, characteristically, ran ahead. "It's like how my mom says the whole country's becoming a plutocracy, everything organized around money, but if the information were actually sorted, if people could see it in order, then finding anything would take, what, seven steps instead of a hundred?" Eva laughed and said that wasn't quite it, or maybe it was, she wasn't sure. She had been thinking about something smaller and closer: how her school liked to pathologize the way her grandfather slowed down after his stroke, the specialists with their labels, when what he needed was a game he could still win and a granddaughter who didn't rush him. And she had been thinking, too, about her aunt in her cosmopolitan apartment in Toronto, who sent postcards from three countries a year but lost the number game every Christmas. Two different women, two ways of moving through the world, and Eva somewhere between, still deciding what her own way would be.

"Do you think it always works?" Dooriya asked, stacking their trays. "Like, even if the list is a million names?"

"I think so," Eva said. "But I haven't tested a million of anything yet." She slid the napkin, still covered in her brackets, into the front pocket of her backpack, next to her phone, where her grandfather's last message was still unread: Rematch this weekend. Bring your little trick.

Sebastian had promised his geography teacher a map by Monday, and by Saturday afternoon the promise had begun to smell like a trap. He sat at the kitchen table with his mother's laptop, a trial version of a geographic information system blinking at him like it was daring him to touch it. The assignment was to overlay flood risk and housing on a map of their own city, and the software seemed to think that "overlay" meant "crash." He clicked a layer, clicked another, and watched the whole river vanish from the screen.

"You've killed the river," said his little sister Priya from the counter, where she was theoretically making toast. "RIP river."

"It's not dead, it's hidden. There's a difference." He right-clicked everything he could find. Somewhere under all these menus, he knew, the floodplain was still there, patient as a cat under a blanket. The trouble was that the software wanted everything codified first: which layer on top, which colors meant what, which shapes counted as housing and which were just sheds the city had never bothered to label. It refused to guess. It was, he decided, the most stubborn thing in the house, and Priya was sitting right there.

She came over anyway, toast in hand, and dropped a worksheet next to his laptop. "You're good at maps. Look at this and tell me it's not a triangle wearing a hat."

It was a population pyramid for Niger, and she was right, it barely looked like a pyramid at all. The bars were widest at the very bottom, stacked with children, narrowing so steeply toward the top that the whole thing resembled a triangle balanced on its tip. Next to it sat Japan's pyramid, which bulged in the middle like a wasp that had swallowed a marble. "We have to write what the shape means," Priya said. "For schools, I think. But I don't get why it matters."

Sebastian almost said the first thing that came into his head, which was that Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world, so of course the base was wide and children made up a huge share of the people. Then he stopped, because the same thought had bent back toward his own map. On his screen, if he ever got the layers to agree, the floodplain ran through the cheapest parts of the city. Cheap housing, lots of families, lots of kids. The two shapes were talking to each other across the table, and he was the only one who could hear it.

"Look," he said, turning the laptop so she could see. He had finally found the layer panel, buried like treasure, and the river was back, a blue vein stitched through the city. He toggled on the flood risk layer and a pale wash of green spread over the south side. Then he added housing, and little squares clustered thick inside the green, like moss growing on the dangerous part of a rock. "That's where the water goes if it floods. And that's where the houses are. Same place."

Priya chewed her toast. "So that's bad."

"It's worse than bad, it's boring," Sebastian said. "Everybody already knows poor people live by the river. The map just says it in green." He sat back, annoyed at his own map, which had taken all afternoon to state the obvious. Then he tapped her worksheet. "But look at your triangle again. All those kids at the bottom. Where do you put schools for that many kids? And now look at my map. Where are the schools?" He pulled up another layer, the one he'd originally thought was useless, and the schools appeared as small orange dots. There were almost none inside the green.

For a while neither of them said anything, which for Priya was a geological event. "So the most kids," she said slowly, "are in the places with the most water and the least schools."

"That's the map I want to make," Sebastian said. He was already dragging layers, stacking them in an order that made a kind of argument: flood risk under housing under schools, each one thin enough to see through, so the whole picture came out like a photograph developed in stages. The software, mollated by correct syntax, finally rendered it without complaint. The south side of the city glowed like a bruise.

He knew, in an honest corner of his mind, that he still wasn't sure what the map proved. Maybe the school data was old. Maybe the flood model was cautious or wild. He couldn't tell from a green wash whether a hundred-year storm meant anything to a kid walking to school in ordinary rain. Those doubts he wrote in small letters at the bottom of the screen, the way you'd confess something in a footnote.

Priya leaned in and read his caption. Then she picked up her worksheet, wrote two sentences about wide bases and classrooms, and pointed her pencil at his screen. "So what you're saying is, your flood map and my triangle pyramid should get married."

"It's not a marriage," Sebastian said. "It's more of a rapprochement." He paused. "Two things that weren't talking to each other, sitting down at the same table."

"Like you and that software all afternoon," Priya said, and stole the last of his toast.

Mackenzie had claimed the table by the tall windows at the back of the library, the one where the afternoon light came in hard and white, because she needed to see her mistakes clearly. In front of her lay the review sheet, problem fourteen circled twice: find the area under the curve of x squared plus seven, from zero to three. She had promised herself she would learn integration before the placement exam on Saturday, because if she passed it she could register for the engineering sequence her first semester instead of wasting a term on remedial math. Her father had said, on the phone, that calculus was just arithmetic with ambition, and she had not argued, though she suspected he was wrong in a way she could not yet name.

Priya dropped into the chair across from her without asking, which was their arrangement. Priya wanted the same exam passed, but for a different reason: she was trying to finish the sequence early so she could graduate in three years and start paying her own rent. She had a notebook already open, a mechanical pencil already clicking. "Did you do fourteen?" she said.

"I did it twice and got two different answers," Mackenzie said. She slid her paper across. Her first attempt ended in nine. Her second ended in thirty. "One of these is wrong and I can't tell which, which is worse than knowing nothing."

Priya looked at the pages for a long moment, then pulled out her own work and laid it beside them. Her answer was thirty too, but her antiderivative was written differently, not x cubed over three but x cubed over three plus seven x, and Mackenzie's first attempt had x cubed over three plus seven x as well while her second had x cubed over three plus seven times x, the whole term, and between those two scribbles sat her entire confusion. "Yours says the seven times x," Priya said. "Mine says plus seven x. Same thing. Where does your nine come from?"

Mackenzie explained, haltingly, that she had second-guessed herself. Somewhere in her memory was the fact that the derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged, and that fact had felt like a trap. If the seven could vanish when you took a derivative, she had reasoned, then maybe it could vanish here too, so she had dropped it, integrated x squared alone, and gotten nine. "But the graph doesn't know I dropped it," she said. "The curve is still sitting seven units higher the whole way across."

Priya was quiet, tapping her pencil against the table's edge, which the library rules technically prohibited. Then she flipped to a blank page and wrote the same problem twice, once with the plus seven and once without, and sketched both curves in quick strokes, one floating above the other like a double exposure. "So the derivative can't tell them apart," she said slowly, "but the area can. The area knows the difference." She looked up. "Do you get how strange that is? Going up, they're identical. Coming back down, they're not."

They were not identical, and Mackenzie felt something settle in her that was not quite understanding, more like the admission that two ways of thinking about the same function were both true at once. Her first instinct had been pure rationalism, a clean rule applied from the top down: constants vanish, therefore drop the seven. Priya's way was the opposite, drawn up from the picture, from the shaded region under a curve that a surveyor or a bridge engineer would actually have to measure. Neither method alone had caught the error. It took the rule and the picture arguing with each other, and even now Mackenzie was honest enough, with herself at least, to admit she could not yet say why reversing a derivative brought the constant back as seven times x instead of seven alone. She could compute it. She could not quite defend it. She wrote both answers in her notebook anyway, one labeled known and one labeled believed.

Around them the library was emptying, the light going from white to gold to something almost melancholic along the spines of the reference books nobody had touched all year. The closing announcement came over the speaker, softened by distance into a voice that seemed to belong to the building itself. Priya gathered her things fast, always fast, and paused with her bag half on her shoulder.

"Saturday," she said. "Table by the windows again, after. I want to know which of us is right about finishing in three years."

"Neither of us, probably," Mackenzie said.

"Then I want to know which of us is less wrong." Priya smiled and zipped her bag, and Mackenzie sat there a second longer, looking at the two curves on the page, the lower one, the higher one, and the space between them.

Landon had claimed the carrel by the periodicals at two o'clock, and by four the empty page in his notebook still had only its original heading: Views of the French Revolution since 1800. Around him the library went on with its afternoon business, a photocopier exhaling somewhere behind the reference desk, rain ticking against the tall windows. He had read three articles and understood roughly none of them, and the effort had begun to enervate him in a way that felt physical, a heaviness in the wrists, a reluctance even to turn a page.

The assignment was the problem. Not the Revolution itself, which he could recite, but the historiography, which required him to stop asking what happened and start asking why each generation of historians had told the story differently. His notes were a list of names, Michelet, Taine, Cobban, each with a one-line verdict he no longer trusted. He pushed the notebook away and went wandering.

In the stacks he found a fat red book someone had left on a cart, an illustrated history of modern Europe, and he flipped through it mostly for the pictures. One spread showed a map of Europe after 1945, with the countries accepting American recovery aid shaded green. France, green. Britain, green. Half of Germany, green. The whole east of the map was blank, pale as an unwashed window. In the caption he found the word Marshall Plan, and then a sentence that stopped him: the Soviet Union refused the aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest. He read it twice. Czechoslovakia had wanted in, and then had not wanted in, or had stopped being allowed to want in. He copied the sentence onto his hand because his notebook was back at the carrel.

On his way to the water fountain he passed the study table by the microfilm drawers, where a girl from his seminar, Priya, sat with a stack of books and a truculent posture, arms crossed over an open text, glaring at it as if it had insulted her family. He sat down across from her without asking, which was the arrangement between them, and read his own hand.

"What's that," she said.

"Nothing. The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid. And Czechoslovakia first showed interest, then had to withdraw."

"So what."

"So the map's blank for a reason." He set the red book on the table between them, open to the pale east. "Look. I've been stuck all day because I keep treating these historians like they're describing the same thing badly. Michelet in the 1840s, the British guys after 1917, this Cobban person in the fifties. But they're all standing somewhere. Like, after 1917 everyone suddenly saw the Terror as a dress rehearsal for Russia."

Priya, whose essay was apparently on the historiography of the Industrial Revolution, and who was therefore also dying, rested her chin on her fist. "My dad says history is written by the victors."

"That's the version people say when they don't want to read the footnotes." He hadn't meant it to come out unkind, and Priya laughed, which he counted as forgiveness. "The victors disagree with each other constantly. That's what the footnotes are."

They worked in a shared quiet after that, and Landon found the pieces beginning to fit, not smoothly but honestly. The nineteenth-century historians who mourned the Revolution were often writing against the revolutions they saw coming; the ones who celebrated it were arming themselves with a precedent. The Cold War historians, Cobban among them, revising the whole account, arguing the Revolution had been less a bourgeois triumph than historians claimed, were revising in a world where the map of Europe had a blank east and a green west, where Czechoslovakia had raised its hand and then lowered it. He didn't think they were lying. He thought they were answering questions their century had asked them, and that a virtuoso of archival method could still be steering by an unexamined compass. That was the idea he wanted, and he wrote it at the top of a fresh page.

But when he tried to close the loop, it wouldn't close. If everything was positioned, then his own essay was positioned too, his own blank spaces shaped by whatever he couldn't see yet, and he couldn't write a paper whose conclusion was that conclusions were impossible without sounding like he was showing off his doubt. He told Priya this, quietly, because the man at the next table had just glared at them over his newspaper.

"So say what you can prove and then say what you can't," she said. "That's allowed. Nobody's going to arrest you for a paragraph beginning however."

"However." He said the word out loud and felt the weight lift slightly. Outside, the rain had thickened, and the library lights had come on against the gray, turning the windows into soft mirrors where the study tables floated, doubled, among the branches. He began to write, and the first sentence came out whole: The historians of the French Revolution have never agreed, and their disagreement is itself the record. Then he crossed out is itself the record, because he couldn't yet defend it, and left the disagreement standing alone.

At closing time Priya packed first and stood behind him reading his last paragraph upside down. "You don't land it," she said.

"I know."

She slung her bag over her shoulder. "Czechoslovakia," she said, tapping his inked hand, "you'll want to wash that off before your mom sees it."

Benjamin had claimed the dining table on Sunday afternoon because it was the only surface large enough for a laptop, a second monitor borrowed from his father's office, and a mug of tea he kept forgetting. On the screen sat the city, or a version of it: cadastral lots in pale grey, the river rendered in an unconvincing blue, and over both of these a layer he had spent the morning coloring in gradients of red. Flood risk and housing, overlaid. His presentation was due Thursday, and so far the map told him only what he had half suspected, which was that the cheap neighborhoods and the wet ones were largely the same neighborhoods.

He was seventeen and had opinions about this, most of them borrowed from a documentary and one very confident aunt. His geography teacher, Ms. Achterberg, had asked for something more careful. "Show me the data doing the arguing," she had said, which Benjamin understood to mean she wanted him to be less interesting.

The problem was the age structure layer. The city's planning department had, with what he considered excessive optimism, published a population pyramid from the last two censuses, and Ms. Achterberg wanted predictions, not descriptions. Benjamin had collated the two pyramids side by side, one from five years before the other, and noticed something odd: the bars hadn't changed size so much as moved. The fat bar that had been at the bottom, in the zero-to-four group, had thinned there and reappeared, almost as fat, one bar up, among the five-to-nines. He sat back. "It's like a wave," he said to the empty room, and felt immediately foolish, and then kept going anyway, because the wave was real. On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, and the bulge he was looking at was still near the bottom. Today's large group of babies was going to be a large group of schoolchildren soon after, which meant, if he traced it forward bar by bar, a large group arriving at the local high school in a string of Septembers he could actually count on his fingers.

His sister Priya came through with laundry balanced on one hip and stopped to look over his shoulder. "What's the red?"

"Flood risk."

"And the little squares?"

"Houses."

She was quiet for a moment, which for Priya was remarkable. "That's our square," she said, pointing. She did not sound alarmed. She sounded like someone confirming a fact she had already filed.

"You're in the orange," Benjamin said, because it was true, and because the distinction between red and orange had seemed important to him right up until he said it out loud.

Their mother was at the counter making dinner, and had been listening in the way she listened, which was ostentatiously not listening. "When I bought that house," she said to the onions, "the agent said it was a hundred-year floodplain, as if that were a warranty." She was, by temperament, mercurial about money and immutable about everything else, and Benjamin had learned to check which mood was operating before asking for anything. This appeared to be the immutable one.

He turned back to the screen and did what he probably should have done first, which was check the veracity of the flood layer against the newspaper archive. The 2011 flood, which his mother still described the way other people described wars, had stopped two streets short of their square. The 1998 flood had not stopped at all. He added both extents to the map as thin outlines, and the map became a different document, less of an argument and more of a memory. Ms. Achterberg's request came back to him: let the data argue. But the data was saying two things at once, that his mother's house had been dry for a generation and that the generation was not a guarantee, and he could not find the tool that would overlay those.

Priya had not moved. "So the babies," she said. "The ones making the wave. Where do they live?"

Benjamin brought the census layer back up and shaded the tracts with the fattest bottom bars. The shading landed, almost entirely, inside the red. He had expected this, and it still did something to his stomach, which he decided was the appropriate professional response. The school that would receive the wave in four years sat on a hill, dry as a bone, and had empty classrooms, because the district had been planning for a shrinking town. He wrote that down. Then he wrote down the thing he did not want to, which was that his own school, on the dry side of the river, was the one the wave would not reach, and that the attendance line between the two ran along a street that also happened to be the line between red and orange.

He worked until dinner, shifting transparency percentages back and forth, making the flood layer bloom and fade over the houses like weather. At the table his mother asked how the project was going, and he said it was going fine, and she looked at him for a second longer than the answer required. Priya passed him the rice without comment.

After dinner he opened the presentation file and made the title slide, and then deleted the title he had written, which was "Flood Risk and Housing," and typed a new one underneath, lower down, in smaller type, where Ms. Achterberg would find it only if she kept clicking. He left both on the slide, one above the other, and turned the transparency of the top layer down to forty percent so you could just see the second one showing through.

The bakery closed at six, and by five fifteen Elliot still had the vocabulary list sequestered in his back pocket, folded into quarters, where the heat of the ovens had softened it into something like cloth. He was supposed to take an online placement test that night, a test that would decide whether he started college in the regular economics section or in the remedial one, and the window to log in closed at midnight. Between now and then there were trays to wash, a register to count, and Rosa, who had opinions about everything and refused to keep them to herself.

"You're telling me," Rosa said, stacking sourdough with the efficiency of someone who had done it ten thousand times, "that if some country is better than us at making everything, better at cars, better at wheat, better at every single thing, we should still trade with them. And we come out ahead." She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at him the way she looked at underproofed dough, with pity and a little disgust. "That sounds like something a loser would say."

Elliot had thought the same thing three days ago. He had read the chapter twice on the bus and something in it kept slipping away from him, evanescent, there on the page and gone the moment he looked up at the passing storefronts. "It's called comparative advantage," he said, which was the phrase on his list, but when Rosa asked him what that actually meant, he started talking about efficiency and being the best at things, and she pounced on it immediately, because that was absolute advantage, that was the exact confusion the chapter kept warning about, and he could feel it, the idea dissolving even as he reached for it.

"Elliot," Rosa said, not unkindly, "you just told me the strong country wins and the weak country wins. Both of them can't win. That's not how anything works." She pointed at the clock. "You've got forty minutes of trays and then you're going to that test knowing less than you did at lunch."

His grandfather lived above the dry cleaner two doors down, and Elliot had arranged to eat dinner there between shifts on test nights, which was how he found himself at the little table with the plastic tablecloth at seven o'clock, still arguing, though now the argument had moved inside his own head and out through his mouth, because his grandfather had asked what was troubling him and Elliot had discovered he couldn't stop talking about it. Something better at everything, he said. Every single thing. And the book says trade helps both of them anyway, and I believe the book, I think, but I can't say why, and tonight at midnight the test closes.

His grandfather buttered a piece of bread with unnecessary care. He had run the dry cleaner for forty years and had opinions of his own, mostly about hedonism, which he blamed for the decline of everything from customer service to popular music, but he set all that aside. He asked a single question. "When they make one car," he said, "what do they give up?"

The question sat on the table between them like a coin neither had picked up. Elliot picked it up. He took the paper napkin and drew two columns, cars and wheat, and started talking about what each country gave up to make each thing, and somewhere in the middle of the napkin he stopped chewing, because the shape of it had appeared all at once, the way the design in a laminate counter appears when you tilt your head. If one country gave up less wheat to make a car, then it had to be giving up more car to make the wheat. It couldn't be less of both. The giving up, the opportunity cost, ran in opposite directions, and if it was low one way it had to be high the other, so with two goods, one country could not hold the advantage in both. Not wouldn't. Couldn't. The arithmetic of it wouldn't allow it. That was why both could gain, and he tried to say why and found he couldn't, not the deeper mechanism, not the why beneath the couldn't, and his grandfather watched him notice that gap and did not fill it for him, only refilled his water.

"The one that gives up less to make it," Elliot said slowly, "that's the one that has the comparative advantage in it. That's the word. And the other country has it in the other thing. Always. It's not a choice they make, it's just what the costs add up to." He looked at the napkin, at his own greasy pencil lines, and laughed once. "Rosa is going to say I'm still describing a loser."

Rosa had closed the bakery alone and was standing in the doorway of the dry cleaner in her coat, holding a paper bag with the day's last almond croissants, which would be stale by morning and were therefore free. She had walked over to tell him she was sorry for needling him, though she would not put it that way, and now she stood listening at the edge of the little table while he turned the napkin toward her and said, "Look, give me two minutes before you decide."

She sat down, took a croissant, and said, "Make it fast. My bus is at nine."

Justine had come to her grandmother's house to escape the group chat, which by Sunday evening had become a tribunal, and it half worked. The kitchen smelled of cardamom because her grandmother had decided, querulously, that nobody visited anymore unless there was cake, and so there was cake, set out on the good plate as if to propitiate some god of grandchildren. Justine sat at the counter with her phone face down and her debate binder open, rehearsing under her breath, when the doorbell rang at the exact minute Dev had said he'd come.

He came in carrying his own binder and a two-liter of ginger ale like a hostage. They were partners for the regional tournament on Saturday, and their last practice had gone badly, not because Dev was bad, but because Justine had told him so in the flattest possible way. "Your closing was weak," she'd said, and then, when he asked what she meant, she'd said, "Just, like, weak," and Shrugged, and the silence after that had lasted four days and generated the tribunal currently raging in the group chat.

They set up on the porch, two folding chairs facing the bird feeder. Dev stood to deliver his constructive speech, and Justine noticed something she'd noticed before but never named: before he began, he rolled his shoulders back, planted his feet wide, and lifted his chin like a man about to be painted into a mural.

"Wait," she said. "Before you start. What is that?"

"What is what?"

"The thing you do. The superhero thing."

He went pink. "It's a power pose. You stand like this for a couple minutes and it changes your hormones. I read about it. There was a study." He held the pose, arms slightly out, looking less like Wonder Woman and more like a scarecrow that had opinions.

Justine took out her phone, because she had learned, the hard way, that checking was cheaper than believing. She found it in three searches, and it was more complicated than Dev's version. The 2010 study had claimed power poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol. Then a larger 2015 replication had found no such hormonal effect at all, though people still reported feeling more powerful. She read it twice. "So it's real and it's not," she said slowly. "The hormones part didn't hold up. The feeling part did."

"Then it works," Dev said.

"Then it works and it doesn't," Justine said, and then stopped, because she recognized the shape of the thing she actually needed to tell him, and it was bigger than the pose.

Last month, before the quarterfinal, she had stood outside the boys' restroom and watched Dev do the pose in the mirror through the cracked door, and she had thought, at the time, that it was why he'd gone out and delivered the most wooden speech of his life. He had felt powerful, apparently, and powerful had made him stiff, had made him gesture like a windmill in a light breeze, had made him use the word "furthermore" four times. She had never said any of this. She had said "weak."

"Okay," she said. "Here's the thing, and I'm going to try to say it better than last time." She put the phone down. "Your arguments Saturday were good. Your second point about the tariff data was the best thing anyone said all round. And then you'd hit a transition and do this." She stood up and did the windmill, arms wide, chin high, and Dev laughed despite himself, a short involuntary bark. "You stand like the pose the whole time you're talking. Like you're holding a position instead of arguing one."

Dev sat down slowly, the superhero leaking out of him. "So I should stop the pose?"

"No. That's the part I'm not sure about." She found she meant it, and it was strange to say a thing she hadn't finished thinking. "The pose makes you feel something, and the feeling is real even if the science isn't, or wasn't, exactly. But the feeling is for before. In the restroom. In the mirror. Then you go out and you talk like a person, and a person isn't a statue." She hesitated. "I think. I could be wrong about the second part. The first part, the hormones, that part's settled. The rest is me."

From inside the house came the sound of the television, which her grandmother kept tuned to a channel where a populist pundit explained, at volume, that elites had ruined everything, including, this evening, breakfast cereal. The screen door creaked open and her grandmother emerged with the cake, set it between the two binders, looked at Dev, looked at Justine, and then, without comment, rolled her shoulders back, planted her feet wide, and lifted her chin at the bird feeder.

"Eighty-one years old," she said, still holding it. "I saw you two through the window. If it works for the young ones, it works for me." She held the pose a moment longer, then cut the cake, her hands steady, her expression unreadable. "I don't feel more powerful," she announced, handing Justine the first slice. "But I feel ready to argue about it."

Dev leaned over and whispered, "Is she available for Saturday?"

"She's the second speaker," Justine said, and cut him a slice too.

The pit at the regional robotics competition smelled like solder and energy drinks, and Makayla had been staring at the same twenty lines of Java for forty minutes. Their scouting app was supposed to pull match data from the volunteer table, rank the other teams, and hand a clean list to the drive team before alliance selection at two o'clock. Instead it handed them a page of nulls. Every robot showed up as "null, null, scored null points," which was less than useless, and Dev, their driver, was standing behind her with his arms crossed like the clock was her personal enemy.

"Fix it fast," he said. "I want the pick list an hour early so I can walk the pits and talk to the top three captains myself." That was Dev's whole season in one sentence: he wanted to be the one who chose, the one shaking hands, the face of the team. Makayla didn't demur out loud, but she filed the request under things that were not going to happen on her current timeline.

She read the Robot class again. She had written it two nights ago in her bedroom, following the pattern from a tutorial: private fields, a constructor, getter methods like getName and getPoints. It looked right. It compiled. She scrolled to the constructor and read it aloud under her breath: name equals name, points equals points. Somewhere behind her, a mentor from another team was telling a rookie that the team treasurer had a fiduciary duty not to spend the entry fee money on a better joystick, and Makayla heard the word without looking up.

"Can I see?" Priya pulled a folding chair over and sat down without waiting for an answer. Priya was their programmer in theory, but she mostly did the mechanical stuff now, and she watched the screen with the patient, slightly jaundiced expression of someone who had seen a lot of code fail at a lot of competitions. "The app's not crashing," she said. "So the fields exist. They're just empty."

"Then the constructor isn't running," Makayla said.

"It's running. You'd get an exception if it weren't."

Makayla put her finger on the line. "I wrote name equals name." She said it slowly, the way you repeat a word until it stops sounding like a word. The parameter was called name. The field was called name. Java had to pick one of them, and it had picked the parameter, both times, on both sides of the equals sign. The field never got anything. The constructor wasn't silently doing nothing, exactly; it was silently assigning a variable to itself, which amounted to the same emptiness. She thought of her English teacher's rule about ambiguous pronouns, how "she told her" could mean three different things depending on who was standing where. She had spent a semester learning to disambiguate sentences for readers, and here was a language that disambiguated for you, bluntly, by taking the nearest name. Except there was a way to say which one you meant.

"You need the keyword," Priya said, and tapped the screen above the line. "this dot name equals name."

Makayla typed it, this.name = name, and then this.points = points, and before she trusted it she wrote a tiny test class in another file. She made one robot, gave it the name "Ironclad" and the number 118, and printed getName. The console answered Ironclad. She made a second one with different values and printed both, and they came back distinct, each object holding its own. She sat back for a second, not triumphant, just quiet. She still wasn't certain she understood the whole rule, only that it worked here, now, in this constructor, and that two hours from now she might hit a case she hadn't imagined. That was fine. Two o'clock was more certain than the rest of it.

"Done," she said, and the pick list spilled out, ranked, real names attached to real numbers. Dev leaned in over her shoulder, reading the top three, already composing his opening line to the first captain. Priya stood and stretched and said she was going to go look at Ironclad's robot in person, because data only told you so much.

"Wait," Dev said. "Give me the list first."

"I'll print you a copy." Makayla hit print, and the page slid out warm from the printer, Ironclad at the top, and she handed it to him without deciding yet whether she would walk the pits with him or go see the robot herself.

The camp was held in the church hall two streets from Grandpa's house, so for two weeks Paige slept in the guest room under the framed photograph of Grandma and got up early to practice. She had been cast as an assistant director, which meant, as far as she could tell, that she was supposed to stand near the director, Mr. Okafor, and learn by standing. On the third morning he handed her the one-act instead. "I have to be at the middle school Tuesday and Thursday," he said. "You'll run the rehearsal. Blocking and everything."

She had directed nothing larger than a video project filmed in one take on her phone. The one-act had five characters and a scene where two of them had to cross a kitchen, open a door, and reveal a third standing on the porch, and every time the actors tried it in the hall they ended up bunched by the refrigerator like people waiting for a bus. Tessa, who played the mother, had opinions about everything and delivered them at volume. Devon, who played the son, went quiet when he was corrected and stayed quiet for ten minutes afterward.

That first night Paige sat at the kitchen table copying names onto index cards and trying to see the stage in her head, which didn't work, because her head kept the stage only when she wasn't looking directly at it. A mug sat at her elbow, left over from Grandpa's coffee, and she slid it across the table to where the refrigerator would be, then walked her fingers toward it and found the same knot of bodies forming in miniature. She was still frowning at the mug when Grandpa came in for his glass of water.

He set a handful of change on the table, leftovers from the paper, and went to bed. Paige looked at the coins for a while, then laid out a nickel for Tessa, a quarter for Devon, a penny for the girl on the porch, and the other two wherever the scene demanded. When the quarter had to reach the door before the penny appeared, the whole geometry opened up: she could see that Devon needed to arrive first and Tessa second, and that Tessa should be near the sink the whole time, not drifting. She moved the coins four more times, drawing the kitchen on a paper napkin around them, and by eleven she had the scene, or at least the scene's skeleton.

At rehearsal the next afternoon she taped an outline of the set on the floor and put the actors in their places before they could argue. Tessa objected that she was being hung out by the sink like a dish towel. "You're the one who opens the door," Paige said, and demonstrated the count herself, walking it, arriving a beat behind Devon the way the quarter had. They ran it six times. On the fourth, Devon stopped moping and started doing something with his hands in his pockets that read, even from the back row of folding chairs, like a boy deciding whether to lie.

Tessa stayed after the others left, eating crackers from the prop box. "Where'd you get the coin thing?" she asked.

Paige told her what she'd found that morning in the camp's one directing textbook, the chapter with the torn cover she'd read on the porch before Grandpa was up. "Blocking," she said, "comes from W. S. Gilbert. Him and other 19th-century directors planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor." Tessa said that was the first interesting thing anyone at the camp had said all week, which was possibly an attack on Mr. Okafor, though Paige chose not to treat it as one. Later, when Devon complained that a bellicose scene between him and Tessa had been staged too politely, with both of them angled toward the audience like presenters, Paige turned them shoulder to shoulder and let the audience watch the argument from behind, which Mr. Okafor, returning on Friday, said was the strongest choice in the whole piece.

The conflict came to a head on the day before the performance. Tessa wanted to change the door reveal; she had decided, during a peroration at Thursday's rehearsal about trusting an actor's instincts, that she should open the door herself and find the porch girl already speaking. Paige had the coin version of the scene in her pocket, worked out in Grandpa's kitchen, and she believed in it, but she could also see that Tessa's version gave the mother the discovery instead of the son, and that Devon had been quietly carrying the whole play on his indecision all week. She tried both. She ran Tessa's once and her own twice, standing in the hall with her arms crossed, watching not the actors but the space around them, the way the coins had taught her to, whether the empty air between the bodies did anything. Tessa's version was louder. Hers was lonelier. She couldn't decide on those grounds alone, so she asked Devon, in front of everyone, whose moment it was supposed to be.

He took his hands out of his pockets. "Mine," he said. "I think it's mine."

"Then we keep it," Paige said, and Tessa picked up her crackers without argument, which was its own small surprise. Paige did not tell her that she'd almost given the moment away, that the coin trick could show you where a person stood but not what a scene meant, or that she would be working that part out, she suspected, for longer than two weeks. Instead she called the scene from the top, and the actors moved, and from her folding chair she could see the paper napkin in her mind, the nickel by the sink, the quarter crossing the kitchen, the penny waiting on the porch outside the door.

The gym smelled like hot glue and printer toner, and Nolan's poster was curling at the corners because he had printed it at eleven the night before, on the family printer that was older than his sister. His table was third from the doors, between a girl growing mold on purpose and a boy who had built a robot that could not, so far, turn left. In front of Nolan sat three sealed tubes of reddish brown gas in a water bath, and next to the bath, a hot plate that had just decided it was done working for the day.

His project was about equilibrium, which he had typed at the top of the poster in a font he now regretted. The tubes held nitrogen dioxide, the gas his chemistry teacher had waved at from a distance while saying the words "don't drop these." In cold water the gas went pale; in warm water it went dark. The whole point was supposed to be that heat nudged the reaction one way or the other, and Nolan was supposed to explain why, smoothly, to a judge, in under ninety seconds. He had the hot water. He had the ice. He had, at the moment, no hot plate.

"Electricity in the gym is on a timer," the mold girl told him, not unkindly, peeling a banana. "Mr. Prasad says it's so nobody burns the school down. Very torpid of them, if you ask me." She pronounced it like a diagnosis and went back to her fungi.

Nolan carried the cold water bath to the judges' table to ask if there was a kettle anywhere in the building, and while he was gone, the trouble arrived in the form of a kid, maybe ten, with a lanyard that said OBSERVER, who had been circling the tables like a small shark. The kid stopped at the next table over, where a sophomore named Priya had a poster about hydrogen as a fuel. Priya was off arguing with the robot boy about extension cords. The kid picked up her marker and started writing on her tablecloth, which was paper, and which she had not intended as paper for other people.

Nolan came back with a kettle borrowed from the teachers' lounge and found the kid deep in arithmetic. "Two H two," the kid was muttering, "plus O two. That's two of the H-twos, so four hydrogens. And the O two has two oxygens." He counted on the paper. "Then two H two O. Two waters. Two hydrogens each, that's four. One oxygen each, that's two."
