He looked up at Nolan with the expression of someone who has caught the universe doing something tidy. "It's the same. Both sides."

"That's the idea," Nolan said, setting the kettle down. "Two moles of hydrogen gas, one mole of oxygen gas, two moles of water. Everything you started with shows up at the end."

"Why?"

Nolan opened his mouth and then closed it, because the honest answer was that he was seventeen hours into knowing anything about chemistry at all, and this kid was asking the kind of question that professors wrote whole books avoiding. "Because atoms don't just wander off," he said. "They keep the score even."

Priya returned, saw her tablecloth, and did not scream, which Nolan thought showed real character. "Oh, that's actually useful," she said, crouching to look at the kid's counting. "I've been trying to explain that for two weeks and you did it in marker." She looked up at Nolan. "Is your hot plate dead? I heard about your hot plate. It's the whole gym, apparently. Everyone's talking about your hot plate."

"My hot plate is not interesting enough to be gossip."

"Beguile yourself if you want," Priya said, "but your tubes are the only project in here that changes color, and right now they're all just sitting there being brown."

That was the problem, put plainly. The judges were starting on the far side of the room. He had ice and he had, now, a kettle of lukewarm teachers'-lounge water, and the demonstration needed heat, and his whole understanding of what heat did was one paragraph he had read four times without it ever quite settling into his head. He poured the kettle water into the bath anyway. It was barely warm. The tubes sat there, faintly pink, torpid as Tuesday.

The kid drifted back over, lanyard swinging. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because I have to explain why they get darker," Nolan said. "And I mostly know that heat pushes it toward the darker stuff, and cold pushes it back, and the system kind of... leans away from whatever you do to it. You add heat, it acts like it's using the heat up. You take heat away, it acts like it's making more." He heard himself say it and stopped. "Wait. Say that again to me."

"Why?"

"No, I mean it. Ask me again why I want them hot."

The kid, game for anything, shrugged. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because when I push on the equilibrium, it pushes back," Nolan said, and the paragraph he had read four times finally walked into the room and sat down. The system wasn't resisting him out of spite. It was doing exactly what a system with two gases on one side and one on the other could do, shifting its weight the only ways it had available. Heat was a push. Cold was a pull. The color was just the system leaning.

"Mr. Prasad says begging the judges works too," Priya offered. "He said it as a joke but he said it twice, so."

The kettle, plugged into the one live outlet behind the mold empire, began its slow climb toward a boil. Nolan stood over the bath with the kid beside him, both of them watching the pink tubes like they were waiting for something to hatch.

"If it works," the kid said, "do I get credit?"

"You get the marker," Nolan said, and lifted the kettle.

The quarry had filled with spring rain again, green-black and cold, and Morgan spread the ocean current map across the flat top of a boulder so it wouldn't blow into the water. She weighted the corners with four chunks of limestone, one of them shaped, if you squinted, like a gavel, which she thought was funny because in the fall she was supposed to be deciding between studying oceanography and studying law. Her father had offered to underwrite either degree, which he said in the tone of a man handing over something heavier than money.

The want was simple and specific: in eleven days she had to give a ten-minute presentation at a summer program's intake interview, and the assigned topic was how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. She had a folder of notes, a printed map with arrows curling like spilled hair across the Atlantic, and no speech. What she did have was Dex, who was floating on an inner tube twenty feet out, and her phone, which had one bar of signal at the very edge of the quarry.

"Come be my audience," she called.

"You come be my lifeguard," Dex called back, but he paddled in anyway, dripping, ebullient about having gone in before June, and sat shivering on the boulder while she taped the map to a sunlit slab of rock like a lecturer at the world's least convenient chalkboard.

"Okay," she said. "Warm water leaves the Gulf of Mexico, moves north along the American coast, then swings east across the Atlantic toward Europe." She traced the arrows. "So far so good."

"Very good," said Dex, who was being a generous audience because he wanted her to return the favor at his own interview, which was about a community garden and which he had not started preparing.

"But here's where I keep getting stuck." She unfolded a second printout, a latitude map, and put her finger on London. "London is at about 51.5 degrees north. Farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. More north than the whole US-Canada border line."

Dex leaned in, water running off his elbows onto the paper. "That cannot be right. Winnipeg is cold. London has, like, rain and cafes."

"Look at the line. All of it, every state, sits south of London."

He stared at the map for a long moment, lips moving slightly, and then said, "Okay, that's going in your talk. Start with that. Everyone falls off their chair."

She wrote it in the margin, and then sat down on the limestone because the problem had come into focus. If London sat that far north, its weather should look like a Canadian prairie, and it didn't, and her job was to say why, when the honest answer was that she could trace the arrows but not yet see the whole machine. The current map showed the ocean as if it were a river with a personality, single-minded and helpful, and that felt too easy, like a lawyer who only ever described one side. Her jurisprudence-minded half wanted to cross-examine the map, and her ocean-minded half wanted to trust it, and for eleven days she had let them argue instead of doing the work.

So she did what she could actually do. She spread both maps side by side on the boulder, the currents over the latitudes, and made herself look at them together, not as rivals but as witnesses to the same event. Where the warm arrow crossed toward Europe, the latitude lines ran on indifferent of it. The water went one way, the geometry another, and the talk, she realized, was the space between them: not a claim that the current was kind, only that it carried heat north and east, and that London existed inside that traffic.

She drafted a message to the program director that evening, sitting on the hood of her car above the quarry, and read it aloud to Dex before sending it.

"Dear Dr. Okafor: For my presentation I'd like to begin with the latitude of London, which surprised me, and use it to ask the question honestly rather than answer it completely. I can describe the Gulf Stream's path. What stays uncertain to me is how much of northern Europe's climate it accounts for, and I'd rather say that plainly than pretend certainty I don't have. Is that acceptable for the format? Sincerely, Morgan Reyes."

"Send it," said Dex. "It's the most lawyer thing you've ever written, and the least lawyer thing, at the same time."

She sent it. Then she folded both maps, put the gavel-shaped stone in her pocket for no reason she could defend, and started down the path to the water, where Dex was already shouting that last one in was a rotten egg.

Levi had spent forty minutes on the last paragraph, and it was the wrong end to start from. The article lay flat on the library table between him and Nadia, a photocopied page from a Portuguese newspaper with a headline about a border town and a vote. She was there to make him speak, which was the part he dreaded, and he had bought himself time by decoding sentences from the bottom up, because the final paragraph had the shortest words.

"You've been on that paragraph for half the period," Nadia said. She slid her water bottle aside and turned the paper so it faced her. "What have you got so far?"

"A man with a van," Levi said. "Possibly two men. Something about receipts."

Nadia laughed, not unkindly. "The whole article is about the plebiscite, Levi. The town voted on whether to merge with the district across the river. The men with the van are at the end for a reason." She tapped the first paragraph, dense with subordinate clauses and words he had not learned. "Start here. Tell me what it says, out loud, even if it's ugly."

He looked at the opening paragraph and felt the specific frustration of knowing that the answer was sitting in front of him in a code he could only read slowly. The first sentence contained the verb votar, which he knew, and a number, and the name of the town. The second sentence gave the margin. By the time he worked through the third sentence, he realized he could already tell someone the core of the story: the town had voted, the result was close, the merge had passed. The rest of the paragraph named the officials and the turnout figure. He said this aloud, haltingly, and Nadia nodded.

"Better. Now the second paragraph without stopping to write anything down."

The second paragraph quoted the regional governor, a man whose statements the paper described with a word Levi had to guess at from context. The governor had warned, in the weeks before the vote, that the neighboring administration was bellicose, that it wanted the river crossing for itself, that the merger would be a surrender dressed as a partnership. Levi assembled this from fragments and gave it to Nadia in three sentences, and she corrected one verb tense and let the rest stand.

"Why did they bury the governor at the end, then?" Levi asked. "He's the loudest person in the article." The final paragraphs were where the van men lived, and a municipal cashier who had absconded with the payroll two days before the vote, a detail the paper reported without comment, as if it were a matter of weather. He had spent forty minutes on the cashier. The cashier, he now understood, was the least important thing on the page, and he had treated him as the key to it.

"Because of how they write them," Nadia said. "Most news articles use the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story." She said it the way she said most things, as though handing over a screwdriver. "If you only have five minutes, read the first paragraph and go."

Levi copied nothing down, but he turned the photocopy over and drew a triangle on the blank side, wide at the top, narrowing to a point, and wrote turnout numbers in the wide part and cashier in the point. It was a small drawing and it made the strategy feel like a thing he could hold, though he was honest enough with himself to notice what the drawing did not settle. Whether the paper was right to rank the governor below the margin, whether the cashier mattered more than the journalists believed, whether importance was a property of the facts or a decision someone had made about them, these were questions the pyramid assumed away. He could read the structure now. He could not yet read the judgment inside it.

"Again from the top," Nadia said. "Out loud, and this time don't stop at words you don't know. Skip them and keep going."

Levi put his finger on the first sentence, took a breath, and began. "A town on the river voted yesterday," he said, "and the vote was close."

Thomas had promised his music theory teacher a marked score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, by Monday, and by Saturday afternoon he still could not find the line where the exposition ended and the development began. He sat in the third row of the empty concert hall with the score open on his knees, a pencil behind his ear, and a programme from last night's rehearsal folded into his pocket. The hall smelled of dust and lemon polish, and somewhere above him a workman on a scaffold adjusted a light.

He had a method, or half of one. In theory class they had tried to codify sonata form into three clean boxes: exposition, development, recapitulation. First theme, second theme, closing theme, then the composer took the material apart, then put it back. But the Mozart on the page kept refusing to sit still inside the boxes, and Thomas suspected the problem was his ear rather than the composer's.

"You're the one doing the analysis," said Priya, coming down the aisle with her violin case. She was rehearsing that evening and had let him in on her guest pass. "Any chance you're wrong about where you drew that line?"

"I'm wrong about most of it." He held up the score, its margins already crowded with arrows and crossed-out brackets. "I thought the second theme started at measure twenty-two, but my marks from Thursday say something different, and Thursday me didn't leave a note."

Priya set her case on a seat and leaned over the page. "Sing the beginning," she said. "The very first theme."

He sang it, thin and unsure, and then hummed the passage he had marked as the second theme. Something about the two didn't fit, and he couldn't say why. Priya plucked a string absently, an open A, and the piano in his head rearranged itself around the sound.

"Play it on the guitar," she said. "You brought the guitar, didn't you. You always bring the guitar."

He had, because his guitar teacher had assigned him a melody project and Thomas, whose hands could manage very little, had planned the entire melody around three chords. "The only ones I know," he admitted, taking the case out. "C, F and G. My guitar teacher says the three primary chords of a major key are built on the first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major that's C, F and G. So my melody goes C, F, G, C, F, G, and back." He strummed them, the sound unexpectedly large in the empty hall.

"Play the Mozart first theme over those," Priya said.

He did, slowly, picking out the melody with his right hand while the left dragged from C to F to G. At the second theme he faltered, then stopped. "It doesn't go back to C," he said. "The second theme sits on G. It's the dominant." He looked up. "So in the exposition the second theme is in G, and when it all comes back at the end, it has to come back in C, or it isn't a recapitulation. That's how I find the line. The recapitulation isn't where the tune returns. It's where the tune returns and stays home."

"Mark it," Priya said.

He drew a firm bracket and wrote recap in the margin, and then, following the same logic backwards, found the place where G took over and the material began to scatter. Development, he wrote, and underlined it twice. But at measure fifty-five he stopped again. The first theme reappeared there, whole and familiar, and he almost marked it, except that his left hand was still sitting on F, not C.

"That's a fake," he said quietly. "It comes back in the wrong key. The real one has to be later, in C." He searched forward, bar by bar, humming under his breath, querulous with himself whenever he lost the thread, until at last the theme settled onto the C chord under his fingers and stayed. He drew the final line and sat back, and for a moment neither of them said anything.

"So Monday you hand it in?" Priya asked, closing her case.

"Half of it," Thomas said. "I know where the sections are. I still can't say why Mozart bothers with the fake one, or what the development is doing besides wandering around. My dad thinks I should drop the elective and take immunology instead, something with a clearer syllabus." He laughed a little. "Maybe the wandering is the point. I don't know yet."

He played his three chords once more, C, F and G, then the first theme over them, and the theme sounded different now that he knew where it was going. Priya picked up her case, and as she started up the aisle she called back over her shoulder, "Still here at six. The piano's unlocked."

Thomas folded the score, took out the pencil, and went to find the stage.

The playground at the edge of the school grounds had been built for children half William's age, but by four o'clock it belonged to the physics students, who spread their worksheets across the slide and the tire swing and argued about acceleration as though the answers were matters of honor. William climbed to the top platform with his notebook and sat with his knees drawn up, the way he had since he was small, except now the platform served mainly as a desk.

The problem that had followed him here concerned a ball launched at an angle, and he had circled it twice on the bus without making a mark toward solving it. "You're treating it like one motion," Priya had told him that afternoon, and he had resented the phrasing, as though he were doing it on purpose. Now, with the wind moving the paper against his hand, he tried what she had suggested: he drew two arrows where the velocity arrow had been, one flat along the ground and one straight down, and for the first time the drawing looked like something that could be handled. The horizontal part would just keep going, unbothered. The vertical part would fight gravity and lose. Two simple motions wearing the costume of one difficult one.

He tested the idea on something he could see. Marcus was at the water fountain by the fence, lobbing wet paper towels at the trash can, missing high and long, always both at once. William watched the arc and thought, not at Marcus but through him. Shorten the flat arrow and the toss lands short. Shrink the standing arrow and it never rises enough. Marcus's arm was supplying both at once and could not seem to supply them separately, which was exactly the trouble William had been having with the ball in the problem, and somehow recognizing the kinship made him feel less stupid about it.

Priya arrived with her own worksheet flapping in her hand, and she was not calm about it. She dropped onto the platform beside him and jabbed her pencil at a diagram of two parallel plates, one marked positive and one marked negative, with a row of arrows drawn between them. "Everyone at the picnic table says my arrows are backwards," she said. "Devon says it doesn't even matter. Does it matter?"

William looked at the drawing. The arrows started at the negative plate and pointed toward the positive one, and something about that arrangement bothered him in a way he could not immediately name. "Which way does a proton go in there?" he asked, because that was the question Mr. Okafor always asked, the one that turned a diagram into an event.

"A proton's positive," Priya said. "So it goes toward the negative plate. That's just attraction." She said it quickly, with the blase certainty she used for things she had decided not to worry about, and William found he could not share it, because if the proton moved toward the negative plate, then the arrows showing the direction of the push had to point the same way the push went, which was toward the negative plate, which meant from the positive one.

"The field points from the positive plate toward the negative plate," he said slowly, turning his pencil over. "That's the direction a positive charge would be pushed. Your arrows are backwards." Priya looked at her diagram for a long moment, then crossed out every arrow with a single hard stroke and redrew them all pointing the other way, from positive toward negative, and William watched her do it and felt the small satisfaction of a thing snapping into place, the same snap he had felt splitting the velocity in two.

"It mattered," Priya said. "Devon owes me a Coke."

They worked until the light went long and orange across the mulch. William finished his ball problem by keeping the two motions separate on the page, letting each one run its simple course, then meeting them again at the same time and place to give one answer. It felt less like solving than like conducting negotiations between two parties who did not know they were cooperating. He was aware, in a way he did not try to put into words, that he was holding two methods of understanding at once: Priya's way of breaking a thing apart to see it plainly, and his own older way of watching a paper towel arc through the air and trusting the shape of it. Neither had won. He suspected the truest approach was some third thing he had not found yet, and he was, for once, not in a hurry about it.

Marcus launched one more towel from the fountain, a beautiful high arc that cleared the trash can entirely and landed in the hedge, and Priya called out, "Too much vertical," and Marcus shouted back that there was no such thing.

Ethan spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with his mother's garden stones, because the backyard wind had opinions of its own. The map showed the North Atlantic as a field of tiny arrows, red ones curling northeast off the American coast like a river inside the sea. Tomorrow he had to stand up in class and explain how the Gulf Stream carried warm water north and why that kept Europe from being as cold as Canada at the same latitude, and he could recite that sentence fine, but reciting felt like borrowing someone else's coat and claiming the tailoring.

Dana came through the gate with her phone already filming, a tripod under one arm and the particular energy of someone on a deadline. She was making a video for the museum's youth contest, five minutes on climate, and she wanted him in it. "You're the only person I know who can talk about water for two minutes without lying," she said, which was her version of a compliment.

"I haven't said anything true yet," Ethan said. He traced the arrows with his finger, the warm current crossing at forty degrees, releasing heat to the air above it as it went, the westerly winds carrying that air toward Ireland and Norway. That much he could see on the page. What he couldn't see was the shape of the whole argument, how the pieces held together, and it bothered him the way a skipped step in a proof bothered him.

"Start with the map," Dana said, adjusting the tripod. "Then the museum footage." She had clips from last weekend, the two of them at the infrared camera exhibit, and she was already picturing the edit: his hand hovering near the screen, glowing white against the dark background of the display. She wanted the video to place, honestly, but more than that she wanted the museum kids who ran the contest to see that a seventeen-year-old could make something serious, not just a slideshow with music.

Ethan looked at the map and then at the phone and then at the grass. He remembered standing at the camera, watching his own palm bloom on the monitor, and Dana offscreen asking why the glowing heat coming off the ground didn't just escape to space, since heat rises. He'd started to answer and then stopped, because the true answer wasn't that heat rises. The ground was giving off heat as infrared radiation, all the time, and above the ground, in the air, were the greenhouse gases, and they absorbed much of that radiation and re-emitted it in all directions.

"Say that part again for the camera," Dana said, sensing he'd landed somewhere.

"Greenhouse gases absorb much of it," Ethan said slowly, "and re-emit it in all directions. Including back down. That's what warms the lower atmosphere." He said it and heard it at the same time, the way you sometimes only understand a sentence once you've committed it out loud. The heat didn't escape because something up there caught most of it and threw a portion of it back.

"So the Gulf Stream heats the air," Dana said, panning from his face to the map, "and the greenhouse gases keep the air from losing that heat right away. The ocean delivers it and the sky holds the door shut."

Ethan considered that. It was almost right, which was more interesting than right. The winds mattered, and the shape of the coast, and he didn't yet know how much of Europe's mildness came from the current and how much from the pattern of air moving around the pole. He'd read arguments on both sides, some claiming the current's contribution was smaller than the textbooks implied, and he couldn't referee between them yet. "I can say the two things work together," he said. "I can't say how much each one does. Not without lying a little."

"Then say that." Dana lowered the phone. "That's the part adults never say. They act like everything's settled." Her older brother had dropped out of his environmental science program last year, calling the whole field a hall of mirrors, and she had privately decided her video would be the opposite of his cynicism: precise about what was known, honest about what wasn't. She hadn't told Ethan any of this. She said instead, "Do the part with the rocks."

He'd brought out three river stones and a bucket of water he'd left in the sun since morning, and now he set them along a line in the grass and poured the warm water in a curving channel past them, the water darkening the earth in a slow S, the way the current curved on the map. "Okay," he said. "The water's the Gulf Stream. The stones are, roughly, Iceland, then the British Isles, then Norway. Boreal places, same latitude as Labrador, but Labrador's frozen ten months a year and Norway grows things." The water sank into the dry ground as he spoke, which was not in his plan, the demonstration literally draining away under him, and Dana laughed so hard she had to lean on the tripod.

They filmed it twice more, and the third time it worked well enough. Afterward Ethan sat on the porch step with the map while Dana reviewed the footage, the afternoon light going long across the yard, the wet curve of grass still visible where the water had run. He thought about tomorrow, standing in front of the class, and decided he would end on the part he didn't know. He would tell them the Gulf Stream warms the air, that the greenhouse gases return much of the heat the ground gives off, and that beyond that, the sizes of things, the exact share of the warming, was still being argued about by people with better math than his.

Dana held up the phone. "Last frame's the best one," she said. "Your hand, glowing, and behind it the whole dark screen going up forever."

Brody pushed the coffee table against the wall and dragged the armchair to where the imaginary stage lights would be. His mother's living room had become a black box theater, minus the black and minus the box, and by Saturday it had to work as the set for a one-act called "The Long Pause," which Mr. Ferrante's drama class had handed over to him because nobody else wanted the directing credit. He wanted it. He wanted it the way you want something you have never once done.

The trouble announced itself on Tuesday. Dana, who played the older sister, sat on the armchair, and Tomas, who played the brother, stood behind her, and for the entire first scene Brody watched the back of Dana's head while she delivered the best lines in the play. He crouched in the kitchen doorway, which he had decided was row F, seat 11, and squinted.

"Tomas, move," he called.

"Where?"

"I don't know yet."

He tried Tomas on the left, then on the right, then kneeling like a man proposing, which made Dana laugh so hard she dropped a page of script. Nothing solved it. Her face stayed aimed at the couch, at the window, at the fake fourth wall, anywhere but at the seats where an audience would sit.

That night he texted his cousin Priya, who had done a summer intensive at a theater in the city. She answered at eleven with a voice memo, and he played it twice while lying on the floor of his room. "You want them to cheat out," she said, sounding half asleep. "Cheating out means the actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while they're talking to the other character, so their face and voice carry." He lay there wondering why nobody had ever told him that bodies could lie, could point one direction and intend another, and whether that was a skill or a kind of honesty he hadn't learned yet.

Wednesday he made Dana and Tomas run the scene again. "Cheat out," he said, tapping his own collarbone to show the angle. Dana swiveled maybe ten degrees toward the doorway. Tomas, who was garrulous by nature and panicked in silence, filled the pause with a speech about how weird it felt.

"It's supposed to feel weird," Brody said. "It's not natural. Real people face each other."

"Then why?"

Because the room isn't real either, Brody thought, and the lights aren't real, and the sister isn't her sister. He didn't say any of that. He said, "Just try it twice and then argue with me."

They ran it. From the kitchen doorway, Dana's face opened up like a door she'd been keeping her shoulder against. Her voice reached him without strain, and the line about the empty bedroom at the end of the hall landed for the first time in a way that made his stomach drop. Tomas cheated out too far, nearly facing the seats, and Brody spent ten minutes adjusting him in small increments, hand hovering near his elbow, like tuning something he couldn't see.

Thursday, a new problem. Cheated out, the two of them looked composed, deliberate, almost formal, and the scene was supposed to be a fight between siblings who knew each other's worst memories. The geometry that made them visible made them careful. Brody sat on the floor with the script and thought about his math homework, about how a lemma was a small thing you proved first so that a bigger proof could stand on it. The angle was like that. It was true, it worked, it carried the voice, but it couldn't be the whole argument. He needed it to hold without anyone noticing it holding.

So he let the fight break the rule on purpose. When Dana stood up and turned her full back to the seats, shouting at Tomas face to face, the sudden wrongness of it did something the angle never could. Then she cheated back out for the quiet last line, and the turn itself became part of the scene, a pivot from fury to something smaller and more exposed.

"Did you plan that?" Tomas asked.

"No," Brody said, and then, honestly, "Sort of. I planned that something like it might happen."

Friday night his mother watched from the stairs with a mug of tea, and Priya, home for the weekend, took the kitchen doorway seat without being told it was his. The run enraptured him so completely that he forgot to take notes, forgot he was supposed to be the one with the pencil, forgot everything except Dana turning ten degrees toward the dark where an audience would breathe.

Afterward Priya said, "The turn at the end. You mean that?"

"I don't know yet," Brody said. "Ask me after Saturday."

He gathered the scattered pages of script off the carpet, squared them against his knee, and set them face down on the armchair where Dana would sit.

Grayson spread the cones across the backyard grass in pairs, six feet apart, then widened them to eight, then ten, because the drills he'd written on the whiteboard last night had looked tidy in his bedroom and looked hopeless now under the actual sky. His team was eleven twelve-year-olds whose passes never arrived. He had watched three games' worth of film on his phone, pausing and rewinding, and the pattern was always the same: a stick stretched out at the blue line, a puck ticking off its blade, a breakout dying before it started. Their passes kept getting blocked. That was the whole problem, one weakness, and Coach Pelletier had handed it to him like a set of keys. "You run Saturday practices," she'd said. "I'll watch from the porch."

The first drill was a simple give-and-go between the cone pairs, and it went badly in a way that taught him something. Dev and Marcus, the two best skaters, snapped flat passes along the grass, crisp and fast, and every time Grayson slid his own stick out to simulate a defender, the ball of tape he was using as a puck struck it and died. "Again," he called, and again, and again, until Marcus stopped with his hands on his knees. "It doesn't matter how hard I pass it. Your stick is just there."

Grayson stood with his stick resting across his shoulders, thinking of his own years on the ice, the passes that had arrived and the ones that hadn't. He had a memory of being nine, in a cold rink in February, receiving a pass that came to him through the air, wobbling slightly and then settling flat onto his blade, and he had never once thought about how it got there. He rolled the taped ball forward, cupped it, and flicked his wrists so it lifted a few inches off the grass, sailed over the stick he'd planted in its path, and dropped down at the base of the second cone. The kids went quiet. Then Dev said, "Do that again."

"It's called a saucer pass," Grayson said, and demonstrated it again, slower this time, the tape rising just off the ground, flying flat, clearing the defender's stick, landing where Marcus's blade was waiting. He made them say the words back to him. He didn't explain the mechanics because he wasn't sure he could; he only knew what his wrists remembered.

By the second hour the backyard had turned into something between a practice and a laboratory. Marcus got it first, his saucers floating over sticks with a lazy confidence that enthralled the younger kids, who crowded around him at the water jug begging to be shown. Dev struggled, launching the tape knee-high, sending it skittering off course. The smallest of them, a boy named Wren whose helmet was two sizes too big, stood at his cone long after his partner had quit for water, flicking the tape over and over, missing, chasing it, flicking again. Grayson noticed him the way he was learning to notice things now, not as a coach cataloguing errors but as a person watching another person refuse to stop. He skated over in his sneakers, set the tape on the grass, and crouched beside him. "You're flipping it like a pancake. Try sliding your hands apart a little." Wren adjusted, tried, and the tape lifted, cleared Grayson's stick, and landed at the far cone. He didn't cheer. He just looked at it lying there, as if verifying it was real.

From Wren's side of the yard, things looked different than they had all morning. The drills Grayson ran weren't like the drills the big coaches ran, all whistles and fury; they were built around one thing at a time, like sentences, and Wren liked sentences, liked the shapes of words even, the phonetics of them, how "saucer" hissed a little at the front and softened at the end, s-aw-sir, a word that did what it described, rising and settling. When Marcus had floated that first perfect pass over Dev's outstretched stick, Wren had felt something loosen in his chest, the same loosening he felt in English class when a metaphor clicked. He picked up the tape again.

"You should teach the little kids the word," he said to Grayson, shy about it, then less shy, because Grayson bent down to listen. "Like, say 'saucer' before you do it, so we know what to look for. Otherwise it just looks like the tape is magic."

Grayson straightened up, and Wren watched something move across his face, the way he weighed it, the way he didn't just say yes right away. Here was a boy of eighteen who had planned a practice on a whiteboard and was now standing in a chewed-up backyard discovering that the plan and the people were two different materials. "We could do that," Grayson said slowly. "Call it out. Though I'm not sure it'll work for everyone. Dev's still fighting it."

"Dev's fighting it because he thinks it's showoff stuff," Wren said, and then worried he'd been facetious about a boy twice his size. "I don't mean, like, mean. I mean he thinks fancy passes are cheating. My dad says that too."

Grayson looked over at Dev, who was standing apart near the fence, spinning a stick in his hands, watching the saucers fly without joining them. He was quiet for a moment, and Wren understood somehow that the coach was doing what Coach Pelletier never did, holding two ideas at once: that a hard, flat, honest pass was a good thing to believe in, and that the saucer was not its opposite but its answer to a stick lying in the way. Whether Dev could be brought to see that, Grayson plainly did not know.

"Okay," Grayson said, and clapped his hands twice, and every head turned. "New drill. Same pairs. But this time the passer calls the pass before he makes it, loud, so the receiver hears it coming." He jogged toward the fence, scooped up a cone, and planted it directly in the passing lane between Dev and his partner, dead center, exactly where a defender's stick would be. "Dev. You first."

The waiting room of Ridgeline Driving Academy smelled like burnt coffee and vinyl, and Charlie spread her papers across two chairs because nobody else was there. Two leases, two floor plans, two sets of fine print. Her mother had said it was Charlie's decision this time, since Charlie was the one moving in with her sister Dana in the fall, closer to the school with the early-college program. The Birchwood lease quoted rent at $950 with "utilities separate." The apartment on Halloran Street quoted $1,040 with "utilities separate" in a smaller font, as if the phrase might go unnoticed if it stayed quiet.

Ron, the instructor, appeared in the doorway with his clipboard and found her surrounded by paper. "Lesson's in twenty minutes. The student before you cancelled." He did not leave, though. He looked at the sheets the way he looked at her parallel parking, patient, waiting for her to notice the problem herself.

"The problem," Charlie said, before he could ask, "is that I can compare the rent but not the utilities. One of these is cheaper than it looks." She tapped Birchwood. Dana had already fallen for the cheaper number and was halfway to lionizing the place, texting their mother photos of the balcony. Charlie did not trust balconies. She trusted math, except the math here had a hole in it.

She called the Birchwood office, and a woman named Priscilla answered. Charlie asked the question Dana had told her was too forward to ask: how much electricity did the previous tenant actually use. Priscilla put her on hold long enough that Ron raised an eyebrow, then came back with a number. "Six hundred kilowatt-hours a month, typical," Priscilla said. "That's how it's billed, by the kilowatt-hour."

Charlie wrote 600 at the top of the page and underlined it twice. Then she called the electric company, because the rate wasn't in the lease anywhere, and a recorded menu finally coughed up a person who said the residential rate was fifteen cents per kilowatt-hour. Fifteen cents times six hundred. She did it on paper because her phone's calculator felt like it could betray her. Six hundred times fifteen was nine thousand cents, which was ninety dollars. Ninety dollars a month, and that was before the fixed monthly charges the company also tacked on, some base fee that existed whether the lights were on or not.

The Halloran apartment had a different trick. Its lease said water and trash were included, which sounded generous until Charlie called that office too and learned that electricity was still separate, with an estimated usage she couldn't get out of anyone. "We don't track that per unit," the property manager said, sounding as though she'd been asked to guess the weight of the moon. So Halloran's true cost stayed quiescent in its paperwork, unknown, unquotable, and Charlie sat with the receiver against her shoulder, staring at the two pages, one with a number she'd dug out of a stranger and one with a blank.

There was a boy in her chemistry class, Marcus, whom she'd privately designated her nemesis since freshman year, mostly because he announced his answers before anyone asked and was usually right. Last spring he had stood up in class and walked through a lab calculation she'd gotten wrong, and she'd spent a week furious about it, and then a month quietly admitting he'd been correct. What she'd learned from that, though she'd never said it aloud, was that being wrong fast was worse than being uncertain slowly. She could still hear him saying "you assumed the volume was constant," and how much that single assumption had cost her grade.

Now she made a second column. Birchwood: $950 plus $90 in electricity plus whatever the fixed charge turned out to be, plus her own water bill. Halloran: $1,040 plus an electricity bill nobody would estimate for her, plus no water bill. Two unknowns, one on each side. She could not make them equal. She could not even promise which one was cheaper, and Dana wanted an answer by Friday.

Ron leaned against the doorframe. "So which one?"

"Whichever one stops hiding things from me," Charlie said. She picked up her pen and wrote, at the bottom of the Halloran page, call back, ask for name of previous tenant, ask them directly. Then she folded both leases together, put them in her bag, and followed him out to the car.

The bus was late, which meant Alyssa had eleven minutes to finish the chapter before Priya caught her pretending she'd finished it last weekend. She had the paperback braced against her knees, the aisle seat empty beside her, the October fields sliding past the windows like something she was supposed to be noticing. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the book club's pick, and she was only forty pages in.

"You're not even to the murder," Priya said, dropping into the seat and poking the page with one finger. Priya had finished it in a single Saturday, which she kept announcing the way other people announced scholarships.

"I'm savouring it."

"You're stalling." Priya leaned over, read the page upside down with the smug fluency of someone who could, and then sat back. "Whatever you think of Dr Sheppard right now, hold on to it. I mean really hold on to it. Take notes if you have to."

"Why?"

"Just do it." Priya pulled out her phone and started texting someone, which was her version of a dramatic exit.

Alyssa did not take notes, but she did pay attention, and Dr Sheppard seemed decent enough: a small-town doctor who noticed things, who narrated the death of his friend Roger Ackroyd with the grief of a man describing a funeral he wished he hadn't attended. She trusted him roughly the way she trusted bus drivers, automatically, without ever wondering whether she should. At the next stop the driver braked so hard her book slid into the aisle, and Priya handed it back with the face of a person holding a live grenade.

The twist, when it came on Thursday, was delivered by Marcus, who hadn't read past page ten and had instead read the last page first, an approach he defended as efficient. "The doctor did it," he said, walking onto the bus. "Sheppard's the murderer. The whole book, he's the one telling it."

"You ruined it," Priya said.

"I efficiented it." Marcus sat across the aisle and looked genuinely pleased with himself. Alyssa sat very still, feeling something rearrange behind her ribs. The narrator. The narrator had done it. The man whose sentences she'd been leaning on for three days was the thing she should have been leaning away from.

She went home and reread the opening chapters that night, hunting. It was all there, not hidden exactly, but folded into his account like a receipt kept in a wallet. Sheppard reported his own actions in the passive, brisk voice of a professional witness; he said he left Ackroyd's house at a certain time and then, with perfect honesty, declined to mention what he did next. He never lied, as far as she could tell. He only drew a fence around the truth, circumscribing it so neatly that she'd mistaken the fence for the world. She fell asleep with the book open on her chest, and in the morning she understood something she couldn't yet say aloud: that the point of view hadn't tricked her so much as she'd handed it her trust, unasked, the way she'd once handed it to a boy named Daniel who'd said he'd been at study group.

At book club, held on the bus's back bench because the library room was double-booked, Priya had brought a list of Sheppard's evasions she'd marked with sticky tabs, and Alyssa had brought her own. When they compared them they matched on only half. The other half were places Priya thought he was hiding something and Alyssa thought he was just being a boring Victorian man about a window latch, and they argued about it for two stops, genuinely, without either of them giving in. Marcus suggested, more than once, that they could resolve it by reading the last page first, and more than once they told him where he could efficient it.

Mrs Okonjo, the history teacher who rode the same route, glanced back at them once but said nothing, which was its own kind of gift. Alyssa noticed her noticing, and noticed herself noticing, and thought, with some alarm, that she was now doing this everywhere. The etymology of the word "narration" had already sent her down a twenty-minute rabbit hole the night before, and she'd begun to suspect every smooth account of anything, including her own, which was exhausting, and which she would not have traded back. Some certainty in her had gone friable, crumbling softly at the edges, and what was growing in its place was harder to carry but harder to break.

"Here's what I still don't know," Priya said as the bus pulled into the school lot. "Did Christie think we'd catch him, or did she want us to feel stupid?"

"Both," Alyssa said.

"That's not an answer."

"It's the answer I have." She closed the book and ran her thumb along the swollen edge of the pages, soft from being reread. Priya held out her hand, and Alyssa handed it over.

Laura had claimed the far table in the periodicals room, the one beside the microfilm cabinets nobody used anymore, and spread her materials across it like evidence at a trial: the briefs, the highlighted transcript, two competing drafts of her opening argument. In three weeks she would stand before a panel of local judges and argue both sides of a First Amendment case, first for the school board that had suspended a student for a viral post, then, after a fifteen-minute silence, against everything she had just said.

She had wanted this. She had chosen it, actually, over the safer debate event, and she remembered telling her mother it would be good for her, learning to see the other side, though she could no longer remember whether she had believed that or only admired it. Now the other side sat in front of her in the form of a concurring opinion whose logic she found both elegant and vaguely reptilian, and she could not tell whether studying it was making her fairer or just making her numb.

The case turned on whether a student's speech, off campus and online, could be punished if it foreseeably disrupted school. Laura's drafts kept drifting into the same shape: passionate for the student, technically competent for the board. When she argued for the student she thought of Marcus, who in eighth grade had been suspended for a joke that traveled farther than he intended, and she thought of him again when she argued for the board, except then he became the reason schools needed authority, and the switch frightened her a little, how quickly the same memory could be rearranged. She tried to make each side its strongest self rather than a straw man, and the drafts grew longer and less certain, her margins filling with objections to herself. A parsimonious reading of the precedent, she wrote, favored the board; everything after that was judgment. But judgment was the whole job.

She was in the middle of this when Devon appeared, sliding into the chair across from her with the pile of notes he'd been carrying around since the courthouse tour their class had taken last week. He had signed up for the same mock court event, arguing a different case, and he wanted to rehearse. Laura agreed, mostly because arguing aloud felt more honest than reading her own handwriting.

His case involved executive power, which was how the trouble started. "So after the impeachment," he said, "the president is out, and then the question is whether the removal was lawful."

"That's not how it works," Laura said, and then paused, because she wasn't sure she could say how it did. She pulled the library's civics guide from the shelf behind her, the fat one with the cracked spine, and turned past the pages she had marked until she found the chapter on Congress. The House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority. She read it aloud, then the next sentence, which was the one Devon had flattened: the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove. Two different thresholds, two different chambers, and the word he had used as if it meant both things at once.

"So impeachment isn't removal," Devon said slowly, writing it down.

"It's the charge. The Senate is the trial." She said it and heard how much she liked saying it, how sure it sounded, and she thought about her two drafts sitting there on the table, each one sure in its turn.

They rehearsed for another hour. Devon argued his side and she cross-examined him, and then they switched, and she found herself defending a position she had torn apart ten minutes earlier, and finding, to her discomfort, that it held. Not because the arguments were equal but because each one assumed a different thing about what school was for, or what a country was for, and the assumptions never touched. Somewhere in there she said the word "homeostasis" to describe the court's instinct, its desire to keep everything balanced and unchanged, and Devon laughed and said that was the most Laura sentence he'd ever heard. She laughed too, but later, walking past the returns desk, she wondered if balance was really what she wanted, or whether it was just what her habits had calcified into: the refusal to commit, dressed up as fairness.

At closing time she packed the two drafts into the same folder, where they pressed against each other like opposing counsel sharing a briefcase. Outside, the streetlights had come on along the library steps, and Devon was still on the third step, rereading his notes about the two chambers and their two different numbers, mouthing the words to himself. Laura stood at the top for a moment, folder under her arm, and realized she still did not know which side she actually believed.

"So which one are you really?" Devon called up to her. "The school or the student?"

"Ask me in three weeks," she said, and started down the steps.

The skate park at six was all long shadows and grinding wheels, and James sat on the flat bottom of the bowl with a physics worksheet folded in his back pocket, half of it already soft with sweat. He had come to watch Rio launch off the coping, but he kept taking the paper out, because the problem refused to behave: a ball leaves the ground at fourteen meters per second at some angle, level ground, no air resistance, and he was supposed to find how long it stays in the air. He had found the vertical part, ten meters per second up, and he had divided by g, which was 9.8, and gotten about one second. Then he had written it in the answer blank. Something about it felt thin.

Rio dropped in, pumped twice, and rose off the lip into the air, board spinning under him. James watched the height of it, the pause at the top where the board seemed to consider its options, and then the fall. He looked back at his number. One second to get up there. But Rio came down after that. The flight wasn't just the rising. It was rising and falling, and if you only counted the climb you were describing half a jump.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," Rio said, rolling over and flipping his board up into his hand.

"Projectile motion," James said. "Supposed to be like this." He nodded at the bowl. "You're the projectile."

"Flattering." Rio squinted at the worksheet. "So what's wrong?"

"Everything's on level ground, no air resistance, which is nothing like you. But I got one second for the whole flight and it feels short." He traced the arc Rio had just made in the air with his finger, up and over. "It took you about that long just going up."

Rio stood with the board under his arm and watched a younger kid push tentatively along the top of the quarter pipe, as if the drop-in might portend something irreversible, which, on a board, it often did. "So count the way down too."

"It's not just counting it. The way down takes the same time as the way up. Exactly the same." James said it and then tested it in his mouth, unsure. Was that true, or was it only true without air, without the friction of the world? He turned the pen over. In the clean world of the problem, rising and falling were mirror images, so the time to the top was half the flight. He wrote two seconds, then crossed it out and wrote the division again, ten divided by 9.8, times two, and got a little over two seconds for the whole jump. From where Dara was sitting, up on the platform with her helmet still on, it looked like the answer had startled him.

She had been half listening while re-lacing her shoes, the way she half listened to most things, filing them for later. But she noticed him sit up straighter, noticed the pen stop moving, and she was curious in the specific way she got curious, which was sideways. She skated over and set her board down.

"What did you find?"

"That I was answering the wrong question," James said. "I found the time to the top of the arc and forgot the fall."

"Is that cheating?"

"It's physics. On level ground with no air, the time of flight is twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g. Rising and falling take equal times." He said it plainly, like reading a street sign, and shrugged. "That's all it is."

Dara tilted her head. She had a whole lineage of skaters behind her, an older cousin who had taught her that tricks were passed down person to person like stories, and she thought physics might work the same way, except the stories were about numbers. "So the whole flight is just the up part doubled."

"Twice the vertical part. The sideways part doesn't even matter for time." He looked at Rio. "When you clear that gap by the fence, how fast you're moving forward changes how far you go. It doesn't change how long you're in the air."

Rio rolled the board under his foot, considering. He dropped in without answering, pumped the transition, and shot off the lip into the still evening air. James watched the whole arc this time, up, the pause, down, and tried to see the two halves of it laid over each other, equal and silent. Dara counted under her breath, "one one-thousand, two one-thousand," and got to a little past two when the wheels touched concrete.

"Close enough," she said, and pushed off toward the bowl.
